abigail-adams-remember-the-ladies.context_blurb:
Spring 1776. The colonies are at war with Britain, and John Adams is far away in Philadelphia at the Continental Congress, helping to write the laws of a nation that does not yet exist. At home in Braintree, Massachusetts, his wife Abigail runs the family farm alone, raises their children and writes to him constantly. She never went to school, but she read her way through her father's library, and she argued like a lawyer.

That March she asked John and his fellow lawmakers to remember the ladies in their new code, and to treat women more generously than their ancestors had. Her reason was hard-headed, not sentimental. Do not hand husbands unlimited power over their wives, she warned, because every man would be a tyrant if he could. If the new laws gave women no voice, she added, women would raise a rebellion of their own. She was turning the Revolution's own logic, no taxation without representation, back on the men who preached it.

John's reply in April was a joke: he wrote that he could only laugh at her extraordinary code, and that he would never give way to what he mocked as the Despotism of the Peticoat. Men, he teased, were masters in name only. Abigail did not drop the argument, and her letter, still in her own handwriting, is the most famous founding-era case for women's place in the new republic.

abolition-of-the-british-slave-trade-wil.context_blurb:
For most of the 1700s British ships carried Africans across the Atlantic in chains, and the trade made fortunes. Then a small band set out to end it: Quakers, preachers, a former slave-ship captain, a freed African author, and a small, sickly Member of Parliament with a beautiful speaking voice named William Wilberforce. Their fight lasted nearly fifty years.

One of them knew the trade from the inside. John Newton had once commanded slave ships himself; after a storm almost drowned him he turned to God, quit the trade, became a pastor, and wrote the hymn Amazing Grace about a lost man saved by grace. In his old age Newton helped steel the young Wilberforce for the fight. The movement also needed a symbol, and the potter Josiah Wedgwood made it. His small jasperware medallion showed an African man kneeling in chains with his hands raised, asking the viewer whether he was not a man and a brother. Supporters wore it as a brooch.

Thomas Clarkson gathered the evidence, riding tens of thousands of miles to interview sailors. He carried a wooden chest with two halves. One half held the honest goods Africa could sell, such as palm oil, ivory, spices and cloth; the other held the tools of the trade in people: handcuffs and leg-shackles of iron, thumbscrews, branding irons, and a device for forcing a captive's jaws open. The box made the whole argument without a word. Ordinary families joined in too. In 1791 the campaigners urged Britain to give up sugar grown by slaves on the West Indian plantations, and some 300,000 households did, many of them led by women who ran the kitchen though they had no vote.

Wilberforce came to the cause through faith. One Sunday in October 1787 his diary named the two great objects God had placed before him: ending the slave trade, and the Reformation of Manners, a drive to improve Britain's morals and public behaviour. In 1789 Clarkson's Quaker allies printed a bird's-eye plan of the slave ship Brookes, her decks crammed with 482 small drawn bodies lying shoulder to shoulder. That figure of 482 was no artist's guess: a law of 1788 had capped the Brookes at exactly that many people, so the poster showed that even the legal maximum was a horror. That same year Olaudah Equiano published his life story, and no pamphlet could match it, because Equiano had lived through the slave ships himself and then bought his own freedom. Readers heard the case from a formerly enslaved African in his own voice, and his book went through nine printings.

Wilberforce brought a bill nearly every year and lost nearly every year. Then, in February 1807, the Commons voted to abolish the trade by 283 votes to 16. As Samuel Romilly praised his long struggle, the House stood and cheered him. Wilberforce sat with his head bowed, weeping, as twenty years of defeats turned at last into victory. Britain then went further, and a Royal Navy squadron off West Africa began hunting slavers at sea. Its most feared hunter, HMS Black Joke, was a former slave ship: the fast Baltimore-built slaver Henriqueta, captured in 1827 and re-armed to chase her own old trade. Wilberforce died in July 1833, three days after hearing that slavery itself would end across the Empire, and Parliament gave the untitled private man an honour it almost never grants: members of both Houses walked in procession and bore his coffin into Westminster Abbey.

The campaign's hardest truths sit at its two ends. Back in 1781, sailors on the Liverpool slaver Zong had flung over 130 living Africans overboard. Then the owners went to court to collect the insurance on them, as if the drowned had been lost cargo, and in 1783 the judges treated it as a quarrel over property, not as murder. Granville Sharp made the case public, and it showed Britain what it meant to call a person property. When Parliament ended slavery itself in 1833, freeing some 800,000 people, it paid out £20 million, a huge share of the national budget, and the whole sum went to the slave-owners as payment for lost property, while the freed people got nothing. The freed were even bound to years of unpaid work as apprentices until 1838. Britain led the world against slavery, and it still paid the masters rather than the enslaved.

abraham-lincoln-the-man-and-leader.context_blurb:
Abraham Lincoln was born in a Kentucky log cabin and grew up on the Indiana and Illinois frontier with less than a year of schooling, teaching himself by firelight. He became a country lawyer, then the sixteenth president, and he held the Union together through the Civil War. Americans still measure their leaders against him.

He stood six feet four inches, a head above most rooms, and he remains the tallest president the United States has ever had, with no one before or since to match him. As a young man he swung an axe for wages, splitting logs into fence rails, and in 1860 the Republicans made that his campaign image, the Rail-Splitter, carrying rails in their parades.

As a store clerk in the village of New Salem, Illinois, he earned the name Honest Abe. Once, realising after closing time that he had overcharged a customer by a few cents, he walked several miles to hand the change back. These stories are cherished frontier legend. So is his wrestling. Legend says he lost only once in about a dozen years. When the rowdy Clary's Grove Boys sent their champion Jack Armstrong against him, Lincoln said the man was as strong as a Russian bear and impossible to throw. The match won him the crowd's respect and Armstrong's friendship for life. A girl of eleven, Grace Bedell, had written in 1860 that his face was too thin and he should grow whiskers. He took her advice, and when his train to Washington reached Westfield, he halted it, called for Grace, and let her see the beard she had asked for.

Lincoln loved mechanical puzzles. After his own flatboats kept getting stuck on river obstructions, he invented a set of inflatable bellows to buoy a boat up and over shallow shoals. His Patent No. 6,469 of 1849 makes him unique: no other president has ever held one. As a lawyer he was just as inventive. In 1858 he defended Duff Armstrong, son of his old wrestling rival, against a witness who swore he had watched the murder by moonlight, and Lincoln opened an almanac to show that the moon that night had hung low and given almost no light. The jury acquitted, and Lincoln had repaid the family that sheltered him when he was poor.

That same year he ran for the Senate against Stephen Douglas. He argued with Douglas in seven famous debates and lost the seat, then edited the debates and published them as a book, which sold widely and made him a national figure. In February 1860 the little-known Illinois lawyer spoke for more than 7,000 words at Cooper Union in New York, quoting the Founders one by one against letting slavery spread west, and he closed by urging his listeners to trust that right makes might and to dare to do their duty. That November he won the presidency.

When the Emancipation Proclamation lay before him on New Year's Day 1863, his hand trembled from hours of greeting visitors, so he steadied it and said that if his name ever went into history, this act would be the reason. At the Gettysburg cemetery that November, Edward Everett, the most celebrated speaker of the day, held the crowd for two hours and Lincoln for barely two minutes, and the next day Everett wrote that he wished his two hours had come as close as those two minutes to the central idea of that occasion. In March 1865, with victory near, Lincoln gave his Second Inaugural Address and, instead of gloating, asked the nation to finish the war bearing malice toward no one and charity toward all, words the Lincoln Memorial now carries on its wall.

Weeks later, on 14 April 1865, he was enjoying a comic play at Ford's Theatre. The actor John Wilkes Booth crept into his box, fired a bullet into his head, jumped onto the stage and cried Sic semper tyrannis, Latin for thus always to tyrants. Lincoln never woke, and died the next morning.

adam-smith-and-the-wealth-of-nations.context_blurb:
Adam Smith was a shy, famously absent-minded Scottish professor of moral philosophy who never married and lived much of his life with his mother in Kirkcaldy, a small town on the Scottish coast. In 1776 he published An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, the book that founded modern economics, and people have argued over it ever since.

The book opens in a pin factory. A lone untrained worker, Smith wrote, could scarcely turn out one pin daily, yet ten men who broke the work into some eighteen separate operations could make upwards of 48,000 pins between them. That is the division of labour: split a job into specialised steps and output explodes. Then Smith asked how a big city finds its food each morning. We do not owe our dinner to the kindness of the butcher, the brewer or the baker, he wrote, but to their regard for their own self-interest.

The man behind the book was an odd one. When he was about four, passing gypsies, a whole band of them, snatched him near his home, and his uncle chased them with a posse until they dropped the boy and ran. His biographer later joked that he would have made a poor gypsy. Lost in talk at breakfast one morning, he rolled up his bread and butter, dropped it into the teapot, poured a cup, and declared he had never met with worse tea. He had only one vanity, and he joked that he was a beau, a dandy, in nothing but his books; he owned the finest private library in Edinburgh.

The book's most famous phrase, the invisible hand, appears in its roughly thousand pages just once, in a single passage about a merchant who seeks only his own gain and is led, without intending it, to serve the public good. The Wealth of Nations appeared in March 1776, sold out within six months, and shared its birth year with the American Declaration of Independence, signed that summer in Philadelphia. Smith later became a customs officer himself. In 1778 he accepted a comfortable salary as one of Scotland's Commissioners of Customs, and out of curiosity he compared the list of forbidden foreign goods with his own wardrobe. Nearly all his neckcloths and handkerchiefs turned out to be contraband. So he burned every one of them, he wrote, to set an example.

Before any of this, Smith was a moral philosopher. In The Theory of Moral Sentiments, published in 1759, he argued that each of us judges his own conduct by picturing how a calm, fair-minded stranger would see it, an inner judge Smith named the impartial spectator. Markets, he believed, rest on that conscience as well as on self-interest. Oddly, Smith never visited a pin factory at all; he took his famous example from a description in Diderot's great French Encyclopédie.

When his dearest friend, the philosopher David Hume, died cheerful and openly unbelieving, Smith published an open letter praising the calm, godless way Hume had met death, and pious Britain was scandalised. Smith's own end came in Edinburgh in July 1790. As he lay dying he called in Joseph Black and James Hutton, his two closest friends, and made them throw sixteen volumes of his unpublished manuscripts into the fire before his eyes. Whatever histories of law and literature they held were lost for ever.

adwa-ethiopia-defeats-italy.context_blurb:
In the 1890s, while European powers carved up Africa, the young Kingdom of Italy set out to make the ancient Christian empire of Ethiopia its colony. Ethiopia's emperor, Menelik II, had been buying modern rifles abroad and binding his regional lords to his crown, and his wife, Empress Taytu Betul, rode and camped with the army.

The quarrel began with a treaty. In 1889 Menelik and Italy signed a pact at Wuchale that he understood as a deal between equals. Then Italy told the royal courts of Europe that Ethiopia was now its protectorate. Italy's whole claim hung on one verb in Article 17, mistranslated: the Amharic text said Menelik could use Italy for his foreign dealings if he wished, while the Italian text said he must. Menelik rejected the treaty, and the two nations went to war.

Taytu proved a shrewd commander. In January 1896 Italian troops were dug into a fort at Mekelle. Instead of storming the walls, she sent about 900 men to seize the garrison's water supply, and within days, with his soldiers dying of thirst, the Italian commander, Major Galliano, surrendered.

Weeks later, on 1 March 1896, Menelik's army crushed the invaders at the Battle of Adwa. Italy had to recognise Ethiopia's independence, and Ethiopia stood as the one African kingdom to beat back a European power in the age of empire.

aesop-s-fables.context_blurb:
Aesop, Greek tradition says, was a slave who lived some twenty-six centuries ago and told short stories in which animals talk and act like people. Each fable ends with a sharp lesson about pride, greed or cleverness. Whether one man named Aesop ever lived is uncertain, but his tales passed through Greek, Latin and French and have never gone out of use.

The best known is The Tortoise and the Hare: the speedy hare, sure of winning, naps halfway through the course, and the slow tortoise trudges past him to win. It gave English the saying that slow and steady wins the race.

In another, a lion spares a little mouse caught beneath his paw, and later, when the lion lies tangled in a hunter's net, the mouse repays him by chewing through the ropes with his teeth. No one is too small to help.

In The Crow and the Pitcher, the bird is parched, and the water lies too low in a tall, heavy jar for its beak, so it drops in pebbles, one at a time, until the water rises within reach. Necessity is the mother of invention, says the moral, and scientists at Cambridge later showed that real rooks can solve the very same puzzle.

african-art-benin-bronzes-and-masks.context_blurb:
In the forest kingdom of Benin, in what is now southern Nigeria, royal Edo metalworkers cast portrait heads of their kings, the obas, and long plaques of warriors and court processions. Europeans who later saw these Benin Bronzes could hardly believe their skill. Many were looted by a British expedition in 1897, and the quarrel over returning them goes on.

The famous bronzes are mostly brass, and the Edo never dug that metal from the ground. Portuguese traders paid for goods in manillas, horseshoe-shaped brass bracelets that served as money, and their brass has been traced as far as the Rhineland in Germany. The Edo casters melted that European money down and recast it as plaques and heads of their own kings and court, turning the traders' cash into royal art.

Benin's most famous treasure is not metal at all but ivory: a little face of the queen mother, Iyoba Idia, made early in the 1500s. Her son, Oba Esigie, hung it at his waist for ceremonies. Around the crown above her face runs a ring of little carved Portuguese heads, the bearded strangers who had just arrived by sea, recording Benin's first meeting with Europe. In 1977 Nigeria made this mask the emblem of FESTAC, a great festival of Black and African arts held in Lagos.

african-decolonization-ghana-1957.context_blurb:
On the night independence came, in March 1957, half a million people gathered to hear Kwame Nkrumah declare the British colony of the Gold Coast free. Nkrumah had studied in America and been jailed by the British, and now he led the first land south of the Sahara to throw off a European empire after the Second World War. He meant it to be the first of many.

Nkrumah threw out the colonial name Gold Coast and called the new nation Ghana, after a great empire of medieval West Africa. The old name only marked a shore where Europeans had bought slaves and metal, but ancient Ghana had sat astride the gold trade across the Sahara, and Arab writers had called it the land of gold.

Nkrumah and his cabinet wore white caps lettered P.G., meaning Prison Graduates, because the British had jailed them in the struggle, and they wore the badge with pride. In his speech he declared that Ghana's independence was worthless unless it was bound up with the total liberation of Africa, the whole continent.

The road to that night had begun in blood. In February 1948 unarmed men who had served Britain in the Gold Coast Regiment during the Second World War marched on Christiansborg Castle to claim the back pay still owed them. The British police chief ordered his men to fire on them, and three veterans fell dead: Sergeant Cornelius Adjetey, Corporal Attipoe and Private Odartey Lamptey. The riots that followed in Accra set the colony on its road to independence.

Ghana's example spread fast. In 1960 alone seventeen new African states, fourteen of them from France, two from Britain and Congo from Belgium, won their freedom and took seats at the United Nations, and the world remembers 1960 as the Year of Africa. Early that year the British prime minister, Harold Macmillan, carried the message south. Standing before the apartheid parliament at Cape Town, every member of it white, he told the government to its face that the wind of change was blowing through the continent. No senior Western leader had said so to South Africa's rulers before.

aggression-unchecked-rhineland-ethiopia-.context_blurb:
Between 1935 and 1938 two dictators, Benito Mussolini of Italy and Adolf Hitler of Germany, tore up the peace settlement of 1919 three times, and each time Britain, France and the League of Nations let them. Every unpunished move taught Hitler that the next one would be easier, and Winston Churchill warned in vain that each made a bigger war harder to stop.

Mussolini struck first, invading Ethiopia in October 1935, and General Emilio De Bono's troops took the town of Adwa within days. It was revenge Italy had craved for forty years. At Adwa in 1896 Emperor Menelik II's army had destroyed an invading Italian force, a defeat so complete that Italy had been forced to accept Ethiopia's independence, and Ethiopia stayed free while Europe carved up nearly all the rest of Africa.

On 7 March 1936 Hitler marched troops into the Rhineland, the German borderland that the Treaty of Versailles had stripped of soldiers and forts, but his force was so tiny beside France's army that his commanders carried secret orders to turn around and pull back over the Rhine if the French resisted. France never moved. That June the exiled emperor of Ethiopia, Haile Selassie, came to Geneva to accuse Italy of gassing his people. No head of state before him had stood up to speak at the League of Nations in person, and as he rose, Italian journalists in the gallery booed and whistled at him until the guards removed them. He spoke in Amharic and warned the delegates that God and history would remember their judgment.

Hitler later confessed to his interpreter, Paul Schmidt, that no hours of his life had strained his nerves like the two days after the march, and that if the French had come in, the Germans would have had to pull back with their tails between their legs. It was the last moment he could have been stopped cheaply.

When the German army rolled over the Austrian border on 12 March 1938, into the land where Hitler was born, it met no bullets, only cheering crowds who threw flowers. Hitler rode in triumph to Linz and on to Vienna, where a roaring crowd heard him proclaim the Anschluss, the union of Austria with the German Reich. Within days, Nazis and jeering crowds dragged Vienna's Jews into the streets and forced them onto their hands and knees to scrub the pavements. A rigged vote in April claimed 99 percent approval for the union, though 300,000 to 400,000 Austrians, Jews and Roma among them, had been barred from voting. Six months later came the crisis over Czechoslovakia.

al-andalus-and-moorish-spain.context_blurb:
For nearly eight centuries, from 711 to 1492, Muslim rulers governed much of Spain and called it al-Andalus. Its capital, Córdoba, ruled by an Umayyad dynasty that had fled a massacre in Damascus, grew into perhaps the grandest city in Europe, a place of libraries, poets and scholars where three faiths shared the streets.

Around 822 a gifted musician named Ziryab came from Baghdad, a man people called the Blackbird because of his dark skin and his beautiful voice, and he changed how Córdoba dressed, ate and made music. The lute, ancestor of the guitar, got a fifth string from him; he swapped the wooden pick for an eagle's quill and brought in the custom of changing clothes with the seasons. While most of northern Europe went pitch-dark after sunset, Córdoba's main streets were lined with oil lamps fixed to the doors and corners of the houses, so that, chroniclers said, a person could walk for miles by their light.

Books were the city's glory. Caliph al-Hakam II sent buyers to Constantinople, Cairo and Baghdad hunting for rare manuscripts, and his library grew so vast that the list of titles alone ran to 44 volumes. Europe's biggest Christian libraries counted their books in the hundreds. Lubna of Córdoba began life enslaved, a skilled copyist in the palace library who could read three languages and had trained in mathematics, and once freed she rose to become al-Hakam's personal secretary. More than 170 women worked as scribes in the city.

At the palace-city of Madinat al-Zahra, the chronicler al-Maqqari wrote, a domed hall held a basin of liquid mercury at its centre, and when servants stirred it, flashes of sunlight rippled over the walls. No digger has ever found that basin, so the tale is legend resting on his word alone.

Historians call this coexistence convivencia, and they judge it real but unequal: Christians and Jews lived as dhimmis, protected but lower in law, and above all they had to pay a special tax, the jizya. They also could not hold the highest offices, build new churches or bear arms, and the peace sometimes broke down in violence. Christian kingdoms in the north slowly fought their way south, and in 1492 Granada, the last Muslim realm, fell.

albrecht-durer-northern-renaissance-prin.context_blurb:
Albrecht Dürer of Nuremberg, who lived from 1471 to 1528, was the greatest artist of the Northern Renaissance. Trained first as a goldsmith, he travelled twice to Italy to master perspective and proportion, and then won fame across Europe with his prints: woodcuts and engravings cheap enough for ordinary people to buy.

In 1515 he made a woodcut of a rhinoceros, an animal he had never laid eyes on; his only guides were a written description and a crude drawing that had come from Lisbon, so he dressed the beast in riveted plates of armour and added a small, twisted second horn on its shoulder that no real rhino has. Europe still took his picture for the true rhino for more than two centuries, until a living rhinoceros named Clara toured the continent in the 1740s and 1750s.

In his self-portrait of 1500 he faced the viewer head-on, long hair falling evenly on both sides and one hand lifted to his chest, a pose painters kept almost only for Christ, so Dürer was deliberately making himself look like the divine Creator. It was a bold claim about the artist as a maker in his own right. He even set the year 1500 above his monogram, AD, so that his initials also read Anno Domini, the year of the Lord.

alexander-graham-bell-and-the-telephone.context_blurb:
Alexander Graham Bell was a Scottish-born teacher of the deaf. His mother and his wife were both deaf, and he spent his life fascinated by how human speech is made. In Boston in 1876 he won the race to send a living voice down a wire, and his telephone changed the way the whole world talks.

The fascination started early. As a boy in Scotland, where his father studied how the mouth and throat form speech, young Alec had the family dog hold a steady growl while he moulded its lips and throat with his hands, until the growl seemed to say How are you, grandmama?

On 10 March 1876, in his Boston workshop, Bell spoke into his new machine, and his assistant, Thomas Watson, heard from a receiver in the next room the first words a telephone ever carried: Bell asking Mr. Watson to come here, because he wanted to see him. The popular tale that Bell had just spilled acid on himself is a myth; no acid appears in his notes or in Watson's.

That year, at a great fair in Philadelphia, Emperor Dom Pedro II of Brazil held the receiver to his ear while Bell, far across the hall, recited Hamlet's famous speech that begins To be or not to be. Lord Kelvin, one of the judges, testified that he heard the faint words. The story that Dom Pedro cried out that the thing talks is only legend. Bell wanted people to answer the new device with a sailor's Ahoy!, but his rival Thomas Edison, building telephones of his own, pushed the friendlier Hello, and Edison's word won.

The patent itself had been a near thing. On 14 February 1876 Bell and his rival Elisha Gray both reached the Patent Office, but Gray filed only a caveat, a preliminary notice that he meant to patent, while Bell filed a complete application, and that difference won Bell patent No. 174,465 in March. Courts and historians have argued about the race ever since.

alexander-hamilton-treasury-national-ban.context_blurb:
Alexander Hamilton was born poor and illegitimate in the Caribbean, orphaned young, and reached New York as a teenager with nothing. He fought on George Washington's staff in the Revolution, co-wrote the Federalist Papers, and as the first Secretary of the Treasury built the young country's system of money and credit from near bankruptcy.

His escape began with a disaster: after a huge hurricane wrecked St. Croix in August 1772, the teenage Hamilton wrote a vivid account of the storm that was printed, and it so impressed local leaders that they raised money to send him to school on the mainland of North America. Today Alexander Hamilton's face is on the ten-dollar bill, and he and Benjamin Franklin are the only two men on circulating American money who never served as president.

As Treasury Secretary he wanted the national government to take over the states' war debts. Virginia and the South, whose states had largely settled their own debts, blocked him. Then, at a private dinner at Jefferson's in June 1790, came a bargain: Madison let the debt plan pass, and in return the permanent national capital went south, to the banks of the Potomac. That is why Washington, D.C., stands where it does.

Jefferson attacked Hamilton's plan for a national bank as unconstitutional, because the Constitution never listed such a power and the Tenth Amendment left the rest to the states. Hamilton answered that the Constitution grants implied powers as well as express ones, so its Necessary and Proper Clause lets Congress charter a bank as a reasonable means to a lawful end. Washington sided with Hamilton in February 1791, and that loose reading of the Constitution, against Jefferson's strict one, still shapes American law.

Hamilton's sharp pen made enemies. In July 1804 he met Aaron Burr, then serving as Vice President of the United States, for a pistol duel at Weehawken, across the Hudson from New York, and Burr shot him; Hamilton had helped wreck Burr's hopes of the presidency and of the governorship of New York. Burr's ball tore through Hamilton's liver and lodged in his spine, and he died the next day.

alexander-the-great-s-conquest-of-the-pe.context_blurb:
In 334 BC a 22-year-old king of Macedonia, Alexander, led his father's veteran army into Asia to conquer the Persian Empire, the greatest power on earth. In eleven years he marched from Greece to India, never lost a battle, and spread Greek language and cities across half the known world. Then, at 32, he was dead.

As a boy he tamed a huge black stallion that threw every rider, because he noticed the horse was spooked by the shifting shadow at its feet and turned its head toward the sun before he mounted. His father, King Philip, wept for joy and told him to seek a kingdom worthy of himself, for Macedonia was too small for him. Alexander named the horse Bucephalus, Ox-head, and rode him for years.

When Thebes rebelled in 335 BC he razed the city, slaughtering about six thousand of its people and selling thirty thousand as slaves, yet he ordered one house spared: the home of the long-dead poet Pindar, whose odes had praised one of Alexander's ancestors. In his first great clash with Persia, beside the Granicus River, a Persian lord's sword cracked his helmet open, and as another Persian raised a blade behind him, his officer Cleitus the Black cut the attacker's arm off, sword and all, with one stroke.

At Gordium an oracle had promised the rule of Asia to whoever could undo a hopelessly tangled knot on an ancient ox-cart, and when Alexander could not untie it, he drew his sword and cut it in two. A bold, direct solution is still called cutting the Gordian knot, though some ancient writers say he simply pulled out the cart's pin. After beating King Darius III at Issus in 333 BC, Alexander captured the Persian king's mother, Sisygambis, along with his wife and daughters, and treated the royal women with such respect that Sisygambis came to love him like a son.

In 332 BC the island city of Tyre resisted him through seven long months, and when Alexander built a causeway into the sea and rolled siege towers along it, the Tyrians packed an old ship with pitch, sulphur and dry branches, set it ablaze and rammed it into the towers. In Egypt he founded Alexandria and trekked across the sands to consult the oracle of Siwa, whose priest hailed him as a son of Zeus-Ammon; because Ammon was pictured with a ram's horns, Alexander's coins began to show ram's horns sprouting from his own head. At Gaugamela in 331 BC his smaller army drove at the heart of Darius's enormous host, and Darius was the first man to break and run; when the Persians saw their own king flee, the whole army collapsed, and the Persian Empire with it.

At a drunken victory feast in 330 BC, his company torched the great palace of Xerxes at Persepolis, and the first to throw a blazing torch after Alexander himself, the accounts say, was Thais, a dancing-girl from Athens, avenging Xerxes' burning of Athens 150 years before. On the Hydaspes, a river of India, he defeated King Porus and his war elephants, and when the wounded Porus was brought before him and asked what treatment he wanted, he answered that he should be treated as a king treats a king. Alexander gave him back his kingdom.

But at the Hyphasis River his exhausted, homesick soldiers refused to march another step east, and the conqueror who had never lost a battle had to turn back, halted not by an enemy but by his own men. On the march home across the Gedrosian Desert, when scouts brought the parched king a helmet holding just enough water for one man, he poured it out on the sand in front of his thirsty army, refusing a comfort his soldiers could not share.

In June 323 BC a fever struck him down at Babylon, aged only 32. Asked on his deathbed who should have his empire, he replied: to the strongest. With no clear heir, his generals tore the empire apart in decades of war. They argued over his body for days, and when the embalmers finally reached it, the ancient reports say, they were astonished to find no sign of decay. His body was entombed in Egypt, where the tomb was a shrine for centuries; today no one knows where it lies.

allied-commanders-eisenhower-patton-maca.context_blurb:
Three American generals became household names in the Second World War: Dwight D. Eisenhower, the calm Supreme Allied Commander in Europe; George S. Patton, the profane, hard-driving tank general; and Douglas MacArthur, the theatrical commander in the Pacific. They quarrelled with their allies and with one another, but together they won the war.

Ordered by President Roosevelt to escape the doomed defence of the Philippines in March 1942, MacArthur reached Terowie station in South Australia and promised the press: I shall return. Washington asked him to soften it to we; he would not, because he meant it as his personal word. Patton carried a pair of ivory-gripped revolvers, and when a reporter called them pearl-handled, he exploded that only a pimp from some cheap New Orleans brothel would carry a pearl-handled pistol.

The invasion of Normandy in June 1944 needed a brief lull in the storms, and after Group Captain Stagg, his chief forecaster, predicted one, Eisenhower weighed the choice alone and then launched the greatest seaborne invasion in history with three plain words: OK, let's go. MacArthur kept his own promise on 20 October 1944, wading ashore through the surf at Leyte and speaking into a radio microphone at the water's edge to tell the people of the Philippines that he had returned.

That December, in the Battle of the Bulge, fog and rain kept Patton's planes on the ground, so he had his chaplain, James O'Neill, compose a prayer asking God for clear skies, gave a copy to every soldier of the Third Army, and, once the weather broke, pinned a Bronze Star on the chaplain. With the air open, the Third Army swung north to rescue the 101st Airborne trapped at Bastogne.

Eisenhower had also faced the chance of disaster. The night before D-Day he handwrote a short note to release if the landings failed, praising the troops' courage and declaring that any blame or fault for the attempt was his alone. In his only sign of nerves he dated it July instead of June; he pocketed it after the landings succeeded, and an aide later rescued it from the wastebasket.

america-enters-world-war-i.context_blurb:
In 1914 Europe went to war, and for nearly three years the United States stayed out. President Woodrow Wilson won re-election in 1916 on the slogan He kept us out of war. Then German submarines and a secret German message changed American minds, and by 1918 fresh American soldiers were pouring into France by the hundreds of thousands.

The first blow fell in May 1915, when a German U-boat off Ireland torpedoed the British liner Lusitania without warning; she went down in eighteen minutes, and nearly 1,200 people died, 128 of them American. In February 1917 Germany went back to sinking ships without warning. By then Germany's foreign minister, Arthur Zimmermann, had wired a coded proposal to Mexico: attack the United States, and Germany would help Mexico win back its lost territory of New Mexico, Texas and Arizona.

British codebreakers in the Admiralty's secret Room 40 caught the message, and when Nigel de Grey had cracked enough to see the offer, he went pale and asked his chief whether he wanted to bring America into the war. The joke was on Germany: for part of its journey across the Atlantic the telegram had travelled over an American wire, a State Department cable that neutral Washington had lent Germany for diplomacy, and Britain had been quietly reading those lines all along. To hide that, the British put out a cover story about a spy in Mexico City. Once the telegram was published, everyone expected Zimmermann to call it a British forgery, but on 3 March 1917, asked point-blank by the reporter William Bayard Hale, he replied that he could not deny it: it was true. On 6 April the United States declared war.

The Allies were in danger all the same, because in 1917 revolution knocked Russia out of the war, letting Germany shift dozens of divisions west for one last knockout blow before the Americans landed in strength. Germany had gambled that America's small army, about 128,000 regulars, would come too late. After the draft, troops reached France at some 10,000 a day.

Americans called their soldiers doughboys, and the best-loved story traces the name to 1916, when General John J. Pershing's infantry hunted raiders on the Mexican frontier and came back caked in white adobe dust, so the cavalrymen jeered at them as adobes, a word that slurred into doughboys. The true origin is still debated. On 4 July 1917, soon after the first troops landed, Pershing's aide, Colonel Charles E. Stanton, stood at Lafayette's grave in Paris, honouring the French nobleman who had fought for American independence, and declared: Lafayette, we are here! In the air, the 94th Aero Squadron painted its planes with Uncle Sam's stovepipe hat tossed into a ring, because on the day America joined the fight an officer quipped that the squadron's hat was in the ring now. Its star pilot, the former race-car driver Eddie Rickenbacker, became America's top ace, with 26 victories.

In June 1918 Germany's last great push drove toward Paris. At Belleau Wood, retreating French troops urged the newly arrived Marines to fall back as well, and Captain Lloyd W. Williams of the 5th Marines scoffed at the idea of retreat: hell, he said, they had just got here. Facing sweeping machine-gun fire through a wheat field as high as their waists, First Sergeant Dan Daly, already twice a winner of the Medal of Honor, rose and led his men forward with a famous curse-laden challenge: come on, did they want to live forever? Tradition says the Germans were so shaken by the Marines' ferocity that they called them Teufel Hunden, Devil Dogs, a nickname the Corps still wears proudly, though historians have never found the German term in the records.

That October Corporal Alvin York, a devout Tennessean who had wrestled with his faith before agreeing to fight, killed more than twenty Germans in one fight and marched back a column of prisoners, and when a general joked that he had captured the whole German army, York answered no sir, he had only got 132. By the Armistice that November, more than two million Americans had served in France.

american-modern-art-hopper-pollock-warho.context_blurb:
In the twentieth century American painters moved to the centre of Western art, and New York took over from Paris as its capital. Three of them show the change: Edward Hopper, the painter of lonely city scenes; Jackson Pollock, who flung paint instead of brushing it; and Andy Warhol, who turned supermarket images into Pop Art.

Hopper's Nighthawks of 1942 shows four people in a bright diner at night behind one seamless wedge of curved glass, and the diner has no door at all, no way in or out, so the viewer is shut outside the scene.

Pollock gave up the easel: he laid his canvas flat on the studio floor and walked around it, pouring and flinging house paint from sticks, trowels and stiff old brushes, so that he could, as he said, be in the painting. In 1956 Time magazine mocked his drip style with a pun that stuck for good: Jack the Dripper. Months later, at 44, Pollock died speeding drunk in his car near East Hampton.

In 1962 Warhol showed not one Campbell's soup can but thirty-two separate canvases, and when the dealer Irving Blum asked why so many, Warhol answered flatly that there were 32 varieties. The Museum of Modern Art now hangs all 32 in four rows of eight. Critics took the soup cans for a cold joke about advertising, but Warhol's reason was personal: for about twenty years he really had eaten Campbell's soup for lunch every day, made for him by his mother, Julia.

american-vocal-traditions-spirituals-fol.context_blurb:
America's songs grew from many roots: spirituals made by enslaved people in the South, ballads carried over from the British Isles, church hymns, and patriotic songs sung by soldiers and schoolchildren. Two of the most famous patriotic tunes began life as something quite different, and their stories show how Americans took what came to hand and made it their own.

In the 1760s a macaroni was a young English dandy dressed in the flashiest fashion, crowned with a towering powdered wig, so when British soldiers sang of a Yankee Doodle who put a feather in his cap and called it macaroni, they were mocking the colonist as a bumpkin who thought one feather made him stylish. The Americans turned the insult around and made Yankee Doodle their own song of defiance.

In September 1814 the lawyer Francis Scott Key spent a night watching the British fleet shell Fort McHenry, and at sunrise saw the Stars and Stripes still above the fort. He fitted his poem to a tune everyone knew, To Anacreon in Heaven, which had begun as the theme song of a London gentlemen's club devoted to wine and music. Anacreon was an ancient Greek poet famous for loving wine. The Star-Spangled Banner became the national anthem only in 1931.

amerigo-vespucci-naming-of-america.context_blurb:
Christopher Columbus crossed the Atlantic first, in 1492, yet two whole continents carry another man's name. Amerigo Vespucci was an Italian merchant and navigator who sailed the coasts of South America a few years after Columbus, and his lively letters spread across Europe in the new age of printed books.

Columbus believed to his death that he had found the far side of Asia, but Vespucci, in a printed letter called Mundus Novus, New World, around 1503, was the first to declare in print that these lands were a whole new continent. The continents are named for the man who first grasped what they were.

In 1507 the German mapmaker Martin Waldseemüller honoured him on a great world map, and he took the label from Vespucci's first name, Amerigo, not from his family name: in Latin Amerigo becomes Americus, and its feminine form is America. So two continents carry a man's given name, and Vespucci, still alive when the map began to spread, seems to have had no idea.

ancestral-puebloans-anasazi-of-the-south.context_blurb:
For more than a thousand years, farming peoples lived in the Four Corners of the American Southwest, where Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado and Utah meet. They grew corn, beans and squash in dry country, built great stone towns, and around 1300 moved away to the south and east. Today's Pueblo peoples, among them the Hopi, are their descendants.

Outsiders long called them the Anasazi, yet the word is Navajo, borrowed from a neighbouring people, and means roughly ancient enemies, which is why Pueblo people prefer the name Ancestral Puebloans. Their most famous homes were tucked into sandstone hollows halfway up the canyon walls, and the largest, at Mesa Verde, is Cliff Palace, with about 150 rooms, hidden until ranchers came upon it in 1888.

Each kiva, a round chamber sunk below the earth for ceremonies, had a small hole in its floor called the sipapu, the portal through which, the builders believed, their ancestors had first come up into this world.

Their grandest building, Pueblo Bonito in Chaco Canyon, rose four or five storeys and held some 800 rooms, and roofing it took more than 240,000 logs hauled from mountain forests over 50 miles off, every one of them carried by people on foot, since they had no wheels, carts or pack animals.

On Fajada Butte above the canyon, three leaning stone slabs let slivers of sunlight fall on a rock-carved spiral: at midsummer one blade of light pierces its centre, at midwinter two blades frame it, and researchers named this stone calendar the Sun Dagger. The artist Anna Sofaer noticed it in 1977. Inside Pueblo Bonito, archaeologists also uncovered the bones of scarlet macaws, tropical parrots from rainforests more than 1,000 miles to the south, brought north as early as AD 900, which proves that Chaco's people traded with distant Mexico.

ancient-china-s-rivers-oracle-bones-shan.context_blurb:
Chinese civilization was born on the plain of the Huang He, the Yellow River, in northern China. There, from roughly 1600 to 1046 BC, the Shang kings ruled, cast magnificent bronzes, and asked their dead ancestors for advice about war, harvests and rain. They are the first Chinese dynasty that writing proves was real.

The river earns its English name honestly: it scoops up so much fine, powdery yellow soil, called loess, that its water turns the colour of straw. That silt also earned it a grimmer name, China's Sorrow. Each flood season the mud settles on the riverbed and lifts it, villagers build the dikes taller to hold the water in, and in the worst stretches the river now flows above the fields and rooftops beside it. Farther south runs China's other great river, the Yangtze, or Chang Jiang, about 6,300 kilometres from the Tibetan mountains to the sea, Asia's longest river and the world's third-longest, after the Amazon and the Nile.

The Shang kings put their questions to the dead. A diviner smoothed a cattle shoulder bone or the underside of a turtle shell, then touched it with a red-hot bronze rod until the bone cracked with a sharp pok, and he read the crack's shape as the ancestors' reply. He carved the question, and later the outcome, right beside it. Many questions were homely: would it rain tomorrow, should the offering be three oxen or five? One king, plagued by toothache, asked whether the pain came from a dead ancestor, father Yi, reaching out from beyond the grave.

Those carved questions are the oldest Chinese writing ever found, and today's Chinese characters descend straight from them: on the bones the sun is a circle with a dot and the moon a crescent, and a modern reader can still recognise both. That unbroken line of more than 3,000 years is the real wonder. Yet for most of that time the bones lay forgotten. Healers ground them into powder and sold it as dragon bone, a fever cure, until the scholar Wang Yirong, in 1899, dosing his own malaria, looked closely at some pieces still whole and saw ancient writing scratched into them. His find stretched China's written history ten centuries further into the past.

The river has its own hero. In legend, Yu the Great tamed its floods over thirteen years, not by damming the water as his father had tried, but by digging channels to lead it to the sea, and he was so devoted that he walked past his own home three times without going in. He went on to found the Xia dynasty.

The bones also record the court's surprises. King Wu Ding once foretold from the cracks that a child born to his consort Lady Hao on a lucky ding-day would bring long good fortune; a scribe later carved the truth on the same bone: she gave birth weeks later, on an unlucky day, and it was not good, for the child was a daughter. That same consort, Fu Hao, appears on about 200 bones, more than any other royal woman, and they show her commanding Shang armies in war, once at the head of 13,000 soldiers, the largest Shang force on record. Her tomb, found untouched in 1976, held hundreds of bronzes and jades.

The river kept its terrible power. In the autumn of 1887 the dikes burst near Zhengzhou, and the raised river fell onto the plain below, flooding some 50,000 square miles and drowning close to a million people, one of the deadliest disasters ever recorded.

The Shang word for divining, bu, was written as a tiny picture of the crack itself, a vertical line with a short branch, and scholars think even its sound echoes the pok of the splitting bone.

angkor-wat-the-khmer-empire.context_blurb:
From about 802 until the 1400s the Khmer Empire ruled much of mainland Southeast Asia from Angkor, in what is now Cambodia. Its kings built a vast city of canals and reservoirs to water their rice fields, and in the early twelfth century King Suryavarman II raised Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument on Earth, first a Hindu temple and later a Buddhist one.

One long carved wall in its east gallery shows the Churning of the Ocean of Milk, a Hindu myth in which gods and demons heave on a giant serpent coiled around a mountain, spinning the mountain to churn the sea and draw out the nectar of immortality. It is a cosmic tug-of-war in stone.

The temple also holds a puzzle. Nearly every Khmer temple faces east, toward the sunrise, but Angkor Wat's main gate faces west, the direction the Khmer linked with death. That is why many scholars think Suryavarman II meant it to be his own funerary temple, a tomb as well as a shrine, though this remains an inference, not a certainty.

anne-frank-and-the-diary.context_blurb:
Anne Frank was a Jewish girl, born in Frankfurt, Germany, in 1929, whose family fled to Amsterdam after the Nazis took power. In 1940 Germany conquered the Netherlands and began deporting its Jews. For two years Anne hid with her family in secret rooms in the city centre, and the diary she kept there became one of the most-read books on earth.

For her thirteenth birthday, on 12 June 1942, Anne chose the present she had spotted in a bookshop the day before: a little autograph book with a red-and-white checked cloth cover and a clasp, which became her diary. She wrote it as letters to an imaginary friend, beginning each entry Dear Kitty, a name she borrowed from a character in a series of Dutch novels.

Within weeks the family went into hiding: Anne, her sister Margot, her parents Otto and Edith, and four others, eight people in all. Their Secret Annex lay behind Otto Frank's office at Prinsengracht 263, and its doorway was hidden by a bookcase that swung aside like a door, so anyone in the hallway saw just an ordinary wall. Armed with glue and a brush, Anne brightened her bare room by pasting up postcards and pictures of film stars from the collection she had kept since before the war. You can still see them on her wall today. The office helpers fed them, above all Miep Gies, who cycled over nearly every day with food and library books, knowing that anyone caught sheltering Jews faced death or a concentration camp. From the attic, through the one window the hiders had not blacked out, Anne watched the sky, the gulls and a tall chestnut tree that she wrote about again and again.

By day the hiders had to stay silent, with no tap running, no toilet flushed and no voice above a whisper, because the men working in the warehouse beneath them had no idea anyone was hiding upstairs. One creak could have given them away. Anne longed to be a writer and journalist, and in an entry of April 1944 she wrote that she knew she could write, and that her deepest wish was to go on living even after her death. That spring Gerrit Bolkestein, a Dutch minister in exile, begged the Dutch people over the radio to keep their diaries and letters from the war years, and Anne at once began rewriting her whole diary on loose sheets as a book she meant to publish, called The Secret Annex.

On 15 July 1944, hearing what she called the approaching thunder that would destroy them too, she still wrote that, in spite of everything, she believed people were truly good at heart. On 4 August 1944 police under the SS officer Karl Josef Silberbauer arrested all eight, along with the helpers Victor Kugler and Johannes Kleiman, and despite decades of searching, who tipped them off has never been proven. Miep Gies and Bep Voskuijl found Anne's notebooks and papers strewn across the floor of the emptied annex, and Miep locked them unread in her desk drawer, later saying it was lucky she never read them, because they named the helpers and she would have had to burn them.

In the end Anne and Margot were shipped to Bergen-Belsen, a camp in the north of Germany. Typhus raged through that cold, filthy camp, and both girls died of it early in 1945, only a few weeks before British troops freed Bergen-Belsen in April. Of the eight who had hidden together, only Otto Frank, Anne's father, survived; Miep gave him the saved diary in July 1945, and in 1947 he published it. It has since appeared in about 70 languages and sold more than 30 million copies.

antietam-the-bloodiest-single-day.context_blurb:
On 17 September 1862, along Antietam Creek near the village of Sharpsburg, Maryland, Robert E. Lee's Confederate army fought George B. McClellan's Union army in the first great battle of the Civil War on Northern soil. Lee hoped a victory in the North would win European recognition for the Confederacy. By sunset more Americans had fallen than on any other single day in the nation's history.

Four days earlier, Corporal Barton W. Mitchell of the 27th Indiana had found three cigars in a field, wrapped in a lost copy of Lee's own secret orders for the campaign, Special Orders No. 191, which showed that Lee had split his army into four parts. A Union officer proved it genuine by recognising the handwriting of Lee's chief of staff, an old colleague from his banking days.

In the centre, Confederates packed into a sunken farm road worn down like a trench and fired into charge after charge for over three hours; about 5,000 men fell there, and soldiers renamed it Bloody Lane. The Irish Brigade, under green flags, lost some 60 percent of its men there in an hour.

At first light the fighting swept through a 24-acre cornfield on a local farm, which changed hands at least six times, and General Joseph Hooker wrote that the gunfire had cut every stalk as closely as a knife could have done, with the dead lying in rows where they had stood. Clara Barton arrived with a wagon of bandages just as surgeons were binding wounds with corn husks, and after a bullet went through her sleeve and killed the soldier she was holding, a grateful surgeon, Dr. James Dunn, called her the angel of the battlefield. She never mended the hole in her sleeve.

To the south, some 450 to 500 Georgians firing from a high bluff stopped more than 12,000 of Ambrose Burnside's men for about four hours, as the Union columns kept jamming toward a single 125-foot stone bridge and falling there, though the creek was shallow enough to wade at several fords close by. It is still called Burnside's Bridge.

Antietam was victory enough for Abraham Lincoln: five days later, on 22 September 1862, he announced the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation, declaring that the enslaved in the rebel states would be free from 1 January 1863. He had been holding that decision back, waiting for a battlefield success, and Antietam also ended Lee's hope of European recognition.

antony-cleopatra-and-the-battle-of-actiu.context_blurb:
Mark Antony was a Roman general, once Julius Caesar's right-hand man, who ruled Rome's eastern half after Caesar's murder. Cleopatra VII, clever and Greek-speaking, was the last pharaoh of Egypt. Their alliance became a love affair and a challenge to Antony's rival in the west, Caesar's adopted son Octavian. In 31 BC the quarrel came to a great sea battle off Actium, on the coast of Greece.

With the battle still in doubt, Cleopatra suddenly broke away under sail with her sixty Egyptian ships, and Antony left his warships in mid-fight and went after her. When he reached her ship he was so ashamed that for three days he sat alone at the prow with his head in his hands, unable to face her.

The fight had been going against him anyway. Antony had brought some 500 big, slow warships, his gold stowed aboard his flagship, the Antonia, but Octavian's admiral Marcus Agrippa had the harpax, an iron-cased harpoon shot on a rope that hooked an enemy ship and reeled it in, and with it he sank fifteen of Antony's vessels.

A year later, trapped in Alexandria and told falsely that Cleopatra was dead, Antony stabbed himself, but the wound was slow to kill him, and because she had sealed herself inside her mausoleum, his men hauled him up through an upper window so that he could die in her arms. Rather than be paraded in chains through Rome, Cleopatra took her own life, and the ancient legend says she let an asp, a small venomous snake, bite her. When the Romans found her, no snake was ever discovered, only tiny marks on her arm.

Octavian's soldiers burst in to find the queen dead and her maid Charmion, swaying, setting her crown straight; when a guard angrily asked whether this was well done, Charmion answered that it was extremely well done, as befitted a descendant of so many kings, and fell dead. Her fellow maid Iras lay dying at the queen's feet. Octavian had wanted her alive to march in chains in his triumph, Rome's great victory parade, so, cheated of his prize, he paraded an image of Cleopatra with the asp instead. Master of the Roman world, he became its first emperor, Augustus, in 27 BC.

apartheid-nelson-mandela.context_blurb:
From 1948 to 1994 South Africa's white-minority government ran a system of laws called apartheid, Afrikaans for apartness. It sorted every citizen by race, took the vote and most rights from Black South Africans, and confined them to set areas. Nelson Mandela, a young lawyer of the African National Congress, became the face of the fight against it, and then of the peace that ended it.

The pass laws were the most hated of all: every Black adult had to carry a pass that people called the dompas, roughly dumb pass, bearing a photograph, fingerprints and stamps that set out where the holder could go, and police could arrest anyone found without it. At Sharpeville in March 1960 police fired on a peaceful crowd protesting the pass laws and killed 69 people, and many of them were shot in the back as they ran away, proof that the crowd had threatened no one. That date is now the UN's day against racial discrimination.

Mandela, born in 1918 into the Thembu royal house, helped found the ANC's armed wing in 1961. At the Rivonia Trial of 1964 he and other leaders stood accused of plotting sabotage, and the gallows was a real possibility. Instead of begging for mercy, Mandela spoke from the dock for three hours about a democratic country in which all races could live side by side, and he ended by calling it an ideal for which he was prepared to die. He was sentenced to life in prison. On Robben Island, off Cape Town, he was the 466th prisoner to arrive in 1964, so his number was 466/64, a number that later named his global charity against poverty and AIDS.

For thirteen years he broke rock in a glaring white limestone pit that damaged his eyes, but educated prisoners tutored the rest in reading, history and politics, smuggling lessons past the guards, and they proudly called their prison the University of Robben Island. At night, on smuggled paper, Mandela secretly wrote the book that became Long Walk to Freedom, and when it was finished he sealed the pages in cocoa tins and buried them in the prison garden. Guards later found a copy while building a wall.

Outside, the young kept fighting. On 16 June 1976 thousands of schoolchildren in Soweto marched against a new rule forcing them to take their lessons in Afrikaans, which they saw as the oppressor's language, and police opened fire. Hector Pieterson, aged twelve, was one of the first to die, and the photograph of his body being carried away shocked the world.

On 11 February 1990 Mandela walked out of prison with his fist raised after 27 years behind bars, and he came out preaching reconciliation, not revenge. In 1994 the country elected him its first Black president. South Africans of every background came to call him by his clan name, Madiba, as if he were one of their own family.

In 1995 South Africa hosted the Rugby World Cup, and at the final against New Zealand, Mandela strode onto the pitch in the jersey of the Springboks, a team most Black South Africans had hated for decades as a whites-only emblem, with the number 6 of the captain, Francois Pienaar, on his back. The stadium, packed with some 60,000 white Afrikaners, people whose government had jailed him, began to chant his first name: Nelson! Nelson! Nelson! South Africa won, 15 to 12.

Years later, as president, Mandela invited Percy Yutar, the prosecutor who had once demanded his hanging, to a private lunch, saying the old man had only been doing his job. Yutar marvelled that any head of government would do such a thing. Mandela chose reconciliation on purpose: he wanted to defeat the system, not merely his enemies.

apollo-11-and-the-moon-landing.context_blurb:
In July 1969 three American astronauts, Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins, flew to the Moon on Apollo 11, keeping President John F. Kennedy's 1961 promise to land men there before the decade was out. Two of them walked on its surface while the third circled overhead, and the whole planet watched.

On 20 July Armstrong climbed down the lander's ladder, set his boot in the grey dust and spoke the line the world remembers, about one small step for man and one giant leap for mankind. He always insisted he had said for a man, though that little word cannot be heard on the tape. An estimated 600 million or more, roughly one person in five on Earth, watched him live on flickering black-and-white televisions, the largest audience in history to that time. With no wind, rain or air on the Moon, nothing will wear away the footprints Armstrong and Aldrin pressed into the dust; they should stay sharp-edged for millions of years.

Getting there took the mightiest machine yet flown. The Saturn V rocket that launched them from Florida on 16 July stood 363 feet tall, higher than a 36-storey building, with five huge engines at its base. When Eagle came to rest in the Sea of Tranquility, a broad, flat lunar plain, Armstrong radioed Houston that Tranquility Base was here and that the Eagle had landed. Aldrin followed him down, looked across the empty, cratered, soundless plain, and summed it up in a pair of words: magnificent desolation.

The world did not see how close the landing came to failing. Seconds before touchdown Armstrong saw that the computer was steering them toward a crater ringed with boulders as big as cars, so he took semi-manual control and flew the lander on past the rocks, hunting for a safe spot. The fuel gauge fell fast as he searched, and when Eagle finally touched down it had only seconds of flying time left, perhaps 25 to 50. After the moonwalk, Aldrin found that his bulky backpack had snapped off a plastic circuit breaker, the switch that armed the engine for the climb back to orbit, and with no spare, he pushed it back in with the plastic tip of a felt-tip pen, keeping metal out of the live circuit.

Other moments stayed private. During the descent the computer had also flashed a 1202 alarm, meaning it was being handed more work than it could keep up with, and Jack Garman, a 24-year-old engineer in Houston, judged in seconds that it was harmless and gave the Go to keep landing. Before the moonwalk, Aldrin, an elder of his Presbyterian church in Texas, sat quietly in Eagle and took Christian communion, the first religious rite on the Moon, with bread and wine from a tiny silver chalice. NASA kept it off the air, having been sued over the Apollo 8 crew's Bible reading.

Above them Michael Collins circled alone in the command ship. Each time his orbit carried him behind the Moon he lost all radio contact, for about 47 minutes, with the whole Moon between him and every other human being. Collins later counted it up: three billion people plus two on the far side of the Moon, and on his side, one man plus God knows what.

apollo-11-moon-landing-1969.context_blurb:
On 20 July 1969 Apollo 11 set two Americans down on the Moon, the climax of a race President John F. Kennedy had launched in 1961 after a string of Soviet space firsts. Neil Armstrong commanded, Buzz Aldrin flew the lander with him, and Michael Collins stayed in lunar orbit. Six more landings followed, and the last men left the Moon in December 1972.

Their spidery lander was called Eagle, and when it settled on the Moon, Armstrong told Houston that Tranquility Base was here and that the Eagle had landed. Armstrong's first act on the surface was a precaution: in case they had to blast off at once, he scooped a little Moon soil into a pocket, the contingency sample, so they would not go home empty-handed. Aldrin followed him down the ladder, gazed at a horizon bare of trees, clouds and life, and named the view magnificent desolation: magnificent for the achievement, desolate for the emptiness. He later used the phrase as the title of his memoir.

The landing had nearly failed. As Armstrong hunted for safe ground, the Capsule Communicator in Houston, Charlie Duke, called out the fuel remaining, sixty seconds, then thirty, and by Mission Control's reading Eagle touched down only about 25 seconds from the point where it would have had to abort. When it landed, Duke was so excited that he stumbled over the word Tranquility, and then told the crew they had a bunch of guys in Houston about to turn blue who were breathing again.

In the final minute the guidance computer had flashed a warning, the 1202 alarm, which meant it was overloaded with tasks, but the young engineer Jack Garman knew by heart which alarms were survivable, assured the flight controllers there was no danger, and the crew got their Go. Meanwhile Armstrong saw through his small window that the autopilot was carrying them toward a crater strewn with rocks the size of cars, so he took manual control and skimmed level past the rocks, which is why Eagle landed long, beyond its planned spot. Before climbing back in, the two men set out science instruments, among them a panel of mirrors that bounces laser beams back to Earth; observatories still fire lasers at it and time the bounce to measure the distance to the Moon within inches.

Even before the moonwalk, Aldrin, an elder of his Presbyterian church, had quietly taken Holy Communion inside Eagle with bread and wine, watching the wine creep lazily up the inside of the chalice in the weak gravity, and historians think nobody had eaten or drunk on the Moon before. NASA asked him to keep it off the air, because the atheist activist Madalyn Murray O'Hair was suing the agency over the Apollo 8 crew's reading from Genesis.

Preparing to leave, Aldrin found his backpack had broken a small breaker switch that armed the ascent engine, their only way home, and since metal in a live circuit was dangerous, he pushed a felt-tip pen, which carries no current, into the broken switch. Of the six American flags Apollo crews planted on the Moon, photographs from orbit show five still upright, but not the first: it stood too close to Eagle, and as they lifted off, Aldrin watched the engine's blast knock it flat.

Collins, circling alone, was cut off from Earth's radio for 47 minutes at a time on every pass behind the Moon, the loneliest man since Adam, a NASA voice said, yet Collins later wrote that he never actually felt lonely.

appeasement-and-the-munich-agreement.context_blurb:
In 1938 Adolf Hitler demanded the Sudetenland, the German-speaking border region of Czechoslovakia, and threatened war to get it. Britain's prime minister, Neville Chamberlain, and France's premier, Édouard Daladier, chose to give way rather than fight. Their policy, appeasement, became the byword for feeding an aggressor in the hope that he will stop.

At Munich that September four men, Hitler, Mussolini, Chamberlain and Daladier, handed Czechoslovakia's border lands to Germany, while the country's own two envoys sat waiting in a hotel and learned their nation's fate only once the four had signed. Czechs still call it the Munich Betrayal: about us, without us. On 30 September Chamberlain waved the signed paper outside 10 Downing Street, told the cheering crowd it meant peace for our time, and advised them to go home to a quiet night's sleep. People often misquote it as peace in our time.

To plead with Hitler in person, the 69-year-old Chamberlain flew to Germany three times that month, though he had never once been up in an aeroplane before. Daladier got a hero's welcome too when his plane landed in Paris, but he understood what had really been signed, and under his breath he muttered about the cheering crowd: the fools. By March 1939 German troops were in Prague, the rest of the country was gone, and Hitler renamed the seized Czech lands the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia. Britain dropped appeasement and promised to defend Poland.

Why had they done it? Chamberlain's generation still remembered the trenches of the Great War, and the appeasers honestly believed they were sparing a whole generation from that horror again. The victims saw it differently. Czechoslovakia's foreign minister, Jan Masaryk, whose country was not even allowed to speak, called what the great powers had done an experiment in vivisection, the cutting open of a creature still alive. When the Commons debated Munich on 5 October 1938, most members were relieved, but Winston Churchill began by declaring that Britain had suffered a defeat both total and unmitigated. The Commons still approved the deal, 366 votes to 144.

The deal was hollow at every level. The Sudetenland held Czechoslovakia's mountain defences, the Beneš Line of 264 heavy blockhouses and some 10,000 pillboxes, and at Munich the whole line passed to Germany without a single shot. Even the compromise that broke the deadlock was a fake: Mussolini presented it as his own neutral plan, but Göring and the German Foreign Office had written it the day before, translated it into French and telephoned it to him in Rome. And the short peace pledge Chamberlain had got Hitler to sign that morning meant nothing to Hitler, who, according to his interpreter, Paul Schmidt, told a worried Ribbentrop not to take it seriously, since it had no further significance whatever.

Chamberlain also boasted of bringing back peace with honour for the second time, hoping to borrow the glory of Benjamin Disraeli, who had used those words on returning from the Congress of Berlin in 1878, but history turned the echo into a rebuke. Even Churchill's most famous verdict, that Britain, offered war or dishonour, had picked dishonour and would get war as well, was polished into that shape later; it reworks words he wrote in private letters before Munich, warning that Britain would choose shame and then have war thrown in. The idea was his; the smooth wording came afterwards.

appomattox-and-lee-s-surrender.context_blurb:
On 9 April 1865, Palm Sunday, in the Virginia village of Appomattox Court House, General Robert E. Lee surrendered the Confederate Army of Northern Virginia to General Ulysses S. Grant, and the Civil War was effectively over. Grant, in a muddy private's coat, met Lee, in his best dress uniform, and offered terms meant to heal rather than humiliate.

They met in the parlour of Wilmer McLean, whose farm at Manassas had been crossed by the war's first great battle, Bull Run, in 1861, when a shell fell through his kitchen chimney; he had moved about 120 miles to escape the war, and he later said that it began in his front yard and ended in his parlour. When the generals left, Union officers stripped the room for trophies, and one tossed a friend the homemade rag doll of Lula McLean, aged seven; the Moore family kept it for more than a century and returned it to the park in 1992, where it is known as the Silent Witness.

Grant knew most of Lee's men were small farmers going home to stripped land, so his terms let every Confederate who claimed a horse or mule take the animal home to plant a spring crop, though army horses were legally government property. Lee said it would have a happy effect. When Lee admitted his army was starving, with some twenty-five thousand men to feed, Grant had 25,000 rations sent across from Union stores to feed them. Grant wrote that he felt sad, not joyful, at the downfall of a foe who had fought so long and so bravely.

On 12 April, as the Confederates marched in to stack their weapons, Union General Joshua Chamberlain had his men salute them at carry arms, and General John B. Gordon, at the head of the column, answered the courtesy: he wheeled his horse, made it bow its head, and dropped his swordpoint to his toe.

A beloved legend says Lee offered Grant his sword and Grant gave it back, but Grant flatly denied it in his memoirs, calling the tale the purest romance: the word sword was never spoken until he wrote it into the terms, which let officers keep their side-arms.

aqueducts-roads-and-roman-engineering.context_blurb:
The Romans did not invent engineering, but they built on a scale the ancient world had never seen: paved roads binding the empire together, aqueducts carrying water for miles, sewers, harbours and baths. Their tools were careful surveying, a remarkable concrete and the arch, and some of their work still stands, and is even still used, two thousand years later.

Appius Claudius Caecus started the Appian Way in 312 BC as a military road for the war against the Samnites, and it eventually stretched to Brundisium, the port at Italy's heel; Romans called it the regina viarum, the Queen of Roads. Around 20 BC Augustus set up the Golden Milestone, a bronze-covered column in the Roman Forum, and every road in the empire, from Britain to Egypt, counted its distance from that single spot. All roads really did lead to Rome.

The Roman arch stands by compression alone: the wedge-shaped keystone at its crown bears down on its neighbours, the voussoirs, and its weight turns into a sideways push that squeezes all the blocks together. Aqueducts used no pumps at all; gravity alone moved the water, down a slope so gentle that the channel to Nîmes in southern France dropped only about 12 metres in 50 kilometres, some 24 centimetres per kilometre. Where it had to leap the valley of the Gardon, engineers raised the Pont du Gard, a bridge 48.8 metres tall in three tiers of arches, its blocks of up to six tons cut so precisely that they hold together without mortar, carrying some 11 million gallons a day.

Roman concrete owed its strength to pozzolana, a volcanic ash from Pozzuoli near Mount Vesuvius that let it set even underwater, and researchers have found that leftover lime in the mix lets it seal its own small cracks when water seeps in. That is why harbour walls and the dome of the Pantheon still survive. Roman highways went down in four layers, from big flat stones at the bottom up to tight-fitting paving on top, and each road was crowned, built higher in the middle than at the edges, so rain ran off into ditches on either side. In 97 AD the emperor Nerva made a retired general, Frontinus, Rome's water commissioner, and his first-hand report on the aqueducts exposed a scandal: wealthy Romans were secretly tapping the public lines to pipe water into their own houses.

aquinas-the-salamanca-school-the-natural.context_blurb:
For four centuries a line of Christian scholars argued that right and wrong are not whatever a king commands but a law written into human nature that reason can read: the natural law. The line runs from a medieval friar in Paris to Spanish professors who asked whether Spain's conquest of the Americas was just, and on to the rights Americans declared in 1776.

It begins with Thomas Aquinas, a big, silent student whom his classmates mocked as the Dumb Ox, until his teacher Albertus Magnus warned that one day this ox would bellow so loudly the whole world would hear. In his vast Summa Theologiae, which wove Christian teaching together with the thought of Aristotle, Aquinas held that one command is built into every reasoning mind, needing no teacher, and that all other moral rules grow from it: good must be done and pursued, and evil shunned. But on 6 December 1273, while saying Mass, he had an overwhelming vision, laid down his pen and never finished the Summa, telling his secretary Reginald that everything he had written now seemed to him like straw. He died about three months later.

The Spanish conquest raised the question in the most practical way. Preaching on Hispaniola in 1511, the friar Antonio de Montesinos thundered at the Spanish settlers who held natives as slaves: were these not men, and did they not have rational souls? One listener who owned slaves himself, Bartolomé de Las Casas, was converted on the spot and became the Protector of the Indians.

Salamanca, then Europe's greatest university, gave its top chair of theology to Francisco de Vitoria. Emperor Charles V, master of half of Europe, sent to him rather than to any bishop for answers on the gravest questions of conscience, among them the legality of Spain's conquests and Henry VIII's divorce from Catherine of Aragon. In a famous lecture of 1539 Vitoria asked by what right Spain ruled the native peoples of the Americas, and concluded that, though not Christians, they truly owned their lands and ruled themselves, a dominion that neither the Pope nor the Emperor could take away. He taught that all peoples, Christian or not, form one moral community, the whole world in some sense one republic bound by a common law of nations, and for that later scholars named him the founding father of international law. Yet he never wrote a book of his own: everything we have of him survives in notes his students took at his lectures, printed after his death.

In 1550 the Spanish crown did something new, halting its conquests and staging a formal debate at Valladolid over whether conquered peoples had rights: Las Casas argued that the natives were fully human with natural rights, while his opponent, the scholar Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda, leaned on Aristotle's idea that some people are slaves by nature. The judges leaned toward Las Casas, but the colonists ignored the verdict. Later the Jesuit Francisco Suárez replied to England's King James I, who was imposing a loyalty oath on Catholics, and James was so enraged that he had the common hangman burn the book outside St Paul's in London.

The rights that the Declaration of Independence places beyond any government's reach came to Jefferson from John Locke, and to Locke from the Dutch jurist Hugo Grotius and from Richard Hooker, a follower of Aquinas; behind them all stood the natural-law tradition of medieval Catholic scholars, Aquinas and the Salamanca school. Writing from a Birmingham jail cell, Martin Luther King Jr. justified disobeying unjust laws with Augustine's old maxim, lex iniusta non est lex: a law that is unjust is no law at all.
