galileo-and-the-telescope.context_blurb:
Galileo Galilei was an Italian mathematician and professor who, in 1609, heard of a Dutch spyglass and built a far better one of his own. Turning it to the night sky, he saw things no human had ever seen, and they convinced him that the Earth goes around the Sun. That conviction brought him before the Roman Inquisition in 1633.

In late 1609 he aimed his telescope at the Moon and, from the long shadows on its face, saw that it was not the flawless sphere of the old teaching but a rugged world covered in mountains and craters. He even estimated that its peaks rose about four miles. In January 1610 he studied Jupiter from a Padua rooftop for several nights, and four specks of light kept moving with the planet: four moons orbiting Jupiter, the first ever found circling another world. We call them Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. In March 1610 he rushed his discoveries into print in Venice in a slim book, Sidereus Nuncius, The Starry Messenger, the first book of science based on telescope observations.

Hoping for a rich patron, he named Jupiter's moons the Medicean Stars after the Medici family, rulers of Florence, and the flattery worked: Grand Duke Cosimo II made him court philosopher and mathematician. He turned the telescope on the Milky Way, the faint white band across the night sky, and found that it was made of countless faint stars, too dim and crowded for the naked eye to split apart.

In the belt and sword of Orion, where the naked eye shows nine stars, his lens revealed about 80 more. The sky was far fuller than anyone had imagined. Saturn puzzled him: it seemed to have bumps on both sides, three bodies almost touching, and when the bumps vanished in 1612 he could not know that he had glimpsed the edges of its rings, turned edge-on to Earth. In 1633, forced before the Roman Inquisition to deny that the Earth moves around the Sun, he is said to have muttered as he rose, And yet it moves, in Italian Eppur si muove, but the story first appeared in print in 1757 and is almost certainly a legend.

Watching Venus night after night, he saw it pass through crescent, half and full phases like the Moon, which was impossible in the old Earth-centred system of Ptolemy, proving that Venus circles the Sun. On 22 June 1633, about 69 and ailing, he knelt in a white penitent's gown at the convent of Santa Maria sopra Minerva and swore to abjure, curse and detest the belief that the Earth moves.

The trial was about pride and politics as well as astronomy. Confined for life to his villa near Florence and going blind, he still finished Two New Sciences, smuggled out and printed abroad in 1638, which laid the foundations of the science of motion that Isaac Newton later built on. galileo-the-telescope.context_blurb:
Galileo Galilei was an Italian mathematician who, in 1609, took a Dutch invention, a tube of lenses that made far things look near, and made it far stronger. Pointed at the night sky, his telescope overturned the astronomy that universities had taught for nineteen centuries. Defending what he saw brought him before the Roman Inquisition in 1633.

In August 1609 he climbed the campanile of St Mark's with Venice's ruler, the Doge, and its senators, and through his spyglass they could pick out ships still far out at sea hours before anyone could see them with the naked eye. The Senate rewarded him with a professorship for life at Padua and doubled his salary. That winter he turned the telescope on the Moon and, reading its moving shadows with an artist's eye for light and shade, saw mountains, valleys and craters, not the perfect, polished ball of heavenly stuff the scholars described. On 7 January 1610 he noticed little stars beside Jupiter, and by 15 January he knew they were four little moons circling the planet, swinging back and forth from one side to the other. That sight broke an ancient belief: here were four bodies plainly orbiting Jupiter, so the Earth could no longer be the one centre around which everything in the heavens turned.

Grinding his own lenses, he pushed his telescopes to twenty or thirty times magnification, and in March 1610 he packed his discoveries, with his own drawings of the cratered Moon, into a slim Latin book, Sidereus Nuncius, The Starry Messenger. The Milky Way broke apart into separate faint stars, and in the Pleiades, six stars to an unaided eye, he found about forty more. His eldest daughter, a nun near Florence called Sister Maria Celeste, mixed medicines for him and wrote him 124 letters that survive, but all of his replies to her are lost.

In the autumn of 1610 he watched Venus pass through phases like a small moon, crescent, half and finally full, and a full Venus could only mean it had swung to the far side of the Sun, so it had to be circling the Sun, not the Earth. To claim the discovery without revealing it, he sent rivals a scrambled line of Latin which, unscrambled, said that the mother of love, meaning Venus, imitates the shapes of Cynthia, meaning the Moon. His lens was too weak to show Saturn's rings, so he took the bulges on either side for two companions; he hid that find in another anagram, announcing a triple planet, and he described the strange bulges as Saturn's ears.

His great book of 1632, a dialogue about the two chief systems of the world, led to his ruin. In it he put Pope Urban VIII's own favourite argument against a moving Earth into the mouth of the fool Simplicio, and the Pope, once his friend, felt personally mocked. On 22 June 1633, threatened with torture and found vehemently suspect of heresy, he knelt in a Roman convent and swore that he abjured, cursed and detested the idea of an Earth travelling around the Sun. Legend says that as he rose from his knees he muttered And yet it moves, though no record from his own time has it and the story appears in print a century after his death.

Confined for life to his villa outside Florence, nearly blind and banned from printing anything, he finished Two New Sciences, a book about how things move and how strong materials are, and friends smuggled it out of Italy to be printed abroad, at Leiden in Holland in 1638. When admirers moved his body to a grand tomb in Florence in 1737, they cut off three fingers, a tooth and a vertebra as relics, and his middle finger still points upward from a gilded glass egg in the Museo Galileo. The Church took 359 years to admit its error: in 1992 Pope John Paul II said publicly that Galileo's judges had been wrong.

gallipoli-campaign.context_blurb:
In April 1915 Britain and France tried to knock the Ottoman Empire out of World War One by forcing a way through the Dardanelles strait to Constantinople. When their warships failed, they landed British, French and above all Australian and New Zealand troops, the Anzacs, on the Gallipoli peninsula, where the invaders clung to the cliffs for nine bloody months.

As the Anzacs scrambled up the cliffs on 25 April, the Ottoman commander Mustafa Kemal flung the men of his 57th Regiment into their path and told them he was not ordering them to attack but to die, because while they died, other troops would have time to arrive and take their place. Kemal later became Atatürk, the founder of modern Turkey, and Turks remember Gallipoli as the birthplace of their nation.

In December 1915 the Allies slipped away by night, and to hide the empty trenches, the Australian lance corporal William Scurry invented the drip rifle: water dripped from one kerosene tin into another below until the lower tin grew heavy enough to pull a rifle's trigger by itself. The rifles kept firing after the men had gone, and the Turks did not notice the withdrawal until it was over. In Australia and New Zealand, 25 April is still Anzac Day.

gandhi-and-indian-independence-movement.context_blurb:
Mohandas K. Gandhi, a British-trained lawyer, came home to India from South Africa in 1915 and over thirty years built the most important nonviolent political movement of modern times against British rule. His method was mass civil disobedience: break an unjust law openly, never strike back, and accept the punishment. India won independence in 1947, and a Hindu nationalist assassinated Gandhi in 1948.

He built a name for the method from two Sanskrit words, satya, truth, and agraha, firmness, so that satyagraha means holding firmly to truth, often translated truth-force. In March 1930, at 61, he trekked some 240 miles to the sea at Dandi to defy the Salt Act, which forbade Indians to collect or sell salt of their own. Next to air and water, he said, salt was perhaps the greatest necessity of life, so the tax hit the poorest hardest. On 6 April he waded into the surf, scooped up a crust of salt from the mud, held it before the crowd and declared that with it he was shaking the foundations of the British Empire. A pinch of his illegal salt later sold at auction for 1,600 rupees.

On 21 May about 2,500 of his followers marched on the Dharasana Salt Works, where police clubbed them down row after row and none of them lifted a hand to shield himself, and the American reporter Webb Miller wrote that they fell like ten-pins, and his report was printed in about 1,350 newspapers. British censors first tried to stop his dispatch.

The famous line about an eye for an eye making the whole world blind is often credited to Gandhi, but historians who searched his letters, speeches and books found no record of him ever saying or writing it; it seems to come from his biographer Louis Fischer summing up his ideas.

gandhi-nonviolent-independence.context_blurb:
Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869 to 1948), a lawyer trained in London, fought for the rights of Indians in South Africa and returned home in 1915 to lead India's struggle against British rule. He drew on Hindu, Jain and Christian ethics and on writers such as Henry David Thoreau, and he became a world symbol of principled, nonviolent resistance.

He called his method satyagraha, truth-force: disobey an unjust law openly, never strike back when you are punished, and accept jail or blows without lifting a hand. For his weapon against the British Empire he chose salt, the plainest necessity of every household in India, whatever its wealth or faith, because the Salt Act forbade Indians to gather it from their own shore and made them buy taxed British salt.

On 12 March 1930 he set out from the Sabarmati Ashram with just 78 followers, but he spoke against the salt tax in a new village every night, and by the time he reached the sea at Dandi, 24 days and some 240 miles later, the procession was more than two miles long. On 6 April he lifted a salt-crusted lump of mud above his head before the crowd and declared that with it he was shaking the foundations of the British Empire. Officials had ground the shore salt into the sand to stop him, but he found a lump anyway, and more than 60,000 Indians, Gandhi among them, were arrested in the protests that followed.

After his arrest, 2,500 unarmed marchers walked into the steel-tipped clubs of the police at the Dharasana Salt Works, and the reporter Webb Miller, who had reported from twenty-two countries over eighteen years, wrote that he had seen nothing like it: not one marcher lifted an arm to ward off a blow. The poet Sarojini Naidu had told them beforehand not even to raise a hand.

In March 1931 the Viceroy, Lord Irwin, signed a pact with Gandhi as an equal, and Winston Churchill, disgusted, sneered at the spectacle of a half-naked fakir striding up the steps of the Viceroy's palace, an insult Indians turned into a mark of pride.

genghis-khan-the-mongol-empire.context_blurb:
Genghis Khan, born on the Mongolian steppe around 1162, united the warring Mongol tribes and from 1206 until his death in 1227 led them in the most devastating conquests in history. His sons and grandsons pushed on into China, Persia, Russia and Eastern Europe, killing many millions while building an empire that also opened Eurasia to trade.

He was born Temujin, for his father gave him the name of a beaten Tatar enemy, and he took the title Genghis Khan only in 1206. Mongol legend says the newborn came into the world clutching a clot of blood in his fist, a sign that he would shed blood and rule. His heirs carried the empire from the Sea of Japan to eastern Europe, roughly one fifth of the planet's land, some 9 million square miles in one unbroken block, the largest land empire without gaps that has ever existed.

When Temujin was about nine, Tatars poisoned his father Yesugei over an old grudge, and his own clan abandoned the widow and her children on the open steppe, expecting them to die. When the rival Merkits stole his wife Borte in a raid, he gathered allies and led a raid to win her back, and that rescue first gave him a name as a leader worth following. Once, in 1202, an archer of the enemy killed his horse beneath him, and when the captured man openly confessed it, Genghis spared him, renamed him Jebe, the Arrow, and made him one of his top generals. He promoted men for ability, not birth. In 1218 a governor of the Khwarezmian Empire accused some 450 Mongol merchants at Otrar of spying and had them killed, and when Genghis sent envoys to demand justice, the Sultan beheaded the chief envoy and shaved the beards of the rest, which meant war.

In February 1220, in conquered Bukhara, Genghis mounted the pulpit of its great mosque and told the terrified people that he was the punishment of God, sent because of their great sins, as the Persian chronicler Juvayni recorded. When an arrow from the walls of Nishapur killed his son-in-law Toquchar, Mongol troops under his son Tolui massacred almost everyone in the city in April 1221 and stacked the heads of men, women and children into three great pyramids. The empire was held together by the yam, a horseback relay with fresh horses waiting every 25 to 30 miles, so messengers could cover up to about 190 miles in a day. Genghis died in August 1227 while fighting the Tangut kingdom, and his grave has never been found, for legend says the men of his funeral escort killed everyone they met on the road to it.

The conquest of Persia was the collapse of a whole people: towns that resisted were wiped out, famine followed, and by one common estimate a population of 2,500,000 fell to about 250,000. The Persian figures are disputed, and estimates of all deaths in the Mongol conquests run from 30 to 60 million. His generals Jebe and Subutai led one army on a scouting ride of more than 5,500 miles in about three years, through northern Persia and the Caucasus, and destroyed a combined army of Rus' princes and Kipchaks beside the Kalka River before riding home. In 2003 geneticists reported one Y-chromosome line shared by about 8 percent of the men in a vast region of Asia, about one man in 200 worldwide, some 16 million, and proposed that it came from Genghis and his sons, though others think it may come from ordinary Mongol warriors.

george-washington-general-and-first-pres.context_blurb:
George Washington was a Virginia planter and veteran of the French and Indian War whom Congress chose in 1775 to command the Continental Army. He lost more battles than he won, yet he kept the army alive for eight years until victory came, and then the new nation chose him as its first president. His greatest acts were the times he gave power away.

On 23 December 1783, with the war won and the only army in the country his to command, he appeared before Congress at Annapolis, handed back his commission and left as a private citizen, saying his assigned work was done. Then he rode hard for his Virginia home, reached it on Christmas Eve and became a farmer again, working his own fields. Americans called him the American Cincinnatus, after the Roman who was called from his plough to rule as dictator in wartime, gave the power back the moment he had won, and returned to farming. His officers founded the Society of the Cincinnati in his honour. In 1789 and again in 1792 he was elected president unanimously: every member of the Electoral College voted for him, 69 votes the first time and 132 the second, which no other president has ever matched.

Legends gathered around him. The famous cherry-tree story, in which young George confesses that he cannot tell a lie, never happened: a travelling preacher and bookseller, Parson Mason Locke Weems, added it to his biography of Washington in 1806 to sell more copies and teach children virtue. The painter Benjamin West told a story that King George III, hearing Washington meant to give up power for his farm, predicted that this would make him the greatest man in the world, though the tale is second-hand.

He had refused power before. At Newburgh, New York, in March 1783, officers who had gone unpaid threatened to turn on Congress, and when his speech failed to move them, Washington put on a pair of spectacles that none of them knew he needed, saying he had grown grey and almost blind in his country's service, and the hardened soldiers wept and gave up the plot. The year before, Colonel Lewis Nicola had written urging him to make himself king, and Washington replied the same day that he viewed the idea with abhorrence, ordering Nicola to put the thought out of his mind for good.

Washington held people in slavery all his adult life; by 1799 there were 317 enslaved people at Mount Vernon. His will singled out his enslaved valet, William Lee, called Billy, who had ridden beside him through the whole war: Lee alone received his freedom at once and a pension of $30 a year for life. Of the 123 people Washington owned himself, his will ordered them freed after Martha's death, which no other slaveholding early president did, though he could not legally free the 153 dower slaves of the Custis estate. Two people he held refused to wait: Martha's skilled seamstress Ona Judge escaped in 1796 and the cook Hercules Posey in 1797, and despite Washington's efforts to recover them, both stayed free and were never recaptured.

In December 1799, dying at Mount Vernon of a throat infection after a long ride across his farms in snow and sleet, he told his secretary Tobias Lear to wait three days before burying him, for he dreaded being buried alive. His doctors had drained about 40 percent of his blood. He had refused a third term in 1796, and for nearly a century and a half no president served more than two, though no law required it: only the force of Washington's example held the line, until the 22nd Amendment wrote the limit into the Constitution in 1951.

german-unification-bismarck-and-blood-an.context_blurb:
Otto von Bismarck, prime minister and later chancellor of Prussia, forged the many separate German kingdoms and duchies into a single empire under the Prussian king between 1862 and 1871. He practised Realpolitik, politics without sentiment, and he believed that armies, railways and well-chosen wars, not speeches and constitutions, would unite Germany.

He told the Prussian parliament in 1862 that the big issues of the age would be decided not by speeches and majority votes, the mistake of 1848, but by iron and blood, a phrase the world remembers the other way round, as blood and iron. It earned him the name the Iron Chancellor. Then he fought three short wars in a row, each removing a rival to Prussian leadership: Denmark in 1864, then Austria in 1866, then France in 1870.

At Königgrätz in 1866 Prussian infantry carried the Dreyse needle gun, a breech-loader they could fire ten or twelve times a minute lying flat, while Austrian soldiers had to rise to their feet to reload from the muzzle, giving Prussia about five shots for every one. Austria lost about 45,000 men, Prussia fewer than 10,000.

In July 1870 Bismarck edited the Ems Dispatch, a royal telegram, cutting it so that a courteous account now sounded like a snub to the French envoy; he called it a red rag for the Gallic bull, and six days later France declared war on Prussia, just as he intended. On 18 January 1871, with German armies besieging Paris, he had the new German Empire proclaimed not in Berlin but in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, to humble France in Louis XIV's own palace. The Prussian king, Wilhelm I, had wanted to be called Emperor of Germany, but Bismarck insisted on the humbler German Emperor so as not to anger the kings of the south, and the slighted Wilhelm stepped down from the dais and refused to shake Bismarck's hand.

gettysburg-and-pickett-s-charge.context_blurb:
From 1 to 3 July 1863, the Union Army of the Potomac under George Meade and Robert E. Lee's Confederate Army of Northern Virginia fought around the small town of Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. Lee had invaded the North hoping to break Northern will. The battle became the turning point of the Civil War, and Lee never invaded the North again.

In three days some 50,000 men were killed, wounded or missing, the most of any battle ever fought in North America. On the morning of 1 July John Buford, a Union cavalry general, held the ridges outside town with a thin screen of horsemen, knowing Lee's whole army was coming, and when asked how things looked, he answered grimly, "The devil's to pay!" His troopers fought on foot, every fourth man holding the horses, and each carried a single-shot carbine that loaded at the breech and could be reloaded much faster than the Confederates' muzzle-loading rifles, which stalled the enemy until Union infantry arrived. The first infantry came under General John Reynolds, who after Chancellorsville had turned down Lincoln's offer of command of the whole army unless he could run it free of meddling from Washington, and minutes after arriving, a bullet killed him. The command had gone to Meade instead.

On 2 July Gouverneur K. Warren, a Union engineer, scrambled up Little Round Top, found only a signal station there, and saw sunlight flashing off enemy bayonets to the southwest, a whole Confederate column coming to seize the hill. Colonel Strong Vincent hurried his brigade up the slope on his own authority, placed the 20th Maine, under Colonel Joshua Chamberlain, at the far end of the entire Union line, and ordered him to hold that ground whatever the cost. Chamberlain's men repelled one Alabama assault after another until their ammunition ran out, and with the enemy thirty yards away he ordered a downhill bayonet charge, which swept up about 400 prisoners. That same day a gap opened in the Union centre, and General Winfield Scott Hancock flung the 262 men of the 1st Minnesota at an oncoming brigade to buy five minutes; the regiment suffered an 82 percent casualty rate, the worst of any Union regiment in a single action.

On 3 July Lee sent about 12,500 men in Pickett's Charge against the Union centre on Cemetery Ridge, and to reach it they had to cross almost a mile of open farmland in full view of Union cannon and rifles. General Longstreet was sure the attack was doomed, and when Pickett asked whether he should advance, Longstreet later wrote, he could not force the order out and only nodded. Of all the attackers, General Lewis Armistead's Virginians got deepest into the Union line, his black hat stuck on the point of his sword and held high so his men could follow, and he crossed the stone wall and laid his hand on a Union cannon before he fell, mortally wounded. Defending that spot was Hancock, and the story goes that the two generals had been dear friends who wept when they parted before the war; dying, Armistead sent his regrets to Hancock, wounded nearby. The charge collapsed in under an hour with some 6,555 casualties, about half the men, and Lee rode among the survivors saying it was all his fault; years later, asked why it failed, Pickett said dryly that he had always thought the Yankees had something to do with it.

giordano-bruno-burned-at-the-stake-1600.context_blurb:
Giordano Bruno was an Italian ex-Dominican friar, poet and daring thinker of the 1500s who fled his monastery and wandered Europe, teaching in Paris, Oxford, Wittenberg and Prague. He argued that the stars were other suns and that the universe might be infinite, full of countless worlds. In 1591 a wealthy Venetian invited him to teach privately, then denounced him to the Inquisition.

Bruno spent seven years in prison and under questioning in Rome before his sentence came in February 1600. Hearing it, Bruno told his judges that perhaps they pronounced the sentence with greater fear than he felt in receiving it. An eyewitness, Caspar Schoppe, recorded almost the same words in a letter that year. Bruno was burned alive in Rome's Campo de' Fiori on 17 February 1600.

He is often called a martyr of astronomy, but his belief in many worlds was just one of the eight final charges, and what doomed him were theological denials: of the Trinity, of Jesus as God made flesh, of the bread becoming Christ's body at Mass, and of Mary's lasting virginity. Cardinal Robert Bellarmine, who would later confront Galileo, reduced the case to eight heretical propositions. Bruno was no modern scientist but a mystic who also believed that souls pass from body to body.

globalization-the-internet-age.context_blurb:
From the late 20th century, cheap container shipping, the opening of closed economies such as China, India and Eastern Europe after communism, and the rise of the internet tied the world together faster than ever before. Most of humanity gained instant, almost free communication, and world trade boomed, though the change also brought industrial decline and political backlash in parts of the West.

On 29 October 1969 the student Charley Kline tried to send the opening message over an early computer network, typing login to a computer at Stanford, but the far machine crashed after two letters, so the first message ever sent was LO. The team sent the whole word about an hour later. In 1937 a young North Carolina truck driver, Malcolm McLean, spent hours on a dock watching men haul his cargo aboard bale by bale, and he wished he could simply lift the whole trailer onto the ship. In April 1956 the Ideal X, an old oil tanker from the Second World War, sailed from New Jersey to Houston carrying 58 of his truck-sized steel boxes, the first true shipping containers, which went aboard in under eight hours instead of days.

In March 1989 the British scientist Tim Berners-Lee handed his boss at CERN, Sendall, a short paper on linking documents across computers, and Sendall scrawled on top, Vague, but exciting, letting the project that became the World Wide Web go ahead. Berners-Lee gave the Web to the world free. The first website lived in 1991 on one black NeXT cube on his desk, and because turning it off would have taken the whole Web down with it, a colleague stuck on it a red-ink note announcing that the machine was a server and must not be powered down.

The engineer Keith Tantlinger designed the twist-lock, a corner fitting that let any crane lift any box and let boxes stack and lock together, and he persuaded McLean's company to give the patent away free of royalties to all comers. That is why a box from any port fits any ship, train or truck. Between 1990 and 2015, as shipping grew cheaper and trade barriers fell, the world added over two billion people, yet the number in extreme poverty fell by almost 1.2 billion, about 130,000 people escaping it every day. The share of humanity in extreme poverty fell from 36 percent to 10.

gothic-cathedrals-chartres-notre-dame.context_blurb:
Between about 1140 and 1350, the master masons of northern France learned to raise churches of astonishing height and light, the style we call Gothic. Two of the most famous stand at Chartres, a cathedral town southwest of Paris, and on an island in the Seine at the heart of Paris: Notre-Dame. Whole towns spent fortunes and lifetimes building them.

On the roof, a true gargoyle is a drainpipe with a monster's face. Rainwater runs down a channel in its back and gushes out of its open jaws, thrown well clear of the walls so that it cannot soak the stone. Inside, Chartres guarded the holiest treasure in France, the Sancta Camisia. Pilgrims believed the Virgin Mary had worn this veil of silk when she gave birth to Jesus, and King Charles the Bald, a grandson of Charlemagne, gave it to the cathedral in 876. The butchers, money-changers, tanners and shoemakers of Chartres each paid for windows, and in the lowest panels the glaziers showed those craftsmen at work in their own trades. In December 1804 Notre-Dame saw Napoleon Bonaparte made Emperor of the French, with Pope Pius VII brought from Rome to crown him. At the high point Napoleon picked up the crown and set it on his own head, a sign that his power came from himself and the people, not from the Church.

In June 1194 fire destroyed most of the old cathedral at Chartres. But priests had sheltered with the veil in the crypt behind iron trapdoors, and when it came out unharmed, the townspeople took its survival as a sign that the Virgin herself wanted a greater cathedral built for her. The west front survived, which is why its two spires do not match. The plain south spire was finished around 1160 in the older Romanesque style, while the architect Jean Texier built the lacy north spire between 1507 and 1513, so more than three centuries separate them. Around 1200 the builders set an eleven-ring labyrinth into the floor. People called it the chemin de Jerusalem, the road to Jerusalem: a believer who could never afford or survive the real journey made a pilgrimage to Jerusalem in miniature here, inching along its path on his knees. Notre-Dame's great voice is Emmanuel, a bell of about 13 tonnes, named in the reign of Louis XIV. It is saved for the greatest feasts of the Christian year, such as Christmas, and for a few great national occasions.

Bishop Maurice de Sully began Notre-Dame in 1163, and it was not complete until about 1345, so generations of masons died before it was done; the men who laid the first stones knew they would never see the towers rise. Their height depended on a trick outside the walls, because a stone vault pushes outward as well as down. The flying buttress catches the roof's outward thrust high on the wall and carries it through the open air to a massive pier, which drives the force down into the ground. Freed of that load, the wall can become a thin curtain of glass. Not every monster on Notre-Dame is medieval, though. The brooding chimeras, among them the winged Le Stryge resting its chin in its hands, were added in the 1800s, during Eugène Viollet-le-Duc's restoration of 1844 to 1864. They drain no water, so strictly they are not gargoyles at all. Chartres nearly died in August 1944, just after its liberation, when American artillery was ordered to shell the cathedral because commanders suspected that German snipers had taken its towers. Colonel Welborn Barton Griffith Jr. would not take that on faith, so he and his driver went inside and climbed the towers, found no snipers there, and had the shelling called off. Hours later Griffith was killed in a nearby town.

The whole style had begun just north of Paris. At the abbey church of Saint-Denis, dedicated in 1144, Abbot Suger used pointed arches and ribbed vaults to open the walls for great windows of stained glass, whose glow he called lux nova, the new light. Every later Gothic cathedral followed his recipe. King Louis IX bought the Crown of Thorns from the bankrupt emperor of Constantinople and built the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris to hold it, a chapel made almost entirely of glass, consecrated in 1248. Yet that whole jewel-box chapel cost Louis less to build than he had paid for the relic it was made to hold.

gothic-cathedrals-chartres-notre-dame-2.context_blurb:
Gothic cathedrals were the great building adventure of medieval Europe. From the 1140s into the 1300s, masons in France and far beyond raised churches so tall and so full of coloured light that they seemed to float. Notre-Dame de Paris is the most famous of them all, and in April 2019 the world watched it burn. What survived, and why the style worked at all, is a story of fire and stone.

High under Notre-Dame's lead roof lay a web of medieval timber that the carpenters nicknamed the Forest. To frame it in the 1200s they felled some 5,000 oaks, and every beam was cut from its own separate tree, which is how the roof earned its name. On the night of 15 April 2019 that ancient wood caught fire and burned almost entirely. Father Jean-Marc Fournier, chaplain of the Paris fire brigade, went in with firefighters passing things hand to hand in a human chain, and he carried out the cathedral's holiest relic, the Crown of Thorns. The spire crashed through the vault. In the wreckage, workers found the copper rooster from its tip, dented but whole, and sealed inside it were three holy relics: a fragment of the Crown of Thorns and bits of bone of Saint Denis and Saint Genevieve, the patron saints of Paris. Some 180,000 bees kept in hives on a ledge about 30 metres beneath the blazing roof came through as well, and once the smoke had cleared their keeper announced that the bees were still alive. Best of all, the three great rose windows, wheels of thirteenth-century glass high in the walls, came through the fire intact.

The building that burned was a triumph of engineering. A round Roman arch shoves hard to the sides, so it needs thick walls to hold it, but a pointed arch sends most of its weight steeply downward, straight into its supports, which let Gothic builders raise taller and thinner walls. Outside, flying buttresses, stone arms leaning against the building, caught the vault's outward thrust and carried it down to heavy piers, so the walls, relieved of the roof's weight, could be filled with vast windows of stained glass. Chartres, southwest of Paris, shows how fiercely people loved these churches. When fire swept the cathedral in June 1194, the story goes, priests sheltered in the crypt behind iron trapdoors and emerged three days later with the town's great treasure, the Veil of the Virgin, unharmed. The town rebuilt on a grander scale. In the new floor lies a labyrinth whose one path winds for about 261 metres, and pilgrims who could never reach Jerusalem shuffled along it on their knees until they reached the centre, a journey to the Holy City in miniature.

In Paris, King Louis IX took the idea to its extreme in the Sainte-Chapelle, built in the 1240s to house the Crown of Thorns, where the upper chapel's walls are almost nothing but stained glass: fifteen windows some 15 metres tall, holding 1,113 coloured panels. The walls seem to dissolve into light.

Two last tales end the story, one a myth and one a warning. Chartres is famous for a deep cobalt blue, said to hide a lost secret no modern glassmaker could copy, but historians call that a romantic myth, because medieval glass recipes survive. The blue has outlasted the reds and greens because its sodium-based cobalt glass proved unusually tough. The race for height also had a limit. Beauvais Cathedral raised the tallest choir vaults in the world, about 48 metres, but the choir fell in 1284, its great tower crashed down in 1573, and the cathedral was never finished.

goya-the-third-of-may-1808.context_blurb:
Francisco de Goya was a court painter to the Spanish royal family when Napoleon's armies invaded Spain in 1808. On 2 May the people of Madrid rose against the French, and the next day French soldiers shot rebels in reprisal. Goya painted those killings in The Third of May 1808, and in old age his art grew darker still.

At the centre of the canvas a labourer in a blazing white shirt kneels in front of the soldiers, arms flung open like Christ on the cross. Look closely at his right palm and you find a dark mark, a nail-wound like the stigmata of the crucifixion, which turns an ordinary man's death into a sacrifice. His face, though, shows raw terror, not a saint's calm.

Old, deaf and bitter, Goya moved into a farmhouse outside Madrid that locals already called the Quinta del Sordo, the Deaf Man's Villa. Between 1820 and 1823 he covered its bare plaster walls with fourteen nightmare scenes, the Black Paintings, among them Saturn Devouring His Son, meant for no eyes but his own. Decades after his death they were peeled from the walls, moved onto canvas and hung in the Prado.

grand-canal-of-china.context_blurb:
China's Grand Canal is the longest waterway people have ever dug, more than a thousand miles of channel linking the rice lands of the south with the capital and armies of the north. Earlier rulers had cut stretches of it, but Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty joined them into one great system in the early 600s, at a terrible cost.

When the canal was complete in 609, Yang toured it in splendour. His fleet of giant dragon-boats sailed in a single unbroken line that, by the old accounts, stretched about 65 miles, some 105 kilometres, from the first boat to the last. That column of ships was longer than many countries are wide.

The splendour hid the suffering. Emperor Yang drove some five million people, women and children among them, to do the digging, and old records say perhaps two million of them died of overwork and disease. That suffering, piled on top of his failed wars against the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo, set off rebellions that overthrew the Sui within a single generation. The dynasty was destroyed by the very lifeline it had built, yet the canal outlived it, and long stretches still carry barges today.

great-famine-in-ireland-and-the-age-of-m.context_blurb:
Between 1845 and 1852 Ireland, then ruled from London as part of the United Kingdom, suffered the Great Famine, An Gorta Mór, the Great Hunger. A huge share of its rural poor lived on tiny rented plots and ate little but potatoes. When the potato crop failed year after year, hunger, fever and eviction tore the country apart and scattered its people across the world.

The killer was Phytophthora infestans, a water mould that had crossed the Atlantic from North America, and it blackened the leaves and rotted the potatoes into slime. It is often called a fungus, but it is not one.

About a million people died, and at least another million left Ireland as refugees, most of them bound for the United States and Canada, so the population fell by more than a million and a half in ten years. The deadliest year of all was 1847, remembered ever since as Black '47. That March, help came from an unexpected place. The Choctaw Nation in Oklahoma, only fourteen years after its own Trail of Tears, collected $170 for the starving Irish. In 2020 the Irish returned the kindness, sending donations to the Choctaw during the pandemic.

Relief from London was clumsy. Robert Peel, the prime minister, secretly shipped in £100,000 of maize from America to be sold cheap in the winter of 1845, but the hard yellow grain was so difficult to cook and digest that the hungry nicknamed it Peel's brimstone. Witnesses tried to make Britain see. The Cork magistrate Nicholas Cummins found six starving skeletons on straw in one hut in Skibbereen, and he wrote to the Duke of Wellington that as soon as he stepped back outside, at least 200 more such phantoms had surrounded him. The Times printed his letter. Those who escaped crowded onto ships so deadly that people called them coffin ships, and in 1847 more than one in ten of the Irish who sailed for Quebec died at sea or in quarantine.

The bitterest arguments are about London's choices. Charles Trevelyan, the Treasury official in charge of relief, shut down Peel's food programmes. He went on to describe the famine as a direct stroke from an all-wise, all-merciful Providence, a sharp but effective remedy, and he blamed the character of the Irish themselves. In 1848 he was knighted for his relief work. All the while, ships carried Irish wheat, oats, butter and calves to England, often under armed guard. Historians still argue over what those exports prove: Austin Bourke pointed out that by 1847 more grain was coming in than going out, while Christine Kinealy argues that policy and merchant profit, not scarcity alone, shaped the death toll.

great-mosque-of-cordoba.context_blurb:
Córdoba's Great Mosque, in southern Spain, was begun in 785 under Abd al-Rahman I, the Umayyad ruler of al-Andalus, on the site of an older Christian church. Enlarged again and again, it became one of the greatest mosques in the Islamic world, a vast prayer hall filled with a forest of columns.

Many of those columns were salvaged from Roman and Visigothic ruins, and they were too short for the lofty roof the builders had in mind. So the builders raised a second layer of arches above the first, a two-storey arcade that lifted the roof to the height they wanted. Striped in red brick and white stone, the doubled arches seem to march away forever in every direction.

After Christian armies took Córdoba in 1236, the mosque became a cathedral, and in the 1500s builders cut a soaring Christian nave through the heart of the old hall. The emperor Charles V had approved the work, but when he saw the result he reportedly told the clergy that they had built something anyone could have built anywhere, and destroyed something unique in the world. The story comes down as testimony, not as an exact record of his words.

great-zimbabwe.context_blurb:
Great Zimbabwe was a medieval granite city on a high plateau in southern Africa, built between about 1100 and 1450 by forebears of today's Shona. Perhaps 20,000 people lived there at its height. Its ruins are the grandest of their kind below the Sahara, and for a century European newcomers tried to steal the credit for them.

When the country around the ruins won its independence, it named itself Zimbabwe after them, from the Shona phrase dzimba dza mabwe, meaning houses of stone. The masons used no mortar at all: they cut and stacked each granite block so precisely that walls up to 11 metres high stand by their own weight. Carvers also made eight tall soapstone birds, each perched on a stone column, and the Zimbabwe Bird is now the nation's emblem, on its coat of arms, banknotes and flag.

Its three parts are the old Hill Complex, perched on a granite outcrop, the walled Great Enclosure beneath it, and the Valley Complex in the lowland. The Great Enclosure's curving wall runs about 250 metres around, and it is the largest ancient stone structure in all of sub-Saharan Africa. Inside it stands the Conical Tower, some 9 metres tall. Archaeologists found that the tower is solid stone all the way through, with neither an entrance nor a chamber inside. Behind the great walls, families lived in daga houses of packed earth and clay. The court's wealth came from great herds of cattle and from gold, mined on the plateau and carried down to Sofala on the coast, then north to the Swahili port of Kilwa and out across the Indian Ocean.

To quarry their blocks, masons lit fires against the granite until the heat cracked it, using the rock's habit of peeling off in flat layers to split it into brick-shaped slabs. The top of the Great Enclosure's outer wall is trimmed with a band of dark stone laid in a double chevron, a zigzag often read as a snake and a sign of fertility. Many scholars read the solid tower as an enormous stone model of a Shona grain bin, showing that the ruler, like a chief with a full granary, fed his people, though its purpose is still debated. The soapstone birds have human lips instead of beaks and five toes instead of talons, and they probably show the bateleur eagle, chapungu in Shona, believed to carry messages from Mwari, God, and from the ancestors. Digging in the ruins, archaeologists turned up Chinese porcelain, Persian glass and beads, and a coin struck by a sultan of Kilwa, proof that this inland city traded across the Indian Ocean. In 1889 the hunter Willi Posselt hacked one bird from its column and paid the local chief for it in blankets and a handful of small goods. It ended up at the Cape Town estate of Cecil Rhodes.

The first European to write about the city, the Portuguese captain Vicente Pegado, called it in 1531 a fortress of stones of marvelous size, with no mortar to join them. Later Europeans would not accept that Africans were the builders. In 1871 the German explorer Karl Mauch sniffed a sliver of a wooden door-beam, decided it smelled like his cedar pencil, and declared that Phoenicians had built the city for the Queen of Sheba. In Rhodes's day Richard Nicklin Hall, sent to restore the ruins, shovelled away up to two metres of buried soil layers, the dated record of who had built the city, because he called them the filth of African occupation. Gertrude Caton-Thompson, a British archaeologist, dug there in 1929, read the layers that remained and proved that Africans, ancestors of the Shona, had built the city in the Middle Ages. Even so, in the 1960s and 1970s Rhodesia's white-minority government leaned on archaeologists to deny it. Paul Sinclair, an archaeologist, reported being threatened with losing his job for saying in public that Black Africans built Great Zimbabwe.

greek-alphabet-and-the-gift-of-vowels.context_blurb:
Around the early 700s BC, Greek traders borrowed a set of letters from the Phoenicians, the seafaring merchants of the eastern Mediterranean. The Phoenicians had been writing for centuries, but their script had a gap, and the Greeks turned that gap into one of history's great inventions. Nearly every alphabet across Europe and the Americas descends from what they did next.

The Phoenicians named each letter after an everyday thing you could point to. Their first letter, aleph, was the word for an ox, and their second, bet, the word for a house, so when the Greeks turned those names into alpha and beta, the word alphabet came to mean, quite literally, ox-house.

Phoenician writing showed only consonants, and a reader had to supply the vowel sounds from memory and context. That suited Phoenician, but Greek written that way would have been hopelessly unclear. So the Greeks took spare Phoenician letters for sounds their own tongue did not use and turned them into vowels, writing down every vowel for the first time and creating the first true alphabet. Aleph became alpha, and the letter he became epsilon. The Etruscans borrowed the Greek letters, the Romans borrowed from the Etruscans, and the Latin letters you are reading now are their heirs.

greek-architecture-doric-ionic-corinthia.context_blurb:
Between the 600s and the 400s BC, Greek architects worked out three orders, or styles, of column: the plain, sturdy Doric of mainland Greece, the slender Ionic with its spiral scrolls from the cities of Asia Minor, and the richly carved Corinthian, the newest of the three. The Romans copied all of them, which is why banks, courthouses and museums around the world still look like Greek temples.

Sometimes Greek builders did without columns altogether. On the south porch of the Erechtheion, on the Acropolis of Athens, the roof sits on the heads of six stone women, the Caryatids, who stand in carved robes and serve as the porch's columns. They are the most famous figures ever used to hold up a building.

The Corinthian capital, crowned with curling leaves, comes with its own legend, which the Roman writer Vitruvius passed on. A young girl of Corinth died, and her nurse left a basket of the child's toys on the grave, with a square roof tile laid on top as a lid. An acanthus plant sprouted beneath the basket, and the heavy tile bent its leaves so that they curled outward, and when the sculptor Callimachus passed by and saw them, he carved that shape into the first Corinthian capital.

greek-fire.context_blurb:
After the western Roman Empire fell, the Byzantine Empire ruled on from Constantinople, and around 672 it gained a terrifying new weapon. A Syrian engineer named Kallinikos is said to have brought the secret with him when he fled to the empire. Sprayed from siphons on the prows of warships, it saved the capital from huge Arab fleets in 677 and 717.

History knows this weapon as Greek fire: a sticky liquid flame that kept burning even on the surface of the sea, so that sailors could not splash it out, and it burned enemy wooden fleets to ash. The memory of those burning ships warned enemies for centuries against attacking the city by sea.

The emperors guarded the recipe on pain of death. In the 900s Emperor Constantine VII told his son, the future emperor, that the secret had come from an angel, who showed it to Constantine the Great, and that no foreigner must ever learn it. The secret was kept so well that the formula was eventually lost, and it is still not fully known today. Scholars guess at naphtha, quicklime and sulphur, but no chemist has ever fully rebuilt it.

greek-mythology-the-twelve-olympians.context_blurb:
The ancient Greeks had no single holy book and no single priesthood, but they shared a great body of stories about their gods, a royal family who quarrelled, feasted and meddled in human lives. Poets from Homer and Hesiod to the playwrights of Athens told their tales, and the Romans later took them over under Latin names.

The Greeks set the gods' palace on Mount Olympus, a real mountain in northern Greece whose summit, at about 2,917 metres, is the highest in the country. Its master was Zeus, king of the gods, who flung thunderbolts down from the sky at anyone who defied him. His children arrived in strange ways. Zeus had swallowed the Titaness Metis while she was pregnant, so when he later suffered a splitting headache and the smith-god Hephaestus split his skull with an axe, Athena sprang out fully grown, wearing armour and shouting a war-cry.

The gods competed for human favour. When Athena and Poseidon both wanted a new city named for them, Poseidon struck the Acropolis rock and brought forth a spring of salt water, but Athena gave the first olive tree, and the people chose her gift and named their city Athens. The olive became the city's wealth. Poseidon, called the Earth-Shaker because the Greeks blamed him for earthquakes, ruled the sea. He was also the god of horses, and myth says he made the first horse out of the white foam that tops the breaking waves. Athena carried the aegis, a goatskin shield. Its centrepiece was Medusa's head, crowned with snakes, which the hero Perseus had cut off and given to her.

The three ruling brothers won their thrones together. When Zeus freed the one-eyed Cyclopes, the grateful smiths forged a weapon for each brother, and for Hades, lord of the dead, they made a helmet that turned whoever wore it invisible, the Helm of Darkness. After they overthrew the Titans, Zeus, Poseidon and Hades did not fight over the world; they drew lots, and Zeus won the sky, Poseidon the sea and Hades the underworld. Hephaestus, the lame smith of the gods, built golden handmaidens to help in his forge, and they could think, speak and move by themselves, which is why they are often called the first robots in literature.

The family's past was violent. Their father Cronus, warned that one of his children would overthrow him, swallowed each baby at birth, until Rhea hid the newborn Zeus and fed Cronus a stone swaddled in a baby's blanket instead. The grown Zeus forced his father to vomit up his brothers, his sisters and the stone, which the Greeks set up at Delphi as the Omphalos, the navel of the world. The Greeks honoured twelve chief gods, the Dodekatheon, but no list was official: some cities and poets gave the twelfth seat to Hestia, goddess of the hearth, and others to Dionysus, god of wine. Hades was never one of the Twelve, because his kingdom lay below, not on Olympus. At Olympia the sculptor Phidias made a seated Zeus of gold and ivory, some 12 metres tall and one of the Seven Wonders, and the geographer Strabo wrote that if the god ever stood up he would burst through the temple roof.

greek-myths-and-heroes-heracles-theseus-.context_blurb:
In Greek myth, the age of heroes came between the age of the gods and the Trojan War. Heroes like Heracles, Theseus and Perseus, often sons of gods, fought monsters, outwitted kings and founded cities. Their stories were already old when the poets wrote them down, they have been retold ever since, and many of them turn on brains as much as muscle.

For his first labour, Heracles faced the Nemean lion, whose golden hide no arrow or blade could pierce, so he wrestled it and choked it to death with his bare arms. He wore its pelt ever after as armour. Athens, meanwhile, had to ship seven young men and seven young women to Crete as tribute, to be fed to the Minotaur in the Labyrinth. Prince Theseus put himself forward as one of the fourteen, planning to kill the monster and end the tribute for good. On Crete, King Minos's daughter Ariadne fell in love with him. She gave him a ball of thread to tie at the entrance and unwind as he went, so he could follow it back out, and that clue of thread is why a clue still means something that leads you to an answer.

Another labour was the Lernaean Hydra, which grew two heads for every one Heracles cut off. So his nephew Iolaus seared each neck-stump with a blazing brand the moment its head fell, and no new heads could grow. Heracles buried the one immortal head under a heavy rock. Perseus began life under a curse. An oracle warned Acrisius, king of Argos, that a grandson of his would kill him, so he shut his daughter Danae in a bronze chamber. Zeus reached her anyway, coming to her as golden rain streaming in through the roof, and she bore Perseus. Grown up, Perseus was sent for the head of Medusa, the Gorgon whose face turned onlookers to stone. Athena showed him how to fight her safely: he looked only at her reflection in his polished bronze shield, so he never met her gaze. Another escape ended in disaster. Daedalus made wings of feathers and wax so that he and his son Icarus could fly away from Crete, but Icarus soared too near the sun, its heat melted the wax, and the feathers came loose. He plunged into the sea that still bears his name.

Ordered to clean King Augeas's filthy stables, home to more than a thousand cattle, before the day was out, Heracles turned the rivers Alpheus and Peneus from their courses and sent them flooding through the yard. King Eurystheus refused to count that labour, because the rivers had done the work. On his way to Medusa, Perseus needed directions from the Graeae, three ancient sisters who shared one eye and one tooth, so he snatched their eye as it passed between them and kept it until they told him the way. Theseus's homecoming turned to grief. He had promised his father, King Aegeus, to hoist a white sail if he lived and leave the black one if he died, but in the joy of victory the promise slipped his mind. Seeing the black sail, Aegeus believed his son was dead and flung himself from the cliffs into the sea, which is why it is called the Aegean.

To win the golden apples, Heracles took the sky on his own shoulders while the Titan Atlas went to pick them. When Atlas refused to take the weight back, Heracles pretended to agree, asking him only to hold it for a moment while he cushioned his shoulders. Then he picked up the apples and walked away. The Minotaur itself had a secret. Minotaur is only a nickname, the Bull of Minos; the creature's own name was Asterion, which means the starry one. And Perseus could not outrun the prophecy. Years later, at athletic games in Larissa, a discus he threw veered off course and struck an old man in the crowd, who turned out to be his grandfather Acrisius. The oracle had come true by pure accident.

greek-natural-philosophy-the-first-searc.context_blurb:
In the 500s BC, in Greek cities on the coast of what is now western Turkey, a few thinkers began to explain nature without stories about the gods, searching instead for natural causes they could reason about. One thinker of Miletus said everything is made of water; others proposed different stuff, or hidden forces. Every later Greek philosopher argued with them.

The boldest answer came from Leucippus and his pupil Democritus. Cut a lump of anything into halves, and the halves into halves, they argued, and at last you must reach a piece too small to divide. They called it atomos, from a, not, and tomos, cut, so the word means uncuttable, and our word atom is their word handed down. Chemists showed some 2,400 years later that matter really is built of tiny particles.

Democritus also asked what our senses truly tell us. Sweetness, bitterness, heat and colour, he taught, are only the way arrangements of atoms affect us. In a fragment that survives, he says that sweet and bitter exist only by custom, and that the only real things are atoms and the void, the empty space they move through. Without that emptiness, he reasoned, the atoms would have nowhere to move.

greek-theater-tragedy-and-comedy-sophocl.context_blurb:
Western drama was born in Athens in the 400s BC, during the city's great age of democracy. Plays were part of religious festivals, and thousands of citizens sat on open-air hillsides to watch tragedies about kings and curses, and comedies that mocked the city's own politicians. Two and a half thousand years later, theatre still speaks their language.

The first actor was Thespis of Athens, who around 534 BC left the chorus and spoke lines alone, in character, and actors are still called thespians after him. The winner of the early contests is said to have received a goat, and tragedy, tragoidia in Greek, joins tragos, a goat, with oide, a song: the goat-song. Every actor hid behind a mask of stiffened linen with a huge painted face that could be read from the back rows. Each mask's mouth flared wide open like a megaphone, throwing the actor's voice out across the vast open-air audience.

The great contest was the City Dionysia, a spring festival in honour of Dionysus, god of wine, where three poets each staged three tragedies and a rowdy satyr play, and judges picked by lot named the winner. Its home was the Theater of Dionysus, cut into the Acropolis on its southern slope so that its curving tiers of seats rose up the hillside, holding some 16,000 people at its height. At its heart lay the orchestra, a level circle of ground for the chorus's singing and dancing, and the word meant simply the dancing place, from the Greek verb to dance.

Across its front row stood 67 marble thrones carved with the names of honoured men, and the grandest, in the very centre, belonged to the priest of Dionysus. Early tragedy allowed only two actors at once, the number Aeschylus used. Sophocles, author of Oedipus the King and Antigone, added a third actor, which made three-way confrontations possible, and he pioneered painted scenery as well. When the young Sophocles first challenged the old master Aeschylus in 468 BC, feelings ran so high that, instead of the usual judges drawn by lot, the general Cimon and his fellow commanders were called in to decide, and Sophocles won.

In Oedipus the King, Oedipus hunts for the criminal whose deed has cursed his city and discovers that he himself killed his father and married his mother, a moment of recognition that Aristotle praised as the perfect tragic reversal. When a plot grew hopelessly tangled, some poets cheated. Stagehands used a crane, the mechane, to swing an actor playing a god over the stage to set everything right, and that trick gave us deus ex machina, Latin for the god from the machine. Comedy was harsher still. Aristophanes made Socrates a laughing-stock in The Clouds of 423 BC, showing him as a windbag who trained young men to cheat their creditors, and at his trial years later Socrates complained that the comedy had poisoned the jurors' minds against him.

greek-war-of-independence.context_blurb:
In 1821 the Greeks rose against the Ottoman Empire, which had ruled them for about four centuries. Their war lasted nearly a decade, with massacres on both sides, and educated Europeans raised on Homer flocked to help them, a movement called Philhellenism. In 1832 Greece was recognised as an independent state, the first new nation of its kind in nineteenth-century Europe.

The most famous volunteer was Lord Byron, the best-known poet in Europe, who gave the Greek cause his fortune. In 1824 he reached Missolonghi, a Greek town under siege, hoping to die as a soldier, yet he never fought a real battle. He fell ill with a fever at 36, and his own doctors, convinced that bloodletting would cure him, bled him again and again with lancet and leeches until he was too weak to recover. His reported last words were that he must sleep now.

The war was decided at sea. On 20 October 1827 an allied fleet of British, French and Russian warships, led by Admiral Edward Codrington of Britain, sailed into the bay of Navarino, where the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet lay at anchor, meaning only to frighten it. Then a British boat rowed over to stop an Ottoman crew from lighting a fireship, a quarrel broke out, a single musket shot rang out, and the anchored fleets erupted into point-blank battle. When the smoke cleared, some sixty Ottoman ships had been sunk or set ablaze, in the last great battle fought entirely by wooden sailing ships.

gregorian-chant-and-medieval-sacred-musi.context_blurb:
Gregorian chant is the single-line, unaccompanied Latin singing of the medieval Western Church. It is named after Pope Gregory the Great, who ruled from 590 to 604 and was later credited with gathering it. For over a thousand years monks and nuns sang it through the day and night, and Western musical notation grew up to help them learn it.

Around the year 1000 Guido of Arezzo, a monk and teacher of singers, found a hymn to Saint John the Baptist, Ut queant laxis, in which each line begins a step above the previous one. He gave the six climbing notes the first syllable of each line, ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la, and with ut later changed to do, they became the do-re-mi that singers still use today.

A century after Guido, the German abbess Hildegard of Bingen, who lived from 1098 to 1179, wrote both the words and the music of the Ordo Virtutum, the earliest musical play that survives. Every Virtue in it sings, but the Devil cannot sing at all; he can only shriek and shout, because Hildegard believed that music was itself the truest way to praise God. More of her chant survives than that of any other named medieval composer.

guadalcanal-campaign.context_blurb:
Guadalcanal is a jungle island in the southern Solomon Islands, where Japan began building an airfield in 1942 to threaten Australia's supply lines. On 7 August 1942, eight months after Pearl Harbor, the US Marines landed there, opening America's first major offensive against Japan, and seized the half-built airstrip, which became Henderson Field. Six months of savage fighting on land, at sea and in the air followed.

Its official name was Operation Watchtower, but Admiral Ernest King had pushed it forward with so little equipment, even on a shoestring as he put it, that the under-supplied Marines bitterly called it Operation Shoestring. Malaria, dysentery and hunger struck them almost as hard as the enemy did.

In mid-September Lieutenant Colonel Merritt Edson, nicknamed Red Mike, and roughly 800 Raiders and paratroopers held a coral ridge south of Henderson Field. About 3,000 Japanese soldiers attacked them three nights running, and some got as far as the runway's edge, while Edson stood just behind his firing line yelling at his men to hold out one more night. They held, losing about 100 men to the enemy's 700 or more, and the survivors named the place Bloody Ridge.

gunpowder-empires-concept.context_blurb:
Historians use the phrase gunpowder empires for the giant states that rose across the Islamic world in the 1400s and 1500s: the Ottomans in Turkey and the Middle East, the Safavids in Persia and the Mughals in India. Their rulers had a weapon that changed the politics of the medieval world, and the moment it proved itself came at Constantinople in 1453.

Constantinople's Theodosian Walls had defied every attacker for a thousand years, but in 1453 Sultan Mehmed II broke them open with a giant bronze cannon, cast by the gunsmith Orban. Orban had first offered his gun to the city's own emperor, Constantine XI, who wanted it but was too poor to pay the price, so Orban took his skills to Mehmed instead. The defenders' would-be weapon brought their own walls down.

Historians argue that guns like Orban's broke the power of the castle-holding nobles, because a rebel lord's walls now fell in days and only a wealthy monarch could pay for such huge cannon, so kings could gather vast empires under their own control. The Safavid shah Abbas even tore down Iran's old fortifications and built an artillery corps that answered to him alone.

gupta-empire-india-s-golden-age.context_blurb:
The Gupta Empire ruled much of northern India from about AD 320 to 550, and Indians have long remembered it as a golden age. Its kings kept a stable gold coinage and a well-run state, and under their peace poets, astronomers, mathematicians and surgeons did work that still astonishes. Its numbers and its science later travelled west and changed the world.

The conqueror Samudragupta, nicknamed the Indian Napoleon, put himself on his gold coins, and one famous coin shows him seated and playing the veena, a kind of lute, a warrior-king who was also a musician. Around 400 Fa-Hien, a Buddhist pilgrim from China, crossed the empire on foot and marvelled that its roads were safe, that criminals were usually only fined, and that the capital, Pataliputra, had a free hospital, funded by gifts, where the poor and sick received food, shelter and medicine. Delhi's Iron Pillar, more than 7 metres of iron set up under a Gupta king some sixteen centuries ago, has stood in the open air ever since and has barely rusted at all. Aryabhata, an astronomer born near Patna in 476, was honoured when India's first satellite, launched in 1975, was given his name.

Aryabhata, writing around 499, claimed that the Earth spins and the sky only seems to turn. To those who said they would feel the motion, he answered that a man in a boat moving downstream sees the motionless riverbank slide backward, and in the same way people on the turning Earth see the fixed stars sweep westward. Indian scholars built the decimal place-value system the world now uses, and in 628 the mathematician Brahmagupta wrote the first known rules for treating zero as a true number that can be added, subtracted and multiplied. The court's greatest poet, Kalidasa, often called the Shakespeare of India, wrote The Recognition of Shakuntala, in which a curse wipes the heroine from King Dushyanta's memory until he sees the ring he once gave her. Indian surgeons were just as bold. A Sanskrit medical text of this era, the Sushruta Samhita, explains how to rebuild a lost nose: the surgeon measured the gap with a leaf, then cut a matching flap of living skin from the cheek or forehead and stitched it in place. Before operating, the book says, the patient should be given wine so that he will feel no pain.

Some secrets took modern science to unlock. In the 1990s the metallurgist R. Balasubramaniam of IIT Kanpur showed that the pillar's iron is unusually rich in phosphorus, about five times richer than modern iron, and over the centuries that phosphorus formed a skin of iron phosphate, about a twentieth of a millimetre thick, that keeps rust out. Surgeons in the Sushruta tradition closed a cut intestine by letting large black ants bite across the wound and then snipping off their bodies, so the locked jaws stayed behind as living stitches. Aryabhata gave pi as 3.1416 but called the value asanna, approaching, and scholars read that one word as a hint that no fraction or finite decimal can ever pin pi down exactly.

gutenberg-s-printing-press.context_blurb:
In the 1440s and 1450s Johannes Gutenberg, a goldsmith of Mainz in Germany, combined a farm press, a new metal for casting letters, oil-based ink and cheap rag paper into one working system. It printed pages far faster than any scribe could copy them, and within fifty years it had changed Europe.

His first great printed book was the Bible, in Latin, the work that launched the age of the printed book in the West. It is nicknamed the 42-line Bible after the lines in each column. The earliest sheets held only 40 lines, but Gutenberg then tightened the spacing to fit two more, most likely to use less of his costly paper. Each copy was priced at around thirty florins of gold, about three years' wages for a clerk: far cheaper than a hand-copied Bible, yet still a small fortune for most people. The deluxe copies were printed on vellum, a fine parchment of calfskin, and each one swallowed about 170 calfskins.

Each tiny letter was cast from type metal, a mix of lead, tin and antimony, soft enough to cast sharply and tough enough to survive thousands of pressings, and printers kept that recipe for centuries. His real secret was the matrix: a steel punch hammered a backwards letter into soft copper, and that one matrix, set in a hand mould and filled again and again with molten metal, could turn out thousands of identical copies of the same letter, each cooling in seconds. The result was speed: in about the time a single scribe needed to copy one Bible by hand, Gutenberg printed about 180.

In March 1455 the churchman Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini, the future Pope Pius II, saw sheets of the Bible at Frankfurt and wrote that the lettering was so neat and clear it could be read without glasses, the earliest eyewitness report of printing. Gutenberg did not enjoy his success. He had borrowed heavily from the Mainz businessman Johann Fust, and in November 1455 Fust sued him and won, and the ruling cost Gutenberg his press and his type. Fust carried on the business with Gutenberg's assistant Peter Schoeffer. The Bibles themselves became treasures, and sometimes victims. In 1921 the New York bookseller Gabriel Wells broke up an incomplete Gutenberg Bible and sold its pages one by one, each boxed in leather alongside an essay by a scholar, calling them Noble Fragments. The rare-book world was scandalised, but the pieces made him rich.

The press went on to shake Europe. After Martin Luther's 95 Theses of 1517, printers poured out his short German pamphlets, which sold well over half a million copies by 1525, and historians call him history's first bestselling author. By 1500, only fifty years after Gutenberg's Bible, presses in about 282 towns had produced over nine million books. Books printed before 1501 are called incunabula, from the Latin for cradle.

gutenberg-s-printing-press-and-the-print.context_blurb:
Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg, a craftsman in the Rhineland city of Mainz, built the machine that made books cheap. His Bible, finished around 1455, was the first major book printed in Europe with movable type, and within fifty years presses were running from Venice to London. He himself lost nearly everything along the way.

His breakthrough was movable metal type: he cast hundreds of small separate letters, locked them together into a page, printed it, then broke the page apart and set the same letters into the next one. One press could now do the work of a roomful of copyists. For the press itself he adapted the screw press that farmers already used to squeeze wine from grapes and oil from olives, turning its force onto a tray of inked type. A scribe with a quill might finish about one page in a day, but a single press, worked by a few men, could print about 3,600. Gutenberg's Bible is known as the 42-line Bible, because each tall column ended up with exactly that many lines after he began with fewer and squeezed in more. In 1999 the American television network A&E, counting down the people who had shaped the past thousand years, ranked Gutenberg first of all, the most influential person of the whole millennium, ahead of every king, scientist and explorer.

Gutenberg had trained as a goldsmith, and that craft taught him to melt and cast metal precisely, the very skill he needed to design a hand mould and a type metal that melted at low heat. The press printed only black text. Each buyer then hired scribes to brush in the red headings and artists to paint the decorations, so no two surviving Gutenberg Bibles look alike. Of the roughly 180 copies, the luxury ones were printed on vellum, calfskin parchment, rather than paper, and each of those used up about 170 calves' hides. Today the surviving copies are priceless, and one nearly cost a thief his life. In 1969 Vido Aras hid in Harvard's Widener Library until closing time, packed its two-volume Gutenberg Bible into a knapsack and tried to climb down the outside wall on a rope, but the 70-pound load pulled him off and he fell six stories. He survived with a fractured skull, and so did the Bible.

Gutenberg had borrowed some 1,600 guilders from the moneylender Johann Fust, and in November 1455, with the Bibles nearly done, Fust sued and won, taking the whole workshop and, with Gutenberg's foreman Peter Schöffer, half of the finished Bibles. Gutenberg was not even the first to use metal letters that could move: the Jikji, a Buddhist book printed that way at Cheongju in Korea in 1377, came some 78 years before his Bible. His true leap was a whole system that flooded a continent with books.

In 1987 one volume of the Doheny copy went under the hammer at Christie's in New York, and Maruzen, a Tokyo firm, paid about $5.4 million for it, then a record for any printed book. Experts now reckon a complete two-volume copy would fetch more than $35 million.

gutenberg-s-printing-press-c-1450.context_blurb:
In the middle of the 1400s a craftsman of Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg, put three ideas together: metal letters cast from a special alloy, an ink that would stick to them, and a press borrowed from another trade. The result printed identical pages faster than any team of scribes, and his Latin Bible was so beautiful that early readers took it for handwork. Yet the man himself remains a shadow.

Gutenberg began as a goldsmith, and that trade taught him to cut steel punches and to strike copper moulds, exactly the metalwork needed to mass-produce type. For his press he adapted the wooden screw press that Rhineland vintners turned every autumn to crush grapes, the wine press, and aimed its even pressure at a tray of inked type. The thin, watery ink of scribes beaded up on metal, so he borrowed from painters and made an ink based on oil, almost a varnish, that clung to the type. His Bible is called the 42-line Bible because he squeezed its columns from 40 lines up to 42, to save costly paper, the most expensive part of the whole job.

While the Bible took about two years, his shop paid its way by printing thousands of indulgences, slips sold by the Church that promised to cancel the punishment owed for a buyer's sins, among them the Cypriot batch of about 1454, sold to fund a crusade. Of about 180 Bibles, most were printed on paper, but a few dozen deluxe copies were printed on vellum, fine animal skin, the same costly surface monks used for their grandest books. The press printed only the black text, leaving gaps that artists filled by hand with coloured initials and red headings, so richer buyers got fancier decoration and no two copies are the same.

To make print look like a scribe's hand, the Bible's type held about 290 different characters, with capitals, small letters, shorthand marks and joined pairs of letters, far more than the alphabet's 26 letters. The work ruined him. In November 1455 his backer Johann Fust sued him before the archbishop of Mainz's court and won, carrying off the press and a share of the finished Bibles just as they were ready to sell, so Fust, not Gutenberg, took the profit. Fust went into business with Peter Schoeffer, Gutenberg's former assistant. In 1457 the two printed the Mainz Psalter, and on its last page they added a colophon, the first printed line recording who made a book and when. Gutenberg's own Bible does not carry his name at all.

Strangely, almost nothing personal of Gutenberg survives. Most of what we know of his workshop comes from one document, the court record of the lawsuit Fust brought against him, the Helmasperger Notarial Instrument, now held by Göttingen's university library. The paper that ruined him is the paper that remembers him. In 1465 Archbishop Adolf von Nassau made the poor old man a courtier, with an allowance of grain, wine and cloth free of tax, and he died in Mainz in February 1468. Not one true likeness of his face has come down to us; every famous portrait of Gutenberg was imagined long after his death.
