gutenberg-s-printing-press-c-1450.title: Gutenberg's Printing Press (C.1450)

gutenberg-the-printing-press.context_blurb:
Johannes Gutenberg, born in Mainz in Germany around 1400, spent decades quietly working on a way to make books by machine. For a thousand years Europe's scribes had copied every book by hand, so even an ordinary volume was costly. His press, finished in the 1450s, kept its basic shape for four hundred years and made books, pamphlets and arguments cheap.

Gutenberg earned his living as a goldsmith, a craft that taught him to cut, melt, cast and polish fine metal, exactly the skills his tiny letters would demand. Earlier European printers cut a whole page of text, in reverse, into a single block of wood, which could print that page and nothing else. Gutenberg's key invention was movable type: small reusable metal letters, set into a page, printed, then pulled apart and rearranged for the next page. For the press itself he rebuilt a wine press, keeping the great turning screw that had crushed grapes and using it to drive a flat plate down onto the paper. His first great book was a Latin Bible of 1,282 pages, the one book nearly every European household wanted, finished at Mainz around 1455.

A monk copying by hand finished only a handful of pages a day, and carved wooden blocks managed about 40, but one of Gutenberg's presses could print about 3,600 pages in a day. Scribes' watery ink slid off smooth metal, so he mixed a new oil-based ink that gripped the type and printed crisp, dark letters. His first pages carried 40 lines in each column, but midway through the job he tightened the spacing to fit two more, to save expensive paper, which is why the book is called the 42-line Bible.

His type metal blended lead and tin with antimony, the clever ingredient, because most metals shrink as they cool but antimony made the mix swell slightly as it set, filling the mould completely and giving every letter crisp edges. Each letter started life reversed on the end of a steel punch, which was driven into soft copper to form a matrix, and one matrix could be filled with molten metal again and again to cast thousands of identical letters. The press left blank spaces where the big capitals and chapter headings belonged, and afterwards artists painted those initials by hand in red and blue, so hardly any two surviving copies look alike.

The earliest work from his shop with a firm date is not the Bible but a batch of church pardon slips, indulgences with blanks for the buyer's name, known to exist by 22 October 1454. His backer, the rich businessman Johann Fust, had lent him about 1,600 guilders, and in 1455, as the Bibles neared completion, Fust sued, won more than 2,000 guilders and seized his entire printing shop, presses and all. Gutenberg was ruined, but the invention spread. When Martin Luther wrote his 95 Theses in 1517 for fellow scholars, printers copied them without his permission, and within about two weeks they had spread across Germany, and within two months across Europe. Historians put it bluntly: no printing press, no Reformation.

hadrian-s-wall-and-the-edges-of-empire.context_blurb:
Around AD 122 the emperor Hadrian, who travelled through every province of his empire in person, visited the far north of Roman Britain and ordered a stone wall built right across northern England, from the North Sea to the Irish Sea. Some eighty Roman miles long, with forts, milecastles and watchtowers, it marked the edge of the Roman world, guarded by soldiers drawn from every corner of the empire.

At Vindolanda, a fort on this frontier, soldiers wrote letters on thin wooden tablets in the years around AD 100, even before the Wall rose. Hundreds survived some 2,000 years in a waterlogged rubbish heap where no air could rot them. One lists a parcel sent to help a soldier through the British cold: socks, along with sandals and underpants, two pairs of each.

The tablets also show what the soldiers thought of the locals. One report scoffs that the Britons do not even get up on horseback to hurl javelins, and calls them Brittunculi, nasty little Britons, a word found nowhere else in all surviving Latin. It is a sneer from the edge of empire, preserved by accident in the mud.

hagia-sophia.context_blurb:
Hagia Sophia rises over Istanbul, the city once called Constantinople, capital of the Byzantine Empire. The emperor Justinian built it in under six years, finishing in 537, and for close to a thousand years it was the greatest church in Christendom. Since then it has been a mosque, a museum and a mosque again, and its walls hold the marks of every age.

Its Greek name means Holy Wisdom, for it was dedicated to the Wisdom of God, not to any saint called Sophia. Tradition says that when Justinian first stepped inside, he looked up at the dome and cried out to King Solomon that he had surpassed him, outbuilding the Temple of Jerusalem, the most famous building in the Bible. At the wishing column, people push a thumb into a worn hole in its bronze casing and twist their hand round, and legend says that if the thumb comes out damp, the wish will come true. The Byzantines believed the moisture was the tears of the Virgin Mary. Eight giant round panels, gold letters on black, carry Arabic calligraphy high on the walls, each about 7.5 metres across, and when people later wanted them taken down, they could not be carried out, because no door was wide enough.

The church exists because an older one burned: in January 532 a brawl between chariot-racing fans in the Hippodrome exploded into the Nika Revolt, and rioters set the old church ablaze. Justinian ordered a new one at once. Centuries later a Viking of the Varangian Guard, the emperor's Norse bodyguard, scratched runes into a marble railing of the upper gallery that roughly say Halfdan was here, and they were rediscovered only in 1964. On 29 May 1453 the young Ottoman sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople, rode straight to Hagia Sophia and that very day ordered it turned into a mosque, and a scholar climbed the pulpit to recite the Muslim declaration of faith.

Its builders, two mathematicians, Anthemius from Tralles and Isidore from Miletus, solved the problem of setting a round dome on a square hall with pendentives, curved triangles of masonry that fill the four upper corners. In 1934 Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the first president of Turkey, made the mosque a public museum, open to people of every faith, where Christian mosaics and Islamic calligraphy were shown side by side. In 2020 the Turkish government made it a working mosque once more.

Forty windows ring the base of the dome, and the light pouring through them makes it seem to float, so that Procopius, a historian of Justinian's own day, wrote that it looked as if it hung from heaven on a golden chain. That first dome was too flat. After earthquakes cracked it and its eastern half fell in 558, Isidore the Younger, nephew of the first Isidore, rebuilt it about 6 metres steeper and taller, the shape it keeps today. In one gold mosaic the Empress Zoe stands next to her husband, but she married three emperors. Whenever she remarried, the workmen cut away the previous emperor's face and fitted the new husband's in its place.

haitian-revolution-and-toussaint-louvert.context_blurb:
In the late 1700s the French colony of Saint-Domingue, the western third of the Caribbean island of Hispaniola, was the richest colony in the world: a sugar and coffee factory worked by hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans. In August 1791 they rose in the largest uprising of enslaved people the world had seen. Thirteen years later they had founded Haiti, the only nation ever born from a successful slave revolt.

Their master strategist was Toussaint Bréda, who around 1792 took the surname Louverture, French for the opening, the one who opens the way, a name said to honour his gift for breaking through enemy lines. He had worked as a coachman, never went to school and taught himself to read, and he studied the Stoic philosopher Epictetus and the political writer Machiavelli. Toussaint outfought Spanish, British and French armies, ended slavery across the island and by 1801 ruled it under the French flag.

Then Napoleon Bonaparte sent a huge army to restore French control. General Brunet, a French officer, invited Toussaint to talks in June 1802 and seized him by treachery. As he was taken aboard the ship for France, Toussaint reportedly told the men who had seized him that in overthrowing him they had cut down only the trunk of liberty's tree, which would grow back from roots that were many and deep. He died in a freezing cell at Fort de Joux in April 1803, but his officers fought on.

In May 1803 General Jean-Jacques Dessalines took the French tricolour, ripped out its white middle stripe, which stood for the white colonists, and had the blue and red joined, and tradition says his goddaughter Catherine Flon sewed them together into Haiti's own flag. On 1 January 1804 Haiti declared its independence.

The victory reshaped the map. With his army destroyed by the rebels and yellow fever, Napoleon gave up on an American empire and in 1803 sold the whole Louisiana Territory to the United States for about $15 million, doubling the size of the young country. France itself refused to recognise Haiti. In 1825 it sent warships and forced the Haitians to pay 150 million francs to the colonists who had owned them, as compensation for the slaves they had lost, a crushing independence debt that took Haiti generations to pay off.

hammurabi-s-code.context_blurb:
Hammurabi was king of Babylon, in what is now Iraq, from about 1792 to 1750 BC, and he built a small kingdom into an empire over much of Mesopotamia. Near the end of his reign he had about 282 laws carved in cuneiform on a black stone monument and set up in public, so that anyone could hear them read aloud. It is the most complete law code to survive from the ancient Near East.

Archaeologists call such a tall, carved stone pillar a stele, and Hammurabi's, more than two metres high, now stands in the Louvre in Paris. Its most famous rule is that the punishment must mirror the crime, the principle lawyers call lex talionis, the law of retaliation: Law 196 says that a man who blinds a nobleman's eye shall have his own eye blinded. In the closing words Hammurabi does not boast of war; he calls himself the shepherd who brings peace, carrying a straight staff, one of the oldest images of a just ruler.

At the top, a carving shows Hammurabi standing before the seated Shamash, the sun god and god of justice, whom any Babylonian would know by the flames that burst out of his shoulders. The laws begin with justice in court. Law 1 says that if a man accuses another of murder but cannot prove it, the accuser himself shall be killed, an early way of putting the burden of proof on the one who makes the charge. The stone had adventures of its own. In the twelfth century BC an Elamite king, most likely Shutruk-Nahhunte, carried Hammurabi's stele off to Susa, in modern Iran, as a trophy, and there a French team under Jacques de Morgan dug it up in 1901.

Many laws turned an eye for an eye into grim exactness. Under Law 230, if a builder's careless house fell and killed the owner's son, the builder's own son was put to death, an innocent child paying for his father's work. Law 218 says that if a surgeon operating with a bronze lancet killed a nobleman, the surgeon's hand was cut off, though Law 215 paid a successful surgeon ten shekels of silver. A man accused of witchcraft was thrown into the Euphrates, and if the river let him come out safe, surviving the plunge proved him innocent and his accuser was executed instead. Punishment followed rank, too. Law 202 says that a man who struck the cheek of someone above his rank was to be lashed sixty times with an ox-hide whip in front of the assembly.

Law 196 blinded the man who blinded a noble, but under Law 198 the man who put out a commoner's eye simply paid a mina of silver, and a slave's eye cost only half the slave's value. The full eye for an eye held only between equals. The law of Moses, written down later by the Hebrews, shared the eye-for-an-eye rule but treated rank very differently: in Exodus, a master who knocked out his slave's eye or tooth had to set the slave free. Hammurabi's code is older by centuries, but the Hebrew law set one standard for the whole community.

han-dynasty-the-silk-road-origins.context_blurb:
The Han dynasty ruled China for four centuries, from about 206 BC to AD 220, one of the great formative ages of Chinese history. Under the vigorous Emperor Wu the empire pushed west into Central Asia, and the trade routes later called the Silk Road opened, carrying Chinese silk as far as Rome. Han scholars, meanwhile, invented paper and an earthquake detector.

The dynasty mattered so much that its name passed to the people themselves: today well over a billion Chinese call their ethnic group the Han people. Its founder, Liu Bang, who overthrew the harsh Qin around 202 BC and became Emperor Gaozu, was born a peasant, a commoner with no royal blood at all.

In about 138 BC Zhang Qian set out westward for Emperor Wu with a party of some hundred men, hoping to win allies against the Xiongnu, nomads of the northern steppe. The Xiongnu caught him and kept him for about thirteen years, and of all who had started, just two came home: Zhang Qian himself and his loyal guide Ganfu. In 105 the court eunuch Cai Lun showed Emperor He a cheap new paper, made by beating tree bark, hemp, old rags and worn-out fishing nets into a wet pulp and pressing it flat to dry. Zhang Heng, a court scholar, unveiled the first known earthquake detector in 132: a bronze jar with eight dragons around it, a ball in each dragon's jaws. When a distant tremor reached it, a pendulum inside swung, and one dragon let its ball fall with a clang into the mouth of a bronze toad waiting beneath.

In the markets of Bactria, a Greek-influenced kingdom far to the west, Zhang Qian was amazed to find cloth and bamboo goods made in Sichuan, back home in China's southwest, proof that trading routes already connected China with far-off lands, though no Han official had ever mapped them. His report to Emperor Wu opened the official Silk Road. He also brought tales of the heavenly horses of Dayuan, a kingdom in the Ferghana Valley: tall beasts that seemed to sweat blood. Dayuan would not sell, so Emperor Wu went to war for them, the War of the Heavenly Horses of 104 and 102 BC, and his armies came home with about 3,000. Silk itself was a state secret, and smuggling silkworm eggs out of China meant death, until, as tradition tells it, monks carried the eggs past the guards inside hollow walking sticks.

Zhang Heng's machine was mocked at first. Then one day a dragon let go of its ball in Luoyang, the capital, though nobody there had felt a thing, and days later a messenger galloped in from the Long region, in Gansu, hundreds of miles away, to report an earthquake exactly where the dragon had pointed. Sima Qian, the court historian, was writing the Shiji, the first great history of China, when around 99 BC he spoke up for a beaten general and Emperor Wu condemned him to death. He chose castration and disgrace over execution so that he could live to finish his history. Far to the west, Romans craved Chinese silk. When rich Roman women paraded in see-through silk, the Senate under Emperor Tiberius answered with a ban that forbade men to wear silk at all. Gan Ying, an envoy of the general Ban Chao, set out in 97 to reach Rome itself. At the Persian Gulf, Parthian seamen, who profited from standing between the two empires, frightened him with stories of a voyage that might last two years and of sailors dying of homesickness on the way, and he turned back.

han-tang-china-astronomers-chang-an-prin.context_blurb:
The Han dynasty, from about 200 BC to AD 220, and the Tang, from the 600s to the 900s, were the two golden ages of imperial China. Their scholars and craftsmen built marvels the rest of the world took centuries to match, from earthquake detectors to printed books, and Chinese skywatchers kept records that astronomers still use.

In 132 the Han scholar Zhang Heng unveiled a bronze jar ringed by eight dragons, each holding a ball over an open-mouthed toad. When a far-off quake shook it, only one dragon let its ball fall, and the direction that dragon faced showed where the quake had struck. Later a ball fell from one dragon at Luoyang, the capital, while the city itself had felt nothing, and days afterward a rider from the west arrived to report a great earthquake at Longxi, about 800 kilometres away, just where the device had pointed. The doubters fell silent.

Under the Tang, Chinese life reached a new splendour. Their walled capital, Chang'an, today's Xi'an, where the Silk Road began in the east, held about a million people, making it the largest city on earth, and Buddhists, Daoists, Zoroastrians and Christians all worshipped there side by side. Tang printers carved whole pages into wooden blocks. In 1900 a monk opened a sealed cave near Dunhuang and found a Diamond Sutra scroll printed from such blocks and dated 868, and no older printed book with a date has ever been found. It was made nearly six centuries before Gutenberg's press.

Chinese astronomers watched the heavens closely, too. On 4 July 1054, under the Song dynasty, court skywatchers recorded a guest star bright enough to see by day for 23 days, and that exploding star left behind the Crab Nebula, still studied through telescopes. Daoist alchemists, hunting for an elixir of immortality, stumbled on gunpowder. By the 900s soldiers were packing it into a tube on a spear to spit flame and shrapnel, and historians call this fire lance the direct ancestor of the gun.

handel-messiah-and-the-hallelujah-chorus.context_blurb:
George Frideric Handel, born in Germany in 1685, the same year as Bach, spent most of his life in London and became the leading composer of Georgian Britain. His best-loved work is Messiah, an oratorio whose words, drawn from the Bible, tell of the life, death and resurrection of Jesus. It was first performed in Dublin in 1742 and in London the next year.

He started writing on 22 August 1741, and by 14 September the whole score was done, orchestra parts and all. All 259 pages of Messiah took Handel just 24 days. His friend Charles Jennens had gathered the words from the King James Bible and the Book of Common Prayer.

The most famous moment is the Hallelujah Chorus, and audiences still rise to their feet when it begins. Legend says the custom started at the London premiere when King George II stood up during the chorus, and since nobody stays seated while the king stands, the whole audience rose with him. Historians doubt the story, because there is no firm evidence the king was even there, and the earliest written mention of the custom comes from 1756.

harriet-tubman-and-the-underground-railr.context_blurb:
Harriet Tubman came into the world enslaved, on Maryland's Eastern Shore, around 1822. She escaped to freedom in Philadelphia in 1849 and then went back into the slave states again and again to lead others out along the secret network of guides and safe houses called the Underground Railroad. Armed with a pistol and a deep Christian faith, she became one of the boldest rescuers in American history.

She was born Araminta Ross, called Minty, and around 1844, when she married a free Black man named John Tubman, she took her mother's name, Harriet. As a teenager she was struck on the head by a two-pound iron weight that an overseer had flung at another enslaved person who was running away, and the cracked skull brought her seizures and sudden fits of sleep for the rest of her days. Because she led her people out of bondage as the prophet had led the Israelites out of Egypt, abolitionists called her Moses. Speaking at a women's suffrage meeting in 1896, she boasted that, unlike most conductors, she had never run her train off the track and never lost a passenger.

On the road she was as hard as iron. She carried a loaded revolver, and once a frightened man in her party wanted to turn back, which could have betrayed them all. She aimed the gun at him and told him he would be free or die. He went on, and reached Canada days later. When she reached a hiding place, the fugitives knew it was time to go by a song: she would sing the spiritual Go Down, Moses as her coded signal. On her last rescue, in 1860, her party included a baby of the Ennalls family, and to keep it from crying as slave patrols passed close by, they quieted it with paregoric, a sleeping medicine made from opium. The abolitionist John Brown, planning his 1859 raid on the arsenal at Harpers Ferry, so admired her knowledge of the routes that he called her General Tubman.

In the Civil War she served the Union as a scout and spy. In June 1863 she led three Union gunboats along the Combahee River in South Carolina, steering them around hidden Confederate mines, in a raid that freed more than 700 enslaved people and made her the first woman to lead an armed assault for the United States. Frederick Douglass, the most famous Black abolitionist, wrote to her that his own work had been done in the daylight and hers in the night, and that apart from John Brown he knew no one who had braved more danger for the enslaved. Around 1898 her old head wound caused such pain that she had a Boston surgeon open her skull, and she refused anaesthetic and bit down on a bullet, as she had seen soldiers do during amputations. Legend says she made 19 trips and freed over 300 people, but the historian Kate Clifford Larson, checking the documents, found about 13 trips and roughly 70 people freed, with 50 to 60 more escaping by following her directions. The true numbers are no less heroic.

harun-al-rashid-and-the-1001-nights.context_blurb:
Harun al-Rashid ruled the Abbasid caliphate from Baghdad from 786 to 809, in what later Muslims remembered as a golden age. His court was famous for its wealth and learning, and later storytellers made him the hero of tales in which he roams Baghdad in disguise, tales gathered into the Thousand and One Nights.

Harun traded gifts with Charlemagne, emperor of the Franks. His most astonishing present was an elephant, alive and well, called Abul-Abbas, which a Jewish envoy named Isaac shipped to Italy and then led on foot over the Alps, reaching Charlemagne at Aachen in July 802. It was the only elephant in Western Europe. Harun also sent a brass water clock that dropped a ball onto a cymbal each hour, while twelve little mechanical horsemen rode out of twelve windows and shut them behind them. The Franks thought it almost magic.

The Nights hold a surprise of their own. Aladdin and Ali Baba, the most famous stories of all, have no old Arabic manuscript. The French scholar Antoine Galland added them in the early 1700s, and he heard both tales from Hanna Diyab, a young storyteller from Syria.

hatshepsut-the-female-pharaoh.context_blurb:
Hatshepsut was an Egyptian ruler of the 1400s BC, the daughter of Pharaoh Thutmose I. After her husband died, she governed for her young stepson, Thutmose III, and then took the throne herself, reigning for about two decades as a full pharaoh. Her reign was peaceful and rich, and her temple at Deir el-Bahri, across the Nile from Thebes, is still a marvel.

Egyptian tradition held that a pharaoh was a man and must look like one, so Hatshepsut ruled as king, not as queen. In her statues and carvings she wears a man's body and the ceremonial false beard that every pharaoh wore. She took the full royal titles, too.

After her death around 1458 BC, Thutmose III had her name and image chiselled off many of her monuments and left her out of the official lists of kings, because to the Egyptians wiping out a name destroyed its owner even in the afterlife. He left the inner carvings of her temple untouched, and she was nearly forgotten until scholars read the hieroglyphs at Deir el-Bahri in the 1800s.

heian-japan-the-tale-of-genji.context_blurb:
In the Heian period, from 794 to 1185, Japan's imperial court at Heian-kyo, today's Kyoto, built one of the most refined cultures in history, devoted to poetry, beauty and manners. Court women, who were not expected to learn classical Chinese, wrote in Japan's own kana script, and one of them created a masterpiece.

Around the year 1000 a court lady we know as Murasaki Shikibu finished The Tale of Genji, the long story of the Shining Prince Genji and his loves, and because it came centuries before the European novel, scholars widely call it the world's first novel.

Even her name is a mystery. Heian manners forbade calling a person by his or her real name, and hers is lost. Shikibu came from her father's post in the Ministry of Ceremonials. Murasaki, meaning purple wisteria, was most likely given to her at court after a heroine of her own creation in the Tale, so the author ended up named after her own character.

henry-ford-and-the-assembly-line.context_blurb:
Henry Ford, a Michigan farm boy obsessed with machines, set out to build a car that ordinary farmers and factory workers could afford. His Model T appeared in 1908, and to make it cheap he kept redesigning the factory as well as the car, at his Highland Park plant near Detroit. Over nineteen years Ford sold more than fifteen million of them.

Before the moving assembly line, putting together one Model T took more than 12 hours, but once the half-built cars rode past the workers, each man doing one small task, the time fell to about an hour and a half. The line started in October 1913. From about 1914 to 1925 every Model T was painted black, because black paint dried fastest, and Ford wrote that a customer could have any colour he wanted so long as it was black. At the peak, a finished Model T came off the line every 24 seconds, and in 1925 Ford was building nearly 10,000 cars a day.

The work was mind-numbing, and in 1913 Ford's worker turnover reached about 380 percent. On 5 January 1914 he announced the five-dollar day, $5 for an eight-hour shift, more than double the old minimum, to stop men quitting and let them afford the cars they built. The full pay came with strings: Ford's Sociological Department sent inspectors into workers' homes to make sure each man drank no alcohol, kept a tidy house and rented no rooms to boarders. A man who failed lost his share of the profits for six months.

henry-hudson-later-north-american-explor.context_blurb:
For a century after Columbus, European captains searched North America for a short passage to Asia, and for the treasure that rumour placed in its interior. None found the shortcut or the gold, but between them they put much of the continent on the map, and several paid for it with their lives.

In 1540 Francisco Vázquez de Coronado led a huge Spanish army north from Mexico in search of Cibola, the fabled Seven Cities of Gold, but the first golden city turned out to be an ordinary Zuni village of mud and stone, with no gold at all. Still hungry for treasure, he trusted a captive guide nicknamed El Turco, who promised a richer kingdom, Quivira, and led the Spaniards onto the plains of what is now Kansas, where they found nothing but villages of grass huts. Pressed for the truth, El Turco admitted that his people had invented Quivira to draw the Spaniards into the wilderness to die. Coronado had him strangled and went home bankrupt.

In July 1609, near the later Fort Ticonderoga, Samuel de Champlain fired a single shot from his arquebus at three Iroquois chiefs and killed two of them at once, and the terrified warriors fled. That shot began generations of French-Iroquois enmity. In June 1611 Henry Hudson's starving crew, trapped all winter in the great Canadian bay later named after him, mutinied and set Hudson, his young son John and about seven loyal or sick men adrift in a small open boat, and they were never seen again. The French explorer La Salle, who in 1682 became the first European to follow the Mississippi by canoe all the way to the sea, later overshot the river's mouth on a voyage by sea and was stranded in Texas. In 1687 his own worn-out men, by then in open revolt, ambushed him and shot him dead.

henry-viii-the-english-reformation.context_blurb:
Henry VIII ruled England from 1509 to 1547. He came to the throne at eighteen, handsome, clever and devout, but his desperate search for a male heir tore England away from the Catholic Church and reshaped the country for good. He married six times, closed the monasteries and executed those who would not bend.

In 1521, long before the break, Henry wrote a book defending the Church's seven sacraments against Martin Luther, and a grateful Pope Leo X named him Fidei Defensor, Defender of the Faith, a title British monarchs still carry. English pupils remember what became of all six queens with a little rhyme: divorced, beheaded, died; divorced, beheaded, survived. In order, Catherine of Aragon was divorced, Anne Boleyn beheaded, Jane Seymour died after childbirth, Anne of Cleves was divorced, Catherine Howard beheaded, and Catherine Parr outlived him.

At the Blackfriars trial in 1529, Henry's first queen crossed the room, knelt before the king and told him she had always been a faithful, humble and obedient wife to him, and had never once shown him a flicker of discontent. Then she refused to accept the court at all. Henry broke with Rome, made himself head of the Church of England and married Anne Boleyn. Condemned in 1536, Anne heard that a skilled swordsman from Calais would behead her, laughed, put her hands round her throat and said she had a little neck.

Sir Thomas More, once Henry's Lord Chancellor, would not take an oath accepting the king as head of the English Church in place of the pope, and on the scaffold in 1535 he told the crowd that he died as the king's loyal servant, but God's servant first.

The deepest reason for the break lay abroad. Clement VII would not grant the annulment, partly over a point of Church law but above all because Catherine was the aunt of Charles V, the Holy Roman Emperor, whose troops had just sacked Rome, and no pope could risk angering such a man. That deadlock led to the 1534 Act of Supremacy.

herodotus-the-father-of-history.context_blurb:
Herodotus, a Greek of Halicarnassus on the coast of what is now southwestern Turkey, wrote in the 400s BC a long book, the Histories, about the great wars between the Greeks and the Persian Empire. He travelled to Egypt and Babylon, questioned people and tried to work out why events happened. That is why he is called the Father of History, though critics also called him the Father of Lies.

He named his work historie, the word that became our history, but to him it meant inquiry or investigation: asking questions and checking the answers rather than simply passing down myths. He trusted what he saw for himself over hearsay.

That habit preserved a famous clue. Pharaoh Necho II, he wrote, had sent a Phoenician crew on a three-year voyage all around Africa. The sailors claimed that as they rounded the far south heading west, the midday sun was on their right, to the north, and Herodotus refused to believe it. No Greek of his day knew that south of the equator the midday sun shines from the north, so his very disbelief makes modern historians think the voyage really happened.

hieroglyphics.context_blurb:
For more than three thousand years the ancient Egyptians carved their sacred writing on temples, tombs and monuments: hundreds of little pictures that stood for whole words, for sounds, or for hints about meaning. Scribes used quicker scripts, hieratic and later demotic, for everyday business. Then the knowledge died, and for fourteen centuries no one could read the pictures.

Greek travellers named the script hieroglyphs, Greek for sacred carvings, while the Egyptians called it the words of the gods. A pharaoh's name was always written inside an oval loop shaped like a rope tied in a ring, and Egyptologists still call that loop by the French name Napoleon's scholars gave it: a cartouche. Names mattered so much because many Egyptians believed that as long as the living still spoke or read a person's name, his or her soul would go on living in the afterlife. Writing itself was a gift of Thoth, the ibis-headed god, patron of every scribe.

The script lasted until Christianity spread through Egypt. The last dated inscription was scratched at the temple of Philae in AD 394 by Esmet-Akhom, a priest of the goddess Isis, and for some 1,400 years afterwards no one on earth could read hieroglyphs. In 1799 French troops building a fort near Rosetta dug up a broken black stone. The stone repeats a single decree of the priests three times, in hieroglyphs, in demotic and in ancient Greek, and because scholars could still read the Greek, it gave them a way in. Jean-François Champollion saw that royal names in cartouches, such as Ptolemy, had to be spelled out in sounds. As the story goes, on 14 September 1822 he burst into his brother's office shouting that he had got it, then fainted and did not recover for five days.

hildegard-of-bingen-medieval-music.context_blurb:
In the 1100s the German abbess Hildegard of Bingen was one of the most remarkable minds of the whole Middle Ages. She founded her own convent, wrote letters of advice to popes and emperors, described visions of a living light, catalogued the healing powers of plants and stones, and composed a great cycle of sung chant.

She also built a language from scratch, the Lingua Ignota, her unknown language, with its own alphabet and about a thousand invented words, possibly the first made-up language in recorded history.

Around 1151 she wrote the Ordo Virtutum, a sung morality play in which the Virtues and a human Soul face the Devil, the oldest play of its kind to survive by more than a century. All the other parts are chanted, but the Devil does not get a single melody: he can only bellow and grunt, because Hildegard held that a creature of sin could never make heavenly harmony.

hindu-arabic-numerals-and-zero.context_blurb:
The numbers we write every day began in India. Indian mathematicians worked out a way to write any number with just ten signs, letting each digit's position give its value, with a special sign, zero, to hold an empty place. Persian and Arab scholars learned the system and passed it to Europe, where Fibonacci of Pisa urged merchants to adopt it in a famous book of 1202.

Around 825 al-Khwarizmi, a Persian scholar at Baghdad's great academy, the House of Wisdom, wrote a book teaching how to calculate the Indian way. When it was translated into Latin as Algoritmi de numero Indorum, his own name turned into Algoritmi, and that is where we get algorithm, the word for any step-by-step method of solving a problem. Another of his books gave us algebra.

The empty place had its own journey. The Indians called it shunya, the void, and Arab scholars translated it as sifr, nothing. That one Arabic word split in two: through Latin and Italian it became our zero, and by a separate road it became cipher, a secret code to be cracked.

hinduism-brahma-vishnu-shiva-core-belief.context_blurb:
Hinduism is a family of religious traditions that grew up in India over some four thousand years, with no single founder and no single holy book; its scriptures range from the ancient Vedas to the Bhagavad Gita. Many Hindus see its countless gods as faces of one ultimate reality, Brahman, and hold beliefs in karma, rebirth and dharma, the duty proper to each life. Its myths are among the most vivid on earth.

Three great gods, the Trimurti, turn the endless wheel of cosmic time: the creator Brahma, the preserver Vishnu, and Shiva, the destroyer, who ends each world so that another can be born. Whenever evil grows strong, Vishnu does not send help from heaven; he takes on a body and is born on earth, in a form called an avatar, and his ten best-known avatars run from Matsya the fish to Kalki, still to come. As the avatar Rama, in the epic Ramayana, he must rescue his wife Sita from the ten-headed demon-king Ravana on the island of Lanka, and Hanuman's monkey army lays a bridge over the sea so that Rama's forces can cross. Shiva keeps a third eye in his forehead, closed except in terrible anger, and when Kamadeva, the god of love, fired an arrow of flowers at him to break his meditation, Shiva opened it and burned Kamadeva to ashes on the spot.

As Nataraja, Lord of the Dance, Shiva dances on one leg in a ring of fire, and beneath his raised foot he crushes Apasmara, the dwarf demon of ignorance. When the holy river Ganga first poured down from heaven, her torrent would have shattered the earth, so Shiva caught her in his matted hair and let her trickle gently down, which earned him the name Bearer of the Ganga. Brahma has four faces, one toward each direction, and each of his four mouths recites one of the four Vedas, the oldest Hindu scriptures, forever. The present age is a dark one, Hindus say, and Vishnu will close it by returning one final time as Kalki. Kalki, his tenth avatar, will ride in on a white horse, bearing a flaming sword, to destroy evil and open a new golden age.

Vishnu once came to the proud demon-king Bali disguised as Vamana, a dwarf, and asked only for the land he could cover in three steps. Then he grew into a cosmic giant: his first stride covered the whole earth, his second the entire sky, and for the third, with nowhere left, Bali offered his own head. When gods and demons churned the Ocean of Milk for the nectar of immortality, the first thing to rise was Halahala, a poison deadly enough to end creation, and Shiva swallowed it but kept it from going down, holding it in his throat, which turned blue and earned him the name Neelakantha. Brahma, though he made the world, has almost no temples, and legend explains that his consort, angry that another goddess had taken her place at a ritual, cursed him so that he would not be worshipped, a curse later softened to allow worship at Pushkar alone.

The demon Hiranyakashipu won a boon that he could be killed by neither man nor beast, by day nor night, indoors nor out, so Vishnu came as Narasimha, a man-lion, and killed him at twilight on the threshold of a doorway, holding him on his lap and using only his claws. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna shows the warrior Arjuna his cosmic form, blazing like a thousand suns and devouring armies like time itself, and in 1945, watching the first atomic test, J. Robert Oppenheimer recalled the line he knew as Krishna's words that he had become Death, the destroyer of worlds. In the Sanskrit, Krishna names himself Time.

hippocrates-and-the-hippocratic-oath.context_blurb:
Hippocrates lived on the Greek island of Kos in the 400s BC and is remembered as the father of medicine. He taught that disease has natural causes, not angry gods, and that a doctor must observe carefully, keep honest records and, at the very least, not make things worse. A whole library of writings, the Hippocratic Corpus, was gathered under his name.

The most famous is the oath young doctors swore. For all his natural medicine, the Hippocratic Oath opens by swearing by Apollo the Healer, then by Asclepius, god of medicine, by Hygieia and Panacea, and by all the gods and goddesses. Doctors still swear updated versions today.

Many people are sure the oath includes the Latin rule primum non nocere, first, do no harm. Yet scholars who searched the ancient text found that the phrase is not in it at all. The closest real Hippocratic line, in a book called Epidemics, tells doctors to help the patient or at least not to harm him, and the Latin slogan has been traced back only to the 1800s.

hiroshima-and-nagasaki.context_blurb:
In August 1945, in the last days of the Second World War, the United States dropped the first atomic bombs ever used in war on two Japanese cities, Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Tens of thousands died in an instant and many more later from burns and radiation. Within a week Japan had given up, and people have argued about the decision ever since.

On 6 August the B-29 Enola Gay, named by its pilot, Colonel Paul Tibbets, after his mother, dropped a uranium bomb on Hiroshima at 8:15 in the morning. The crews nicknamed the two bombs Little Boy, the uranium bomb for Hiroshima, and Fat Man, the heavier, rounder plutonium bomb dropped on Nagasaki three days later. On 15 August Emperor Hirohito spoke on the radio, asking his people to endure the unendurable, and the shock for millions was that most Japanese had never before heard the emperor speak. He never used the word surrender. The suffering went on for years. Sadako Sasaki was two when the Hiroshima bomb fell and twelve when leukaemia struck her, and because legend says that whoever folds a thousand paper cranes is granted a wish, she folded more than 1,300 before she died in 1955.

Within a mile of the hypocentre nearly every building fell. Yet one ruin, the A-Bomb Dome as it is known today, still stood with its outer walls and the bare skeleton of its dome, because the bomb exploded almost directly overhead and the blast pressed straight down through it rather than shoving it over. Everyone inside died. At a bank, the flash bleached the pale stone steps lighter, except for one dark patch where a person had been sitting, whose body shielded the stone in the instant of death. The steps are now in Hiroshima's Peace Memorial Museum. Nagasaki was never the first choice for the second bomb. On 9 August smoke and haze hid the city of Kokura through three bombing runs, so the crew flew on to Nagasaki, a near miss that writers have since called the luck of Kokura. The engineer Tsutomu Yamaguchi, burned in Hiroshima on a work trip, went home to Nagasaki and was back at work on 9 August, telling a doubtful supervisor about the Hiroshima explosion, when the second bomb went off. He survived both.

Nagasaki's bomber, Bockscar, nearly did not make it back: a stuck pump had locked away hundreds of gallons of fuel, and the long wait over Kokura had burned much of the rest. When it thumped down on Okinawa, the flight engineer reckoned there was under five minutes' worth of fuel left in the tanks. On the night of 14 August, young army officers who wanted to fight on broke into the Imperial Palace grounds. They were hunting for the phonograph discs on which the emperor had recorded his surrender speech, but palace staff hid them, the coup failed, and the broadcast went out. In Nagasaki, the old heart of Japanese Christianity, the bomb burst only some 500 metres from Urakami Cathedral, killing about 8,500 of its 12,000 worshippers. One of its bells came out of the rubble whole, and believers hung it from a log and rang it for Mass on Christmas Eve 1945.

Behind the decision lay a dreaded alternative. The Americans were planning Operation Downfall, an invasion of Japan itself, and on Okinawa roughly 35 percent of the Americans engaged had become casualties. Truman told his advisers he hoped the invasion would not turn into an Okinawa stretching from one end of Japan to the other. Forecasts of the cost ranged from tens of thousands of American dead to Truman's later figure of up to a million casualties. Historians still argue over what forced Japan to give up, and many point to a second blow on 8 August, when the Soviet Union declared war and sent over a million troops into Japanese-held Manchuria. Some, like Ward Wilson, call the Soviet attack the bigger shock; others give the bombs first place.

hitler-s-rise-to-power.context_blurb:
Adolf Hitler, an Austrian-born lance corporal of the First World War, entered German politics in the bitter chaos after Germany's defeat in 1918. He led the Nazi Party, which preached hatred of Jews and dreams of conquest. In 1923 he tried to seize power by force and failed; ten years later he took it through the openings of a democracy, and destroyed that democracy within months.

On the night of 8 November 1923 Hitler burst into a crowded Munich beer hall with about 600 armed SA men behind him, jumped on a chair and silenced the crowd by shooting a pistol into the ceiling, yelling that the national revolution had begun. The Beer Hall Putsch collapsed within a day. Jailed in Landsberg prison in 1924, Hitler dictated his ideas to his devoted fellow prisoner Rudolf Hess, and the result was Mein Kampf, My Struggle, the Nazi playbook.

Ten years later, on 30 January 1933, Hitler was named chancellor of Germany. That night columns of SA and SS men, tens of thousands strong, paraded through Berlin holding flaming torches, a sight that has stood ever since for a democracy lighting the way for its own destroyer. Four weeks later the Reichstag, Germany's parliament, caught fire. Police caught a 24-year-old Dutch bricklayer, Marinus van der Lubbe, a former communist, inside the burning building, and he confessed to setting the fire alone.

The movement's rituals grew out of 1923. When some 2,000 Nazis marched through Munich the day after the beer hall, police at the Feldherrnhalle opened fire and sixteen marchers died. A banner drenched in their blood became the movement's holiest relic, the Blood Flag, and every new SA and SS flag was consecrated by being touched to it. In the same gunfire Hermann Göring was shot in the groin, and the morphine he was given for the pain left him addicted for the rest of his life. The fire of 1933 gave Hitler his chance. Within a day Hindenburg, at Hitler's urging, signed the Reichstag Fire Decree, which cancelled free speech, a free press, the right of assembly and the privacy of letters. Within days the police arrested thousands of Communists, among them Communist deputies of the Reichstag, before the March election.

How had a failed rioter come so far? After 1923 Hitler decided that guns and barricades had failed him and that he would seize power legally instead, through elections, using democracy to destroy it from the inside. He never won a majority. But when the Great Depression threw millions of Germans out of work, the Nazi vote leapt from about 800,000 in 1928 to about 14 million in July 1932, making them the largest party in parliament.

Even then, voters did not hand him the country. With the Nazis at about 37 percent and short of a majority, the former chancellor Franz von Papen struck a backroom deal and persuaded the aged President Hindenburg that Hitler could be kept on a leash, a harmless puppet in their hands, with only three Nazis in a cabinet of eleven. Papen made himself vice-chancellor. On 23 March 1933, with SA and SS men packing the hall, the Reichstag voted on the Enabling Act. The Act let Hitler make his own laws without parliament, and he won the Catholic Centre Party's votes by promising to protect the Church, a promise he soon broke. One man stood up to him: the Social Democrat leader Otto Wels, who told Hitler that freedom and life could be taken from them, but not their honour, and his 94 deputies cast the only votes against. It was the last free speech in the German parliament for twelve years.

homer-and-the-trojan-war-iliad-and-odyss.context_blurb:
The Iliad and the Odyssey, long poems credited to a poet named Homer and written down perhaps in the 700s BC, are the oldest great works of Western literature. The Iliad tells of the Greek siege of Troy, a city in what is now northwest Turkey; the Odyssey follows the hero Odysseus on his ten-year voyage home.

When Polyphemus, a one-eyed giant, shut Odysseus and his men in his cave, Odysseus told the giant his name was Nobody, so when the blinded Cyclops roared for help, crying that Nobody was killing him, the other Cyclopes shrugged and went away. Determined to hear the deadly song of the Sirens and live, he stopped his sailors' ears with beeswax and had them bind him upright to the mast, with orders to tie him tighter if he begged for release. When he finally reached Ithaca after twenty years, disguised as a beggar, the first to know him was his old hunting hound Argos, lying on a dung heap, who wagged his tail one last time and died.

After ten years of war, the Greeks pretended to sail home and left on the beach a huge wooden horse, hollow inside, which the Trojans hauled within their walls, and that night the warriors hidden in it climbed out and opened the gates. Sailing home, Odysseus had to pass between the whirlpool Charybdis and Scylla, a many-headed monster on a cliff, and he steered close to Scylla, who snatched six of his men, one in each of her mouths. In the Iliad, before the city fell, the Trojan prince Hector bid farewell to his wife at the gate. When he reached for their baby son, Astyanax, the child shrank back screaming, terrified of his father's bronze helmet and its nodding crest of horsehair, so Hector laughed, set the helmet on the ground and kissed him.

Back home, when his old nurse Eurycleia washed the disguised stranger's feet, she felt the scar a wild boar's tusk had torn in his leg when he was a boy, and she nearly cried out his name. Then came the contest of the great bow that only Odysseus could draw: every suitor failed even to string it, but the ragged beggar strung it as easily as a singer strings a lyre and shot an arrow through a whole row of axe-heads before turning the bow on the suitors. The Iliad, meanwhile, is the story of Achilles, the greatest Greek warrior, who sulked in his tent after a quarrel. When his dearest friend Patroclus, fighting in Achilles' own armour, was struck down by Apollo and killed by Hector, Achilles poured ashes over his head and lay face-down in the dust, then vowed to kill Hector.

The Iliad opens on a single word, menis, meaning the rage of Achilles. Everywhere else Homer saves that word for the wrath of the immortal gods, so by using it for a man's anger he makes Achilles' rage seem almost more than human. Yet Homer's Achilles is no invulnerable superman. In Book 21 the Trojan Asteropaios grazes Achilles' forearm with a spear, and dark blood gushes out. Some famous lines are not Homer's at all. The line about Helen's face launching a thousand ships was written by Christopher Marlowe for Doctor Faustus, his English play about a scholar who trades his soul to the Devil.

The famous weak spot comes from a later legend, first told by the Roman poet Statius around AD 90: his mother dipped the baby Achilles in a magic river, holding him by the heel, so the heel was the one place Paris's arrow could kill him. Nor does the Iliad tell the whole ten-year war: it covers only about fifty days near the end and closes with Hector's funeral, before the wooden horse ever appears. Homer's stock phrases, the wine-dark sea, rosy-fingered Dawn, swift-footed Achilles, led the scholar Milman Parry to argue that the epics were sung aloud from memory, generation after generation, long before anyone wrote them down. Heinrich Schliemann, a businessman convinced the Iliad was history, dug into the mound of Hisarlik in the 1870s and found the buried city where Homer set Troy. Then, at Mycenae in Greece, he raised a gold funeral mask from a grave and, as the story goes, announced that he had gazed upon the face of Agamemnon. Scholars now date the mask centuries before any Trojan War.

homer-s-epics-iliad-and-odyssey.context_blurb:
Two great poems stand at the start of Western literature: the Iliad, about the Greek siege of Troy, and the Odyssey, about the hero Odysseus and his ten-year struggle to get home. The Greeks credited both to a poet named Homer. For a thousand years Greek children learned to read from them, and Virgil, Dante, Milton and Joyce all drew on them.

After ten years of siege, Odysseus devised a trick: the Greeks set fire to their tents and put to sea, pretending to give up. They left behind a huge wooden horse, hollow inside; the Trojans dragged it through their walls, and after dark the warriors hidden in its belly climbed down and unbarred the gates. On the voyage home, when the man-eating Cyclops Polyphemus penned the Greeks in his cave, Odysseus gave his name as Nobody, Outis in Greek, so that when he blinded the giant, Polyphemus could only howl to his neighbours that Nobody was hurting him, and they left him alone. Next morning Polyphemus guarded the doorway, running his hands over each ram's woolly back as the flock went out, but Odysseus and his men hung underneath the animals, gripping their bellies, and passed out unnoticed.

To hear the Sirens, whose song lured sailors onto the rocks, and live, Odysseus plugged his crew's ears with beeswax and had them tie him to the mast and ignore him, binding him tighter when he begged to be freed. Between the ship-swallowing whirlpool Charybdis and the many-headed Scylla on her cliff, he steered away from the whirlpool, and Scylla's heads plucked six sailors off his deck as he watched helplessly.

At home in Ithaca, over a hundred suitors had moved into his palace and pressed his wife, Penelope, to marry one of them. She promised to choose once she had finished weaving a funeral cloth. By day she worked at the loom where all could see, but every night she secretly unravelled the day's work, and she kept the trick going for about three years until a servant betrayed her. When Odysseus returned in a beggar's rags, the first to know him was his old dog Argos, lying on a dung heap, who pricked his ears, wagged his tail and died. Then Odysseus set the suitors a contest with his own great bow, which none of them could so much as bend far enough to fit the string, and he strung it with ease and sent a single arrow through twelve axe-heads in a row. Then he turned the bow on the suitors.

The two poems run to nearly 28,000 lines of strict verse, yet for centuries no one wrote them down: bards carried them entirely in memory, passing them from singer to singer, helped by stock phrases they knew by heart.

The Iliad tells only a slice of the war. It covers a few weeks of the tenth year and ends not with the horse or the sack of the city but with the burial of Hector, Troy's prince, while Troy still stands. After killing Hector, Achilles dragged the corpse through the dust and refused to give it up. Then old King Priam, Hector's father, came secretly by night into the Greek camp, alone and unarmed. He knelt before Achilles and kissed the hands that had slain his son. The two enemies wept together, and Achilles gave the body back. In the 1870s Heinrich Schliemann dug into the mound of Hisarlik in Turkey and found city upon ruined city, along with a gold hoard he called Priam's Treasure, but he had dug too deep: the gold was more than a thousand years older than the Trojan War. Still, he had found the real site of Troy.

hungarian-revolution-1956.context_blurb:
In October 1956 students and workers in Soviet-ruled Hungary rose against the Stalinist regime forced on them after 1945. A peaceful student protest in Budapest swelled within days into a national uprising that toppled the hated leaders and made the reformer Imre Nagy prime minister. Nagy announced free elections and Hungary's exit from the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact.

On 23 October a crowd of perhaps 100,000 surrounded the giant bronze statue of Stalin in Budapest, workers cut through it with blowtorches and pulled it down with a steel rope, and only his boots were left standing on the pedestal. Hungarians nicknamed the place Boots Square. Protesters also cut the communist emblem out of the middle of their flags with scissors, and the flag with a hole became the lasting symbol of the revolution.

In early November Soviet tanks rolled back into Budapest and crushed the revolt, killing thousands, while about 200,000 Hungarians fled west. Nagy took refuge in the Yugoslav embassy and came out only when he was handed a written guarantee that he could leave safely, but the Soviets seized him, and after a secret trial he was hanged in June 1958.

ibn-battuta-s-travels.context_blurb:
In 1325 Ibn Battuta, a 21-year-old Berber scholar of Islamic law, left Tangier in Morocco to make the pilgrimage to Mecca, and simply kept going. He crossed three continents, served sultans as a judge and reached as far as China and the empire of Mali. Back home, he dictated his memories to a court secretary, and the book became the Rihla, the Journey.

All told he travelled about 75,000 miles, some 120,000 kilometres, roughly three times as far as Marco Polo, and he was away from home for 24 years.

His travels were full of danger. In 1341 Delhi's sultan chose him to escort a vast gift to the emperor of China: slaves, singers, dancers, horses, cloth and swords. Near Calicut a storm wrecked his ships, and every gift was lost. Fearing what the sultan would do if he came back without the gifts, he slipped away to the Maldive Islands and served there as a qadi, a judge, for nearly two years.

ibn-battuta-the-great-muslim-traveler.context_blurb:
Ibn Battuta, born in Tangier in Morocco in 1304, set off alone at twenty-one on the pilgrimage to Mecca, meaning to return soon. Instead he wandered for nearly thirty years, through the Middle East, India, the Maldives, probably China and the empire of Mali, by camel, horse, foot and ship. He kept no diary; around 1352 to 1355 he dictated the whole story from memory to a scribe, Ibn Juzayy, and it became the Rihla, the Journey.

He covered about 75,000 miles, and since the Earth's waistline at the equator is roughly 25,000 miles, that was enough to circle the globe three times. The journey began in tears. Reaching Tunis with no companion to cheer him, he burst into bitter tears, so lonely was he, until a stranger befriended him. On a bandit-haunted stretch of the road to Mecca, so feverish he could barely sit his horse, he lashed himself to the saddle with the cloth of his turban rather than fall behind the caravan.

Later the Sultan of Delhi, Muhammad bin Tughluq, sent him to China with a vast gift for the emperor, but before he had even sailed, a storm smashed his ships in the harbour near Calicut and sank the treasure. Afraid to face the brutal sultan, he drifted to the Maldive Islands. Its rulers, desperate for a scholar who knew Arabic and Islamic law, showered him with pearls and gold and would not let his ship leave, so that he would stay as their judge.

Crossing the Sahara, he reached the rich empire of Mali, and at the court of Mansa Sulayman, brother of the famous Mansa Musa, he watched subjects grovel before the ruler, pound the earth with their elbows and throw dust and ashes over their own heads. It is the first eyewitness account of a West African kingdom by an outside traveller.

ignatius-loyola-the-jesuits.context_blurb:
Ignatius of Loyola was a proud Spanish nobleman and soldier who, after a terrible wound in 1521, gave his life to God. He went on to found the Society of Jesus, the Jesuits, approved by the pope in 1540, who became the schoolmasters of Catholic Europe and its boldest missionaries, carrying the faith to India, Japan and the Americas. He died in Rome in 1556.

Defending the fortress of Pamplona on 20 May 1521, the young soldier then called Iñigo was hit by a cannonball that shattered one of his legs and badly wounded the other, and he never soldiered again. Jesuits still mark the date as Cannonball Day. Laid up in bed, he asked for tales of knights, but the only reading in the house was a book of saints' lives and another on the life of Christ, and soon he was wondering whether he could do what Saint Francis had done.

The leg healed crooked, with a knob of bone jutting out below the knee that spoiled the line of his fashionable tight hose, so the vain ex-soldier had surgeons saw off the bone and stretch the leg straight, with no painkiller, and he never cried out. He called it butchery, and he limped for the rest of his life.

His conversion was slow. Riding on his mule, he met a Muslim traveller who insulted the Virgin Mary, and unsure whether he ought to chase the man down and kill him, he dropped the reins and let the mule choose at a fork in the road; it took the other way. In 1522 he climbed to the monastery of Montserrat and spent a whole night on watch, like a knight, at the Black Madonna's altar. At daybreak he handed his rich clothes to a poor man, put on sackcloth, and left his sword and dagger hanging by the altar as a sign that his soldiering was over.

Living for nearly a year in a cave at Manresa, fasting, unkempt and at times close to despair, he worked out the Spiritual Exercises, a course of meditations laid out stage by stage that Jesuits still guide people through on silent retreats. His friend Francis Xavier, one of the first Jesuits, carried the order east, and when he landed in Japan in 1549, no Catholic priest had ever been there. To win a hearing from Japan's lords, he brought gifts they had never seen, among them a mechanical chiming clock, a music box, spectacles and muskets. When he died in 1552 on a small island within sight of China, sailors packed his body in quicklime to strip the flesh, but months later the coffin was opened and the body was found fresh and undecayed, as if he had just died. It now lies in a glass casket in Goa, in India. In 1614, by order of the Jesuits' superior general, Xavier's right forearm, the arm said to have baptised tens of thousands, was cut off at the elbow and carried to Rome as a relic, and it is still shown there in the Gesù.

illuminated-manuscripts-book-of-kells.context_blurb:
In the centuries after Rome fell, Irish monks copied the Gospels by hand and decorated them with spirals, knotwork and strange beasts. The most famous of their books is the Book of Kells, made around the year 800 and now kept at Trinity College in Dublin. Its pages are so dense with detail that a reader can stare for an hour and still miss things.

The monks hid jokes and little creatures in the patterns. On the page devoted to the name of Christ, two cats pin down two mice nibbling a communion wafer, and an otter lies on its back holding a fish. A whole tiny zoo plays around the holy name.

Such work amazed medieval visitors. Around 1185 the travelling writer Gerald of Wales, also known as Giraldus Cambrensis, was shown a gospel book in Ireland so crowded with fine spirals and interlace that it hardly seemed human. He wrote that it seemed made by an angel rather than a man, and ever since, people have applied his words to the Book of Kells. It records his wonder, not who really painted it.

illuminated-manuscripts-book-of-kells-li.context_blurb:
Between about 700 and 800, monks in Ireland and northern England made some of the most beautiful books in history: gospel books handwritten on vellum, a fine calfskin, and blazing with giant decorated letters, interlace in red and gold, and whole pages of saints and symbolic beasts. The two greatest are the Book of Kells, now in Dublin, and the Lindisfarne Gospels, now in the British Library in London.

The Lindisfarne Gospels come from a holy island off the coast of Northumbria. Eadfrith, a monk of the island who rose to be its bishop, did all of it himself: he wrote every word and painted every picture. He became bishop in 698 and died in 721.

The Book of Kells had a narrower escape. In 1007 thieves stole it from the church at Kells for its gold and jewelled cover, and when it turned up nearly three months later, the cover had been ripped off and the pages left buried under a sod of earth. The book survived; the gold did not. To paint a yellow that glittered like real gold, its monks ground a pigment called orpiment, which is made of arsenic, so they were handling poison.

impressionism-monet-and-the-movement.context_blurb:
In the 1860s and 1870s a band of French painters, among them Berthe Morisot, Camille Pissarro, Edgar Degas, Claude Monet and Pierre-Auguste Renoir, broke with the official art world of Paris. They painted outdoors, caught shifting light with quick, loose strokes, and chose modern subjects like railway stations and boulevards over myths and battles. Mocked at first, their work is now among the most loved art on earth.

Painting outdoors was hard until the paint tube: before it, artists squeezed oil paint out of tied-off pig's bladders, pricked with a pin, which leaked, burst and dried out within days. John Goffe Rand's collapsible tin tube, patented in 1841, set them free. In Impression, Sunrise, painted in 1872, Monet let Le Havre's harbour melt into grey dawn fog. The eye goes straight to the one blazing thing in it, a little orange sun, its reflection broken into ripples on the water. When the critic Louis Leroy sneered at it in an 1874 review that dubbed the painters Impressionists, they took up the jeer and wore it proudly as the name of their movement.

Rejected by the official Salon, the rebels held their own show in April 1874 in the studio of the photographer Nadar, and while the Salon drew some 400,000 visitors, only about 3,500 came to theirs. Their society lost money and broke up that December.

Their trick was broken colour: instead of mixing a smooth tone on the palette, they laid small dabs of pure colour side by side, and the mixing happens inside the eye of whoever is looking, so the picture shimmers. From about 1912 cataracts clouded Monet's sight so badly that he could hardly tell one colour from another, so to know which paint he held, he went by the printed words on each tube's label. His pictures turned muddy red and brown until he had surgery in 1923.

inca-road-network-machu-picchu.context_blurb:
The Inca ruled an empire that stretched thousands of miles along the Andes, from today's Colombia to Chile, and they ran it without wheels, without horses and without writing. Instead they built roads over deserts and some of the highest passes on earth, kept their accounts in knotted string, and raised Machu Picchu, a royal estate on a saddle between two peaks that the Spanish never found.

Their Royal Road, the Qhapaq Ñan, ran some 40,000 kilometres across Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Argentina and Chile, about the distance around the whole Earth. Royal orders flew along it in relays: runners called chasquis waited in huts a few kilometres apart, and each sprinted one short leg flat out and handed the message on, so it could travel 240 kilometres or more in a day. As he ran up to the hut, the arriving chasqui blew a conch-shell trumpet, the pututu, so that the fresh runner was already moving at the handoff. Across deep canyons the road crossed swaying rope bridges woven from twisted mountain grass, the thin ichu, weak alone but enormously strong when hundreds of strands are braided together. Villagers still rebuild one, the Q'eswachaka, by hand every June.

Martín de Murúa, a Spanish chronicler, reported that when the emperor in his mountain palace craved ocean fish, chasquis relayed it up from the coast, some 350 to 400 kilometres, so fast that it arrived still alive. With some 12 million subjects to tax and storehouses to track, Inca record-keepers used bundles of knotted strings called quipus, a main cord hung with dozens or hundreds of knotted cords. To feed armies far from any farm, they made chuño, potatoes that keep for years, by leaving them to freeze on cold Andean nights and then stomping them underfoot by day to squeeze out the water, again and again. It was freeze-drying, centuries before electricity. At Machu Picchu, masons armed only with stone hammers, sand and bronze chisels fitted huge blocks with no mortar, so tightly that even today not even the thin blade of a knife fits into the joints of many walls. At the top of the site stands a carved stone pillar, the Intihuatana, the Hitching Post of the Sun, which casts almost no shadow at noon near the equinoxes and helped Inca astronomers track the sun's yearly path. The American explorer Hiram Bingham brought the overgrown ruins to the world's attention in 1911.

The builders had no wheeled carts, horses or oxen; their only pack animal was the llama, which carried about 30 kilograms some 20 kilometres a day, and everything else moved on human backs. At Moray, near Cusco, sunken rings of terraces drop into the earth like giant bowls, and from top to bottom the temperature changes by up to 15 degrees. With some twenty small climates in one spot, archaeologists think the Inca used Moray as a laboratory to find out which crops grew best at each height.

On a quipu, a knot's position along the cord set its value, ones, tens, hundreds and up, so a place on the cord left empty, without any knot, stood for zero. Today most quipus are unreadable, because Spanish colonists burned many as pagan objects and the spoken key that explained each one, passed from keeper to keeper, father to son, died with the knot-keepers. Scholars have catalogued more than 900, yet most remain silent.

inca-stonework-and-sacsayhuaman.context_blurb:
The Inca were among the finest stonemasons in history. In their capital, Cusco, and at the great fortress of Sacsayhuaman on the hill above it, they shaped blocks weighing many tons without iron tools, wheels or draught animals, and set them without a speck of mortar. When the Spanish arrived in the 1530s, they built churches and mansions on top of Inca foundations.

The blocks were cut to fit so precisely that even today not even a sheet of paper will slide into the joints between them. In one Cusco street, part of the old palace of the ruler Inca Roca, the famous Twelve-Angled Stone, a single green block, was carved with twelve corners, each one matched to a neighbouring stone. It locks so tightly that the Spanish could never pry it loose.

Cusco sits in earthquake country. When tremors struck, the interlocking Inca blocks shifted slightly and settled back into place, so the walls danced instead of cracking, while the newer Spanish buildings on top cracked and fell.

indian-numerals-zero-decimal-system.context_blurb:
The digits the whole world uses, nought to nine, written in columns where each place has its own value, were worked out by Indian mathematicians in the Gupta era and the centuries after. Europeans call them Arabic numerals, but Arab mathematicians called them Indian numerals, because they knew where they came from. The system reached Europe through Baghdad and Italian merchants.

Al-Khwarizmi, a Persian mathematician of the 800s, explained the Indian numerals in a book that survives in Latin as Algoritmi de numero Indorum, and the scribes' Latin version of his name became our word algorithm. The oldest written zeros survive in the Bakhshali manuscript, 70 leaves of birch bark dug up near Peshawar in 1881, where zero appears as small dots, and Oxford's carbon dating put some leaves as early as the 200s or 300s AD.

In 628 the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta explained negative numbers with an image from money, calling positive numbers fortunes and negative numbers debts, so that the product of two debts is a fortune, which is to say a minus times a minus makes a plus.

indian-ocean-trade-spread-of-indian-cult.context_blurb:
For more than two thousand years the Indian Ocean has been one of the busiest highways on earth. From early in the first millennium AD, Indian traders, Hindu priests and Buddhist monks sailed east to the coasts and islands of Southeast Asia, carrying Sanskrit, Indian gods, scripts and temple art. Kingdoms from Funan to the Khmer Empire grew out of the blend.

What made the trade possible was the monsoon, which flips direction with the seasons, blowing from India toward Southeast Asia from June to September and back again from October to March, so a sailor could ride one wind out and the other home. Borobudur, in central Java, the greatest Buddhist temple anywhere, was raised around 800 from some two million volcanic stones, and they hold together with no mortar, locked only by their shapes.

Gajah Mada, chief minister of Java's Majapahit empire, swore the Palapa Oath, vowing, as legend tells it, to eat no food flavoured with spices until the whole island chain was united under Majapahit. In Cambodia the Khmer king Suryavarman II built Angkor Wat in the 1100s as a Hindu temple to the god Vishnu, its galleries carved with scenes from the Mahabharata and Ramayana, and only later did it become Buddhist.

Historians call this spread Indianization, and they stress that no Indian army imposed it: Indian merchants settled in the ports, bringing priests and monks, and local rulers invited these holy men to court, because Indian gods, Sanskrit and ceremony made a king look grander.

indulgences-tetzel.context_blurb:
In medieval Catholic teaching, an indulgence reduced the time a soul had to spend in purgatory, the place of cleansing before heaven. By 1517 the pope was raising money to rebuild St Peter's Basilica in Rome, and Albert of Mainz, an ambitious young German churchman, ran the sale across much of Germany. His star preacher was the Dominican friar Johann Tetzel.

Tetzel set up beside parish churches and promised that an indulgence could free a dead loved one from purgatory. His sales jingle promised that as soon as a coin clinked into the coffer, a soul leapt out of purgatory.

Buyers thought every coin went to St Peter's, and Tetzel thought so too. But by a secret deal, half the German money went to repay the banker Jacob Fugger, who had lent Albert of Mainz some 20,000 guilders to buy his archbishopric. In Wittenberg the friar Martin Luther was so outraged by the selling that he wrote his Ninety-Five Theses, and the Reformation began.

indus-valley-civilization-harappa-mohenj.context_blurb:
Some 4,500 years ago a great urban civilization grew up beside the Indus River, in today's Pakistan and northwest India, flourishing at the same time as Egypt and Mesopotamia. Its cities, Harappa and Mohenjo-daro the best known, had grid streets, standard fired bricks, drains and uniform weights. Yet we cannot read its writing, and we do not know who ruled it or exactly why it faded after about 1900 BC.

Long before archaeologists dug there, local farmers, who kept finding bones and old objects in a lonely brick mound, called it in Sindhi Mohenjo-daro, the Mound of the Dead. At the heart of its raised citadel lies the Great Bath, a watertight brick pool some 12 metres long with broad stairs at both ends, the oldest public water tank yet found. Its most famous artwork is a bronze girl only about ten centimetres high, standing with a hand on her hip, chin raised and her left arm covered in bangles, known as the Dancing Girl. Children played with clay bullock carts whose wheels turned, animals with nodding heads, and a little monkey that slid down a string pulled through it.

The cities were planned in advance: their main streets ran in a strict grid, north to south and east to west, with avenues twice as wide as the side lanes. Almost every house had its own toilet, draining into covered brick sewers under the streets, the world's first city-wide sanitation system. On roughly half of their thousands of carved seals appears one creature, always facing right, a one-horned bull that scholars nickname the unicorn, though no one knows what real animal, if any, it shows.

Traders in cities hundreds of miles apart used matching stone weights shaped like little cubes, and each weight was double the one before, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and on, with no king's stamp to enforce the match. Strangest of all, unlike Egypt or Mesopotamia, these huge cities have yielded no palace, no royal tomb and not a single name of a king. At the city of Dholavira, ten large signs of white gypsum, each over a foot tall, were set into a wooden board above the north gate, and this line of writing has been nicknamed the world's oldest billboard. Nobody can read it.

An old theory held that invaders massacred Mohenjo-daro's people, and scattered skeletons were offered as proof, but the archaeologist George Dales re-examined the bones and found they bore no wounds at all. The Indus cities show almost no signs of war. One small seal shows a horned figure sitting cross-legged like a yogi among a buffalo, a rhino, a tiger and an elephant, and John Marshall, the excavator, suggested in 1931 that he was an early form of Shiva, Lord of Animals, a reading still debated. The script, some 400 signs with no Rosetta Stone to unlock it, has defeated a century of scholars, and in January 2025 the chief minister of Tamil Nadu, M. K. Stalin, offered one million US dollars to anyone who can crack it.

industrial-revolution-textiles-and-the-f.context_blurb:
The Industrial Revolution began in late eighteenth-century Britain, and the first thing it transformed was cloth. For thousands of years spinning and weaving had been slow handwork done in cottages. In about fifty years, a string of English inventors built machines that did the work of many hands, and mill owners gathered workers under one roof to run them by the clock.

In the mid-1760s James Hargreaves built the spinning jenny, a frame holding eight spindles, so one worker could spin eight threads at once where an old spinning wheel spun one. Later jennies held as many as 120. In 1771 Richard Arkwright opened Cromford Mill on the River Derwent, where a water wheel drove the machines and some 200 workers kept time by the clock instead of the daylight, and he is remembered as the Father of the Factory System.

Around 1779 Samuel Crompton crossed the spinning jenny with Arkwright's water frame, and because a mule is a cross between a horse and a donkey, his machine was called the spinning mule. It spun thread fine enough for delicate muslin.

The machines ruined many hand-workers. From 1811 men who smashed the new machines signed their threatening letters Ned Ludd, but historians say this leader almost certainly never existed; the Luddites took their name from an imaginary man. In 1812 Parliament's Frame Breaking Act made wrecking a machine punishable by death by hanging, even if no one was hurt, and at York in January 1813 fourteen Luddites were hanged. Lord Byron used his first speech in the House of Lords, in February 1812, to defend them, arguing that hunger and want, not hatred of machines, had driven the men to it.

A 1788 survey of 143 water-powered mills found that two-thirds of all the workers were children, a fact that helped push Parliament to pass the Factory Act of 1833, which banned mill work under the age of nine.
