interwar-western-breakthroughs-the-expan.context_blurb:
Between the two world wars, Western science made two discoveries that reshaped the modern world: the universe is expanding, and a humble mould can kill deadly germs. Both came from a few people who kept paying close attention, and one of them was a priest.

Returning to his cluttered London laboratory in 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that a patch of blue-green mould on one dish had wiped out the germs in a ring all around it. Before he named the germ-killing substance penicillin, after the mould Penicillium, Fleming simply called it mould juice. In 1927 the world's leading physicists gathered at the Solvay Conference in Brussels for a photograph some call the most intelligent ever taken, and the only woman in it, Marie Curie, alone among them had won the Nobel Prize in both physics and chemistry.

One October night in 1923, Edwin Hubble caught a faint star of the Andromeda nebula on a glass plate, first marked it N for nova, then realised it was a variable star whose brightness could measure distance, and scrawled VAR! in red ink, proof that Andromeda lay well beyond our own galaxy. In 1927 Georges Lemaître, a Belgian physicist ordained a Catholic priest in 1923, worked out from Einstein's own equations that the universe must be expanding, beating Edwin Hubble's measurements by two years.

At the Solvay Conference, Einstein told Lemaître that his calculations were correct but his physics was abominable, though years later he called Lemaître's idea the most beautiful explanation of creation he had ever heard. The astronomer Fred Hoyle, who favoured a rival Steady State universe and thought the idea nonsense, gave it its everyday name on BBC radio in 1949 when he called it the Big Bang.

In February 1941 a policeman, Albert Alexander, became the first patient given penicillin, and the drug was so scarce that his doctors filtered it out of his urine and injected it again. Even that was not enough; the supply ran out, and he died in March.

invasion-of-poland-and-blitzkrieg.context_blurb:
On 1 September 1939 Nazi Germany invaded Poland and began the Second World War in Europe. Britain and France declared war two days later but sent no real help, and on 17 September the Soviet Union struck from the east. Outgunned in the air and in armour, Poland fell in about five weeks, and the two invaders divided it between them.

The first shots of the war came from the Schleswig-Holstein, an elderly German battleship that had steamed into Danzig days before, dressed in flags for a supposed courtesy call. Hidden below its deck were more than 200 German marines, and at dawn its guns opened on Westerplatte, a tiny Polish base. Major Henryk Sucharski's 200 or so men had been told to hold for twelve hours, but with no help coming they beat off thirteen assaults by some 3,400 Germans and held out for seven days. The German general was so impressed that he let Sucharski keep his sabre. Overhead, Ju 87 Stuka dive-bombers howled down on their targets, because engineers had fitted them with small wind-driven sirens, called the Jericho Trumpets, purely to terrify the people below.

The little town of Wieluń had no soldiers and no anti-aircraft guns, yet from about 4:40 that first morning Stukas pounded it for hours, destroying most of its centre, beginning with the hospital. Poland did not simply collapse. On the first day, at Mokra, the Wołyńska Cavalry Brigade won a battle with the help of Armoured Train No. 53, which steamed right up to the Panzers and fired into them at point-blank range. The famous tale of Polish horsemen charging tanks with lances is a myth: at Krojanty the 18th Pomeranian Uhlans drew sabres and charged German infantry resting on foot, scattering them, until armoured cars arrived. An Italian reporter saw the dead horses afterwards, assumed they had charged tanks, and the legend was born.

In Blitzkrieg, lightning war, fast tanks punched through the lines while radios linked every unit, and the Stukas served as flying artillery, diving almost straight down to smash targets ahead of the Panzers. The invasion was built on a lie. The night before, in an operation code-named Himmler, SS men dressed in Polish uniforms faked an attack on the German radio station at Gleiwitz and left a body in Polish uniform as proof, so that Hitler could claim he was only hitting back. Then on 17 September more than 600,000 Soviet troops poured across Poland's eastern border, under the secret Molotov-Ribbentrop pact that had already split Poland in two, and Stalin's foreign minister, Vyacheslav Molotov, told the world on the radio that the Polish state had ceased to exist and the Red Army came only to protect its Ukrainians and Belarusians. On 22 September, at the captured fortress of Brest-Litovsk, the German general Guderian and the Soviet commander Krivoshein breakfasted together, and the two armies staged a joint military parade before the Germans handed the fort to the Red Army.

The Red Army took up to 450,000 Polish prisoners, and in 1940 Stalin's secret police, the NKVD, shot about 22,000 Polish officers, police and members of the educated elite at Katyn and other sites, then for decades blamed the Germans. Poland had fought back with brains, too. In July 1939, at Pyry near Warsaw, the mathematicians Henryk Zygalski, Jerzy Różycki and Marian Rejewski handed the British and French their reverse-engineered copies of the German Enigma machine and the methods to read it. That gift later powered Britain's codebreakers at Bletchley Park.

investiture-controversy-canossa-1077.context_blurb:
In the late 1000s Pope Gregory VII and the German king Henry IV, ruler of the Holy Roman Empire, fought over a question that sounds narrow but was enormous: who should appoint the bishops of Christendom, the Church or the king? Bishops ran great estates and held real power, so both men needed them loyal. The quarrel is called the Investiture Controversy.

In January 1077 Henry crossed the freezing Alps to Canossa castle in northern Italy, where the pope was staying, and for three days he stood barefoot in the snow before the gate, dressed only in rough wool, begging to be forgiven. It is the most famous penance of the Middle Ages, and Henry made it because Gregory had excommunicated him and his own nobles were threatening to depose him.

The fight centred on the ceremony that made a bishop: whoever handed the new bishop his ring, the sign of his bond to his church, and his staff, the crook-shaped crozier, showed who outranked whom. A year before Canossa, in 1076, Henry had sent a furious letter addressed not to the pope but to Hildebrand, Gregory's birth name, calling him a false monk and ordering him to come down from his throne and be damned through all the ages.

Going to Canossa came to mean humbling yourself before an enemy, and in 1872, in his own fight with the Catholic Church, the German chancellor Otto von Bismarck vowed that Germany would not go to Canossa. The story did not end at the castle gate. Within a few years Henry led an army against Rome, chased Gregory out and put a rival in his place. Gregory died in exile at Salerno in 1085, and the words later carved on his tomb have him say that he loved justice and hated wickedness, and that this was why he died in exile.

The deepest root of the quarrel lay in Gregory's own claims. In 1075 he set out the Dictatus Papae, a list of 27 sweeping statements of what a pope may do, including the power to remove an emperor, and it declared that every prince should kiss the pope's feet and no one else's. That clash of spiritual and royal power helped shape the Western idea that Church and state are separate authorities.

iron-curtain-churchill-s-fulton-speech.context_blurb:
Ten months after the war in Europe ended, in March 1946, Winston Churchill, Britain's wartime prime minister, took the stage at a small college in Fulton, Missouri, with President Harry Truman sitting behind him. The Soviet Union had been a wartime ally, and many in the West did not want to hear it called a threat.

Churchill warned that from Stettin on the Baltic to Trieste on the Adriatic an iron curtain had descended across Europe, sealing the lands under Soviet control away from the free nations of the West. The speech was titled The Sinews of Peace, but history remembers it as the Iron Curtain speech, and the phrase named the divide of the next forty years.

Churchill had given reporters printed copies of his text, but he ad-libbed past it, so stenographers in the hall had to piece some of his most quoted lines back together from their shorthand. Within two years rigged elections, purges and a communist coup in Czechoslovakia made his warning look prophetic.

iron-working-in-sub-saharan-africa-nok.context_blurb:
The Nok culture of central Nigeria, on and around the Jos Plateau, is one of the earliest iron-working cultures in Africa south of the Sahara. It flourished some 2,500 years ago and left behind striking hollow terracotta heads and figures, with elaborate hair and pierced eyes, the oldest known figure sculptures made south of the Sahara.

The culture was found by chance: in 1943 a farmer near Jos gave the British archaeologist Bernard Fagg a clay head that had served as the top of a scarecrow among his yams, and that head, named after the nearby village of Jemaa, became the first find of the lost Nok culture.

Nok artists pierced the nostrils, mouths, ears and pupils of their hollow heads, and the holes were not only for looks: when the clay was fired, they let trapped heat and steam escape so the figure did not crack. At Taruga, archaeologists found iron-smelting furnaces beside old flaked stone blades and dated the smelting to between 400 and 100 BC, which shows that the Nok skipped bronze entirely, jumping straight from stone tools to iron.

isaac-newton-and-universal-gravitation.context_blurb:
Isaac Newton, born in 1642 at Woolsthorpe, a farmhouse in Lincolnshire, became perhaps the greatest scientist who ever lived. He worked out the laws of motion, the law of gravity that binds the heavens, and the nature of light and colour, and he published his system in 1687 in the Principia. He was also a secret alchemist and a fierce, vengeful rival.

He arrived on Christmas Day, premature and tiny, and few thought he would last a week; his mother, Hannah, liked to say he could have fitted inside a quart mug. His father had died three months before. In the summer of 1665 the Great Plague, which carried off roughly one Londoner in four, closed Cambridge University, and the 22-year-old Newton went home to the farm for nearly two years. Sitting in the garden there, he watched an apple fall straight to the ground, never sideways or upward, and wondered why. His great idea was that the same invisible pull that brought the apple down was also keeping the Moon circling in its orbit, one law for the heavens and the earth.

At Woolsthorpe he blacked out his room, admitted a single narrow ray of sun through a hole in the shutter, passed it through a glass prism, and saw a band of rainbow colours spread across the far wall: white light is made of all the colours. The only first-hand account of the apple comes from his friend William Stukeley, who had it from Newton's own lips in the 1720s, and in it Newton only saw the apple drop to the earth; the cartoon apple bouncing off his head is a later embellishment. The original tree at Woolsthorpe blew down in a storm in the early 1800s, yet that very tree is still alive in the orchard, because it grew on where it fell, from its own living roots.

His law of universal gravitation is an inverse-square law: the pull weakens with the square of the distance, so two bodies twice as far apart pull on each other with only one quarter of the force, not half. As he finished the Principia, Robert Hooke publicly claimed the inverse-square idea as his own, and the furious Newton struck Hooke's name out of almost every place it appeared in the manuscript. The book nearly went unprinted, because the Royal Society had just spent all its money on an expensive illustrated book about fishes, so the astronomer Edmond Halley paid for the printing himself.

Gottfried Leibniz, a German mathematician, and Newton each claimed to have invented calculus first, and when the Royal Society, with Newton as its president, set up a committee to judge, Newton packed it with his supporters and secretly wrote its 1713 verdict himself. After the economist John Maynard Keynes bought a hoard of Newton's private papers in 1936 and found about a million words on alchemy and far more on religion, he declared that Newton was not the first of the age of reason but the last in the line of the magicians.

isaac-newton-gravity-and-motion.context_blurb:
Isaac Newton was born in Lincolnshire in 1642, the son of a farmer who died before he was born, and went to Trinity College, Cambridge, as a poor student who earned his keep by serving richer ones. Out of quiet years of private work came the laws of motion, the law of universal gravitation and a new theory of light, gathered in 1687 into his great book, the Principia.

When the plague closed Cambridge in 1665, Newton went home to Woolsthorpe and in less than two years laid the groundwork for gravity, optics and calculus, a stretch scholars call his annus mirabilis, his wonderful year. He let a single beam of sunlight pass through a triangular prism in a darkened room and watched it fan out on the wall into a broad band of every colour of the rainbow, though most people had thought white light plain and colourless.

In 1726 the elderly Newton took tea under some apple trees with his friend William Stukeley and told him that, long ago, he had seen an apple drop straight down to the earth and wondered why; the apple striking his head is later myth. The tree, a rare old variety called Flower of Kent, still stands at Woolsthorpe: when a storm blew it flat in the early 1800s, it grew on where it fell, from its own living roots. In 1668 Newton built the first telescope of its kind, using a curved, polished mirror instead of a glass lens to gather the light, because lenses smeared starlight into coloured fringes, and King Charles II was shown the new instrument.

Newton's daring leap was that the pull drawing the apple toward the Earth's centre reaches far out into space, and the very same force keeps the Moon circling the Earth, one law for heaven and earth. In the Principia he set out three laws of motion, and the third explains why a cannon jumps backward as it fires: for every action there is a reaction, equal in size and pushing the opposite way. When Edmond Halley called on him in 1684 to ask what curve a planet would trace if the Sun's pull faded with distance, Newton instantly answered: an ellipse. Asked how he knew, Newton said he had already worked it out by calculation years earlier. Then he could not find the paper and had to work it out again.

His law of gravity is an inverse-square law, so if you double your distance from the centre of the Earth, the pull falls not to one-half but to a mere quarter of its former strength. In his crucial experiment of 1666 he sent a single colour from the prism's band through another prism, and its colour stayed exactly the same, which proved that white light already contained every colour and the prism merely sorted them out. Halley paid to print the Principia because the Royal Society had wasted its budget on a lavish flop, a History of Fishes, and when the Society later fell behind on Halley's salary, it paid him in leftover copies of the fish book. When Newton and the German Gottfried Leibniz fought over who had invented calculus, the Royal Society's committee ruled for Newton in 1713, and historians later found that Newton, the Society's president, had secretly written much of its report himself.

Decades earlier Johannes Kepler had found three separate rules of planetary motion, among them that each planet travels an ellipse, and in the Principia Newton proved that all three follow automatically from his single law of gravity. The planets obey Kepler because they obey Newton. Even Newton's most famous humble saying, that he was only a boy playing with pebbles and shells on the seashore beside the great ocean of truth, is found nowhere in his own writings; it is fond tradition.

islamic-art-and-architecture-alhambra-do.context_blurb:
From the 600s onward, Islamic artists and builders created one of the richest traditions on earth, stretching from Spain to India. Because sacred Islamic art avoided pictures of people and animals, they poured their genius into geometric patterns, flowing plant designs called arabesques and the art of beautiful writing. Its great monuments range from Jerusalem's Dome of the Rock to the Alhambra in Granada.

To Muslims the Quran is the very word of God, and writing it out in the loveliest possible hand became an act of devotion, so calligraphy, beautiful writing, rose above every other art. Jerusalem's Dome of the Rock, finished around 691 under the caliph Abd al-Malik and the earliest Islamic building to survive, was raised over a bare rock that sits at its very centre, sacred to Muslims, Jews and Christians alike.

In the Alhambra, the palace of Granada's last Muslim rulers, the ceiling of the Alhambra's Hall of the Two Sisters glitters like a starry sky with muqarnas, honeycomb plasterwork of more than 5,000 tiny cells falling from a central star. The court poet Ibn Zamrak wrote verses for the walls that speak as the room itself, and in this hall the room announces that it is a garden, adorned with beauty.

In the 1890s mathematicians proved that a design repeating endlessly across a flat surface can do so in only 17 basic ways, and the Alhambra's tilemakers, working by hand centuries earlier, are famously said to have used all 17. The Dome of the Rock holds a forgery. More than a century after it was built, the caliph al-Ma'mun had Abd al-Malik's name scraped from the dedication and his own carved in. But he forgot the date, so the inscription still reads year 72 of the Islamic calendar, a year that falls a hundred years before his reign.

islamic-art-calligraphy-and-geometric-pa.context_blurb:
Islamic sacred art grew up under a strong tradition warning against images of living beings, especially in places of worship, for fear they would become idols. Instead, Muslim artists built two astonishing visual traditions: stylised Arabic writing and intricate geometric patterns drawn with compass and straightedge. In palaces and in the miniature paintings of Persian and Mughal courts, though, artists did paint people and animals.

Because the Quran is held to be God's own speech, Arabic calligraphy of its verses became the highest of all Islamic arts, and making it, or even gazing on it, counted as worship.

The geometry was startlingly advanced. On the walls of Isfahan's Darb-i Imam shrine, completed in 1453, tilemakers used just five shapes, girih tiles, to build a pattern that never repeats, a near-perfect quasicrystal tiling of the kind Roger Penrose worked out in the West some five centuries later. A Harvard student, Peter Lu, recognised it in 2007.

islamic-golden-age-algebra-optics-medici.context_blurb:
Between about the 700s and the 1200s the Islamic world, from Spain to Central Asia, enjoyed a golden age of learning. In Baghdad, Cairo, Córdoba and Bukhara, caliphs and princes paid to have Greek, Persian and Indian books hunted down and translated into Arabic, and Muslim, Christian and Jewish scholars argued over them and built on them. Europe later caught up largely by reading their work.

In Baghdad the caliph al-Ma'mun ran a great library and translation centre, the House of Wisdom, and tradition says he paid translators the weight of each finished book in gold, a detail that is famous but missing from the early records. The Persian scholar Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, born around 980 in Central Asia, had memorised the entire Quran by the age of ten and was practising as a physician in his teens.

The Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi wrote books that reached Europe in Latin, where scribes mangled his name into Algoritmi, the root of algorithm, a step-by-step procedure a computer can follow. Avicenna's Canon of Medicine, finished around 1025, remained the standard medical textbook in Islamic and Christian schools for about 600 years, until roughly 1650.

In Cairo, the scholar Ibn al-Haytham had promised al-Hakim, the feared caliph of Egypt, that he could tame the Nile's floods with a dam, then found it impossible. Knowing that failure meant death, he feigned complete madness, and he stayed safely under house arrest for years until the caliph died. Studying light, he let a tiny point of it into a closed chamber with no other light, and an upside-down image of the street outside appeared on the back wall; he called it the dark room, and in 1604 the astronomer Johannes Kepler gave such a device the Latin name of the same meaning that it still carries, camera obscura.

His experiments also overturned what Euclid and Ptolemy had taught, that beams streamed out of the eyes to see; in fact light bounces off objects into the eye. The golden age ended in 1258, when Hulagu Khan's Mongols took Baghdad, slaughtered tens of thousands and destroyed the House of Wisdom, and survivors said that so many books were thrown into the Tigris that the river ran black with ink for days.

islamic-golden-age-science-and-math.context_blurb:
From about the 700s to the 1200s the Islamic world was the most advanced scientific civilisation on earth. Its caliphs gathered Greek, Persian, Indian and Syriac learning, paid translators lavishly, and set scholars to work on medicine, chemistry, astronomy, optics and mathematics. Much of that knowledge later reached Christian Europe through the translation schools of Toledo and Palermo.

Its powerhouse, around 820, was the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, a library, a school and an observatory in one, where scholars working for the Abbasid caliphs turned foreign science into Arabic. There al-Khwarizmi wrote a book whose title contained al-jabr, which gave us algebra, but al-jabr first meant setting broken bones, the work of a bone-setter, because his method restores an equation to wholeness. Europeans also took from him the sign that holds an empty place, so that 105 is not mistaken for 15, together with its Arabic name, sifr, meaning empty, which became both cipher and zero. Astronomers carried the astrolabe, a brass disc with a movable map of the heavens that told the time and place, and its Greek name means star-taker.

Al-Khwarizmi also explained the Indian numerals, nought to nine, in a book whose Latin title, Algoritmi de numero Indorum, turned his name into the word algorithm, any step-by-step method of calculation. In Cairo, Ibn al-Haytham, known in Europe as Alhazen, studied light. He described how a dark, closed room with one tiny hole in its wall fills with an inverted image of the scene outside. His name for such a room, al-bayt al-muzlim, means the dark room, and its Latin name, camera obscura, coined by Johannes Kepler in 1604, means the same; the device is the ancestor of the camera.

Around 1020 he overturned the theory of Euclid and Ptolemy, who had taught that the eye sends out rays that reach out and feel distant objects, by proving with experiments that we see because light bounces off things and travels into the eye. Muslims also made the astrolabe serve their faith: it fixed the hours of the five daily prayers from the sun's height and pointed each worshipper toward Mecca, the direction of prayer called the qibla. In 10th-century Aleppo, Mariam al-Astrulabi built astrolabes so ingenious that she is remembered among the earliest women engineers we know by name, and a thousand years later astronomers named an asteroid, found in 1990, after her.

Ibn al-Haytham insisted that claims be tested by experiment, and he wrote that whoever seeks the truth must turn himself into an enemy of everything he reads, questioning every authority. The famous story says that when Caliph al-Hakim summoned him to dam the Nile and he saw that the river was simply too great to tame, he faked being insane to escape execution, and spent about ten years under house arrest writing his Book of Optics. The golden age ended in blood in February 1258, when Hulagu Khan's Mongols took Baghdad and wrecked the House of Wisdom, and chroniclers wrote that the Tigris ran black with the ink of all the books thrown into it.

island-hopping-strategy.context_blurb:
After Midway in 1942 turned the tide, the United States began fighting its way back across the Pacific toward Japan. Rather than capture every Japanese-held island in turn, American commanders seized only the islands they needed for airfields and bases and jumped past the strongest Japanese fortresses. The strategy was called island-hopping, or leapfrogging.

Commanders summed it up with the motto of Willie Keeler, an old-time baseball batter who placed his hits where no fielder stood: hit 'em where the fielders ain't. The bypassed garrisons, cut off from supplies and bombed from nearby airfields but never invaded, were left to wither on the vine, useless to Japan's war effort.

The offensive came in two great thrusts: General Douglas MacArthur drove up through New Guinea toward the Philippines, while Admiral Chester Nimitz's fleets crossed the open Central Pacific, taking the Gilberts, then the Marshalls, then the Marianas. Rabaul, the greatest Japanese stronghold in the South Pacific, with tens of thousands of troops, was never stormed; the Allies cut it off and bombed it, and in September 1945 they simply walked in to accept its surrender.

The lesson had been learned in blood at Tarawa in November 1943, where Marines charging the fortified islet of Betio head-on suffered over 3,000 casualties in 76 hours, so later commanders chose to go around the strong points rather than throw men straight at them.

In February 1944 carrier aircraft of Operation Hailstone destroyed some 45 ships at Truk Lagoon, the Japanese fleet's great forward base. Then the fleet simply sailed past Truk and left its garrison of some 28,000 to starve. The real prize was the Mariana Islands, Guam, Saipan and Tinian, because from there the new B-29 bombers could reach Japan itself. Leapfrogging had its surprises: some of the stranded garrisons planted gardens from seeds that submarines brought in, and survived far better than expected, though they were still useless to Japan.

italian-unification-risorgimento-garibal.context_blurb:
In 1815 Italy was not a country but a patchwork of kingdoms, duchies, papal lands and Austrian provinces, each with its own ruler and dialect. The movement that joined them into one nation is called the Risorgimento, the Resurgence. Its two great faces were the dashing soldier Giuseppe Garibaldi and the patient statesman Count Camillo di Cavour, prime minister of Piedmont-Sardinia, serving King Victor Emmanuel II.

As a young exile Garibaldi had fought for a dozen years in South America, with rebels in Brazil and Uruguay, and because he had battled on two continents, Italians called him the Hero of the Two Worlds. In 1860 he led about a thousand volunteers, the Thousand, to invade Sicily, and because they all wore red shirts, they were known as the Redshirts.

The expedition had no ships, so on the night they sailed from Quarto near Genoa, 5 May 1860, his lieutenant Nino Bixio seized two steamers, the Piemonte and the Lombardo, from the Rubattino shipping company. At Calatafimi on 15 May, as the Redshirts' uphill charge against Bourbon troops on the hilltop began to falter, Garibaldi told Bixio, as tradition has it, that here they would make Italy or die.

By October he had conquered Sicily and Naples, and when he met Victor Emmanuel II at Teano on 26 October 1860, he hailed him as King of Italy, handed over everything he had won and took no crown, retiring to the island of Caprera with no reward.

Cavour, who built unity through diplomacy, became the first prime minister of the new Kingdom of Italy in 1861 but died of malaria that June, whispering on his deathbed, it is said, that Italy was made and all was safe. When Italy became a kingdom in March 1861, its king kept his old title, Victor Emmanuel II of Piedmont-Sardinia, instead of becoming the first of Italy, and historians read that choice as a hint that Piedmont had swallowed the rest of Italy rather than joined with it as an equal.

jacques-louis-david-and-neoclassicism.context_blurb:
Jacques-Louis David, who lived from 1748 to 1825, was the leading painter of French Neoclassicism, a severe style modelled on ancient Rome. He painted for three very different masters, the French crown, the Revolution and Napoleon, and he put his talent at the service of each in turn.

In 1784 the royal government commissioned his Oath of the Horatii, three Roman brothers vowing to give their lives for Rome, a picture of loyalty the crown hoped would serve its own cause. When the Revolution came, David became a deputy in the National Convention. In January 1793 the painter who had worked for the crown cast his vote for the death of King Louis XVI, his former patron. He later served Napoleon as First Painter to the Emperor.

David turned a murder into an altarpiece. When the revolutionary leader Jean-Paul Marat was stabbed in his bath in 1793, David painted him dead in the tub with one arm hanging limp. He copied that drooping arm from Michelangelo's Pietà, the sculpture of the dead Christ lying across Mary's lap, turning the murdered man into a kind of Christ lowered from the cross. He even painted Marat's diseased skin smooth and clean.

jainism-mahavira.context_blurb:
Jainism is one of India's oldest living faiths, born some twenty-five centuries ago, in the age of early Buddhism. Its great teacher was Mahavira, whose title means Great Hero. Jains count him the twenty-fourth and last Tirthankara, or ford-maker: a soul who won full freedom from the cycle of rebirth and showed others the crossing.

At the heart of Jain life sits ahimsa, the vow to harm no living thing, and Jain monks keep it more strictly than almost anyone on Earth. As a Jain monk walks along, he brushes the path in front of him with a soft broom before each step, so that no ant is crushed beneath his foot. He wears a small cloth over his mouth, the muhpatti, so that he will not breathe in an insect, and he strains his drinking water to spare the tiny lives swimming in it.

Mahavira, born Vardhamana into a royal family, left his throne behind and in the end shed even his clothes, wandering naked for twelve and a half years. Centuries later his followers split over that very point. The Digambara, whose name means sky-clad, hold that a true monk must own nothing at all, not even a garment, and so go naked as their founder did. The other branch, the Svetambara or white-clad, dresses its monks and nuns in plain white robes.

james-madison-father-of-the-constitution.context_blurb:
James Madison of Virginia was a small, quiet, bookish man who did more than anyone else to design the United States Constitution. In the summer of 1787, delegates from the states met in Philadelphia to replace a national government that was failing, and Madison came better prepared than any of them. That is why Americans call him the Father of the Constitution.

His preparation began with books, a great many of them. From Paris, his friend Thomas Jefferson sent him two trunkfuls of books about ancient and modern leagues of states, and Madison wrote back thanking him for the "literary cargo." Madison read them to learn exactly where earlier republics had broken down.

He reached Philadelphia early with an entire new government already drafted, the Virginia Plan, which divided power among three branches that could check one another. His fellow Virginian Edmund Randolph presented it to the delegates at the end of May, and the convention hammered out the whole Constitution using Madison's draft as its starting point.

Next the states had to be persuaded to accept the new frame of government, so Madison wrote essays in its defence under the pen name Publius. His most famous reply to the fear of tyranny came in Federalist No. 51: if men were angels, he wrote, nobody would need government at all, and since they are not, the system must set ambition against ambition. He went on to serve as the fourth president.

james-watt-and-the-steam-engine.context_blurb:
James Watt was a Scottish maker of scientific instruments who, in the 1760s and 1770s, rebuilt the steam engine so thoroughly that it could drive the Industrial Revolution. Before him, steam engines were wasteful giants that did little but drain mines. After him, steam turned mills and factories and later pulled trains, and his name is printed on every light bulb in your house.

A much-loved tale, spread by his cousin Marion Campbell, says the spark came when young James sat by his aunt's fire and watched the steam from her kettle lift its lid and let it fall, over and over. The story is almost certainly a myth; Watt himself said a Dr John Robison first turned his mind to steam in 1759. The true beginning came later. In 1763, while he was repairing instruments for the professors at Glasgow's university, Watt was handed a little working model of a steam engine, built to Thomas Newcomen's older design, that would not run properly. Fixing it showed him how much heat that design threw away.

The Newcomen engine wasted its fuel in an absurd way. To pull its piston down, it squirted cold water into the cylinder to turn the steam back into water, and then it had to warm the chilled cylinder up again before every new stroke, burning most of its coal on that alone. Watt's cure was the separate condenser: the used steam was let out into a second chamber and cooled there, while the working cylinder stayed hot all the time. He patented it in 1769, and the same coal now did roughly twice the work. The idea arrived all at once during a Sunday walk in May 1765, as he crossed Glasgow Green, the city's common, and he later said the whole machine was arranged in his head before he had passed the golf-house.

Building the engine was harder than imagining it. No workshop could make a cylinder truly round, so steam hissed past the piston and the engine wheezed. The ironmaster John Wilkinson saved it by turning his machine for boring out cannon barrels onto Watt's cylinders. It cut them so true that, as his later partner boasted, a 50-inch cylinder was not out by the thickness of an old shilling anywhere.

Watt also needed a businessman. He was a nervous man who dreaded haggling, and in a letter of 1772 he admitted he would sooner stand before a loaded cannon than settle a bill or strike a bargain. So he joined Matthew Boulton, the confident owner of the Soho works outside Birmingham, who sold what Watt built. Their first engine for a paying customer started work in March 1776 at the Bloomfield Colliery in Tipton, where it pumped out the floodwater that rose in the shafts as the miners dug deeper. That same year the writer James Boswell toured Soho, and Boulton told him proudly that he sold there what all the world longed for: power. To show mill owners what an engine was worth, Watt invented the horsepower, the work one horse could do in a minute, which he fixed at lifting 33,000 pounds by one foot, and he priced each engine by the number of horses it replaced. Watt died in 1819, and in 1882 scientists gave his name to the unit that measures power, meaning how fast work gets done: the watt.

Behind the condenser lay real science. Watt's friend Joseph Black, a Glasgow professor, had found that boiling water into steam soaks up a great hidden store of heat, which he named latent heat, and that steam gives all of it back the moment it turns to water again. Chilling the steam inside the working cylinder threw that heat away on every stroke; condensing it somewhere else kept it. Watt's last great trick made the engine look after itself. In 1788 he added the centrifugal governor: two metal balls whirling on a spindle swung outward as the engine sped up and, as they rose, throttled the steam to slow it again. He borrowed the idea from the regulators of windmills, and it was among the earliest machines to correct their own behaviour.

jamestown-the-first-english-colonies.context_blurb:
Jamestown, planted on a swampy island in a Virginia river in 1607, was the first English colony in America that lasted. It began as a business venture: the Virginia Company of London sent about a hundred men across the ocean hoping for gold. They found none. They starved, fought and nearly gave up, yet on that same muddy riverbank both American self-government and American slavery began.

The colonists crossed the winter ocean in three small ships, the Susan Constant, the Godspeed and the Discovery, which left the Thames in the last weeks of 1606. The Susan Constant was the biggest, with about 71 people aboard, while the Discovery was a tiny pinnace carrying about 21. Around their new fort lived the Powhatan, a chiefdom of more than thirty tribes ruled by Wahunsenaca, whom the English called Powhatan. His young daughter Amonute had a family nickname, Pocahontas, which meant roughly the playful one, a girl full of mischief. Many colonists were gentlemen who thought digging was beneath them, so Captain John Smith told them flatly that any man who refused to work would get nothing to eat, a rule taken from the New Testament. In the Starving Time of 1609 to 1610, with Powhatan warriors penning them inside the fort, the settlers ate their horses, dogs, cats and rats, and at last boiled and chewed the leather of their boots and shoes. Only about 60 were still alive by spring.

In June 1610 the last survivors gave up, loaded their boats and headed downriver for England, but a few miles on they met a relief fleet sailing in, and its new governor, Lord De La Warr, sent them straight back to the fort. The colony survived almost by accident. What finally made it pay was tobacco: the local Virginia leaf was too harsh to sell, so in 1612 John Rolfe, a settler, planted sweeter Spanish seed from the Caribbean, a strain he named Orinoco, which fetched high prices in London. Soon colonists were growing it even in Jamestown's streets. Then in July 1619 the House of Burgesses gathered in the Jamestown church, the first assembly in English America whose members the settlers themselves had elected to make their laws. It brought together twenty-two burgesses, two from every one of eleven settlements.

Smith had arrived with a past like an adventure novel. By his own telling, he had been captured fighting the Turks in Hungary and sold as a slave, then killed his master and escaped on foot across Russia and Poland. Later historians doubt some of his tales. In 1613 the English seized Pocahontas as a hostage; she was baptized Rebecca, and she married the tobacco planter John Rolfe in April 1614, a match that brought a few years of calm called the Peace of Pocahontas. In August 1619 the English privateer White Lion reached Point Comfort with about twenty captive Angolans, people whom privateers had taken by force from a Portuguese slave ship. So the year that brought elected lawmakers to English America also brought its first enslaved Africans. In 2013 Smithsonian scientists examined the bones of a fourteen-year-old English girl they named Jane, and the chop and knife marks on her skull proved for the first time that starving colonists had eaten their dead.

The best-known Jamestown story may be the least reliable. Smith later wrote that the child Pocahontas threw herself over him to save him from execution, but many historians think the scene was really an adoption ceremony, in which Powhatan's people symbolically killed Smith and brought him back to life as a chief under Powhatan. She was a child and he was 27; there was no romance, and Smith may have written the rescue tale years later, once she was famous. In 1616 Pocahontas sailed to England as Lady Rebecca, where she found Smith alive after years of hearing he was dead. By Smith's own account she recalled how Powhatan had named him his father, and then told him bluntly that his countrymen lie a great deal. She fell ill as her ship set out for home and died at Gravesend in March 1617, about 21 years old.

jan-van-eyck-and-the-northern-renaissanc.context_blurb:
Jan van Eyck was a Flemish painter of the early 1400s who worked in the rich trading city of Bruges as court painter to the Duke of Burgundy. A generation before the Italian Renaissance reached its height, he painted merchants, their furs, their brass chandeliers and their little dogs with a realism so sharp that it stunned every artist who saw it.

His most studied painting is the Arnolfini Portrait of 1434, a double portrait of a wealthy merchant couple posed side by side in their bedroom. On the far wall hangs a small convex mirror, and in it van Eyck painted the entire room seen from the back: the couple from behind, and two more people who have just come in at the door. One of them, dressed in red, may be the painter himself, arriving as a guest or a witness. Van Eyck was proud of his work and signed it with the words "Jan van Eyck was here."

For centuries, followers of the Italian biographer Giorgio Vasari said that oil paint itself was van Eyck's invention. It was not; painters were using it already. What he did was perfect it, building each picture from many thin, see-through layers of oil glaze over a careful drawing, so that light passes into the paint, bounces off the panel underneath and glows back out. Egg tempera, the older paint, dried too fast to be layered like that, which is why his colours seem to shine like jewels lit from within.

japanese-american-internment.context_blurb:
On 19 February 1942, ten weeks after Japan bombed Pearl Harbor, President Franklin Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066. Under it the Army forced roughly 120,000 men, women and children of Japanese descent out of their West Coast homes and into ten remote camps ringed with barbed wire. None had been charged with a crime, and none was given a trial.

The removal came fast. Families got as little as two days' warning, and each could bring along only what its members were able to carry by hand, so homes, farms and shops were lost in a single weekend. Soldiers tagged people with numbers like pieces of luggage and held them first at fairgrounds and racetracks, some families in horse stalls. Tatsuro Masuda, a grocer in Oakland, had stretched a huge banner across his shop the day after Pearl Harbor reading "I AM AN AMERICAN," and in March 1942, as he was made to close the store, the photographer Dorothea Lange captured it. One young citizen, the welder Fred Korematsu, refused to go so that he could stay with his girlfriend; he underwent minor plastic surgery and took the alias Clyde Sarah, until the FBI arrested him in May 1942. Young men from these families volunteered by the thousands to fight for the country that had imprisoned their parents, and their unit, the 442nd Regimental Combat Team, took as its motto the gamblers' cry "Go For Broke," meaning bet everything you have.

What later shocked Americans most was that about two-thirds of the prisoners were American citizens, most of them born in the United States. Their soldier sons fought with startling courage. In the last weeks of the war in Italy, a German rifle grenade smashed the right arm of Lieutenant Daniel Inouye, who had already taken a bullet in the stomach. That ruined fist still clutched a live grenade of his own, so Inouye prised it out with his left hand and threw it into the German bunker. He lost the arm and later served fifty years as a senator for Hawaii.

The Supreme Court upheld Korematsu's conviction in December 1944 by six votes to three, accepting at face value the Army's plea of "military necessity." Justice Robert Jackson dissented with a famous warning: the ruling would now lie about like a loaded weapon, ready for any authority able to dress up a plausible claim of urgent need. Justice Frank Murphy, also dissenting, said the order fell into the ugly abyss of racism. That October, in the Vosges Mountains of France, the 442nd battled five days through the forest to reach the Lost Battalion, some 200 Texans cut off by the Germans, and it suffered more casualties than the number of men it saved. For its size and length of service, it became the most decorated unit in American history. On 29 April 1945, scouts of the Japanese-American 522nd Field Artillery broke open the gates of a Dachau sub-camp in Bavaria, where some 3,000 prisoners were set free, and some of those soldiers had enlisted straight out of America's own camps for Japanese families. In 1982 a federal commission concluded that the camps had served no military purpose and blamed them on race prejudice, war hysteria and the failure of political leadership.

The deepest wrongs came out slowly. In 1943 every prisoner over seventeen had to fill out a loyalty questionnaire, and one of its items demanded a renunciation of loyalty to Japan's emperor. That was a trap for the older immigrants, the Issei, because American law forbade them ever to become citizens: if they gave up Japan, they would belong to no country at all. About 12,000 who answered no were sent to the Tule Lake camp. Searching the National Archives in 1981, a lawyer and a researcher found the proof that the government had hidden a Navy report judging almost no Japanese Americans a danger, and had altered the Army's case, to win before the Supreme Court. In 1983 Judge Marilyn Hall Patel erased Korematsu's conviction in the same San Francisco courthouse, and in 1988 Congress apologized and paid $20,000 to every surviving prisoner.

japanese-art-hokusai-s-great-wave-and-wo.context_blurb:
Katsushika Hokusai was a Japanese artist who lived from 1760 to 1849 in Edo, the city we now call Tokyo. He made ukiyo-e, "pictures of the floating world": colour woodblock prints of actors, beauties and landscapes, sold cheaply to ordinary townspeople. One of his prints, a monstrous wave about to fall on three fishing boats, is now among the most copied pictures on Earth.

The print belongs to a series of views of Mount Fuji, and that is the secret of it. Framed in the hollow beneath the curling crest, far away in the distance, sits a tiny Mount Fuji, Japan's highest mountain, made small and calm by the wave in front of it. Hokusai designed it around 1831, when he was about 70 years old, long after most artists have done their best work. He called himself the Old Man Mad About Drawing and believed his finest pictures were still ahead of him.

In its own day the Great Wave was cheap street art: carvers and printers turned out thousands of copies, and each sold for about as much as a bowl of soba noodles. People used them up, so of perhaps 8,000 printed, only about 113 early impressions survive.

When Japan opened its ports to the world in the 1850s, Hokusai's prints first reached Europe crumpled up as cheap packing paper around shipments of porcelain. Around 1856 the French artist Felix Bracquemond found some used as wrapping and was electrified, and a craze for Japanese art, Japonisme, swept through European painting. Vincent van Gogh wrote to his brother that the waves were claws and the boat was caught in them, and the crest really does break into white fingers reaching down for the boats.

joan-of-arc.context_blurb:
In the 1420s England held much of northern France after a long, grinding war, and the French prince Charles had never been crowned. Then a teenage farm girl from Domremy in eastern France announced that God had sent her to drive out the English. Within months Joan of Arc had broken the siege of Orleans and seen Charles crowned; within two years she was burned as a heretic.

At about thirteen she began to hear voices, often when the church bell had just sounded: first Saint Michael the archangel, and then Saint Catherine and Saint Margaret, two martyred virgins. In 1429 she reached the prince's court at Chinon, and Charles tried to catch her out by slipping into ordinary clothes among his courtiers while someone else sat in his chair of state. Joan passed by the man on the throne and singled out the real, disguised Charles in the crowd, a moment remembered as the Recognition, though it is legend rather than proven fact. She sent her men for a sword she had never seen, telling them it lay buried behind the altar at Sainte-Catherine-de-Fierbois, under the floor, and when they dug there the rusty blade was waiting.

Before the fighting at Orleans she dictated a letter commanding the English to leave France in God's name, and she warned them that if they stayed, she would strike them with a clash of arms greater than any France had seen in a thousand years. She could neither read nor write it herself. During the siege in May 1429 an English arrow buried itself where her neck meets her shoulder, yet that same day she returned to lead the final attack that broke the siege. The English gave up about nine days after she arrived. On 17 July 1429 Charles VII was crowned at Reims, a city that had thrown open its gates to him, with Joan beside him, banner in hand. Asked why her white banner deserved that place of honour, she replied that it had borne the burden, so it was right that it should have the honour too.

In May 1430 Burgundian soldiers dragged her off her horse at Compiegne, and they later sold her on to the English for money. Locked in the tower of Beaurevoir castle, she jumped from the very top in a desperate bid to escape, and lived.

At her trial in Rouen in 1431 the judges asked whether she was in God's grace. A yes would sound like pride, and a no would be a confession. She answered that if she was not, she prayed God would put her there, and if she was, she prayed God would keep her so, and the court notary said the judges were left stupefied. She signed a recantation and agreed to wear a dress, a promise that ought to have spared her. But while she slept, her jailers took the dress away and left her nothing to wear except the forbidden men's clothes. She put them back on and was condemned as a relapsed heretic.

On 30 May 1431, at about nineteen, she died at the stake in Rouen's Old Market; a friar held up a crucifix for her to fix her eyes on, and she died calling out the name of Jesus three times. Afterwards the executioner, Geoffroy Therage, gathered her ashes and, on English orders, threw them into the Seine, so that nobody could keep any piece of her as a relic. Soon after, badly shaken, Therage came to two friars and confessed that he was terribly afraid of damnation, because he had burned a saint. A legend that grew with her fame said Therage swore her heart would not burn, however fierce the flames, and lay whole in the ashes.

Twenty-five years later the Church reopened her case. Isabelle Romee, Joan's elderly mother, came to Notre-Dame to plead for her, and the new court declared the old verdict void and branded the dead judge, Bishop Cauchon, the true heretic. The public executioner of Rouen then ripped the pages of her death sentence out of the record and set them on fire. In 1920 the Catholic Church made her a saint.

john-adams-second-president-xyz-affair.context_blurb:
John Adams of Massachusetts was a stubborn, prickly lawyer who helped lead the American Revolution, served eight years as George Washington's vice president, and then became the second president of the United States, from 1797 to 1801. His life shows both faces of a man who prized the law: a brave stand for a fair trial, and a harsh law against his own critics.

In 1770, after British soldiers shot five colonists dead in the Boston Massacre, Adams, a patriot himself, agreed to defend the accused soldiers in court when no other lawyer in town would touch the case. He believed even hated enemies deserved a fair trial. Six of the eight soldiers walked free, and the jury convicted the other two only of manslaughter. Adams later counted it among the best services he ever did his country.

As president, during a bitter quarrel with revolutionary France, Adams signed the Sedition Act of 1798, which turned printed attacks on the government or the president into a federal crime if officials judged them false and malicious. Federal courts prosecuted at least 26 people, mostly newspaper editors who backed Thomas Jefferson. The first man tried was the Vermont congressman Matthew Lyon, who spent four months behind bars for sneering at Adams's love of pomp. From his jail cell Lyon ran for re-election and won by a landslide, turning his punishment into a public rebuke of Adams. The backlash helped Jefferson defeat Adams in 1800.

john-cabot-the-northwest-passage-search.context_blurb:
John Cabot was a Venetian captain working out of the English port of Bristol. In 1497 King Henry VII sent him west in the little Matthew to find a short sea road to Asia. He found the coast of Newfoundland instead, and his voyage started England's long and deadly hunt for a Northwest Passage over the top of America.

When Cabot stepped ashore on 24 June 1497, he found fire pits, snares and cut trees that showed people lived there, yet in the whole of his short landing he never met a single one of them face to face. He planted a cross and raised the banners of the king, the Pope and Saint Mark of Venice. Back in Bristol, his sailors bragged about the Grand Banks, where cod swarmed so thickly that the men only had to let down stone-weighted baskets over the side and pull them up full. England, they boasted, would never need Iceland's fish again.

Later captains chased Cabot's dream and paid dearly. In 1576 the first Englishman to seek the passage, Martin Frobisher, carried home a heavy black rock that he was sure held gold, and one expert agreed with him, so English fleets went back and hauled home about 1,225 tons more. It was iron pyrite, fool's gold, worth nothing at all, and some of the useless rock was reportedly dumped as gravel to pave streets. In 1611 Henry Hudson's ship froze fast in the vast bay later named for him, and after a starving winter his crew mutinied, pushed Hudson, John, his teenage son, and seven sick or loyal men into a small open boat, and cut the rope. None of them was ever seen again.

In the 1840s Sir John Franklin took two warships, Erebus and Terror, into the Arctic, and all 128 of his men died after the ships froze fast near King William Island. For more than a century British officials ignored what the Inuit said about where the ships had gone down. Searchers found Erebus in 2014 and Terror in 2016, right where Inuit witnesses had placed them, and Terror was so well preserved that its drawers were still closed and its cabins intact.

john-calvin-calvinism.context_blurb:
John Calvin was a French scholar of the 1500s who became one of the great leaders of the Protestant Reformation. From the Swiss city of Geneva he built a strict, disciplined church whose ideas spread to Scotland, the Netherlands and later North America. His story holds both lasting achievement and one of the ugliest burnings of the age.

Calvin was born Jehan Cauvin at Noyon, in northern France, in 1509, and before he joined the Reformation he studied law at Orleans to become a lawyer. Geneva was only his adopted home. In 1536 he was simply travelling through Geneva, longing for a quiet life of books, when Guillaume Farel, a fiery preacher, pleaded with him to remain, and when Calvin said no, Farel warned that God would curse his studies if he refused. Calvin later wrote that he would rather have died a hundred times than take up that cross, but he stayed.

In 1553 Calvin's Geneva condemned the Spanish doctor Michael Servetus to the stake for denying the Trinity. Calvin urged the council to use the sword instead, a quicker death, but it refused. The executioners built the fire from green oak branches still in leaf, and the damp wood burned so slowly that Servetus took about half an hour to die. Servetus had also made a true medical discovery: blood travels from the heart into the lungs and returns, and his was the first European account of it in print. He had tucked the description inside Christianismi Restitutio, a book of forbidden theology, because he believed the soul lived in the blood, so when nearly every copy was burned along with him, the discovery was almost lost.

Calvin worked himself to death and died in 1564, aged 54, and at his own request he was buried without any marker, so that nobody could make his grave a place of pilgrimage; the spot is still unknown. The five points people sum up as TULIP were not his writing at all: a Dutch synod, the Synod of Dort, drew them up in 1618 and 1619, more than fifty years after his death, to answer the followers of Jacob Arminius.

john-locke-and-natural-rights.context_blurb:
John Locke was an English doctor and philosopher of the 1600s whose ideas about freedom shaped the American Declaration of Independence. He argued that people are born free and equal, that their rights come from nature rather than from any king, and that a government earns obedience only by protecting those rights. In his own lifetime, saying so could get a man hanged.

Locke trained as a physician first. In 1668 he directed a dangerous operation to drain a huge cyst on the liver of Lord Ashley, his patron, and fitted a silver tube into Ashley's side to let it go on draining. Ashley, the future Earl of Shaftesbury, said Locke had saved his life, and wits joked that his liver would need a silver tap forever. In his great book on how we come to know things, published in 1689, Locke argued that a newborn's mind holds no ideas at all: it is like white paper with nothing written on it, and experience alone fills it in. People later called this the blank slate.

Friendship with Shaftesbury, a fierce enemy of the king's party, made Locke a marked man. When a plot to kill King Charles II came to light around 1683, Locke slipped out of England, saying it was for his health, and went into exile in Holland. There, with the king's agents hunting him, he lived under false names, one of them Dr. van der Linden. His Two Treatises of Government, which defended a people's right to depose their king, came out in 1689 with no author's name on it, because writing such a thing could send a man to the gallows. He denied writing it all his life and owned up only weeks before his death in 1704, in a codicil, a late addition, to his will, which nobody would read until he was gone.

The First Treatise demolished Robert Filmer's book Patriarcha. Filmer claimed kings ruled by God's grant because their power had passed down from Adam, the first man, in one unbroken chain, and Locke mocked the idea, arguing that no living king could prove himself Adam's rightful heir. Property, Locke said, begins with labour: wild apples and open land belong to everyone in common until a person mixes his own work with them, by picking, ploughing or building, and so makes them his.

Locke's natural rights to life, health, liberty and possessions demand only that other people let you be and do you no harm, which is why a beggar and a lord can each hold all of them at once. They never require anyone to give you anything. People leave the lawless state of nature and join together under a government, he wrote, chiefly to protect their property, by which he meant the lives, liberties and estates that already belong to them. Government is a trust, and a ruler who sets out to seize the people's property or enslave them breaks it, so the people may rise up, dissolve that government entirely and start again.

A century later, in 1776, Thomas Jefferson borrowed Locke's rights of life, liberty and property for the Declaration of Independence, but in place of property he wrote the pursuit of happiness. Jefferson counted Locke among his three greatest heroes, beside Bacon and Newton.

john-paul-ii-s-warsaw-homily-be-not-afra.context_blurb:
In October 1978 the Polish cardinal Karol Wojtyla became Pope John Paul II, the first pope in more than four centuries who was not Italian, and the first from a country ruled by communists. Poland's Communist government ran the press, the police and the schools, and it called the state officially atheist. In June 1979 the new pope came home on a long pilgrimage.

It was the first time any pope had visited a Soviet-bloc country. At his open-air Mass in Warsaw's Victory Square, about a million Poles interrupted his sermon with the chant "We want God!", a roar that the writer Peggy Noonan said swelled to thunder. It was a public rejection of the atheist state's claim on Polish life.

The regime fought back with its cameras. Afraid of what pictures of the vast crowds would reveal, the government told state television to keep its lenses off them, and the broadcasts lingered instead on a bare brick wall and the faces of old people, as if young Poles did not care. Viewers saw through the trick, and the clumsy lie became a symbol of the regime's dishonesty. Within a year the electrician Lech Walesa had helped found Solidarity, the first independent trade union in the Soviet bloc.

joseph-lister-and-antiseptic-surgery.context_blurb:
In the 1860s Joseph Lister was a surgeon at the Royal Infirmary in Glasgow, and nearly half of his patients lived through their operations only to die days later, when their wounds festered and rotted. Doctors called it hospitalism and shrugged. Surgeons wore blood-stiffened coats as badges of experience. Lister set out to stop the dying, and his answer changed surgery forever.

His clue came from France. The chemist Louis Pasteur had shown that rotting and fermenting were the work of tiny living organisms drifting in the air, not of bad air itself. Lister guessed that the same germs were getting into wounds, and he hunted for something that would kill them. He chose carbolic acid, because he had heard that the town of Carlisle was using it to purify the stench of its sewage works, and he soaked his dressings in it. His first patient, eleven-year-old James Greenlees, whose leg a cart wheel had crushed in August 1865, healed without deep infection and kept his leg.

Many London surgeons would not believe in killers they could not see, and they went on operating with unwashed hands and instruments. One surgeon made fun of Lister openly, telling his nurses to shut the door so that Mr. Lister's germs could not get in. Lister kept publishing and lecturing, and within twenty years his methods, refined into sterile technique, had conquered the operating theatre.

julius-caesar-crossing-the-rubicon.context_blurb:
Early in 49 BC Julius Caesar, the Roman general who had spent eight years conquering Gaul, led soldiers across a little river called the Rubicon, the border of Italy itself. Bringing an army over it was an act of war against the Roman Republic. The civil war that followed destroyed the Republic, and "crossing the Rubicon" still means passing a point of no return.

As he committed his men, tradition says, Caesar declared that the die is cast: like a gambler's throw, the move could not be taken back. For all its fame, the Rubicon was little more than a stream, a shallow brook that a soldier could wade across, so the whole drama lay in law and symbol rather than in the water. That evening Caesar sat through a gladiator show at Ravenna so that nobody would guess his plan, then slipped away after dark in a hired carriage drawn by mules borrowed from a bakery, taking a roundabout road. He brought only a single legion across, the Thirteenth, about 5,000 legionaries with some 300 horsemen, and he gambled on speed and shock instead of numbers.

The river marked where Italy began, and Roman law forbade a general coming back from the provinces to lead his army past it; doing so was treason, punishable by death, for Caesar and for every soldier who followed him. Suetonius tells a legend that while Caesar hesitated, a huge and beautiful figure appeared on the bank playing a pipe, then snatched a trumpet from a soldier, blew the call to battle and crossed the river, and Caesar took it as a sign to follow. At dawn he seized the town of Ariminum and drove south so fast that terrified refugees ran ahead of him, and when word got to Rome, rumour had swollen his one small legion into an immense army. Pompey, the consuls and much of the Senate fled the city.

Why risk it all? The Senate, with Pompey behind it, had ordered Caesar to give up his army and come home to Rome as a private citizen, and without troops or office he expected his enemies to put him on trial. So he chose war. In Appian's account, Caesar stood at the water's edge and told his friends that holding back would bring great trouble on himself, but crossing would bring it on all mankind, and then he plunged across like a man inspired.

The famous words may not be quite what he said. Neither Caesar's own account of the civil war nor any letter Cicero wrote that winter records the line; the scene we know was written down by Plutarch and Suetonius, more than a century and a half after the crossing. Plutarch even says Caesar spoke Greek, not Latin, at the river, quoting the comic playwright Menander: let the die be flung, a daring cry meaning let the game begin. For centuries three Italian streams each insisted it was the real Rubicon, until Benito Mussolini settled the quarrel by decree in 1933, renaming a riverside town Rubicone; scholars backed his choice in 1991, though it is still debated.

justinian-and-the-surviving-eastern-byza.context_blurb:
When the western half of the Roman Empire fell to invaders in the 400s, the eastern half lived on, ruled from Constantinople on the Bosphorus, and its people still called themselves Romans. In the 500s its emperor Justinian set out to win the lost West back and to raise a church that would outshine every other on Earth: Hagia Sophia, the Church of Holy Wisdom.

Constantine the Great had dedicated the city in May 330 as his eastern capital, naming it Constantinople after himself, and the Romans hailed it proudly as New Rome. For a thousand years it ruled the eastern empire. After rioters burned the old church in 532, Justinian set an army of over ten thousand builders to work, and the new Hagia Sophia was finished in about six years, in December 537, when great cathedrals elsewhere took a century or more. Legend said its high altar, made of gold and silver melted with pearls and powdered gems, changed colour as you walked around it, gleaming gold from one side, then silver, then deep sapphire.

The historian Procopius, who saw it new, wrote that the church was so full of light that it seemed not to come in from the sun but to be produced by the building itself. The trick was a ring of forty windows around the base of the dome, which seems to float on a band of light.

For almost 1000 years no cathedral on Earth was larger, until Seville Cathedral was finished in 1520. Such splendour cost a fortune, perhaps 15,000 to 20,000 pounds of gold. In the middle of the work, says one Byzantine account, Justinian sat down in despair because the gold to complete it had run out.

Justinian also dreamed of restoring the whole empire. His best general, Belisarius, crushed the Vandal kingdom in North Africa in 533 and 534, then invaded Italy and in 536 took back Rome itself from the Ostrogoths. Justinian's lawyers gathered all of Roman law into one great body, and their textbook for students, the Institutes, opens by defining justice as the constant and unending will to render to every person his due, what he is owed. That law became the foundation of civil law across Europe.

justinian-and-theodora.context_blurb:
Justinian ruled the eastern Roman Empire from Constantinople from 527 to 565, and his wife Theodora ruled beside him as a true partner. He was born a peasant and she was the child of a racetrack animal-keeper, yet together they survived a revolt, rebuilt their capital, rewrote Roman law and won back lands the empire had lost.

Justinian, born Petrus Sabbatius into a Latin-speaking peasant family in the Balkans, rose through his uncle Justin I and worked through the night so tirelessly that courtiers called him the emperor who never slept. Theodora spent her childhood behind the scenes at the Hippodrome, the vast chariot-racing stadium, because her father Acacius kept and trained the bears there for the Green racing faction. When he died, the family was left destitute, and she earned her living on the stage and, by the old accounts, as a prostitute. Roman law forbade a senator, a man of high rank, to marry an actress, so around 524 the emperor Justin I, Justinian's uncle, issued a new law that let the wedding go ahead. Theodora became empress in April 527.

In January 532 the Blues and the Greens, rival racing fans who normally hated each other, united against the emperor and set the capital ablaze, roaring "Nika!", the Greek for "Win!", the cheer they shouted at their charioteers. With a rival emperor proclaimed and ships waiting in the harbour, Justinian was ready to flee, but Theodora refused, declaring, as Procopius tells it, that imperial purple is a fine burial shroud: better to die an emperor than live a fugitive. The speech may be Procopius's polished version, but her courage held the throne. Justinian then raised a new Hagia Sophia, crowned by a dome so vast that, ringed by forty windows at its base, it seemed to float, and Procopius wrote that it looked as though it hung from heaven on a golden chain.

Theodora never forgot her hard girlhood: she founded the Metanoia, or Repentance, convent on the Bosphorus, where she bought enslaved prostitutes out of bondage, repaying their owners and giving each woman clothes and money. She also hid persecuted clergy of her own Miaphysite faith in the palace. In 534 Belisarius, Justinian's great general, paraded the treasure of the conquered Vandal kingdom through Constantinople, and among it gleamed the golden menorah of the Temple in Jerusalem, which Rome had looted long before and the Vandals had stolen from Rome. In 540, when Belisarius reached Ravenna, the Ostrogoth capital in Italy, the cornered Goths offered to make him their own emperor of the West; he pretended to accept, rode into the city and then seized it for Justinian.

Under Justinian, the lawyer Tribonian led a commission that sorted ten centuries of conflicting Roman rulings into the Code, the Digest and the Institutes, together called the Corpus Juris Civilis. That body of law became the foundation of the civil-law systems still used across much of the world today. In the church of San Vitale in Ravenna, gold mosaics show Justinian and Theodora on opposite walls beside the altar, each carrying a gift for the Mass, and both wear a halo, marking them as rulers chosen by God.

Then in 541 bubonic plague reached Constantinople and killed a huge share of its people, emptying Justinian's treasury and his armies and wrecking his dream of restoring the whole old empire. It is still remembered as the Plague of Justinian.

justinian-s-code-corpus-juris-civilis.context_blurb:
When Justinian became emperor of the eastern Roman Empire in 527, Roman law was a jungle: a thousand years of statutes, imperial decrees and the opinions of famous jurists, heaped up and often contradicting one another. He gave the brilliant lawyer Tribonian the job of clearing it. The result, the Corpus Juris Civilis or Body of Civil Law, still shapes law across much of the world.

Tribonian's team, free to trim and reword the old writings wherever they clashed, squeezed some three million lines from more than two thousand books into a single work of just fifty books, the Digest. The whole Corpus had four parts: the Code of imperial statutes, the Digest of the great jurists, the Institutes, a textbook for students, and later the Novellae, the new laws Justinian issued afterward. The Digest preserves nearly everything that survives of Rome's greatest legal writers.

In the West the books were all but forgotten. Some five centuries after Justinian they turned up again in northern Italy, and around 1088 Irnerius, a Bologna teacher, began to lecture on them, helping to launch Europe's first universities. His grateful students called him lucerna juris, which means lantern of the law. Through his school, Justinian's law became the seedbed of the civil law of continental Europe.

kamikaze-pilots.context_blurb:
In the last year of the Pacific War, as American fleets closed in on Japan, the Japanese high command formed squadrons of pilots whose mission was to crash their bomb-laden planes into Allied ships. More than three thousand of these young men died. Their attacks sank about fifty warships and damaged hundreds more, a heavy toll that still could not stop the American advance.

The high command named them kamikaze, divine wind, borrowing an old legend. In 1274 and again in 1281, the Mongol ruler Kublai Khan sent huge fleets to invade Japan, and both times typhoons wrecked the ships at sea before his armies could conquer the islands. Japanese tradition remembered those storms as a divine wind sent by the gods, and in 1944 the high command cast its suicide pilots as a new one.

Propaganda showed the pilots dying gladly for the Emperor. Lieutenant Yukio Seki, who led the first organised kamikaze attack in October 1944, a five-plane strike on American carriers, rejected that picture. Before he took off, Seki told a reporter that he was giving his life not for the Emperor or the empire but for his beloved wife. He also called the tactic a waste of skilled flyers, saying he could land a 500-kilogram bomb on a carrier deck without crashing into it.

katyn-and-the-soviet-invasion-of-poland-.context_blurb:
On 17 September 1939, barely two weeks after Hitler invaded Poland from the west, Stalin's Red Army invaded from the east under the secret Nazi-Soviet Pact and took hundreds of thousands of Poles prisoner. In the spring of 1940, on an order drawn up by the secret-police chief Lavrenty Beria and signed by Stalin and his Politburo, the NKVD murdered about 21,857 of them, officers, police and professors, to rob Poland of its educated class.

The NKVD's chief executioner, Vasily Blokhin, killed roughly 7,000 prisoners himself across twenty-eight April nights, and because the heavy recoil of Soviet revolvers made his hand ache after a dozen shots, he brought along German-made Walther pistols instead. The German guns later helped the Soviets hide their crime.

In April 1943 German troops dug up mass graves in Katyn forest and announced that the NKVD had done the shooting. Moscow blamed the Nazis and set up a commission under Nikolai Burdenko that duly declared the Germans guilty, and the Western Allies kept silent because they needed Stalin against Hitler. The Soviet Union kept up that lie for forty-seven years, and only on 13 April 1990, forty-seven years to the day after the Germans announced the graves, did it admit that its own NKVD had done the killing. Beria's signed order was made public in 1992.

kepler-s-laws-of-planetary-motion.context_blurb:
Johannes Kepler was a German mathematician of the early 1600s and a devout Lutheran who believed the heavens were written in God's own geometry. Working from the most exact sky measurements ever made, he found three laws that describe how planets really move, overturning a belief two thousand years old. His laws later gave Isaac Newton the clue he needed to explain gravity.

Kepler's treasure was the life's work of his Danish employer, Tycho Brahe, who had measured the planets with the naked eye at his observatory on an island in the Baltic, more precisely than anyone before the telescope, and who died suddenly in Prague in 1601. Two days later Kepler became Imperial Mathematician and took charge of the records. Astronomers had always insisted that planets move in perfect circles, but Tycho's records of Mars showed Kepler that it travels in an ellipse, a squashed oval, with the Sun off to one side at one of its two focus points.

A planet speeds up as it nears the Sun and dawdles far from it. Kepler's second law captures exactly how: the line joining the Sun to the planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times.

The answer had cost him years. He had built a tangled scheme of little wobbling circles for Mars, and when he saw that it had been a plain ellipse in disguise the whole time, he scolded himself in print for being a foolish bird. In The Harmony of the World, in 1619, he argued that each planet, quickening and slowing along its orbit, sings like a voice in a heavenly choir, so the planets are literally making music. He even punned that Earth sings mi, fa, mi, because misery and famine rule our home.

When his third law, linking a planet's year to its distance from the Sun, finally came to him, he wrote that he surrendered to a sacred frenzy, for he had stolen the Egyptians' golden vessels to build a tabernacle for his God. To Kepler, finding the harmony of the heavens was an act of worship.
