magellan-s-circumnavigation.context_blurb:
In September 1519 Ferdinand Magellan, a Portuguese captain sailing for Spain, set out with five ships and about 270 men. Portugal's king had refused to back him, so Spain's young King Charles I did. Three years later a single battered ship came home, having sailed right around the world for the first time in history, but Magellan was not aboard.

Going around the world was not what Magellan set out to do: he meant to reach the Spice Islands, the Moluccas, by sailing west, so that Spain could break Portugal's grip and buy cloves straight from where they grew. In the winter of 1520, at Port San Julian far down the coast of South America, his men marvelled at the tall local people, whom Magellan called Patagao, and by legend the region's name, Patagonia, means the land of people with big feet. The fleet found its passage at the continent's tip in October 1520, a strait 350 miles long that now bears Magellan's name. While the ships were still fighting their way through it, the crew of the San Antonio mutinied and secretly sailed home to Spain, abandoning the expedition and carrying off much of its food.

In November 1520 Magellan led the remaining ships out into a vast, calm ocean that no European had crossed, and because they met no storms, he named it the Pacific, the peaceful sea. It was far bigger than anyone had guessed. The crossing took about 98 days, and when the biscuit ran out and the water turned rotten, the starving sailors soaked the ox-hides that protected the rigging in the sea, heated them on the embers and ate them, along with sawdust and rats. Without fresh food they fell sick with what we now call scurvy, and Antonio Pigafetta, the expedition's diarist, wrote that the men's gums swelled up over their teeth until they could not eat; nineteen died.

Magellan's end came on 27 April 1521, in a fight on the Philippine island of Mactan, where he waded ashore in armour with about fifty men against some 1,500 warriors led by Chief Lapulapu, and a spear through his unarmoured leg brought him down in the surf. His body was never returned to his men. The Basque captain Juan Sebastian Elcano took command of the last ship and brought it home, finishing the first voyage around the world. Of the five ships that sailed, only the Victoria sailed all the way around the world; even the flagship Trinidad never made it home. When the Victoria reached Seville on 8 September 1522, only 18 starving men were aboard, out of the roughly 270 who had set out.

The voyage left two strange proofs that the world is round. When they put in at Cape Verde in July 1522, the crew's logbook, kept every day for three years, said Wednesday while the islanders insisted it was Thursday: by always sailing west around the globe, the crew had gained a whole day, the first real proof of what became the International Date Line. Magellan's interpreter, an enslaved man from Malacca named Enrique, may have beaten everyone around the world. Carried east to Europe years before, he now sailed west with Magellan. At Limasawa in the Philippines in March 1521, the local people understood his Malay, which meant he had travelled right round the globe to a place where his own language was spoken.

magna-carta-1215.context_blurb:
In June 1215 King John of England, hated by his barons, was forced to accept a long charter limiting his own power: Magna Carta, the Great Charter. Most of it dealt with narrow feudal grievances, and it was cancelled within weeks. Yet reissued again and again, it became a founding stone of English liberty and of constitutional law across the English-speaking world.

John's troubles began abroad: in 1204 he lost Normandy and his family's French lands to King Philip II of France, and the heavy taxes he wrung from his barons for a failed reconquest bred fury. In August 1213 Archbishop Stephen Langton read the barons a forgotten charter that Henry I had granted at his coronation in 1100, giving them a written precedent on which to build their own demands. On 17 May 1215 the rebel barons seized London, the capital, while the king was away, leaving John little choice but to bargain. In June the two sides met on neutral open ground, the meadow of Runnymede beside the River Thames between Windsor and Staines, as the charter itself records. John never signed Magna Carta with a quill; like every medieval king, he made it binding by pressing his great wax seal into it. The charter ran as one unbroken block of 63 provisions, and the clause numbers people quote today were added by editors long after John's reign.

Clause 39, the most quoted of all, protected every free man from arrest, prison, loss of land or exile unless his peers judged him lawfully or the law of the land allowed it, and that judgment by one's peers grew into trial by jury. Clause 40 bound the crown never to sell justice to anyone, nor to deny it or delay it, and it is one of the few clauses still on the British statute book. But about ten weeks after Runnymede, Pope Innocent III, whose vassal John had made himself, declared the charter shameful, illegal and void forever, because the king had been forced into it. In October 1216, fleeing a French invasion, John tried to cross the Wash, a stretch of tidal sands and quicksand on the east coast, and tradition says the incoming sea engulfed part of his baggage train, including the crown jewels, which have never been found. Days later, on the night of 18 to 19 October 1216, John died of dysentery at Newark Castle. His nine-year-old son became Henry III, and the boy's regents reissued the charter to win the barons back.

The most radical clause, 61, set up a council of 25 barons who could seize the king's castles and lands if he broke the charter and did not repair the wrong within 40 days, which in effect gave legal cover to rebels taking up arms against their king. It was dropped from the very first reissue. Clause 39 protected only free men, while the unfree villeins, perhaps half of England's people, were tied to their lords' estates and left outside its protection. The version that lasted was not John's: Henry III reissued a settled charter in 1225, and in 1297 Edward I made it statute law, the version that lived on in English law. Even a humble order to rip out the fish-weirs, traps that were silting up the Thames, the Medway and other rivers, survived as law into the 1960s, long after the grand clauses were gone.

mahabharata-ramayana-epics.context_blurb:
The Mahabharata and the Ramayana are the two great Sanskrit epics of ancient India, shaped over many centuries from older spoken tales and still retold across South and Southeast Asia. The Mahabharata tells of a feud between two families of royal cousins, the Pandavas and the Kauravas, that ends in a vast war. The Ramayana tells how Prince Rama rescues his wife Sita from Ravana, the demon king of Lanka.

The Mahabharata is the longest poem ever composed, some 100,000 verses and 1.8 million words, roughly ten times as long as Homer's Iliad and Odyssey put together. It is about four times the length of the Ramayana. Ravana carries Sita off to his island fortress of Lanka, and Rama's army of monkeys and bears cannot follow across the sea. But the mighty monkey Hanuman, son of the wind god Vayu, prays, swells to a giant's size and leaps the whole ocean to Lanka in a single bound from the top of Mount Mahendra.

When Ravana's demons catch Hanuman spying and set his oil-soaked tail alight to shame him, he bounds from roof to roof and sets fire to all of Lanka, sparing only the grove where Sita is held. In the Mahabharata, King Yudhishthira, eldest of the five Pandava brothers, gambles away everything in a rigged game of dice, even his wife, Queen Draupadi, and when Prince Dushasana tries to strip her before the court, Krishna makes her sari endless, so it unwinds and unwinds until Dushasana collapses.

Brahma, the creator, had granted Ravana a boon: no god and no demon could ever kill him. In his pride Ravana never bothered to ask for safety from mere mortals, and that gap in his boon is why Rama, only a man, can kill him in the end.

On the eve of the great battle of Kurukshetra, the warrior Arjuna talks with his charioteer, who is the god Krishna, and that dialogue is the Bhagavad Gita. The patriarch Bhishma held a boon that let him decide for himself when he would die. Arjuna's arrows brought Bhishma down at Kurukshetra, and so many of them stood in his body that they held him off the ground, so he lay suspended on a bed of arrows for weeks, teaching Yudhishthira, until the holy season of Uttarayana came.

mandate-of-heaven-zhou-dynasty.context_blurb:
In 1046 BCE a Chinese army under King Wu crushed the Shang dynasty and set up a new one, the Zhou. The new rulers had to explain why toppling a king backed by the heavens could be right, and their answer shaped Chinese politics for more than two thousand years: a ruler who governed badly could lose his right to rule.

According to the Duke of Zhou, Heaven gives power to a virtuous ruler and withdraws it from a cruel one, and this heavenly grant became known as the Mandate of Heaven, or Tianming. The Shang had fallen, he said, because Heaven had already rejected them. The Zhou themselves outlasted every other Chinese dynasty, ruling for about 800 years until 256 BCE, though their real power faded long before the end.

To make the last Shang king the very image of a ruler Heaven had abandoned, the Zhou blackened his memory and renamed him Zhou, a character meaning the grimiest strap on a horse's saddle. The Han scholar Wang Chong already dismissed the lurid tales about him as the victors' propaganda.

Centuries later Mencius, asked by the king of Qi whether killing the tyrant Zhou of Shang had been the murder of a king, replied that he had heard of the execution of a mere fellow called Zhou, but never of a ruler being slain, because a cruel tyrant is no true king. The Mandate's boldest idea was that Heaven speaks through ordinary people: the Book of Documents says that Heaven sees as the people see and hears as the people hear, so a king who loses his people's loyalty has already lost Heaven. Floods, famines and revolts could be read as Heaven's verdict, and Mencius taught that the people matter most and the ruler least.

manhattan-project.context_blurb:
The Manhattan Project was the top-secret American effort in the Second World War to build an atomic bomb before Nazi Germany could. At its peak it employed more than 125,000 people and cost some two billion dollars. Under the physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer, its scientists at Los Alamos, New Mexico, built the first atomic weapons in 1945 and opened the nuclear age.

It began with a warning: in August 1939 the Hungarian physicist Leo Szilard wrote a letter to President Franklin Roosevelt, signed by Albert Einstein, cautioning that Nazi Germany might beat America to an atomic bomb. At Los Alamos, Richard Feynman, a young physicist, passed idle hours learning to open the locked safes that held the bomb's secrets, and one safe opened to 27-18-28, the first digits of the mathematical constant e, 2.71828. The German-born refugee physicist Klaus Fuchs worked on making the plutonium bomb implode, and all the while he was passing what he knew of the bomb to Soviet intelligence through a courier named Harry Gold; he was caught only in 1949.

Oppenheimer named the first test Trinity, and it took place on a barren stretch of New Mexico desert that old travellers had called Jornada del Muerto, the Journey of the Dead Man. While they waited, the scientists ran a betting pool on the size of the explosion, and I. I. Rabi, arriving last, took the only number left, 18 kilotons, which turned out almost exactly right, so he won. At 5:29 on the morning of 16 July 1945 they set off the Gadget, a steel ball of explosives and plutonium perched on a steel tower 100 feet tall, and the blast turned the tower to vapour, so that only the stumps of its legs remained. The fireball melted the desert sand around it into a crust of faintly radioactive, light-green glass, later named trinitite. The test's director, the physicist Kenneth Bainbridge, turned to Oppenheimer and told him bluntly that now they were all sons of bitches. Twenty years later Oppenheimer said that, watching the fireball, he had remembered words from the Bhagavad Gita, a sacred Hindu text, in which the speaker says he has become Death, the destroyer of worlds. His brother Frank, standing beside him at the test, remembered Robert's real words in the moment as much plainer: it worked.

Little Boy, the Hiroshima bomb of 6 August 1945, worked like a gun barrel, shooting one lump of uranium into a second. Fat Man, which fell on Nagasaki on 9 August, used plutonium instead and worked by implosion: a carefully timed shell of explosives squeezed a plutonium ball inward. Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, found guilty of giving the Soviets atomic secrets, were executed at Sing Sing prison in June 1953, the only American civilians put to death for spying during the Cold War. Years later Ethel's brother, David Greenglass, admitted that he had lied on the stand about her typing the spy notes.

manorialism-the-medieval-peasant.context_blurb:
In medieval Europe most people lived on manors, farming estates owned by a lord, with fields, meadows, woods, a mill and a village of peasant households. Most peasants were serfs: not slaves, but bound to the land, owing the lord labour, crops and fees in return for strips of land of their own. It was a hard life, and sometimes the villagers pushed back.

Breaking northern Europe's heavy, wet clay took a great iron-shod plough that only a team of eight oxen could drag, so families that owned only two had to pool their animals with the neighbours just to plough at all. That is one reason peasant farming was so communal. Before a serf could tend his own crops, he owed week-work: two or three days of unpaid labour every week, and more at harvest, on the demesne, the part of the manor the lord kept for himself.

At a serf's death the lord claimed a death-tax called the heriot, the dead man's best beast, his finest ox or cow, and the church often claimed the second-best as well, so a grieving family lost its two most valuable animals at once. Peasants also had to grind their grain at the lord's mill and pay him a share of the flour. Abbot Richard of St Albans, around 1331, confiscated about eighty hidden hand-mills from the townspeople and had the millstones cemented into the floor of the abbey parlour as a lasting humiliation. Fifty years later, on 12 July 1381, the Peasants' Revolt reached St Albans, and the townsfolk tore those millstones out of the abbey floor, broke them into pieces and handed the fragments round as trophies.

Slowly, farming grew richer. Villages learned to rotate three fields, one sown with winter grain, one with beans and peas and one left resting, and with no notion of chemistry, they had hit on real science: the beans and peas were returning nitrogen to the soil that the grain had worn out. The extra food helped the population grow and towns spread around the years 900 to 1000.

mansa-griots-african-oral-tradition.context_blurb:
Across West Africa, especially in the Mande-speaking lands of the old Mali Empire, history was kept not in books but in trained memory. Hereditary musician-historians called griots, or jeli, carry a community's family lines, wars, births and deaths in song, and a griot could even speak hard truths to kings. The epic of Sundiata, founder of the Mali Empire in the 1200s, has passed from griot to griot for over seven hundred years.

As he recites, a griot often plays the kora, a harp-lute with 21 strings whose body is a halved gourd with a cowhide face; the strings were traditionally made from fishing line. A griot is a living library who carries unwritten history line by line.

Because nothing was written down, an old griot's death means the loss of everything he carried. The Malian writer Amadou Hampate Ba, who warned UNESCO of that loss in 1960, put it in a famous line: when an old man dies in Africa, it is as though a whole library has gone up in flames. Some of West Africa's most famous modern singers still come from griot families.

mansa-musa-and-the-mali-pilgrimage.context_blurb:
In the early 1300s Mansa Musa was king of Mali, a West African empire that controlled the gold fields of the upper Niger and the trade routes across the Sahara. In 1324 he began the hajj, the pilgrimage of Muslims to Mecca, with a caravan so rich that it shook the economy of Egypt and carried his fame all the way to Europe.

His title, mansa, meant ruler or emperor, literally the king of kings. In Egypt, Musa explained how he had come to the throne, and the scholar al-Umari wrote it down. Musa's predecessor, he said, was sure the Atlantic must end somewhere and sent 200 ships to find its far shore. Only one came back, and its captain reported that the rest had been swallowed far out at sea by a mighty current flowing like a river through the open ocean. That king then sailed off himself with 2,000 ships and never returned, and so Musa became king. It is told as legend.

At the head of his procession walked five hundred attendants, each carrying a staff of pure gold weighing four to six pounds. Behind came some 80 to 100 camels, each loaded with about 300 pounds of gold dust, in a caravan of perhaps 60,000 people. A later legend says that every Friday of the journey he had a brand-new mosque built wherever he happened to be.

In Cairo he showered every emir and official at the sultan's court with loads of gold, and so much poured in that he crashed the price of gold across Egypt. Gold there had always fetched at least 25 silver dirhams per mithqal, but after his visit a mithqal sold for 22 or less, and al-Umari, collecting stories in Cairo around 1340, found it had stayed cheap for about twelve years. Told to kiss the ground before the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad, Musa at first refused, then bowed while declaring aloud that he made obeisance to God who created him. On the way home the richest king in the world ran short of money and borrowed gold from Cairo's merchants at a steep rate, which drew gold out of the market and helped push its price back up.

Back home around 1325 he ordered the Djinguereber Mosque built at Timbuktu, and with no stone quarries anywhere near, his builders raised it in mud brick. Under his patronage Timbuktu became a city of scholars around its Sankore mosque, and in its markets books were among the most valuable goods for sale. In 1375 the Majorcan mapmaker Abraham Cresques painted him on the great Catalan Atlas, enthroned and crowned in the middle of West Africa, holding out a big gold nugget toward a camel rider, and called him the richest and noblest king of those lands.

mansa-musa-the-mali-empire.context_blurb:
In the early 1300s Mansa Musa ruled the Empire of Mali, a vast West African realm that held the goldfields of the upper Niger and the trading cities on the southern edge of the Sahara. His pilgrimage of 1324 and 1325, with thousands of followers and camels loaded with gold, made him the first ruler from south of the Sahara to become famous across the Middle East and Europe.

In the Mandinka language mansa meant king or emperor, so his name simply means King Musa. Musa told the Egyptians that the king before him, often called Abu Bakr II, would not believe the Atlantic had no far shore, so he gave up his throne and sailed west with some 2,000 vessels and never returned, and that is how Musa became king. Modern historians suspect Musa may simply have pushed him aside, so the tale is told as legend.

Mali's wealth came from trading its plentiful gold for salt, which the south badly lacked and prized like treasure, while at the desert town of Taghaza the stuff lay so thick that houses, and even the mosque, were built of salt slabs. The traveller Ibn Battuta saw people there cut salt into pieces and spend it as money. To guard the secret of his real mines at Bambuk and Bure, Musa spread the rumour that in Mali gold grew up out of the ground like a plant. About two-thirds of the gold in the medieval Mediterranean came from West Africa.

In 1324 Musa crossed the Sahara on the hajj, the pilgrimage Muslims hope to make at least once, to the holy city of Mecca in Arabia, a trek of some 2,700 miles. When the caravan neared a city, 500 men marched in front of the king, each carrying a gold staff weighing about six pounds, followed by riders with red-and-gold flags. In Cairo the Mamluk sultan expected him to kiss the floor on his knees, and Musa at first refused; then, on a companion's whispered advice, he bowed, declaring that his reverence went to the God who had made him.

His gifts of gold in Cairo were so lavish that the metal's price collapsed. When al-Umari, an Arab writer, came to Cairo about twelve years later, gold there was still cheap: a mithqal that had never sold below 25 silver dirhams now fetched 22 or fewer. On the journey home the great king actually ran out of cash, and to pay his way across the Sahara he had to take loans of gold from the merchants of Cairo, 50,000 dinars from one man alone. About fifty years after his pilgrimage, the Majorcan mapmaker Abraham Cresques drew him on the 1375 Catalan Atlas, crowned, with a sceptre in one hand and a giant gold nugget held out in the other toward a camel-riding merchant.

Back home he raised the Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu from banco, an earthen mud brick, and, renovated many times since, it still stands nearly seven centuries later. Timbuktu grew rich on gold, yet the traveller Leo Africanus reported that the most profitable merchandise in the city was books, manuscripts carried south across the Sahara. Online lists now crown Musa the wealthiest human who ever lived, but the historian Hadrien Collet and others point out that the old maps called him richest only in his own region, and that his true fortune is impossible to calculate. He was staggeringly rich; the famous number is simply made up.

mao-s-great-leap-forward-cultural-revolu.context_blurb:
Mao Zedong led the Chinese Communists to victory in 1949 and ruled China until his death in 1976. Two of his campaigns, the Great Leap Forward of 1958 to 1962 and the Cultural Revolution that began in 1966, killed tens of millions of his own people. The first caused the deadliest famine ever recorded; the second turned China's young people against teachers, parents and the Party itself.

In 1958 Mao ordered China to wipe out sparrows for eating grain seed, and whole cities hammered pots, pans, gongs and drums without pause, so the birds had nowhere to settle and fell from the sky exhausted. With the sparrows gone, insects swarmed the fields and ate far more of the crops, and around 1960, persuaded by the bird scientist Tso-hsin Cheng, the leaders had to import some 250,000 live sparrows from the Soviet Union. Mao also wanted China to outproduce Britain in steel, so peasants built backyard furnaces in their fields and, with no scrap iron, threw in their woks, cooking pots and kitchen knives and even their iron hoes and ploughs, producing useless pig iron and leaving nothing to farm with. Officials faked enormous harvests to please Mao, and one propaganda photo showed a boy perched on a field of wheat, as if the stalks were thick enough to hold him, when he was really standing on a hidden table.

At the Lushan Conference in July 1959, Defence Minister Peng Dehuai alone dared tell Mao that the Great Leap was starving the countryside, and Mao threw him out of power, branding him a right-opportunist, a warning to every official who might tell the truth. At a secret meeting in Shanghai that March, Mao had told officials to take as much as one third of the grain, and the historian Frank Dikotter, quoting Party archives, records that he said it was better to let half the people die so that the other half could eat their fill. Even as roughly 30 to 45 million people starved, the government shipped about 7 million tons of grain abroad in 1959 and 1960, selling it for hard currency or giving it away as foreign aid. In Xinyang, in Henan province, about a million of 8.5 million people died around 1960, many at the doors of Party granaries that were full of grain the officials were forbidden to hand out.

Under Mao almost everyone was expected to carry Quotations from Chairman Mao, the Little Red Book, and recite from it daily; around a billion copies had been printed by 1966, and misquoting it could bring punishment. In 1966 Mao launched the Cultural Revolution and sent gangs of teenage Red Guards to smash the Four Olds: old customs, old habits, old culture and old ideas. At struggle sessions the Red Guards made their victims kneel in tall paper dunce caps and hold the jet plane for hours, arms wrenched up behind them while their heads were forced down. Liu Shaoqi, who had been president of China, was labelled the nation's chief capitalist roader, battered at struggle meetings and allowed to die untreated in a prison in Kaifeng in 1969. From 1968 the Party sent some 17 million city teenagers Down to the Countryside for years of farm labour, and one of those teenagers, Xi Jinping, has led China since 2012.

marbury-v-madison-judicial-review.context_blurb:
Marbury v. Madison was the 1803 Supreme Court case that gave American courts one of their greatest powers. In the last hours of John Adams's presidency, William Marbury was appointed a justice of the peace, but his signed commission never reached him. Thomas Jefferson's new Secretary of State, James Madison, refused to deliver it, and Marbury sued.

The chief justice who heard the case, John Marshall, had a hidden tie to it: as Adams's outgoing Secretary of State, he was the very official who had failed to get Marbury's commission delivered before Jefferson's people took over. Marshall was in a trap: ruling against Marbury would bless the government ignoring the law, but ordering Madison to deliver would invite Jefferson to defy the Court.

So Marshall held that Marbury had a right to his commission but that the statute letting him sue in the Supreme Court broke the Constitution, and in surrendering that minor power the Court won a mighty one: the power to declare a law passed by Congress void when it conflicts with the Constitution. This is judicial review, and Marshall's words still guide it: no act of the legislature that goes against the Constitution can be valid.

marco-polo-the-silk-road-to-cathay.context_blurb:
In the late 1200s the young Venetian Marco Polo set out east along the Silk Road with his father and uncle, and he spent nearly a quarter of a century serving Kublai Khan, ruler of the Mongol empire and of China, which Europeans called Cathay. He saw cities bigger than any in Christendom and inventions Europe had never heard of, and his book of wonders amazed and puzzled readers back home.

He described a strange fuel the people of Cathay dug in lumps from beds in the mountains and burned to heat their homes, black stones that stayed alight all night: coal, almost unknown in Europe. Kublai paid for things with sheets of mulberry bark pressed flat and stamped with his red seal, and since he could spend tree bark as treasure, Polo said the Khan had mastered the alchemists' secret. When the Polos finally headed home, the Khan gave them a golden tablet, a paiza about a foot long, warning that anyone who failed to honour its bearers would be killed, and it worked as a passport that commanded horses, food and lodging across the whole empire.

In 1298, a prisoner of war in Genoa after a naval defeat, Polo told his adventures aloud to his cellmate Rustichello of Pisa, a writer of Arthurian romances, who wrote them down. When he lay dying in Venice in 1324, friends at his bedside urged him to confess, for his soul's sake, that his book was full of lies, and he answered that he had not told half of what he saw. The story comes down through Jacopo d'Acqui, a Dominican friar who told it in his chronicle.

marconi-radio-and-broadcasting.context_blurb:
Guglielmo Marconi was a young Italian inventor who believed that the invisible electromagnetic waves Heinrich Hertz had produced in 1887 could carry signals across miles of countryside without any wire. Italian officials ignored him, so he took his idea to Britain. By 1899 he was sending messages across the English Channel, and his wireless soon became standard on ocean ships, famously calling rescuers to the sinking Titanic in 1912.

On 12 December 1901, on Signal Hill in Newfoundland, Marconi and his assistant George Kemp flew a wire aerial on a kite and caught a signal fired from Cornwall, some 2,000 miles away across the Atlantic: the letter S in Morse code, three faint dots, repeated over and over. They had chosen S because three quick dots were the easiest pattern to pick out of the static; some later scientists doubted whether he really heard it.

Soon radio carried more than code: on Christmas Eve 1906, operators at sea, used to nothing but clicking Morse, heard a man's voice and the sound of a violin, as Reginald Fessenden broadcast from Brant Rock, Massachusetts, playing O Holy Night on his violin, singing and reading from the Bible.

marcus-aurelius-the-philosopher-emperor.context_blurb:
From AD 161 to 180 Rome was governed by Marcus Aurelius, the last of the so-called Five Good Emperors and the nearest thing Rome ever had to a philosopher king. He spent much of his reign fighting Germanic tribes along the Danube while plague and war drained the empire. In spare hours he wrote down private reflections in a notebook that became one of the most-read books of ancient philosophy.

As a boy, Marcus Annius Verus so charmed the old emperor Hadrian with his seriousness that Hadrian punned on his family name, Verus, meaning true, and called him Verissimus, the truest. Marcus said the greatest gift of his life came from the philosopher Rusticus, who lent him the discourses of Epictetus, a teacher born a slave, and so the Stoic philosophy passed from a former slave to the ruler of the world.

When plague and endless war drained the treasury, he refused to load his suffering people with heavier taxes and instead auctioned off palace treasures in Trajan's Forum, even the silk robes woven with gold that belonged to his wife, to pay his soldiers. In the war against the Quadi, the men of the Thundering Legion were parched and trapped when rain suddenly poured down, and the historian Cassius Dio says they caught it in their mouths, shields and helmets and drank and fought at the same time. Dio put the rain down to Harnouphis, an Egyptian magician, but the Christian writer Tertullian claimed it came because Christian soldiers in the legion had prayed for it.

When the general Avidius Cassius rebelled on a false rumour that Marcus had died and was then killed by his own officers, a centurion brought Marcus the rebel's head, but Marcus would not even glance at it and ordered it buried, for he had hoped to show Cassius mercy. Over the centuries more than twenty bronze statues of mounted emperors and generals went into the melting pot, but medieval Christians spared the great bronze horseman of Marcus because they mistook him for Constantine, Rome's first Christian emperor. Marcus broke the custom of the Five Good Emperors, who had chosen heirs by adoption on merit, by leaving the throne to his own son, Commodus, one of Rome's worst emperors.

Marcus wrote his notebook on campaign: a line in its first book places him among the Quadi beside the river Granua, in a soldier's tent on the battlefront, in what is now Slovakia. Though he was a Roman emperor and a native Latin speaker, he wrote the Meditations in Greek, the language of philosophy. He never meant anyone to read it and gave it no title; copyists later added the Greek heading Ta eis heauton, meaning To Himself. The famous poster line about our deeds echoing in eternity is not his at all: it was written for Gladiator, a big Hollywood film of 2000 about a fictional Roman general named Maximus. His real lines are plainer: stop arguing about what a good man should be, and be one.

marie-curie-and-radioactivity.context_blurb:
Marie Curie, born Maria Sklodowska in Warsaw in 1867, grew up in a Poland that Russia, Germany and Austria had divided between them. She became the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, discovered two new elements with her husband, Pierre, and gave a name to the strange energy that pours out of certain atoms. That energy made her famous, and in the end it killed her.

In the 1880s the University of Warsaw would not admit women, so Maria and other Polish women studied in the Flying University, secret evening lessons that moved from home to home to escape the police. She later worked as a governess to pay for her sister Bronya's studies in Paris, then followed her there and graduated first in physics at the Sorbonne.

In Paris, Marie and Pierre found that pitchblende ore gave out more radiation than all the pure uranium inside it could explain, and they reasoned that hidden, more powerful new elements must be in the rock. Marie coined a new word for what elements such as uranium were doing as they gave off invisible rays: radioactivity. In 1898 they announced the first new element, and Marie named it polonium after her homeland, Poland, which had been erased from the map, a defiant act of patriotism. Radium followed that December.

Proving that radium existed took her about four years of boiling and stirring roughly seven tons of ore with an iron rod nearly as big as herself, and in 1902 it yielded a mere tenth of a gram of pure radium chloride. They worked in a leaky wooden shed with no ventilation, and when the German chemist Wilhelm Ostwald visited, he said it looked like something between a horse stable and a shed for potatoes. She loved to slip into the workroom at night to see her tubes of radium glowing on their own in the dark, like faint fairy lights.

She won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903, shared with Pierre and Henri Becquerel, and the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1911, and she is still the only person ever to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. She refused to patent her method of isolating radium, so that every laboratory and hospital could use it free, even though it left her too poor to buy radium herself. In the First World War she equipped some twenty vehicles with X-ray apparatus and drove them to the battlefields, so that surgeons could locate bullets and shrapnel, and the soldiers called them the petites Curies, the Little Curies.

She carried glowing radium in her pockets and kept it in her desk with no idea of its danger, and she died in 1934 of aplastic anaemia, brought on by years of exposure to radiation, from her radium and from the X-ray work of the war. In 1995, when France moved her remains to the Pantheon in Paris to lie among the nation's great minds, they were sealed in a lead lining as a precaution against radioactivity. She was the first woman laid there for her own achievements.

marshall-era-economic-miracles-japan-wes.context_blurb:
After the Second World War, West Germany and Japan lay in ruins, yet within a generation both had become industrial giants, in what people called economic miracles. American Marshall Plan aid helped, but much of the recovery came from within: freer markets, high saving and skilled workers. In West Germany the turning point came from one economist, Ludwig Erhard.

Under price controls, German shopkeepers hid their goods rather than sell them at the official prices, and a black market thrived. One Sunday in June of 1948, while Allied generals still governed, Erhard abolished the controls on his own authority. When the American general Lucius Clay warned him that his advisers called it a terrible mistake, Erhard told him not to listen to them, because his own advisers told him the same thing.

By the next morning, goods that had been hoarded for years were back in the shop windows, and the black market melted away, because merchants could at last sell at real prices. West German industrial output jumped from about half of its 1936 level in May 1948 to more than three-quarters by December, and the Wirtschaftswunder, the economic miracle, had begun.

marshall-plan.context_blurb:
Two years after the Second World War ended, much of Europe was still rubble: bombed factories, empty shops, and families facing another winter of hunger. In 1947 the United States answered with the Marshall Plan, named for Secretary of State George Marshall. Over four years America shipped grain, coal, fuel and factory machines worth about 13 billion dollars to sixteen Western European nations, and the help rebuilt half a continent.

Marshall unveiled the idea at Harvard on 5 June 1947, tucked inside a commencement speech that lasted just eleven minutes. He had warned no reporters, and Harvard's own president did not know a great announcement was coming. American policy, Marshall said, took aim at no nation and no creed; its only enemies were poverty, hunger, chaos and desperation. That line made the plan a war on suffering itself. Congress later insisted that every crate, sack and fuel drum carry a shield in red, white and blue reading "For European Recovery," with the words "Supplied by the United States of America" beneath, so that no European could miss where the help came from. Ordinary Americans had moved even before Washington did: in 1947 a Friendship Train gathering gifts of food for the hungry of France and Italy pulled out of Hollywood with eight freight cars, and so many towns along the route loaded it up that it rolled into New York with 270 boxcars.

Getting the plan through Congress took cunning. President Harry Truman deliberately gave the credit away. He grumbled that any bill carrying his own name would flop over and die, but if it was named for the General, even the worst Republican on Capitol Hill could vote for it. To run the program, Truman chose a carmaker with no diplomatic experience at all, Paul Hoffman, the president of the Studebaker automobile company. The largest single share, about a quarter of all the money, went to Britain, because Washington believed that reviving Europe's biggest industrial powers was the key to reviving everyone else. In 1953 Marshall himself received the Nobel Peace Prize, the first professional soldier ever to win it.

Behind the kindness lay hard strategy. In France and Italy, Communist parties were winning a fifth to nearly a third of the vote, and the plan was racing to bring back prosperity before the Communists could take power through free elections. The offer was open to the Soviet bloc too. Stalin's foreign minister, Vyacheslav Molotov, came to Paris with close to a hundred economic advisers, and on 2 July 1947 he stormed out, rejecting the whole plan as "totally unsatisfactory." Stalin feared that American dollars would pull Eastern Europe out of his grip, so he turned down free aid to keep it, and he forbade his satellite states to accept a cent. In 1949 he built a rival bloc, Comecon, which chained those countries to trade run from Moscow and shut them off from Western technology.

In western Germany, money alone was not the whole story. On a Sunday in June 1948, the same week a new Deutsche Mark replaced the worthless Reichsmark, the economist Ludwig Erhard abolished the old wartime price controls overnight, and he did it without first asking the Allied occupation authorities. The black market melted away and shop shelves filled. West Germans called the boom that followed the Wirtschaftswunder, the economic miracle. Within a decade the West was outgrowing France and Britain, while East Germany, run on a Soviet-style command economy, stagnated and never caught up.

martin-luther-the-95-theses.context_blurb:
Martin Luther was a German monk who taught the Bible at the small university of Wittenberg. In 1517 he challenged the way the Church raised money by selling forgiveness, and his protest split Western Christianity in two. Every Protestant church today traces its separation from Rome back to the quarrel this one stubborn professor began.

Luther had never planned to be a monk at all. In July 1505 a bolt of lightning struck the ground beside him, and the terrified law student cried out to Saint Anna for help, vowing to become a monk. He kept his word and entered a monastery at Erfurt. Twelve years later he was enraged by indulgences, paper certificates the Church sold with the promise that they would cut short the time a dead loved one's soul spent in purgatory. The friar Johann Tetzel, who peddled them across Germany, sang a jingle promising that the instant a coin rang in his money chest, a soul sprang up out of purgatory. To Luther, that was forgiveness being sold for cash.

Luther's Ninety-five Theses were written in Latin, for scholars to argue over, but within weeks they had been turned into German, and the new printing press carried them across the country. Copies came off presses in Basel, Leipzig and Nuremberg, and a debate meant for professors became a movement for everyone. Hidden behind the sales was an ugly deal. Officially the money was paying for Pope Leo X's great new church of St. Peter in Rome, but half of what Tetzel raised was quietly going to Archbishop Albert of Mainz, to pay off the debt he had run up buying his high church office. When the pope gave Luther sixty days to take everything back, Luther answered on 10 December 1520 by tossing the papal order into a bonfire at Wittenberg's Elster Gate while students cheered.

In 1521 Emperor Charles V summoned him to the city of Worms. The emperor promised him a safe-conduct, a sworn guarantee of free passage, yet everyone remembered that the reformer Jan Hus had trusted the same kind of promise at Constance in 1415 and had been burned at the stake anyway. Luther went regardless. Ordered to retract his writings, he refused, saying he neither could nor would take anything back, since it was neither safe nor honest for a Christian to act against his conscience. The emperor declared him an outlaw. His protector, Frederick the Wise of Saxony, had his men fake a kidnapping on the road and carry Luther off to Wartburg Castle, where he grew a beard and lived as a knight called Junker Joerg, Knight George. There, in only eleven weeks, he turned the whole New Testament from Greek into everyday German, a Bible printed so widely that it helped shape the modern German language.

The deeper story starts with the Theses themselves. The very first one set the tone: when Jesus told people to repent, Luther argued, he meant a believer's whole life to be one of repentance, not a single debt settled with a coin. Even the famous scene may be a legend. The picture of Luther hammering the Theses to a church door comes from Philip Melanchthon, who was not yet in Wittenberg in 1517, while Luther's own account says he sent them by mail, in a letter to Archbishop Albert. He sent his protest straight to the very man whose debts the indulgences were paying.

martin-luther-the-protestant-reformation.context_blurb:
Martin Luther was a German monk and Bible professor in the town of Wittenberg who, in 1517, attacked the Church's sale of forgiveness. Within a few years half of Germany was reading him, the pope had thrown him out of the Church, and the emperor had made him an outlaw. The Reformation he began split Western Christianity for good.

It started with a thunderclap. In July 1505, when lightning struck right beside the young law student, Luther shouted a vow to Saint Anne, begging her to help him and promising to become a monk. He sold his law books and entered a monastery, to his father's fury. Twelve years later, on 31 October 1517, he finished ninety-five arguments against the sale of indulgences, and by tradition he nailed the list to the door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg, which served the university as a notice board. In 1523 he arranged the secret escape of twelve nuns from the convent at Nimbschen, who rode out in a merchant's covered wagon hidden among empty herring barrels. One of them, Katharina von Bora, married him in 1525: the runaway nun and the renegade monk.

What enraged him was a salesman. The friar Johann Tetzel sold indulgences with the Church's claim that they reduced the punishment a buyer owed for his sins. Tetzel's catchy rhyme promised that as soon as a coin rang in his chest, a soul sprang free of purgatory. Part of the money went to rebuild St. Peter's in Rome, and to Luther, selling forgiveness for cash was a betrayal of the faith.

Open defiance followed. In 1520 Pope Leo X gave him sixty days to recant, and on the last of them Luther led his students to Wittenberg's Elster Gate and threw the papal order into a bonfire, along with books of Church law. At the Diet of Worms in 1521, Emperor Charles V had a table piled with Luther's books and ordered him to take it all back. Luther would not, unless Scripture itself proved him wrong. His conscience, he said, was held captive by the Word of God, and to act against it was neither safe nor right. The emperor made him an outlaw whom anyone might kill, so his protector, Frederick the Wise, staged an ambush on the road and hid him in Wartburg Castle. To pass unnoticed, Luther let his beard grow and dressed as a minor nobleman, the knight Junker Joerg. There he spent about eleven weeks translating the entire New Testament into German, inventing new German words where the language had none. Legend says he hurled an inkwell at the devil there; in truth he fought the devil with ink, by translating.

The words most people remember, "Here I stand," followed by his saying that he could do nothing else and asking God to help him, were probably polished in the first printed account rather than spoken exactly that way. Printing made him. His Theses crossed the German lands in two weeks and Europe in two months, and between 1517 and 1520 thirty of his pamphlets ran through some 370 editions. Johann Cochlaeus, who hated Luther, grumbled that even tailors and shoemakers were devouring the German New Testament, treating it as the spring of all truth. He meant it as an insult, but it proves how hungrily ordinary Germans read the Bible for themselves.

marx-engels-and-the-communist-manifesto-.context_blurb:
In the winter of 1847, a small revolutionary club in London asked two young German exiles, Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, to write down its beliefs. Their short pamphlet, the Communist Manifesto, called for workers to overthrow the owners and abolish private property. In the next century, regimes built on its ideas under Lenin, Stalin, Mao and Pol Pot killed somewhere around a hundred million people. The story begins here.

Printed in London in late February 1848, the pamphlet's first line warned that a spectre was haunting Europe, the spectre of communism. Marx was then a poor, brilliant, quarrelsome exile with a growing family. His daughters never called him Karl; they called him Moor, a nickname he had earned at university for his jet-black hair and dark complexion. Engels had a nickname too: the General.

Months before, Engels had drafted the program like a school catechism, twenty-five questions with a brief reply to each, under the title Principles of Communism, and Marx reworked it into flowing prose. The finished Manifesto closed with its most famous rallying cry, calling on the working men of every land to unite. Just before it, the authors told the workers they had nothing to lose but their chains. At first almost nobody read it. Then, within a day of its publication, revolution broke out in France, and the upheavals of 1848 spread across the continent.

Engels lived a double life. In 1842 his family sent him to their cotton mill in Manchester, and a spirited Irish factory worker named Mary Burns, who knew the slums, guided him safely through the wretched district called Little Ireland. What he saw became his 1845 book on the English working class. In 1850 a Scottish writer, Helen Macfarlane, made the first English translation of the Manifesto, and in place of the spectre she had a frightful hobgoblin stalking through Europe. Marx, meanwhile, lived in real poverty in London's Soho, where the family sometimes ate only bread and potatoes. His bright son Edgar, a boy who loved to bellow the Marseillaise, died in his father's arms on 6 April 1855. Only three of Jenny Marx's seven children grew up. By day Engels was a rich mill executive who rode to hounds with the gentry; by night he sent thousands of pounds to the Marx family, money that paid for the long research and writing of Das Kapital. Capitalist profits funded the great attack on capitalism. Marx finished the first volume standing at his desk, because boils had broken out on his rear, and he hoped the bourgeoisie would remember his carbuncles until their dying day. When Marx was buried at Highgate in 1883, only about eleven mourners came, and Engels told them that just as Charles Darwin had found the law of nature's development, his friend had found the law of history's.

The ideas outlived the men. The Manifesto claimed that all history was the story of a struggle between economic classes, an idea at the core of Marx's view of the past and still his claim, not a settled fact. In 1844 Marx called religion the sigh of the oppressed and the heart, as he put it, of a heartless world, and then came the line everyone remembers: it was the opium of the people, a painkiller for a hard life. His tomb carries his 1845 jab at the thinkers before him: philosophers had only explained the world in various ways, while the real task was to change it. His followers did try to change it, and the twentieth century paid the price.

mary-anning-the-fossil-hunter-of-lyme-re.context_blurb:
Mary Anning was born in 1799 in Lyme Regis, a little seaside town in Dorset, England, beneath cliffs crammed with the bones of sea creatures some two hundred million years old. Her family was poor, and her father, a cabinetmaker who sold curiosities to tourists, died when she was eleven. Selling fossils kept them alive, and Mary became one of the greatest fossil finders who ever lived.

Her life began with a near miracle. In August 1800, lightning struck an elm where a woman stood holding the baby Mary, killing three women, and the limp child was carried home and revived in a tub of hot water. The town later joked that the bolt explained her sharp curiosity. In 1811 her brother Joseph dug a four-foot skull like a crocodile's out of the cliffs, and months later twelve-year-old Mary went back and freed the rest of the animal, a skeleton some seventeen feet long. At the British Museum, Charles Konig named the creature an ichthyosaur, meaning fish-lizard, because it swam like a fish yet was an air-breathing reptile. The work was dangerous, since the cliffs crumbled in every storm. In October 1833 a landslide came down on her little terrier Tray and killed him in an instant before her eyes, and Mary herself escaped by a moment.

Science did not pay the bills, and the Annings hunted bones to keep from starving. They sold that first ichthyosaur to Henry Hoste Henley, a local gentleman who was lord of the manor of Colway, for about 23 pounds. On 10 December 1823 Mary found her most startling monster, the four-flippered Plesiosaurus, with a neck so long, around 35 vertebrae, that experts who saw only drawings refused to believe it. In December 1828 she uncovered the first pterosaur ever found outside Germany, a flying reptile that William Buckland of Oxford named Pterodactylus macronyx.

She was a sharp thinker as well as a finder. Inside ichthyosaur skeletons she kept finding polished lumps that scholars called bezoar stones, and when she broke them open and saw fish bones and scales, she worked out that they were fossilised droppings. Buckland named them coprolites and, unusually, gave her credit. Others did not. When William Conybeare showed her plesiosaur to the Geological Society of London in 1824, using the drawing she had made, he never mentioned her name at all. Friends helped when she faced ruin. In 1830 Henry De la Beche painted Duria Antiquior, a scene of ancient Dorset swarming with her reptiles, and sold prints to raise money for her, and it became the first picture of deep time that ordinary people everywhere could see.

The great men took a long time to trust her. Georges Cuvier of France, the mightiest naturalist of his day, called her plesiosaur's neck impossible and accused her of gluing together bones from different animals to make a fake, until the 1824 Geological Society meeting proved the skeleton genuine and he admitted his mistake. She knew who profited from her work. Her friend Anna Pinney recorded Mary's bitter complaint that the learned men had sucked her brains, publishing books she had filled while she gained nothing. Even her legend got away from her. Many people say the tongue-twister about selling seashells was written about her. Stephen Winick, a folklorist at the Library of Congress, found that the rhyme was older folklore, that Terry Sullivan's 1908 song came more than a century after her birth, and that the song never mentions her at all.

mary-wollstonecraft-and-women-s-rights.context_blurb:
Mary Wollstonecraft was an English writer, born in 1759, who taught herself, worked as a governess and joined the radical writers of London. In 1792, in the middle of the French Revolution's arguments over the rights of man, she published her Vindication, a fierce defence of women's rights. She argued that women seemed weaker than men only because society denied them the education men received.

Her goal was not to turn the tables. She wrote that she had no wish for women to rule over men, but to have power over themselves: the power to reason and to govern their own lives. Reason, she argued, belongs to both sexes, so if rights rest on reason, denying girls a real education makes no sense.

That put her on a collision course with Jean-Jacques Rousseau, the most admired writer of the age. In his book Emile, Rousseau's model girl, Sophie, is raised only to please a man. Wollstonecraft quoted his advice and dismissed it in a few words, branding it the philosophy of lasciviousness. She died in 1797, just after giving birth to a daughter who grew up to be Mary Shelley, the author of Frankenstein.

mauryan-empire-ashoka-the-great.context_blurb:
The Mauryan Empire was the first state to unite almost all of India under one ruler, from about 322 to 185 BC. Its greatest emperor, Ashoka, began as a ruthless conqueror like his grandfather and father. Then one terrible war changed him, and he spent the rest of his reign carving messages of mercy into stone across the subcontinent. He is remembered for the conquest he refused to repeat.

The dynasty began in fear. Ashoka's grandfather, Chandragupta Maurya, overthrew the last Nanda king in 321 BC, yet he so dreaded assassins that he never slept in the same bedroom two nights running. Around 305 BC he beat Seleucus, once one of Alexander the Great's generals, and sealed the peace by giving him five hundred war elephants, which Seleucus later used to win the Battle of Ipsus. Legend says the adviser Chanakya fed Chandragupta tiny doses of poison to make him immune; when the pregnant queen ate from his plate and died, her unborn son was saved and named Bindusara for a drop of the poison that touched him. That child became Ashoka's father.

Ashoka then conquered the kingdom of Kalinga, and the slaughter haunted him. What makes his Rock Edict 13 nearly unique in the ancient world is that the victorious king himself had the death toll of his own war carved in stone: a hundred thousand slain, a hundred and fifty thousand carried off, and many more dead afterwards. Where another king would boast, Ashoka recorded his deep remorse and grief over the killing. He renounced war and declared that from then on he would seek only conquest by Dhamma, winning people over by teaching them to live rightly.

He spread that message on rocks and pillars. Rock Edict 1 boasts that the royal kitchen, which once killed thousands of animals a day, now killed just a pair of peacocks and one deer, and the deer not always. At Sarnath, where the Buddha first preached, a pillar was crowned with four lions set back to back, facing outward. Carved from one block of sandstone some 2,300 years ago, that lion capital still carries a mirror-like polish that shines today. Modern India adopted the four lions as its national emblem. Beneath them sits the Wheel of Law, and a 24-spoke version of it, the Ashoka Chakra, now stands at the centre of India's national flag.

Ashoka sent his own children abroad as missionaries. His daughter Sanghamitta, a Buddhist nun, carried a sapling of the Buddha's own tree to Sri Lanka in a golden vase, and the tree she set in the earth at Anuradhapura is still alive, the oldest planted tree with a recorded planting anywhere on Earth.

Then the emperor vanished from memory. In almost all his inscriptions he used not the name Ashoka but the title Devanampiya Piyadasi, Beloved of the Gods, so after his empire collapsed nobody knew who had carved them, and his identity stayed lost for about two thousand years. Even the Brahmi script became unreadable. In 1837 James Prinsep, a British scholar, deciphered it, and an old chronicle from Sri Lanka that named the same king let him prove that Beloved of the Gods was the lost emperor Ashoka. In 1915 an edict found at Maski settled it, naming him outright as Devanampiya Ashoka.

maya-astronomy-and-the-long-count-calend.context_blurb:
The Maya built their stone cities across southern Mexico, Guatemala and Belize, and for centuries their priest-astronomers watched the Sun, the Moon and above all the planet Venus with nothing but their eyes. They wove several calendars together, including the Long Count, which numbered the days from a mythical starting point far in the past. Its cycle that ended in 2012 meant a new beginning to the Maya, not the end of the world.

Their mathematics was as bold as their stargazing. Maya numbers needed only three marks: a dot meant one, a bar meant five, and a picture of a shell meant zero. With those three signs a scribe could write any number at all. The Maya dreamed up zero on their own, over a thousand years before the idea finally reached Europe by way of India and the Arabic numerals. Only a handful of peoples in all history ever invented zero from nothing.

Most of what they wrote is gone. Diego de Landa, a Spanish bishop, heaped up every Maya bark-paper book he could seize in 1562 and burned them at Mani, and after the conquest only four Maya books were left on Earth. The finest of them ended up in a library in Dresden, Germany, and took its name from the city. It nearly perished a second time in February 1945, when the Allied firebombing of Dresden soaked it with water, yet it stayed readable.

That book shows how precise the Maya were. Its tables count the cycle of Venus as 584 days, while the true average is 583.92, so with the naked eye the Maya missed by less than a tenth of a day. They even built in a correction, like a leap year, to keep the count from drifting.

maya-writing-and-the-dresden-codex.context_blurb:
The Maya were the only people in the Americas before Columbus known to have a full writing system, one that could record any sentence of their spoken language. They carved it on temples, painted it on pottery and folded it into bark-paper books for more than a thousand years. Then the Spanish came, and for centuries nobody could read a word of it.

The man who did the most damage also left the key. Bishop Diego de Landa burned nearly all the Maya books he could lay hands on in 1562, but in his own account of Yucatan he wrote down a list pairing Maya glyphs with the letters of the Spanish alphabet. For centuries that "de Landa alphabet" seemed useless, because the signs never matched up.

In 1952 a young Soviet scholar, Yuri Knorozov, spotted the mistake: when de Landa asked for the letter b, the Maya scribe drew the sign for the syllable be, because the script was a syllabary in which each glyph stands for a spoken syllable. The useless list became the Rosetta Stone of Maya writing. Knorozov cracked the code from photographs in Moscow and did not see a Maya ruin until 1990.

mccarthyism-the-red-scare.context_blurb:
In the late 1940s and early 1950s, as the Cold War began, Americans feared that Soviet spies and secret communists were burrowing into their government. Some really were. But Senator Joseph McCarthy of Wisconsin turned the fear into a crusade of accusation without evidence that wrecked careers, and his name became a word for exactly that. The Red Scare is a story of real spies and real injustice at once.

The hunt began in Congress and Hollywood. In 1947 a House committee demanded that ten screenwriters and directors, among them Dalton Trumbo, say whether they had ever joined the Communist Party, and when the Hollywood Ten refused, they were sent to prison and blacklisted by the studios. Trumbo kept writing under false names, paid a fraction of his old fees. When his script The Brave One won an Oscar in 1956, nobody came up to claim it, and the gossip columnist Hedda Hopper demanded to know who the hell Robert Rich was. Real spying was going on too. In 1948 the former communist Whittaker Chambers led investigators to his Maryland farm and pulled rolls of spy film out of a hollowed-out pumpkin, evidence against the State Department official Alger Hiss. Hiss was convicted of perjury. In Albuquerque, the Soviet courier Harry Gold and the spy David Greenglass, a machinist from Los Alamos, proved who they were by fitting together the torn halves of a Jell-O box top.

McCarthy seized the moment. In Wheeling, West Virginia, in February 1950, he waved a paper he said listed communists in the State Department, but as the number shifted from 205 to 57 to 81 to 10, he never revealed the list and never proved a case against a single person on it. When Senator Millard Tydings called the charges a fraud, McCarthy's staff spread several hundred thousand copies of a faked photo showing Tydings chatting with the American Communist leader Earl Browder, and Tydings lost his seat. Yet the spies were not imaginary. The physicist Klaus Fuchs passed bomb plans from Los Alamos to Moscow, and experts reckon he let the Soviets build their first atomic bomb one to two years earlier. In June 1953 Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were electrocuted in Sing Sing prison, and Ethel survived the first jolts, so it took five to kill her.

The fall came in 1954. In March the broadcaster Edward R. Murrow turned McCarthy's own filmed words against him on See It Now and told Americans that they were not descended from fearful men. The showdown that finished McCarthy began over a favour: his chief counsel, Roy Cohn, had spent months bullying the Army to give a cushy posting to his friend G. David Schine, a drafted private. In the televised hearings that followed, McCarthy smeared a young lawyer, Fred Fisher, and the Army's counsel, Joseph Welch, asked him whether, at long last, he had no sense of decency. The room burst into applause. That December the Senate condemned him, and he drank himself to death; he died at 48 in 1957 of alcoholic liver failure, though the official certificate blamed acute hepatitis.

The full truth came out only later. The Venona project's decoded Soviet cables named Julius Rosenberg as a spy, but prosecutors could not use them in court because they were still classified, and they stayed secret until 1995. In 2001 Ethel's brother, David Greenglass, admitted that he had lied at the trial and had never seen her type anything, to shield his own wife. Julius truly spied, but Ethel may have died on her brother's perjury.

mecca-the-kaaba-and-the-hajj.context_blurb:
Mecca, in western Arabia, is the holiest city of Islam and the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad. Every Muslim who is able is expected to make a pilgrimage there at least once, and each year about two million pilgrims come. They follow rituals that Muhammad himself performed on his farewell pilgrimage in the seventh century.

At the centre of the Grand Mosque stands the Kaaba, a cube-shaped stone shrine draped in black cloth, and pilgrims walk around it seven times. Its name means cube, and Muslims everywhere face it when they pray. Each man lays aside his own clothes and wraps himself in the ihram, a pair of plain white sheets, so that in the vast crowd no one can tell a king from a beggar, all equal before God.

Set in one corner of the Kaaba is the Black Stone, which pilgrims try to touch or kiss. In 930 the Qarmatians, a sect of raiders, carried it off to eastern Arabia, and when it came back some twenty-two years later, it was broken into seven pieces. That is why it is still cemented together inside a silver frame.

medieval-jewish-life-persecution.context_blurb:
In medieval Christian Europe, Jewish communities lived as a protected but second-class people. Kings taxed them, expelled them or shielded them as it suited their purses, mobs blamed them for plagues and murdered them, and laws barred them from most trades. Yet in Muslim Spain and beyond, Jewish scholars and physicians thrived and wrote works still read today.

Moses Maimonides was a boy when conquerors ordered the Jews of Cordoba to convert, leave or die, so his family fled, and he became a physician at Saladin's court; his tomb at Tiberias declares that from Moses to Moses there was none like Moses. The first Moses is the prophet and the last is Maimonides, ranked as the greatest Jewish mind since the lawgiver himself. His Guide for the Perplexed joined Aristotle's philosophy to the Torah.

In 1516 the city council of Venice forced every Jew onto a small island that had once held a foundry, called a geto in Venetian, and that is how the world got the word ghetto. The council's guards locked the gates from outside each night and opened them only when the great bell of St Mark's rang in the morning.

medieval-knight-s-arms-armor.context_blurb:
A knight of the late Middle Ages in full plate armour was one of the costliest war machines his world could build. Hinged steel covered him from crown to toe, shaped to turn aside blades and arrows, and equipping one man could cost a village a whole year's income. Every piece had its own name, and every knight trained from boyhood to wear it.

The helm guarded his head, the gauntlet his hand and the greave his shin, while the sabaton was a steel shoe for his foot, ending in a long sharp toe. Knights also loved legendary swords. For centuries the cliff village of Rocamadour in France kept an old sword lodged in the rock above a chapel and called it Durendal, the blade of the hero Roland, until in June 2024 someone pulled it out and stole it.

In the Song of Roland, the dying Roland tries to keep Durendal from his enemies by smashing it on a rock. Instead the stone cracked in two and the blade came through without a mark, because, the poem says, its golden hilt held holy relics. Real armour was less magical but cleverer than people think. A full suit weighed only about twenty to twenty-five kilograms spread across the body, so a knight swung into the saddle on his own with one foot in the stirrup, and the story of a crane hoisting him onto his horse is a myth. That myth comes from an 1843 joke in Punch magazine and a 1944 film.

A knight sealed in steel needed a sign. Heraldry painted each family's symbols on its shield, in colours with their own names, such as gules for red and azure for blue. Its rule of tincture banned metal on metal and colour on colour, because a coat of arms had to be read in an instant across a battlefield, and only strong contrast made that possible.

medieval-medicine-the-calendar-daily-lif.context_blurb:
Medieval doctors inherited a theory from Greek and Arab writers: the body held four fluids, called humours, and health meant keeping them in balance. Bleeding, purging, special diets and remedies timed to the stars all aimed at that balance. Barbers doubled as surgeons, village women served as midwives and herbalists, and the whole year ran by the church calendar.

Barbers pulled teeth, lanced boils and drained blood into bowls, and the striped pole outside a barbershop began as their sign, the red standing for blood and the white for the bandages. Legend says the first poles were the stained bandages themselves, hung out to dry and twisting into a spiral in the wind. Feast days set the farming year. Ploughing could start at Candlemas, and the first loaf went to the lord at Lammas. Michaelmas, on 29 September, closed the harvest, and on that same day the peasants' rent fell due to the lord.

The humours left their mark on English. A cheerful, rosy person was called sanguine, from the Latin word for blood, because doctors believed he had more blood than any other humour.

Sometimes real knowledge broke through. In 1537 the boiling oil used to seal gunshot wounds gave out on Ambroise Pare, a French barber-surgeon, so he tried a soothing salve instead, and next morning the men he had salved were resting easily while the men burned with oil lay in agony. He concluded that he only bandaged a man and God healed him. In 2015 a Nottingham University team brewed an eye salve from Bald's Leechbook, a thousand-year-old Anglo-Saxon book of remedies, and found that it killed MRSA, a modern superbug that resists antibiotics. Only the full mixture worked, as if its maker had tuned the recipe.

medieval-universities-scholasticism.context_blurb:
In the twelfth and thirteenth centuries Europe invented the university: a self-governing body of teachers and students in cities like Paris, Bologna and Oxford. Young men from all over Christendom came to study the liberal arts, then law, medicine or theology, all in Latin. Gowns, degrees and graduation ceremonies still come down to us from these medieval scholars.

At Bologna the students ran everything, through a guild with an elected student Rector. The students there hired their professors and paid them out of their own pockets, so the teachers worked for the class. A master who started his lecture late or came unprepared was fined out of his pay, nine Bolognese pounds for a late start, and students elected official denouncers to report him. The greatest scholar of the age had a rough start. When the young Thomas Aquinas chose to join the Dominicans, the begging friars, his rich family seized him and kept him locked in a tower of their castle for about a year. He would not give in. Because he was huge and almost never spoke in class, his classmates called him the Dumb Ox, but his teacher Albert the Great warned that this ox's bellowing would one day fill the world.

The word university does not mean all-embracing learning. The Latin universitas simply meant a guild or corporation, the same word used for merchants and craftsmen, so it named the people, not the buildings. Books were hand-copied and costly, so in a lecture the master read the set text aloud, word by word, while students copied it, and then he explained it; the word comes from the Latin for a reading. In early Paris the brilliant logician Peter Abelard drew crowds, and when he and his pupil Heloise had a son, they named the boy Astrolabe, after an instrument for measuring the stars. In 1209 a deadly fight with townspeople drove a band of scholars out of Oxford, and the town where they settled became the home of Cambridge.

The university's freedom had limits. A scholar became a master by winning the licentia docendi, the license to teach, and it was granted not by the university but by the Church, through the chancellor of the local bishop. Students could fight back, though. In 1229 Paris saw history's first great student strike, set off when students quarrelled with a tavern keeper over their bill for wine, and the queen's guards killed several of them. The masters stopped teaching for two years and won a papal charter of freedom.

The deepest fights were over ideas. In 1277 Bishop Etienne Tempier of Paris condemned 219 propositions, among them the claim that all human beings share one single intellect, which would deny each person his own soul. The method of the age, scholasticism, was patient debate. Each article of the Summa Theologica opens with the arguments against Aquinas's own view, stated at their strongest, before he gives his reply and answers each one.

medieval-women-s-lives-roles.context_blurb:
Medieval women lived under heavier legal limits than their fathers and brothers. Yet the record is full of women who ruled estates and kingdoms, ran trades and great abbeys, wrote books and argued with popes. Their story shatters the easy picture of silent women shut away, from queens and saints down to the village brewer.

Eleanor of Aquitaine, heiress to a great duchy in southern France, was first queen of France as the wife of Louis VII, and after the pope annulled that marriage, she wed Henry II and was crowned queen of England. Ordinary women found their own independence. Most trades were closed to them, but brewing ale at home was women's work. Women who sold their extra ale from their own front doors were called alewives, and the trade gave them money of their own.

In 1147 Eleanor did not stay home while Louis went on the Second Crusade: she rode east toward the Holy Land with her own company of ladies from Aquitaine. Two centuries later, a widow broke new ground. When the plague killed Christine de Pizan's husband in 1389, she had young children, a niece and her own mother depending on her, and rather than remarry she made her living as a professional writer, the first woman in Europe known to do so.

Church women held real power. In 664 the Northumbrian king Oswiu chose the abbey of Hilda of Whitby to host the synod that settled how the English Church would fix the date for Easter. Hildegard of Bingen, around the age of sixty, made four preaching tours between 1158 and 1170, preaching sermons to crowds of men in cities like Cologne. She also wrote to popes and emperors.

Both women fought for room of their own. Around 1150 Hildegard broke free of the abbot who housed her nuns and founded her own monastery at Rupertsberg. In 1405 Christine answered the poets who painted women as wicked with The Book of the City of Ladies, building a walled city for the great women of history.

mendel-and-the-birth-of-genetics.context_blurb:
Gregor Mendel, a friar of the Augustinian order, lived at the monastery of St. Thomas in Brno, in what is now the Czech Republic. In the 1850s and 1860s he ran one of the most patient experiments in the history of science in the monastery garden, and he discovered that living things pass on their traits in separate units, the ones we now call genes.

From 1856 to 1863 he grew and crossed about 28,000 plants, most of them pea plants, because peas were cheap, bred fast and showed clear traits such as seed colour and stem height. He counted every result and found that the traits came back in steady mathematical ratios.

In 1865 he explained his findings to some forty people at the local natural history society, and the scientific world ignored them for about thirty-five years. He became abbot and died in 1884 almost unknown as a scientist. Near the end, the story goes, he told a colleague, "My time will come." In 1900 three botanists, Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak, rediscovered his laws on their own and gave the monk his due.

mendel-and-the-foundations-of-genetics.context_blurb:
Gregor Mendel was an Augustinian friar, later abbot, at a monastery in Brno, in today's Czech Republic. For eight years he crossbred ordinary garden peas, kept careful counts of tens of thousands of plants, and did the arithmetic. Out of those counts came the laws of heredity, the foundation of modern genetics.

His key trick was to follow one trait at a time. When he crossed round-seeded peas with wrinkled ones, every offspring was round, but when those hybrids pollinated themselves, the wrinkled seeds came back in about a quarter of the next generation, a ratio of roughly three round to one wrinkled. The wrinkled trait had been hidden, not blended away. Mendel called the trait that shows dominant and the one that hides recessive.

In 1865 he read his results to a little scientific society, and in 1866 he published them, but almost no one understood them, and he died in 1884 still ignored. In 1900 Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak each worked out the same laws independently, then found Mendel's forgotten paper and saw that he had reached them thirty-five years before them. They said so publicly, and his name has carried the science ever since.

mexican-independence-and-father-hidalgo.context_blurb:
In 1810 Mexico was New Spain, a vast colony ruled from Madrid for three hundred years, with Spanish-born officials at the top and the Indian and mixed-race poor at the bottom. In the parish of Dolores, north of Mexico City, lived Miguel Hidalgo, a Creole priest who had read Enlightenment books and secretly joined a plot against Spanish rule.

Warned that the plot had been discovered, he struck first. Before dawn on 16 September 1810, Hidalgo rang his church bell, gathered his parishioners and urged them to take up arms against Spain, and that call is remembered as the Grito de Dolores, the Cry of Dolores. Mexicans still celebrate it every 16 September, and each year the president rings Hidalgo's bell again.

On the march the next day, at the church in Atotonilco, Hidalgo took down a banner of the Virgin of Guadalupe, the patron of Mexico, and made it his army's standard. The dark-skinned Virgin drew thousands of Indian and mixed-race fighters to his cause. Hidalgo was captured and executed the following year, but independence came in 1821.
