michelangelo.context_blurb:
Michelangelo Buonarroti, a Florentine who lived from 1475 to 1564, was a sculptor, painter, architect and poet, and he worked for a long line of popes who both adored and infuriated him. In his own mind he was always a sculptor first. His David, his Pieta and the Sistine Chapel ceiling were treated as miracles even in his own lifetime.

People who saw the awesome power of his work called the man himself Il Divino, the Divine One. Older sculptors showed David after the battle, standing over Goliath's head, but Michelangelo carved him before the fight, tense and alert, measuring his enemy.

The marble for the David had lain outside for some twenty-five years after two sculptors gave up on its cracks and veins, and Florentines called the block Il Gigante, the Giant. The famous tale of Michelangelo painting the Sistine ceiling lying down is false: he painted standing upright on his own scaffolding, his head bent back and paint dripping onto his face. Even his face told a story: as a teenager in the Medici garden, a jealous fellow student, Pietro Torrigiano, punched him so hard that he shattered his nose, leaving it crooked for life.

In 1499, after hearing pilgrims credit his Pieta to another sculptor, Michelangelo slipped into the chapel by night and cut his name with a chisel along the sash across Mary's chest, the only work he ever signed. When the David was finished, more than forty men took four days to roll the statue, some six tonnes of marble, half a mile across Florence.

Rivals and critics troubled him. His biographer Condivi claimed that the architect Bramante pushed the ceiling job onto Michelangelo hoping the sculptor would fail at a painter's task. In 1509 he wrote a comic sonnet complaining of his aching neck and dripping beard, and he ended it by saying he was in the wrong place and was no painter. When the papal official Biagio da Cesena called the nudes of the Last Judgment fit for a bathhouse, Michelangelo painted him into hell as Minos, the judge of the damned, with donkey ears and a snake biting his groin. The pope joked that his power did not reach into hell, so Biagio stayed there.

Michelangelo died in Rome, and to bring him home his nephew smuggled the body past the guards wrapped in a bale and labelled as ordinary merchandise. He lies in Santa Croce in Florence. The line about seeing an angel in the marble is almost certainly not his, but in a genuine sonnet for Vittoria Colonna he wrote that the more the marble wastes away, the more the statue grows.

michelangelo.title: Michelangelo

michelangelo-sistine-ceiling-and-david.context_blurb:
Michelangelo Buonarroti, who lived from 1475 to 1564, was the giant of the Italian Renaissance: sculptor, painter, architect and poet. He considered sculpture his true calling, yet popes kept forcing brushes into his hands. Two of his works stand above almost everything else in Western art: the marble David in Florence and the Sistine Chapel's painted ceiling in Rome.

Unveiled in Florence in 1504, the David was carved from one block of marble and rises about 17 feet, roughly three times the height of a man. The legend of Michelangelo lying on his back to paint the Sistine ceiling is a myth; he painted on his feet, high on a wooden scaffold, craning his neck. In 1991 an attacker, Piero Cannata, pulled a hammer from under his jacket and broke off part of one of David's toes before he was stopped.

Before Michelangelo claimed the block in 1501, two other sculptors had started on it and given up, and it lay for decades in the cathedral yard, where Florentines nicknamed it il Gigante, the Giant. In the Creation of Adam, the most famous fingers in art never actually meet: a tiny gap keeps God's hand and Adam's apart.

David's head and right hand look oversized because he was meant to stand high on the roofline of Florence Cathedral, to be seen from far below. Florence judged him too magnificent for that and set him by the town hall instead. Workers knocked down an archway to free him, and more than forty men rolled him over fourteen greased logs to the town hall. When Michelangelo began painting the chapel's vault in 1508, he threw out Bramante's hanging scaffold, because its rope anchors would have punched holes in the very surface he had to paint. His first big scene, the Flood, was ruined when mould bloomed across the fresh plaster, because a plaster mix that worked in Florence failed in the damp air of Rome, and he had to chip it off and start again.

Earlier, Donatello and Verrocchio showed David triumphant over Goliath's head, but Michelangelo chose the tense instant before the battle, the sling resting on David's shoulder. Miserable on the scaffold, he sent Giovanni da Pistoia a comic poem and ended it by saying flatly that he was not a painter.

Close study shows him growing as he worked. He painted the nine Genesis scenes backwards, from the Drunkenness of Noah toward the altar, and his figures grew bigger and bolder as he went. Some scholars think the prophet Zechariah has the face of Pope Julius II, who once struck Michelangelo with a stick, and that the boy behind him is making the rude fig gesture at the pope. That reading is a tradition, not a proven fact.

ming-china-zheng-he-s-treasure-fleets-th.context_blurb:
The Ming dynasty ruled China from the fourteenth to the seventeenth century. Its emperors moved the capital to Beijing, rebuilt the Great Wall in stone and brick, and in the early 1400s sent the Muslim eunuch admiral Zheng He on seven huge voyages, with fleets of hundreds of ships, across the Indian Ocean as far as East Africa.

In 1414 his fleet brought home a live giraffe from Africa, and the court hailed it as a qilin, a gentle Chinese unicorn said to appear only under a wise ruler. The Yongle Emperor had it painted, though he said good government mattered more than omens.

China stood ready to rule the seas, decades before Columbus. Instead, once the seventh voyage came home in 1433, the court let the treasure fleet decay and forbade ocean voyages with its sea-ban laws, and decades later, by the usual account, officials destroyed the records of the expeditions. China turned inward just as European ships began to venture out.

ming-dynasty-the-forbidden-city.context_blurb:
The Ming dynasty ruled China from 1368 to 1644, after the Chinese threw out their Mongol overlords. Its founder rose from utter poverty to the throne, and his son, the Yongle Emperor, moved the capital north to Beijing and built a walled palace there between 1406 and 1420. Ming and then Qing emperors lived in that Forbidden City for nearly five hundred years, until 1912.

The founder, Zhu Yuanzhang, was sixteen when plague killed his parents and his elder brother within weeks, and he survived by entering a Buddhist monastery and begging for food in the streets. From that beggar's bowl he climbed to the throne as the Hongwu Emperor. The palace earned its name because any ordinary person who entered or left it without the emperor's permission could be executed. His son, Yongle, sent fleets under the admiral Zheng He as far as the coasts of Arabia and East Africa. Columbus crossed the Atlantic with three ships and under a hundred men, but one of Zheng He's fleets numbered some 300 ships carrying about 28,000 men.

The palace was built as a map of heaven. Legend says its builders stopped half a room short of the 10,000 rooms of the Heavenly Emperor's palace, building 9,999 and a half, though a 1973 survey counted 8,707. Its Chinese name means Purple Forbidden City, and the purple pointed to the North Star, Polaris, the still point around which the whole sky turns, just as the world was meant to turn around the emperor. The throne halls are paved with golden bricks, clay tiles fired for months near Suzhou and shipped north on the Grand Canal, named not for any gold but because they ring like metal when struck. Yongle had seized the throne by making war on his nephew, the Jianwen Emperor, who vanished when the Nanjing palace burned in 1402, and legend says he slipped away dressed as a wandering monk and lived almost forty years more.

The central doorway of the Meridian Gate was for the emperor alone; the empress used it once, on her wedding day, and the three highest scorers in the empire's civil-service examination each walked through it once as well. Learning was prized that highly. When Zheng He brought a giraffe home from Africa in 1414, Yongle's courtiers declared it a qilin, a creature that appears only under a perfectly wise ruler, which gave the usurper a stamp of approval from heaven. Yongle set some 2,000 scholars to compile the Yongle Encyclopedia, more than 11,000 volumes by 1408, and it stayed the largest encyclopedia on Earth until Wikipedia passed it in 2007. The Ming had a dark side too. In 1380 Hongwu accused his chancellor, Hu Weiyong, of treason and had over 15,000 officials and their families killed, and he is said to have complained that he punished a few each morning, only to find others committing the same crime by evening.

The greatest navy on Earth did not survive. After Yongle died, Confucian officials called the voyages wasteful, and around 1477, according to the story, the court official Liu Daxia hid or burned Zheng He's records so that no emperor could send the fleets out again. China turned inward just as Europe began sailing out.

ming-voyages-of-zheng-he.context_blurb:
Zheng He was a Chinese Muslim eunuch who, between 1405 and 1433, led seven giant naval expeditions for the Ming emperors. His fleets of hundreds of ships and tens of thousands of men crossed the Indian Ocean to Arabia and East Africa, collecting tribute and showing off China's power. Then China called the ships home for good.

In 1414 a live giraffe arrived at court from overseas, and Yongle's courtiers hailed it as a qilin, a gentle unicorn from old legend that appears only when Heaven blesses the throne. By the old Ming records, his greatest treasure ships ran about 400 feet long, so huge that all the ships of Columbus and Vasco da Gama put together could have fitted on one deck. A rudder post some 36 feet long, dug up at a Nanjing shipyard in 1957, hints at their scale.

These fleets sailed some sixty to ninety years before Columbus made his Atlantic crossing of 1492, and long before da Gama reached India. After Zheng He died, Liu Daxia, an official of the War Ministry, fearing future rulers might copy the voyages, is recorded as destroying the fleet's logs and charts, and the maps were lost forever.

In 1409 the fleet set up a stone at Galle, on Ceylon, that thanks three gods side by side: the Buddha in Chinese, Vishnu in Tamil and Allah in Persian. Lost for centuries, it turned up in 1911 as the cover of a roadside drain.

moctezuma-ii-and-the-spanish-conquest-of.context_blurb:
Moctezuma II ruled the Aztec empire from Tenochtitlan, a shining island city in a mountain lake, when Hernan Cortes and a few hundred Spanish soldiers arrived on Mexico's Gulf coast in 1519. Within two years the empire was gone, brought down by Spanish steel and horses, by disease, and by huge armies of Indigenous warriors who hated Aztec rule. The soldier Bernal Diaz left the great eyewitness account.

Before he took the throne, Moctezuma had been a war leader and high priest of the war god Huitzilopochtli, and his name means roughly he who frowns like a lord. When the Spanish first saw Tenochtitlan rising from the water, Bernal Diaz wrote, it looked like the enchantments told in the romance of Amadis, and some men asked whether they were dreaming. When Moctezuma met Cortes on the causeway in November 1519, he gave him collars of red shells hung with golden shrimp, each some eighteen inches long. Cortes later built a navy in the mountains. The shipwright Martin Lopez built him thirteen small warships far from any water, and they were hauled overland in pieces and put back together on the shore of Lake Texcoco. The last emperor, Cuauhtemoc, whose name means Descending Eagle, led the city's defence to the very end in August 1521.

The conquest was not a few hundred Spaniards against an empire. Cortes spoke Spanish to Geronimo de Aguilar, who put it into Maya for a Nahua noblewoman, La Malinche, who then spoke to the Aztecs in Nahuatl, so every word passed through two interpreters and three languages. His greatest allies were the Tlaxcalans of Tlaxcala, a people the Aztecs had never conquered, who sent warriors by the tens of thousands because they were sick of Aztec tribute. The deadliest weapon was one the Spanish never meant to bring: smallpox, which killed millions across Mexico in 1520, among them Moctezuma's successor. In May 1520 Cortes's captain Pedro de Alvarado attacked unarmed Aztec nobles at a festival, and Aztec accounts say his men began by cutting off the arms of the man beating the great drum. On the Night of Sorrows, 30 June 1520, the Spanish tried to slip out along a causeway, and soldiers who had stuffed their clothes with stolen gold sank and drowned, dragged down by its weight. When Cuauhtemoc was caught fleeing by canoe, he touched the dagger at Cortes's belt and asked Cortes to kill him with it, having done all he could for his city.

Some famous scenes are later inventions. Cortes never burned his ships; he had them stripped of anchors, sails and rigging and run aground, so that his men could not sail home. Aztec accounts written decades afterwards tell of eight omens, among them a grey bird with a mirror in its head in which Moctezuma saw warriors riding strange deer, that is, men on horses. Historians treat those omens as largely a story told after the conquest. Even Moctezuma's death in June 1520 is disputed: Bernal Diaz wrote that stones thrown by his own Aztec people struck him, while some Indigenous sources say the Spanish killed him.

mongol-empire-genghis-khan.context_blurb:
In the early 1200s a steppe chieftain's son united the quarrelling tribes of Mongolia and launched some of the most devastating conquests in history. As Genghis Khan he and his heirs took northern China, Central Asia, Persia, Russia and Baghdad, and killed millions in cities that resisted. Yet the same empire also made the Silk Road safe and tied Asia and Europe together.

He was born around 1162 and named Temujin, after a Tatar warrior his father had captured, and the name meant of iron, or blacksmith. Genghis Khan, probably meaning universal ruler, was a title he took in 1206. His warriors rode with a deadly weapon. The Mongol composite bow, built from layers of horn, sinew and wood, needed a pull of over a hundred pounds yet was light enough to shoot at full gallop, striking targets some 350 yards away. By the 1290s the Mongols held the largest unbroken block of land any empire has ever ruled, nearly 23.5 million square kilometres. Messages crossed it on the Yam, a chain of relay posts where fresh horses and new riders stood ready, so that urgent news could cover 200 miles in a day.

For the most urgent mail a rider wore a belt hung with bells, and their jingling warned the next station from far off to have a fresh horse waiting. A messenger also carried a paiza, a metal tablet that served as his passport, opening with the words "By the power of eternal Heaven" and threatening death to anyone who disrespected him. Under this Mongol peace the roads grew so safe that people said a young woman could carry gold across the whole realm and come to no harm. In battle the Mongols loved one trick. At Mohi in Hungary in April 1241, Subutai's horsemen pretended to run away, then wheeled round and shot down the Hungarians chasing them.

Merit, not birth, made Mongol generals. Subutai, who conquered thirty-two nations, was born a blacksmith's son, without a drop of royal blood and with no kinship to the Khan. Revenge drove the great war in the west. In 1218 Genghis sent a caravan of some 450 merchants to Otrar, and the governor, Inalchuq, called them spies, killed every one and took their goods. When the Shah beheaded Genghis's envoy too, the Mongols invaded. Genghis died in 1227, and his grave has never been found. Tradition says his escort killed travellers who saw the funeral, and riders drove their horses over the grave until it was trampled flat.

The conquests were soaked in blood. In 1221, after the Persian city of Nishapur killed Genghis's son-in-law, Tolui had every inhabitant put to death, the poet Attar among them, and the severed heads were stacked into three pyramids as a warning. In 1258 Genghis's grandson Hulegu sacked Baghdad, and because Mongol custom forbade spilling royal blood on the ground, he had the caliph rolled up in a carpet and trampled to death by horses. Chroniclers said the Tigris ran black with ink from the city's libraries. A 2003 genetic study found one family line of Y chromosomes in about 8 percent of men across the old empire, some 16 million men, and suggested it came from Genghis and his sons. Later researchers have questioned that link.

mongol-threat-to-europe-subutai-1241.context_blurb:
In 1241 a Mongol army led by Subutai, the greatest general of Genghis Khan's empire, burst into central Europe. Within two days it destroyed a Polish army and a Hungarian one, and no force left in Europe could stand against it. Chroniclers believed the end of the world had come, and the pope wrote letters trying to learn who these riders were.

At Legnica on 9 April and at Mohi on 11 April, the Mongol horse-archers played the same trick on the heavily armoured knights: they charged, turned and fled, and when the knights broke ranks to chase them, the riders led them into a waiting ambush.

By the end of the year the Mongols were closing on Vienna and meant to ride on to the Atlantic. Then, far away in Mongolia, the Great Khan Ogedei died on 11 December 1241, and Mongol custom called the princes and their armies all the way home to choose his successor. They turned east and never came back. Europe was saved not by any victory but by the death of one man on the far side of Asia.

monitor-versus-merrimack-ironclads.context_blurb:
In March 1862, during the American Civil War, the age of wooden warships ended in Hampton Roads, Virginia. The Confederates had rebuilt a burned Union frigate, the Merrimack, with iron armour and renamed her CSS Virginia. The Union answered with a strange new ironclad designed by the Swedish engineer John Ericsson, the USS Monitor.

With its flat iron deck lying almost awash and a single round turret rising from the middle, the Monitor looked so odd that sailors called it a cheesebox floating on a raft. The turret could turn its two big guns to fire in any direction without turning the ship.

The Virginia struck first, on 8 March. She drove her heavy iron ram into the wooden sloop Cumberland, and as the Cumberland sank, the ram snapped off and stayed stuck inside her. Her chief engineer said the Virginia was like a wasp that could sting only once and leave the sting in the wound. The next morning the Monitor and the Virginia fought the first battle between ironclads, and neither could sink the other.

montesquieu-and-separation-of-powers.context_blurb:
Charles-Louis de Secondat, Baron de Montesquieu, was a French judge and nobleman who gave modern democracies one of their master ideas. In 1748 his great book, The Spirit of the Laws, argued that liberty survives only when the powers of government are split among separate hands that check each other. The men who wrote the American Constitution quoted him more than almost anyone.

At his moated chateau outside Bordeaux he lived as a country lord who grew and sold wine, and he fussed over every harvest. He first won fame in 1721 with the Persian Letters, a novel told in letters home from two Persian visitors to Paris, which let him mock French kings and priests safely through foreign eyes. His great book of 1748 named three powers, the legislative, which makes laws, the executive, which carries them out, and the judicial, which judges cases, and he warned that freedom dies when one person or group holds all three. Going nearly blind from cataracts in his last years, he kept working by dictating his words to secretaries until his death in 1755.

His reasoning started from a hard truth about people. Anyone given power, he wrote, tends to abuse it and to stretch his authority to its limit. So he did not wait for good rulers; he argued that the nature of things demands that power be set up to check power. He knew the danger from the inside, because for about eleven years he had been a judge, presiding over the criminal court of the high court of Bordeaux. In 1751 the Catholic Church placed his masterpiece on its list of forbidden books, and the ban only spread its fame.

He sorted governments by the passion that keeps each alive: a republic runs on virtue, a monarchy on honour, and a despotism on fear. His influence crossed the ocean. In Federalist No. 47, James Madison called Montesquieu the oracle whom everyone always consulted and cited on the separation of powers. When the scholar Donald Lutz counted the authors quoted by American writers from 1760 to 1805, Montesquieu's great book came first among human authors, beaten only by the Bible.

Madison sharpened the lesson. Gathering the lawmaking, enforcing and judging powers into the same hands, he wrote, may justly be called tyranny's very definition. Montesquieu wanted judges to apply the law exactly as written, nothing more than the mouth that pronounces the words of the law, with no power to soften it or harden it. And in Federalist No. 51 Madison wrote that ambition must be made to counteract ambition, so that each branch's hunger for power blocks the others.

monteverdi-and-the-birth-of-opera-palest.context_blurb:
Opera, a drama sung from start to finish, was born in Italy around 1600, when Florentine composers tried to bring back the sound of ancient Greek theatre. Claudio Monteverdi, who lived from 1567 to 1643, turned the experiment into great art. A generation earlier, Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina had perfected the sacred music of the Catholic Church.

In Monteverdi's L'Orfeo of 1607, the singer Orpheus reaches the river of the dead and wins his way across by singing so beautifully that the ferryman Charon is charmed into rowing him over. In the aria Possente spirto, Monteverdi piled up organ, violins, cornetts and harp to make the song itself the magic. L'Orfeo is the oldest opera still regularly staged today.

Palestrina's fame rests partly on a legend. At the Council of Trent, some churchmen wanted to ban music in which many voices sang different lines at once, because it buried the sacred words. A beloved story says his Missa Papae Marcelli, its words clear because the voices often moved together, showed that such music could be holy and understandable, and so saved the tradition from being banned. Modern scholars say his name probably never came up in the Council's debates.

mosque-architecture-minaret-dome-mihrab.context_blurb:
A mosque is a Muslim house of prayer, and most mosques share a few features that follow from how Muslims worship. A dome often crowns the prayer hall, and a slender tower, the minaret, carries the call to prayer out over the city. Inside there are no pews or statues, only carpets on which worshippers kneel and touch their foreheads to the ground.

In one wall of every mosque is a niche called the mihrab, and it exists to show the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca, which all Muslims face when they pray. The earliest mosques marked that direction with a painted line or a staff stuck in the ground.

The call to prayer goes back to Bilal, a freed African slave and one of Muhammad's first companions, famous for his beautiful voice. When Muhammad took Mecca in 630, he had Bilal climb to the top of the Kaaba and from there call the newly conquered city to prayer for the first time. Minaret towers came later.

mound-of-empires-end-atlantic-slave-trad.context_blurb:
Between the early 1500s and the 1860s, European ships carried about 12.5 million enslaved Africans across the Atlantic to labour on the plantations of the Americas. African kings and merchants captured most of them in wars and raids and sold them on the coast; European traders bought them, chained them and shipped them. Then, at the end, British Christian campaigners led the fight to end the trade.

Ships sailed a triangle: goods such as cloth and guns went to West Africa, captive Africans went west across the ocean on the Middle Passage, and sugar, tobacco and cotton went home to Europe. Olaudah Equiano, an Igbo boy kidnapped at about ten, saw the slave ship and its sailors and was terrified that the white men were about to eat him. His 1789 book became a powerful weapon against slavery. In 1787 the potter Josiah Wedgwood made a medallion of a kneeling African in chains, asking whether he was not a man and a brother. Women wore it as jewellery, and the cause became something people carried. In 1807, after twenty years of defeats, William Wilberforce saw the House of Commons ban the slave trade by 283 votes to 16, and as the members rose to cheer him, he stayed in his seat and wept for joy.

Abolitionists first printed a plan of the Brookes in Plymouth in 1788, and Thomas Clarkson spread it far and wide: a slave ship packed with more than 400 people, in which each grown person had only sixteen inches of width to lie in. The Royal Navy's most successful slave-ship hunter, HMS Black Joke, had herself been a slave ship, carrying some 3,000 captives to Brazil before the Navy seized her in 1827.

African rulers ran the inland end of the business. The Asante kings sold war captives to British and Dutch traders for guns, and used the guns to conquer more land and take still more captives. Europeans waited at the shore and bought their captives from kingdoms such as Dahomey because they judged raiding inland too deadly for themselves. The voyage was a horror. Equiano saw two chained captives, preferring death to such misery, force their way through the netting and leap into the sea. In 1781 the crew of the Liverpool ship Zong, short of water, threw about 132 Africans alive into the sea over several days.

The law treated them as cargo. When the Zong's owners claimed insurance for the dead, Lord Mansfield said the case was the same as if horses had been thrown over the side. The crew's excuse collapsed when records showed the ship had water to spare. Even an African king protested. In 1526 Afonso I of Kongo wrote to the king of Portugal that slavers were kidnapping his people, even his own relatives, and marking them with red-hot branding irons. He was ignored.

mozart-the-prodigy-composer.context_blurb:
Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, born in 1756 in Salzburg, in Austria, was performing for royalty and writing music while still a small child. In a life of only thirty-five years he poured out operas, symphonies, concertos and church music that stand at the heart of Western classical music. He died in Vienna in 1791 with a great work unfinished, and his fame only grew.

At his baptism one of his names was written in Greek, Theophilus, which in Latin became Amadeus, and both mean beloved of God. His father Leopold, a Salzburg music teacher, copied the boy's first tunes into his sister Nannerl's notebook, and the very first, written at about five, was a short minuet.

By the age of three he could already pick out tunes on the harpsichord. When he was six, Leopold took him and Nannerl on a grand tour to Munich, Vienna, Paris and London, where the child performed for kings and queens at Europe's grandest courts. In London he played for George III and Queen Charlotte.

He was still a child, though. When the scientist Daines Barrington tested the eight-year-old for the Royal Society, the boy sight-read perfectly and invented songs as he went, then suddenly left the harpsichord to go and play with his pet cat. At fourteen, in the Sistine Chapel during Holy Week of 1770, he heard Allegri's Miserere, a choral work the Vatican guarded jealously, and after that single hearing copied the entire piece down from memory. His opera Don Giovanni ends when the stone statue of a man the villain murdered comes to supper, and when the Don refuses to repent, it drags him down through the flaming floor into hell.

Legends cling to his genius. The story goes that on the night before Don Giovanni opened in Prague in 1787, he had not yet written the overture, and he composed all of it overnight in roughly three hours. When Emperor Joseph II supposedly complained that one opera had too many notes, Mozart is said to have answered that it had just as many as were needed. Both tales are famous but unproven. In 1791 a messenger in black brought an anonymous order for a Requiem, the Mass for the dead, and the sick, worn-out Mozart came to believe he was writing it for his own death. He died before finishing it; the last music in his own hand is the first eight bars of the Lacrimosa, and his pupil Franz Xaver Sussmayr completed the rest.

Scholars keep track of his huge output with the Kochel catalogue, giving each work a K. number, from K. 1, the minuet he wrote at five, to K. 626, the Requiem.

mozart-vs-salieri-the-poisoning-myth-vs-.context_blurb:
A famous legend says that Antonio Salieri, the court composer in Vienna, was so jealous of Mozart's genius that he poisoned him. Alexander Pushkin's verse play spread the idea, and the 1984 film Amadeus fixed it in everyone's mind. Historians have found no evidence for it at all; Mozart died of an illness in 1791, and Salieri was a respected colleague.

The two men even worked together. In 1785 Salieri, Mozart and a musician named Cornetti jointly wrote a cantata celebrating the recovery of the singer Nancy Storace, who had lost her voice and got it back. The score was thought lost until a musicologist found it in a Prague archive in 2015.

Far from a jealous nobody, Salieri served as Vienna's imperial music director for thirty-six years and often taught for free. Among his pupils were Beethoven, Franz Schubert and the piano master Carl Czerny. Beethoven even dedicated three violin sonatas to him.

muhammad-and-the-origins-of-islam.context_blurb:
Muhammad was born in Mecca, in western Arabia, around 570, and lost both parents young. Muslims believe that from about 610 God revealed the Quran to him through the angel Gabriel. Persecuted in Mecca, he and his followers moved to another city, built a community there, and by his death in 632 most of Arabia had accepted the new faith.

As a young man he drove caravans between Mecca and Syria and dealt so honestly that Meccan merchants called him al-Amin, the Trustworthy. Around 595 the wealthy widow Khadija, who was about forty and had hired the twenty-five-year-old to run her caravans, admired his character so much that she asked him to marry her. She became the first person to believe in his message.

When Mecca's clans rebuilt the Kaaba and nearly came to blows over who would put the holy Black Stone back in its corner, Muhammad spread a cloak, put the stone on it and had a man from each clan lift one corner, so all shared the honour. Around 610, in a cave on Mount Hira, he said the angel Gabriel gripped him and commanded him three times: Recite! The first verses of the Quran followed. His followers paid a price. Bilal, an enslaved convert, was pinned on burning sand under a boulder by his master, and through the torture he would say only "One, One," meaning that God is One. Abu Bakr later bought his freedom.

The leaders of Mecca pressed Muhammad's uncle, Abu Talib, to silence him. Muhammad vowed that even if they set the sun in his right hand and, in his left, the moon, he would not give up his mission. In 622 the clans plotted to kill him in his bed. His young cousin Ali ibn Abi Talib lay down in Muhammad's bed as a decoy while the prophet slipped away. Hiding in the Cave of Thawr with Abu Bakr as the searchers came close, Muhammad told his frightened friend not to grieve, because God was with them. The refugees settled in the oasis of Yathrib, renamed the City of the Prophet, which is known today as Medina. That migration, the Hijra, became Year One of the Islamic calendar, and Muslims still count their years from it.

Older stories filled out the history. Years before, persecuted Muslims had fled to the Christian king of Aksum, and when Ja'far, Muhammad's cousin, recited to him what the Quran says of Mary and of Jesus, the king wept until his beard was wet and refused to hand them back to Mecca. A tracker named Suraqa, chasing the 100-camel bounty, let Muhammad go after his horse sank in the sand, and years later, after Persia fell, Caliph Umar made him wear the captured bracelets of the Persian emperor, just as Muhammad had promised. In Medina, Muhammad bound the penniless emigrants from Mecca to the local helpers by pairing each emigrant with a helper as his brother. A pious legend says the searchers never looked inside the cave because a spider had spun a web across its mouth and a dove sat on her eggs at the entrance, though scholars find no reliable report of it.

mummification-and-the-afterlife.context_blurb:
For three thousand years the ancient Egyptians preserved their dead, because they believed the soul needed its body to live on in the next world. Embalmers emptied and dried the body, wrapped it in linen with amulets, and sealed it in nested coffins with a mask over the face. Food, furniture and scrolls of spells went into the tomb to help the dead on their journey.

Thinking the brain worthless, embalmers pushed a long hook up through the nose, stirred the brain into liquid, drained it out and threw it away. To dry the body they buried it in natron, a salt they called netjry, the divine salt, scraped from dry desert lakebeds. When Howard Carter opened Tutankhamun's innermost coffin in the 1920s, the boy king's face lay under a solid-gold death mask, two hammered sheets weighing about ten kilograms.

Embalmers carefully left one organ inside, the heart, because Egyptians believed it held a person's thoughts, feelings and character and would be needed at the final judgment. The liver, lungs, stomach and intestines went into four canopic jars, each lid carved as the head of a guardian god, one of Horus's four sons: a man, a baboon, a jackal or a falcon. While he cut, the chief embalmer wore a mask of the jackal-headed god Anubis, so that for those hours he became the god of the dead. The Greek traveller Herodotus, around 440 BC, wrote that the priests kept the body in natron for seventy days and that embalming longer than that was forbidden.

In the judgment of the dead, Anubis placed the heart in one pan of a scale and a single ostrich feather, the feather of Maat or truth, on the other. Beside the scale crouched Ammit, the Devourer, built from the three great man-eaters of the Nile, the crocodile, the lion and the hippopotamus, waiting to swallow a heart heavy with sin. So a green heart scarab was laid over the chest, carved with a spell that pleaded with the heart not to testify against its owner, a bribe to keep it quiet at the scales.

The name canopic is a European mistake: early travellers confused the organ jars with a Greek legend about Canopus, the helmsman of Menelaus, who was said to be worshipped in the shape of a jar. And though embalmers tossed the brain away, the Edwin Smith Surgical Papyrus, copied around 1600 BC from older writings, gave the first known written description of the brain and its folded surface.

mussolini-and-fascist-italy.context_blurb:
Benito Mussolini built fascism in Italy after the First World War from nationalism, hatred of Marxism, veterans' anger and street violence. He took power in 1922, crushed every rival party, invaded Ethiopia, allied with Hitler and led Italy into the Second World War, where his armies were beaten again and again. He fell in 1943 and died at the hands of Italian partisans in 1945.

He named his movement after the fasces, carried before Roman judges: a bundle of wooden rods bound around an axe, meaning strength through unity. He began as a socialist newspaper editor, but in 1914 the Socialist Party expelled him because he demanded that Italy join World War I while the party wanted neutrality. His propaganda made him Il Duce, the Leader, who was always right, and his staff left the lights in his office burning all night so that people would think he never stopped working.

When about 25,000 Blackshirts marched on Rome in October 1922, Mussolini was not with them; he was at the opera in Milan, close enough to the Swiss border to flee if the bluff failed. The king handed him power anyway.

In 1932 Mussolini and the philosopher Giovanni Gentile wrote The Doctrine of Fascism, which declared that the State stands above the individual, and that the individual exists to serve it. That is the real creed of fascism. In April 1945 he tried to escape to Switzerland in a German coat and helmet, but partisans at Dongo knew his bald head and heavy jaw from a thousand posters. They shot him the next day.

nato-vs-warsaw-pact.context_blurb:
In the Cold War two military alliances faced each other across Europe. NATO, founded in April 1949 by the United States, Canada, Britain, France and other Western nations, promised that an attack on one member was an attack on all. The Soviet Union answered with the Warsaw Pact. For decades their armies and nuclear weapons stood face to face along the Iron Curtain.

NATO's first head, the British general Lord Ismay, joked that the alliance existed to keep the Americans in, the Russians out and the Germans down. Moscow formed the Warsaw Pact only in 1955, five days after West Germany was allowed to join NATO, and put all its armies under one Soviet commander.

NATO's all-for-one rule, Article 5, has been used only once, after the September 11, 2001 attacks on the United States, when Europe came to America's aid. In August 1968 the Soviet-led alliance sent its tanks into its own member Czechoslovakia to crush the Prague Spring, and the Czechs, with no army to match them, tore down and painted over their street signs so the tank columns got lost.

The Warsaw Pact punished members who tried to leave. When Hungary's leader Imre Nagy announced in 1956 that Hungary would quit the Pact, Soviet tanks crushed Budapest, and Moscow later had Nagy hanged and buried in an unmarked grave. No NATO member was ever invaded by its allies for trying to leave.

navajo-code-talkers.context_blurb:
In the Second World War the United States Marine Corps recruited hundreds of Navajo men to send battlefield radio messages in their own language. Navajo was unwritten and spoken by almost no outsiders, and the Code Talkers wrapped it in a code of their own. The Japanese never broke it, and the program stayed secret for decades.

They gave war machines animal names: a tank was a tortoise, a fighter plane a hummingbird, and a submarine the iron fish. Every term had to be memorized, because no codebooks went into the field. In the first two days on Iwo Jima, six Code Talkers sent and received more than 800 messages, and the signal officer, Major Howard Connor, marvelled that not one of them held a mistake.

When Japanese troops took a Navajo soldier, Sergeant Joe Kieyoomia, prisoner on Bataan and tortured him to translate the messages, he could not, because he had never been trained in the code, and the coded words were nonsense even to a native speaker.

nazi-ghettos-warsaw-ghetto-uprising.context_blurb:
After conquering Poland in 1939, the Nazis forced Polish Jews into sealed city districts called ghettos, a step toward murdering them. In November 1940 they walled more than 400,000 Jews into the Warsaw Ghetto, where hunger and disease killed tens of thousands. In 1942 the SS began shipping the people to the Treblinka death camp. In April 1943 the survivors fought back.

The deportations began in the summer of 1942. Janusz Korczak, a doctor who ran an orphanage of nearly 200 children, was offered forged papers and escape, but he refused, led his children to the train in orderly rows, and died with them at Treblinka. Resistance grew. When German soldiers came back for more victims on 18 January 1943, Jewish fighters opened fire with a few smuggled weapons, and after several days of this the Germans pulled their troops out of the ghetto. That small success proved that armed defence was possible.

On 19 April 1943 the SS marched in to destroy the ghetto for good. The main fighting force, the Jewish Combat Organization or ZOB, was led by Mordecai Anielewicz, a youth leader and poet who was just 24 years old. Fighters of a second group, the Jewish Military Union, seized a stronghold on Muranowski Square and flew the blue-and-white Zionist banner beside the red-and-white flag of Poland for about four days. One fighter recalled that a typical member went into battle carrying a pistol, five grenades and five Molotov cocktails, against more than 2,000 German soldiers with tanks and cannon. Unable to win street by street, SS commander Jurgen Stroop had the ghetto burned down around the fighters, block by block. As one commander, Marek Edelman, put it, the flames beat them, not the Germans.

Stroop expected to clear the ghetto in three days, but the fighters and the families hiding in bunkers held out from 19 April to 16 May, nearly a month. On 23 April Anielewicz wrote to his deputy that his life's dream had come true, because he had lived to see Jews defending themselves with arms. When it was over, Stroop sent Heinrich Himmler a boastful illustrated report titled The Jewish Quarter of Warsaw Is No More! To crown his triumph, on 16 May Stroop dynamited Warsaw's Great Synagogue. His report later helped hang him.

The fighters knew they could not win. Edelman explained that they fought so that the Germans alone would not get to choose the time and place of their deaths. On 8 May the Germans found the command bunker at 18 Mila Street and pumped gas inside, and rather than fall into the hands of the SS, Anielewicz and many of his fighters took their own lives. The historian Emanuel Ringelblum's secret archive, Oneg Shabbat, saved about 35,000 pages of records by sealing them in milk cans and metal boxes and burying them, and some were dug up after the war.

nazi-ideology-and-the-nuremberg-laws.context_blurb:
Adolf Hitler's Nazi Party taught that Germans were a pure Aryan race whose blood the Jews were poisoning. Once in power in 1933, the Nazi state turned that hatred into law, propaganda and finally violence. The Nuremberg Laws of 1935 stripped German Jews of their rights, and the road they built led to the Holocaust.

On 1 April 1933, in the first nationwide action the state organized against Jews, SA storm troopers stood outside Jewish shops and offices holding signs that told Germans to defend themselves and not to buy from Jews. Julius Streicher's hate paper, Der Sturmer, posted in glass cases on street corners, printed the same slogan on every issue: The Jews are our misfortune. On the night of 9 to 10 November 1938, Nazi mobs set fire to over 1,400 synagogues and wrecked thousands of shops, and the shattered windows littering every street gave that night its name: Kristallnacht, or Night of Broken Glass. Joseph Goebbels gave the signal; the violence came from the top. From September 1941, on Reinhard Heydrich's order, every Jew aged six or older had to wear a yellow Star of David marked Jude when out in public.

In 1938 Streicher's press printed a picture book for children called The Poisonous Mushroom, which taught that a Jew was like a deadly mushroom hidden among good ones. After Kristallnacht the regime blamed the victims, fining German Jews a billion Reichsmarks and seizing the insurance money owed for their own wrecked property. The Nuremberg Laws banned marriage and love between Jews and other Germans, and the Nazis named the new crime Rassenschande, race defilement, sending thousands to camps for it.

The laws were made on 15 September 1935. The first, the Reich Citizenship Law, made only people of German blood full citizens, so every Jew was demoted from citizen to mere subject of the state. An official chart sorted people by their grandparents, with white circles for German blood, black circles for Jews and shaded ones for those of mixed descent. Hitler called the Reichstag to the Nuremberg party rally to pass them, the only sitting of the Nazi-era parliament ever held outside Berlin. The drafts were thrown together overnight, one scrawled on the back of a menu.

The deepest absurdity sat at the core. The Nazis claimed that Jewishness lay in the blood, but no test could find it, so they decided whether a grandparent was Jewish by whether he or she had belonged to the Jewish religion. Justice came for some. Sentenced to death at Nuremberg for his propaganda, Streicher shouted "Purimfest 1946!" on the gallows, sneering with the name of the Jewish feast that celebrates a persecutor's downfall.

nazi-soviet-molotov-ribbentrop-pact.context_blurb:
In August 1939, days before the Second World War began, Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union, sworn ideological enemies, signed a pact in Moscow. Foreign ministers Joachim von Ribbentrop and Vyacheslav Molotov promised that their countries would not attack each other, and a secret protocol split eastern Europe between Hitler and Stalin.

At the banquet on the night of 23 August, Stalin lifted his glass of sparkling Crimean wine and drank to the health of Adolf Hitler, saying he knew how much the German nation loved its Fuhrer. The man who had denounced fascism for years now promised not to betray his new partner.

Then they acted. German troops poured into western Poland on 1 September, and the Red Army came in from the east on 17 September. On 28 September the two dictators fixed their new border in a treaty whose title paired Boundary with the word Friendship, while Polish cities still smoked. The two powers were partners until Hitler invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941.

nazi-soviet-pact-of-1939.context_blurb:
In 1939 Hitler's Germany and Stalin's Soviet Union, the bitterest enemies in Europe, one fascist and one communist, shocked the world by signing a pact. Their foreign ministers, Ribbentrop and Molotov, met in Moscow on 23 August and promised publicly that neither country would attack the other for ten years.

At a Kremlin dinner that same night, Stalin himself raised his glass and drank to Adolf Hitler's health. He reportedly said he knew how much the German people loved their Fuhrer. The leader of world communism toasting the leader of fascism showed that the two regimes were now partners, not opposites.

A secret protocol, which the Soviets denied for fifty years, carved up eastern Europe, splitting Poland and handing the Baltic states between the two powers. Both powers acted on it within weeks: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September, the Red Army followed on 17 September, and the Soviets went on to seize the Baltic states and attack Finland. Moscow admitted the protocol existed only in 1989.

negative-rights-vs-positive-rights-what-.context_blurb:
In 1776 the Declaration of Independence said that people are endowed by their Creator with unalienable rights. Thinkers call such rights negative: rights to be left alone, which ask everyone else only to hold back. Positive rights, to housing, healthcare or a job, need someone else's work to supply them. That is why the Bill of Rights is mostly a list of things the government may not do.

The Declaration's third right is the pursuit of happiness, a right to chase happiness, not a promise that anyone will hand it to you. John Locke's older list had named property in that place.

The French writer Frederic Bastiat drew the line sharply in his 1850 book The Law. If you carried off your neighbour's bread yourself, a judge would punish you. So a law that takes one man's bread and gives it to another, Bastiat argued, is still theft, only carried out by the law instead of by hand; he called it legal plunder. The strongest case on the other side came from Franklin Roosevelt, whose 1944 Second Bill of Rights held that freedom is hollow without a job, a home and medical care. Bastiat's answer is that such a right can be filled only by forcing someone to provide it.

nero-caligula-and-the-mad-emperors.context_blurb:
After Augustus, Rome was ruled by his family, the Julio-Claudians, and two of them became history's models of power gone mad. Caligula, who ruled from AD 37 to 41, grew cruel and wildly extravagant until his own guards murdered him. Nero, who ruled from AD 54 to 68, turned paranoid and murderous and loved performing on stage more than governing.

As a toddler in his father Germanicus's camp on the Rhine, Gaius wore a tiny copy of the soldiers' boot, the caliga, so the troops called him Caligula, Little Boots. As emperor he hated the name. In July of AD 64 Rome's Great Fire began in shops packed with flammable goods beside the Circus Maximus and raged for about six days.

The famous picture of Nero fiddling while Rome burned is impossible, because the fiddle was not invented until more than a thousand years later. The historian Tacitus reports only a rumour that Nero sang about the fall of Troy. When people whispered that Nero had started the fire, Tacitus says, he blamed Rome's Christians instead and had them torn by dogs, crucified or burned alive as torches.

In AD 68, declared a public enemy and abandoned by his guard, Nero killed himself, and Suetonius records his dying boast: what an artist was perishing in him. His death ended the dynasty.

new-weapons-of-wwi.context_blurb:
The First World War turned Europe's factories against its own young men. Between 1914 and 1918 both sides rushed out terrifying new weapons: poison gas, tanks, fighter planes with forward-firing guns, and machine guns that cut down whole lines of attackers. By the war's end, nearly every tool of modern mechanized war had been invented, and millions had died learning to face them.

In April 1915, near Ypres, German troops released a greenish-yellow cloud of chlorine from thousands of buried cylinders, and the wind carried it into the French and Algerian trenches in the war's first large gas attack. On 15 September 1916, at the Somme, the British sent the first tanks into battle, and the diamond-shaped Mark I crossed trenches on caterpillar tracks that ran right around its whole body.

Canadian soldiers at Ypres, still without gas masks, heard an officer reportedly shout for them to urinate on their handkerchiefs and tie them over their faces, because the ammonia in urine partly neutralised the chlorine.

Machine guns, firing some 600 rounds a minute, did the worst killing. Gunners angled them so their streams crossed no man's land from the sides, and a soldier who swerved to dodge one gun simply walked into the next gun's line of fire. On the Somme's first day such fire helped cause close to 60,000 British casualties.

In the air, pilots could not fire forward without shooting off their own propellers. In 1915 Anthony Fokker, a Dutch designer, gave Germany a gear in which a cam driven by the engine halted the gun at the instant a blade passed in front of the muzzle. Now a pilot aimed his whole plane at the enemy, and Allied airmen called themselves Fokker fodder.

new-world-crops-potato-maize-tomato.context_blurb:
For thousands of years, farmers in the Americas bred wild plants into foods that would one day change every kitchen on Earth. After Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492, those crops sailed east in the great swap of plants and animals called the Columbian Exchange. Within two centuries the potato, maize and the tomato fed Europe, Africa and Asia.

Tomatoes, potatoes and chili peppers all came from the Americas, so before 1492 there was no tomato sauce in Italy, no potato in Ireland and no chili in India or Korea. Farmers in southern Mexico spent some 9,000 years turning a scrawny grass called teosinte into maize, and they planted it together with beans and squash in one mound, a trio called the Three Sisters. The corn gave the beans a pole to climb, the beans fed the soil and the squash shaded out weeds.

Europeans did not trust the newcomers at first. The tomato belongs to the same family as deadly belladonna, also called deadly nightshade, and its leaves are genuinely poisonous, so Europeans feared the fruit as poison for two hundred years. Around 1785 the army pharmacist Antoine-Augustin Parmentier planted potatoes outside Paris, guarded them by day and withdrew the guards each night, betting that villagers would sneak in to steal such a precious crop. The tale is told as legend, but France did take to potatoes.

The Italian word pomodoro, first printed in 1554, means golden apple, a hint that the first tomatoes Italians saw were yellow.

The potato's success brought one terrible danger. By the end of the eighteenth century, around two in five Irish people lived on potatoes alone. When a water mould called late blight rotted the crop from 1845, more than a million people in Ireland died and some two million more emigrated, most of them to America.

north-africa-and-el-alamein.context_blurb:
From 1940 to 1943 the Second World War raged across the deserts of Libya and Egypt, as German and Italian forces fought the British and their allies for the Suez Canal and Middle Eastern oil. The German commander, Erwin Rommel, ran rings around his enemies with his Afrika Korps. In late 1942 General Bernard Montgomery finally beat him at El Alamein, in Egypt.

Rommel's lightning raids, striking and vanishing across the open desert, won him the nickname the Desert Fox. At El Alamein his engineers laid roughly 500,000 mines in bands as much as five miles deep, and his soldiers called those minefields the Devil's Gardens. When Montgomery's Eighth Army won in November 1942, Winston Churchill ordered Britain's church bells to be rung in celebration, the first time they had sounded in years.

Montgomery's opening attack was called Operation Lightfoot, a grim joke, because his infantry had to cross the minefields first, stepping lightly enough not to set the mines off before the heavier tanks followed. Rommel was sick in Germany when the battle began, and General Georg Stumme, commanding in his place, dropped dead of a heart attack near the front on the second day.

The British won partly by trickery. In Operation Bertram they hid tanks under canvas to look like lorries, built dummy tanks and laid a fake water pipeline that grew a few miles a day. Wilhelm von Thoma, a German general the British captured, afterwards confessed that he had been fooled on both the timing and the place of the attack.

Rommel's end was bitter. On 14 October 1944, accused of a part in the July plot against Hitler, he was given a choice between a public trial for treason, with his family punished, and a hidden death, and he chose a cyanide capsule. The Nazis gave him a hero's state funeral and blamed his war wounds.

north-korea-the-prison-state.context_blurb:
North Korea was founded in 1948 under the Soviet-backed communist Kim Il Sung, and three generations of his family, Kim Il Sung, Kim Jong Il and Kim Jong Un, have ruled it ever since. It is one of the most closed and cruel states on Earth: a cult of the ruling family, total control of information, and prison camps where whole families die for one relative's offence.

Satellite photos at night show South Korea blazing with light and the North almost totally black, except for one bright spot, the capital, Pyongyang. When the Soviet Union collapsed, the North lost the cheap fuel that ran its power plants.

Hunger followed in the 1990s. When famine killed hundreds of thousands, the regime refused to call it a famine and named it the Arduous March, after a tale of the young guerrilla Kim Il Sung leading a march through deep snow. Under the rule of guilt by association, if the state charges one person with a political crime, it can send three generations of the family, grandparents, parents and children, to the prison camps.

nuclear-arms-race-mad.context_blurb:
The United States built and used the first atomic bombs in 1945, and the Soviet Union, helped by spies, tested its own in 1949. The two superpowers then raced to build hydrogen bombs and missiles that could cross the world in half an hour. By the 1960s each could destroy the other, and that grim balance kept the peace.

In 1952 the United States set off the first true hydrogen bomb, Ivy Mike, on the coral island of Elugelab in the Marshall Islands, and when the steam cleared the island was simply gone, replaced by an ocean crater more than a mile across. In 1961 the Soviets answered with the Tsar Bomba, the most powerful bomb ever built, and its mushroom cloud climbed about 67 kilometres, almost eight times the height of Mount Everest.

The bomb was too fat for its Tu-95 bomber, so engineers took off the bomb-bay doors and it rode half-exposed under the plane. It had been designed for 100 megatons, but engineers halved its power, because at full strength its fallout would have soaked the bomber crew and a quarter of the Soviet Union. When Sputnik went up in 1957, Americans panicked because its rocket, the R-7, was the first intercontinental ballistic missile anywhere in the world, able to carry a warhead to any American city.

The man behind the Soviet hydrogen bomb, Andrei Sakharov, came to fear it. At the 1955 banquet for the first Soviet H-bomb, he toasted the hope that their devices would always explode over test sites and never over cities. A marshal mocked him for it. Sakharov became the regime's most famous critic, and when the Nobel Peace Prize went to him in 1975 and he was barred from leaving the country, his wife, Yelena Bonner, read his speech in Oslo.

The doctrine that neither side dared strike first was named Mutual Assured Destruction by Donald Brennan, who opposed it and chose the acronym MAD to mock the idea of keeping peace by promising to annihilate each other.

nuremberg-trials.context_blurb:
In November 1945, six months after Germany surrendered, Britain, the United States, France and the Soviet Union put twenty-two surviving leaders of the Nazi regime on trial before an international military tribunal. The charges were waging aggressive war, war crimes and crimes against humanity. The trial ran almost a year, and twelve men were sentenced to hang. It set the rule that individuals answer for such crimes.

The Allies held the trial in Nuremberg on purpose, because it was the city where the Nazis had staged their giant party rallies every year. Its Palace of Justice had also survived the bombing, with a prison attached. Hermann Goering, the most senior Nazi in the dock, was sentenced to hang, but about two hours before his execution in October 1946 he crushed a smuggled cyanide capsule between his teeth and died in his cell.

On 29 November 1945 the prosecutors dimmed the lights and showed an hour of film shot by Allied soldiers in the freshly liberated concentration camps, and the whole courtroom sat in stunned silence. The prison psychologist Gustave Gilbert secretly gave the defendants intelligence tests, and they scored as near-geniuses and geniuses, with Hjalmar Schacht highest at 143. These were not stupid brutes.

Rudolf Hess, once Hitler's deputy, claimed for days that he had lost his memory, then stood up on 30 November and admitted he had faked the amnesia for tactical reasons. When Robert Jackson, the chief American prosecutor, charged that Germany had prepared for war in secret, Goering retorted that he did not remember reading America's own published plans for mobilization either, and Jackson lost his temper. The Polish-Jewish lawyer Raphael Lemkin had coined a new word in 1944 for the destruction of a whole people, genocide, and he fought to get it into the Nuremberg case.

The deepest meaning lay in the choice to hold a trial at all. Jackson opened by saying that when victorious nations held back from vengeance and handed their captives to the law, it was one of the greatest tributes that Power had ever paid to Reason. The court ruled that a man who commits such a crime cannot clear himself by claiming he was only obeying his government or his commanders, though it may lessen his punishment. The propagandist Julius Streicher shouted "Purimfest 1946!" on the gallows because exactly ten men were hanged that night, like the ten sons of Haman in the Book of Esther.

The trial had flaws. Soviet prosecutors urged the court to blame the Germans for the Katyn massacre of Polish officers, but the Western judges would not convict, because the Soviet secret police had committed it themselves. Moscow admitted the truth in 1990. Albert Speer, Hitler's architect and armaments chief, admitted in open court that he shared responsibility for the regime's crimes, and historians think that is why he escaped the gallows and got twenty years in prison instead.

olmec-civilization-and-the-colossal-head.context_blurb:
The Olmec, who flourished on Mexico's hot Gulf Coast from about 1500 to 400 BC, are often called the mother culture of Mesoamerica. Their art, their ritual ballgame and their calendar passed down to the Maya and the Aztecs. They are best known for colossal stone heads, some standing taller than a person and many tons in weight.

The Olmec carved seventeen giant heads, and because every one has its own face, its own nose and cheeks, scholars think they are portraits of particular Olmec rulers rather than gods.

The heads are a marvel of engineering, because the Olmec had no metal tools, no wheeled carts and no beasts to pull loads. Their great ceremonial centres at San Lorenzo and La Venta needed stone the swampy lowlands could not supply. Each needed a single boulder of basalt, and the nearest source, in the Tuxtla mountains, lay more than a hundred kilometres away. The Olmec floated the multi-ton boulders downriver on rafts and rolled them across land on logs.

operation-barbarossa.context_blurb:
On 22 June 1941 Adolf Hitler sent Germany's armies into the Soviet Union, his partner under the 1939 pact. He planned it as a war of annihilation, fought to wipe out Soviet communism and its officials as well as to seize land. German armour drove deep toward Moscow, but the Red Army held. The war in the east became the deadliest ground war in history and broke Nazi Germany.

Over 3.8 million Axis soldiers crossed a front nearly 2,900 kilometres long, from the Baltic to the Black Sea, in the biggest land invasion the world has ever seen. Hitler named it after the medieval emperor Frederick I, whose nickname Barbarossa means Redbeard in Italian. At Brest Fortress, the first place struck, cut-off defenders held out long after the front moved on, and one scratched on the wall that he was dying but would not surrender, and bade farewell to the Motherland.

Stalin had brushed off warnings from Churchill and from his own spies, and when the blow fell, he withdrew to his country house and stayed out of sight for days. On the first day the Luftwaffe destroyed more than a thousand Soviet planes, most of them parked in neat rows on their airfields. But the Germans had planned to win before autumn. Caught in summer uniforms when winter struck, freezing German soldiers stuffed newspaper and straw inside their coats, and about 100,000 suffered frostbite. By early December they were some fifteen to twenty miles from Moscow, and legend says the nearest soldiers could see the spires of the Kremlin.

Before the frost came the rasputitsa, the Russian season of bottomless mud in spring and autumn, which swallowed tanks, trucks and horses. In August Hitler overruled his generals and turned south to trap the Soviet armies at Kiev, where the Soviets lost more than 600,000 men, and he boasted that it was the greatest battle in world history. The detour cost him the time he needed to take Moscow.

From the start the invasion was a war of murder. Days before it began, Hitler's high command sent out the Commissar Order, which told German troops to shoot any Soviet political officer they captured rather than hold him as a prisoner. Behind the front, four SS killing squads, the Einsatzgruppen, shot some 500,000 people in nine months, most of them Jews, in what is called the Holocaust by bullets. At the Babyn Yar ravine outside Kiev, on 29 and 30 September 1941, an SS unit under Paul Blobel machine-gunned 33,771 Jews, a number taken from the killers' own report.

origins-of-parliament-the-english-common.context_blurb:
In the 1200s English kings who needed money for their wars began calling not only great lords and bishops but elected men from the counties and towns to a meeting. A rebel earl, Simon de Montfort, pushed that idea further than anyone before him, and the assembly he shaped grew into the House of Commons. Parliaments across the world descend from it.

The word parliament comes from the French parler, to speak, so long before it meant lords and commons making laws, a parliament was simply a talking-place, a speaking. In 1264 the barons rose against King Henry III. Before they fought at Lewes, the rebel barons sewed white crosses on their tunics, like crusaders on a holy mission. They won and captured the king. The king's brother, Richard of Cornwall, hid in a windmill, and the rebels jeered at him to come down out of it, calling him a wicked miller. In 1265 de Montfort ordered every major town to send two burgesses, ordinary townsmen, to sit beside the barons and bishops.

De Montfort was not even English. Born in France around 1208, he had married Eleanor, King Henry's own sister, so he rose against his brother-in-law. At Lewes, young Prince Edward routed the Londoners and chased them for four miles, and when he returned, his father the king had been beaten and captured behind him. De Montfort's pairing of two knights from every county with two burgesses from every town grew into the House of Commons.

The end came at Evesham in 1265. Edward's men flew banners captured from Kenilworth Castle, and the old earl took them for his own reinforcements arriving to save him. The captive Henry III had been forced into de Montfort's colours, and his own son Edward's soldiers almost cut him down by mistake until a knight shouted who he was. De Montfort died hacked to pieces as a traitor.

The idea outlived him. In 1258 the barons had already bound Henry with the Provisions of Oxford, with Parliament meeting three times a year, and a chronicler mocked that assembly as the Mad Parliament. Even earlier, clause 12 of Magna Carta, in 1215, forbade the king to levy any great tax except by the kingdom's common counsel. In 1295 Edward I made the summoning of knights and burgesses the regular rule in his Model Parliament, justifying it with a Latin maxim: what concerns everyone must be approved by everyone. The crown banned visits to de Montfort's grave, but pilgrims crept to Evesham Abbey anyway to honour him as a saint. A book recorded some 200 miracles credited to him.

parthenon-and-the-greek-architectural-or.context_blurb:
The Parthenon is the great marble temple of Athena on the Acropolis of Athens, built from 447 to 438 BC under the statesman Pericles. The architects Iktinos and Kallikrates designed it and the sculptor Phidias directed its carving. The Greeks developed three styles of column, called orders, and Romans, Renaissance builders and modern architects copied them all.

The Roman architect Vitruvius wrote that the Doric, the oldest and plainest column, was modelled on the sturdy body of a strong man. The slimmer Ionic column, which he said copied a woman, is crowned with a pair of spiral curls, called volutes, that look like curled-up rams' horns. Inside stood Phidias's statue of Athena, almost 40 feet tall, built over a wooden core and covered in ivory for her skin and gold for her robes and armour. On her open right hand she held Nike, the winged goddess of Victory, herself a full statue the height of a person. The temple's sculptures were never bare white; scans show the Greeks painted them in bright colours, including Egyptian blue, which weather later wore away. An earlier temple to Athena, still unfinished, had stood on the spot until 480 BC, when the army of the Persian king Xerxes burned it to the ground.

The builders played tricks on the eye. A perfectly straight column looks thin in the middle, so they gave each one entasis, a gentle swelling at the middle that makes it look truly straight. The outer columns all lean slightly inward, and if you extended them upward, they would meet at a single point about a mile and a half above the temple. Athena's robes held more than a ton of gold, and Phidias made the gold panels removable, so the city could strip them off and spend the gold to pay for a war.

Legend clung to the sculptor. On Athena's shield Phidias secretly carved his own bald, aged face and his friend Pericles among the fighters, and when people noticed, the sculptor was tried for impiety. Ancient writers say he may have died in prison or exile. Vitruvius told how the sculptor Callimachus saw a basket on a young girl's grave with acanthus leaves curling around it and carved a stone basket ringed with such leaves, the Corinthian capital. The grooved blocks in a Doric frieze, called triglyphs, are stone copies of the sawn-off ends of the wooden roof beams in the older timber temples.

pasteur-germ-theory-and-vaccines.context_blurb:
Louis Pasteur was a French chemist, born in 1822, who helped prove that many diseases are caused by germs and that weakened germs can protect people and animals from those diseases. He was not the first to suggest germ theory, but his experiments and public demonstrations convinced the world. Germ theory and vaccines have added decades to human lives.

Pasteur boiled broth in flasks with long, curving swan necks, and it stayed clear for as long as the flask stood upright, but tipping it let the dust trapped in the bend slide down into the broth, which soon clouded. Germs came from the air, not from the broth itself.

In May 1881 he vaccinated 24 sheep against anthrax, left 24 unprotected, and then infected all of them in front of farmers and vets, and two days later every unvaccinated sheep lay dead while every vaccinated one was alive. In 1885 nine-year-old Joseph Meister, bitten fourteen times by a rabid dog, received a course of Pasteur's untested vaccine, never developed rabies, and became the first person ever saved from it. Meister later worked as gatekeeper of the Pasteur Institute in Paris, watching over the crypt below, where Pasteur's tomb lies.

The triumph had a hidden side. About a hundred years on, the historian Gerald Geison studied Pasteur's private notebooks and found that the anthrax vaccine had been made with a chemical method from his rival Henri Toussaint, whom Pasteur never credited.

paul-revere-s-ride-lexington-and-concord.context_blurb:
On the night of 18 April 1775, the Boston silversmith Paul Revere and William Dawes rode out to warn the Massachusetts militia that British troops were marching to seize patriot weapons at Concord and perhaps to arrest Samuel Adams and John Hancock. At dawn the first shots of the American Revolution rang out at Lexington. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's poem of 1860 made the ride a legend.

The patriots' signal from the steeple of the Old North Church was one lantern if the British left by land and two lanterns if they crossed by water, and that night the sexton, Robert Newman, hung two. Years later, in his Concord Hymn of 1837, Ralph Waldo Emerson praised the embattled farmers at Concord's North Bridge for firing a shot that was heard round the world.

The lanterns burned for less than a minute, but one of the two real lanterns survives and can still be seen in the Concord Museum. Two friends got Revere out of Boston by rowing him across the Charles River in a small boat, slipping past the British warship Somerset, and a horse waited for him in Charlestown. He almost surely never shouted that the British were coming, since most colonists still called themselves British and the mission was secret; his real warning was that the regulars were coming out.

Newman escaped from the church by climbing out a back window, and when the British arrested him the next day, he blamed another man who had already fled. Revere borrowed his horse from Deacon John Larkin, and its famous name, Brown Beauty, comes only from a family tradition that someone wrote down generations afterwards, in 1930. When a British sergeant on guard hissed at him to keep the noise down, Revere, by his own account, snapped that the sergeant would have noise enough before long. Longfellow's hero gallops all the way to Concord, but the real Revere never got there: a British patrol caught him at a roadblock in Lincoln and took his horse. At dawn on Lexington Green, among about 70 militiamen, stood Prince Estabrook, a Black man then held as a slave, who was wounded in the fight.

A young doctor, Samuel Prescott, who had joined Revere and Dawes on the road, escaped the patrol by jumping his horse over a stone wall, and he alone reached Concord to raise the alarm. Tradition says the militia captain, John Parker, told his men not to fire unless fired upon, but that if the British meant to have a war, it should begin right there. Badly outnumbered, Parker then ordered his men to scatter. As they turned away, a single shot rang out, and to this day no one knows whether a colonist or a British soldier fired it. British volleys killed eight militiamen.

At Concord's North Bridge, some 400 militia faced about 90 British soldiers. When a British volley killed one of the militia, Major John Buttrick of Concord shouted to his fellow soldiers to fire, for God's sake, and Americans fired back in formation for the first time. The redcoats fell back, and on the long march to Boston thousands of militiamen fired on them from behind stone walls.

pearl-harbor.context_blurb:
On the morning of Sunday, 7 December 1941, planes from Japanese aircraft carriers struck the American Pacific Fleet at its anchorage in Hawaii. In under two hours they sank or damaged the battleships, wrecked hundreds of aircraft and killed about 2,400 Americans. Japan hoped to buy time for its conquests in Asia. Instead the attack united a divided nation and brought the United States into the Second World War.

As the first wave arrived and found the ships still sleeping, the lead pilot, Mitsuo Fuchida, radioed his carrier three words to say the enemy had been caught completely unaware: Tora! Tora! Tora! On the battleship Nevada the band was playing the national anthem for the 8 a.m. flag-raising when a Japanese plane strafed the deck, and the musicians played on to the end, just faster. Kenneth Taylor and George Welch, two young Army pilots, drove from an all-night dance to a small airfield at Haleiwa and flew their P-40 fighters into battle still wearing the formal tuxedo-style mess dress they had worn to the party. The Arizona still lies on the harbour floor, and the drops of oil that rise from her each day are called the tears of the Arizona. On 8 December Franklin Roosevelt asked Congress to declare war, calling 7 December a date which will live in infamy; his draft had said world history until he changed it by hand.

The worst blow fell on the Arizona: an 1,800-pound armour-piercing bomb punched through her deck and set off her forward ammunition magazine, and the ship blew apart, killing 1,177 of her crew. When the Oklahoma rolled over, the shipyard worker Julio DeCastro heard trapped sailors hammering SOS inside, and his crew cut through the steel hull and pulled out 32 men. Doris Miller, a cook on the West Virginia who had never been trained on the guns because the Navy kept Black sailors off them, dragged his wounded captain out of danger and then fired a heavy machine gun at the attackers, becoming the first Black American to receive the Navy Cross.

There were warnings. Roughly an hour earlier, Joseph Lockard and George Elliott at the Opana radar station had reported a huge flight of planes 132 miles away, and Lieutenant Kermit Tyler, the officer on duty, waved it off, believing it was a flight of American B-17 bombers expected that morning. Japan meant to hand over a long note in fourteen parts, breaking off negotiations, half an hour before the strike, but its embassy was so slow typing it that the Americans received it only after the bombs had fallen. So the raid went down in memory as a sneak attack.

The attack also failed in its main aim. All three Pacific carriers, the Enterprise, Lexington and Saratoga, were away from the harbour and escaped, and carriers like them went on to carry the fight back across the ocean, all the way to Japan. The famous line in which Yamamoto fears he has awakened a sleeping giant appears in no letter or diary of his; it comes from the 1970 film Tora! Tora! Tora!

pericles-and-the-golden-age-of-athens.context_blurb:
Pericles was the aristocrat and general who led Athens in its golden age, the generation between the Greek victory over Persia and the long war with Sparta. Elected general year after year for some thirty years, he made Athens a naval empire, rebuilt the Acropolis, and championed its democracy. He died of plague in 429 BC, and Athens never had another leader like him.

His speeches were so thunderous that comic poets said he had a thunderbolt on his tongue and nicknamed him the Olympian, as if he were Zeus. They mocked his looks too, calling him Squill-head after a knobbly sea-onion. Sculptors almost always showed him with a helmet tipped back on his brow, politely hiding his unusual, elongated skull. Around 447 BC he began rebuilding the Acropolis, and its crown was the Parthenon, a white marble temple to Athena, the city's protector.

In front of Phidias's giant gold-and-ivory statue of Athena lay a shallow pool of olive oil, which kept the ivory from cracking and reflected the goddess's image. On her shield, among Greeks fighting Amazons, Phidias slipped in small portraits of Pericles and of himself, and he was dragged into court for impiety. In his funeral speech of 431 BC, recorded by Thucydides, Pericles said Athens was called a democracy because its government served the many, not the few. Once a man followed him around the marketplace cursing him all day, and Pericles bore it in silence, then at nightfall told a servant to take a torch and walk the man safely home.

The temple's columns lean slightly inward and swell at the middle, yet to a viewer below the finished building looks perfectly straight and upright. The glory had a price. The Delian League was an alliance against Persia, led by Athens and funded by its members, but in 454 BC Athens moved the league treasury from Delos to its own city and spent the money on its own temples, quietly turning its allies into the subjects of an Athenian empire. When rivals said he was decking out Athens like a vain woman, Pericles offered to pay for the buildings himself if his own name were carved on them, and the assembly at once told him to use public money.

His last years were bitter. At the start of the war with Sparta, Pericles packed the country people inside the city walls, a plague tore through the crowded city, and in 429 BC it killed Pericles himself. His law of 451 BC made only children of two Athenian parents citizens, so after plague killed his lawful sons, he had to beg the assembly to set aside his own law for his son by Aspasia, a woman from Miletus.
