phillis-wheatley-poet-of-the-founding-er.context_blurb:
Phillis Wheatley was kidnapped from West Africa as a small child and sold in Boston in 1761. The family that bought her taught her to read English and Latin, and by her teens she was writing poems admired in Boston and London alike. She was freed after her book appeared, but she died in poverty in 1784, about thirty-one years old.

The Wheatleys named her after the very slave ship that had brought her to Boston, a schooner called the Phillis. They guessed she was about seven because she was losing her front teeth.

So many people refused to believe an enslaved girl could write such poems that eighteen leading Bostonians, John Hancock among them, examined her and signed a statement that the poems were hers, and when her poems were printed in London in 1773, she became the first African American ever to publish a book of poetry.

Late in 1775 she wrote a poem to George Washington in which she invented a goddess to stand for the new nation, Columbia, a name that poets went on to use for America itself. Washington wrote back praising her talents and met her in 1776.

phoenician-sea-traders-and-tyre-s-purple.context_blurb:
The Phoenicians were seafaring traders from city-states on the coast of what is now Lebanon. From about 1200 BC their ships ranged across the whole Mediterranean, and they founded colonies as far west as Spain, including Carthage, which later fought Rome. They also spread the alphabet that the Greeks adopted and passed on to Europe.

Their most famous product was a dye. The city of Tyre made royal purple from a spiny sea snail called the murex, and it took the crushed glands of some ten thousand snails to colour a single garment. Twelve thousand snails gave barely 1.4 grams of dye, enough to trim one robe. Under Rome a pound of the dye cost more than its weight in gold, so only kings and emperors wore it.

The Greeks named the traders for that dye: the Greek word phoinix, the root of Phoenician, meant reddish-purple. The Phoenicians were, in a sense, the purple people.

picasso-and-cubism.context_blurb:
Pablo Picasso, born in Malaga in 1881, moved to Paris as a young man and became the most influential artist of the twentieth century. With the French painter Georges Braque he invented Cubism, which broke with the single viewpoint painters had used since the Renaissance. He worked in painting, sculpture, ceramics and prints until his death in 1973, and his cruelty to several women in his life is now part of how he is judged.

Family legend says his very first word was piz, baby talk for lapiz, the Spanish word for a pencil. At his baptism the priest wrote down a string of more than a dozen first names, honouring saints and relatives, ending in Ruiz y Picasso. Cubism let a single picture show one object from several viewpoints at the same moment, so a nose might sit beside an ear seen from the side. In 1937, after German and Italian planes bombed the Basque town of Guernica, he painted a huge mural in nothing but grey, black and white, so it would strike viewers like a newspaper photograph.

Most of the town's men were away at the front, so the bodies he painted in the rubble are mostly those of women and children. Yet from the broken sword in a dead soldier's hand, Picasso let a single flower grow as a sign of hope. The story goes that during the German occupation of Paris, a Gestapo officer pointed at a photo of the mural and asked whether Picasso had done that, and he answered, "No, you did." He had called his 1907 painting of five women The Brothel of Avignon, after a red-light street in Barcelona, but the poet Andre Salmon, a friend, renamed it Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, and Picasso hated the change.

Around 1908 the French critic Louis Vauxcelles sneered that Braque's blocky landscapes were made of little cubes, and the insult gave the movement its name. In 1912 Picasso and Braque, working like climbers roped together, began gluing newspaper, wallpaper and labels onto the canvas, inventing collage.

Picasso refused to explain his symbols. Pressed for decades to say what the horse and the bull in Guernica secretly meant, he answered that the bull was just a bull and the horse just a horse. He vowed the painting would not go to Spain until liberty returned, so it waited in New York until the dictator Francisco Franco had died, and it reached Spain in 1981.

pizarro-and-the-conquest-of-the-inca.context_blurb:
Francisco Pizarro was an ageing, unlettered Spanish adventurer who in 1532 led a tiny band into the empire of the Inca, high in the Andes of South America. Within a year he had captured the emperor Atahualpa, collected a fortune in gold and silver, and killed him anyway. A few hundred Spaniards brought down one of the largest states on Earth.

At Cajamarca, facing Atahualpa's army of some 80,000 warriors on the hills, Pizarro had only about 168 men, 62 on horseback and 106 on foot.

The friar Vicente de Valverde handed Atahualpa a Bible and ordered him to submit to Spain and to God, and when the book told him nothing, the emperor threw it to the ground, which the Spanish seized on as their excuse to attack. Taken prisoner, Atahualpa promised to fill a whole room with gold up to a red line as high as he could reach, then fill it twice over with silver. The Ransom Room still stands in Cajamarca.

Spanish eyewitnesses wrote that when swords cut off the hands and arms of the nobles carrying Atahualpa's litter, they kept holding it up with their bleeding stumps until they were killed. After the ransom was paid, the Spanish sentenced Atahualpa to be burned alive, and when he accepted baptism to escape the fire, they strangled him with an iron garrote in the same square instead.

The empire was already broken when Pizarro came. Disease had killed the emperor Huayna Capac, and his sons fought over the throne. A five-year civil war had just ended, in which Atahualpa's generals defeated and captured his brother Huascar, and Pizarro exploited the wreckage.

pizarro-and-the-spanish-conquest-of-the-.context_blurb:
Between 1532 and 1533 the Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro, with fewer than two hundred men, toppled the Inca Empire of Peru. He seized the emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca, high in the Andes, took a vast ransom and then killed him. But disease, an Inca civil war and native allies did as much as Spanish steel.

Even before Pizarro landed, smallpox, racing ahead of the Spanish, had killed the last strong emperor, Huayna Capac, around 1527, and his sons Huascar and Atahualpa went to war over the throne. At Cajamarca a friar handed Atahualpa a holy book, and since Inca gods spoke aloud through oracles, the emperor lifted it to his ear, heard no voice and threw it on the ground. Pizarro waved a white scarf and a cannon fired. Held prisoner, Atahualpa reached up and drew a line on the wall of his room and promised to fill the room to that height with gold.

Pizarro had only about 168 Spaniards, with a few cannon and guns, against some 80,000 Inca warriors, yet his men killed thousands in the town square in one afternoon. The eyewitness Pedro Pizarro wrote that when the Spanish hacked at the litter-bearers, the wounded men kept holding the emperor's litter up on their stumps and shoulders. A story says that earlier Hernando de Soto galloped his warhorse at Atahualpa, an animal the emperor had never seen, and reined in just feet from his face, but Atahualpa did not flinch a muscle. Much of the ransom was stripped from the walls of the Coricancha, the temple to the Sun in Cusco, which had been sheathed in plates of solid gold.

Though the ransom was paid, Pizarro's men sentenced Atahualpa to burn, and since in Inca belief a body destroyed by fire could never reach the next life, he accepted Christian baptism so that he would be strangled instead. A legend says the captive emperor learned chess in a few weeks and once whispered to Hernando de Soto to move the rook, which won the game.

The conquest did not end there. In 1536 the Spanish puppet ruler Manco Inca turned on them and besieged Cusco for nearly a year, and his forces destroyed all four rescue armies the Spanish sent from Lima. The Spanish won with the help of tens of thousands of native allies, above all the Canari and the Chachapoya, who had suffered under Inca rule. The conquerors then fought over the loot, and in 1541 followers of Pizarro's executed partner Diego de Almagro stormed his palace in Lima and assassinated him.

plato-the-academy-and-the-republic.context_blurb:
Plato was an Athenian aristocrat of the 300s BC who became the most influential philosopher of the ancient world. He was devoted to Socrates, and after Athens executed his teacher in 399 BC, Plato spent his life writing philosophical conversations on justice, love, knowledge and the nature of reality. One modern thinker said all Western philosophy is a series of footnotes to Plato.

His real name was Aristocles; his wrestling coach nicknamed him Plato, from the Greek for broad, because of his broad, powerful shoulders. Around 387 BC he founded a school in a grove of olive trees outside Athens named for the hero Akademos, and from it we get the word Academy. In nearly all of his written dialogues Plato never speaks himself; the leading voice is his old teacher Socrates, who never wrote anything down. The legend of Atlantis, the mighty island that sank beneath the waves, first appears in two of Plato's own books, Timaeus and Critias, and scholars think the philosopher Plato invented it to make a political point.

In his most famous image, prisoners chained in a cave since childhood see only the flickering shadows that a fire behind them casts on the wall, and they mistake those shadows for the whole of reality. A freed prisoner climbs painfully out into daylight and at last looks at the Sun, which stands for the Form of the Good, the highest object of knowledge. When Plato defined a human as a featherless animal on two legs, the story goes, Diogenes the Cynic plucked a chicken, carried it into the Academy and announced, "Behold, Plato's man!"

The Republic describes an ideal city. Plato argued that cities would never be free of misery until power and true wisdom belonged to the same person, the philosopher-king. His guardians spend some thirty-five years in study and fifteen more in lesser posts, so they rule only at about the age of 50. To make each class accept its place, the rulers spread what Plato openly calls a noble lie: that each soul has a metal mixed into it, gold for rulers, silver for soldiers and bronze or iron for workers. In The Open Society and Its Enemies, the twentieth-century philosopher Karl Popper read the Republic as the first blueprint for a closed, totalitarian society. That is one serious modern reading, and Plato's admirers dispute it.

In 2024 scholars read a scroll charred by Vesuvius at Herculaneum and learned that Plato, dying at about eighty and clear-headed to the end, found breath to complain that a flute-girl had a poor sense of rhythm. The scroll also says he was buried in a garden at the Academy.

polar-exploration-amundsen-peary-shackle.context_blurb:
In the decades around 1900, the Heroic Age of polar exploration, small teams on skis, with sledges and dogs or ponies, raced to the ends of the Earth. The Norwegian Roald Amundsen reached the South Pole first, in December 1911, beating the Briton Robert Falcon Scott by about a month. Scott's whole party died on the way back, while Ernest Shackleton later brought every one of his men home alive.

Amundsen, who had learned dog-driving from the Inuit, took 52 dogs and planned in advance exactly which dogs to shoot along the way, feeding them to the dogs that were left and to his men. Scott's motor sledges failed him, and his ponies weakened in the cold until they were shot. In 1915 Shackleton's ship Endurance was locked in the frozen Weddell Sea, and in November the pressing ice crushed her hull and she sank, leaving his men on the drifting floes.

After the crew reached Elephant Island, where no rescue ship would look, Shackleton and five men set out in April 1916 in the James Caird, a 22-foot open boat, to sail 800 miles over the world's stormiest ocean and fetch help from South Georgia.

Scott's party had no such luck. Captain Lawrence Oates, his feet ruined by frostbite, knew he was holding back his starving friends, so he walked out of the tent into a blizzard, saying he was just going outside and might be some time.

The North Pole brought a bitter quarrel. Robert Peary claimed it in April 1909, days after Dr. Frederick Cook said he had stood there a year earlier. Cook's claim fell apart when investigators showed he had also lied about being the first to climb Denali, then called Mount McKinley. Peary's own claim is still disputed.

policy-of-appeasement-and-munich-1938.context_blurb:
By 1938 Adolf Hitler had remilitarized the Rhineland and swallowed Austria. Then he demanded part of Czechoslovakia. Britain's prime minister, Neville Chamberlain, and France's premier, Edouard Daladier, chose to give way rather than risk another world war, a policy called appeasement. Six months after their deal at Munich, Hitler took the rest of Czechoslovakia, and in 1939 war came anyway.

Hitler's target was the Sudetenland, a mountain border region of Czechoslovakia where some three million ethnic Germans lived. Chamberlain's umbrella, which he carried everywhere, became the cartoonists' symbol of appeasement. Hitler himself sneered at the silly old man with his umbrella. On 27 September, as Londoners dug trenches and tried on gas masks, Chamberlain said on the radio that it was horrible to do so over a quarrel in a faraway country between people of whom Britons knew nothing. Home from Munich, he told the cheering crowd outside Downing Street that he had brought back peace with honour, and peace for our time.

Chamberlain, then 69, flew to Hitler three times in two weeks, and the first flight took him to Berchtesgaden, Hitler's retreat high in the Bavarian mountains. Signed in the small hours of 30 September by Hitler, Chamberlain, Daladier and Mussolini, the agreement handed the Sudetenland to Germany, to be occupied within ten days, and not one Czechoslovak sat at the table while their country was carved up. The two Czech envoys were kept waiting in another room and called in at 1:30 a.m. to hear the verdict, and one of them recorded that Chamberlain yawned openly, without even trying to hide it. In March 1939, when Hermann Goring threatened to flatten Prague from the air, President Emil Hacha collapsed and then signed his country over to Hitler.

Not everyone was fooled. When cheering crowds in Paris showered Daladier with flowers, he muttered to an aide, "Ah, the fools!" In the Commons debate, Winston Churchill opened by calling Munich a defeat, total and unmitigated. He warned it was only the first sip of a bitter cup, yet the House approved the deal by 366 votes to 144. Alfred Duff Cooper resigned from the cabinet, saying he could accept war with honour or peace with dishonour, but war with dishonour was too much.

Chamberlain's defenders make a serious case. In 1938 the Royal Air Force had few modern fighters. During the delay before war, Britain built Chain Home, a coastal radar network that proved one of the war's most valuable advantages. By the Battle of Britain, Fighter Command flew modern Spitfires and Hurricanes.

polynesian-wayfinding-settling-the-pacif.context_blurb:
Between about 1500 BC and AD 1300, Polynesian voyagers settled the vast triangle of the Pacific from Hawaii to New Zealand to Easter Island, an area bigger than several United States put together and almost all of it water. They sailed double-hulled canoes and found specks of land thousands of miles apart by reading the stars, the swells and the birds. The art nearly died, then came roaring back in the 1970s.

When European scholars looked for the instruments the navigators had steered by, they found none at all: no compass, no sextant, no chart, because everything was carried in the navigator's memory and senses. The great Micronesian navigator Mau Piailug, from the tiny island of Satawal, began his training as a baby, when his family placed him in tide pools so he could feel the sea's pull. White terns sleep on land and fly out to fish at dawn, so a navigator who sees them at dawn heading out to sea turns his canoe back the way they came, toward the land behind them. The Marshall Islanders made stick charts of coconut ribs and shells showing how swells bend around islands, but they studied them on shore and never carried them to sea. In 1976 Mau guided the voyaging canoe Hokule'a over more than 2,500 miles of open ocean to Tahiti, using no instruments, and when it arrived, about 17,000 people, half the island, came down to the shore to greet it.

Under cloudy skies Mau steered by the swells alone, lying in the hull and feeling the canoe's motion through his own body, and he could pick out eight separate swells at once. Near the low Tuamotu atolls, a navigator watched for a faint green tint on the undersides of the clouds, thrown up by the shallow lagoon of an island still hidden below the horizon. In 1769 the Polynesian priest and navigator Tupaia drew Captain James Cook a chart from memory of about 130 islands, naming 74 of them. Settlers carried a whole transported landscape in their canoes: live pigs, dogs and chickens, and plants such as taro, breadfruit and coconut, to turn an empty island into a home.

A single star is useful for steering only until it climbs too high. So navigators followed star paths, switching from star to star through the night, and the greatest held more than 150 stars in their heads, each with its exact bearing. Polynesians were already growing the sweet potato, a plant from South America, by about AD 1200, strong evidence that their voyagers reached the Americas and sailed home again. Navigators also told of te lapa, the flashing, streaks of light that dart toward land from beneath the water far out at sea.

The deepest secrets were ways of thinking. In the Caroline Islanders' method called etak, the navigator pictures his canoe sitting still while an unseen reference island slides backward past one star after another. The star compass is not an object at all but a map held in memory of the point on the horizon where each star rises and where it sets, and the Hawaiian Nainoa Thompson relearned it from Mau so he could navigate the canoe himself.

pompeii-and-the-eruption-of-vesuvius-79-.context_blurb:
In AD 79 Mount Vesuvius, above the Bay of Naples, erupted and buried the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum under deep ash. Thousands died, and the disaster froze an entire Roman town in place: bakeries, shops, graffiti, meals on tables and the dead where they fell. It is our clearest window into everyday Roman life.

The teenage Pliny the Younger, watching from across the bay, later wrote that the great cloud rising over the mountain looked most like an umbrella pine tree, with a tall trunk spreading into branches. Bodies had rotted away inside the hardened ash and left hollows, so in 1863 the archaeologist Giuseppe Fiorelli poured liquid plaster into them and recovered the last poses of the dead. The famous casts are plaster, not bone, and they show faces, clothing folds and dying positions. At the door of the House of the Tragic Poet, a mosaic of a snarling chained dog carries the Latin words cave canem, Beware of the Dog.

One cast shows a guard dog left chained at the House of Orpheus, twisted onto its back as it strained against its collar while the ash rose around it. In one bakery oven archaeologists found about 80 round loaves that the heat had baked black and rock-hard, like charcoal. One loaf still carries its baker's stamp: Celer, slave of Quintus Granius Verus. Stepping stones let people cross the muddy streets, and the gaps between them were spaced so that cart and chariot wheels could roll through. Generations of wheels wore ruts inches deep into the paving.

Pliny the Younger's two letters to the historian Tacitus are prized because they are the only eyewitness account of the eruption that survives. They tell of his uncle, Pliny the Elder, admiral of the fleet. When a woman named Rectina begged for rescue, the old admiral steered toward the burning mountain, telling his helmsman that fortune favours the bold. At Stabiae, as burning pumice rained down, he and his companions tied pillows on their heads with cloths before walking out. He died there. Pompeii's streets held more than 80 thermopolia, counters set with jars that sold hot food and wine to go, like ancient fast-food bars.

Science keeps finding more. In 2020 Pier Paolo Petrone's team found that the heat at Herculaneum had turned one young man's brain into black glass, like obsidian. In 2023 the student Luke Farritor used scans of an unopened Herculaneum scroll to read its first recovered word, porphyras, meaning purple. And though tradition dates the eruption to 24 August, carbonized autumn fruit and the heavy clothing on the victims suggest it came in the colder season, probably October.

potos-silver-mountain.context_blurb:
In 1545 Spanish colonists found the richest silver deposit the world had ever seen, Cerro Rico, the rich hill, above the town of Potosi in the high Andes of what is now Bolivia. A boomtown of up to 160,000 people grew on its freezing slopes. Its silver became the world's money, and the forced labour that dug it cost countless Indigenous lives.

Potosi silver was minted into the eight-real Spanish coin, nicknamed pieces of eight, which became the first truly global money, and the dollar sign probably comes from it. The city's coat of arms boasted that Potosi was the treasure of the world, the king of mountains and the envy of kings.

Its wealth entered the language: around 1615 Cervantes used the saying vale un Potosi, worth a Potosi, and Spaniards still say it of anything worth a fortune.

In 1573 Viceroy Francisco de Toledo imposed the mita, a forced-labour draft named from the Inca word for a turn, which made villages across sixteen provinces send men to the mountain, about 13,500 at a time. Cave-ins and mercury poisoning killed so many workers, by some estimates millions over the colonial centuries, that Cerro Rico was called a mountain that eats men. Spanish galleons carried the silver from Acapulco to Manila every year from 1565 to 1815, and somewhere from one third to one half of the silver mined in the Americas ended up in China, soaked up by its taxes and trade.

prague-spring-1968.context_blurb:
In 1968 Alexander Dubcek, the reforming leader of Communist Czechoslovakia, loosened censorship and promised socialism with a human face. For a few months Czechs and Slovaks spoke freely for the first time in twenty years. Then in August the Soviet Union and its Warsaw Pact allies invaded to crush the reforms, and Czechoslovakia stayed under Soviet control until 1989.

The army did not fight back, so ordinary people fought the tanks with no weapons at all, repainting the road signs so the columns got lost, with one sign for Moscow pointing back the way the invaders came. They argued with the bewildered soldiers in the streets instead of shooting at them.

The occupation stayed. In January 1969 Jan Palach, a twenty-year-old student at Charles University, set himself on fire in Wenceslas Square, and he signed his farewell letter "Torch No. 1," warning that others would follow. He died three days later, and his sacrifice helped inspire the dissident Vaclav Havel, who led the revolution of 1989.

pre-columbian-monumental-art-maya-aztec-.context_blurb:
The peoples of the ancient Americas and the Pacific raised some of the world's most astonishing monuments without wheels, draft animals or iron tools. The Maya built stepped pyramids, the Aztecs carved colossal stones for their capital, Tenochtitlan, and on remote Easter Island the Rapa Nui people carved giant stone figures called moai. Later Europeans could hardly believe local people had made them, but archaeology proves they did.

At the spring and autumn equinoxes, sunlight and shadow on El Castillo, the great pyramid of Chichen Itza, form a snake of light that seems to slither down the staircase to a carved serpent's head at its foot. The pyramid is a calendar too, with 365 steps in all. On Easter Island, archaeologists who dug around about 150 of the famous heads found that they have whole bodies, buried up to the shoulders by centuries of soil.

Island legend said the moai walked, and in 2012 the archaeologists Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo put it to the test: eighteen people with three ropes rocked an upright replica from side to side, so that it waddled forward. The Aztec Sun Stone, a basalt disk of some 24 tons, has four panels around its centre recording four earlier worlds, every one of them destroyed in turn, by jaguars, wind, fiery rain and flood. The Aztecs believed they lived in the fifth.

In 1978 electric-company workers in Mexico City struck a great carved disk of the moon goddess Coyolxauhqui, shown beheaded and cut to pieces by her brother, the sun god Huitzilopochtli. The find led archaeologists to dig out the buried Templo Mayor, the great temple of the Aztec capital.

prince-henry-the-caravel-and-navigation-.context_blurb:
Prince Henry of Portugal, who lived from 1394 to 1460, is remembered as Henry the Navigator, though he hardly went to sea. He paid for and pushed a long campaign of voyages down the west coast of Africa, taking a share of the profits. His captains sailed new ships with new tricks, and a generation after his death the Portuguese reached India by sea.

Sailors feared Cape Bojador, a low headland on the African coast, believing the sea beyond it boiled with monsters, until in 1434 a Portuguese captain, Gil Eanes, sailed past it and came home alive. To prove he had really walked the desert shore beyond the cape, Gil Eanes brought home a handful of little flowers the Portuguese called St. Mary's roses.

From the dhows of Arab sailors the caravel took the three-cornered lateen sail, which let a ship zigzag forward against a wind blowing straight at it. The famous navigation school Henry is said to have run at Sagres never existed; writers made it up long after his death, and the real voyages sailed from Lagos.

Getting home was the hardest part. With the volta do mar, the turn of the sea, a captain steered away from home, out into the open Atlantic, looping northwest until he caught the westerly winds, and then ran east back to Portugal. Navigators had found their latitude by the height of the Pole Star, but near the equator the star sank below the horizon and vanished, so they had to measure the sun instead. In 1485 Portuguese scholars drew up the first daily tables of the sun's height.

prince-henry-the-navigator-sagres.context_blurb:
Prince Henry of Portugal, a younger son of the king, almost never went to sea himself. From the 1420s until his death in 1460 he paid for voyage after voyage down the African coast, each captain pushing a little farther than the last. His captains also brought back enslaved Africans, a dark part of his legacy.

The great barrier was Cape Bojador, south of the Canary Islands, where sailors swore the sea boiled and no ship could return. In 1434 Gil Eanes finally rounded it, found calm water, and brought home wild roses he had picked on the far shore as proof.

To come home against the Atlantic winds, Henry's shipwrights built the caravel, a small and shallow ship. Instead of one big square sail, the caravel carried triangular sails, which let it beat back against a headwind. Its shallow hull let it work close to the coast, and the ships of Columbus and da Gama grew from it.

prince-shotoku-early-japan-yamato-nara.context_blurb:
Prince Shotoku was a Japanese statesman of the late 500s and early 600s who helped build the Japanese imperial state. He lived as Japan was eagerly borrowing ideas from China and Korea. He championed Buddhism, built great temples such as Horyu-ji, sent embassies to China and wrote a moral code for officials, though modern scholars debate how much of this was really his.

Around 552 the Korean king Seong, ruler of Baekje, sent the Japanese court a gleaming bronze statue and holy scriptures, and with them Buddhism arrived in Japan. In 604 Shotoku created twelve court ranks that a man could earn by merit, and each official showed his rank by the colour of his cap.

Shotoku never ruled in his own name; from 594 to 622 he served as regent for his aunt, the Empress Suiko.

In 607 his envoy, Ono no Imoko, carried a letter to the Sui emperor of China from the Son of Heaven where the sun rises to the Son of Heaven where the sun sets, casting Japan as the land of the rising sun and China as the land of the setting sun, two rulers on the same level. The emperor was angry, but he still sent an envoy back. The last of Shotoku's Seventeen Articles warns that important matters should never be decided by one person alone, but discussed with many.

prohibition-and-the-gangster-era.context_blurb:
In January 1920 the Eighteenth Amendment took effect and the United States went dry: making, selling or shipping alcohol became a federal crime. Millions of Americans kept drinking anyway. The trade went underground, and its profits built the most notorious gangs in the country's history, above all in Chicago, until repeal came in 1933.

Thirst simply moved behind closed doors. All over the country people opened secret bars with no sign outside, where a customer whispered a password at the door and everyone inside spoke softly so that nobody outside would hear, and from that hushed rule they took their name: speakeasies. By some estimates New York City alone had as many as 100,000 of them by 1925.

The Chicago trade belonged above all to Al Capone, who had dozens of rivals killed to keep it. Everyone knew him as Scarface, because years earlier, in a brawl at the Harvard Inn on Coney Island, he had insulted Frank Galluccio's sister, and Galluccio's knife slashed his left cheek three times, leaving scars that never faded.

On Valentine's Day 1929, Capone moved to wipe out the North Side Gang of his rival Bugs Moran. Four gunmen walked into the S-M-C Cartage garage on North Clark Street, where seven of Moran's men were waiting. Because the killers wore police uniforms, the gang members took it for an ordinary raid and obediently faced the wall, hands up, to be searched; then the guns opened fire. Moran himself, the man Capone really wanted dead, was running late that morning, and when he saw what looked like a police car parked by the garage, he turned around and walked away, missing the slaughter of his own men by minutes.

Capone made tens of millions a year, yet no prosecutor could prove he had killed anyone. What finally caught him was his money: IRS agents traced the cash from his gambling business, showed that he had never reported any taxable income, and in 1931 a jury convicted him of income tax evasion. He got eleven years, a $50,000 fine and a bill for back taxes, without a single charge for bootlegging or murder.

Meanwhile a small squad of Prohibition agents under Eliot Ness kept smashing Capone's breweries, and when the gang offered them fat bribes, they turned the money down in public, so the newspapers named them the Untouchables. Their raids hurt Capone's business, but it was the tax men, not Ness, who put him behind bars.

ptolemy-and-the-geocentric-universe.context_blurb:
Claudius Ptolemy was a Greek-speaking astronomer who worked in Roman Alexandria, in Egypt, around 150 AD. He packed centuries of Babylonian and Greek sky-watching into one huge textbook, in which the Earth stands still at the centre while the Sun, Moon, planets and stars wheel around it.

Ptolemy gave his book a plain Greek title, the Mathematical Composition. In the ninth century Arab translators called it al-majisti, from al-, meaning 'the', and a garbled form of the Greek megiste, 'greatest', so the name Almagest means The Greatest. That accidental nickname outlived Ptolemy's dull title in every language.

In Ptolemy's scheme each planet rides a small circle whose centre travels around a larger one, yet even that left his forecasts off. His fix was the equant, an imaginary point set off-centre on the far side from the Earth, and seen from that point a planet sweeps out equal angles in equal times. The trick let a planet seem to speed up and slow down while the maths stayed accurate, and the model lasted until Copernicus, who rejected the equant because it broke perfectly even circular motion.

pythagoras-and-his-theorem.context_blurb:
Pythagoras was born on the Greek island of Samos in the sixth century BC and settled in Croton, a Greek colony in southern Italy. There he founded a brotherhood that was part school and part religion. His followers shared their lives, believed that souls are reborn in new bodies, and treated numbers as the hidden structure of the world. He wrote nothing that survives, so fact and legend are tangled.

The brotherhood guarded its secrets fiercely. A newcomer had to keep complete silence, not speaking a single word, for five years before he could meet the master in person. A member who broke the rules was thrown out for good, and the others then raised a tombstone for him as though he had died, because to them the outcast no longer existed.

The rules included a strange ban on eating fava beans, and a legend says it killed Pythagoras. Fleeing from enemies, he came to a field of beans and would not cross it, since trampling the plants meant breaking his own law, so he halted at the edge, and his pursuers caught him and killed him there.

Other tales made him more than a man. Aristotle recorded the legend that Pythagoras had a golden thigh, which he showed at the Olympics and to Abaris, a visitor from the far north, as a sign that he was the northern Apollo come to earth. The brotherhood's holiest shape was the tetractys, a triangle of ten dots, one on top, then two, then three, then a base of four, and the initiates swore their secret oath by it. Ten was their perfect number.

Their faith that whole numbers rule everything had a weak spot: some lengths can never be expressed as a ratio of two whole numbers. A famous legend says that Hippasus, the member who let this secret out, drowned at sea as a punishment from the gods. Historians doubt the story, because no ancient writer actually credits him with finding these irrational numbers.

Even his famous theorem may not be his own. Plimpton 322, a Babylonian clay tablet written about 1800 BC, lists sets of whole numbers that fit right triangles, which shows that Babylonian scribes knew the rule more than a thousand years before Pythagoras was born. Tradition credits the Pythagoreans with giving the rule a strict proof, and with the grander idea that numbers are the hidden order of reality.

qin-shi-huang-china-s-unification.context_blurb:
In 221 BC the king of Qin, a hard-fisted western state, conquered the last of his rivals and ended centuries of war among China's kingdoms. He gave himself a brand-new title, Qin Shi Huang, roughly 'First Emperor of Qin', and ruled with ruthless efficiency. His dynasty barely outlived him, but the single China he forged became the pattern for every later dynasty.

To make one country out of many, he made everything the same. Each kingdom had minted its own money, so he swept it all away for one coin, the banliang, a round disc pierced through the centre by a square hole, the circle standing for heaven and the square for the earth. That shape remained the look of Chinese money for over twenty centuries. Carts built in one region stuck fast in the deep ruts of another, so he fixed a single axle width for every cart in the empire, and any wagon could roll down any road. In the north the old kingdoms had each raised separate walls against the horsemen of the steppes, and the emperor drove armies of soldiers and convicts to link those walls and lengthen them into one continuous barrier, the beginning of the Great Wall. Countless workers died building it.

He had nearly not lived to rule. In 227 BC, while he was still only King of Qin, the little state of Yan sent an assassin, Jing Ke, to his court with a map offered as a gift. A poisoned dagger lay rolled up inside the map, and as the scroll was unrolled to its end, the blade appeared. The king tore free, and when his court physician hurled a medicine bag at the assassin, he finally drew his long sword and cut Jing Ke down.

Once he was emperor, he longed to live forever. In 219 BC he dispatched an alchemist, Xu Fu, with a fleet bound east for Mount Penglai, home of the immortals, to fetch the elixir of life, and legend says the ships carried some three thousand boys and girls along with many craftsmen. Xu Fu never came back.

In 213 BC, on the advice of his chancellor Li Si, he had the empire's private libraries put to the fire, sparing only practical works on medicine, farming, forestry and divination, along with the records of Qin itself. Verse, the chronicles of the kingdoms he had destroyed and the works of thinkers he distrusted all burned.

The next year, the historian Sima Qian wrote, the emperor ordered roughly 460 scholars in his capital, Xianyang, buried alive in pits, and he publicised the killings as a warning. When his eldest son, Fusu, warned that such cruelty would stir up revolt, the emperor sent him away into exile on the far northern frontier, a decision that doomed the young man once his father was gone.

Qin Shi Huang died in 210 BC, and the eunuch Zhao Gao grabbed the real power. To learn who at court would follow him whatever he said, Zhao Gao led a deer into court and loudly called it a horse; those who honestly said deer were later put to death, and 'point at a deer and call it a horse' has been a Chinese saying ever since for using raw power to make people repeat a lie they know is false. The dynasty the First Emperor meant to last ten thousand generations fell apart within about four years of his death.

Sima Qian wrote that craftsmen built a model of China inside, with mercury made to flow like the Yellow River, the Yangtze and the seas. The mound has never been opened, but when scientists tested its soil they found mercury at many times its natural level, concentrated in just the places where the old historian had put the rivers. Nobody knew that some eight thousand clay soldiers, each the size of a living man, stood buried nearby until March 1974, when local farmers digging a well near Xi'an broke into the pits by accident. Craftsmen shaped the warriors from roughly ten basic face moulds and then finished each one by hand, so that no two soldiers share exactly the same face.

queen-victoria-and-the-british-empire-at.context_blurb:
Victoria became queen of Britain in 1837 at eighteen and reigned until her death in 1901, sixty-four years. In her time Britain ruled the largest empire the world had ever seen, and the Industrial Revolution remade daily life, so 'Victorian' became the name of a whole confident, industrial century.

Her age showed itself off at the Great Exhibition of 1851 in Hyde Park, in London. The gardener Joseph Paxton designed its hall, a vast greenhouse of iron and glass nicknamed the Crystal Palace, and workers raised it in only nine months. Instead of felling the tall old elm trees on the site, Paxton built right over them, so living, full-grown elms stood inside the palace.

Victoria and her German husband, Prince Albert, had nine children, who married into royal houses across the continent. A generation later her grandchildren sat on many of Europe's thrones, and she became known as the Grandmother of Europe. Then in 1861 Albert died of typhoid at forty-two. Victoria dressed in black for the remaining forty years of her life and shut herself away from public view for so long that people called her the Widow of Windsor.

Eight times men tried to kill her. The last was Roderick Maclean, who fired a pistol at her at Windsor station in March 1882, enraged that the queen had paid no attention to some verses he had mailed to her. Eton schoolboys waiting nearby rushed at Maclean and beat him with their umbrellas before the police could reach him.

A jury needed only five minutes to find Maclean 'not guilty, but insane'. Victoria was furious that a man who fired at the queen could be called not guilty of anything. She pressed Parliament, and a new law of 1883, the Trial of Lunatics Act, turned the verdict around to 'guilty, but insane', the form British law kept for decades.

quetzalcoatl-the-feathered-serpent.context_blurb:
Quetzalcoatl, the Feathered Serpent, was one of the great gods of ancient Mexico, a lord of wind, learning and the morning star. The Aztecs worshipped him, but he was far older than their empire: the builders of Teotihuacan carved him on a great temple, the Toltecs honoured him at Tula, and the Maya knew him as Kukulkan.

His name is a picture. In Nahuatl, the Aztec tongue, the word coatl is a snake, while quetzalli is the shimmering emerald tail-feather of the quetzal, a rainforest bird whose long green plumes were prized like jewels. Put together, the two words make a serpent dressed in feathers.

At Teotihuacan his temple bristles with some 260 carved stone serpent heads. In 2003 archaeologists found a sealed tunnel running far beneath it, packed with offerings of jade and jaguar bones and a tiny model mountain landscape. Most startling of all, liquid mercury lay in shimmering pools in the depths, apparently placed there so the tunnel would stand for the watery underworld.

quipu-the-inca-knotted-string-records.context_blurb:
The Inca ruled an empire stretching down the Andes from what is now southern Colombia to central Chile, with censuses, taxes, armies and storehouses to track, yet they had no writing of any kind. Instead they kept their records on quipus, and trained readers called quipucamayocs could recall a province's accounts from a bundle of cords.

A quipu looks like a fringe, one main cord with dozens or even hundreds of thinner strings hanging from it, and the numbers lived in knots tied along those strings, read by where each knot sat. It worked like a spreadsheet made of string.

Quipus counted in tens, and the height of a knot on its string set its place value, just like the columns in which we write numbers. The ones sat at the bottom, near the free end, the tens above them and the hundreds higher still, with a gap between each place, and an empty gap with no knot meant zero. To record 586, a reader tied a long knot wound six times near the bottom, a cluster of eight simple knots in the tens place and five in the hundreds.

ramesses-the-great.context_blurb:
Ramesses II, called the Great, ruled Egypt for about sixty-six years in the thirteenth century BC. He covered the land with monuments, from the rock-cut temples of Abu Simbel to the Ramesseum, and fought the Hittite Empire for Syria.

His most famous battle, at Kadesh in 1274 BC, really ended in a bloody draw, and the Hittites still held the city afterward. Ramesses told the story his own way, carving it across the walls of temple after temple as a glorious victory he had won almost alone, boasting that he smashed thousands of Hittite chariots single-handed. It is one of the oldest pieces of war propaganda known.

Three thousand years after his death, Ramesses travelled again: in 1976 his mummy was flown to Paris to be saved from a fungus that was eating it. To let the dead king enter France legally, Egypt issued him a genuine modern passport, and on the line for his occupation it read King (deceased). When his plane landed, French soldiers greeted him with the full honours due a visiting head of state.

rape-of-nanjing.context_blurb:
In December 1937 the Imperial Japanese Army captured Nanjing, then the capital of China. Over the following weeks Japanese soldiers murdered prisoners and civilians, most historians say between 100,000 and 300,000 people, and raped and looted across the city. A few Westerners who stayed set up a Safety Zone.

One of them was John Rabe, a German who ran the Siemens office in the city and belonged to the Nazi Party. His zone gave shelter to over two hundred thousand Chinese. Japan was Hitler's ally, so when Japanese bombers came over, Rabe gambled that the pilots would not attack the swastika, and he stretched a huge Nazi flag over the crowd like a canopy. Some 600 refugees camped in his own house and garden.

Minnie Vautrin, an American missionary who taught at Ginling Girls' College, opened its grounds to as many as ten thousand women and children. When Japanese soldiers came hunting for women, she stood with her own body between them and the people they wanted. The refugees she protected called her the Goddess of Mercy.

raphael.context_blurb:
Raphael, born Raffaello Sanzio in Urbino in 1483, was the young star of the High Renaissance in Italy. Pope Julius II called him to Rome in 1508, and for twelve dazzling years he painted the papal apartments, altarpieces and portraits while running a huge workshop, until he died at thirty-seven.

His most famous fresco, The School of Athens, gathers the great thinkers of ancient Greece in one vast hall. At its centre Plato points a finger up toward his heaven of perfect ideas, while his pupil Aristotle stretches out his hand flat, palm turned down toward the earth, the solid world we can touch. Those two gestures sum up the whole split between the two men. When Raphael finished the Sistine Madonna, he felt its lower edge looked bare, so as an afterthought he added a pair of small cherubs leaning on a ledge, and the two of them have since escaped the painting to decorate postcards and mugs all over the world.

Tradition says that the white-bearded Plato wears the face of the aging Leonardo da Vinci, the great master of the generation before, whom Raphael admired above all living painters.

In 1511 Raphael slipped next door to look at the newly finished ceiling of the Sistine Chapel. Afterward he painted one last figure into his fresco, the gloomy philosopher Heraclitus, slumped by himself on the steps, and most scholars see in that scowl the face of Michelangelo, his great rival.

Raphael died on Good Friday 1520, his thirty-seventh birthday, and Rome mourned him like a prince. He was laid to rest in the ancient Pantheon, a burial place few painters have ever been granted. At the funeral, the story goes, the pope himself bent down to kiss the dead artist's hand.

reagan-s-evil-empire-the-coalition-that-.context_blurb:
Ronald Reagan, elected American president in 1980, set out to win the Cold War, not merely contain it, and in 1983 he called the Soviet Union an evil empire. Britain's Margaret Thatcher and Pope John Paul II pressed the Soviet bloc beside him until it fell in 1989 to 1991.

Thatcher's nickname came from the enemy. Speaking at Kensington Town Hall in January 1976, while she led the Conservatives in opposition, she warned that Moscow was bent on world domination. Within days Red Star, the newspaper of the Soviet army, mocked her as the Iron Lady, meaning it as an insult. She seized the name, telling her constituents that yes, she was an iron lady, and wore it proudly ever after.

In 1987 Reagan stood at the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin and demanded that Gorbachev tear down the Wall. The fiercest fight against that line came from his own advisers: officials of the State Department and the National Security Council tried again and again to strike it, and his White House chief of staff, Howard Baker, called it unpresidential. Reagan overruled them all and kept it in.

reason-deism-and-religion-in-the-enlight.context_blurb:
In the 1600s and 1700s, the age of the Enlightenment, Europe's thinkers tried to test everything by reason, including God. Few of them became atheists. Most argued instead over what reason could show: was the orderly universe the work of a Maker, and how much of the old faith should a reasoning person keep?

The best-known picture came from the English clergyman William Paley, whose Natural Theology of 1802 asked readers to imagine crossing a heath: a stone lying there might have lain there forever, but a watch, its parts fitted together for a purpose, must have had a maker. Nature, with contrivances like the eye, pointed the same way.

Reason cut both ways. One winter, in 1819, the aging Thomas Jefferson set out to keep Jesus's moral teaching and drop the miracles, so he took a razor to six New Testaments, sliced out the passages he trusted and pasted them into a blank book. His gospel ends at the sealed tomb, with no resurrection. Yet the same century burned with heart-religion. In 1738 John Wesley sat in a small gathering in London's Aldersgate Street while someone read aloud Luther's preface to the letter to the Romans, and he felt his heart strangely warmed, suddenly certain that Christ had rescued him. That moment helped launch Methodism.

The greatest scientist of the age built the design argument into his physics. In 1713 Isaac Newton added a closing section to the second edition of his masterwork, the Principia, arguing that so lovely a system of the sun, the planets and the comets could proceed only from an intelligent and powerful Being.

Even the Church's fiercest mocker agreed. Voltaire was no atheist, and in a poem of 1772 he wrote that he could not imagine this clock of a universe existing with no clockmaker.

The sharpest blow came from David Hume, whose Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion appeared in 1779, after his death. His character Philo grants that like effects have like causes, then pounces. We believe a watch has a maker because we have seen craftsmen making watches, but nobody has ever watched a universe being made, so the comparison has nothing to stand on. Hume left the matter unsettled, for readers to weigh.

reconstruction-and-the-reconstruction-am.context_blurb:
Reconstruction was the dozen years after the American Civil War, 1865 to 1877, when the United States tried to rebuild the South and decide what freedom meant for four million people just freed from slavery. For a few years Black men voted and held office; then terror, court rulings and political bargains undid most of it.

Congress wrote the new freedom into the Constitution. In December 1865 the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery everywhere in the United States. The Fourteenth, in 1868, made citizens of everyone born or naturalised in the country, freed people included, and promised that no state could deny any person equal protection under its laws, the clause courts would one day use to strike down segregation. In 1870 the Fifteenth barred any state from denying a man the vote because of his race, his colour or his previous condition of servitude, so a man could not be turned away for having once been a slave.

Freed families wanted farms of their own, and in January 1865 General William T. Sherman settled about 18,000 of them on confiscated coastal plantations, in plots of up to forty acres, with army mules lent to some, so the dream took the name forty acres and a mule. Within months President Andrew Johnson reversed the order and had the families evicted, and most sank into sharecropping.

Terror rose to meet the change. In 1866 six Confederate veterans in Pulaski, Tennessee, formed a secret society of costumes and fake-Greek titles, the Ku Klux Klan, and it soon turned to hunting freed Black families. In 1867 the former Confederate cavalry general Nathan Bedford Forrest became its first leader, under the chilling title Grand Wizard.

For a time Black Americans reached the halls of power. In 1870 Mississippi sent Hiram Revels to Washington as the first Black member of the Senate, in a seat left empty since 1861. Senator James Nye of Nevada hailed it as justice: in the place of Jefferson Davis, the proud Mississippi senator who had quit in 1861 to lead the Confederacy, came a man of the race Davis would have kept enslaved forever. Blanche Bruce, born a slave in Virginia, served Mississippi for a full term, and on 14 February 1879 he presided over the United States Senate, the first Black American and the only former slave ever to do so.

At Colfax, Louisiana, on Easter Sunday 1873, more than three hundred armed White men, many of them Confederate veterans, besieged the Black defenders of the courthouse with a cannon and set it ablaze. When the trapped men raised white flags to surrender, the attackers shot them down anyway. Between 62 and 153 Black men died, against 3 White men. In 1876 the Supreme Court, hearing the Colfax case as Cruikshank, decided that Washington's Enforcement Acts could restrain only state governments and not private mobs, which left no federal power to punish the killers, and they all walked free.

Southern states then found ways around the Fifteenth Amendment without writing race into the law. Poll taxes and reading tests kept poor men from the polls, but a grandfather clause let a man skip them if his ancestors had been voters in the days before the war, and because the forebears of freedmen had themselves been enslaved, illiterate White men voted and Black men did not. With such tricks, Black registration in Mississippi fell from tens of thousands in the late 1860s to under 9,000 by 1892.

Segregation came next. In 1892 New Orleans activists chose Homer Plessy to test Louisiana's law separating train passengers, because by ancestry he was seven-eighths White and could pass as White, so the conductor had to be tipped off in advance to arrest him. In 1896 the Supreme Court upheld the law, seven to one, with its doctrine of separate but equal. The lone dissenter, Justice John Marshall Harlan, answered that "our Constitution is color-blind" and tolerates no classes among citizens, words history later vindicated.

Frederick Douglass, who escaped slavery to become the nation's leading Black voice, called the vote no favour from the powerful but a natural right, the single great power through which every civil right is won, enjoyed and kept.

redrawing-the-map-of-europe.context_blurb:
When the First World War ended in November 1918, four empires collapsed at once, and the peacemakers who met in Paris in 1919 had to redraw the map of central and eastern Europe. President Woodrow Wilson wanted every nation to rule itself. The borders they drew righted some old wrongs and planted the grievances of the next war.

Poland had vanished from the map for 123 years, ever since Russia, Prussia and Austria divided it among themselves in the late 1700s, but when all three of those empires fell in 1918, Poland rose again as an independent nation. Its great port posed a puzzle. Danzig was overwhelmingly German, yet Poland needed it, so the peacemakers handed it to neither country and made it a Free City of its own under the League of Nations, with its own flag, money and stamps.

The war swept away four old ruling houses, Russia's Romanovs, Germany's Hohenzollerns, the Ottoman sultans and the Habsburgs of Austria-Hungary, whose last emperor, Karl I, lost his throne in 1918 and died in exile at thirty-four. Twenty years later the next war began at Danzig. On 1 September 1939 the old German battleship Schleswig-Holstein opened fire on the Polish garrison at Westerplatte, in the harbour of Danzig, the first shots of the Second World War.

To give Poland a road to the sea, the treaty cut a strip from West Prussia and Posen running north to the Baltic, the Polish Corridor. That strip left East Prussia stranded, cut off by land from the rest of Germany, a wound Hitler never stopped pressing. Czechoslovakia's new borders followed the old frontier of Bohemia and so took in about three million German speakers, the Sudeten Germans, and in 1938 Hitler used them as his excuse to tear the country apart.

That was the trap in Wilson's principle of self-determination. Europe's peoples lived mixed together, village by village, so a border that freed one people trapped another. Millions of Germans and Hungarians found themselves overnight as minorities in foreign states, and their grievances fed the next war.

religious-liberty-at-the-founding-virgin.context_blurb:
In most of colonial America one church was established by law: the government backed it and taxpayers paid its ministers, whatever they themselves believed. After the Revolution, Virginia led the break. Thomas Jefferson drafted the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, and James Madison pushed it through the state assembly in 1786. It declared that the state could compel no one to attend or fund any church, and could punish no one for what he believed about God.

During the debate some lawmakers tried to insert the name Jesus Christ into the statute's reference to the Author of religion, which would have protected Christians alone, and when the assembly voted them down, Jefferson wrote that the law was meant to shelter Jew and Gentile, Christian and Muslim, the Hindu, and unbelievers of every sort.

The new nation then made the principle national: the First Amendment of 1791 packs two rules into one line, so that Congress may set up no official national church and may not stop anyone from freely practising his own faith.

rembrandt-dutch-golden-age.context_blurb:
Rembrandt van Rijn (1606 to 1669) was the greatest painter of the Dutch Golden Age, when Amsterdam's merchants ran a trading empire across the globe and wanted paintings on their own walls. He was a master of light and deep shadow and of the ordinary human face, and though he died poor, his pictures are now among the most valuable on earth.

His most famous canvas, painted in 1642, has Captain Frans Banning Cocq striding out of a doorway at the head of his militia company. Over the centuries candle smoke and yellowing varnish darkened it so badly that everyone took it for a night scene, and it got the name The Night Watch. When restorers cleaned it in the 1940s, the scene turned out to take place in broad daylight, though the nickname stuck anyway. In the middle of the crowd glows a little girl in gold, the company's mascot, with a dead chicken hanging from her belt, and its claws are a joke, because the company's men were the Kloveniers, whose emblem was a golden claw.

Rembrandt also kept a diary in paint for forty years, painting, etching or drawing his own face about a hundred times, from a cocky young success in rich furs to a worn old man, the fullest record of any single face before modern times.

His first great group portrait, Nicolaes Tulp's anatomy lesson of 1632, shows a real corpse. The city permitted just a single public dissection each year, always on an executed criminal. The body was that of the thief Aris Kindt, hanged on 31 January 1632 and cut open before the audience that very same day.

The Night Watch suffered surgery of its own. When the city hung it in its Town Hall in 1715, the canvas was too big for its spot between two columns, so officials simply cut the canvas down on every side, taking the widest slice from the left, and two whole militiamen vanished. The strips were never found. In 2021 the Rijksmuseum made the painting whole again with an artificial-intelligence program, which studied a small seventeenth-century copy of the full picture by Gerrit Lundens and painted back the missing edges stroke by stroke.

renaissance-humanism-petrarch.context_blurb:
Francesco Petrarca, called Petrarch in English, was an Italian poet and scholar of the 1300s, often named the father of Renaissance humanism. He spent his life hunting forgotten Latin books in monastery libraries and writing letters in polished classical Latin. The movement he started taught Europe to learn from the ancient Greeks and Romans directly, and it reshaped schooling for centuries.

The humanists' battle cry was ad fontes, Latin for to the fountainheads, meaning return to the original sources: instead of trusting medieval digests that retold the ancients at second hand, a student should drink from the spring itself and read the classics in their own Greek and Latin.

Petrarch had a fresh eye for the world. In April 1336 he climbed Mont Ventoux in southern France, ignoring an old shepherd who had found nothing up there but rocks and brambles, because he went up for nothing but the view from the summit, the first person since ancient times, he claimed, to climb a mountain for that pleasure alone. On Easter Sunday 1341, on Rome's Capitoline Hill, he was crowned with laurel, an ancient honour for poets and victors unused for more than a thousand years, which is why we still speak of a poet laureate.

In 1345, in Verona's cathedral library, he discovered Cicero's long-lost private letters and copied the whole collection himself, and then he wrote a letter back to Cicero, dating it from the birth of the God whom the old Roman never knew, a gentle reminder that Cicero had died in 43 BC, decades before Jesus was born. To Petrarch, the thousand years since Rome fell looked like a wasteland of ruins and barbarous Latin. He called that age darkness, and so gave us the idea of the Dark Ages, a gloomy era standing between two ages of light. Historians now find the label far too harsh, but it stuck. When death came in July 1374, at his house in Arqua, the story goes that he was slumped over his desk with his head on a book of Virgil, the Roman poet he loved best.

His followers turned that learning into power. Coluccio Salutati, chancellor of Florence for thirty-one years, wrote Latin so sharp that Florence's great enemy, Duke Giangaleazzo Visconti of Milan, is said to have grumbled that one Salutati letter did him more damage than a thousand Florentine horsemen. Poggio Bracciolini used the idle weeks of a long Church council to scour abbey libraries. Around 1416, at the monastery of St Gall, Poggio came upon the only complete copy of Quintilian's handbook on public speaking, mouldy but whole, shut in a dungeon at the foot of one of the abbey's towers, a place so foul, he wrote, that not even a condemned criminal would be kept there. Early in 1417, in another monastery in Germany, Poggio rescued the one surviving copy of the lost poem of Lucretius, On the Nature of Things, which taught that all things are made of tiny atoms colliding in empty space.

Greek came back too: in 1397 Salutati invited the Byzantine scholar Manuel Chrysoloras to Florence, where he began teaching the ancient Greek language in public, the first time anyone had done so in Italy for some seven hundred years. Racing to copy the rediscovered books, Poggio's friend Niccolo Niccoli developed a quick, slanting hand of his own, and printers later cast that hand in metal as italic type.

Even the word humanist began as student slang: in medieval Italian universities students nicknamed each professor after his subject, the jurista for law and the artista for the arts, so the umanista was the teacher of grammar, rhetoric, poetry, history and moral philosophy, all studied through the classics of Greece and Rome. It named a teacher of those old books, not the modern worldview the word later came to mean.

renaissance-reformation-music-as-western.context_blurb:
In the 1500s composers across Europe brought polyphony, choral music in which many independent voices weave together, to a height that set the standard for Western music for centuries. Catholic Rome and Protestant England both produced masters, and they wrote their music to glorify God in worship.

When an Italian piece for forty voices arrived in London around 1567, a duke wondered aloud whether any Englishman could equal it. Thomas Tallis replied by writing Spem in alium, a motet for forty voices arranged in eight choirs of five. According to an account written down decades later, after the first performance the duke, delighted, took the gold chain from around his own neck and hung it on Tallis.

In Rome the great master was Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina, whose clear, flowing masses later composers treated as the model of sacred polyphony. When he died, Palestrina was laid in a lead coffin under the floor of St Peter's, and two Latin words on it crowned his life's work: Musicae Princeps, Prince of Music.

renaissance-science-as-the-work-of-belie.context_blurb:
The men who launched modern astronomy in the 1500s and 1600s were, almost all of them, devout Christians who believed they were reading God's second book, the book of nature. A Catholic churchman moved the Earth, a Danish nobleman measured the stars, and a pious German mathematician found the laws of the planets.

Nicolaus Copernicus, a canon of Frombork Cathedral in Poland, put the Sun at the centre of the heavens, yet for years he kept his great book unpublished, afraid of being laughed at. Tradition says the first printed copy of De revolutionibus reached him on his deathbed, on the very day he died in May 1543, so that he could die in peace. He aimed high, dedicating the book to Pope Paul III, and in that dedication he said it was mockery from Aristotle's followers, not from the Church, that he feared.

The Danish nobleman Tycho Brahe was a wilder character. At twenty, quarrelling with another young nobleman over which of them was the better mathematician, he fought a duel by night with swords, lost the bony bridge of his nose, and wore a metal one ever after, fixing it on with paste from a little flask. His king, Frederick II, gave him the whole island of Hven, where he built Uraniborg, the finest observatory in Europe. A famous story says Tycho kept a tame elk there that got drunk on beer at a feast in a nobleman's castle, tumbled down the stairs and died.

Tycho's assistant, the German Lutheran Johannes Kepler, inherited his careful records. In October 1604 a brand-new star flared in Ophiuchus, though everyone believed the heavens never changed, and it burned so fiercely that people could see it in broad daylight for more than three weeks. Kepler charted it for a year; it was a supernova, the last one seen with the naked eye in our galaxy. Working through Tycho's precise observations of Mars, Kepler then broke two thousand years of perfect-circle astronomy, showing that the planets travel in ellipses, stretched ovals, with the Sun sitting off-centre at one focus.

Kepler's genius did not shield his family. While he served as the Holy Roman Emperor's mathematician, his elderly mother, Katharina, spent more than a year in jail on a charge of witchcraft. At a hearing in 1621 the executioner laid out his tools before her to frighten her into confessing, but she refused, saying they could pull every vein from her body and she would still have nothing to confess. Kepler believed a leaked draft of his own Somnium had helped feed the rumours. That tale of a journey to the Moon, imagining the view of our planet hanging in the Moon's sky, featured a witch-mother much like Katharina, and Carl Sagan and Isaac Asimov both hailed it as the very first science-fiction story.

Kepler's first grand idea, in 1596, was beautiful and wrong: he was sure he had uncovered God's blueprint for the planets in the five Platonic solids, perfect shapes such as the cube and the pyramid, fitted one within another to fix the spacing of the six known planets. He kept that faith in God's geometry all his life. In his Harmonices Mundi of 1619 he announced his third law, which ties the length of a planet's year to how far it lies from the Sun, and he heard in that order real cosmic music, the harmony of the world, the song of the spheres.

Galileo Galilei held that honest science and honest faith cannot truly conflict, since God is the author of two books, the Bible and the world itself, and the book of nature, he said, is written in the language of mathematics. Isaac Newton, who tied all of this together into one physics in his Principia, closed the 1713 edition with a claim about origins: so beautiful a system of sun, planets and comets could only come from the counsel and rule of a Being both intelligent and powerful.

righteous-rescuers-schindler-wallenberg.context_blurb:
During the Holocaust, while Nazi Germany murdered the Jews of Europe, a few outsiders risked their own lives to save some of them, and Israel honours such people as the Righteous Among the Nations. Two of the most famous were nothing alike: Oskar Schindler, a German businessman who came to occupied Krakow to get rich, and Raoul Wallenberg, a young Swedish diplomat posted to Budapest in 1944.

Schindler was a Nazi Party member out for money, and in 1939 he acquired a Krakow factory later nicknamed Emalia. Emalia turned out enamelware, mostly pots and pans for the German army, and because the army ranked that work as vital to the war, the Jewish workers Schindler brought in from the ghetto were protected from deportation. When German troops emptied the Krakow ghetto on the night of 13 March 1943, killing thousands and sending the rest to the camps, Schindler had told his workers to sleep at the factory instead of going home, so they were out of reach.

Wallenberg's weapon was paper: he designed a Swedish protective passport, the Schutzpass, a blue-and-gold document bearing Sweden's three crowns, so official-looking that Nazi officials honoured it, and about twenty thousand Jews are said to have been saved by it. He also rented some thirty-two buildings, declared them Swedish soil, and sold the bluff by draping them in giant Swedish flags and hanging official-sounding signs such as "The Swedish Library." Nearly ten thousand people hid inside. When trains crammed with Budapest Jews stood ready to roll toward Auschwitz, Wallenberg scrambled onto the boxcar roofs and handed his passes down through the openings while Arrow Cross gunmen fired over his head, and then he walked dozens of pass-holders off the train.

Late in 1944 Schindler moved factory and workers to Brunnlitz, in the Czech lands, supposedly to make shells. Itzhak Stern and Mietek Pemper cooked the record books so the SS believed shells were pouring out, but Brunnlitz barely produced a single usable shell, and the sham kept its prisoners classed as essential war workers, and so alive. That January two frozen cattle cars from an Auschwitz sub-camp were left at the plant, with a dozen of the people inside already dead. Schindler's wife, Emilie, would not hand the living back to the SS: she had an engineer cut the iced-over doors open with a soldering iron, then nursed the hundred or so frostbitten survivors back to health herself. On screen Schindler types the famous list himself, but historians say the real one was drawn up by Marcel Goldberg, a Jewish clerk working for the SS, and redrawn more than once, with some places on it bought.

That January, as the Red Army closed in on Budapest, the SS meant to blow up its ghetto with some seventy thousand Jews inside. Through an Arrow Cross officer, Pal Szalai, Wallenberg warned the German commander, General Gerhard Schmidhuber, that if the ghetto died he would personally see the general hanged as a war criminal. The massacre was called off. Days later, on 17 January 1945, Soviet counter-intelligence seized Wallenberg as a suspected spy, and the man who had saved so many from one tyranny vanished into the prisons of another, never seen free again. His last recorded words said he was going to Malinovsky's and did not yet know whether as a guest or a prisoner. The Soviets claimed he died in prison in 1947, but Sweden declared him dead only in 2016.

At the war's end Schindler, a Nazi Party man, had to run from the Allies. His workers gave him a ring made from a prisoner's melted gold tooth crown, engraved in Hebrew with the Talmud's teaching that to save one life is to save an entire world. Bribes and food for his workers had eaten his fortune, and he died poor in 1974. At his own wish he was buried in Jerusalem, on Mount Zion, the only former member of the Nazi Party laid to rest there in honour. By the 1990s his workers' descendants numbered more than six thousand, outnumbering all the Jews left in the whole of Poland, who were fewer than four thousand.

rise-of-islam-expansion-to-europe-s-edge.context_blurb:
In the early 600s Muhammad, a merchant of Mecca in western Arabia, began to preach that the one God had spoken to him. Within about a century the faith he founded, Islam, had built an empire whose armies swept across the Middle East and North Africa into Spain, until they were turned back in the middle of France.

Around 610, Muslim tradition says, Muhammad was about forty and praying alone in the mountain cave of Hira near Mecca; there the angel Gabriel seized him and gave a single command, "Recite!" Muhammad protested that he could not read, but the angel repeated it; in Arabic the word is iqra. In 622, warned that the Quraysh, Mecca's ruling tribe, meant to kill him, Muhammad escaped with his friend Abu Bakr some two hundred miles north to Yathrib, which took a new name: Medina, meaning simply the City. The caliph Umar later made that flight, the Hijra, Year 1 of the Islamic calendar.

In August 636 Khalid ibn al-Walid's Arab army met a far larger Byzantine force by the Yarmuk River, on today's border of Syria and Jordan. A blinding sandstorm blew straight at the Byzantines, their line broke, and the fleeing soldiers were herded into the steep ravine of Wadi al-Ruqqad, where many plunged from the cliffs onto the rocks below. Byzantine rule in Syria never returned.

In the spring of 711 the Berber general Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed from Africa with about seven thousand men and landed beneath a towering rock at Spain's southern tip, which his troops called Jabal Tariq, Tariq's Mountain; worn down over the centuries, that Arabic name became Gibraltar.

In 732 Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi led an army over the Pyrenees into Gaul and burned Bordeaux, but near Tours the Frankish leader Charles Martel packed his foot soldiers into a solid wall that the horsemen charged again and again and could not break. The emir died there, and the advance into Europe turned back at its farthest edge.

rise-of-medieval-towns-guilds-commerce.context_blurb:
After about the year 1000, Europe's towns grew again along rivers, coasts and crossroads. Behind their walls, merchants and craftsmen ran their own markets, courts and militias, and organised each trade into a sworn brotherhood called a guild. Their freedom was new, and they guarded it fiercely.

A serf who fled his lord and stayed a year and a day within a chartered town's walls could no longer be reclaimed, and Germans put that escape into a proverb, Stadtluft macht frei: the air of a town makes a man free. A boy entered a trade such as baking or smithing as an apprentice at about twelve, then worked for wages as a journeyman. Only by making one flawless example of his craft, judged by the guild's masters, could he become a master himself, and that test piece, his masterpiece, gave us the word for any great work. If the masters turned it down, he might stay a journeyman for life.

Many German market towns raised a giant statue of Roland, one of Charlemagne's knights, gripping a drawn sword in the market square, as a sign that the town was free and kept its own market. Bremen's Roland, set up in 1404, stands more than ten metres high, the biggest free-standing statue of medieval Germany.

Merchants linked the towns into trading leagues, and the greatest, the German Hanse, reached from the Baltic to the Atlantic. At its wharf of Bryggen in Bergen, Norway, teenage trainees faced savage initiation games meant to toughen them for the hard life of a merchant: older traders threw a boy into the harbour three times on a rope and beat him with sticks whenever he came up.

A commune was born when every townsman swore to his fellow townsmen that all would defend one another, a promise between equals that ran sideways rather than upward like a vassal's vow of obedience to his lord. That shared oath made the town a legal person, able to hold property and pass its own laws. In the Holy Roman Empire a town's charter of liberties, with the right to hold markets, run courts and tax itself, had to be bought, and the townsmen usually paid not their resentful local lord but the power over his head, the king or emperor.
