rise-of-militarist-japan.context_blurb:
In the 1920s Japan had a parliament and party cabinets. Over the next decade army officers who believed Japan deserved an empire in East Asia seized control through plots, murders and staged incidents, and dragged the country into a war of conquest in China whose cruelty is still remembered.

It began in Manchuria, in China's vast north-east, where Japan's Kwantung Army guarded the South Manchuria Railway. On the night of 18 September 1931, Japanese officers exploded a bomb on their own railway line near Mukden and pinned it on Chinese troops. The blast was so feeble that it damaged only a metre and a half of one rail, and a scheduled train from Changchun crossed the very spot minutes later and reached Shenyang on time, which gave the fake away. That night some five hundred Japanese attacked a Chinese barracks holding about seven thousand soldiers, yet only two Japanese died against roughly five hundred Chinese, because Chiang Kai-shek, hoping to avoid the war Japan was spoiling for, had the garrison under orders not to resist.

Japan's army overran all of Manchuria and dressed it up as an independent country, Manchukuo, and for a famous face on its throne it chose Puyi, who had been the last emperor of China until the 1911 revolution deposed him as a little boy. Real power stayed with the Kwantung Army's commander, who could veto anything Puyi did.

On 15 May 1932 a band of eleven young naval officers forced their way into the home of Prime Minister Inukai Tsuyoshi, and when the old man tried to reason with them, telling them that they would understand if he could explain, they answered, "Dialogue is useless," and shot him. They had meant to kill Charlie Chaplin too, who had just landed in Japan, hoping to provoke a war with the United States, but at that hour Chaplin was at a sumo match with the prime minister's son, which probably saved both their lives. The killers got astonishingly light sentences, a sign that civilian rule was crumbling. When the League of Nations voted forty-two to one in February 1933 to brand Japan the aggressor, its chief delegate, Yosuke Matsuoka, led his delegation out of the hall, announcing that Japan was not coming back.

On 26 February 1936 some fourteen hundred rebel soldiers, led by young army officers, seized the snowy heart of Tokyo and murdered the finance minister, Takahashi Korekiyo, and other leaders, but Prime Minister Keisuke Okada lived: while he hid in a closet, the killers mistook his brother-in-law for him and shot the wrong man. In July 1937, beside the Marco Polo Bridge outside Beijing, Japanese troops on manoeuvres claimed that a soldier, Private Shimura Kikujiro, was missing and demanded to search the town of Wanping, and they kept pressing even after Shimura had already returned to his own unit. Shots followed, and the quarrel became full-scale war.

That December the Japanese army took Nanjing, then China's capital, and for some six weeks its soldiers murdered prisoners and civilians, raped women and girls, and burned whole districts. The postwar International Military Tribunal for the Far East found that more than 200,000 people had been killed in the Rape of Nanking; the Chinese government puts the toll at 300,000, and some historians give lower estimates. Minnie Vautrin, an American missionary who ran Ginling Girls College, sheltered some ten thousand women and girls there, and when Japanese soldiers came to drag victims away, she planted herself at the gate and kept them out. The strangest shield belonged to John Rabe, a German businessman and Nazi Party member: because Germany was Japan's ally, his membership and his swastika flag held soldiers back from a Safety Zone where some 200,000 Chinese civilians took refuge.

At home, papers ran a breathless tale of officers named Toshiaki Mukai and Tsuyoshi Noda racing to be first to kill a hundred people with a sword, but most historians treat those reports as war-glorifying propaganda, since Noda himself later said he had killed only four or five men in real combat and that the rest were prisoners. Both were executed at Nanjing in 1948. That year General Iwane Matsui, the overall commander, was hanged for not preventing the atrocities, but Prince Yasuhiko Asaka, the emperor's uncle, who commanded the troops inside the city during the massacre, received immunity as a member of the imperial family and was never tried.

rise-of-mussolini-and-italian-fascism.context_blurb:
Benito Mussolini invented fascism. A blacksmith's son from northern Italy, he founded the movement in Milan after the First World War, bullied and bluffed his way to power in 1922, and turned Italy into a one-party dictatorship, the model that Adolf Hitler and other strongmen would copy.

The movement began small: on 23 March 1919, in a hall on Milan's Piazza San Sepolcro, Mussolini launched the Fasci di Combattimento before a crowd of only about two hundred people, yet within three years it ruled Italy. He named it after the fasces, the ancient Roman emblem of power, a bundle of wooden rods tied around an axe and carried on the shoulders of the attendants, called lictors, who walked ahead of Rome's magistrates. The rods stood for the power to flog and the axe for the power to behead.

Fascism's founder had started on the far left. His father, Alessandro, a village blacksmith and fiery socialist, named the boy born in 1883 after Benito Juarez, the Mexican president he admired. The son grew into a star of the Socialist Party, editing its newspaper and lifting its readership from twenty thousand to a hundred thousand, but in 1914 he called for Italy to join the First World War, and that November the Socialists expelled him from the party.

After the war his Blackshirt squads made the streets their own. Their signature way to break a socialist, a journalist or a union man was to seize him, hold him down, force his jaws apart and pour castor oil, a violent purgative, down his throat by the litre, so that he lost control of his bowels in front of the crowd. People summed up their methods as the truncheon and castor oil.

Four days before the march on the capital in October 1922, sixty thousand Blackshirts massed in Naples. Before those ranks Mussolini put his aim in one blunt line, declaring that the Fascist programme was a simple one: to rule Italy. The marching columns were fewer than thirty thousand poorly armed men. Mussolini did not lead them: he stayed safely in Milan and came to Rome by train only after the king had already invited him to form a government.

The march could have been crushed, for Luigi Facta, the prime minister, had prepared an emergency order placing the country under a state of siege that would have let the army stop the columns, but King Victor Emmanuel III, fearing bloodshed and perhaps a rival for his throne, refused to sign it. Instead the king asked Mussolini to become prime minister; the march worked because the king flinched. In power, Mussolini took the title Il Duce, the Leader, from the Latin dux, a war chief, and he became the pattern of the all-powerful strongman, so much so that Hitler's own title, Fuhrer, meant the same thing.

Next he rigged the rules. In 1923 Mussolini forced through the Acerbo Law, the work of Giacomo Acerbo, under which whichever party list came first with at least a quarter of the vote won two-thirds of all the seats in Parliament. The 1924 election held under it was Italy's last competitive vote until 1946. On 30 May 1924 the socialist deputy Giacomo Matteotti stood up in Parliament and accused the Fascists to their faces of winning that election by fraud and violence, and eleven days after, a squad of Fascists under Amerigo Dumini kidnapped and murdered him. The killing nearly brought Mussolini down, but the regime survived.

Foreign visitors who heard about the beatings often waved them away with one cheerful boast: Mussolini, at least, had made the trains run on time. The journalist George Seldes heard it everywhere, yet historians call it mostly a legend: much of the railway repair came before the Fascists, and only the big tourist expresses kept to their timetables. In Milan in October 1925, on the third anniversary of the march, Mussolini packed his creed into a formula that became the regime's motto, carved on its monuments: everything inside the State, nothing outside it, nothing against it. The State, not the individual, was supreme.

rise-of-stalin-and-the-ussr.context_blurb:
When Vladimir Lenin died in 1924, Joseph Stalin outmanoeuvred his rivals for control of the Soviet Union, drove Leon Trotsky into exile, and by about 1929 ruled alone. He set out to turn a nation of peasants into an industrial giant by force, and to destroy anyone, even inside his own party, who might stand in his way.

Stalin's first Five-Year Plan, launched in 1928, demanded staggering leaps, more than doubling coal and tripling pig iron, and the regime grew so obsessed with building single plants, dams and steelworks bigger than anything in the capitalist West that Western observers mocked the craze as gigantomania. The showpiece was Magnitogorsk, a complete steel city built on open ground in the Urals beside a mountain rich in iron ore, so that the ore for its furnaces lay right at hand. In 1935 the miner Alexei Stakhanov was said to have hewn 102 tons in one shift, fourteen times his quota, but the record was staged: a support team did his loading and propped up the tunnel while every ton was credited to Stakhanov alone. The Party made him the hero of a Stakhanovite movement of record-breakers; only in 1988 did a Soviet newspaper admit the feat had been puffed up.

In 1936 Stalin turned his secret police on his own people in the Great Purge. The terror at its height is called the Yezhovshchina, the Yezhov era, after Nikolai Yezhov, the head of the secret police, who stood barely five feet tall and was known as the Bloody Dwarf. In three great Moscow show trials, the prosecutor Andrei Vyshinsky, armed with beaten confessions and little else, heaped abuse on Lenin's old comrades, calling them vermin and mad dogs of Trotskyism, and he ended one tirade with a command to the judges: "Shoot the mad dogs!"

Vasily Blokhin, the secret police's chief executioner, personally killed tens of thousands, more than any other official executioner on record, and before each shift he pulled on a leather butcher's apron, a leather cap and long leather gloves to keep the blood off his uniform. Yezhov's own turn came when Stalin had him arrested and shot in 1940, and censors then erased him from a famous 1937 photograph of the two men strolling beside the Moscow-Volga Canal, leaving a blank patch of water where Yezhov had walked.

Behind the purges stood a whole system of slave labour, the Gulag, which Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn would later expose in The Gulag Archipelago. Its first showpiece, the White Sea-Baltic Canal, was hacked out between 1931 and 1933 by some 126,000 prisoners using only crude hand tools, picks, shovels and wheelbarrows, with no real machinery at all, and somewhere between twelve and twenty-five thousand of them died digging it. In the countryside, a 1932 decree of Stalin's government, remembered as the Law of Spikelets, made a handful of leftover ears of grain gleaned from a collective-farm field into theft of socialist property, so a starving peasant could be shot for picking them up. Meanwhile the man-made famine in Ukraine, the Holodomor, killed roughly 3.9 million Ukrainians.

Marshal Mikhail Tukhachevsky, father of the Red Army's deep-battle tank doctrine, faced a secret one-day trial in June 1937 for a German plot he had never joined and was shot within hours, and when investigators opened his prison file decades later, they found the pages of his confession spattered with his own blood. His death began the beheading of the Red Army on the eve of war.

Long before the Plans began, the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises had argued in 1920 that a fully socialist economy could not work, because once private property was abolished there would be no real market prices, and without them a planning ministry like Gosplan could never know what anything was truly worth. Friedrich Hayek added that the knowledge needed to run an economy is scattered among millions of people and can never be gathered into one office, and the Plans' bottlenecks, faked reports and shortages bore them out. People who play down the Great Purge talk vaguely of half a million dead, but the NKVD, Stalin's secret police, kept count, and its own files log 681,692 executions in 1937 and 1938 alone, besides some 116,000 deaths in the camps. The honest scholarly range runs from 700,000 to 1.2 million killed.

robert-boyle-and-the-birth-of-chemistry.context_blurb:
Robert Boyle, born in 1627 into one of the richest families in Ireland, spent his fortune on something new: testing nature by experiment and reporting the results in plain words for anyone to repeat. A founder of the Royal Society in London and a devout Christian, he is often called a father of modern chemistry.

In 1659 his young assistant, Robert Hooke, built him an air pump, a big glass globe on a brass cylinder, which could pump the air out of it. Most people thought a vacuum was impossible. A bird shut inside drooped and died as the air was drawn out, but when Boyle let the air flood back in quickly enough, the bird revived, proof that animals cannot live without air.

In 1661 Boyle published The Sceptical Chymist, a book written as a sharp debate, which attacked both the four ancient elements of fire, air, earth and water and the alchemists' three principles of salt, sulfur and mercury, and demanded that chemistry stand on experiments rather than secret authority.

To find the rule that governs a gas, Boyle trapped some air in the sealed short arm of a J-shaped glass tube and kept pouring mercury into the long end, and he found that when the air was squeezed into half its space, its pressure doubled. Boyle's Law says that at a fixed temperature, pressure times volume stays the same.

robin-hood-the-outlaw-legend.context_blurb:
Robin Hood is the outlaw hero of English legend: an archer living with his Merry Men in Sherwood Forest, robbing the rich to help the poor and defying a crooked sheriff. His story grew in ballads sung in markets and taverns in late medieval England, and whether a real Robin ever lived is unknown.

In the most famous scene, Robin enters an archery contest, finds a rival's arrow already in the centre of the target, and shoots so true that his own arrow splits it lengthwise, which is why archers still call that rare shot a Robin Hood. Sir Walter Scott made the feat famous in his 1819 novel Ivanhoe.

The legend ends darkly: old and dying, betrayed by the Prioress of Kirklees, who has bled him to death, Robin shoots one last arrow from her window and asks his men to bury him wherever it falls. Little John holds him up for the shot, and a mound near Kirklees is still shown to visitors as Robin Hood's Grave.

rodin-and-modern-sculpture-the-thinker.context_blurb:
Auguste Rodin, who lived from 1840 to 1917, was the French sculptor who did more than anyone to begin modern sculpture. He let rough tool marks show, gave his figures raw emotion instead of polished calm, and broke the old rules about how a monument should stand.

His most famous statue, The Thinker, started life as a little figure of the poet Dante, seated high on Rodin's huge bronze doors, The Gates of Hell, and brooding on the souls of the damned in his own Inferno. Foundry workers nicknamed it The Thinker, and in 1904 Rodin enlarged it into the giant the world knows.

For his monument to the Burghers of Calais, the six townsmen who in 1347 gave themselves up to King Edward III, ropes around their necks, to save their town, Rodin refused the usual tall pedestal and wanted his life-size figures set right on the ground, so that passers-by would meet the condemned men eye to eye. Calais at first hoisted them onto a high base anyway; only in 1924 did the city lower them to the ground, where they stand today.

roentgen-and-the-x-ray.context_blurb:
Wilhelm Roentgen was a physics professor at the University of Wurzburg in Germany. In late 1895, working with a glass vacuum tube wrapped in black cardboard, he noticed a coated screen across his darkened laboratory glowing when no light could reach it. Unseen rays were passing through the cardboard, through wood, and even through flesh.

Roentgen had no idea what the rays were, so he named them after the letter that stands in algebra for an unknown quantity, X, and the name X-rays stuck around the world, though some called them Roentgen rays in his honour.

That December he made a picture of the left hand of his wife, Anna Bertha, showing the dark shadows of her bones with her ring still around one finger, and when she looked at the bones of her own living hand, she cried out that she had seen her death. No one had ever looked inside a living body before. Within months doctors were using the rays to find bullets and broken bones.

roman-concrete-the-lost-dome-and-medieva.context_blurb:
The Romans built with a concrete so tough that their harbours, aqueducts and domes still stand after two thousand years, some of them in seawater. After Rome fell, the recipe was lost, and for centuries builders could only stare at what the ancients had done.

The Pantheon's dome in Rome, finished under the emperor Hadrian around AD 126 and 43 metres across, stayed the widest in the world for more than thirteen centuries, until in 1436 Filippo Brunelleschi completed the great dome of Florence Cathedral, having first studied the Pantheon closely.

The concrete held a secret, too: experts had long dismissed its little white lumps, called lime clasts, as sloppy mixing, but in 2023 Admir Masic and Linda Seymour of MIT showed that the lumps heal the concrete's cracks, because water seeping in dissolves them and the lime recrystallises to seal the gap. Their Roman-style test piece closed its crack within two weeks, while an ordinary one stayed broken. The Romans made the lumps by mixing in quicklime hot, a trick modern concrete has never used.

roman-engineering-aqueducts-roads-concre.context_blurb:
The Romans left most theory to the Greeks, but as practical engineers they have rarely been matched. Across a vast empire they built paved highways, channelled fresh water into their cities, and invented a concrete that let them raise vaults and domes no one had attempted before. Much of it still stands.

Their first great paved highway, the Appian Way, was begun in 312 BC on the orders of the censor Appius Claudius Caecus and ran from Rome to the port of Brindisi in Italy's heel, and Romans proudly called it the queen of roads, regina viarum. It also served as a grim noticeboard. In 71 BC, after Crassus crushed the slave revolt led by Spartacus, he had six thousand captured rebels crucified in a line along the Appian Way, a warning to every traveller about the price of rebellion. In 20 BC Augustus set up the Golden Milestone, a gilded bronze post in the Forum, and every great road and every milestone in the empire measured its miles from that one post, so all roads really did lead to Rome.

The Pont du Gard, near Nimes in southern France, is the tallest aqueduct bridge Rome ever built, raised around AD 50 with three tiers of arches nearly fifty metres high and limestone blocks, some weighing six tonnes, cut so precisely that they hold together almost without mortar. Yet such soaring arches were the exception. Rome's aqueducts ran for some 780 kilometres, yet arches carried barely 47 of them: about 94 percent of the water flowed hidden in tunnels and buried trenches, and arcades appeared only where a valley dropped away.

Every arch rested on a simple trick: wedge-shaped stones were laid over a wooden frame until the last stone, the keystone, was driven in at the top, and at that moment the ring locked solid and the frame could be taken away. The wedges turn the weight above into a sideways squeeze, so the arch bears its load as one block.

The Romans' boldest concrete work is the Pantheon, raised under Hadrian almost nineteen centuries ago, whose dome, without a single steel bar inside it, is still the largest dome of plain unreinforced concrete on Earth. The great round opening at its crown, the oculus, is more than a window: by leaving the top open, the builders removed the heaviest and most dangerous part of the dome, and gave the ring of concrete around the hole something to push against.

The concrete itself hid a secret that scientists cracked only recently. In 2023 an MIT team led by Admir Masic broke a test block made the Roman way and let water flow through the break, and within two weeks the crack had sealed itself and the water stopped, while a modern block went on leaking. The heroes were the little white lumps called lime clasts, long blamed on sloppy mixing: when water seeps into a crack, a clast dissolves, and its lime recrystallises as calcium carbonate that plugs the gap. Masic argues that the Romans made those lumps on purpose by tossing dry, caustic quicklime into the wet mix instead of soaking it first, so the batch grew scorching hot and baked in reactive lumps of lime, ready to crack open and dissolve when rain reaches them. Roman harbour walls go one better: the volcanic ash in them, pozzolana, keeps reacting with seawater for centuries, growing rare interlocking crystals inside the concrete, so the walls have grown stronger with age.

roman-law-and-its-lasting-legacy.context_blurb:
Roman law is one of the West's greatest inheritances. It grew from the customs of a small Italian city into the legal system of an empire, and its ideas, that law must be written down for all to read and that some rules of justice bind every people, still shape courts from Paris to Buenos Aires.

For generations the plebeians, Rome's common people, kept losing in court, because the law was unwritten custom known only to a small circle of patrician priests, who could bend it against them. In 451 BC the plebeians made the city name a board of ten, the decemviri, to set it down in writing, and the result was the Twelve Tables, posted in the Forum on bronze for every citizen to read. Around 387 BC the Gauls under Brennus sacked and burned Rome and destroyed the original tablets, yet the laws were never repealed and remained the foundation of Roman justice for centuries. Cicero recalled that in his grandfathers' day schoolboys learned the whole code as a required song, chanting it from memory, a custom that had died out by his own time.

The Tables could be savage. A debtor who could not pay was held and shown in the market on three market days, and if nobody settled the debt, Table III let his creditors cut him into pieces and share him out, a rule so grim that even Romans debated whether it meant the man's body or only his property. The other choice was to sell him as a slave across the Tiber. Table IV allowed a father to sell his son as a bondsman, but it hid a loophole: a son sold three times by his father went free of him for ever, and later lawyers turned that rule into the ritual for freeing a son on purpose, the origin of emancipation.

Roman jurists also reached for something higher than any written statute. They spoke of natural law, ius naturale, a justice binding on all peoples whatever their own laws say, and modern thinkers trace human rights and international law back to that idea and to its partner, the law of nations. Cicero's best-known definition of natural law, true law as right reason in harmony with nature, stood in his dialogue On the Republic, and when that work was lost for centuries, the passage survived only because a Christian writer, Lactantius, had quoted it.

The jurist Julius Paulus put the burden of proof into a few Latin words that Justinian's Digest preserved: proof falls on the one who makes a claim, not on the one who denies it, so the accuser must prove the case and the accused need prove nothing. It is the ancestor of the presumption of innocence. The emperor Trajan went further, ruling that suspicion alone must never condemn anyone and that it is better to let a guilty man's crime go unpunished than to condemn an innocent one, words that Blackstone, the English jurist, later echoed.

By Justinian's time, in the 500s, ten centuries of statutes and legal opinions had grown into a contradictory tangle. The emperor Justinian I set the brilliant jurist Tribonian to sort it out, and the result was the Corpus Juris Civilis, the Body of Civil Law, in four parts: the Codex of imperial decrees, the Digest of the jurists' opinions, the Institutes for students, and the Novels, Justinian's new laws. Tribonian's team boiled some two thousand books by nearly forty jurists down to the fifty books of the Digest, and Justinian, determined that his law should never again be twisted, made it the only law that could be cited in court and forbade anyone to write commentaries on it. Yet the Digest reached us by a thread: it survives almost entirely in a single hand-copied manuscript made soon after the original, kept at Amalfi, carried off to Pisa as war loot in 1155, and brought to Florence in 1406, its home ever since.

Around 1070 to 1100, scholars at Bologna got hold of the nearly forgotten Digest, and a teacher named Irnerius read it aloud and wrote short explanations, called glosses, between its lines and in its margins. His successors, the glossators, built a curriculum on those notes, Bologna grew into the first great law school of Europe, and Justinian's code became the backbone of modern European civil law.

roman-pantheon-and-the-concrete-dome.context_blurb:
The Pantheon in Rome is the best-preserved great building of the ancient world: a round temple fronted by a columned porch and crowned by a vast concrete dome, finished under the emperor Hadrian around AD 125. Nearly nineteen centuries later it is still in use, and its dome still astonishes engineers.

Its name joins two Greek words, pan, all, and theon, gods, because it was raised to honour every god of Rome together rather than a single one. There are no side windows: all the daylight pours in through one round opening, nearly nine metres wide, at the crown of the dome, and the Romans called it the oculus, the eye. When it rains, water falls straight through onto the marble floor, but the floor never floods, because the Romans built it raised and gently humped in the middle, with about twenty-two hidden drain holes to carry the rain away.

The inscription on the porch credits Marcus Agrippa, but Agrippa's earlier temple on the site had burned down long before, and the building we see was raised by Hadrian, who left the old inscription in place instead of carving his own name. That modest choice confused visitors for centuries. Inside hides perfect geometry: the height from the floor to the top of the dome, about 43.3 metres, equals the width across, so a giant sphere would fit snugly within, touching both floor and crown. Most pagan temples were quarried for stone after Rome fell, but in 608 the Pantheon was consecrated as a Christian church, Santa Maria ad Martyres, and so it gained caretakers instead of looters.

The dome's deepest secret is how it keeps from crushing itself. Its concrete was made with pozzolana, a grey volcanic ash from Pozzuoli near Mount Vesuvius, which reacts chemically with lime and water and sets rock-hard, even underwater, instead of merely drying. The builders also lightened the mix as the dome rose, with heavy travertine and basalt at the base, brick and tufa in the middle, and at the top pumice, a volcanic rock so full of holes that it floats on water. The rings of sunken square panels inside, five rings of twenty-eight, called coffers, are beautiful, but their real job is to cut dead weight out of the dome.

In 1625 Pope Urban VIII, of the powerful Barberini family, stripped the bronze from the porch to melt into cannons, and Romans mocked him in Latin, Quod non fecerunt barbari, fecerunt Barberini: the Barberini had done what even the barbarians never did.

The concrete even repairs itself: in 2023 MIT scientists showed that the little white lumps of lime in it, long sneered at as careless mixing, let Roman concrete heal its own cracks, since water seeping in dissolves the lime, which recrystallises and glues the crack shut. For about thirteen centuries no one built a wider dome, until Filippo Brunelleschi, who had travelled to Rome to study the Pantheon's ancient structure for himself, built the great dome of Florence Cathedral between the 1420s and 1436.

romantic-era-composers-chopin-tchaikovsk.context_blurb:
The Romantic composers of the 1800s poured personal emotion, drama and national feeling into music, with bigger orchestras and bolder harmonies than the Classical masters before them. Three giants show the range: Frederic Chopin, the Polish poet of the piano; Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky of Russia; and Richard Wagner of Germany, who dreamed of opera as total drama.

Chopin lay dying in exile in Paris in 1849, so afraid of being buried alive that he asked for his heart to be removed after his death and taken back to Warsaw, and the physician Jean Cruveilhier took it out and sealed it in a crystal jar of cognac. His sister Ludwika carried it home past Austrian and Russian border guards who searched travellers' luggage, smuggling the jar hidden under her cloak. It rests today inside a pillar of the Holy Cross Church in Warsaw.

In his 1812 Overture, a hymn to Russia's victory over Napoleon, Tchaikovsky made the music roar like a real battle by writing in live cannon fire, sixteen shots in all, alongside the pealing church bells of Moscow.

Wagner's Ride of the Valkyries, written for the warrior maidens who carry fallen heroes to Valhalla, found a second life in the 1979 war film Apocalypse Now, blaring from loudspeakers on attack helicopters as they swoop on a village. Wagner built his own theatre at Bayreuth, paid for chiefly by King Ludwig II of Bavaria, and there he hid the whole orchestra in a sunken, hooded pit beneath the stage, invisible to the audience, so that nothing would distract from the drama. He called that hidden space the mystic gulf.

romanticism-delacroix-and-turner.context_blurb:
Romanticism swept European art from the late 1700s into the mid-1800s, prizing emotion, imagination and nature at its wildest over the cool order of Neoclassicism. Its two great painters were Eugene Delacroix in France and the Englishman Turner, whose loose, stormy brushwork pointed the way toward Impressionism.

At the centre of Delacroix's Liberty Leading the People, painted in 1830 for the July Revolution that toppled Charles X, a bare-breasted woman in a red Phrygian cap, half goddess of Liberty and half fighting woman of the people, charges over the fallen on the barricade with a musket in one hand and the French tricolour in the other. She is an early Marianne, the symbol of France, and people often mistake the scene for the great revolution of 1789.

To paint Snow Storm, his 1842 picture of a steamboat in a blizzard off a harbour, Turner said, he had the sailors lash him to the mast for four hours in the blizzard, and he did not expect to escape alive. Some scholars doubt the story, so it is best told as his own legend.

romulus-and-remus-the-founding-legend.context_blurb:
Every Roman child knew how the city began. The legend says that twin brothers, Romulus and Remus, founded Rome in the mid-700s BC, and that the city took its name from Romulus. Historians treat the tale as myth, but it told the Romans who they were: a people born of a god, raised in the wild and founded in blood.

Their mother, Rhea Silvia, had been forced to become a Vestal Virgin so that she would bear no heirs, yet she bore the twins, the story says, because their father was Mars, the god of war. Her uncle Amulius, who had seized the throne from her father, Numitor, ordered the babies placed in a basket and abandoned beside the River Tiber. The basket drifted until it snagged among the roots of a wild fig growing beneath the Palatine Hill, close to the cave where a she-wolf lived. Before any human found them, the she-wolf came down and let the twins suckle her milk, and the image of the wolf nursing the boys became the city's most famous emblem.

A shepherd, Faustulus, and his wife, Acca Larentia, found the boys and raised them as their own, so the princes grew up as shepherds, herding flocks on the hills and never knowing they were of royal blood.

As young men they set out to found a city of their own, but they quarrelled over where. They agreed to settle it by augury, watching the sky for birds sent by the gods: Remus watched first and saw six vultures, but then Romulus saw twelve vultures, and each brother claimed the victory. When Romulus began building his wall on the Palatine, Remus jumped over it to mock him, and Livy tells that Romulus killed his brother in anger, crying that so would perish anyone else who leapt his walls. Plutarch preserves another version, in which a man named Celer struck the blow.

rorke-s-drift-and-the-anglo-zulu-war.context_blurb:
In January 1879 a British army invaded the independent Zulu kingdom of King Cetshwayo in southern Africa. On a single day it suffered one of its worst defeats and then made one of its most celebrated stands.

At Isandlwana a Zulu army of some 20,000 overran a British camp of about 1,800 men and killed more than 1,300 of them, using the formation called the buffalo's horns and chest: the chest pinned the enemy in front while the two horns swept round both flanks to encircle them. A partial eclipse darkened the field at the height of the battle.

That afternoon the Zulu moved on to the little mission station of Rorke's Drift, held by about 150 British soldiers. Lieutenants John Chard and Gonville Bromhead chose to stand, because fleeing across open country with the wounded meant death. With no time to build real defences, the garrison stacked bags of maize and boxes of army biscuits into walls and fired from behind them. Through the night they beat back a Zulu force of perhaps 4,000 warriors, and eleven Victoria Crosses, the empire's highest award for bravery, were given for that defence, the most ever for a single action.

rousseau-and-the-social-contract.context_blurb:
Jean-Jacques Rousseau, the Geneva-born writer of the 1700s, argued that modern civilisation had gone badly wrong and that a just state must rest on the will of the whole people, not on kings or churches. The French revolutionaries quoted him constantly, and he has been loved and feared ever since.

His book The Social Contract, published in 1762, opens with a line known around the world: man is born free, Rousseau wrote, yet everywhere he is in chains. His aim was to show how authority could be made legitimate. Within weeks, the authorities in both Paris and Geneva condemned that book and his Emile as dangerous and burned them in public.

Emile was a whole book on raising a child well, and Rousseau became the great prophet of childhood's natural goodness, yet he left each of his own five children, soon after birth, at the foundling hospital in Paris, where few babies survived.

Rousseau taught that laws bind only when they voice the general will, the shared will of the whole people for the common good, and he pushed the idea to a chilling edge: whoever refuses to obey it, he wrote, must be forced to be free. The Jacobins called him their muse, and in 1794, defending the Terror, Robespierre fused virtue and terror together: virtue without terror, he said, is powerless, and terror without virtue is murderous. Those who resisted the general will went to the guillotine. Hegel argued that Rousseau's ideas led straight to the Terror; other scholars insist Rousseau himself would have condemned it.

russian-revolution-of-1917.context_blurb:
In 1917 Russia had two revolutions. In February, hungry crowds and mutinous soldiers brought down Tsar Nicholas II and three centuries of Romanov rule. In October, Vladimir Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power in the capital, Petrograd, and within months they had crushed the country's first freely elected parliament and begun a one-party dictatorship.

It began on 23 February 1917, International Women's Day, when women textile workers marched through Petrograd demanding bread, joined by strikers from the giant Putilov works, until some 200,000 people filled the streets. Nicholas ordered the garrison to crush the bread riots, but on 27 February the soldiers of the Volynsky Regiment mutinied, refused to fire on the crowds, turned their guns around and joined them, and other regiments followed. Within days his generals warned the Tsar that he had lost the army, and he gave up the throne stranded aboard his royal train at Pskov.

Lenin was stuck in exile in Zurich, and Germany, hoping he would take Russia out of the war, carried him home across German territory in a sealed train, with a chalk line on the carriage floor separating the Russians from their German escorts. Back in Petrograd in April, he boiled his whole programme down to three words that war-weary, hungry Russians could chant in the streets: peace, land and bread.

In October the Bolsheviks struck. The takeover was no vast popular rising but a tight, planned seizure of key buildings, run by Leon Trotsky, who chaired the Military Revolutionary Committee of the Petrograd Soviet, while Lenin stayed in hiding until the final hours. On the night of 24 October Lenin crept through the city to the Bolshevik headquarters at the Smolny Institute in a worker's coat, a slipping wig and a dirty bandage round his jaw as if he had toothache, and a comrade, Antonov-Ovseyenko, said he looked like a schoolteacher or a dealer in second-hand books. The next night the cruiser Aurora gave the signal to attack the Winter Palace, but contrary to the famous image it never bombarded the building: it fired a single blank shell. Most of the palace's defenders had drifted away, hungry and leaderless, and among the last to stand guard was a battalion of women, the 2nd Women's Battalion of Death, about 140 strong, beside a few hundred young cadets. The ministers inside were simply arrested.

In November 1917 the Bolsheviks let Russia hold its first free national election, in which over 40 million people cast ballots, and the Socialist-Revolutionaries won the most seats, 324, while Lenin's party came a distant second with 183. When the elected Constituent Assembly met in January 1918, it defied the Bolsheviks for one thirteen-hour session, until the anarchist sailor commanding the guard, Anatoli Zheleznyakov, closed it with four words, "The guard is tired." The Bolsheviks locked the doors, and the assembly never met again. The heroic picture of the Winter Palace stormed by surging crowds comes mostly from Sergei Eisenstein's 1927 film October, and from a 1920 mass re-enactment, both bloodier than the nearly bloodless real event.

sakharov-havel-the-dissidents-of-conscie.context_blurb:
Under communism in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, telling the truth in public could cost a man his career, his freedom or his life. Two men who paid that price and won anyway were the Soviet physicist Andrei Sakharov and the Czech playwright Vaclav Havel.

Sakharov began as a maker of weapons: he headed the team that designed the USSR's hydrogen bomb, and in October 1961 a scaled-up version, the Tsar Bomba, exploded over the Arctic with the force of fifty megatons, and no bomb since has matched it. Havel's story ended in triumph. In late November 1989, as the Velvet Revolution swept the country, vast crowds in Prague's Wenceslas Square pulled out their keys and jingled them all at once, ringing a goodbye to the communist regime.

The bomb's maker became its conscience. In 1975 Sakharov won the Nobel Peace Prize, praised as the voice of humanity's conscience, but Moscow refused to let him go to Oslo, so his wife, Yelena Bonner, his partner in dissent, read his Nobel lecture there in his place. After he condemned the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, the regime banished him to Gorky, a city closed to foreigners. In December 1986 a KGB man came to the flat with two electricians and fitted a telephone, saying nothing about why, and the next day it rang: Mikhail Gorbachev himself was on the line, ending Sakharov's exile. Sakharov used the call at once to press for the release of other prisoners of conscience. In June 1989, at the new Soviet parliament's first Congress, when Gorbachev cut off his microphone and snapped at him for not respecting the Congress, Sakharov answered that he did respect it, but that he respected the country and its people more. On 14 December 1989, resting at home before going back to argue against one-party rule, he told his wife that tomorrow there would be a battle, and that evening his heart gave out.

Havel started as a stagehand in a Prague theatre and wrote absurd comedies, and his play The Memorandum, staged in 1965, mocked communist office life with an invented bureaucratic language that every clerk had to learn and no one could actually speak. In 1976 the regime jailed the members of an underground rock band with long hair, The Plastic People of the Universe, for extreme vulgarity, and outrage at that trial moved Havel and others to write Charter 77, a human-rights manifesto published in January 1977. Imprisoned in 1979, he could write his wife, Olga, only a single letter of four pages each week, with no cross-outs and no humour allowed, and his jailers threw him into solitary for one act of defiance: speaking up for an illiterate Roma prisoner. Those letters became the book Letters to Olga.

After the revolution had ended four decades of communist rule peacefully, Havel closed a Prague speech on 10 December 1989 with the creed it stood on, that truth and love would prevail over lies and hatred, a line that memorials across the country now bear. On 29 December the Federal Assembly, still packed with the Communist deputies whose regime had jailed him, elected Havel president unanimously, with not one vote against and no abstentions. Within one year he had moved from a cell to the castle.

The seed of Sakharov's change was planted in 1955, at the banquet after his first hydrogen bomb's successful test. Sakharov raised a toast in the hope that the bombs would burst only above proving grounds and never above cities, and when a Soviet marshal answered with a crude parable and a toast to using them in war, Sakharov felt his conscience stir against the weapon he had made, a feeling he said never left him.

saladin-and-the-recapture-of-jerusalem.context_blurb:
In the late 1100s the Muslim sultan whom Europeans called Saladin united Egypt and Syria and drove the Crusaders back toward the sea. A Kurd born around 1137 in Tikrit, in modern Iraq, he won the respect of friend and enemy alike for his mercy and his word, though he could be ruthless too. Saladin was the Crusaders' clipped form of Salah ad-Din, an honorific title meaning Righteousness of the Faith, which he had earned defending Islam.

A shaky truce held in 1187 until Reynald of Chatillon, lord of the desert castle of Kerak above the caravan roads to Mecca, ambushed a rich Muslim caravan, killed its people and refused to return the goods, and Saladin swore an oath to kill Reynald with his own hand.

That July he trapped the Crusaders on dry, high ground beside a twin-peaked hill, the Horns of Hattin, above the Sea of Galilee, after taking the springs. His men beat drums and chanted through the night. They set the dry grass alight as well, and on the morning of 4 July the smoke blinded and choked knights already maddened by thirst. The Christians had marched into battle behind their holiest relic, the True Cross, believed to be wood from the cross of Jesus, but Saladin's warriors cut down the bishop of Acre who guarded it, seized it, and later paraded it to Damascus.

In his tent Saladin offered his prisoner, King Guy of Lusignan, iced rose-water in a cup, but when Guy passed it to Reynald, Saladin would not let Reynald drink, because by custom a captive given food or drink by his captor could not be killed, and Saladin would not let hospitality shield the truce-breaker. He said he had not invited that evil man to drink, and struck Reynald down himself, keeping his oath. Guy he spared, telling him that kings do not kill kings, but he had the captured Templar and Hospitaller knights, the warrior monks he saw as his most implacable enemies, beheaded, sparing only the Templar Grand Master.

In September Saladin besieged Jerusalem. Remembering 1099, he first swore to take the city by the sword, until its last Christian commander, Balian of Ibelin, threatened that the defenders would kill their five thousand Muslim prisoners and destroy the city's Muslim holy places, the Dome of the Rock among them, rather than die without a fight. Saladin agreed instead to let the people ransom themselves. He set the price at ten dinars for a man, five for a woman and two for a child, a deliberately low and sliding scale. The mercy shone brighter by contrast, for when the First Crusade stormed the same city in 1099, its knights had slaughtered the Muslims and Jews of Jerusalem in the streets, even those sheltering in the Al-Aqsa Mosque. Many historians think the old accounts exaggerated the toll, but Saladin's restraint was measured against them.

He had the golden cross torn from the Dome of the Rock, and the Al-Aqsa Mosque, which the Crusaders had used as a palace and in one wing as stables, washed with rose-water, recarpeted and adorned again with verses of the Quran. Some emirs wanted the Christians' holiest shrine, the Holy Sepulchre, razed, but Saladin refused and let Christian pilgrims keep visiting it on payment of a fee, and allowed native Christians and Jews to stay in the city.

Europe answered with the Third Crusade, led by England's Richard the Lionheart. When Richard lay sick with a raging fever outside Acre in 1191, Saladin sent his enemy fresh fruit and snow carried down from the mountains to cool his drinks, a courtesy, whether or not it happened just so, that made Saladin a legend of chivalry in Europe. In 1192, fighting at Jaffa, Richard lost his horse and was left on foot among the enemy, and Saladin, through his brother al-Adil, sent him two Arabian horses, because so brave a king should not have to fight on foot. The two men traded gifts and courtesies through the whole war, yet never once met.

Saladin gave so much to the poor that his treasurers hid money from him, and when he died in Damascus in 1193, his treasury held one gold coin and forty-seven pieces of silver, not even enough to pay for his funeral.

saladin-richard-the-lionheart-third-crus.context_blurb:
In 1187 Saladin, sultan of Egypt and Syria, recaptured Jerusalem from the Crusaders, and Europe answered with the Third Crusade, with England's King Richard I at its head. The two kings became famous enemies and, in a strange way, admirers of each other, capable of great courtesy and of great cruelty.

Richard, huge and fearless, cared more for fighting than for governing, and even before he sailed east, minstrels were praising his reckless charges, so that in his own lifetime he was already Coeur de Lion, the Lionheart. His enemy, Yusuf, was a Kurd from Tikrit in modern Iraq who ruled Egypt and Syria from about 1174, and Salah ad-Din, which Europeans shortened to Saladin, was an honorific title meaning Righteousness of the Faith.

Saladin's greatest victory came on 4 July 1187 at Hattin, near the Sea of Galilee. Having taken the only springs, he left the Crusaders to bake in their thirst. His men set the dry grass and brush on fire, and on the morning of 4 July the smoke rolled over the parched Crusaders and choked their throats. The Christians had carried a fragment of the True Cross at the head of their army, and after the rout Saladin's men fixed the captured relic upside-down on a lance and paraded it to Damascus. The Kingdom of Jerusalem never got it back.

Saladin had the exhausted King Guy of Lusignan brought to his tent and gave him rose-water chilled with snow brought from Mount Hermon, and as Guy drank, Saladin assured him that kings never kill kings. Among his people, giving a captive a drink meant his life was safe. But when Guy passed the cup to Raynald of Chatillon, the lord who had plundered Muslim caravans in time of truce, Saladin struck the cup from his hands, saying he had not offered that evil man a drink, and killed Raynald himself.

When Jerusalem surrendered that October, Saladin did the opposite of the First Crusaders, who in 1099 had slaughtered Muslims and Jews by the thousand: he spared the city and let its people buy their freedom with a ransom. The price was ten dinars for a man, five for a woman and two for a child, and when many of the poor could not pay, Saladin and his brother al-Adil let thousands go free.

In 1191 Richard took Acre, and when Saladin dragged his feet over the ransom he had promised, Richard marched some 2,700 Muslim prisoners to the hill of Ayyadieh and had them all beheaded in full view of Saladin's army, and Saladin answered by executing his own Christian captives. The two chivalrous rivals could slaughter too. Yet when Richard lay burning with fever in the desert heat, Saladin sent across the lines fresh fruit and snow brought down from the mountains to cool him, and is said to have offered his own physician. Richard, hoping to end the war without more slaughter, even proposed that his sister Joan marry Saladin's brother al-Adil, and that the couple rule Jerusalem together. The plan came to nothing; Richard wrote that Christians objected to such a marriage without the Pope's consent.

At Jaffa in 1192 Richard's horse went down under him and he battled on foot, and al-Adil, whom the Crusaders called Saphadin, sent two fine Arab warhorses to him in the thick of the battle. Richard accepted them as a gift between worthy enemies, though he and Saladin never met face to face. Saladin gave so freely to the poor that, after his death in Damascus in 1193, his treasury held just one gold coin and some forty-seven silver pieces, not even enough to bury him.

samuel-morse-and-the-telegraph.context_blurb:
Samuel Morse was an American portrait painter who, in middle age, turned inventor. He believed a message could flash instantly down a wire from city to city by making and breaking an electric circuit, and with his partner Alfred Vail he built a telegraph and a code of dots and dashes that carried the world's long-distance messages for a century.

On 24 May 1844, in a room of the US Capitol in Washington, Morse tapped out the first message on the line to Vail in Baltimore, 38 miles away: a verse from the Bible, chosen by Annie Ellsworth, the teenage daughter of the patent commissioner, "What hath God wrought."

To give the commonest letters the shortest signals, Vail went into a newspaper office in Morristown, New Jersey, and counted how many pieces of metal type the printers kept for each letter, since printers stock the most of the letters they use most. That is why E, the commonest letter in English, is a single dot. The most famous signal of all, the distress call SOS, agreed on by the world's governments in 1906, is three dots, then three dashes, then three dots again, a short, even rhythm that is almost impossible to mistake for anything else.

samurai-shoguns-bushido-feudal-japan.context_blurb:
From the late 1100s to the 1860s, Japan was ruled in practice by military governments, with the emperor kept as a sacred figurehead in Kyoto. Its warriors, the samurai, were a hereditary class who served great lords called daimyo, and their code of loyalty and honour was later celebrated as bushido, the way of the warrior.

Under the Tokugawa family, from 1603 to 1868, the emperor reigned in name while the shogun, the supreme military ruler, commanded the armies, roads, taxes and castles from his fortress capital at Edo, today's Tokyo. The man who reigned was not the man who ruled. A samurai wore two swords together, a long katana and a shorter wakizashi, a pair called the daisho, big-little, and no farmer, merchant or monk was allowed to carry both.

A samurai who had lost his honour might be sentenced to seppuku, ritual suicide by cutting open his own belly. A trusted swordsman, the kaishakunin, stood behind him and cut off his head the moment he made the cut, a mercy stroke that spared him a slow death.

The shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu, in 1635, to stop the great lords from ever growing strong enough to revolt, made each daimyo spend every other year at Edo, paying for two great households and costly processions between them, and when a lord went home to his province, his wife and heir stayed behind in Edo as hostages. The system was called sankin-kotai, alternate attendance. When Lord Asano was forced into seppuku, his forty-seven lordless samurai swore revenge on his enemy, Kira, and to fool Kira's spies, Oishi Kuranosuke, their leader, passed more than a year playing a drunken good-for-nothing in the pleasure quarters of Kyoto. Then, on a snowy night in January 1703, the forty-seven stormed Kira's mansion in Edo and killed him; the shogun praised their loyalty, then ordered all of them to commit seppuku.

The Hagakure, bushido's best-known text, opens with the claim that a samurai's way lies in dying. Its author, Yamamoto Tsunetomo, a samurai long retired, spoke it aloud to a scribe in about 1709, and he had never seen a real battle. Bushido was largely written down during the long Edo peace, by men looking back on war rather than fighting it.

saratoga-1777-the-turning-point.context_blurb:
In the summer of 1777, in the American War of Independence, General John Burgoyne led a British army down from Canada along Lake Champlain, meaning to seize the Hudson valley and split New England from the other rebel colonies. The other British columns never came, and the Americans under Horatio Gates, with Benedict Arnold leading fiercely in the field, trapped him at Saratoga in upstate New York.

On 17 October 1777 Burgoyne surrendered his whole army, and every royal court in Europe was stunned, because never before had a complete British field army laid down its arms to anyone, anywhere.

When the news reached Paris that December, France, which had been secretly sympathising with the rebels but avoiding open war, moved fast: in February 1778, thanks to Benjamin Franklin's diplomacy, it signed a formal alliance with the United States and entered the war openly on the American side. French soldiers, ships and money followed, and Britain now faced a war it could lose.

sargon-of-akkad-s-empire.context_blurb:
Sargon of Akkad, who ruled in Mesopotamia in the 2300s BC, conquered the city-states of Sumer and built what historians count as the world's first empire, stretching from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean coast of Syria. He made Akkadian, a Semitic language, the language of his government, and his model shaped every later Mesopotamian empire.

A legend on clay tablets written down long after his reign tells that his mother, a priestess who dared not acknowledge a son, sealed his basket with tar and laid it on the Euphrates, where a water-drawer named Akki lifted him out and raised him, a tale strikingly like the Bible's story of baby Moses, pulled from the Nile among the bulrushes.

Sargon made his daughter Enheduanna chief priestess of Nanna, the moon god, at Ur, and there she wrote hymns in praise of Inanna, a goddess, and signed them with her own name some forty-three centuries ago, ages before Homer, which makes her the first author in history whom we know by name.

scipio-zama-and-the-destruction-of-carth.context_blurb:
Rome fought three wars against Carthage, the great trading city on the coast of North Africa, between 264 and 146 BC. In the second, the Carthaginian general Hannibal crossed the Alps with war elephants and ravaged Italy for fifteen years; in the third, Rome wiped Carthage off the map.

The war turned when the Roman general Scipio carried the fight to Africa and drew Hannibal home, and in 202 BC, at Zama, near Carthage itself, Scipio defeated Hannibal, the man whose name Roman mothers had used to frighten their children. Hannibal sent eighty war elephants against the Roman front, but Scipio had opened wide lanes between his units and had his men blare trumpets and clash weapons against shields, and the terrified beasts stampeded harmlessly down the empty lanes, some even turning to trample Hannibal's own horsemen. Scipio's other secret was the fast Numidian horsemen Hannibal had once used to beat the Romans, for now they rode for Rome under their king, Masinissa, swept Hannibal's cavalry from the field and struck his infantry from behind.

Rome stayed afraid. Decades later, Cato the Elder loathed Carthage so fiercely that whatever the Senate was debating, even the city's drains, he finished with the same demand: Carthage must be destroyed. To show that Carthage was still rich and dangerous, Cato once dropped a ripe fig from his toga in the Senate house, and as senators admired its size, he told them it had been picked only three days' sail from Rome.

After a three-year siege, Rome stormed Carthage street by street in 146 BC, and the general who razed it was Scipio Aemilianus, the adopted grandson of the Scipio who had beaten Hannibal at Zama. Its people were sold as slaves and the city was put to the torch. Yet as Carthage burned, Scipio Aemilianus wept, quoted Homer's lines on the fall of Troy to his friend the historian Polybius, and confessed his fear that Rome itself would one day suffer that fate. Later writers claimed that the Romans also sowed the ground with salt so nothing could grow there, but no ancient source mentions it, and historians think the tale was most likely invented in the 1800s. The true record is harsh enough.

seneca-falls-and-the-women-s-rights-move.context_blurb:
On 19 and 20 July 1848, some three hundred people met in the Wesleyan Chapel at Seneca Falls, a small town in upstate New York, for America's first convention on women's rights. Its leaders were Elizabeth Cady Stanton, a young mother with a sharp pen, and Lucretia Mott, a famous Quaker preacher and abolitionist.

On the first morning they found the chapel locked and no key to be had, so they lifted Stanton's eleven-year-old nephew, Daniel Cady Eaton, through an open window, and he opened the door from inside. Stanton modelled her Declaration of Sentiments on Jefferson's Declaration of Independence, and to its most famous line she added two words, and women, so that it declared all men and women created equal. She claimed the founders' own natural-rights principle for women rather than rejecting it.

James Mott, Lucretia's husband, presided, because in 1848 even these reformers did not think it proper for a woman to chair a public meeting. Every resolution passed unanimously except the demand for women's right to vote, which nearly failed until Frederick Douglass, who had escaped slavery and was the only Black person present, rose and argued for it. His newspaper's masthead read: Right is of no Sex, Truth is of no Color.

One of the hundred signers was Charlotte Woodward, a nineteen-year-old glovemaker who wanted to keep her own wages, and when women at last won the vote nationwide through the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920, she was the only signer still alive, though too ill to cast the ballot she had waited 72 years for.

Even Lucretia Mott had begged Stanton to drop the vote, warning that it would make them ridiculous, but Stanton held that the ballot was the right that protected every other right, and kept it in. The press mocked it fiercely, and the campaign it began lasted seventy-two years.

september-11-2001.context_blurb:
On the morning of 11 September 2001, nineteen al-Qaeda hijackers, Islamist terrorists, seized four American airliners. They crashed two into the World Trade Center's twin towers in New York and a third into the Pentagon outside Washington, while the fourth came down in a field in Pennsylvania. Almost three thousand people were killed, in the deadliest terror attack of modern times.

As office workers fled down the stairwells, New York City firefighters were heading up them, toward the fire and the people stranded on the floors above, and 343 of them died that day, the worst loss in the department's history. Among them went Father Mychal Judge, the fire department's Franciscan chaplain, who was killed by falling debris in the North Tower while praying over the dying, and he was recorded as Victim 0001, the first certified death of the attacks.

In the South Tower, Welles Crowther, a young equities trader of 24, guided people who were trapped to a stairway, then climbed back for others, his face covered against the smoke by the red handkerchief he had carried since boyhood, and survivors who never saw his face remembered him only as the man with the red bandana. He made three trips up to the 78th-floor sky lobby before the tower fell with him inside.

The fourth plane, United Flight 93, was probably bound for the US Capitol, but its passengers and crew fought back. Sandra Bradshaw, a flight attendant, called her husband to say farewell and told him she was in the galley boiling water to hurl at the hijackers. On another call, the operator Lisa Jefferson heard the passenger Todd Beamer ask the others whether they were ready, and then say, "Let's roll." Moments later they rushed the cockpit, and the plane crashed near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, far short of Washington.

In the wreckage at Ground Zero, a burned Callery pear, half dead, turned up; parks workers nursed it for years, and since 2010 it has stood at the 9/11 Memorial, known to New Yorkers as the Survivor Tree.

shaka-zulu-the-zulu-kingdom.context_blurb:
Shaka ruled the Zulu from 1816 until his half-brothers murdered him in 1828, and in that time he turned a small clan in today's South Africa into the most feared military power in the region. He did it by reinventing how his warriors fought, and he ruled with a ferocity that his own people came to dread.

Shaka replaced the long throwing spear with the iklwa, a short spear whose wide iron blade was nearly a foot long, so that his warriors had to close in and fight hand to hand. Its very name, iklwa, imitates a sound: the wet, sucking noise the broad blade made as it was pulled from a wound. In his battle plan, the bull horns, seasoned warriors formed the chest and met the enemy head-on, while two horns of fast young men raced around both sides to surround the foe, and a reserve, the loins, waited behind to plug any gap.

Around 1818, at Gqokli Hill, Shaka faced Zwide of the Ndwandwe, whose army was twice the size of his, but the Ndwandwe were packed so tightly on the slope that they could not hurl their long spears, and Shaka's men charged down on them and stabbed them with the short iklwa.

When his mother, Nandi, died in 1827, Shaka's grief became a terror: he banned planting and the use of milk, put thousands to death for mourning too little, and even had cows slaughtered so that their calves would know what it was to lose a mother, as he had.

Shaka's wars are linked to the Mfecane, the crushing, a time of war, hunger and whole peoples on the move across the south of the continent from the 1810s to the 1840s, out of which new nations were forged, among them Lesotho, which Moshoeshoe built by drawing scattered clans to a mountain stronghold. The usual estimates put the Mfecane's dead at one to two million; some historians argue that drought, the slave trade and European pressure drove it too and that those tolls are inflated, while others defend them.

shakespeare.context_blurb:
William Shakespeare, a glovemaker's son born in 1564 in Stratford-upon-Avon, a small Warwickshire market town, went to London as a young man and became the greatest playwright in the English language. He acted with, wrote for and part-owned a company whose open-air playhouse on the Thames's south bank drew everyone from the poorest Londoners to the queen.

The cheapest place at his Globe theatre cost a single penny and bought no seat at all, only standing room in the open yard at the foot of the stage, and those penny fans were called groundlings. Archaeologists digging the Globe's yard have found the cracked hazelnut shells and orange peel they dropped. English law and custom kept women off the public stage, so Juliet, Lady Macbeth, Cleopatra and every other heroine was first played by a boy whose voice had not yet broken.

On performance days a flag flew over the Globe, and by tradition it showed Hercules carrying the whole world on his shoulders, to match the theatre's name. On 29 June 1613, during Henry VIII, a stage cannon fired for the king's entrance set the thatched roof alight, and within an hour the Globe was ashes, yet no one died, and the only injury was a man whose breeches caught fire, which he put out with a bottle of ale. Shakespeare was baptised on 26 April 1564, so historians set his birth a few days earlier, on 23 April, and by tradition he died on that same date, 23 April 1616, his fifty-second birthday.

The Globe itself rose out of a quarrel over land. When the lease ran out on the ground beneath the company's old playhouse, The Theatre, the actors still owned the timber, so over a few December nights in 1598 they took the building apart beam by beam and ferried it across the Thames. On the south bank it became the Globe, finished in 1599. Hamlet asks whether to be or not to be, but the speech that calls all the world a stage belongs to another play, As You Like It, where the gloomy lord Jaques follows a man's life through seven stages, from infancy to old age.

Many actors will not say Macbeth inside a theatre, believing the name brings fires, injuries and ruined shows, so they call it the Scottish Play. Anyone who slips must leave the room, turn around three times, spit and ask to be let back in. His will gave his house and the bulk of his fortune to Susanna, his elder daughter, and squeezed in one short bequest for his wife, Anne Hathaway: his second-best bed. Historians think it was the couple's own marriage bed, since the best bed was kept for guests.

In 1596 Shakespeare's only son, Hamnet, a twin to his sister Judith, died at eleven, and scholars have long been struck that the boy's name is almost the same as that of Hamlet, the grief-stricken prince of his later tragedy. Shakespeare is the most quoted author in the Oxford English Dictionary, which credits him with the first written use of some 1,700 words, everyday ones like frugal, obscene and puppy-dog, and he often made new words by turning one part of speech into another, as with bedazzle. In 1623 two fellow actors, Heminges and Condell, published thirty-six of his plays in a single volume, the First Folio, and for roughly half of them it is the only source: Macbeth, The Tempest, Twelfth Night and others had never appeared in print, and without it they would be lost today. His grave in Stratford's Holy Trinity Church bears a four-line rhyme, believed to be his own, blessing anyone who leaves the stones alone and cursing anyone who digs up the grave and moves his bones.

One legend explains the curse on the Scottish Play: at its very first performance, it says, the boy cast as Lady Macbeth died suddenly, and Shakespeare himself had to rush on and play her. It is a story invented to explain the bad luck, not a recorded fact.

shakespeare-the-plays-and-the-language.context_blurb:
William Shakespeare, who lived from 1564 to 1616, left Stratford-upon-Avon for London, became part-owner of the Globe theatre and wrote some thirty-seven plays and 154 sonnets. His English was so inventive that ordinary speech is still full of his words and phrases, and he remains the most performed playwright on Earth.

A penny, as cheap as a loaf, bought the cheapest place at the Globe, which was no seat at all but standing room in the open-air pit, the yard, at the foot of the stage, and the standing crowd there were nicknamed the groundlings. Richer playgoers paid more to sit in the covered galleries. Women were forbidden on the English stage until 1660, so teenage boys played every one of his heroines, Juliet and Lady Macbeth and Cleopatra among them. Over 1,700 words still in use are first found in writing in his works, and in Henry VI, Part 1, he became the first writer to set down the word eyeball. He may have coined some of these words and merely been the first to write down others.

In Macbeth three witches cook up a spell around their pot, chanting again and again, Double, double toil and trouble, while the fire burns and the cauldron bubbles. In Hamlet's graveyard scene, a gravedigger turns up the skull of Yorick, the old court jester who used to carry little Hamlet on his back a thousand times, and holding it, the prince sees how death brings king and clown alike to dust.

The Prologue of Romeo and Juliet calls the pair star-crossed lovers, and since people then believed the stars ruled human fate, that one phrase warns the audience from the first minute that fate itself is set against them and their love is doomed. So when Juliet stands on her balcony asking wherefore art thou Romeo, she is not looking for him in the dark: wherefore means why, and she despairs that the boy she loves was born a Montague, her family's sworn enemy. The same play gives the first written wild-goose chase, which then meant not a bird hunt but a horse race in which every rider had to follow the leader's twisting path, like geese flying after the lead bird. In Macbeth, Lady Macbeth, her husband's partner in the murder of King Duncan, later walks in her sleep, rubbing her hands and crying out against a damned spot, because she imagines the king's blood still on them, a stain her guilt can never wash away.

Hamlet's soliloquy that begins To be, or not to be, the most famous speech in English drama, wrestles with whether to go on enduring life's suffering or to escape it through death. In Henry V, the Chorus apologises that one small round playhouse must hold the vast battlefield of Agincourt, calls the Globe "this wooden O," and asks the audience to piece out the armies with their thoughts. The Globe burned down in 1613 when a stage cannon fired during Henry VIII set its thatch alight, and the eyewitness Sir Henry Wotton reported a single injury, a man with his breeches on fire, who doused the flames with his bottle of ale. When the theatres reopened, on 8 December 1660, the first professional actress the English stage had ever seen walked on, by most accounts Margaret Hughes, and the heroine she played was Desdemona, in Othello.

About half his plays, Julius Caesar, The Tempest and Macbeth among them, had never been printed in his lifetime, so if Heminges and Condell had not collected them in the First Folio in 1623, they would have vanished for ever. Ben Jonson, once his rival, praised him in verse at the front of that book as the Sweet Swan of Avon, after the river of his birthplace, and declared that he was not of an age, but for all time.

shays-rebellion-1786-87.context_blurb:
In the winter of 1786 to 1787, debt-ridden farmers in western Massachusetts rose in arms under Daniel Shays, a veteran of the Revolutionary War. The state was squeezing them with heavy taxes to pay its war debts, and the courts were seizing their farms and jailing debtors, so the rebels shut the courts down.

Shays had served from Bunker Hill to Stony Point and come home without his pay, only to be hauled into court for debt, and the sword that Lafayette had given him for his service, a handsome ceremonial blade, he sold for cash, to the shame of his fellow officers. He stood for every veteran the new republic had left broke.

In January 1787 the rebels marched on the federal arsenal at Springfield, and Massachusetts crushed them with a militia paid for by Boston merchants. Congress, under the Articles of Confederation, could neither tax nor raise an army and had been all but helpless, and that frightened Washington and other leaders into calling the Constitutional Convention, which met in Philadelphia in May 1787 to build a stronger government.

shostakovich-s-fifth-music-coded-under-s.context_blurb:
Dmitri Shostakovich was the great Soviet composer of Stalin's time, and his career was a long struggle to write music that would satisfy a murderous regime without betraying his own conscience. In January 1936 Stalin went to the Bolshoi to see his opera, Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District, and left before the final curtain.

Two days later Pravda, the Party's newspaper, ran a savage unsigned editorial headed Muddle Instead of Music, and to be attacked by name in Pravda could cost a man his life. Historians now credit the propagandist David Zaslavsky with writing it. By his son Maxim's account, Shostakovich then slept fully clothed on top of the blankets with a small packed suitcase on the floor beside him, so that if the secret police came in the night, they would not drag him away in his pyjamas.

His Fifth Symphony of 1937, written while Stalin's secret police sent his friends to the Gulag, ends in a blaring victory that officials cheered as loyalty, but a disputed memoir, Solomon Volkov's Testimony, quotes him saying the rejoicing was forced, like being beaten with a stick and made to march off cheering.

siege-of-leningrad.context_blurb:
From September 1941 to January 1944, German and Finnish armies ringed Leningrad, the Soviet Union's second city, now St Petersburg, and set out to starve its people into surrender. The siege lasted 872 days and killed roughly a million people, most of them civilians who died of hunger and cold.

In the worst winter, at the end of 1941, an ordinary citizen's daily bread ration fell to about 125 grams, and once the real grain ran out, the bakers padded the loaves with sawdust, cellulose and chaff. Leningrad's lifeline ran over the ice of Lake Ladoga, the Road of Life, and since over 300 lorries plunged through the thin ice in two winters, the drivers kept their cab doors open to leap clear if it cracked. The road still evacuated some 1.4 million people and carried in over 1.5 million tonnes of supplies.

An eleven-year-old girl, Tanya Savicheva, wrote each death in her family on a fresh page of a small alphabet notebook, one flat line at a time, and her last three pages record that the Savichevs had died, that everyone had died, and that only Tanya was left. She was evacuated, but died in 1944, aged fourteen.

On 9 August 1942 the conductor Karl Eliasberg led Shostakovich's Seventh, the Leningrad Symphony, inside the besieged city, and because only about fourteen of the forty players of the radio orchestra were still alive there, soldiers were pulled from the front line to fill the empty chairs. Three musicians died of hunger during rehearsals, and loudspeakers blared the concert at the German trenches. General Leonid Govorov made sure German guns could not drown it out, opening Operation Squall, some 3,000 shells on the German batteries, and he told Eliasberg afterward that his gunners had played their own instrument in the symphony too.

At the Vavilov Institute, which held the world's first seed bank, nine scientists starved to death rather than eat the roughly 380,000 samples of rice, grain and nuts they guarded; one died clutching a packet of peanuts. The man who had built that collection, the botanist Nikolai Vavilov, did not die in the siege at all: Stalin had him arrested in 1940 after he clashed with the pseudo-scientist Trofim Lysenko, and in January 1943 he died in a Soviet prison, starved on mashed cabbage and mouldy flour.

sinking-of-the-lusitania.context_blurb:
The Lusitania was a giant British ocean liner of the Cunard line, and the German embassy had printed warnings in New York newspapers before she sailed. On 7 May 1915, during the First World War, she was steaming toward Liverpool off the south coast of Ireland when the German submarine U-20 put a torpedo into her side.

Everyone assumed so vast a ship would stay afloat for hours, but she went down in about 18 minutes, and 1,198 people died, 128 of them Americans, which helped turn American opinion against Germany. Only about 763 people survived.

Her attacker, Kapitanleutnant Walther Schwieger, was puzzled that one torpedo had sunk her so fast, and the reason was a violent second explosion deep within the hull just after the torpedo struck. Historians still argue over its cause: coal dust, a bursting boiler or steam line, or the war munitions in her hold, for she really was carrying millions of rifle rounds and cases of shrapnel shells.
