smallpox-and-the-demographic-collapse.context_blurb:
When Europeans reached the Americas after 1492, their deadliest weapons were invisible. The peoples of the Americas had lived apart from the Old World and its crowd diseases for thousands of years, and in the century after Columbus a series of epidemics swept through them in the worst population collapse in recorded history.

The worst killer of all was smallpox, which covered its victims in agonising sores and marked those who lived with deep pits, sometimes blinding them. Steel and gunpowder accounted for only a small part of the dying: by one widely cited estimate some 56 million people had died by 1600, perhaps nine in ten of the Native population, and Old World epidemic diseases did the overwhelming majority of the killing. In Europe smallpox carried off about one victim in three, but in the Americas it could wipe out half a village or more, because Native peoples had never been exposed to it and so had no acquired immunity, which historians call a virgin-soil epidemic.

In 1520 the Aztec general Cuitlahuac led the uprising that drove Hernan Cortes out of Tenochtitlan on the night the Spanish called the Night of Sorrows, and he was crowned emperor in triumph, but smallpox killed him after a reign of only about eighty days. The epidemic gave Cortes time to regroup before his final siege. An Aztec survivor told the friar Bernardino de Sahagun that the sick lay helpless like corpses, and many who outlived the disease itself died anyway, because whole families fell ill at once and no one was well enough to bring them food or water, so they starved. The disease raced ahead of the Spanish down the Andes and very likely killed the Inca emperor Huayna Capac and his chosen heir, so when Francisco Pizarro landed in Peru with a band of under two hundred, he found the empire already torn by a war of succession between the brothers Huascar and Atahualpa.

The Taino of Hispaniola, the first people Columbus met, numbered about 60,000 in a census of 1508, but after enslavement, war and the first smallpox epidemic in the New World in 1518, they had fallen to about 400 by the mid-1500s, a whole people all but gone in two generations. In New England an epidemic of 1616 to 1619, the Great Dying, killed as many as nine in ten of the coastal peoples, and when Tisquantum, known to the Pilgrims as Squanto, came home from years of captivity in Europe in 1619, he found he was the last of the Patuxet left alive. So when the Pilgrims landed in 1620, the place they settled and named Plymouth was the emptied Patuxet village, with dwellings still standing and the bones of the dead lying unburied.

The dying went on for centuries: in 1837 the fur-trade steamboat St. Peter carried smallpox up the Missouri to Fort Clark, in today's North Dakota, and the Mandan, some 2,000 people living in round earth-lodge towns, were cut down in three months to about 25 survivors. More than 17,000 Native people died along the river.

John Winthrop, the Puritan governor of Massachusetts, wrote in 1634 that the natives near the colony were nearly all dead of smallpox, and he read it as God's favour, saying that the Lord had thereby cleared the colonists' title to what they possessed. In 1763, during Pontiac's War, the British defenders of besieged Fort Pitt gave two visiting Delaware envoys blankets from the fort's smallpox hospital, and the trader William Trent wrote that he hoped it would have the desired effect. General Jeffery Amherst separately urged spreading the disease with blankets. Smallpox was already circulating there, so the blankets' effect is uncertain; the intent is documented.

Not every killer was smallpox: the cocoliztli epidemic of 1545, which killed millions in New Spain as its victims burned with fever and bled from the eyes and mouth, stayed a mystery until 2018, when Johannes Krause's team read DNA from victims' teeth and found a Salmonella bacterium that causes a typhoid-like fever. In 2019 Alexander Koch and his colleagues argued that the Great Dying may even have cooled the planet: so much abandoned farmland, some 56 million hectares, grew back into forest that the new trees drew enough carbon dioxide from the air to deepen the Little Ice Age around 1600. The argument is serious, but not settled.

social-darwinism-and-the-civilizing-miss.context_blurb:
After Charles Darwin made natural selection famous, writers of the late 1800s borrowed his language for human societies. Their Social Darwinism held that strong races, nations or classes were destined to rule the weak, and imperialists turned it into a moral story in which conquest was both natural and kind.

The slogan survival of the fittest was not Darwin's: the British philosopher Herbert Spencer coined it in 1864 as another name for what Darwin had called natural selection, the phrase Darwin actually used in On the Origin of Species, and Darwin only borrowed Spencer's words later. In February 1899 Rudyard Kipling's poem The White Man's Burden pressed America to take the Philippines and govern them, calling the people there sullen, half-devil and half-child, and casting empire as a thankless duty. Theodore Roosevelt called it poor poetry but good sense for expansion.

In July 1885 Jules Ferry, who had twice led France's government, told the Chamber of Deputies that the superior races had a right because they had a duty, the duty to civilise the inferior races, the classic statement of the civilising mission. In the same debate the deputy Camille Pelletan challenged him, asking what kind of civilisation had to be imposed with cannonballs, and calling it another form of barbarism. Pelletan asked whether those peoples did not have the same rights as the French, as masters of their own houses.

William Graham Sumner, an American sociologist, claimed that whoever rose to the top must be nature's fittest, but to a biologist fitness means only how many offspring a creature leaves, not strength, cleverness or moral worth, and it never ranks which people deserve to rule. The leap from biology to the moral worth of peoples was never legitimate.

social-upheaval-after-the-plague.context_blurb:
Between 1347 and 1351 the Black Death killed roughly a third of Europe's people. The survivors found the old order shaken: lords tried to hold down wages by law, peasants pushed back, and in England in 1381 a great revolt marched on London itself.

With so many dead, farms and towns were short of hands, and the surviving peasants found that their labour had become precious, so they could ask for much higher wages than ever before. Under Edward III, England's rulers passed the Ordinance and the Statute of Labourers, in 1349 and 1351, which made it a crime to seek or offer more than the old wages, but by 1352 Parliament admitted the law had failed: workers were still demanding double and treble the old rate.

The plague also bred terror and fanaticism. Around Michaelmas 1349 Robert of Avesbury, a chronicler, saw more than 600 flagellants arrive in London from Flanders, men who bared their backs twice a day and lashed them bloody with knotted whips, hoping their suffering would persuade God to lift the Black Death. The Brethren of the Cross grew so quickly that the Church took alarm, and the Pope condemned them in a bull of 20 October 1349 as an impious sect to be suppressed. France had its own rising, the Jacquerie, in 1358, and when its leader, a well-off farmer named Guillaume Cale, came to truce talks near Mello, Charles II of Navarre's nobles seized him, saying chivalry's rules did not protect a peasant, then tortured him and cut off his head. At least 20,000 peasants were killed as the revolt was crushed.

In England the spark came on 30 May 1381, when the royal tax collector John Bampton rode into the Essex village of Brentwood with armed men to squeeze out a hated poll tax, the same sum from rich and poor alike, and the villagers drove him out, and within days the Peasants' Revolt was blazing across the south-east. At Blackheath, outside London, on 12 June, the radical priest John Ball stirred the rebels with a rhyming question: when Adam dug and Eve spun, who then was the gentleman, meaning that since the first man and woman both worked with their hands, no one was born a lord.

On 14 June the rebels forced their way into the Tower, dragged out Archbishop Simon Sudbury and the treasurer Robert Hales, beheaded them, and set their heads on London Bridge. They torched the Savoy, John of Gaunt's splendid palace, but, declaring that they fought for truth and justice and were no thieves, they took almost nothing from its treasure and destroyed it instead.

At Smithfield on 15 June the rebel leader Wat Tyler was cut down in front of the boy king, Richard II, just fourteen, and as the furious crowd bent their bows, the boy rode straight out to them and told them to follow him as their leader, turning a massacre into a procession. Richard had signed charters abolishing serfdom and pardoning the rebels, and the peasants went home thinking they had won, but on 2 July, once the danger had passed, he formally revoked every one. By November at least 1,500 rebels had been executed or killed in battle, and John Ball was hanged, drawn and quartered. Yet the lords could never again push the price of work as low as before the plague.

socrates-trial-and-death-by-hemlock-399-.context_blurb:
Socrates of Athens, who fought for his city and went about barefoot questioning everyone in the marketplace, became the founding hero of Western philosophy. In 399 BC, at about seventy, he was tried, condemned and put to death, and the way he died made him the image of a thinker who will not betray his questions.

He never wrote a word himself, teaching only by talk in the streets, so everything we know of him comes from his students, above all Plato and Xenophon. His mission began, he said, when his friend Chaerephon asked the oracle at Delphi whether any man was wiser than Socrates, and the priestess answered that no one was. Puzzled, since he believed he knew nothing, he questioned politicians, poets and craftsmen, and concluded, in Plato's Apology, that he was wiser only in this: he alone saw how far his own ignorance reached, while they thought they knew what they did not. The famous saying that he knew that he knew nothing is a later paraphrase. In 404 BC the Thirty Tyrants, a murderous junta seizing rich men's property, ordered Socrates and four others to arrest an innocent man, Leon of Salamis, for execution, and while the other four went, Socrates simply walked home, though it could have cost him his life.

In 399 BC his accusers charged him before a jury of 500 citizens with impiety, failing to honour the city's gods and bringing in new spirits, and with corrupting the youth of Athens by teaching them to question their elders. In his defence he called himself a gadfly, sent by the god to sting the city, a great but sluggish horse, awake. He told the jury he would choose death over silence, because a life without examination is not worth living for a human being. Found guilty by a narrow margin and invited to propose his own penalty, he joked that he deserved to dine at the city's expense for the rest of his life, the honour Athens gave its Olympic champions. Only when Plato and Crito offered to pay did he propose a fine instead, and the jury chose death.

The execution waited about a month, because no one could be put to death in Athens while the sacred ship sent each year to Delos to honour Apollo was away, and that year contrary winds held it back. His friend Crito came at dawn with an escape arranged and the guards bribed, but Socrates refused, picturing the city's Laws standing before him and calling him to account: he had lived his whole life under their protection, and could not break the city's verdict now that it harmed him.

Then he drank the hemlock, walked about until his legs grew heavy, and lay down, and the poison worked as a slow paralysis: a cold numbness crept upward from his feet, slowly climbing toward his heart. His last words were a small instruction to Crito, that they owed a rooster to Asclepius, the god of healing, as if thanking the god for curing him of life.

solferino-and-the-founding-of-the-red-cr.context_blurb:
On 24 June 1859, near the village of Solferino in northern Italy, French and Piedmontese armies fought the Austrians in a long, savage battle of the war for Italian unity. Tens of thousands were left dead or wounded, and the armies' medical services broke down. A Swiss businessman, Henri Dunant, on his way to see Napoleon III about an Algerian land deal, walked into the aftermath.

The women of Castiglione turned their church into a hospital and tended French, Italian and Austrian soldiers side by side, and as they worked they kept saying Tutti fratelli, meaning that all are brothers. That scene became the seed of Dunant's idea for a neutral society to aid the wounded of every side. In 1864 delegates in Geneva chose the new Red Cross's emblem by reversing the colours of the Swiss flag, a white cross on red, to make a red cross on a field of white, in honour of neutral Switzerland. The Geneva Conventions grew from the same campaign.

solidarity-the-polish-workers-movement.context_blurb:
Solidarity was the independent trade union that Polish workers founded in August 1980 at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdansk, the first free union anywhere in the Soviet bloc. Within months it had some ten million members, and in 1989 it swept Poland's first partly free elections, ending communist rule there.

When the strike began that August, Lech Walesa, an electrician the shipyard had sacked years before for organising, was locked outside, so he scaled the shipyard's fence, about twelve feet high, and the strikers promptly made him head of their strike committee.

On 31 August 1980 Walesa signed the Gdansk Agreement, which let Polish workers organise their own unions, with a huge souvenir pen bearing a portrait of the Polish-born Pope John Paul II, joining the workers' cause to the faith that fed it. Walesa later won the Nobel Peace Prize and in 1990 became Poland's first president after communism.

song-dynasty-the-civil-service-exam-scho.context_blurb:
The Song dynasty ruled China from 960 to 1279, and in wealth, cities, printing, science and art it may have led the world. Its emperors chose their officials not by birth or bribery but by gruelling written examinations on the Confucian classics, and the scholar-officials who passed them ran the empire.

The founding emperor, Taizu, a general who had seized the throne, put scholars above soldiers on purpose, and in 973 he added a final round, the Palace Examination, in which he examined the leading candidates in person and set their ranking himself. The man who came first in the whole empire, the zhuangyuan, saw his name at the head of the yellow Golden List and rode through the streets in a horseback parade, a celebrity overnight. The ladder was real: in 1148 and again in 1256, counts of graduates showed some 57 percent from families with no official rank at all, so a poor farmer's boy who learned the classics could outrank a general's son who had not passed.

To stamp out favouritism, from 992 candidates' names were covered and numbers put in their place, and because a grader might still know a man's handwriting, from 1015 clerks recopied every paper by hand before it was marked, and two graders scored each one with a third to break ties. As later records of the same exam tradition describe, each candidate was shut for days in a cramped, roofless brick cell, bringing bedding, food, ink and a chamber pot, and its only furniture was two wooden boards: one served as his desk, the other as both his seat and his bed. The compound gates stayed sealed until the exam ended, so when a candidate died at his desk, as some did, officials wrapped the body in a mat and threw it over the wall.

Sichuan's coins were made of iron, so heavy and bulky that local merchants began trading paper notes instead, and in 1023 the state took over, opening an office in Chengdu that issued the jiaozi, the first paper money any government ever issued. Some four centuries before Gutenberg, around 1041 to 1048, Bi Sheng, a commoner, created movable type, carving each character into sticky clay as thin as the edge of a coin and baking it hard, so that each piece could be reused page after page. We know of it only because Shen Kuo wrote it down. The earliest known gunpowder recipes appear in the Wujing Zongyao, a military manual of 1044, and before long Song troops were binding gunpowder tubes to spears, making the fire lance, the ancestor of every gun ever carried into battle.

Su Song, a Song official, completed an astronomical clock tower some forty feet tall at Kaifeng in 1094; a great water wheel drove it, a bronze sphere on top followed the stars, and every hour little costumed figures popped out of doors to ring bells and beat drums. When the Jurchen Jin armies sacked Kaifeng in 1127, they carried the clock north piece by piece, but no one could make it run again, and when Su Song's own son, Su Xie, also failed to rebuild it, he concluded that his father had kept back essential parts on purpose. Shen Kuo, writing his Dream Pool Essays in 1088, described the first true navigator's compass, a needle rubbed on lodestone and hung from a silk thread, and he noticed that it pointed slightly east of true south, a discovery Europe would not make for centuries.

songhai-empire-askia-the-great.context_blurb:
After the empire of Mali declined in the 1400s, the Songhai people built an even larger empire along the great bend of the Niger in West Africa, rich with gold trade and Muslim learning. Its greatest ruler, Askia Muhammad, called Askia the Great, took the throne in 1493 by defeating the son of the old king at Anfao.

His capital, Gao, stood on the banks of the Niger River, which watered its fields and bore its trading canoes along the edge of the Sahara, and under Askia it grew to some 100,000 people. The empire's jewel was Timbuktu, where the Sahara meets the grasslands, a hub of the gold trade and of Islamic learning with around 100,000 people and some 150 to 180 Koranic schools, where scholars taught at the Sankore Mosque.

In 1497 Askia made the pilgrimage to Mecca with hundreds of horsemen, handed out 100,000 gold pieces in alms in the holy cities, and in Cairo the Abbasid caliph named him Caliph of the Sudan, ruler for the faith in West Africa. On the way home he recruited scholars from Egypt and Morocco to teach in Timbuktu. After ruling for about 37 years with a professional standing army and specialised ministers, Askia was buried at Gao in a stepped pyramid built of mud and earth, just over ten metres tall and bristling with wooden stakes used as permanent scaffolding. It is now a World Heritage Site.

In 1591 Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur of Morocco sent an army across the whole Sahara, and at the Battle of Tondibi its arquebuses and cannon, firearms the Songhai did not have, cut down the huge Songhai cavalry, with its spears, swords and bows, in about two hours. The Songhai tried to stampede a herd of a thousand cattle into the Moroccan line, but the roar of the guns and cannon panicked the beasts, which turned and trampled the Songhai's own ranks. The largest empire in West African history broke apart.

soviet-mass-deportations-and-the-brutal-.context_blurb:
In August 1939 Hitler and Stalin signed a pact whose secret clauses split eastern Europe between them. For the peoples of eastern Poland and the Baltic states, the war that followed brought not one tyranny but two, and when the Red Army later drove the Germans back, its victory came with crimes the Soviet Union hid for fifty years.

Hitler invaded Poland from the west on 1 September 1939, and on 17 September Stalin's Red Army poured across Poland's eastern border to take its share. On the freezing night of 10 February 1940 the Soviet secret police hammered on doors across occupied eastern Poland, gave families minutes to pack, and loaded about 139,000 people onto cattle trains for Siberia, and almost half of them were children under sixteen. Soviet occupation of the Baltic states brought mass deportations too, more than 200,000 people between 1940 and 1953, and one Soviet official put the scheme for Lithuania in a line survivors never forgot: Lithuania would remain, but without Lithuanians.

On 5 March 1940 Lavrentiy Beria, the secret police chief, asked leave to execute some 22,000 Polish prisoners, officers, policemen and other professionals, and Stalin wrote his signature of approval across it. The men were shot in the back of the head, some 4,400 of them in Katyn Forest, and for fifty years the Soviet Union blamed the Germans, until 1990, when Moscow at last admitted the truth and named 21,857 of the dead. When Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941, the NKVD, pulling out of western Ukraine, slaughtered the political prisoners in its jails instead of releasing them, some 10,000 to 40,000 in eight days, and Nazi propaganda then blamed the killings on Jews to incite pogroms that took still more innocent lives. After a brief amnesty in 1941, General Wladyslaw Anders led more than 110,000 Polish deportees, orphans among them, across the Soviet border into Persia, and from there the freed Poles scattered to New Zealand, Mexico and British Africa, among other distant places.

In May 1944 Stalin's regime branded a whole people, the Crimean Tatars, collaborators with the Germans and loaded some 183,000 of them onto sealed cattle trains for Uzbekistan, where about a fifth were dead within eighteen months. The Volga Germans, the Chechens and others met the same fate.

As the Red Army pushed west through eastern Europe in 1944, its soldiers, many of them farm boys from poor villages, grabbed wristwatches so eagerly that some wore a row of them on each forearm. When the war photographer Yevgeny Khaldei staged his famous picture of a Soviet flag raised over the Reichstag in May 1945, he darkened the smoke over Berlin and scratched out one telling detail, a second wristwatch on a soldier's other arm. The advance also brought mass rape on a vast scale, which the historian Antony Beevor called the greatest in history: by his estimate at least 1.4 million women in East Prussia, Pomerania and Silesia alone, and some 100,000 more in Berlin.

soviet-war-in-afghanistan.context_blurb:
In December 1979 the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan to prop up a failing communist government against Muslim guerrillas, the mujahideen. Moscow expected a short war; instead it fought for nearly ten years, losing some 15,000 soldiers, while somewhere between 850,000 and over a million Afghan civilians died and more than five million fled as refugees.

The invasion began with Operation Storm-333 on 27 December 1979: Soviet commandos stormed Kabul's Tajbeg Palace in about forty minutes with one aim, to kill Hafizullah Amin, the Afghan ruler. Eleven days earlier a KGB plot to poison his lunch had failed when a Soviet doctor who knew nothing of it saved his life. The Soviets' most feared weapon was the Mi-24 Hind, a heavily armoured attack helicopter armed with rockets and a gun in its nose, so tough that rifle bullets bounced off it, and the Afghan fighters called it the flying tank.

In his home valley, the Panjshir, the guerrilla commander Ahmad Shah Massoud, the Lion of Panjshir, beat off nine Soviet offensives between 1980 and 1985 the same way each time: the Soviets could push him out, but he came back the moment they left. Then, in September 1986, Ghaffar, a mujahideen engineer, launched five new American Stinger missiles, shoulder-fired and heat-seeking, near Jalalabad, and brought down three Mi-24s in quick succession, breaking the Hind's rule of the skies. The CIA had funnelled the missiles through Pakistan in a secret programme called Operation Cyclone.

In February 1986 Mikhail Gorbachev said aloud at the 27th Party Congress what Soviet leaders were never meant to admit: Afghanistan had become a bleeding wound. On 15 February 1989 the commander of the last troops, General Boris Gromov, made himself the very last soldier out, walking on foot across the Friendship Bridge over the Amu Darya into Soviet territory. In 1991, under three years later, the Soviet Union itself collapsed, and historians count the drained treasury and humiliating defeat of the Afghan war among the blows that brought it down.

spanish-civil-war.context_blurb:
In July 1936 General Francisco Franco and other army officers rose against Spain's elected Republican government, and three years of civil war followed. It became a proxy war: Hitler and Mussolini sent planes, tanks and men to Franco, while Stalin's Soviet Union armed the Republic. Franco won in 1939 and ruled Spain until 1975.

Some 40,000 foreign volunteers from 52 countries came to fight Franco, about 2,800 of them Americans in the Abraham Lincoln Battalion, and a fiery communist speaker called La Pasionaria gave the Republic its battle cry, No pasaran, they shall not pass. When the Condor Legion and Italian bombers set the Basque town of Guernica ablaze on 26 April 1937, its wooden houses burned, yet the Basque parliament house survived, and beside it the sacred oak under which Basque lords had sworn for centuries to respect the people's freedoms. Wolfram von Richthofen, who planned and commanded the raid, was the younger cousin of the First World War ace Manfred von Richthofen, the Red Baron, and his diary called the burning a complete success.

The Republic's side tore at itself. Orwell, a hopeful socialist, joined the POUM militia to fight Franco, but in May 1937, when fighting broke out in Barcelona's streets, he watched the Soviet-backed communists turn their guns on their own allies, the anarchists and his own POUM, and brand them fascist traitors, a lesson that later helped shape his novel 1984. That June the NKVD, Stalin's secret police, tortured to death Andreu Nin, a POUM leader who had once been Trotsky's secretary, then staged a fake escape and branded him a Nazi spy. When people chalked the question of where Nin was on the walls, the regime mocked them with an answer meant to brand him a fascist: in Salamanca or in Berlin, Franco's headquarters and Hitler's capital.

Hitler used Spain as a dress rehearsal, testing his newest aircraft and tactics, and barely three months after a victory parade for his Condor Legion airmen in Berlin on 6 June 1939, he launched the real war by invading Poland to the east.

spanish-galleons-the-manila-trade.context_blurb:
After Spain took the Philippines in the 1560s, one great galleon a year, nicknamed La Nao de China, sailed between Manila and Acapulco in Mexico, carrying silver from the mines of Spanish America west across the Pacific. For 250 years it was the first steady link between the Americas and Asia.

The silver bought Chinese silk, the real prize of the homeward voyage, since a roll of it fetched about ten times its Manila price in the Americas, and as much as a third of all the silver mined in Spanish America flowed to China this way.

The trade winds made the westward run simple, yet for years no captain could find a route back east, until in 1565 the Basque friar and navigator Andres de Urdaneta tried the opposite of the obvious: he sailed far north, almost to the latitude of Japan, caught the Kuroshio Current and the westerly winds, and rode them home to California and down to Acapulco. His first crossing took 129 days.

sparta-s-helots-and-the-krypteia-the-pri.context_blurb:
Sparta's famous warriors could train for war all their lives because others did their work: the helots, a conquered Greek people held in bondage on their own land, who outnumbered their Spartan masters about seven to one. The Spartans lived in constant fear of a helot revolt, and they ruled by terror.

Each year the ephors, Sparta's chief magistrates, began their term by formally declaring war on the helots, so that a Spartan who killed one carried no blood-guilt: the killing counted as a clean act of the state. Young Spartans were even sent out by night with daggers to murder helots.

Thucydides tells how the Spartans once promised freedom to the helots who had fought most bravely for them, and about two thousand came forward, crowned themselves with garlands and went round the temples, and soon afterward every one of them vanished, and no one ever learned how each had died. It was a trap to destroy the helots most able to lead a revolt.

sparta-the-agoge-and-warrior-society.context_blurb:
Sparta, a city-state in the southern Peloponnese, built its whole society around one aim: producing the finest heavy infantry in Greece. Its citizens were a small warrior class living off the labour of a vast enslaved population, and every Spartan, from birth, belonged first to the state.

At seven a Spartan boy was taken from his family by the state and enrolled in the agoge, a harsh communal upbringing meant to make him a soldier, with only enough reading and writing to get by. The boys were kept hungry on purpose so they would learn to steal food and grow cunning, and a boy who was caught got a flogging, not for the theft but for getting caught, as a careless thief. When a son marched to war, a Spartan mother, it was said, gave him his great round shield with the words "Either this or upon this": come home carrying it in victory or carried dead upon it, for to throw away a shield and run was the ultimate disgrace. The saying is attributed to Queen Gorgo and is best treated as legend.

Spartan men ate together every night at a common mess, and its famous black broth, prized as tough soldier's fare, was pork cooked in its own blood with vinegar and salt, so foul to outsiders that a visitor from Sybaris joked that now he understood why Spartans did not fear death. Plutarch tells of a boy who hid a stolen fox cub beneath his cloak, and when the animal clawed and bit at his belly while he talked with his elders, he kept silent and let it tear into him until he died, rather than be found out. Spartans told it as proof of trained endurance; it is best treated as legend.

Spartans were famous for laconic speech, short and cutting, named after their region, Laconia. In 480 BC, when the Persian king Xerxes, at the pass of Thermopylae, demanded that King Leonidas and his 300 Spartans lay down their arms, Leonidas sent back two words in Greek, molon labe: come and take them. Around 346 BC Philip II of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great, warned them that if he invaded Laconia he would raze their city to the ground, and the Spartans replied with a single word: If.

A newborn belonged to the state: the father carried it before the tribal elders, who inspected it, and according to the tradition Plutarch preserved, a baby they judged sickly or deformed was left to die in a chasm at the foot of Mount Taygetus. No infant remains have ever been found there, so this too may be legend. The helots who outnumbered the Spartan citizens about seven to one were mostly Messenians, a whole neighbouring people Sparta had conquered in the 700s and 600s BC and enslaved on their own land, where they kept their own families and gods and never forgot who they were. To keep them terrified, Sparta ran the krypteia: the toughest young Spartans were armed with daggers and sent out at night to murder any helots they met, above all the strongest. Spartan women, alone in Greece, could own and inherit land and trained as athletes, and asked why Spartan wives alone held sway over their husbands, Queen Gorgo replied that only Spartan women gave birth to real men.

Thucydides records the darkest trick: the Spartans offered freedom to the helots who had fought best for them, some two thousand put on garlands and toured the temples as free men, and a little later they all secretly vanished, and no one ever knew how each had died. Sparta's power finally broke in 371 BC, when the Theban general Epaminondas smashed its army at Leuctra and then marched into Messenia and freed the helots, destroying the slave labour the whole Spartan system rested on. He founded the city of Messene for them, and Sparta was never again a great power.

spartacus-and-the-slave-revolt.context_blurb:
Spartacus was a Thracian gladiator who in 73 BC led the largest slave revolt in Roman history. For two years his army of runaway slaves, which grew to some 70,000, roamed Italy and beat one Roman force after another, until the rich general Marcus Licinius Crassus crushed it in 71 BC.

It began when about seventy gladiators at a training school in Capua decided to break out, and with the proper weapons under lock and key, they raided the kitchen and armed themselves with cooking knives and roasting spits. On the road they captured a wagon of real gladiators' weapons. Gaius Claudius Glaber, a Roman commander, cornered them on Vesuvius and blocked its only path down, but the rebels wove ladders from the wild grapevines that covered the slopes, climbed down the cliff he thought impossible, and wiped out his camp from behind.

When his officer Crixus was killed, Spartacus held funeral games and turned the Roman spectacle upside down, making about 300 Roman prisoners kill one another as gladiators for an audience of slaves. Before his last battle in 71 BC, Spartacus had his warhorse brought out and killed it with his sword, saying that if he won he would have plenty of fine horses from the enemy, and if he lost he would need none. He charged straight for Crassus, cut down two centurions, and died surrounded; his body was never found. Crassus took 6,000 rebels alive and nailed them to crosses lining the Appian Way all the way from Capua to Rome, as a warning to every slave in Italy.

spread-of-buddhism-into-china-xuanzang.context_blurb:
Buddhism reached China from India along the Silk Road and became one of China's great traditions. In the 600s a young monk named Xuanzang, troubled that the scriptures in Chinese were poor translations, made an epic sixteen-year journey of some 10,000 miles to India and home again in search of the originals. Long after his death, a Ming novel, Journey to the West, turned him into a fantasy hero guarded by three magical companions, the most famous being the Monkey King, Sun Wukong.

In 629 he slipped out of the Tang capital, Chang'an, in secret, defying Emperor Taizong's ban on travel to the west, to fetch the true Buddhist scriptures from India itself. Alone in the Gobi, he spilled his water bag into the sand and spent four days and five nights without a drop among camel dung and bones, until his horse bolted of its own accord and bore the dying monk to a spring. Dying of thirst and tempted to turn back, he kept whispering a vow: he would not go one step east without the true scriptures.

In the oasis kingdom of Gaochang, King Qu Wentai loved the monk so much that he tried to keep him for ever as his court chaplain, and Xuanzang refused all food until the king gave way; the two swore brotherhood, and he promised to return to teach. Crossing the ice of the Bedel Pass in the Tian Shan mountains took some eight bitter days, and three or four of every ten men in his party froze to death. In 630 he passed through Bamiyan, in today's central Afghanistan, and described its two colossal painted Buddhas carved into the cliffs, the earliest written record of the statues the Taliban dynamited in 2001.

In 643, after thirteen years of study in India, at King Harsha's eighteen-day assembly at Kanauj he reportedly out-argued 500 Brahmins, Jains and rival Buddhists in defence of his Mahayana school. In 645 he came home to Chang'an a national hero, with 657 Sanskrit texts loaded on twenty-two horses, and in 652 the Big Wild Goose Pagoda, 64 metres tall today, was built to house them, where he spent the rest of his life translating.

st-francis-of-assisi-the-friars.context_blurb:
Francis of Assisi, the son of a rich Italian cloth merchant, gave up his fortune in the early 1200s to live in poverty, work with his hands and preach in plain words. The order of friars he founded spread across Europe within a generation, and he is loved still for his gentleness.

Around 1206 his angry father dragged him before the Bishop of Assisi to get his money back, and there in the square Francis stripped off his fine clothes, handed them over, and declared that from then on he would say only Our Father who art in heaven, no longer calling Pietro di Bernardone his father. The bishop covered him with his own cloak.

In 1223, in the mountain village of Greccio, Francis staged the first live nativity scene, filling a manger with straw and setting a real ox and a real donkey beside it, so that villagers who could not read could see the birth of Jesus for themselves. It is the origin of the Christmas crib.

st-peter-s-basilica-and-the-renaissance-.context_blurb:
St Peter's Basilica in Rome, raised over the traditional grave of the apostle Peter, took more than a century to build from the early 1500s and passed through the hands of Bramante, Michelangelo and Bernini. It is the largest church in the world and the heart of the Roman Catholic Church.

Donato Bramante began by demolishing the twelve-hundred-year-old church that Constantine had built on the site, pulling down its nave so hastily that priests were still saying Mass amid the rubble, and Romans punned on his name to call him Maestro Ruinante, Master Wrecker. Michelangelo was 71 when he took over the project in 1547, and he refused to take any pay, doing it, he said, only for the love of God and in honour of the Apostle, and he held to that for the rest of his life, dying at 88 with the drum of his dome built but not the dome itself.

When nine hundred men, 140 horses and dozens of winches hauled a 350-ton Egyptian obelisk upright in the square in 1586, Pope Sixtus V ordered silence on pain of death, but as the strained ropes started smoking, a sailor named Benedetto Bresca shouted, "Water to the ropes!" The story says the wetted ropes held, and his town won the right to supply the Vatican's Palm Sunday palms. Gold letters taller than a man circle the inside of Michelangelo's dome, quoting Jesus in Matthew's Gospel, Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church, a pun because the name Peter means rock.

Bernini's colonnade, 248 columns curving round the square in four rows, topped by 140 statues of saints, was, he said, the motherly arms of the Church reaching out to gather in everyone who entered, believers, heretics and unbelievers alike. To help pay for the new church, the friar Johann Tetzel toured Germany selling indulgences with Pope Leo X's blessing, and his rhyming pitch, in German, Sobald das Geld im Kasten klingt, die Seele aus dem Fegefeuer springt, promised that the instant a coin rang in the money chest, a soul leapt out of purgatory. It enraged Martin Luther, a monk, who attacked indulgences in his theses of 1517; some scholars doubt Tetzel coined the line himself.

stamp-act-no-taxation-without-representa.context_blurb:
The Stamp Act of 1765 made American colonists pay for a British revenue stamp on nearly every piece of printed paper, to help cover the cost of the French and Indian War and the troops still stationed in America. It was the first direct tax Parliament had laid on the colonies, and they had no members in Parliament at all.

Wills, newspapers and court papers all needed a stamp, and so, oddly, did two pastimes made of paper and bone: playing cards and dice. Since no deed, will, court filing or ship's clearance was valid without a stamp, many colonial courts and ports simply shut their doors and stopped working rather than buy the stamps, freezing legal and commercial life.

In May 1765 a new member of Virginia's House of Burgesses, Patrick Henry, raged against the act so fiercely that a law student of 22, listening from the doorway, Thomas Jefferson, remembered the speech all his life. Henry warned that Caesar had had his Brutus, and Charles the First his Cromwell, one ruler stabbed to death and the other beheaded, and that George the Third might profit by their example. When the Speaker cried "Treason!", Henry, as the famous story goes, did not flinch, but finished his sentence by saying that if this was treason, they should make the most of it. In Parliament, Charles Townshend had described the colonists as children raised by British care, but Isaac Barre answered that they were sons of liberty, and the resistance proudly took the name Sons of Liberty.

On 14 August 1765 a Boston crowd hanged a straw figure of Andrew Oliver, the stamp distributor, from a huge elm, cut off its head and burned it, and that elm became the Liberty Tree. Oliver resigned three days later. On 26 August a mob wrecked the mansion of Lieutenant Governor Thomas Hutchinson room by room, and besides his furniture and cash it destroyed thirty years of his manuscripts, among them the notes for the history of Massachusetts he was writing.

That October leaders from nine colonies gathered in New York's City Hall, the building later called Federal Hall, as the Stamp Act Congress, the first time the separate colonies had joined in protest against a tax, and declared that the colonists could be taxed only with the consent of their own elected representatives. They did not object that the tax was steep; they said it broke an essential principle of the English constitution, that no subject may be taxed without his own consent, a consent that only their own assemblies, not a distant Parliament, could give. Parliament claimed that its members spoke for every British subject, even colonists who elected no one, a doctrine called virtual representation, but the Maryland lawyer Daniel Dulany tore it apart in a 1765 pamphlet: not one voter in England would ever feel a tax laid on America, so Parliament could not truly represent the colonists when it taxed them.

By 1 November every stamp seller had resigned or fled, but what forced Parliament's hand was pain in Britain itself: colonial merchants boycotted British goods, and London merchants, some of them bankrupted, begged Parliament for repeal. On 18 March 1766 Parliament repealed the Stamp Act, but that same day it passed the Declaratory Act, asserting that Parliament could make laws for the colonies in all cases whatsoever, and the quarrel that would become a revolution was only postponed.

star-spangled-banner-fort-mchenry.context_blurb:
In September 1814, two years into the War of 1812, a British fleet came up Chesapeake Bay to take Baltimore. First it had to knock out Fort McHenry, which guarded the harbor. For some twenty-five hours British ships hurled bombs and rockets at the fort, and an American lawyer named Francis Scott Key watched every minute from the water. What he saw at the end gave the United States its national anthem.

All night Key could not tell through the smoke and rain whether the fort had fallen. At first light he had his answer: the huge American garrison flag was still flying over Fort McHenry, and the sight moved him to write the verses we now sing as The Star-Spangled Banner. A smaller storm flag had flown through the wet night; the giant one was most likely hoisted that morning.

That giant flag was Major George Armistead's idea. The fort's commander ordered it in 1813, a full year before the attack, and his reason was blunt: he wanted a flag so large that the British would have no difficulty spotting it from far away. It measured forty-two feet long and thirty high, and each of its stars and stripes was two feet across. A Baltimore widow, Mary Pickersgill, sewed it with help from her daughter, two nieces and Grace Wisher, a teenage servant. Her own house was far too small to hold it, so the women spread the cloth at night across the floor of Claggett's brewery nearby and stitched the pieces together there. She was paid $405.90, more than most people in Baltimore earned in a year.

Key was out in the harbor because of a rescue. With the prisoner-agent John Skinner he had gone to the enemy fleet under a truce flag and won the release of Dr. William Beanes, an American doctor the British had captured. But the two negotiators had spent their visit aboard the British flagship Tonnant just as the fleet made ready to strike Baltimore, and they had seen its full strength. The British would not let men who knew their plans slip ashore to warn the city, so they held all three Americans until the bombardment was over, and Key watched it from behind enemy lines.

stoicism-and-epicureanism-hellenistic-ph.context_blurb:
After Alexander the Great died in 323 BC, the free Greek city-states fell under the power of great kingdoms, and the thinkers of Athens turned from politics to a more personal problem: how can one person live well in a world he cannot control? Two rival schools gave answers that are still with us, and both of their names became everyday English words.

Around 300 BC Zeno of Citium began teaching in the busy agora of Athens, in the shade of the Stoa Poikile, the Painted Porch, a long roofed colonnade whose walls showed scenes of great battles. His followers were first called Zenonians, and then simply the people of the Stoa: the Stoics. Zeno taught that wealth, fame, pain and even death are neither truly good nor bad, and that freedom means wanting only what lies in your own power. That is why a stoic, to this day, is someone who meets pain or bad news calmly. The word is named after a porch.

Epicurus taught in a garden on the edge of Athens, and the English word epicure, which now means a lover of rich food and fine wine, turns his teaching upside down. He warned that overindulgence only ends in pain. For Epicurus real pleasure was simple: a mind at peace and free of fear, which he called ataraxia, a plain meal of bread and water, and friends to share good conversation with. The two schools agreed on more than they liked to admit, and both are enjoying a revival as practical guides for ordinary life.

strategic-bombing-and-tokyo-firebombing.context_blurb:
The Second World War was the first war in which whole cities were bombed on an industrial scale. Germany struck Warsaw, Rotterdam and London; Britain and America answered by burning Hamburg, Berlin and Dresden; and in 1945 American B-29 bombers set the cities of Japan on fire. Historians, moralists and veterans have argued over the record ever since.

The worst single night came over Tokyo. In early 1945 General Curtis LeMay, a blunt, cigar-chewing bomber commander, bet that Japan had little to shoot at bombers flying low in the dark. So he had most of the guns and armor pulled out of his B-29s, making them lighter, so that each plane could carry more firebombs and come in low and slow at 5,000 to 9,000 feet rather than the usual 32,000. Pathfinder planes first burned a giant X across the target, and the main force dropped napalm on a city of dry wooden houses. Winds of 65 miles an hour whipped the flames into a firestorm, and Tokyo had only 8,000 firemen and, by one account, exactly three long ladders.

That raid, called Operation Meetinghouse, on the night of 9 to 10 March 1945, killed some 100,000 people, more in one night than the atomic bomb at Hiroshima or the one at Nagasaki, and it remains the deadliest air raid in history. It burned out sixteen square miles and left more than a million people homeless.

Some death tolls became weapons themselves. After British and American bombers struck Dresden in February 1945, Joseph Goebbels's propaganda ministry claimed a quarter of a million dead, and the writer David Irving later pushed figures of 150,000 or more. In 2010 a commission of historians appointed by the city of Dresden reported, after six years of study, that the dead numbered about 25,000, roughly a tenth of the Nazi figure. The historian Donald Miller noted that most victims did not burn: about seven in ten suffocated on carbon monoxide as the firestorm sucked the air out of the cellars where they hid. An American prisoner of war, Kurt Vonnegut, survived in an underground meat locker and turned the night into his novel Slaughterhouse-Five.

stravinsky-rite-of-spring-riot-1913.context_blurb:
Igor Stravinsky was a young Russian composer writing ballets for Serge Diaghilev's Ballets Russes, the most daring dance company in Paris. His third score for Diaghilev, The Rite of Spring, told of a pagan ritual sacrifice in prehistoric Russia. Its first night, in 1913, became one of the most famous scandals in the history of the theatre.

The newly opened Théâtre des Champs-Élysées was full of fashionable Parisians that May evening, and they expected graceful ballet. Instead the orchestra hammered out pounding, clashing rhythms while Vaslav Nijinsky's dancers stamped about with their toes turned in. Within minutes the crowd split into two camps yelling over the music, one side crying marvellous and the other ridiculous, until the rival spectators came to blows and were fighting one another in the seats. A ballet had started a brawl, and the scandal made Stravinsky famous overnight.

The surprise came a year later. In 1914 the conductor Pierre Monteux performed the score again, purely as a concert, the orchestra alone without any ballet on the stage. This time the audience cheered the music with delight, and the score people had fought over soon became one of the celebrated classics of the century. Without Nijinsky's jarring choreography the notes could win a crowd; the riot had been as much about the stamping dancers as about the music. Stravinsky kept composing for almost sixty more years and is counted among the most influential composers of the twentieth century.

suez-crisis-1956.context_blurb:
In 1956 Egypt's president, Gamal Abdel Nasser, seized the Suez Canal, the great shipping lane joining the Mediterranean to the Red Sea. French engineers had built it in the 1860s, and an Anglo-French company still ran it. Britain, France and Israel secretly planned a war to take it back. Their failure marked the end of Britain as a global superpower.

Nasser chose a dramatic way to strike. On 26 July, speaking to a vast crowd in Alexandria, he slipped a code word into his speech: de Lesseps, the name of Ferdinand de Lesseps, the Frenchman who had built the canal. The moment the engineer Mahmoud Yunis heard the name, his team began taking over the canal, and Nasser said it about fourteen times in ten minutes to be sure they could not miss it. The United States and Britain had refused to lend him money for his Aswan High Dam, so he announced that the canal's tolls would pay for it instead.

In late October Israel, Britain and France attacked, and on the ground they were winning. But they had kept the American president, Dwight Eisenhower, in the dark, and he turned on them with money instead of soldiers. Eisenhower blocked hundreds of millions of dollars in credit that Britain badly needed, and he threatened to sell off the American government's holdings of British pound bonds, which would have sent the pound crashing just as Britain's reserves were running out. Britain and France gave in and accepted a United Nations ceasefire on 6 November. Nasser became a hero of the Arab world, and the British prime minister, Anthony Eden, resigned within months.

sugar-plantations-the-encomienda-system.context_blurb:
When Spain conquered the islands of the Caribbean, and then Mexico and Peru, its colonists wanted gold and they wanted workers. Sugar became the richest prize of all, and the labor systems the Spanish built to grow it shaped the Atlantic world for three centuries. A friar of the Dominican order, Bartolomé de las Casas, spent his life exposing what those systems did to Native peoples.

The first system was the encomienda, which the governor Nicolás de Ovando set up on Hispaniola in 1502. Its name comes from the Spanish verb encomendar, meaning to entrust. On paper the Crown entrusted a group of Indian villagers to a colonist, who owed them protection and Christian teaching in return for their labor. In practice it became a license to work people to death.

The richest grants went to the conquerors. After he brought down the Aztec empire, Hernán Cortés received a single encomienda in Mexico covering more than 23,000 families of Native laborers, the forced work of tens of thousands of people handed to one man. The sugar mills were deadly. Three heavy rollers crushed the cane, and if a worker's hand caught between them they would drag in his arm and then his whole body before anyone could halt them. So a second worker always stood ready with a hatchet or cutlass to hack off the trapped arm; losing an arm was the merciful outcome. Next the juice was boiled down in the scorching boiling house, and the thick syrup set hard in clay molds. The molds were shaped like cones, so the sugar came out as a tall cone-shaped loaf weighing fifteen to twenty pounds.

Some Native leaders fought back. The Taino chief Hatuey watched the Spanish lay waste to Hispaniola and resolved to warn Cuba before the conquerors reached it, so he and his people paddled across the sea to Cuba in canoes. There he led guerrilla raids until the Spanish hunted him down with war dogs, and in 1512 they burned him at the stake at Yara. In 1516 Hispaniola got the Americas' first sugar mill, built with cane brought over from the Canary Islands. Sugar was the most labor-hungry crop in the colonies, and the work was so deadly that a mill hand was said to last only about seven years before heat, disease, injury and overwork killed him. As the Native peoples died, planters turned to Africa for new workers, and sugar's endless hunger for labor drove the Atlantic slave trade, the horror this plantation system is most remembered for.

Spain covered the conquest with paperwork. From 1513 commanders had to read out a document called the Requerimiento, written by the jurist Juan López de Palacios Rubios, which ordered the listeners to obey the Pope and Spain's king or face war. Soldiers read it in Spanish or Latin to people who understood none of it, and often to nobody at all: to empty beaches and to villages whose people had fled, to prisoners already captured, and even from the decks of ships the moment a coast came into sight. Las Casas, who watched the ritual, said it left him unsure whether he ought to laugh at it or weep. In his eyewitness account he also described the conquistadors' war-mastiffs, big dogs the Spanish bred and trained to hunt people down and tear them apart like prey.

Reformers like Las Casas finally moved Emperor Charles V. His New Laws of 1542 declared the Indigenous peoples free subjects of the Crown who could never be made slaves, and they struck at the encomienda with the rule colonists hated most: a grant could no longer pass to an heir, but went back to the Crown when its holder died, so the system would die out with the men who held it. In Peru the grant-holders rose in revolt under Gonzalo Pizarro, and in 1546 his men killed Blasco Núñez Vela, Peru's first viceroy, in battle rather than give up their grants. The Crown had already backed down and dropped the inheritance ban in 1545. As the encomienda faded, Spain put the repartimiento in its place, called the mita in Peru. Rather than hand people over to one master, it made each Indigenous village send a rotating share of its men to work for set periods. Meant as a reform, it was often just as deadly for the men sent down the silver mines.

sumer-and-the-first-city-states.context_blurb:
More than five thousand years ago, on the hot, flat plain where the Tigris and the Euphrates run toward the sea, in the south of modern Iraq, the Sumerians built the world's first cities: Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Umma and others. Each walled city had its own ruler and its own god, whose temple stood at its heart. Sumer gave the world writing, schools, written laws and some of its oldest stories.

The first of them was Uruk. By about 3100 BC some 40,000 people crowded behind its walls of mud brick, which made Uruk, as far as archaeologists can tell, the first true city ever built and the largest place on Earth in its day. To keep track of so many people and goods, the Sumerians invented writing, pressing wedge-shaped marks into wet clay with a reed. The earliest tablets hold no poems and no prayers: nearly all of them are accounts of grain and livestock, recording who owed what to whom. Writing began as bookkeeping. Each city's ruler bore the title lugal, which means, quite bluntly, big man. He might also be called en, lord, or ensi, governor, and he usually served as high priest of the city's god as well. The Sumerians played, too. At Ur the archaeologist Leonard Woolley dug up boards of shell and lapis lazuli inlay from about 2600 BC, and the curator Irving Finkel later pieced together its rules using a Babylonian tablet, so the Royal Game of Ur, a race to bring seven pieces across the board, is the oldest board game anyone can still play.

The first person in history whose name we know was no king. Kushim, at Uruk around 3100 BC, kept the tally of barley for a beer brewery at the temple of the goddess Inanna, and that bookkeeping job is the only reason the name was ever written down. One tablet lists 134,813 litres of barley owed to Kushim's brewery over 37 months. The Sumerians counted in sixties rather than tens, because sixty splits evenly into halves, thirds, quarters, fifths and sixths. The Babylonians inherited the system, and it never left us: it is why an hour holds sixty minutes and a circle 360 degrees. The first author known by name was a woman. Around 2300 BC Enheduanna, daughter of King Sargon of Akkad, served at Ur as high priestess of Nanna, the moon god, and she wrote hymns to the goddess Inanna and signed her own name to them.

Kings built on a vast scale. Gilgamesh's epic, among the oldest poems anywhere, credits King Gilgamesh with Uruk's great wall, some nine and a half kilometres around, and it opens with a challenge: go up on the walls of Uruk yourself, walk along them, study the brickwork and judge whether it is not baked brick, fired in a kiln. Around 2100 BC King Ur-Nammu began the Great Ziggurat of Ur, a stepped tower about thirty metres high that his son Shulgi finished. Three staircases led to a shrine at the top, and the Sumerians believed that shrine was the moon god Nanna's own home on earth, the place he had chosen to live. The cities also fought each other constantly. Around 2475 BC King Eannatum of Lagash crushed the neighbouring city of Umma in history's first well-recorded war between states, and he raised a stone to boast of it. It is called the Stele of the Vultures, because carved along its top are vultures flying away with the cut-off heads of the defeated enemy.

Some of Sumer's secrets lie in humble objects. At Uruk, excavators have found one cheap, rough bowl in its thousands, all pressed in molds and all much the same size: the bevel-rim bowl, the first mass-produced object in history. These bowls held a fixed daily ration of grain for each worker, the first sign of a true division of labour, with people working at special jobs and paid in measured portions of food. Death came to Ur's royalty, too. In one grave Woolley found 68 women in red gowns and gold headdresses lying in neat rows, with six armed men at the entrance. He called it the Great Death Pit and concluded that these were servants who had followed a dead royal master into the grave, perhaps by poison, though some skulls show blows to the head. It remains his reading of the evidence, not a settled fact.

sumerian-inventions-wheel-plow-sail.context_blurb:
The Sumerians, who built the first cities in southern Mesopotamia, in modern Iraq, more than five thousand years ago, were tireless inventors. Their potters, farmers, boatmen and number-keepers came up with tools so useful that we still rely on some of them every day, usually without knowing where they came from.

Their most famous invention began in a pottery workshop. Around 4000 BC potters at Uruk set a heavy disk spinning and shaped wet clay on it, which let them make smoother, thinner pots far faster than by hand. This potter's wheel is among the oldest wheels anywhere, and it came centuries before anyone stood a wheel on its edge and put it under a cart. The oldest one that survives, found at Ur, dates to about 3100 BC. The Sumerians also counted in sixties rather than tens, because sixty divides evenly by 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. That base-60 system outlived them by thousands of years: it is why each hour has sixty minutes and each minute sixty seconds. It is also why a full circle has 360 degrees.

Around 2500 BC Sumerian farmers built the seed-plow, a machine that did two jobs in a single pass. A pair of oxen hauled it across the field; as its wooden blade opened a fresh furrow, a farmer poured seed into a funnel on top, and the seeds dropped straight down into the newly cut earth. It took a team of three: one to lead the oxen, one to hold the plow and one to feed in the seed. On the rivers, from around 3000 BC, Sumerian boatmen used sails to push heavy cargo up the Tigris and Euphrates against the current. An old folk story says the idea came from washing day: someone watched wet laundry hung out to dry swell and pull in the breeze, and reasoned that a bigger cloth could drive a boat. The tale is plausible, but nobody can prove it.

One small tablet even preserves a farming manual. An expedition of the University of Chicago and the University of Pennsylvania found it in southern Iraq in 1949. From around 1700 BC, it records a father's advice to his son on the whole barley year, and it is known today as the Farmer's Almanac. Its instructions are precise: each seed should go into the furrow about two fingers deep.

sundiata-keita-the-lion-king-of-mali.context_blurb:
Sundiata Keita founded the Mali Empire in West Africa in the 1200s. His life is told in the Epic of Sundiata, which griots, the hereditary bards of the Mande peoples, have sung for more than seven hundred years. Much of it is legend, but the tale of a crippled boy who grows up to become the Lion of Mali is still performed across West Africa today.

His mother was Sogolon, the king's hunchbacked second wife, and the boy was named for her. Sundiata joins her name to jata, the Mande word for lion, so his epic name means Sogolon's Lion. His birth name was Sogolon Djata, and as emperor he took the title Mansa, king. The epic begins with a hard truth: for years the boy who would found an empire could not walk. While he dragged himself along the ground, his father's other wife, Sassouma Bereté, made fun of mother and son alike.

The turning point came when Sogolon was insulted over some baobab leaves that no one would fetch for her. The boy called for an iron bar that took six men to carry, and gripping it he pulled himself onto his feet for the first time. As he rose, the legend says, the bar bent under his strength into the shape of a bow. Later, driven into exile with his mother by jealous rivals, he grew into a hunter and a warrior. Meanwhile his homeland fell to Soumaoro Kanté, who ruled the Sosso people and was feared as a sorcerer. The epic paints Soumaoro as a monster: in a secret room carpeted with human skins, he displayed as trophies the heads of nine kings he had defeated.

Sundiata came home at the head of an alliance of neighbouring peoples, and around 1235 he met Soumaoro at the Battle of Kirina. Sundiata knew the secret that could undo the sorcerer's spells, the spur of a white rooster, so he fixed one to the point of an arrow. Wounded by that arrow, Soumaoro lost his power and vanished into the Koulikoro mountains. Kirina is remembered as the founding moment of Mali, which went on to rule much of West Africa for two centuries.

Around 1236 the victorious Sundiata called the heads of the clans together at Kouroukan Fouga, a clearing of granite rock, and proclaimed the Manden Charter, the new empire's constitution. For centuries it lived only in memory, handed down by speech, and today scholars hail it as among the first declarations of human rights. Its articles say that taking food to satisfy hunger is not robbery, that women must share in governing, and that before clearing land by fire a farmer must check the trees for fruit or flowers. UNESCO added it to its heritage list in 2009.

sunni-shia-split.context_blurb:
Islam's oldest and deepest division began in 632, when the Prophet Muhammad died in the oasis city of Medina. The believers he left behind had to decide who would lead them next, and their quarrel split the faith into two branches that still exist: the Sunni majority and the Shia. Both share the same Qur'an, the same prophet and the same pillars of worship.

The split began as an argument over who should take Muhammad's place at the head of the community. At a meeting in a roofed courtyard called the Saqifa, the senior companion Abu Bakr, Muhammad's close friend and father-in-law, was acclaimed as the first caliph. Another faction insisted that Muhammad had already chosen Ali ibn Abi Talib. Ali was family twice over: Muhammad's first cousin, orphaned as a boy and raised in the Prophet's household, and later his son-in-law, married to his daughter Fatima. By tradition Ali was the first boy or man to embrace Islam, at about eleven. His supporters became the shi'at Ali, the party of Ali: the Shia.

For the Sunni, Ali became the fourth of the rightly guided caliphs, in 656; for the Shia he is the first Imam. In 661 a Kharijite rebel, Abd al-Rahman ibn Muljam, attacked Ali in the Great Mosque of Kufa with a blade he had smeared with poison, so that even a single wound would kill, and Ali died about two days later. He is believed to lie in the great shrine at Najaf, one of the holiest places in the Shia world.

The deepest Shia wound came in 680. Ali's son Husayn, the Prophet's grandson, would not pledge loyalty to Yazid, the Umayyad caliph, and on the plain of Karbala, in Iraq, thousands of Umayyad soldiers closed around him. With Husayn stood only some seventy to a hundred people, family and followers together. That morning al-Hurr ibn Yazid, the cavalry officer whose horsemen had first stopped Husayn's march, was so moved by Husayn's words that he rode across to Husayn's side and was killed fighting for him. The little band was overwhelmed on 10 October 680. Husayn's head was cut off and carried to Yazid in Damascus, and the surviving women and children were led away as captives.

Each year Shia Muslims relive Karbala with mourning processions on Ashura, the tenth of Muharram. Forty days later comes Arba'in, when pilgrims walk to Husayn's tomb, often more than twenty million at once, many times the two or three million who make the Hajj to Mecca, which makes Arba'in the largest yearly gathering of people on earth.

surrealism-dali-s-melting-clocks.context_blurb:
Surrealism began in Paris in 1924, when the French writer André Breton set out to make art from the hidden images of the unconscious mind. Surrealist painters filled their canvases with dreams: everyday objects in impossible scenes. The most famous of them was the Spanish painter Salvador Dalí, a superb craftsman and a born showman with a waxed moustache and a pet ocelot.

In 1931 Dalí painted The Persistence of Memory, a bare dreamscape where pocket watches hang limp and droopy, as if they had melted. A physicist once asked whether Einstein's relativity, which says that time can stretch, had given him the idea. Dalí said no. He had been inspired by something far homelier: a Camembert cheese turning runny in the sun one summer evening. He called his watches the camembert of time.

Look closely at the lower left of the painting. One orange pocket watch lies face down with its case shut, the only watch in the picture that stays hard, and it is swarming with black ants, the creatures Dalí painted again and again as his sign of rot and decay. Soft time melts away; hard time is eaten. The image became one of the most copied pictures of the twentieth century, and dream scenes like it still turn up in films and advertising today.

suttee-thuggee-and-foot-binding-ended-by.context_blurb:
In the nineteenth century, reformers set out to end three old customs that cost countless lives in India and China: suttee, in which a widow died in the flames of her dead husband's pyre; Thuggee, a secret brotherhood of highway stranglers; and the binding of girls' feet. Some reformers were British officials and missionaries, others were Indians and Chinese working within their own traditions, and they often worked side by side.

The Thugs roamed India's roads in bands, joining travellers for days and winning their trust with shared meals and easy talk before turning on them. Each strangler killed with the rumal, a cloth handkerchief knotted at one end to give his hand a grip. The spade the gang used to dig secret graves was held sacred to the goddess the cult worshipped. In China, foot-binding began when a girl was small. Her toes were folded under until they broke, then her arch was snapped, and the foot was bound tighter year after year. The prized ideal was a foot of about three inches, called the golden lotus; a four-inch foot ranked lower as a silver lotus, and five inches or more made an iron one. Families saw a tiny foot as a daughter's ticket to a good marriage.

For years the British rulers of India left suttee alone, fearing that a ban would set off a religious revolt. Two unlikely allies pushed them: the Baptist missionary William Carey and the Hindu reformer Raja Ram Mohan Roy, who argued that Hindu scripture did not actually require the burning. On 4 December 1829 the Governor-General, Lord William Bentinck, signed a regulation declaring suttee illegal. In the eyes of the law, helping to burn a widow was now the killing of a human being, not a sacred rite, and those who took part could be tried as her murderers.

Carey was also the government's official translator into Bengali, and the new order reached him on a Sunday morning. Believing that every hour of delay might cost another widow her life, he gave his pulpit to a fellow preacher and worked to have the decree in Bengali by that same evening. In the 1830s William Sleeman, a British officer, set out to break the Thugs. His great weapon was the approver: a prisoner from the cult who would turn informer and guide the soldiers to the men of his old gang. The most important, Feringheea, led Sleeman in 1831 to graves near the village of Salohda, and his testimony helped identify 283 of 289 Thugs seized near Jhansi. By 1839 Sleeman declared the cult destroyed.

In China, early campaigners argued against foot-binding from the Christian faith and won few hearts. Alicia Little, who started the Natural Foot Society at Shanghai in 1895, took a cleverer route on her tours: she showed audiences X-ray photographs of crushed and folded feet, set beside quotations from Confucius, arguing from health and from China's own tradition instead of from religion. Chinese reformers joined the fight, and Kang Youwei's Anti-Footbinding Society claimed 300,000 members. The Republic of China banned foot-binding in 1912, though the last factory making lotus shoes, in Harbin, closed only in 1999.

taiping-rebellion.context_blurb:
From 1850 to 1864 the Taiping Rebellion tore through southern and central China. Its leader, Hong Xiuquan, raised an army of peasants, miners and the poor, captured the great city of Nanjing and ruled from it for more than a decade, while the Qing emperors, already weakened by the Opium Wars, fought him back city by city.

Hong was a village schoolteacher who had failed the imperial civil service examination four times. After one failure he fell sick with a fever and dreamed that an old man with a golden beard took out his organs and handed him a sword to sweep demons from the world. Years later he read a Christian pamphlet by Liang Fa and decided what the dream had meant: the old man was God his father, Jesus was his elder brother, and Hong himself was the younger brother of Christ, sent to rid China of demons. In 1851 he proclaimed himself Heavenly King of the Taiping, the Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace.

The war he started was the deadliest of the nineteenth century anywhere on earth. Estimates of the dead run from 20 to 30 million people, many times the toll of the American Civil War fought in the same years, which makes the Taiping war one of the bloodiest in all of human history. It shattered central China, exposed how weak the Qing had become, and began the long collapse of imperial China that ended in 1911.

taj-mahal.context_blurb:
Beside the Yamuna, in the city of Agra in northern India, stands the Taj Mahal, a white marble building with a great onion dome and four slender minarets. The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan ordered it in the 1630s, and it became the most famous monument in India and one of the most photographed buildings on earth.

The Taj is a monument to grief. In 1631 Shah Jahan's beloved wife Mumtaz Mahal died giving birth to their fourteenth child, and the emperor built the Taj as her tomb. About 20,000 craftsmen worked on it for some twenty-two years, from 1632 to 1653, cutting and carving white marble from the quarries of Makrana. The poet Rabindranath Tagore later called it a teardrop resting on the cheek of time.

Shah Jahan designed everything in perfect balance, each tower and hall mirrored by its twin, with his wife's tomb at the exact center beneath the dome. Only one thing spoils the symmetry, and that is the emperor's own grave. When Shah Jahan died, his son Aurangzeb had him buried in the space beside Mumtaz, slightly off center to the west, so the coffin of the man who planned the perfect balance is the one thing that breaks it. Aurangzeb had already seized the throne and locked his father up in nearby Agra Fort, where the old emperor spent his last years, from 1658 to 1666, gazing across the river at the Taj.

tang-dynasty-golden-age-of-poetry-arts.context_blurb:
The Tang dynasty ruled China from 618 to 907, and the Chinese still look back on it as their golden age. Its capital drew merchants, monks and envoys from all over Asia, and its poets wrote verses Chinese children still learn. Then, at the height of its glory, one rebellion tore the empire apart.

Chang'an was the biggest city in the world, with about a million people inside its walls of packed earth. The Tang laid it out as one giant checkerboard of straight avenues, with the palace at the northern end, because they believed the grid copied the order of the heavens: the capital was the cosmos rebuilt on earth. Envoys from Japan and Korea took its plan home, and the Japanese capitals of Nara and Heian-kyo, later called Kyoto, and the Korean capital of Gyeongju were all built in its image. Inside, the city was divided into 108 walled wards. At dusk some 800 drumbeats sounded the curfew and every ward gate shut, and a commoner found in the streets after that could expect arrest and a beating. The inner walls were there less to keep enemies out than to keep the city's own people shut in at night.

In the 740s the wandering poet Li Bai, born in 701 in the Silk Road town of Suyab, came to Chang'an. The veteran court poet He Zhizhang, reading his wild, thundering poem The Road to Shu, hailed him as the Banished Immortal, a spirit thrown out of heaven to live on earth, and the name stuck for good. He Zhizhang loved wine as much as Li Bai did. Once, with no money for the bill, he took off the golden-tortoise ornament that marked his high rank at court and handed it across the tavern counter for a drink. Li Bai's short poem Quiet Night Thoughts, in which a traveller takes moonlight on the floor for frost and then looks up at the moon, homesick, is the first poem most Chinese children learn by heart. In 744 Li Bai met Du Fu, a younger and graver poet, and the two spent a season on the road together as sworn friends. The friendship ran mostly one way: Du Fu wrote about a dozen poems to or about Li Bai, and Li Bai sent back only one.

The Tang age was a great age of Buddhism too. In 629 the monk Xuanzang left Chang'an against the emperor's law and walked the Silk Road to India, where he studied for years at Nalanda. He came home in 645 with 657 Sanskrit scriptures loaded on horses, and centuries later his journey inspired the Ming novel Journey to the West. Tang printers spread such scriptures by cutting whole pages into wooden blocks and inking them, long before Gutenberg. The Diamond Sutra, a Buddhist scroll printed in 868 with a woodcut picture at its head, is the oldest complete printed book in the world that carries a date.

The golden age broke in 755, when the general An Lushan rose in revolt. That year Du Fu wrote of rich families behind red-lacquered gates, whose wine went sour and meat went bad while frozen and starving people lay dead along the road. When he reached his own home, he learned that his little son had starved to death. In 756, as Emperor Xuanzong fled the rebels, his guards mutinied at Mawei Station, blamed the family of his beloved consort Yang Guifei for the disaster, and would not march on until he ordered her death. The emperor gave in, and his servant Gao Lishi saw to it that she was strangled. An Lushan crowned himself emperor, but he grew bloated, half blind and suspicious of everyone. In 757 a servant, Li Zhu'er, cut him down inside his tent, in a plot backed by An's own son, and the dying rebel shrieked that his killer was a thief from within his own household. The census shows the wreckage: the count of 754 recorded nearly 53 million people, and the count of 764 found only about 17 million, through death, flight or the collapse of the count itself.

Li Bai died in 762, and nobody knows how. The Chinese have always preferred a legend: drunk in a boat one night, the poet reached out to hug the moon's reflection on the water, tumbled in and drowned. The moon shines through so many of his poems that the story feels right.
