tenochtitlan-the-floating-aztec-capital.context_blurb:
Tenochtitlan, the capital of the Aztecs, rose on an island in Lake Texcoco, high in the Valley of Mexico. The Mexica people founded it around 1325 on a swampy islet, and within two centuries it had become one of the great cities of the world, ringed by water and fed by gardens built in the lake itself. In 1521 Hernán Cortés destroyed it.

The Mexica had wandered for years in search of a home. Huitzilopochtli, their god, had promised them a sign to mark the spot, and on the island, the legend says, they found it: an eagle perched on a cactus, devouring a snake. That scene sits today at the center of the Mexican flag. The city's name, in the Mexica language of Nahuatl, paints the same picture: tetl, stone, plus nochtli, prickly-pear cactus, plus tlan, place, so Tenochtitlan means the place of the prickly pear growing out of a stone. When the Spaniards under Cortés first looked down on the city in 1519, its white towers and temples rising from the water, the soldier Bernal Díaz compared it to the enchantments in the knightly romance of Amadís, and he wrote that some of the men wondered aloud whether what they were looking at was a dream.

Tenochtitlan was huge. Its people numbered two hundred thousand or more, perhaps twice that, which made it bigger than most cities in Europe, London and Paris included. To feed them, farmers grew crops in the lake on plots called chinampas, nicknamed floating gardens. Each plot began as open water: the farmers built it up from the lake bed in layers of mud, rotting plants and reeds until it stood about half a metre above the surface. There were no coins in the markets. Shoppers paid for small things with cacao beans, and for big purchases, Díaz noted, traders measured out goose quills filled with gold dust, white quills clear enough to show the gold, valued by their length and thickness.

In truth the chinampas never floated. Farmers planted willow trees along the edges of every plot, and the willows' deep roots gripped the lake bottom and held each garden fast. The greatest market of all was at Tlatelolco, the sister city next door; in a letter to his king, Cortés counted more than sixty thousand people there on a single day. Yet the crowd was orderly, Díaz said, because every kind of goods had its own fixed place, cloth here, cacao there, obsidian blades, jade, feathers, jaguar skins and food each in theirs, and judges sat in the market to settle quarrels. Three long stone causeways joined the island to the shore, but the builders left gaps in them, crossed by loose wooden beams that people could lift out. Canoes slipped through the gaps, and in war, pulling up the beams turned each gap into a moat that attackers could not cross. The Spaniards learned this on the Noche Triste, the Night of Sorrows, in June 1520: the gaps trapped Cortés's men as they fled the city, and many drowned, some dragged under by the gold stuffed in their clothes.

The lake around the city was salty, so fresh water had to travel more than four kilometres by aqueduct from springs on the hill of Chapultepec. Begun in 1418 and wrecked by a flood in 1449, it was rebuilt by Nezahualcoyotl, the poet-king of Texcoco, with two channels instead of one, so that either could be shut down for cleaning or repair while its twin kept the city supplied. Nezahualcoyotl and the Aztecs also split the lake with a dike some sixteen kilometres long, finished around 1453. Besides holding back floods, it kept the brackish eastern water apart from the fresh, spring-fed water around Tenochtitlan, so it let them control how salty the lake beside the city stayed. But the aqueduct was also the city's weak point. The island had no spring or well of its own, so when Cortés besieged Tenochtitlan in 1521 he broke the aqueduct apart and cut off its drinking water, turning the Aztecs' own engineering against them.

teotihuacan-city-of-the-gods.context_blurb:
Northeast of today's Mexico City lie the ruins of Teotihuacan, the greatest city of ancient Mexico. Its builders raised giant pyramids along a straight ceremonial road and traded across Mesoamerica, yet they left no written name for themselves or their city. Around 550 its heart went up in flames, and its people faded from history.

Centuries later the Aztecs wandered among its empty pyramids, awed. In their own language, Nahuatl, they named the ruin Teotihuacan, the City of the Gods, roughly the place where the gods were born. Down the middle runs a boulevard some four kilometres long and forty metres wide, lined with stepped platforms. The Aztecs took those platforms for tombs and called the road the Avenue of the Dead, though they were really ceremonial buildings, not graves.

In 1971 a hidden tunnel came to light beside the Pyramid of the Sun; it ran about a hundred metres under the pyramid and ended in a sealed chamber shaped like a four-leaf clover. Many scholars think it was a sacred place of emergence, the womb of the earth from which the first humans were born. Another temple bristles with some 260 carved heads jutting out of its walls: fanged feathered serpents, the god the Aztecs would later call Quetzalcoatl, alternating with a second figure in a war headdress.

In its prime, around 400 to 500 CE, perhaps 125,000 people lived in Teotihuacan. No city in the Americas was bigger before the 1400s, and archaeologists count it among the six biggest cities anywhere on Earth in its day. Its wealth ran on obsidian, a volcanic glass, and Teotihuacan held the only source of the green kind in Mesoamerica, which its craftsmen shaped into blades and masks. That green glass has turned up as far off as the Maya city of Tikal in Guatemala, more than a thousand kilometres away, proof of how far Teotihuacan's traders reached.

Its builders had a signature style too: a sloping wall, the talud, under a flat, picture-framed panel, the tablero. That pairing works like a fingerprint, and wherever archaeologists find it in distant ruins, it tells them that Teotihuacan's influence reached that far. The city welcomed strangers: Zapotecs from Oaxaca had one neighbourhood, and Gulf Coast merchants in round houses had another. Scientists proved that many of these people were born far away by running chemical tests on their bones and teeth, which keep a record of the water and food of a person's childhood home.

In the 1980s, excavators working under the serpent temple found more than two hundred sacrificed people laid in the ground with their wrists bound behind them when the temple was dedicated, around 150 to 200 CE. Many wore necklaces made of actual human teeth and jawbones. In 2003 heavy rain opened a sinkhole at the foot of that temple, and the archaeologist Sergio Gómez went down into a sealed tunnel that no one had entered for some eighteen centuries. At its far end, pools of liquid mercury lay on the floor. Powdered pyrite on the walls glittered like stars, as if the builders had made a starry underworld.

Teotihuacan's reach could turn to conquest. On 16 January 378, a warlord called Siyaj K'ak' arrived at Tikal under the authority of a Teotihuacan lord known as Spearthrower Owl, and the king of Tikal, Chak Tok Ich'aak, died on the very day he came. Within a year a boy said to be Spearthrower Owl's son sat on the Maya throne. Many scholars read those matching dates as a coup: a foreign power from Teotihuacan seizing control of Tikal.

Around 550, fire swept the city's center. Sifting the ruins, archaeologists found that the burning had not fallen evenly: it fell on the palaces and temples of the rulers, while ordinary homes were largely spared. That points many of them to a revolt by the city's own people, not a foreign army.

Strangest of all is the silence about who ruled. Egypt buried its god-kings in gold, and the Maya boasted of their kings in carved stone, but Teotihuacan has given up no royal tomb, no portrait of a ruler and not one carving that names a king. From that silence, a good many experts conclude that Teotihuacan had no single monarch, and that noble houses shared power in a kind of collective rule.

terracotta-army.context_blurb:
Qin Shi Huang was the ruthless warlord who crushed his rivals, united China in 221 BC and made himself its first emperor. He meant to go on ruling after death, so he had an army made to guard his tomb near the modern city of Xi'an: some eight thousand life-sized soldiers of clay, set out in battle order with real bronze weapons. For twenty-two centuries the army lay buried and forgotten.

Then, in the dry spring of 1974, Yang Zhifa and his neighbours were sinking a well when, about four metres down, a shovel struck something hard: a clay head. The farmers took it for a pottery god. In fact they had broken into a pit holding thousands of life-sized clay soldiers, the Terracotta Army.

Stroll along the ranks today and something uncanny appears: no two warriors share a face. The sculptors built the heads from about ten basic molds, then pressed extra clay onto each one by hand to give every man his own features, hair and expression. They showed rank as well, making the generals taller than the foot soldiers.

The soldiers were once brightly painted, with rosy skin, black hair and robes in vivid colours, and that paint survived more than two thousand years in the sealed dark. But it lay on a thin coat of lacquer that dried and curled the moment it met dry air. When archaeologists dug the warriors out, their colours began to change within about fifteen seconds and flaked away within four minutes, which is why most of the army looks bare and grey today.

teutoburg-forest-varus-loses-three-legio.context_blurb:
In AD 9 Rome was pushing its frontier east of the Rhine, into the dark forests of Germania. The governor there, Publius Quinctilius Varus, marched three legions, the 17th, 18th and 19th, along narrow, boggy paths through the Teutoburg Forest, trusting a guide he knew well. Over three days of running fights the Germanic tribes destroyed his army almost to a man, and Varus killed himself rather than be taken.

The guide was the traitor. Arminius, a Cherusci chieftain, had grown up in Rome as a hostage, trained as a Roman officer and been made a Roman citizen and knight. He was commanding a squadron in Varus's own army, trusted by his general, even as he secretly arranged the ambush.

When the news reached Rome, the aged emperor Augustus fell apart. For months he left his hair and beard uncut, and he beat his head on the doorposts and cried out for Quintilius Varus to give him back his legions; in Latin the cry was Quintili Vare, legiones redde. For the rest of his life he kept the day of the disaster as a day of mourning.

The defeat ended Rome's dream of ruling Germania. The legions never again tried to hold the land beyond the Rhine, and the river stayed the empire's frontier for centuries.

the-abbasid-caliphate-and-baghdad.context_blurb:
In 750 a new family of caliphs, the Abbasids, overthrew the Umayyad dynasty and took charge of much of the Muslim world. Their capital, Baghdad, rose beside the Tigris in today's Iraq and grew into the largest and most learned city of its age, a meeting place for scholars of many faiths, until the Mongols stormed it five centuries later.

The caliph al-Mansur founded the city in 762 and gave its core a shape no capital had used: a perfect circle about two kilometres across, laid out, it was said, to display the geometric order he had admired in the books of Euclid. The everyday name, Baghdad, was the name of a Persian village that stood there before, but al-Mansur's official name for his city was a hopeful one: Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace. Ringed walls enclosed the Round City, pierced by four gates, and each gate took its name from the distant city its road ran toward: the Kufa Gate, the Basra Gate, the Damascus Gate and the Khorasan Gate, where the great road to Central Asia began. At the very center, inside an almost empty plaza, stood the caliph's palace and main mosque. The caliph's Golden Gate Palace wore a great green dome that could be seen from far across the city.

To dazzle Charlemagne, emperor of the Franks, Harun al-Rashid, the most famous of the Abbasid caliphs, sent him a live elephant, Abul-Abbas. An envoy called Isaac the Jew led the beast across North Africa and over the Alps, and in July 802 it reached Charlemagne's court at Aachen, where it lived until it died of pneumonia in 810. Oddly, the gift lives only in Frankish memory: their royal annals and Einhard's biography of Charlemagne name the elephant, yet no surviving record from Baghdad mentions the present at all.

Harun's Baghdad was a capital of learning. At the House of Wisdom, scholars rendered Persian, Greek, Syriac and Sanskrit learning into Arabic. Much of the hardest Greek work fell to Syriac-speaking Nestorian Christians, who already knew both tongues, a reminder that Christians, Jews, Zoroastrians and Muslims built the golden age together. There the scholar al-Khwarizmi wrote a book of mathematics with the Arabic word al-jabr in its title, and that one word grew into the English algebra. His own name, turned into Latin as Algoritmi, gave us the word algorithm. At their peak in the ninth and tenth centuries, Baghdad's streets may have held a million people, the biggest crowd of any city in the world. Its only rival was Chang'an, the capital of Tang China, at the far eastern end of the Silk Road, and the two were the twin giants of the medieval world. Harun's court lived on in legend too. He, the poet Abu Nuwas and the vizier Jafar turn up again and again in The Thousand and One Nights, where the caliph slips through his city by night in disguise, adventures that are storytelling, not court record.

A later caliph, al-Ma'mun, loved knowledge just as much. Around 830 he sent astronomers to the level plain of Sinjar, where one party headed due north and the other due south, each pacing out the distance that covered exactly one degree of the planet's curve. Once they knew how long a single degree was on the ground, they could calculate how big the whole Earth is, and their result came remarkably close to the truth.

In 1258 the Mongol commander Hulagu Khan brought his army against Baghdad. The last caliph, al-Musta'sim, still had twenty thousand horsemen, but the Mongols beat them before the real fight began: they broke the dikes on the canals beside the Tigris and flooded the ground behind the army, trapping the riders in mud and water. In February the Mongols stormed the city and ended the Abbasid line. Mongol custom forbade shedding a ruler's blood on the earth, so they rolled al-Musta'sim up inside a carpet and trampled him to death under their horses, though some sources say he was starved instead.

A legend says the Mongols flung so many books into the Tigris that its water turned black with ink. The historian Michal Biran found that story of total ruin overblown: Baghdad's learning was wounded, not wiped out, and big libraries were open for teaching again within two years.

the-american-home-front-rosie-the-rivete.context_blurb:
When the United States entered the Second World War in December 1941, millions of American men left to fight, and the country's factories had to arm a world war. Women took their places by the millions, welding, riveting and building ships, tanks and planes, while every family at home learned to make do with less. The nickname for those women was Rosie the Riveter.

The sacrifices began in the kitchen. In 1942 the government started rationing food so the troops overseas could be fed, and every family received a booklet of stamps to tear out and trade for scarce goods. The first thing rationed, on 27 April 1942, was sugar, about a pound for each person every two weeks, and the booklet itself was nicknamed the Sugar Book. Coffee followed that November, after German U-boats sank the ships bringing it from Brazil.

The factories raced the war itself. Could American yards turn out cargo ships faster than U-boats sank them? At Kaiser's Richmond shipyard in November 1942, crews set out to answer that, snapping together some 250,000 parts into one Liberty ship in four days, fifteen hours and twenty-nine minutes. The ship was the SS Robert E. Peary.

The name came first from a song. In 1942 Redd Evans and John Jacob Loeb wrote Rosie the Riveter, and in 1943 it became a hit for the Four Vagabonds, an African-American vocal group. In the song Rosie works overtime on the riveting machine to protect her sweetheart, Charlie, a Marine, by building the planes he would fly. Norman Rockwell gave her a face. On a Saturday Evening Post cover for Memorial Day 1943, he painted a brawny Rosie posed like a prophet on the Sistine Chapel ceiling, a rivet gun across her knees and her name on her lunch pail. Under her shoes, to show whom she was fighting, lay a crushed copy of Hitler's Mein Kampf.

The factories kept speeding up. At Ford's Willow Run plant, a mile long, production chief Charles Sorensen boasted that it would build a bomber an hour, which sounded impossible for a four-engine B-24 Liberator. By April 1944, with two shifts of nine hours each, six days in seven, Willow Run made his boast come true, rolling out a new B-24 every 63 minutes. Charles Lindbergh, who worked for Ford as a test pilot, called the plant the Grand Canyon of a mechanized world.

The most famous picture of all had the quietest start. In 1942 the artist J. Howard Miller painted a woman in a bandana flexing her arm under the words We Can Do It!, as a short-lived morale poster for the Westinghouse company. It was up on the factory walls for a fortnight or so and then disappeared for decades, so the image now seen as the very symbol of wartime women was hardly known during the war itself.

the-ancient-hebrews-and-monotheism.context_blurb:
The ancient Hebrews, the people who became the Jews, lived in a world crowded with gods: every city, river and storm had its own. Over many centuries, from Abraham through Moses and the prophets, they came to a different conviction, that there is one God who made everything and judges everyone. Judaism handed that belief on to Christianity and Islam, and it reshaped the moral language of the West.

Their central daily prayer, the Shema, takes its name from its first word, Hear, and it declares that the LORD, Israel's God, is one. In a world of countless gods, that single word sums up the whole faith. The Book of Exodus tells how Moses led the Hebrews out of slavery in Egypt. When the tenth and last plague fell on Egypt, each Hebrew family killed a lamb and daubed its blood on the door frame with a sprig of hyssop, and when death came for the firstborn of Egypt, it passed over every house marked with blood. Jews have kept that night ever since as Passover. At Mount Sinai, Moses spent forty days with God and came down carrying two stone tablets inscribed with the Ten Commandments, only to find the people dancing around a golden calf they had cast from their melted jewellery. In his fury he shattered the tablets and had to climb the mountain again for a second set.

The Hebrews' God also had a name unlike any other. Earlier in Exodus, when God spoke to Moses out of a burning bush, Moses asked by what name he should announce Him to the Israelites. God answered not with a label but with a statement of His own existence, I AM WHO I AM, and told Moses to say that I AM had sent him. In the scriptures the personal name of God is written with four Hebrew letters, YHWH, called the tetragrammaton. Jews held it too holy to speak, and readers said Adonai, my Lord, instead. Out of that old reverence, English Bibles still print the word LORD in small capital letters wherever the holy name stands.

Hebrew scripture tells the people's whole story as a single covenant, a binding pact between God and Israel. It begins when God promises Abraham that a great nation, loyal to Him alone, will spring from his family, and so Abraham is remembered as the father of monotheism. Its first chapter carries what Rabbi David Wolpe has named the greatest gift Judaism gave the world. Dignity is not earned by rank or wealth but given to every human being alike, because each one is made in the image of God. Historians count that idea, the imago Dei, among the headwaters of universal human rights. Disaster came in 587 or 586 BC, when the army of the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar broke into Jerusalem, burned Solomon's Temple and dragged the people into exile. Jews still mourn the Temple every year on the fast of Tisha B'Av.

Long before that fall, the prophet Amos had raged at the rich who cheated the poor with crooked scales. To him, wronging widows and orphans was an offence against God Himself, and he cried out for justice to roll down like waters and righteousness like a stream that never runs dry. In 1979, digging in a tomb outside Jerusalem, archaeologists found two tiny silver scrolls, each about two and a half centimetres long, once worn as protective charms. Dating to about 600 BC, four centuries before the Dead Sea Scrolls, they carry the Priestly Blessing, The LORD bless you and keep you, and are the oldest known passages of the Hebrew Bible.

Far from home, the exiles poured out their grief in Psalm 137. It opens by the rivers of Babylon, where the captives sat down and wept when they remembered Zion. Their exile ended when Persia's Cyrus the Great took Babylon in 539 BC and allowed the captives to return. The Hebrew Bible honoured this foreign king with a title it gave no other outsider: in the Book of Isaiah, God calls Cyrus his anointed one, the word that in Hebrew is messiah.

the-ancient-olympic-games-at-olympia.context_blurb:
Every four years for more than a thousand years, Greeks from every city travelled to Olympia, a sanctuary of Zeus in the western Peloponnese, for the greatest festival of their world. Tradition dates the first games to 776 BC. They were an act of worship as much as sport, and a win made a man the most famous athlete in Greece.

Yet a champion took home no gold and no money. His only prize was a crown of leaves cut from wild olive, the kotinos, sliced with a golden sickle from a sacred tree at Olympia that Hercules himself was said to have planted. The glory was the reward.

Greek athletes competed completely naked. Orsippos of Megara, the story goes, shed his loincloth in the middle of a race around 720 BC, ran on and won, and from then on athletes stripped bare, their bodies displayed as a tribute to Zeus.

The festival even tamed war. The Greek city-states fought each other almost without end, but before each games, heralds set out from Elis, the city that ran the festival, to proclaim the ekecheiria, the holding of hands. While that truce lasted, every war had to stop and no army could set foot in Elis, so athletes and up to 40,000 spectators could make the journey in safety. In time the truce stretched to three months.

The most famous champion was Milon of Kroton, a wrestler who won the boys' crown in 540 BC and then five men's crowns in a row, six Olympic victories in all. Legend says he built his strength by hoisting a newborn calf onto his shoulders every day and carrying it until it grew into a full-grown bull. The story adds that he finally carried the bull around the stadium, then killed it and ate the whole thing in a day.

Cheating was rare, partly because the judges had a clever punishment. Anyone who bribed an opponent or broke the rules owed a heavy fine, and the money paid for bronze statues of Zeus, called Zanes, set in a row along the path into the stadium, so every competitor walked past the record of a cheater's shame on the way in. Their stone bases still stand at Olympia.

the-assyrian-war-machine.context_blurb:
From its heartland in the north of today's Iraq, the Assyrian Empire ruled the ancient Near East for some three centuries, from about 900 to 612 BC. Its kings built the most fearsome army the region had ever seen and used terror on purpose, boasting in stone of their cruelties. Yet the same kings gathered the first great library, and its ruins saved some of humanity's oldest stories.

The Assyrians kept the first real standing army in history, up to 200,000 men, and they could afford so many because they armed them with iron. Iron was cheap enough to turn out in bulk. When Ashurnasirpal II opened his new capital, Kalhu, in 879 BC, he feasted 69,574 guests for ten days and had the menu cut into stone, listing 1,000 oxen, 14,000 sheep, 10,000 eggs and 10,000 jars of beer. King Ashurbanipal, who ruled at the empire's height from 668 to 631 BC, bragged of a rarer gift: he was able to read and write. Most kings left writing to their palace scribes, but Ashurbanipal had trained as a boy like an apprentice scribe, mastering the wedge-shaped cuneiform script and even the ancient Sumerian language. He turned that passion into the world's first great library, ordering cities across his empire to send copies of every text they had, until over thirty thousand tablets of clay filled his palace at Nineveh.

The Assyrians broke rebels with a chilling policy: they marched whole peoples off to distant lands. When Sargon II took Samaria, capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, he recorded leading away 27,290 of its people, and the exiled northern tribes became known as the Ten Lost Tribes. In 701 BC Sennacherib invaded the Hebrew kingdom to the south. At Lachish his men piled up a siege ramp of some three million stones, about 20,000 tons, to haul a one-ton battering ram up to the walls. It is the only Assyrian siege ramp ever found, and inside it archaeologists recovered the iron chain that once swung the ram. Next he laid siege to Jerusalem, where King Hezekiah held out. Sennacherib's own six-sided clay prism brags that he penned Hezekiah inside Jerusalem like a caged bird, yet it never claims the city fell. Babylon, a holy city, rebelled against him in 689 BC, and Sennacherib meant to blot it out of memory. His own inscription says how: he dug canals and drowned the ruins under water until the site became a mere meadow.

For centuries Nineveh seemed untouchable, though Nahum, a Hebrew prophet, had foretold its ruin in a short book of the Bible. In 612 BC an alliance of Medes and Babylonians besieged the city and broke in after only three months. They burned Nineveh and fired Ashurbanipal's palace, but the blaze did not destroy his library: as the shelves collapsed, it baked the clay tablets rock-hard and preserved them for us to read. Among them was the Epic of Gilgamesh, the oldest great story ever written, whose hero rides out a flood that drowns the world and lets a dove fly from his boat. The brutal Assyrians are the reason the poem survives at all.

The Assyrians never hid their cruelty; they carved it in stone as a warning. Ashurnasirpal II boasted that when a city rebelled, he flayed all its chiefs and covered a pillar by the city gate with their skins, words meant to be read aloud so that rival cities would give up in terror. The walls of Sennacherib's Nineveh palace showed the fall of Lachish, with captives put to death before the enthroned king, beneath a label calling him king of the world. Long after he died, an unknown hand gouged out the king's face. Even the art of terror could be great art. On a panel from Ashurbanipal's royal lion hunt, carved around 645 BC, a dying lioness pierced by arrows drags her paralysed hind legs and roars, and many call it among the finest works of art the ancient world produced.

The tablets waited underground for more than two thousand years. In 1872 George Smith, a scholar who had taught himself, was studying one of them at the British Museum when he found in it a flood that drowned the world and a boat grounding on a mountaintop, much like the story of Noah. The story goes that he was so excited he began tearing off his clothes and ran around the room shouting.

the-atlantic-triangular-slave-trade.context_blurb:
From the early 1500s to the 1860s, European merchants ran a trade that carried millions of captive Africans across the Atlantic to work the plantations and mines of the Americas. Their ships sailed a great triangle between Europe, Africa and the New World, and on its middle leg, the Middle Passage, human beings were the cargo.

Along what Europeans named the Slave Coast, traders bought people not with coins but with cowrie shells, tiny white shells gathered in the faraway Maldive Islands and shipped west by the ton as ballast. The Bight of Benin alone took in some thirty billion of them over nearly four centuries. Captives were held in coastal forts such as Elmina and Cape Coast Castle, and at the end they were driven in chains through one last doorway, where small boats waited to carry them out to the ships. It is remembered today as the Door of No Return, because no one who passed through it ever came home. Most Americans would guess that the ships went mainly to the United States, but Portugal's sugar and gold colony of Brazil received the most by far, about 46 percent of all the Africans landed in the New World, almost half. Just some 388,000 landed directly in mainland North America, fewer than four in every hundred of the roughly 10.7 million who survived the crossing; the rest went by the millions to Brazil and the Caribbean.

The triangle paid for itself. Guns, iron and cloth went out from Europe to buy captives on the African coast, and the captives were traded for sugar and molasses on the plantations of Brazil and the Caribbean. The molasses sailed north to New England, where colonists distilled it into rum, and the rum went back across the ocean to pay for more captives. A hard truth stands beside the European guilt. European buyers seldom went inland to hunt people themselves; the captives reached the coast, already chained, in the hands of other African kingdoms, such as Dahomey, the Oyo Empire and the Asante, which made war on their neighbours and sold the prisoners for guns, cloth and shells. Dahomey, which held the slave port of Ouidah, grew so rich on the trade that Britain had to force it to stop selling captives in 1852. Neither truth excuses the other.

Elmina Castle, which the Portuguese raised on the coast of Ghana in 1482, was the first European building in Africa below the Sahara. Beneath it, hundreds of enslaved men waited in chains in a dark stone dungeon, and directly on the floor above them the Portuguese built a Christian church, worshipping overhead while the captives suffered below. As a boy, Olaudah Equiano was seized from his home and carried onto a slave ship. Years later, a free man in Britain, he published his Interesting Narrative in 1789, which fed the campaign against the trade, and he remembered his terror when the strange crewmen with red faces and long loose hair first took him below. He was sure that the white men meant to eat him.

The abolitionists fought back with pictures. In 1788 they printed a plan of the slave ship Brookes with 482 people packed in rows, its legal limit, and more than 7,000 copies made it the most famous image of the whole movement. Yet the ship's own records showed it had once crammed in as many as 740. Britain banned its own slave trade in 1807, after a long campaign by William Wilberforce and his allies, and then sent the Royal Navy after everyone else's. Its West Africa Squadron hunted slavers off the African coast for half a century, seizing about 1,600 ships and setting free about 150,000 Africans found chained below their decks.

Scholars have pieced the ships' own logbooks and sales records together into a database, and it shows that between about 1525 and 1866, about 12.5 million Africans were packed into ships for the voyage west. About 10.7 million lived to step ashore, so somewhere between 1.2 and 2.4 million died in the crossing itself, and many more died in the raids and the forced marches to the coast. More than 1,500 British sailors died on that station, most of them from tropical fever rather than enemy guns, and people at the time reckoned the price at one sailor dead for every nine Africans set free. At its height the campaign swallowed about 2 percent of Britain's national income.

the-atomic-bomb-and-the-manhattan-projec.context_blurb:
In the Second World War the United States set out, in deep secrecy, to build an atomic bomb. The Manhattan Project gathered the finest physicists of the age under J. Robert Oppenheimer, and in less than three years it went from a pile of bricks in Chicago to a fireball in the New Mexico desert, and then to Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

The first step came on 2 December 1942. Beneath the stands of the University of Chicago's football field, in a converted squash court, Enrico Fermi's team had built a pile of uranium and graphite blocks about twenty feet tall. At 3:22 in the afternoon they drew out the control rods, and Chicago Pile-1 produced the world's first controlled nuclear chain reaction, one that kept itself going.

Nobody had prepared a speech. Instead the physicist Eugene Wigner brought out a bottle of Chianti he had bought in advance, and everyone sipped it in silence from paper cups. Then Arthur Compton phoned James Conant with the news in a code he made up on the spot: the Italian navigator had landed in the New World. The navigator was Enrico Fermi, an Italian like Columbus. Conant asked how the natives were, and Compton told him they were very friendly.

The bomb itself was tested before dawn on 16 July 1945, at a desert site the scientists called Trinity. The plutonium device, nicknamed the Gadget, was hoisted on a 100-foot steel tower, and when it went off at 5:29 in the morning, the blast vaporized the tower completely. General Thomas Farrell described a searing light many times brighter than the midday sun. The heat melted the desert sand at ground zero into chunks of radioactive green glass, which the scientists named trinitite.

Oppenheimer, who had directed the whole project, said afterwards that the sight brought to mind words from the Bhagavad Gita, the sacred Hindu poem, and he spoke them again on film in 1965: now he had become Death, the destroyer of worlds. Fermi, meanwhile, was doing science on the spot. As the blast wave swept by, he let scraps of torn paper fall from about six feet up and paced off how far the wind carried them, about two and a half metres. From that he estimated the bomb's explosive yield at roughly ten thousand tons of TNT, within a factor of two of the true figure of about nineteen thousand.

Weeks later two bombs fell on Japan, and they were built in two different ways. Little Boy, dropped on Hiroshima, was a gun-type weapon that shot a uranium slug down a barrel into a second piece. Fat Man, dropped on Nagasaki, used the design proven at Trinity: a shell of high explosives around its plutonium core went off all at once and crushed the core inward until it exploded.

the-automobile-and-the-internal-combusti.context_blurb:
The modern car was born in Germany in the 1880s, in the workshop of the engineer Karl Benz in Mannheim. His machine was small, slow and noisy, and many people doubted it would ever be useful, until his wife Bertha took it out on the road and showed the world what it could do.

Benz finished the machine in 1885. It ran on three wheels, with a single-cylinder, four-stroke gasoline engine at the back that gave just three-quarters of one horsepower, and it was designed from the start to move under its own power, rather than being a carriage with an engine strapped on. He named it the Benz Patent-Motorwagen, and on 29 January 1886 it won German patent number 37435, often called the birth certificate of the automobile.

One morning in August 1888, without a word to Karl, Bertha took the car and set off with her two teenage sons for her mother's home town, a drive of about 66 miles and the first long-distance car journey in history. Along the way the fuel line choked up, and she cleared it with her hat pin. She wrapped a frayed ignition wire with her garter, had a blacksmith mend the drive chain, had a cobbler nail leather onto the brakes, which made the first brake linings, and bought fuel at a pharmacy in Wiesloch, the first filling station in the world. Her trip proved to a doubting public that the car really worked.

the-aztec-empire-and-the-triple-alliance.context_blurb:
The empire the Spaniards called Aztec was really a partnership of three lake cities in the Valley of Mexico, led by Tenochtitlan, the island capital of the Mexica people. For less than a century it ruled much of central Mexico through war, tribute and fear, until Hernán Cortés and his allies brought it down.

For some 175 years the Mexica wandered, seeking the home that Huitzilopochtli, their god, had promised. In 1325, on a swampy islet, they saw his sign at last: an eagle perched on a cactus, a nopal. There they founded Tenochtitlan, and the scene still sits at the center of Mexico's flag. When Hernán Cortés's soldiers first saw the city in November 1519, its pale towers gleaming above the lake, the conquistador Bernal Díaz del Castillo thought of the enchantments in the tale of Amadís, and he recalled decades later that some of the men asked whether it was not all a dream. In the twin city of Tlatelolco stood a market that amazed Díaz with its goods and its good order. On a busy day up to 60,000 people came to trade there, paying with cacao beans and cotton cloaks instead of coins, while judges sat at hand to settle quarrels, as Cortés reported.

The empire's finest fighters were the Eagle and Jaguar Warriors, who went to war dressed as those fierce creatures. Aztec battle aimed to take captives rather than to kill, because the priests taught that the sun would die without human blood. A common-born man who took four enemy warriors alive was raised into these noble ranks.

Feeding an island city took ingenuity. Farmers built chinampas, plots about 2.5 metres wide and 30 long, raised from lake-bottom mud on frames of reed right in the shallow water of the lake, with willows rooted at their edges to anchor them; some 12,000 hectares of them ringed the city. At the heart of the city rose the Templo Mayor, some 60 metres tall, with two shrines on its summit: one painted red for Huitzilopochtli, god of war and the sun, and one painted blue for Tlaloc, god of rain.

The empire itself was born in 1428. Led by their ruler Itzcoatl and his adviser Tlacaelel, the Mexica joined the cities of Texcoco and Tlacopan to throw off the rule of Maxtla, the tyrant of Azcapotzalco, and the three cities swore to split the spoils and fight their future wars together. Historians call that pact the Triple Alliance, and it, not a single emperor, is what we mean by the Aztec Empire. The alliance ruled its conquests in an unusual way. It left each defeated city's own ruler in place and simply demanded tribute twice a year, and if the payments ever stopped, the armies came back. Officials called calpixque gathered tribute from 38 provinces, and the spoils were split two-fifths to Tenochtitlan, two-fifths to Texcoco and one-fifth to Tlacopan. Nezahualcoyotl, who ruled Texcoco from 1402 to 1472, was a warrior, an engineer who built a dike against the lake's salt water, a lawgiver and a builder of terraced gardens. Yet what keeps his name alive, and earned his portrait on the 100-peso note, is that he composed philosophical poems on life and death that still survive; Mexicans remember him as the Poet-King.

Tlacaelel, who counselled four kings one after another, never took the throne, yet tradition remembers him as the secret architect of the empire's might. He raised Huitzilopochtli above every other god and swelled human sacrifice far beyond anything before. Tradition also says he ordered the old painted books of history burned, claiming they were full of lies, and had the Mexica past rewritten to make his people a chosen nation. Sacrifice was carved into the temple itself. At the foot of one stairway lay a round stone about 3.25 metres across, carved with the moon goddess Coyolxauhqui, dismembered by her brother the war god, and captives killed above were flung down the steps onto it. On 21 February 1978, electric-company workers digging in a Mexico City street struck the stone by accident, and their find led archaeologists to dig out the entire temple. Spanish chroniclers wrote of skull racks holding 130,000 heads, numbers historians treat as exaggerations. But since 2015 archaeologists have dug out a real tower of skulls, the Huey Tzompantli, with more than 600 of them, and the tests overturned an old assumption: the dead were not only captured warriors but women and children as well.

the-aztec-empire-tenochtitlan.context_blurb:
Tenochtitlan, the capital of the Aztecs, stood on an island in Lake Texcoco in the Valley of Mexico. The wandering Mexica founded it in 1325, and within two centuries it was one of the biggest cities on Earth, a place of canals, causeways, temples and gardens that left the first Spaniards who saw it lost for words.

The Mexica had searched the valley for years for a home. Their war god Huitzilopochtli had promised a sign to mark the spot: an eagle perched on a cactus, the prickly pear. The sign appeared on a little island, and there they built their city, and the eagle on its cactus is the emblem at the heart of the Mexican flag today. They fed the city from chinampas, long garden beds that farmers heaped up from the shallow lakebed out of mud, reeds and decaying plants, and farmers paddled their canoes along the narrow canals between them. Astonishingly, the gardens are still alive: at Xochimilco in Mexico City, now a World Heritage Site, farmers still work the plots and canoes still glide along the canals between them.

By the early 1500s, somewhere between 200,000 and 400,000 people lived in Tenochtitlan, about five times as many as in the London of Henry VIII. Three stone causeways, which doubled as dikes, crossed the water to the mainland, and each was broken by gaps spanned with wooden bridges that defenders could lift out and take away, leaving an attacking army stranded at the edge. At the center rose the Templo Mayor, a stepped double pyramid crowned not with one shrine but with two, side by side: one for the war god Huitzilopochtli and one for the rain god Tlaloc, the war that built the empire beside the rain that fed it.

The city's very name tells its founding story. In the Mexica language, Nahuatl, Tenochtitlan joins tetl, rock, to nochtli, the prickly-pear cactus, with an ending that means place, so it names the place where the prickly-pear cactus grows on a rock. In November 1519 Hernán Cortés led his Spaniards over the pass between two volcanoes, and the city appeared below them, its white towers rising out of the lake. Bernal Díaz del Castillo, one of the soldiers, compared it to an enchanted vision from the romance of Amadís, and he wrote that some of the veterans wondered aloud whether it was all a dream.

The chinampas were astonishingly productive. An ordinary field yielded a single crop of grain each year, two in a good season, but the lake gardens, anchored by willows whose roots gripped the soil and watered constantly by the canals, could give up to seven harvests a year. The markets matched the farms. In a letter to King Charles V in 1520, Cortés described the great market of Tlatelolco, in the twin city beside the capital, as twice the size of the market of Salamanca, with more than sixty thousand people trading there every day. Moctezuma, the emperor, had his own zoo, and his aviary of ten rooms held pools of fresh and of salt water for quetzals, macaws and eagles, along with jaguars, pumas and snakes. Some three hundred keepers saw to it that every creature got its proper food.

Nobody could drink the salty water of Lake Texcoco, so fresh water came to the city along an aqueduct from the springs of Chapultepec hill, a few miles west. The engineers built it as two terracotta channels side by side, each more than four kilometres long, so that one could be shut off and scrubbed clean while the other kept the drinking water flowing. The same lake threatened floods, and to keep its brackish water away from the fresh water around the city, a dike some 12 to 16 kilometres long was finished around 1453. Its designer was the neighbouring king Nezahualcoyotl of Texcoco, remembered as much as a celebrated poet as for his engineering.

the-aztec-sun-stone-calendar-stone.context_blurb:
The Aztec Sun Stone is a giant disk carved from a single block of basalt that weighs about 24 tons and measures nearly twelve feet across. After the Spanish conquest it spent centuries underground beneath Mexico City, until it came to light again in 1790. Today it is the most famous single work of Aztec art.

At the center glares a snarling face that most scholars identify as Tonatiuh, the sun. Where its tongue should be, a stone sacrificial knife juts from its open mouth, and on each side of the face a clawed hand grips a human heart.

The carving also tells the Aztec story of time. In Aztec belief, the world had been made and destroyed four times already, its earlier ages ended by devouring monsters, hurricanes, a rain of fire and a great flood. Their own age was the Fifth Sun, marked on the stone by the sign Nahui Ollin, 4-Movement, and they believed it too would end, torn apart by earthquakes.

the-bantu-migrations.context_blurb:
Over some two thousand years, Bantu-speaking farmers spread out across half of Africa, from the forests of Cameroon to the far south of the continent. Today their descendants speak about 500 related languages, and the story of how they travelled has been pieced together from crops, rubbish pits and, above all, words.

The family takes its name from its own word for human beings. In these languages the root -ntu means a person: umuntu is one person, and with the plural prefix ba- the word abantu, or Bantu, means people.

When Bantu farmers reached the far south, they met Khoisan peoples who spoke with clicking sounds, and they borrowed the clicks into their own speech. That is why Zulu and Xhosa, alone among the Bantu languages, are full of clicks. Xhosa wears one right at the front of its own name: the Xh that opens the word is itself a click.

Even the great forest crop of the Bantu, the banana, came from far away, from Southeast Asia. At Nkang in Cameroon, archaeologists found tiny plant-stones called phytoliths in ancient rubbish pits, proof that bananas were growing in central Africa about 2,500 years ago, far earlier than anyone expected. The find hints at contact across the Indian Ocean long before written records.

Scholars mapped the whole migration without digging up a single traveller's skeleton. Instead they compared the living Bantu languages pair by pair, counting how many words each pair still shares, a method called lexicostatistics. The more words two languages share, the more recently their speakers parted, so the words themselves reveal which peoples parted from which, and when.

the-barbarian-invasions-and-the-sack-of-.context_blurb:
In the fourth and fifth centuries, the western Roman Empire was battered by Germanic peoples on the move and by the Huns of the steppe. Rome itself, untouched by a foreign army for some eight hundred years, fell to the Visigoths in 410 and to the Vandals in 455, and the shock echoed across the Christian world.

The trouble began on the Danube in 376. Fleeing the Huns, tens of thousands of Goths under Fritigern begged the emperor Valens for refuge inside the empire. Starving in their camps, they fell prey to two Roman officers, Lupicinus and Maximus, who traded them dog meat at the price of one Gothic child per dog, sold into slavery. The outraged Goths rose in revolt, and in 378 at Adrianople they destroyed the eastern Roman field army and killed Valens himself. Rome's own cruelty had made them its enemies.

Late on 24 August 410, Alaric's Visigoths broke into Rome and looted it for three days, the first time a foreign enemy had taken the city since the Gauls nearly eight centuries before. Yet for its age the sack was oddly merciful. Alaric, an Arian Christian, ordered his men to spare the churches and everyone who fled inside them, and those who took refuge in the basilicas of St Peter and St Paul came out unharmed. The news stunned Christians who had believed Rome eternal. Around 413 Augustine, the bishop of Hippo, began his great answer to the pagans who blamed Christianity for the fall. He called it The City of God: every earthly city, even Rome, is mortal, he argued, but the city of God endures.

Then came the Huns. Their warlord Attila led his horsemen out of the steppes and ravaged the empire from the Balkans to northern Italy, and terrified Christians took his rampage for a punishment from Heaven. They called him Flagellum Dei, the Scourge of God, and the name has clung to him ever since.

In 455 Rome fell again, this time to Genseric, king of the Vandals. Every earlier conqueror had marched down through Italy, but Genseric ruled from Carthage in North Africa, and he shipped his whole army across the open Mediterranean and put it ashore where the Tiber meets the sea. Pope Leo I went out to plead with him, and Genseric agreed to spare the people if the gates opened without a fight; then he looted the city at leisure for two weeks, even stripping the gilded bronze tiles from the roof of the Temple of Jupiter.

The Vandals' name outlived them. In 1794 Henri Grégoire, a French bishop, watched revolutionaries smash works of art during the French Revolution and coined the word vandalisme to shame them by comparison with the Vandals. So a fifth-century people became a modern insult.

the-believing-scientists-of-the-revoluti.context_blurb:
Many people picture the Scientific Revolution of the 1600s as science breaking free of religion. Its leaders tell a different story. Johannes Kepler, Blaise Pascal, Robert Boyle and Isaac Newton remade our picture of the planets, numbers, matter and motion, and each was a man of deep faith who saw his science as a way of reading the mind of God.

Kepler had trained to become a Lutheran pastor and turned to astronomy only because a teacher steered him toward mathematics. He believed he was not inventing the laws of the planets but tracing patterns already laid down, and he prayed that in his work he was thinking God's thoughts after Him. Pascal, in France, showed his genius as a teenager. Watching his father toil night after night over tax accounts, the young Pascal designed a calculating machine of brass gears and dials, later called the Pascaline, that could add up sums by itself. Newton, the father of modern physics, hid a second life of the mind. The economist John Maynard Keynes acquired a trunk of Newton's private papers in 1936, expecting mathematics, and found pages on church history, on the prophecies of the Bible and on dating ancient events. Newton, Keynes decided, was not the first scientist of the age of reason but the last of the magicians, who read stars and Scripture alike as one great puzzle left by God.

Pascal's deepest secret came out only after his death in 1662. A servant noticed something stiff hidden in the lining of his coat: a folded sheet of parchment. For eight years Pascal had carried it, sewing it into each new coat himself, and it recorded a night when he met God. Across the top, in capital letters, stood a single word: FIRE.

Kepler's faith was tested at home. When his mother, Katharina, was accused of witchcraft, he set his work aside to defend her, and she spent more than a year chained in a cell, facing the stake. In a written defence he dismantled the accusations point by point with careful medical reasoning, showing that the supposed curses were ordinary illnesses, and in 1621 she went free. Boyle, the chemist behind Boyle's Law, brought the same demand for evidence to his Bible. He taught himself Hebrew, Greek, Syriac and Aramaic, the original tongues of Scripture, so that no translator could fool him about what it said. In his will he paid for a yearly series of public lectures in London to defend Christianity against unbelievers, and the Boyle Lectures still go on after more than three hundred years. He set one strict rule: the speakers must never argue about quarrels among Christians themselves, because he wanted the talks aimed outward, at doubters. Pascal, meanwhile, wrote that a human being is a thinking reed, the frailest thing in nature, which a puff of wind can kill. Yet, he argued, a man crushed by the whole universe would be the nobler of the two, because he knows he is dying, while the universe knows nothing of what it does.

When the Royal Society tried to make Boyle its president in 1680, the highest honour in English science, he turned it down because the office required an oath, and his conscience would not let him swear one. Newton had privately rejected the Trinity, believing later hands had tampered with the Bible to slip it in, yet Cambridge required professors like him to be ordained in a church that taught it. Unwilling to take holy orders in a faith he doubted, in 1675 he quietly obtained a royal exemption, signed by Charles II, that freed the holder of his chair from the rule.

The famous core of the Memorial hails the God of that night as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and then, sharply, not the God of the philosophers and of the learned. One of the sharpest reasoners alive was insisting that he had met a living person, not a theorem proved on paper. Boyle, Newton and Kepler looked out at a cosmos so orderly that its motions could be predicted years ahead. To them, nature obeying exact laws was the handwriting of a lawgiver who had designed it, and the strongest evidence for Him, since laws imply a lawgiver. Boyle paid for printing Bibles, Newton wrote more about God than about physics, and to Kepler geometry was the mind of God.

the-bering-land-bridge-and-peopling-of-t.context_blurb:
Nobody knows exactly when or how the first people reached the Americas. The old Clovis First timeline held that they came late, walking down an inland corridor between the great ice sheets of North America. Two remarkable finds, one in New Mexico and one in Chile, have pushed the story much further back, and the question is still open and hotly debated.

In the gypsum flats of White Sands, New Mexico, scientists have found human footprints dated to 21,000 to 23,000 years ago, among the oldest traces of people anywhere in the Americas. One trackway there freezes a hunt: a lone human crept up behind a giant ground sloth as big as a car, and the prints show the moment the cornered beast reared up on its hind legs and spun round to face its hunter. Another set shows an adult carrying a toddler back and forth across the mudflat.

Far to the south, at Monte Verde in Chile, the archaeologist Tom Dillehay excavated a bog and found a camp about 14,500 years old, so well preserved in the waterlogged ground that wooden tent frames and scraps of animal hide had survived. The bog had even kept the print of a child's foot, pressed into the clay, and that tiny trace shattered the Clovis First timeline. Monte Verde lies near the southern end of South America, yet people were living there before the inland corridor between the ice sheets could even be crossed, so they cannot have come that way. Many scientists now look instead to a coastal route, the kelp highway.

the-berlin-wall-goes-up-1961.context_blurb:
After the Second World War, Berlin lay deep inside communist East Germany, split between a free western half and a Soviet-run eastern half. Millions of East Germans used the open city as their door to the West, so in August 1961 the regime of Walter Ulbricht slammed it shut. For twenty-eight years the Berlin Wall divided families and killed people who tried to cross.

In the early hours of Sunday, 13 August 1961, while Berliners slept, East German soldiers tore up streets and strung about 43 kilometres of barbed wire through the middle of the city. Germans still call that day Stacheldrahtsonntag, Barbed Wire Sunday. Two days later a 19-year-old border guard, Conrad Schumann, was posted beside a low coil of the wire. He threw down his submachine gun and jumped it into West Berlin, and Peter Leibing's photograph of him in mid-air, Leap into Freedom, became the defining image of the Wall's first days. On Bernauer Strasse the border ran along the house fronts: the apartments stood in the East, but stepping out of the front door put you on a Western pavement. When the East sealed the doors, people escaped by climbing out of their upper-floor windows, knotting bedsheets into ropes or jumping into nets held open by West Berlin firemen while East German police tried to drag them back. Below ground, a few of West Berlin's subway lines still passed under the East. The East sealed those stations with bricks and stationed sentries on the dim platforms, and Western trains crept through without stopping. Berliners called these sealed and guarded stops Geisterbahnhöfe, ghost stations.

The Wall existed to stop people leaving. Before 1961 about 3.5 million East Germans, roughly one in five of the population, had fled to the West, some 2,400 of them on 12 August alone, the most ever in a single day. Two months earlier, at a press conference in June 1961, Walter Ulbricht, who led East Germany, had flatly denied any such plan, insisting that nobody intended to build a wall; he was the first official even to say the word. The sealing of the border was a secret operation, code-named Rose. All that first night armed soldiers stood over every stretch, and their loaded guns were aimed at the work crews putting up the barrier, so the workers themselves could not flee. The builders of the Wall were prisoners too. On Bernauer Strasse, on 22 August, 58-year-old Ida Siekmann threw her bedding out of her window and jumped before the firefighters below had opened their rescue sheet beneath her. She died on the way to hospital, the day before her 59th birthday, the first person to die at the Wall. Others went under it. In October 1964, after five months of digging, West Berlin students finished a tunnel 145 metres long and 12 metres deep, from a bakery cellar in the West to an outhouse in the East, and 57 people crawled through it to freedom, the biggest escape in the Wall's history. It is remembered as Tunnel 57.

The Wall killed in plain sight. On 17 August 1962, an 18-year-old bricklayer named Peter Fechter made a run for the Wall near Checkpoint Charlie. East German guards fired 35 shots, and he fell back wounded into the death strip, where he lay screaming for about fifty minutes; the Eastern guards left him there, and all that Western police could do was throw bandages over. As he bled to death, the crowd on the Western side screamed Mörder, Murderers, at the guards again and again. The regime never called its Wall a prison. Officially it was the Anti-Fascist Protection Rampart, built to keep Western fascists out, yet every watchtower gun, floodlight and guard dog along the death strip faced inward, toward East Germany's own citizens. A government that points its guns at its own people has confessed what its wall is for. In June 1963 President John F. Kennedy faced an enormous West Berlin crowd. Democracy was not perfect, he said, but free nations had never had to build a wall to keep their people in, and he finished in German with Ich bin ein Berliner, I am a Berliner, which the crowd roared back.

the-bhagavad-gita-s-battlefield-dilemma.context_blurb:
The Bhagavad Gita is one of the best-loved scriptures of Hinduism. It opens on a battlefield in ancient India, moments before a war between two branches of one royal family, and it is told as a conversation between the warrior Arjuna and his charioteer, Krishna. The question Arjuna asks there, what a good man owes his duty when duty means killing, has echoed for centuries.

Arjuna asks Krishna to drive their chariot out between the two armies. Facing him he finds the men he loves: Bhishma, his grandfather; Drona, who taught him; his cousins and their sons. His limbs give way, and his bow Gandiva slips from his hand. He tells Krishna it would be a sin to kill his own kin and teachers for the sake of a kingdom, and he will not fight. His collapse is moral, not cowardly, and the Gita's first chapter is even named for his despair.

Krishna's reply is the Gita's most-quoted teaching, nishkama karma, selfless action. A person has a right to do his duty, Krishna says, but no claim on its fruits: do the duty, and surrender all attachment to how it turns out. Many centuries later Gandhi called the Gita his mother and built his nonviolent movement on acting from duty without clinging to results.

the-big-three-yalta-and-potsdam.context_blurb:
In 1945, with the Second World War nearly over, the leaders of the three great Allied powers met twice to decide the shape of the peace: at the Black Sea resort of Yalta in February, and at Potsdam near Berlin that summer. Their bargains finished off one tyranny, Nazi Germany, and handed half of Europe to another, Stalin's.

The press called them the Big Three: Franklin Roosevelt of the United States, Winston Churchill of Britain and Joseph Stalin of the Soviet Union. Churchill loved the secret code name for the Yalta summit, Argonaut, which winked at the Greek myth of Jason and his Argonauts sailing the Argo to the Black Sea coast to win the Golden Fleece; Yalta, too, lay on the Black Sea.

Stalin lodged Roosevelt's party in the Livadia, the fifty-room summer palace of the old tsars. Worn out by the long journey, the president looked round at the marble splendour and joked that it offered every comfort of home. At Yalta, Stalin agreed to turn on Japan once Germany had been beaten for three months, and he named his price: Japanese-held South Sakhalin, the Kuril Islands and the naval base at Port Arthur. He kept the bargain almost to the day, and Russia still holds South Sakhalin and the Kurils, in a quarrel with Japan that has never been settled.

Roosevelt, the youngest of the three, looked ghastly at Yalta, hollow-eyed and some thirty pounds underweight, and Churchill's doctor, Lord Moran, privately gave him only a few months. Moran was right: Roosevelt died of a stroke at Warm Springs, Georgia, on 12 April 1945, about two months later and less than a month before Germany surrendered. So when the leaders met again at Potsdam in July, Harry Truman sat in Roosevelt's chair. Then, partway through, Churchill vanished from the table too: British voters had turned him out in a general election, and on 26 July the new prime minister, Clement Attlee, took his place.

No question at Yalta caused more argument than Poland. Britain had declared war in 1939 for Poland's sake, but Stalin's Red Army already held the whole country, and the West had little leverage left. Poland's new eastern border followed the Curzon Line and cost it about 48 percent of its prewar land, roughly half the country. At Potsdam, Truman took Stalin aside and mentioned, as if in passing, that the United States now had a mighty new weapon. Stalin barely reacted and said only that he hoped they would make good use of it against Japan, because Soviet spies had already told him about the atomic bomb. That same day, reportedly, he ordered his own bomb program speeded up. Poland's betrayal ran to the end. The Poles had fielded the Allies' fourth-largest army; their airmen fought over Britain in 1940, and more than 900 Poles died taking Monte Cassino. Yet at London's great Victory Parade in 1946, Britain, unwilling to anger Stalin, left the Polish forces out entirely.

The bargaining had started months before Yalta. At a meeting in Moscow in 1944, Churchill jotted on a half-sheet of paper how the Balkans would be shared, ninety percent Soviet here, ninety percent British there, and Stalin ticked it with his blue pencil. Churchill, calling it a naughty document that might look cynical, suggested they burn it, but Stalin told him no, he should keep it. At Yalta, Stalin also promised free and unfettered elections in Poland. When his foreign minister Molotov fretted that the wording might tie their hands, Stalin told him never to mind; they would do it their own way later. Moscow installed a communist government instead, and Poles waited until 1989, forty-four years, for a truly free election. Another clause at Yalta required Britain and America to return to Stalin every Soviet refugee they held, even people who rioted or hurt themselves rather than go. British and American troops used rifle butts and bayonets on those who refused, and many who went back faced a firing squad or the gulag. The writer Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn called this hushed-up affair the last secret of the Second World War. Finally, at Potsdam the Big Three shifted Poland's border some 200 kilometres west, to the Oder and Neisse rivers, onto land that had been German. Some 12 million Germans lost homes their families had owned for generations, one of the largest forced migrations in history, and the official agreement asked only that the transfer be orderly and humane.

the-black-death-1347-1351.context_blurb:
Between 1347 and 1351 a plague swept Europe from Sicily to Norway and killed people faster than they could be buried. Nobody then knew its cause. Modern science has traced its germ, its path and its true toll, and has knocked down some famous myths along the way.

It reached Western Europe in October 1347, when twelve Genoese trading galleys, home from the Crimea, put into the harbour of Messina in Sicily. Their sailors were already dead or dying of plague, and the horrified townsfolk drove the ships back out to sea, but too late: within weeks the disease was all over the island. In four years it killed between a third and a half of all Europeans, emptying whole villages and taking priests, doctors and gravediggers with everyone else; the historian Ole Benedictow argues the true share was nearer 60 percent. Victims found agonising lumps rising in the armpit, neck or groin, swollen lymph nodes that could grow to the size of an apple. Such a swelling is called a bubo, which is why this form of the disease is named bubonic plague. No one alive then called it the Black Death; that label is first found in English in 1755, centuries later. People in the 1300s spoke of the Great Pestilence or the Great Mortality.

The germ, Yersinia pestis, travelled in fleas riding on black rats. It clogged the flea's gut so that the insect could never fill its stomach, and every time it tried to feed, it vomited plague-laden blood straight back into the bite. In Florence in 1348 the writer Giovanni Boccaccio saw the dead tipped by the hundreds into huge trenches and packed in layers with earth between them, he wrote, like cargo stowed in a ship. In 1349 bands of flagellants, robed in white with red crosses, went from town to town, flogging themselves morning and evening and pleading with God to end the plague. They stayed in each town for thirty-three days and a half, a day for each year that Christ was said to have lived on Earth. Frightened Christians blamed the Jews, claiming they had poisoned the wells. On 14 February 1349 the townsmen of Strasbourg seized their Jewish neighbours, about two thousand people, and burned them alive in a wooden house, though the plague had not yet even reached the city; rumour and fear alone drove the massacre. Later, cities learned to defend themselves. In 1448 Venice made ships and travellers from infected places wait in isolation for quaranta giorni, forty days, before entering, and from that phrase comes our word quarantine.

How did the plague reach Europe? The notary Gabriele de' Mussi told a famous story. Khan Jani Beg's Mongols of the Golden Horde were besieging Caffa, a Genoese fort in the Crimea, when plague broke out in their camp, so they catapulted their own plague corpses over the walls into the city, and fleeing Genoese carried the disease home. Modern historians doubt the tale for a simple reason: records show that de' Mussi was never at Caffa but stayed home in Piacenza, Italy, the whole time. In 1348 Pope Clement VI condemned the murderers of Jews as seduced by the Devil and exposed the well-poisoning charge with one plain fact: Jews were dying of the plague just as Christians were, so they could hardly be its cause. With so many workers dead, the survivors could demand far higher wages, and the lords took fright. In 1351 Edward III's Parliament passed the Statute of Labourers to freeze wages by law at their old, pre-plague levels. It largely failed, and the anger it stirred helped spark the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.

DNA has rewritten the beginning of the story. Skeletons in a Nestorian Christian cemetery at Kara-Djigach, near Lake Issyk-Kul in the Central Asian mountains of modern Kyrgyzstan, carry the plague germ, and their gravestones date to 1338 and 1339, long before it touched the Mediterranean. And many people believe the nursery rhyme Ring around the rosie hides a memory of the plague. Folklorists say it does not, and the proof is simple: the rhyme first turns up in print only in the late 1700s or the 1800s, centuries after the Black Death. The plague reading was invented in the mid-1900s, and the folklorist Steve Roud called it complete nonsense.

the-blitz.context_blurb:
In the autumn of 1940 Hitler turned his air force, the Luftwaffe, against the cities of Britain, beginning with London. The British called the long bombing the Blitz. Night after night ordinary people huddled in shelters while their streets burned, and their refusal to break became one of the great stories of the war.

It began on Saturday, 7 September 1940, remembered as Black Saturday, when some 348 bombers set the East End docks ablaze from Tower Bridge to Woolwich and killed about 430 people. They came back the next night and the next: London was bombed for 57 nights in a row. Many families did not go down into the Underground stations. They sheltered at home, in arched huts of corrugated steel sunk halfway into the back garden and heaped with earth, named after the minister Sir John Anderson: the Anderson shelter.

On 13 September a bomb struck Buckingham Palace while King George VI and Queen Elizabeth were at home. The poor dockland districts had suffered worst of all, and the queen said she was glad they had been bombed, because now she felt she could at last look the people of the East End in the face. On the night of 29 December 1940, incendiaries turned the old City of London into a sea of fire. From a rooftop the Daily Mail photographer Herbert Mason caught the dome of St Paul's Cathedral rising unharmed above the smoke and flames, and his photograph, St Paul's Survives, became a symbol of defiance. Volunteers of the St Paul's Watch had saved the church; one fire bomb burned through the lead of the dome but fell outward onto a gallery, where they put it out.

Coventry was hit on 14 November 1940. The raid left St Michael's Cathedral a burned-out shell, and no other English cathedral was destroyed in the war; so total was the ruin that the Germans coined a verb, koventrieren, for razing a city. In the ruins the cathedral's provost, Richard Howard, ordered two words cut into the wall behind the shattered altar: Father Forgive. He pointedly left out the word them, so that the prayer took in his own nation as well as the enemy. A stonemason bound two charred roof beams into a cross, and three medieval roof nails became the first Cross of Nails, a symbol of reconciliation around the world.

the-british-raj-in-india.context_blurb:
Britain ruled India until 1947, more than three hundred million people in what are now India, Pakistan and Bangladesh. Its rule brought railways, a single code of law and the end of some cruel customs. It also brought a great rebellion crushed by force and famines met with cold neglect.

Britain's most famous crown jewel is Indian. In 1849, when the East India Company conquered the Punjab, its eleven-year-old Sikh ruler, Duleep Singh, was made to hand over to Queen Victoria the Koh-i-Noor, a diamond whose Persian name means Mountain of Light. In 1852 it was cut down from 186 carats to 105.6, and by tradition it brings bad luck to any man who wears it, so only Britain's queens have worn it.

The British also wired the land together. On 16 April 1853 India's first passenger train ran 21 miles from Bombay to Thane, with 400 riders in fourteen carriages, cheered along the way, behind three locomotives named Sahib, Sindh and Sultan. By 1900 the network had grown to nearly 25,000 miles, the fourth-largest in the world.

In 1857 much of India rose in revolt. The spark was a rumour about the new Enfield rifle, whose greased paper cartridge a soldier had to bite open: word spread that the grease was the fat of cows and pigs, the one sacred to Hindus and the other unclean to Muslims. No proof was ever found, but the fear that the British meant to break their faith was enough. On 29 March, on the parade ground at Barrackpore, the sepoy Mangal Pandey called on his comrades to rise, fired at a British officer and cut him with a sword. When troops moved in on him, he turned his long musket on his own chest and pulled the trigger with his foot. He survived the wound and was hanged on 8 April. The rebels rode on to Delhi, burst into the Red Fort and proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar, the frail old heir of the Mughal dynasty, emperor of all Hindustan. He accepted with regret, for Zafar was a celebrated poet who had never wanted a throne and wished to be a poet, not a king. When Delhi fell, Major William Hodson captured him and shot his sons, and the British exiled him to Rangoon, where he died in 1862. In Jhansi, Rani Lakshmibai, a widowed queen, would not give up her state, which the British had seized under the Doctrine of Lapse, a rule that took any state whose ruler died without a natural-born son. Vowing she would never surrender her Jhansi, she raised an army that included women and rode to war, and on 17 June 1858 she died fighting near Gwalior, sword in hand.

Britain governed this vast land with astonishingly few men. The Indian Civil Service never grew much beyond 1,200 British officers, and each district officer was at once judge, police chief and tax collector over an area as big as a small country. The service was nicknamed the steel frame, the skeleton on which the whole Raj rested. Some British rulers also took on cruel customs. Lord William Bentinck, the governor-general, banned sati across Bengal in 1829, the burning of widows on their husbands' funeral pyres, ordering that it stop absolutely and immediately, after years of campaigning by William Carey, a Baptist missionary, and Ram Mohan Roy, a Hindu reformer.

The Raj's darkest chapter was famine. The Great Famine of 1876 to 1878 killed about eight million Indians. In the middle of it the viceroy, Lord Lytton, staged a lavish week of celebrations in Delhi to proclaim Queen Victoria Empress of India, while his government shipped a record 320,000 tons of wheat to Britain. His relief wage for a whole day of heavy labour was a grain ration of about 1,600 calories, which the historian Mike Davis later compared to the ration at the Buchenwald concentration camp.

the-buddha-siddhartha-gautama.context_blurb:
Some twenty-five centuries ago, in the north of India, a prince of the Shakya clan named Siddhartha Gautama gave up his palace to discover why people suffer, and became the Buddha, the Awakened One. Buddhist tradition tells his life as a chain of vivid scenes, from his birth in a garden to the night he sat beneath a fig tree and woke up.

Tradition says Queen Maya gave birth to him beneath a tree in Lumbini's garden, and that she died only a few days later, so her sister Mahapajapati Gotami raised the boy. An old sage, Asita, left his mountain to visit the baby and saw on his body all thirty-two signs of a great man. Then the seer wept, not for the child but for himself: the boy would become a Buddha, and Asita, too old to wait, would die before he grew up to teach.

His father walled him inside luxurious palaces so that he would never know hardship. But at 29 the prince ventured beyond the walls and met, for the first time in his life, a man bent with age, a man wracked by disease and a dead body. His charioteer Channa told him that age, sickness and death come to every living being. Then came a fourth sight: a wandering holy man, calm and serene amid all that suffering, who filled the prince not with dread but with hope that there might be a way out. One night he slipped away on his white horse, Kanthaka, who carried him across the Anoma River to the forest's edge. There he cut off his hair with his sword, put on beggar's robes and sent his royal ornaments home with Channa. Tradition says the loyal horse's heart broke at the parting, and he died. For six years Siddhartha starved himself in the forests as a wandering ascetic. So little was left of him, the old account says, that when he touched his belly he could feel his spine. That near-starvation convinced him that tormenting the body was a dead end.

Neither palace luxury nor self-torture had brought him enlightenment. Then, the story goes, he heard a musician tuning a stringed instrument and saw his answer: wound too tight, the string snaps; too loose, it will not play; only tuned rightly does it make music. He called that balance the Middle Way. Sujata, a milkmaid, found him close to death and gave him a golden bowl of milk-rice, which brought back his strength. He set the empty bowl on a river and vowed that if he was destined to reach enlightenment that day, it should float upstream against the current; it did, before it sank. He sat down under a sacred fig tree to meditate, and the demon Mara attacked him with storm, flood and a demon army. When those failed, Mara sent his three daughters, named for three pulls on the human mind: Craving, Aversion and Desire.

At the climax Mara demanded to know who could witness that Siddhartha had earned enlightenment, and his demon host shouted that they bore witness for their master. Siddhartha had nobody to speak for him, so without a word he reached down and touched the ground, calling the earth itself to witness, and the earth shook in reply. That gesture is carved into countless statues of the Buddha. His awakening came that night in three stages: first he saw all his past lives; next, how karma drives the endless round of death and rebirth; and in the third and deepest watch, as the morning star rose, he grasped the Four Noble Truths, the truths about suffering and its end. He was about 35. The fig tree became the Bodhi tree, the tree of awakening. A cutting from it, which Emperor Ashoka sent to Sri Lanka in 288 BC, grew into the tree that still lives at Anuradhapura, the oldest planted tree on Earth with a known planting date.
