the-carolingian-renaissance.context_blurb:
In the late 700s and the 800s, Charlemagne, the great emperor of the Franks, and his advisers set out to pull western Europe out of a long slump in learning. They brought in scholars from Britain and elsewhere, spread a cleaner, easier handwriting and set monks across the empire copying ancient books by hand. Historians call it the Carolingian Renaissance.

Nearly everything we still have of ancient Rome's writing passed through the hands of monks, and the copying reached its peak under Charlemagne. Count every Latin book that survives from all the centuries before 800 and the total is under 2,000, yet the one century after 800 has left more than 7,000. That single boom is the main reason the ancient authors reach us at all.

Some survived by a thread. Take Lucretius, the Roman poet, and his great poem On the Nature of Things, which very nearly vanished. Every copy made in the Renaissance goes back to books that Carolingian monks copied in the 800s, and of those Carolingian copies just two still survive, nicknamed the Oblongus and the Quadratus.

the-caste-system-varnas.context_blurb:
For some three thousand years Indian society has been divided into hereditary groups whose members did particular work and married within their own group. The oldest scheme, named in the ancient Vedic scriptures, had four ranks, the varnas: priests, warriors, merchants and farmers, and laborers. Below them all were people treated as untouchable.

The Rig Veda, the oldest Hindu scripture, tells how the ranks were born. A cosmic giant, Purusha, was sacrificed, and from his body came the four varnas: the Brahmin priests from his mouth, the warriors from his arms, the Vaishya traders from his thighs and, from his feet, the Shudra laborers and servants. The order of the body mirrored the order of rank, from the mouth that speaks sacred words down to the feet that do the menial work.

Today varna is usually rendered as caste, but in the Rig Veda's Sanskrit it literally meant color, or outward appearance. What that color referred to is debated. Many scholars read it as symbolic, since each varna was linked with a color, and the old idea that caste began as a racial ranking by skin tone is largely a nineteenth-century colonial theory, now widely disputed.

The top three varnas shared a privilege that the Shudras were denied. Their boys received a sacred thread at an initiation ceremony and gained the right to learn the Vedas, a second, spiritual birth, so they were called dvija, the twice-born.

The old law codes enforced the lines brutally. The Laws of Manu kept the holy verses of the Vedas from the lower ranks, and the Gautama Dharmasutra, a code written after it, ordered molten lead poured into the ears of a Shudra who listened to them. Those laws still stung in the twentieth century. Ambedkar, a reformer born an untouchable who went on to draft much of independent India's constitution, held the Manusmriti, the Laws of Manu, more responsible than any other text for giving caste its scriptural backing. On Christmas Day 1927, in front of a crowd gathered at Mahad, he tore it up and burned it page by page. His protest grew out of a campaign to let untouchables drink from the public Chavdar Tank.

the-christianization-of-scandinavia-the-.context_blurb:
In the tenth and eleventh centuries the Scandinavian peoples, whose longships had terrorized Christian Europe, became Christian themselves, sometimes peacefully and sometimes by royal force. The old gods lived on in sagas and poems, but within a few generations the public sacrifices to them came to an end.

Iceland nearly tore itself apart over the new faith. In 1000 its parliament broke into hostile pagan and Christian camps, and to avoid war both sides agreed to accept the ruling of one man, the pagan lawspeaker Thorgeir Thorkelsson. Thorgeir spent a day and a night silent beneath a fur cloak, then rose and declared that the whole of Iceland would take the Christian faith. The pagans accepted it without bloodshed, and Thorgeir softened the blow: people could still worship the old gods in private and still eat horse meat.

The old religion had a grim side. Adam of Bremen wrote that at the great temple of Uppsala in Sweden the pagans held a nine-day feast once in nine years, killing nine males of each kind of creature. The bodies of the men, dogs and horses were hung together in the sacred grove beside the temple, and a Christian who had seen it told Adam he counted 72 corpses hanging there.

In Norway, King Olaf Tryggvason spread the faith by sermon and by sword. At Maerin, Snorri Sturluson's saga says, Olaf strode up to Thor's idol, gleaming with gold and silver, and with the ornamented staff he carried struck the god off his pedestal; his men then toppled all the other idols.

the-christmas-truce-of-1914.context_blurb:
At Christmas 1914, four months into the First World War, British and German soldiers in the trenches of Flanders laid down their rifles for a day. Without orders, and against their officers' wishes, the enemies met in no man's land. Nothing like it ever happened on the Western Front again.

It began on Christmas Eve, when the British saw small fir trees lit with candles along the German parapets and heard carols drifting across the mud. Private Oswald Tilley wrote that the British began O Come, All Ye Faithful and the enemy took it up immediately, singing the Latin version, Adeste Fideles, so both armies sang one hymn across the wire. Silent Night was sung that night too.

On Christmas morning the enemies left their trenches to shake hands in the open ground between the lines and trade presents: cigars, schnapps for rum, sausage for English corned beef, chocolate, badges and buttons. A British corporal, John Ferguson, said that in no time they were talking like old friends. The souvenir every British soldier wanted most was a German spiked helmet, the Pickelhaube.

the-civil-rights-movement-as-moral-victo.context_blurb:
In the 1950s and 1960s, black Americans and their allies fought to end legal segregation in the United States. They won not by tearing down the American system but by holding it to its own founding promise, that all men are created equal, with courage, nonviolent protest and the courts.

On 1 December 1955 in Montgomery, Alabama, Rosa Parks, a 42-year-old seamstress, refused to surrender her seat on a city bus to a white rider and was arrested. People later said her feet must have hurt; she answered that the only tired she was, was tired of giving in. Black citizens then refused to ride the buses, walking or sharing cars for 381 days. Yet the city never yielded on its own: the boycott ended in victory only when a federal court ruled Alabama's bus segregation laws unconstitutional and struck them down. On Bloody Sunday, 7 March 1965, John Lewis and Hosea Williams led some 600 marchers out of Selma, Alabama, across the Edmund Pettus Bridge, demanding the ballot. Alabama state troopers clubbed them back, and Lewis's skull was fractured. The televised brutality helped pass the Voting Rights Act of 1965. On 28 August 1963, at the great March on Washington, Martin Luther King told the crowd of his dream that his four children would one day live in a nation where people would look past the color of their skin and judge them by their character.

In May 1963, in Birmingham, Alabama, more than a thousand black children walked out in pairs from the city's 16th Street Baptist Church in the Children's Crusade. Birmingham's police boss, Bull Connor, turned attack dogs and high-pressure fire hoses on them, and the televised pictures shocked the world. That September, less than three weeks after King's speech, Ku Klux Klan members bombed the same church on a Sunday morning. The blast killed four girls getting ready for the service: Addie Mae Collins, Carole Robertson and Cynthia Wesley, all 14, and Denise McNair, 11. The battle went back decades. In 1896, in Plessy versus Ferguson, the Supreme Court had ruled 7 to 1 that segregation was lawful as long as the separate facilities were equal. Homer Plessy, counted as seven-eighths white under the race laws of his time, had deliberately taken a seat in a railroad car reserved for whites in New Orleans to challenge Louisiana's Separate Car Act, knowing he would be arrested.

The tide turned in 1954 with Brown versus Board of Education. The Court leaned on a test from the 1940s in which the psychologists Kenneth and Mamie Clark offered black children dolls that differed only in skin color. About two-thirds of the children chose the white doll, and many called the black doll bad, evidence that segregation taught black children they were inferior. Under Chief Justice Earl Warren, a unanimous Court ruled segregated schools inherently unequal and overturned Plessy. Thurgood Marshall, the lawyer who had argued for the children, later became the first black justice of the Supreme Court, in 1967. At the March on Washington, King described the nation's founding charters, the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution, as a promissory note, a promise to pay, signed to every American. America, he said, had given its black citizens a bad check, one that came back marked insufficient funds, but he refused to believe the bank of justice was bankrupt.

The movement stood in a long line. In Rochester, New York, on 5 July 1852, Frederick Douglass, who had escaped slavery, asked a Fourth of July audience what their holiday meant to the American slave. He praised the signers of the Declaration as brave men and pledged to honour their memory. His charge was not that the creed was wrong, but that America, by keeping slaves, was betraying the creed it was founded on. Even in 1896 one justice saw the same truth. John Marshall Harlan dissented alone from the Plessy ruling, writing that there was no caste here, because our Constitution is color-blind and neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens. His lonely dissent became the principle that the civil rights laws of 1964 and 1965 finally wrote into law.

the-closing-of-the-islamic-golden-age-al.context_blurb:
Abu Hamid al-Ghazali, a Persian scholar born around 1058 at Tus, became one of the most influential thinkers in the history of Islam. He attacked the Greek-minded philosophers of his faith and fused mysticism with orthodox theology. Some later writers blamed him for the end of the Islamic golden age of science; the record turns out to be more complicated.

Later Muslims honoured him with a towering title, Hujjat al-Islam, the Proof of Islam, and called him the renewer sent to revive the faith for his century. Teaching in Baghdad in the 1090s, he argued that nothing in nature acts by its own power: every event is God's own act, renewed at each instant. Point to a flame touching cotton, he said, and ask what sets it alight. Not the fire, which is only the occasion, but God, who burns the cotton directly every single time. Centuries later the philosopher David Hume would also doubt that we ever truly see a cause at work.

A century and a half after al-Ghazali, the golden age suffered its most famous blow. In 1258 Hulagu Khan, Genghis Khan's grandson, took Baghdad, and his Mongols seized the last Abbasid caliph, al-Musta'sim. They would not spill royal blood on the ground, so they rolled him up in a carpet and trampled him under their horses. Legend says they hurled so many books into the Tigris that the river ran black with ink; historians call that an exaggeration, since big libraries reopened within about two years, but the destruction of Baghdad's books was real.

Back at the height of his fame, around 1095, al-Ghazali held the grandest professorship in Islam, at the Nizamiyya college of Baghdad. Then, in front of a hall full of students, his throat closed and he found he could not speak a word. He lost his appetite, gave up his chair and left Baghdad to wander for more than ten years as a poor Sufi. When he came back to writing he produced his masterwork, the Ihya, or Revival of the Religious Sciences, which joined law, theology and mysticism in one vast whole. The later scholar al-Nawawi praised it extravagantly: if all the other books of Islam were lost, he said, the Ihya alone would be enough.

His fiercest work, The Incoherence of the Philosophers, savaged the Muslim thinkers who followed the Greeks. A century later the Spanish philosopher Averroes answered it passage by passage, and cheekily titled his reply The Incoherence of the Incoherence. Averroes lost the argument in the Islamic world, but the same book made him a giant in Christian Europe. Not all learning drowned in 1258, either. Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, a polymath who rode with the Mongols, rescued what manuscripts he could and took them to a new observatory that Hulagu built for him at Maragha in 1259, whose library is said to have grown to hundreds of thousands of volumes. And Neil deGrasse Tyson and other modern critics say al-Ghazali killed science in Islam by calling mathematics the devil's work. Researchers who checked his writings found no such line. He actually wrote that anyone who thinks Islam is defended by denying the mathematical sciences commits a great crime against religion.

In The Incoherence, al-Ghazali did more than disagree. He condemned three doctrines of Avicenna and al-Farabi as kufr, outright unbelief: that the world is eternal, that God knows only universals and not particular things, and that there is no bodily resurrection. Behind him stood an older quarrel. The rationalist Mu'tazila, who drew on Greek philosophy, taught that reason could discern good and evil unaided and that God had created the Qur'an. Their rivals, the Ash'aris, held that human reason must bow to revelation, and the Ash'ari view won and became Sunni orthodoxy. In law, too, historians describe a closing of the gate of ijtihad, the scholar's fresh reasoning on new problems. From about the eleventh century, teachers held that the four founding schools had settled the great questions and urged taqlid instead: following established precedent without reasoning things out for oneself. The reformer Muhammad Abduh later blamed that turn for leaving the Islamic world unable to adapt while Europe went through its Renaissance and Industrial Revolution.

the-colosseum-and-gladiator-games.context_blurb:
The Colosseum in Rome, begun by the emperor Vespasian around 72 CE on the drained site of Nero's private lake and opened by his son Titus in 80, was the greatest arena of the ancient world. Some 50,000 Romans packed its tiers to watch beasts hunted, criminals executed and gladiators fight, a show of engineering and cruelty together.

Its real name was the Flavian Amphitheatre. The nickname came from the Colossus, a bronze statue about a hundred feet tall that stood beside it, showing the emperor Nero remade as the sun god; the name Colosseum only truly stuck around the year 1000. On hot days sailors rigged a vast linen awning, the velarium, over the crowd on about 240 wooden masts. Its name comes from the Latin for sail, and handling a sail that size was sailors' work, so the crew came from the Roman war fleet at Misenum, near Naples. Where you sat showed who you were. The emperor and the senators had ringside seats, knights and citizens sat behind them, and the topmost tier, as far as possible from the sand, was crammed with the poor, slaves and women. A beaten gladiator did not simply beg. He raised a single finger to the editor, the official who sponsored the games, in a formal plea for release called ad digitum, and the editor, swayed by the roaring crowd, decided whether he lived.

Before tunnels were dug beneath the arena, its floor could be sealed and the ring flooded with aqueduct water. At the opening games of 80 CE, the historian Cassius Dio records, Titus staged a full sea battle with real ships, re-enacting an old fight between the Corcyreans and the Corinthians. Later the arena was built over the hypogeum, a warren of passages and cages on two levels. About 28 elevators, hauled by teams of enslaved men, could lift a caged lion or leopard up a shaft and pop it through one of some 32 trapdoors, so the beast seemed to appear out of nowhere in front of the crowd. Gladiators were paired by contrasting styles. The retiarius fought almost without armour, carrying a trident with three prongs and a weighted net, against the heavily armoured secutor, the chaser, whose smooth helmet gave the net nothing to snag on. A day at the arena ran to a grim timetable: beast hunts in the morning, the execution of condemned criminals at noon, and gladiator duels in the late afternoon. The morning and midday killings were deaths staged as a show, but most afternoon duels did not end in death, partly because a dead fighter could cost his sponsor up to fifty times the rental fee.

The poet Martial left the only surviving ringside report of one particular duel, between Priscus and Verus at the opening games. They were so evenly matched that the exhausted crowd begged for an end, and Titus declared both men winners and gave each the wooden sword that meant freedom. A gravestone in Sicily records the career of the gladiator Flamma, a secutor: 34 fights, 21 wins, 9 draws, and 4 lost bouts in which he was granted the crowd's mercy. The stone marks those four with one Latin word, missus, spared, four times; the popular tale that he turned down his freedom four times is a legend the stone does not support. Films show thumbs up to live and thumbs down to die, but Roman writers mention only a turned thumb and never say which way meant what. The familiar version comes from a Victorian oil painting, Jean-Léon Gérôme's Pollice Verso of 1872, and the classicist Anthony Corbeill has even argued that thumbs up may have meant kill. Nor does any ancient writer place the martyrdom of Christians, fed to lions, inside this arena. The real persecutor came earlier: Tacitus says Nero had Christians burned alive as human torches in his gardens in the 60s, more than a decade before the Colosseum opened. Even the famous greeting to Caesar from those about to die appears only once in Roman history, and not from gladiators. At a staged naval battle on Lake Fucinus in 52 CE, prisoners condemned to die in the battle shouted it to the emperor Claudius, who joked back, Or not, and they took it as a pardon and refused to fight.

the-columbian-exchange.context_blurb:
When Christopher Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492, he joined two halves of the world that had been apart for thousands of years. Plants, animals and germs began to flow both ways, and the swap changed what people ate, how they lived and how many of them survived, on every continent.

Before Columbus, the potato grew only in the high Andes of South America. Carried to Europe, the humble tuber fed its swelling towns, and historians credit it with perhaps 12 to 25 percent of all the population growth in Europe, Asia and Africa between 1700 and 1900.

Horses had vanished from the Americas some ten thousand years earlier, and Columbus shipped about two dozen across from Spain on his second voyage of 1493. From the Aztec court came chocolate. The emperor Montezuma II served Hernán Cortés a bitter, frothy brown drink in a gold cup, xocolatl; the Spanish stirred in sugar, took it home, and it became a craze among Europe's rich. The tomato had a harder welcome. For more than two centuries many Europeans called it the poison apple and kept it only as a garden ornament, and in 1597 the English herbalist John Gerard called the plant rank and stinking. Alfred Crosby, an American historian, named the whole two-way swap in his book of 1972: the Columbian Exchange.

The deadliest cargo was invisible. In 1520 smallpox, a disease the Aztecs had never known, swept through their capital, Tenochtitlan, killing about 40 percent of its roughly 200,000 people within a year, among them the new emperor, Cuitlahuac. An Aztec survivor remembered sores erupting from head to foot, and the epidemic did more than Spanish swords to bring the city down. Portuguese traders carried cassava, a starchy American root, to Africa in the 1500s, where it slowly crowded out older grains such as sorghum and millet; it still feeds more Africans than any other crop.

In Europe the tomato's bad name had a twist. Rich diners who ate it off pewter plates sometimes fell ill, while the poor, eating from wooden trenchers, stayed well. A chemist later found why: old pewter contained lead, and the sour juice leached it out, so the tomato took the blame for the plate. The chemist Joe Schwarcz notes the amount was probably too small to truly poison anyone. The exchange reached China too. In 1593 the Fujianese merchant Chen Zhenlong smuggled the sweet potato out of the Philippines, where the Spanish guarded it closely, by winding the living vines around a rope that ran along his ship's hull. Promoted as a famine crop for barren hillsides, it helped China's population nearly triple between 1500 and 1900. When Po'pay led the Pueblo peoples in driving the Spaniards from Santa Fe in 1680, thousands of their horses ran loose and drifted north. Within fifty years the Comanche had become the first nation of mounted bison hunters on the Plains, and their southern empire, Comancheria, grew rich on horses and bison. Disease may have crossed the other way too. A long-told account blames returning sailors for syphilis, which struck the army of France's King Charles VIII at the siege of Naples in 1494 and went on to kill as many as five million Europeans; historians still debate whether it truly came from the Americas.

The exchange's darkest result reshaped even the climate. Epidemics cut the native population of the Americas from about 60 million to some 6 million, by one 2019 estimate, and fields the size of France turned back into forest. A team under Alexander Koch calculated that the new forests drew down enough carbon dioxide to cool the globe around 1610, helping bring on the Little Ice Age, a long spell of bitter cold across the world.

the-columbian-exchange-and-indigenous-di.context_blurb:
The Columbian Exchange, the great trade in crops, animals and germs between the hemispheres that began with Columbus, enriched the diets of the whole world. For the native peoples of the Americas it also brought catastrophe: Old World diseases they had never met killed them by the millions and helped small Spanish forces topple great empires.

Chocolate began as xocolatl, a bitter Aztec drink of ground cacao. Cortés brought cacao back to Spain around 1528, and there cooks sweetened it with sugar, later adding vanilla, and turned it into a luxury. Horses had once roamed the Americas, then died out about ten thousand years before Columbus came. He shipped some 24 Andalusian horses on his voyage of 1493, Cortés brought them to Mexico in 1519, and Plains peoples such as the Comanche and the Sioux grew into superb horsemen.

In Europe the potato banished many old famines. Yet by the 1840s some four million Irish people, half the island, ate almost nothing else, and a grown man got through twelve to fourteen pounds of potatoes a day; that dependence set the stage for the Great Famine. The tomato, by contrast, was distrusted for centuries. Europeans grew it only as an ornament, and some whispered it was poisonous, before it became the base of countless Mediterranean sauces.

Why did the germs strike so hard? For millennia Europeans had shared their homes with cows, chickens and pigs, and so with the illnesses those animals breed, and they had built up some resistance. Native Americans had lived for some fifteen thousand years with almost none of those animals and had no defence. Historians argue that smallpox and the other diseases of the Old World, far more than Spanish weapons, explain how a few hundred soldiers could topple the Aztec and Inca empires. Hispaniola, where Columbus landed in 1492 and Europeans first settled, felt the full force first. Perhaps a million Taino lived there; by the middle of the 1500s only a few hundred were left.

In Mexico the Franciscan friar Motolinia wrote that the Aztecs died in heaps, like bedbugs. Entire families perished together, and since nobody remained to bury them, the survivors pulled their houses down on top of the dead, so that their homes became their tombs. The name for the whole swap is surprisingly recent. The historian Alfred Crosby invented the phrase Columbian Exchange in a book of that name in 1972, and he also coined virgin soil epidemic for an outbreak among people who have never met a disease and so have almost no defence.

Moctezuma's successor, Cuitlahuac, won what no other Aztec leader had: in a bloody battle by night he chased Cortés's Spaniards out of the capital. But smallpox, carried by one infected man in the expedition of Pánfilo de Narváez, had reached the city, and after just eighty days on the throne Cuitlahuac died of it. In the Inca empire the disease ran ahead of the conquerors, passing from one community to the next. Around 1527, some five years before Francisco Pizarro and his men arrived, smallpox killed Huayna Capac, the emperor, together with Ninan Cuyochi, the heir he had chosen. With no clear successor, his sons Huascar and Atahualpa, half-brothers, fell into a civil war that left the empire shattered when the Spanish came. In 1680 the Pueblo peoples revolted and expelled the Spaniards from New Mexico, who abandoned their herds as they fled. Some three to five thousand horses were set loose, and trading carried them north and east to peoples such as the Comanche, Sioux and Cheyenne. And one disease may have sailed the other way. Soon after Columbus's crews came home, a savage outbreak of syphilis struck the army of King Charles VIII of France at the siege of Naples in 1494, and historians still argue over whether his sailors carried it from the Americas or it was already lurking unrecognised in Europe.

the-computer-pioneers-babbage-lovelace-t.context_blurb:
The computer has two founding stories, a century apart. In Victorian England, Charles Babbage designed a mechanical calculating engine and Ada Lovelace saw what it might become. In the twentieth century Alan Turing turned the idea of a computer into mathematics, and then into machines that helped win a war.

Lovelace, born in 1815, was the daughter of the most famous poet in England, the wild Romantic Lord Byron, who walked out while she was still an infant; she never knew him. Her mother steered her hard toward mathematics, hoping to keep her from inheriting Byron's stormy temperament. In the 1830s and 1840s Babbage was designing his Analytical Engine, the first mechanical computer, and Lovelace became his brilliant collaborator. In an 1843 letter he begged her to forget the world and its troubles and called her the Enchantress of Number. Turing, a century later, was a serious marathon runner as well as a mathematician. In 1948 he trained for a place on Britain's Olympic team, and his best time was just 11 minutes or so behind the man who won the Olympic silver that year; an injury, not a lack of speed, kept him out.

Lovelace saw that the Engine could work with symbols of any kind, not only numbers, and she explained it with a picture from the textile mills. The Jacquard loom wove its patterns by following stiff cards punched with holes, and in the same way, she said, punched cards could tell Babbage's Engine how to handle symbols. Babbage had his own famous moment. Members of Parliament kept asking him whether the machine would still give right answers if it were fed wrong numbers. In his memoir of 1864 he wrote that he could not even understand the confusion of ideas behind such a question: a machine does only what it is told, so wrong figures in mean wrong answers out, an early form of the rule garbage in, garbage out.

In 1843 Lovelace added a series of notes, lettered A to G, to her translation of a lecture on the Engine. The last, Note G, set out step by step how the machine could calculate the Bernoulli numbers by itself, and it is honoured as the first computer program; while working it out she even caught a mistake in Babbage's own mathematics. During the Second World War, at the secret codebreaking centre of Bletchley Park, Turing designed the Bombe, an electromechanical machine that tested millions of rotor settings at speed to break the German Enigma cipher. The first went to work on 18 March 1940. It built on a Polish machine made by Marian Rejewski's team, who had broken into Enigma before the war, and breaking Enigma is thought to have shortened the war.

Turing's deepest idea came earlier. In his 1936 paper On Computable Numbers, he pictured a bare-bones device that moves along an endless tape, reading and writing symbols according to a table of rules, and he proved that one such machine could carry out any computation at all. That universal Turing machine is the founding idea of every general-purpose computer, which runs whatever program it is given. John von Neumann said the central concept of the modern computer came from Turing's paper. Lovelace herself had doubted that such an engine could ever truly think: it could originate nothing, she wrote, and could only follow the orders people gave it. When Turing asked in 1950 whether machines could be intelligent, he took her challenge seriously, named it the Lovelace objection and answered it in the paper that proposed his imitation game, now called the Turing Test.

the-constitution-separation-of-powers-ch.context_blurb:
In 1787 a convention in Philadelphia wrote the Constitution of the United States. Its authors had just won their freedom from a king in a long war, and they feared any one person or body holding all the power. So they divided the government and set each part to check the others, a design that has now lasted for well over two centuries.

They divided federal power three ways. Congress, under Article I, makes the laws; the President, under Article II, carries them out; and the courts, under Article III, judge them. A President who dislikes a bill may veto it, but Congress can still make it law, without his signature, if two-thirds of the House and two-thirds of the Senate pass it again, a bar so high that overrides are rare. George Washington used the veto sparingly, only twice in eight years. His first, on 5 April 1792, killed a bill dividing up seats in the House among the states, which he judged unconstitutional because it broke the rule of no more than one representative for every 30,000 people. Removing an official takes both chambers. The House impeaches, which means it formally accuses; the Senate then holds the trial and votes on whether to remove the official, and conviction needs two-thirds of the senators.

In 1868 the Senate tried President Andrew Johnson, impeached after his bitter fights with Congress over Reconstruction and charged with firing his Secretary of War, Edwin Stanton, in defiance of the Tenure of Office Act. The deciding vote fell to Senator Edmund Ross of Kansas, and in a silent chamber he said not guilty. Thirty-five senators voted to convict and nineteen to acquit, one vote short of two-thirds, so Johnson stayed in office. Since then the House has impeached two more presidents, Bill Clinton in 1998 and, twice, Donald Trump, and the Senate convicted none of the three, so not one was removed from office. Treaties need the Senate too: the President signs them, but they bind the nation only when the Senate approves them by a two-thirds vote. In 1919 and again in 1920 the Senate refused to approve Woodrow Wilson's Treaty of Versailles, keeping the United States out of the League of Nations.

The courts' great check came from Chief Justice John Marshall. In Marbury versus Madison, decided on 24 February 1803, he struck down an act of Congress as unconstitutional and so established judicial review, the courts' power to cancel laws that break the Constitution. It is the duty of the judges, he wrote, to say what the law is. Congress holds what many call the strongest check of all, the power of the purse. Article I forbids any money leaving the Treasury except under a law Congress passes, so Congress can cut off the money even for a war the President has ordered.

James Madison explained the logic in the fifty-first Federalist paper. Because people are flawed and grasping, ambition must be made to counteract ambition, with each branch's appetite for power set against the others; and if men were angels, he wrote, no government would be necessary. Strangely, the words judicial review appear nowhere in the Constitution. The Court claimed the power for itself in the Marbury case, and then used it so cautiously that it did not strike down another act of Congress for 54 years, until the Dred Scott case of 1857. The design has lasted. Scholars who studied all the national constitutions drafted since 1789 found that the median one lasts only about 19 years before it is scrapped. The American Constitution has never been replaced: it has run for more than 230 years, over ten times that span, with only 27 amendments.

the-counter-reformation-council-of-trent.context_blurb:
The Council of Trent was the Catholic Church's great answer to the Protestant Reformation. Meeting on and off in the mid-1500s at Trent, a mountain city in the north of Italy, the bishops restated Catholic teaching against Martin Luther, cleaned up real abuses in the Church and launched the movement called the Counter-Reformation.

In April 1546 the council named one Bible as the sole authentic scripture: the Latin Vulgate, which Saint Jerome had translated centuries earlier, and it ruled that only the Church could approve new translations. Its most genuine reform targeted real decay. Many priests were badly trained, and some bishops pocketed the income of dioceses they had never set foot in, so the council ordered every diocese to build a seminary where its priests would be trained, and it required bishops to live in their own dioceses.

The council's politics were stormy. In 1547 the pope's legates used a typhus scare to move the council south to Bologna, inside the Papal States, where Emperor Charles V had no sway. Charles, who wanted the council within his own reach, ordered his own bishops not to follow it to Bologna, and the sessions there produced no decrees.

Trent struck straight at Luther's teaching of salvation by faith alone, sola fide. Its decrees insisted that good works, alongside faith, keep a person's justice alive and make it grow, and decree after decree ended with one fearsome Latin word for anyone who denied it: anathema, meaning cursed and cut off. Protestants had smashed images; Catholic artists answered with the most theatrical art Europe had ever seen, the Baroque. Its showpiece is Gian Lorenzo Bernini's marble Ecstasy of Saint Teresa, carved between 1647 and 1652 for a church in Rome. It freezes the vision Teresa of Avila described, in which an angel drove a fiery golden spear into her heart, a pain she called so sweet she could not wish it gone.

the-crusades.context_blurb:
The Crusades were holy wars that Latin Christians waged from 1095 into the 1200s, at first to win Jerusalem and the Holy Land from Muslim rule. They mixed real devotion with greed and cruelty, and they ended with one crusading army sacking the richest Christian city on Earth.

In 1095 Pope Urban II urged Europe's knights to go east and win Jerusalem back. According to Robert the Monk, who chronicled the scene at the Council of Clermont, the crowd roared back three words, God wills it, Deus vult, and Urban answered that God had given them that cry to use in battle. A man who joined swore his vow in public and sewed a cloth cross onto his tunic and cloak, and from that cross came the very name: a crusader was one who had taken the cross.

The First Crusade took Jerusalem in 1099, and the crown was offered to Godfrey of Bouillon. He refused to be crowned king; a golden crown had no place, tradition says he answered, in the city where Christ had worn a crown of thorns. He took the humbler title Defender of the Holy Sepulchre. Around 1118 Hugues de Payns and eight companions formed a band of fighting monks to guard pilgrims on the dangerous roads to Jerusalem, sworn to poverty and chastity like monks, yet armoured and armed like knights. Based on the Temple Mount, they became the Knights Templar. A half-legendary story from 1212 tells of a French shepherd boy, Stephen of Cloyes, who led thousands of children south to Marseille, certain that God would split the sea open so that they could walk to the Holy Land, as Israel had crossed the Red Sea. The sea never parted, and by tradition many children were stranded or sold into slavery, though historians debate how much of the tale is true.

What drove the crusaders? Fulcher of Chartres, who marched with them, recorded the Pope's promise: any man who died on the road or fighting the enemy would have every one of his sins forgiven at once. The reward was forgiveness, not loot, and historians also point to the protection of pilgrims and Byzantium's plea for help after its defeat at Manzikert in 1071. When the crusaders stormed Jerusalem on 15 July 1099, they slaughtered its people. Raymond of Aguilers, who saw it, wrote that men rode through blood at the Temple of Solomon up to their knees and their horses' reins. Eighty-eight years later the tide turned. In July 1187 Saladin caught the crusader kingdom's whole army, waterless under a blazing sun, on the twin hills known as the Horns of Hattin, and fired the dry scrub around them so that smoke choked the parched knights. Then he crushed them and captured their holiest relic, a fragment of the True Cross.

The Fourth Crusade went most badly astray. Unable to pay Venice the 85,000 silver marks promised for their ships, the crusaders let the blind old Doge Enrico Dandolo, some ninety years of age, steer them first against Zara, a Catholic city, which they sacked. It was the first time a crusading army had attacked fellow Catholics, and Pope Innocent III briefly excommunicated the whole crusade. Then, in April 1204, they stormed and sacked Constantinople, Christendom's richest city. The Byzantine writer Niketas Choniates watched them wreck the church of Hagia Sophia, lead mules into its sanctuary to haul away the silver, and set a drunken prostitute on the patriarch's throne to sing and dance. Dandolo shipped home four horses of gilded bronze from Constantinople's Hippodrome, and they still crown the façade of St Mark's in Venice. Innocent, who had launched the crusade himself, wrote in fury that the crusaders, dripping with Christian blood, had spared neither age nor sex, and that the Greeks now, with reason, detested the Latins more than dogs.

the-cyrus-cylinder-and-early-imperial-to.context_blurb:
Cyrus the Great founded the Persian Empire, the largest the world had yet seen, and conquered Babylon. Unlike many conquerors before him, he let defeated peoples keep their gods and go home, and a small clay object buried in Babylon tells the story in his own words.

In 1879 Hormuzd Rassam dug a small barrel of baked clay out of the foundations of Esagila, the temple of the god Marduk in Babylon. About nine inches long, it carries some 45 lines of cuneiform recording the deeds of Cyrus, and it is called the Cyrus Cylinder.

On it Cyrus boasts that after taking Babylon he gathered up the peoples whom earlier kings had dragged off as captives and returned them to their own homes, and sent the seized statues of their gods back to their own temples. The Book of Ezra credits him with the same policy toward the exiled Jews, letting them go home to rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem, though the cylinder itself never names Jerusalem or the Jews.

The cylinder is often sold as the first declaration of human rights, a label the Shah of Iran promoted in 1971 when he gave a replica to the United Nations. Irving Finkel of the British Museum, who knows the object well, rejects that label: there were no human rights in antiquity, he says, and the cylinder is royal propaganda about restoring peace, not a charter of rights. Historians treat it as a real early experiment in imperial tolerance.

the-diet-of-worms.context_blurb:
In April 1521 the monk Martin Luther, whose attacks on the Church had set Germany alight, was summoned before the young Emperor Charles V at the imperial assembly, or diet, in the city of Worms. Commanded to recant what he had written, he refused, declaring that his conscience was bound by the Word of God.

Schoolbooks end his speech with a ringing claim that he stood there and could do nothing else, and a final prayer for God's help. Historians are more careful. The refusal on grounds of conscience is well documented, but those famous closing words were added later and are missing from the earliest records of what he said.

The emperor then declared Luther an outlaw whom anyone could kill without penalty. His protector, Frederick the Wise, staged a fake ambush and hid him in Wartburg Castle. There Luther let his beard grow and passed as Junker Jörg, a knight, Knight George. In his hiding place he translated the whole New Testament from Greek into German in about three months.

the-domesday-book-1086.context_blurb:
Twenty years after the Norman Conquest of 1066, William the Conqueror wanted to know exactly what his new kingdom held and what it owed him. In 1086 he sent officials into every corner of England to record who owned each estate, each field and each farm animal, the most thorough survey of its age.

The English gave the finished record a grim nickname. Just as no soul could appeal the verdict of the Last Judgement, Doomsday, no landholder could argue with what the survey said, and so it became the Domesday Book. Around 1179 the royal treasurer Richard FitzNeal explained the name in exactly those terms: from it, as from the Last Judgement, there was no further appeal.

The survey rested on sworn local testimony. In each district, sworn juries of local men vouched for each entry, and William made sure neither side could rig the record: every jury was made up half English, half Norman, so neither the conquered nor the conquerors could fix it alone.

the-dust-bowl.context_blurb:
In the 1930s the southern Great Plains of the United States dried up and blew away. Drought and wind lifted the bare topsoil into enormous black storms that buried farms, choked people and drove families off the land, and the disaster had been largely made by the plow.

The worst came on 14 April 1935. The morning dawned clear and blue over Oklahoma, and families headed outdoors. Then, at 2:49 in the afternoon, a black wall of dust some 500 to 600 feet high came racing down from the north at up to 60 miles an hour. Witnesses thought the world was ending, and people groped for the walls of their own homes. The day is remembered as Black Sunday. The Associated Press reporter Robert Geiger was caught in that storm, and in his story the next day he called the whole stricken region the Dust Bowl, a name that never left it.

The plow had set up the disaster. Before the settlers came, the native buffalo grass held the soil with roots up to five feet deep. Then, during the wheat boom of the First World War, gasoline tractors pulling disc plows let a single farmer break 50 acres of prairie in one day, where a horse team managed 3, and when the drought came, nothing anchored the dried topsoil.

Washington took notice. In the spring of 1935 Hugh Bennett, a soil scientist, was pleading with Congress for money to fight the storms, and he timed his testimony so that the sky outside the Capitol went dark with dust carried from the plains as he talked. A senator glanced up and remarked that it did look like dust. Soon afterward Congress passed the Soil Conservation Act, which set up the Soil Conservation Service as a permanent agency; in time it bought back over ten million acres to return to grass.

the-early-muslim-conquests.context_blurb:
After the Prophet Muhammad died in 632, Arab armies burst out of Arabia under the banner of the new faith of Islam. Within about a century they had built an empire that stretched from Spain on the Atlantic to the Indus River, some 13 million square kilometres, the largest the world had yet seen.

In April 711 a Berber general, Tariq ibn Ziyad, crossed from Africa into Spain with about 7,000 men and landed at the great rock that guards the strait. The Arabs called it Jabal Tariq, the Mountain of Tariq, and over the centuries the name wore down into Gibraltar.

Khalid ibn al-Walid, the Arabs' most famous general, is said never to have lost a battle. Legend says he won his title, Sayf Allah, the Sword of Allah, at the battle of Mu'tah, holding firm against the enemy so fiercely that eight swords shattered in his hands. At al-Qadisiyyah, in a battle that raged for four days in November 636, the Persians sent some 33 war elephants trampling into the Arab lines. The Muslim soldiers learned to blind the beasts and cut their trunks and girths, and the panicked elephants stampeded back through their own Persian ranks.

That victory won the Arabs the most sacred prize of the Sasanian Persian empire, the Derafsh-e Kaveyan, the jewelled battle banner of the Persian kings. Its great central jewel was cut up and the pieces sold in Medina. In 711, the same year Tariq landed in Spain, Muhammad bin Qasim, a young general, led an army through Makran at the empire's eastern end and conquered Sindh, on the Indus River at the edge of India. In a single year the conquests touched both the Atlantic and the Indus.

Why did the old empires give way so fast? Historians point to exhaustion. Byzantium and Sasanian Persia had bled each other white in a long war from 602 to 628, and both were spent when the Arabs struck.

the-economic-verdict-how-the-west-bankru.context_blurb:
The Cold War was a contest of economies as much as of armies, and by the 1980s the Soviet Union was losing it. Its central planners tried to run a whole nation's production from offices in Moscow, setting prices by decree instead of letting buyers and sellers set them, and the results were empty shelves and enormous waste.

In 1989 Boris Yeltsin, then a rising Soviet politician, dropped in unannounced at a Randall's grocery in Houston and spent twenty minutes walking past shelves stocked with some 30,000 everyday products. The plenty was so far beyond anything in the Soviet Union that he suspected the store had been specially staged to fool him. On the flight afterwards, his aide said, the last of Yeltsin's Bolshevism collapsed, and Yeltsin asked aloud what had been done to his people.

A famous Soviet parable shows the problem in miniature. A nail factory was given its quota by weight, so its managers met the plan perfectly by making one single gigantic nail, useless to anyone; when the planners switched the quota to the number of nails, the factory churned out millions of tiny worthless pins. Nikita Khrushchev himself grumbled that weight targets produced chandeliers so heavy they pulled the ceilings down.

In 1920 the economist Ludwig von Mises explained why. With no market in which factories and machines are bought and sold, nothing tells the planners what capital is really worth, so a state that owns everything cannot know whether it uses its resources well. The Soviet record bore him out: its price agency fixed some 24 million prices by hand, yet the yearly plan could balance only around 2,000 goods, and almost everything else ran on guesswork. Friedrich Hayek added the deeper objection that the knowledge of millions of changing local needs can never be gathered into one office.

the-eiffel-tower-and-the-1889-world-s-fa.context_blurb:
Gustave Eiffel's iron tower rose over Paris for the World's Fair of 1889. Many of the city's artists hated it, and it was supposed to stand for only twenty years, yet it outlived its critics and became the best-known symbol of Paris.

In 1887, before it was finished, Guy de Maupassant, Alexandre Dumas the younger and the architect of the Paris Opera, Charles Garnier, signed a protest in the newspaper Le Temps calling the tower useless and monstrous. A beloved legend says Maupassant afterwards lunched almost daily at the restaurant inside the tower, because it was the one place in Paris from which he could not see the tower he hated.

Nobody meant it to last. Eiffel's permit ran for twenty years, and Paris had the right to demolish it on 1 January 1910 and sell its iron for scrap. Eiffel saved it by making it useful, as a giant radio antenna. Wireless experiments began there in 1898, by 1908 its signals reached 3,700 miles, and in the First World War its station picked up a coded German message about an agent called H-21 that helped convict the spy Mata Hari.

the-electricity-pioneers-faraday-tesla-f.context_blurb:
Electricity went from a parlour curiosity to the power behind the modern world in about a century and a half. Benjamin Franklin showed that lightning was electric, Michael Faraday found how to make electricity move machines, and Nikola Tesla and Thomas Edison fought a bitter war over how to send it into every home.

In June 1752, during a thunderstorm outside Philadelphia, Franklin flew a silk kite into the storm clouds with a metal key hanging from its wet string, his son William beside him. When he brought his knuckle near the key, a spark leapt from the key to his knuckle, proof that the electricity in a storm cloud was the same as the spark in a laboratory. Franklin also gave electricity its everyday words. He swept away the awkward labels vitreous and resinous and named the two sorts of electric charge positive and negative, coined the word battery and invented the lightning rod. Faraday, a blacksmith's son born in 1791, got almost no schooling; at fourteen he went to work for a London bookbinder, and he taught himself science by reading the very books he bound, among them an encyclopedia's article on electricity. In 1821 his little homopolar motor became the first device to turn electric current into continuous motion: a wire whirling round and round a magnet, the ancestor of every electric motor. In the 1880s the War of the Currents broke out over how to wire America. Edison backed direct current; Tesla and his partner, the industrialist George Westinghouse, championed alternating current. AC won because transformers can step it up to high voltage and send it hundreds of miles, while Edison's DC faded out within about a mile.

In 1812 the young bookbinder heard the chemist Humphry Davy lecture at the Royal Institution, took careful notes and then used his own craft to catch Davy's eye: he bound the notes into a handsome volume of some 300 pages and sent it to him. In 1813 Davy hired him as a laboratory assistant. Tesla, a Serbian-born inventor, conceived the AC motor in a single flash in 1882 while strolling in a Budapest park and reciting Goethe's poetry to a friend. He had no paper, so he drew the design in the dirt with a stick. In 1899, in a laboratory high in Colorado Springs, Tesla set out to show that energy could travel wirelessly. His giant Tesla coil, as tall as a house, hurled bolts of man-made lightning up to 135 feet long, with a crash reportedly heard fifteen miles away.

Faraday's greatest find came in 1831. He wrapped two coils around an iron ring, one on each side, not touching, and switched the current in the first on and off; each time, a pulse of current leapt up in the second. He had discovered electromagnetic induction: a changing magnetic field creates an electric current, the principle behind every generator since. In 1895 the first great hydroelectric plant opened at Niagara Falls, and Tesla and Westinghouse's alternating current, made by the falling water, carried power 26 miles by copper wire to light the streets and homes of Buffalo. The rivalry turned ugly. The electric chair's first victim, William Kemmler, died on 6 August 1890 in a botched execution: one jolt did not finish him, and a second set his head smoking. Westinghouse, whose AC had been used in the chair to smear it, remarked bitterly that an axe would have done the job better.

Edison, who had once spoken out against the death penalty, fought dirty. To frighten the public away from alternating current, he staged gruesome travelling shows, electrocuting live animals in front of crowds, and he quietly helped develop the electric chair with an AC generator so that execution might be called being Westinghoused. Faraday, a devout member of a small Christian sect, the Sandemanians, turned down a knighthood and would not be buried in Westminster Abbey among kings and heroes. He wished to remain plain Mr Faraday to the end. Tesla's 1888 deal with Westinghouse paid him two and a half dollars per horsepower of AC the world would ever use, a contract that might have made him the first billionaire in history. When the company was close to ruin, Tesla reportedly tore the contract up to save it, trading a future fortune for loyalty.

the-emancipation-proclamation.context_blurb:
In the middle of the Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln turned the fight to save the Union into a fight to end slavery. His Emancipation Proclamation, signed on New Year's Day 1863, declared the enslaved people of the rebel states free, and it set in motion the end of slavery across the United States.

Its most quoted words declared that the enslaved in the rebel states were, from that day, thenceforward and forever free, words Lincoln chose to sound permanent, not provisional. Black Americans, free and enslaved, crowded into churches all over the country on the last night of 1862, many of them meeting in secret, and prayed as they waited for midnight, when the Proclamation would take effect. That vigil, Watch Night, also called Freedom's Eve, is still kept every New Year's Eve. In South Carolina, under the live oaks of Camp Saxton, an officer read the Proclamation aloud to a regiment of former slaves, the First South Carolina Volunteers. As the flag of the United States was handed to them, an old man began to sing in a cracked voice, two women joined him unbidden, and soon the whole crowd was singing My Country, 'Tis of Thee. Their colonel, Thomas Wentworth Higginson, wrote that it seemed the choked voice of a race at last unloosed. In faraway Texas the news came late. On 19 June 1865, two and a half years after the Proclamation took effect, General Gordon Granger of the Union army reached Galveston and proclaimed that all slaves were free. That day became Juneteenth, the oldest yearly holiday marking the end of slavery in America.

As he took up the pen, Lincoln told those present that he had never been surer he was right, and that if history remembered his name it would be for this, because his whole soul was in it. He signed, looked up and said simply that it would do. He had drafted the Proclamation months earlier, but Secretary of State William Seward warned that, issued after Union defeats, it would sound like the last shriek of retreat. So Lincoln waited for a victory, and it came at Antietam on 17 September 1862, the bloodiest single day in American history; five days later he announced the Proclamation. It also added something aimed at winning the war: freed Black men would be received into the armed service of the United States to garrison forts and man vessels. Nearly 200,000 Black soldiers and sailors went on to fight for the Union.

To his cabinet Lincoln confided that the timing also kept a private promise to God: he had solemnly vowed that once General Lee was driven back from Pennsylvania, he would crown the result with a declaration of freedom for the slaves. On the day itself a great crowd filled Boston's Tremont Temple, with runners going back and forth to the telegraph office. As midnight came and went without a word, Frederick Douglass said they were waiting as for a bolt from the sky that would rend the fetters of four million slaves, and when the word finally came, the hall burst into song. The signed original no longer exists. After the war it was given to a charity fair in Chicago to raise money for wounded soldiers, and it burned in the Great Chicago Fire of 1871; the copy in the National Archives is the neatly engrossed version Lincoln also signed.

No president could simply decree slavery away, so Lincoln grounded the act in his power as commander-in-chief and called it a war measure, fit and necessary for putting down the rebellion, tying it to military necessity. That limit meant that slaves in the loyal states, such as Kentucky and Maryland, stayed enslaved. Only an amendment to the Constitution could end slavery everywhere: the 13th, ratified on 6 December 1865.

the-english-longbow-crecy-agincourt.context_blurb:
During the Hundred Years War with France, the English longbow was the most feared weapon in Europe. At Crécy in 1346 and at Agincourt in 1415, common English archers cut down the flower of French knighthood, and the bows and skeletons raised from a sunken Tudor warship show what it took to draw one.

The war bow was a giant beside a sporting bow: cut from a single stave of yew, it stood about six feet tall, as tall as the man who drew it. Its arrows, about 30 inches long, were made to punch through a knight's mail and plate rather than slash flesh, and the bodkin point was the head built for that one job, a short, narrow, square-sectioned steel spike. Henry V took an outnumbered army into battle at Agincourt in October 1415, and it was built around common bowmen: some 5,000 longbowmen stood beside only about 1,000 men-at-arms, five archers for each man-at-arms. Every bowman drove a sharpened wooden stake into the mud before him, angled toward the enemy, so the line became a hedge of spikes that would impale a charging horse or make it shy away.

The yew stave worked like a natural spring. Bowyers kept the pale sapwood on the bow's back, where bending stretches the wood, because sapwood resists stretching, and the dark heartwood toward the archer, on the belly, because it resists being crushed. The bows raised from Henry VIII's warship the Mary Rose, which sank off Portsmouth in 1545, needed about 150 pounds of force to draw, some up to 185, three or four times the pull of a modern Olympic bow of 40 to 50 pounds. At Crécy in 1346 the French hired some 6,000 Genoese crossbowmen. A trained longbowman could loose 10 to 12 arrows a minute while a crossbowman was still winding his weapon, and the Genoese, caught without their big pavise shields, were outshot and fled, only to be ridden down by their own French knights. Rain had churned Agincourt's ploughed field into a bog, and French knights in full plate sank knee-deep as they advanced. Many who fell in the crush were trampled, suffocated or drowned in the mud before they could rise. A popular legend says the archers jeered at the defeated French with a two-fingered salute, waving the two fingers that French knights had sworn to chop from the hand of every archer they captured: the index finger and the middle finger. No medieval source records it; the chronicler Jean de Wavrin says the threat was to cut off three fingers, and the gesture story appears only in the 1970s.

Making an archer took a lifetime, so in 1363 Edward III commanded all fit Englishmen to shoot at the butts on holidays and outlawed games like football that drew them away. At Crécy, King John of Bohemia, fifty years old and blind, begged his knights to lead him forward so he could strike one blow with his sword. They tied all their horses' reins to his and rode into the fight together, and at dawn they were found dead in a circle, their horses still bound together. The 16-year-old Black Prince, Edward III's son, was hard pressed that day, and a messenger begged the king, watching from a windmill, to send help. Edward refused: he wanted the boy to win his spurs, and the honour of the day, himself. The Mary Rose skeletons show the price. Years of hauling a 150-pound bow, begun in childhood, left their mark on nearly one man in five aboard: the archers can be picked out by a left arm and shoulder overbuilt and twisted by the strain.

the-epic-of-gilgamesh.context_blurb:
The Epic of Gilgamesh, written in ancient Mesopotamia, is the oldest great story we still have, older than the Iliad or the Hebrew Bible. It tells of Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, of his wild friend Enkidu, and of his doomed search for a way to escape death.

Scribes first wrote it down almost four thousand years ago, the earliest Sumerian versions dating to about 2100 BC, by pressing a cut reed into soft clay tablets to make wedge-shaped marks, the script called cuneiform. The gods made a shaggy wild man, Enkidu, as Gilgamesh's equal. Before he ever saw a city, Enkidu lived far out in the wild among the animals, eating grass beside the gazelles and drinking at the waterhole with the beasts.

The poem opens by boasting of its hero, the strongest of kings and builder of Uruk's great walls: Gilgamesh is two-thirds divine and one-third mortal, the son of the goddess Ninsun and the priest-king Lugalbanda. When Enkidu came to Uruk, he blocked the king's path in a doorway, and the two giants crashed together and wrestled. Gilgamesh won, but Enkidu's strength so impressed him that the two became inseparable friends, and their friendship is the heart of the whole story.

Together they set out for the Cedar Forest and its monstrous guardian, Humbaba. The sun god Shamash sent thirteen great winds to pin the monster and blind him, and when the beaten Humbaba begged for mercy, the heroes cut off his head. Back in Uruk the goddess Ishtar demanded that Gilgamesh marry her. He refused and mocked her, and in a rage she sent the Bull of Heaven against the city. The heroes killed it, and as a final insult Enkidu tore off the bull's haunch and flung it up at Ishtar as she watched from the walls.

Then Enkidu died, and Gilgamesh could not accept it. For a week he mourned by the corpse and let no one bury his friend, until a maggot dropped from Enkidu's nose. Then he knew death was final, and terror of his own death sent him searching for immortality. His search led him to Utnapishtim, who had survived the great flood. A god told him to tear his house apart for timber and build a vessel, and it was no ordinary ship but a giant cube, 120 cubits on every side, with seven levels inside, which he filled with his family, craftsmen and animals. When the waters began to fall, he sent out three birds from the stranded boat. The dove came back, and so did the swallow, but the raven found the waters gone and never returned. At the very end, Gilgamesh won a thorny plant from the sea floor with the power to restore youth. He laid it aside while he bathed, and a snake slipped up and swallowed it; as the snake slid away it shed its skin, which, the storytellers said, is why snakes renew themselves, while Gilgamesh went home empty-handed.

The epic lay buried for two thousand years. In 1872 George Smith, a self-taught scholar at the British Museum, was fitting together a broken tablet from Nineveh when he found a flood story, with a ship grounded on a mountaintop and birds released to find land. He jumped to his feet and dashed around the room, even tearing at his clothes. The news stunned Victorian London, because the tale sounded so familiar: the hero warned by a god, the boat built to save his household and the beasts, the landing on a mountain, the birds sent out to find land. It closely matches Noah's Ark in the Book of Genesis, though the Mesopotamian version was written down centuries earlier. Most ancient stories are anonymous, but the standard Babylonian version, finished around 1200 BC, has a named author: the scribe-priest Sin-leqi-unninni, one of the few authors from antiquity whose name we still know.

the-exodus-and-the-birth-of-a-covenant-p.context_blurb:
The Book of Exodus tells how Moses led the Hebrew slaves out of Egypt, through the sea and the desert, to the edge of a promised land, and how at Mount Sinai they became a people bound to God by covenant. For three thousand years it has been the great story of liberation, retold by every people that longed to be free.

Moses and Aaron, his brother, faced Pharaoh with one demand from their God: let my people go, so that they may serve Him in the wilderness. Pharaoh sneered that he did not know this LORD, and many centuries later enslaved people seized on the words as their own cry for freedom. To show God's power, Aaron threw down his shepherd's staff and it became a snake. Pharaoh's magicians did the same with their staffs, but Aaron's snake swallowed up every one of theirs. Later, when the magicians could not copy the plague of gnats, they admitted it was the finger of God. When the tenth plague came, every Hebrew family smeared a lamb's blood on its door frame. Exodus says the LORD struck down every firstborn son in Egypt but passed over the marked houses and spared everyone inside, which is why the festival has been called Passover ever since. When the freed slaves set out into the trackless desert, God went before them, the story says, as a column of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night, so they could travel at any hour.

Pinned against the sea, with Egypt's chariots closing in, the Israelites saw Moses raise his hand over the water; all night an east wind held the sea back, and they walked across its dry bed between walls of water. When Pharaoh's army rushed onto the seabed in pursuit, God clogged their chariot wheels so that they drove with difficulty, and then the sea came back over Pharaoh's army. At Mount Sinai, while Moses spent forty days with God, the restless people talked Aaron into melting their gold earrings into a calf and bowed down to it. When Moses came down, he burned the calf, ground it to powder, scattered it on water and made the Israelites drink it.

Earlier, tending flocks on Mount Horeb, Moses had seen a bush blazing without ever burning up. A voice from the fire sent him to free the slaves, and when he asked what name to give the people, it answered, in the old English of the King James Bible, I AM THAT I AM, in Hebrew ehyeh asher ehyeh, and told him to say that I AM had sent him. Hungry in the wilderness, the people found the ground one morning frosted with fine white flakes, bread from heaven, they believed. They asked one another man hu?, meaning What is it?, and the name manna keeps that startled question. After forty years of wandering, Moses, by then 120 years old, climbed Mount Nebo alone and looked out over the Promised Land. He was allowed to see it but never to enter it, and he died there on the mountain.

English Bibles name the waters Moses divided the Red Sea, but the Hebrew name is Yam Suph, which means Sea of Reeds; the familiar Red Sea came from the Greek translators of the scriptures and stuck for two thousand years. In the haste of the escape, with the bread too rushed to rise and the people loading up Egypt's silver and gold, Moses kept an old promise: he carried out the bones of Joseph, who generations earlier had made his family swear to take him along when God led them out. The story kept inspiring the oppressed. In 1776 Benjamin Franklin proposed that the new United States put on its Great Seal a picture of Moses stretching out his hand as the sea swallowed Pharaoh's chariots, under the motto Rebellion to Tyrants is Obedience to God. Enslaved African Americans sang Go Down, Moses, and they gave Harriet Tubman, who went back into slave country time after time to guide others north on the Underground Railroad, the name of Exodus's own liberator: Moses.

the-factory-system-and-textile-mills.context_blurb:
In the late 1700s Britain's cotton industry moved out of cottages and into factories. A handful of inventors built machines that spun and wove far faster than hands could, mill owners gathered workers under one roof to tend them, and the factory system was born, bringing great wealth and, for many children, great misery.

Around 1764 James Hargreaves, an illiterate weaver from Lancashire, built the spinning jenny. An ordinary spinning wheel spun one thread at a time; his first jenny spun eight threads at once, so one spinner could do the work of eight. Legend says the idea came when his daughter knocked over a spinning wheel and he saw its spindle still turning upright, which suggested that several spindles could stand in a row and spin together; it is a charming tale, not a documented fact. Richard Arkwright, a Lancashire man born in 1732, began as a barber and wig-maker in Bolton before he patented his water frame in 1769 with the help of the clockmaker John Kay. Arkwright's mill at Cromford, opened in 1771, was the first cotton-spinning mill in the world to run on water power, and from 1772 it worked two thirteen-hour shifts, so its machines turned day and night, around the clock. By his death in 1792 the former wig-maker was said to be the richest man in Britain without a title.

Machines frightened many workers. In 1768 an angry mob, afraid the jennies would steal the hand spinners' work, broke into Hargreaves's house near Blackburn and smashed his machines, sparing only the jennies with twenty spindles or fewer; Hargreaves fled to Nottingham. Cromford ran by the clock. Its gates were locked promptly at six each morning and evening, and a worker who came even a little late lost that day's pay and was fined a second day's wages on top. Arkwright brought in workers from outside the district, mostly women and children, some only seven years old, and built them a whole settlement with cottages, pubs, shops, a school and chapels, making Cromford the world's first purpose-built factory village. The youngest children worked as scavengers, crawling under the moving machines to sweep up loose cotton. In 1832 one of them, David Rowland, told a parliamentary committee that because the machines never stopped, he often had to lie flat to avoid being caught. At Lowell, Massachusetts, mill owners cut the pay of their young women workers by an eighth in February 1834. About 800 of the mill girls walked out, and when they all withdrew their savings at once, two of Lowell's banks faced a run.

Around 1779, in a little upstairs room of a Bolton manor house that he called his conjuring room, Samuel Crompton finished a machine he had been building secretly. He named it the mule because, like the animal born of a horse and a donkey, it crossed two earlier machines, Hargreaves's jenny and Arkwright's water frame. Weaving was mechanized by a country clergyman. Edmund Cartwright, rector of Goadby Marwood, had never built a machine until a visit to Arkwright's mills in 1784 inspired him, and in 1785 he patented the first power loom. Britain banned the export of its textile machines and even forbade skilled mill workers to leave. Samuel Slater, aged 21, escaped the ban in 1789 by sailing for America disguised as a farmhand, carrying Arkwright's designs entirely in his memory, without a single drawing. Back home he was branded Slater the Traitor. Robert Blincoe, an orphan from a London workhouse, was seven when he was sent to the mills in 1799, and he ended up at notorious Litton Mill. Many argue that his 1828 memoir of beatings and starvation inspired Charles Dickens's Oliver Twist. Michael Sadler's committee heard in 1832 from 89 men and women who had worked as children, through days of 12 to 16 hours. When exhausted children nodded off at the machines late at night, they testified, the overseers beat them awake. That testimony drove the Factory Act of 1833, which limited children's hours and first sent government inspectors into the mills.

the-fall-of-the-western-roman-empire-476.context_blurb:
The Western Roman Empire did not fall in a day. Over two centuries it was split in two, sacked by Goths and Vandals and ruled by puppet emperors, until in 476 a Germanic commander quietly set the last one aside. Historians still argue over when, and why, it really ended.

Around 285 to 293 the emperor Diocletian divided the empire into an eastern and a western half to make it easier to govern. The western half collapsed in 476, but the eastern half, ruled from Constantinople and later called the Byzantine Empire, survived nearly a thousand years longer, until 1453. In 410 Alaric's Visigoths broke into Rome and plundered it; no foreign army had entered Rome for almost eight centuries. In Bethlehem the scholar Jerome put down his work and grieved that the city that had captured the whole world had now been captured itself. In June 455 King Gaiseric's Vandals sacked Rome for two full weeks, even stripping the bronze tiles from the roof of the Temple of Jupiter. Their name lives on: in 1794, during the French Revolution, a French bishop coined the word vandalism for wild, needless destruction. No great battle marked the end on 4 September 476. When Odoacer, a Germanic general, advanced on the capital, the boy emperor, a puppet about ten years old, was forced to step down: Romulus Augustulus. His name was haunting, for Romulus had founded Rome and Augustus had been its first emperor. Odoacer did not kill him. He spared the boy with a pension of 6,000 gold coins a year and sent him to live at the Castellum Lucullanum, a grand seaside villa near Naples, where the last emperor retired into comfortable obscurity.

Romans mocked the powerless boy even while he reigned. Augustulus means Little Augustus, a sneer at a child who never truly ruled, and Greek speakers called him Momylus, little disgrace. The real power behind the throne was the boy's father, Orestes, commander of the army, who had set his son there. Orestes had once taken dictation as secretary to Attila the Hun, the Scourge of God. Nor did Odoacer crown himself. He shipped the imperial crown and purple robes across the Adriatic to the emperor Zeno in Constantinople, declaring that the West needed no emperor of its own, and ruled as King of Italy. Odoacer's own end came in 493, when Theodoric the Great, king of the Ostrogoths, invited him to a peace feast at Ravenna and cut him down with a single stroke of his sword. Looking at the body, tradition says, Theodoric remarked that the wretch could not have had any bones in him.

Few who lived through 476 thought anything had ended; to them Odoacer's coup was one more shuffle of rulers. The year became the Fall of Rome only centuries later, when the British historian Edward Gibbon made it the great turning point in his eighteenth-century history of Rome's decline and fall. Many historians argue that Romulus does not even count. Julius Nepos, a rival who had fled to Dalmatia, was still treated in Constantinople as the lawful Western emperor until two counts, Ovida and Viator, killed him near Salona in 480, so by that reckoning the last Western emperor died that year. And why did Rome fall? Historians have never agreed. In 1984 the German scholar Alexander Demandt listed every reason ever put forward and counted 210, among them invasions and money troubles but also stranger ideas, such as that Romans bathed too much.

the-fertile-crescent-mesopotamia-s-river.context_blurb:
Civilization began in the Fertile Crescent, an arc of good land in the Middle East. At its heart lay Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq, where farmers first grew enough food to feed cities, and where people first wrote, built great temples and organized kingdoms.

The ancient Greeks named the land after the Tigris and Euphrates, the two great rivers that both rise in the mountains of eastern Turkey and run down to the Persian Gulf. Mesopotamia is Greek for the land in the middle of rivers, from mesos, middle, and potamos, river.

Rain almost never fell on southern Mesopotamia, yet it fed Uruk and Ur, among the earliest great cities. The secret was the yearly flood: every spring the rivers overflowed, and as the water sank back it left a fresh layer of river mud, or silt, that fertilized the fields for free. One grain ruled those fields. Barley tolerated the salty, sun-scorched southern soil better than any other crop, and Sumerians even paid each other in it and made their daily bread from it; wheat and emmer were saved for beer and luxury foods.

Some five thousand years ago the Sumerians added a seed funnel to the plow, so one trip down the field both opened the furrow and sowed it: as the blade cut the earth, seed poured down the funnel and was planted in the furrow. It took a crew of three to run, one leading the ox, one steering and one pouring the grain.

Irrigation changed everything. Before farming, almost everyone spent the whole day finding food, but now a few farmers could raise much more grain than their households needed. That surplus freed other people to take up their own crafts and trades, as potters, weavers, priests, scribes and rulers, and that division of labour is what made the first cities possible.
