the-final-solution-and-wannsee-conferenc.context_blurb:
The Holocaust was the murder of Europe's Jews by Nazi Germany. In January 1942 leading Nazi officials gathered at a villa outside Berlin to organize what they called the Final Solution of the Jewish question: the killing of every Jew in Europe. One copy of their own minutes survives, and it shows how calmly they planned it.

Fifteen high-ranking Nazis gathered on 20 January 1942 in a villa beside Lake Wannsee, in a leafy Berlin suburb; the SS had bought the house as a private retreat. The setting was as pleasant as the plan was monstrous. They had not come to debate whether to murder Europe's Jews, because Adolf Hitler had already decided that at the top. Their task was to coordinate how to do it, getting every government ministry to work together on the logistics of genocide. The chairman was Reinhard Heydrich, the SS general in charge of the Gestapo and the whole Nazi security apparatus, a man other Nazis dreaded; Hitler called him the man with a heart of iron. The whole meeting took about 90 minutes. Adolf Eichmann, who took the notes, later put it at between an hour and an hour and a half.

These were not ignorant thugs. Eight of the fifteen men at the table held doctorates, and ten had been to university; educated men administered genocide as paperwork. Heydrich put the target of the Final Solution at about eleven million Jews, and his list went far beyond the lands Germany held: it reached into Britain and into neutral nations such as Sweden, Switzerland, Ireland, Spain, Portugal and Turkey. Heydrich did not outlive the year. In Prague on 27 May 1942, Jozef Gabčík and Jan Kubiš, agents trained in Britain, waited at a sharp bend for his open car. Gabčík's gun jammed, and Kubiš hurled a grenade at the Mercedes; Heydrich died of infected wounds on 4 June. The SS gave his name to its murder campaign at the death camps of Belzec, Sobibor and Treblinka in occupied Poland: Aktion Reinhard, which killed about 1.7 million people.

Eichmann's chart counted the Jews of each country like goods in an inventory, about 11 million people in all; it entered Ukraine's Jews, for instance, as 2,994,684. The written minutes never use the words murder or kill. Jews driven to death on road gangs were said to drop out through natural diminution, and deportation was called evacuation to the East. The protocol even planned for the toughest survivors of that labour: if freed, it argued, they could become the germ cell of a new Jewish revival, so they too were to be treated accordingly, that is, killed. At his trial in 1961 Eichmann recalled that near the end, as butlers poured cognac, the officials dropped the polite language and spoke openly about methods of killing, about liquidation and extermination. The SS had run off roughly thirty copies of the minutes, and as the Reich fell it burned almost every one. Just one survived, copy number 16, which the American prosecutor Robert Kempner found in 1947 among seized Foreign Office files; it is the chief proof that the conference happened. When Israel tried Eichmann in Jerusalem in 1961, he seemed less a monster than a fussy, colourless clerk who said he had only obeyed orders. The philosopher Hannah Arendt, who watched the trial, coined a phrase for evil carried out by ordinary functionaries: the banality of evil.

the-first-crusade-capture-of-jerusalem-1.context_blurb:
In 1095 Pope Urban II summoned Western Christendom to a holy war to win back Jerusalem. Over the next four years tens of thousands set out on the First Crusade, and in July 1099, after terrible hardship and terrible crimes, they took the holy city in a storm of slaughter.

At the Council of Clermont the crowd answered Urban's call with two Latin words, Deus vult, meaning that God wills it, and he told them to make those words their battle cry. Each man who took the vow sewed a cloth cross onto his outer clothing, on the right shoulder or between the shoulders, so the crusaders were called crucesignati, those signed with the cross, and from the cross came the word crusade.

Before the knights set out, the preacher Peter the Hermit raised a ragtag People's Crusade of peasants and townsfolk with no military training and led it across Europe in 1096. This first wave was destroyed long before the knights' armies ever reached the Holy Land: the Seljuk Turks ambushed and slaughtered it at Civetot on 21 October 1096. The crusaders went hungry through the long siege of Antioch in 1098. Peter Bartholomew, a peasant, claimed that Saint Andrew had appeared to him and revealed a relic buried under a church floor, and on 14 June the men dug in the Church of St Peter and found the Holy Lance, the spear that had pierced Christ's side. The fired-up army broke the siege. Many doubted the find, and in April 1099 the peasant offered to prove it genuine by ordeal: he walked a narrow path between two walls of fire. He was terribly burned and died twelve days later. In late 1098 the crusaders besieged the Syrian town of Ma'arra, and when their food ran out, some of them cooked and ate the flesh of the dead, as Ralph of Caen and Fulcher of Chartres, priests who marched with them, recorded with horror.

Outside Jerusalem the crusaders had no wood, because the defenders had felled all the trees around the city. The Genoese commander Guglielmo Embriaco took his own ships apart at Jaffa and hauled the timber inland to build two huge siege towers. On 8 July 1099 a priest announced that the dead bishop Adhemar had appeared to him in a vision with orders, and about 15,000 crusaders walked barefoot in procession around the city walls, ending on the Mount of Olives, while the defenders jeered from above. The final assault came on 15 July. A Flemish knight, Lethold of Tournai, leapt from the siege tower of Godfrey of Bouillon and was the first crusader over the city wall, and when the defenders saw him there, their line broke.

The crusaders butchered the Muslims and Jews of Jerusalem. Raymond of Aguilers, who saw it, wrote that in the Temple and porch of Solomon men rode in blood up to their knees and bridle reins, the most quoted account of the slaughter. For all the horror, the crusaders' own losses in storming the walls were surprisingly small: modern historians treat the medieval death tolls as huge exaggerations, and the scholar Conor Kostick puts the crusader dead at about 3,000. The victors wanted Godfrey of Bouillon as their king, but he would not be called king; legend has him say that a golden crown did not belong on his head in the city where Christ had worn one of thorns. He took the title Defender of the Holy Sepulchre instead. The crusaders also turned Muslim holy sites into churches. The al-Aqsa Mosque on the Temple Mount, where Solomon's Temple was believed to have stood, became Templum Salomonis, the Temple of Solomon, and a knightly order made it its headquarters and took its name from it: the Knights Templar.

the-forgotten-allies-of-the-east-polish-.context_blurb:
Poland suffered and fought as hard as any nation in the Second World War, yet its allies often forgot it, and one of them betrayed it. Two stories show both sides of that record: a Polish mathematician's triumph before the war, and the Polish capital's lonely uprising near its end.

Poland's greatest secret weapon was a mathematician. Marian Rejewski began attacking Germany's Enigma machine in December 1932, seven years before the war, without a captured machine or a single stolen page. Working from patterns in intercepted messages, he deduced the hidden wiring of its rotors by pure mathematics, using the algebra of permutations. A British codebreaker later called it the mathematical theorem that won the Second World War.

The Polish Home Army rose against the German occupiers of Warsaw on 1 August 1944 and fought on for 63 days. Stalin's Red Army halted just across the Vistula and watched the city burn. When Britain and the United States wanted to fly in supplies, Stalin refused to let their planes even land at Soviet airfields, dismissing the rising as an adventure. The uprising was crushed: some 150,000 civilians and 20,000 Home Army fighters died, and Heinrich Himmler ordered the city razed so that no stone would remain standing.

the-french-revolution-s-terror-as-the-en.context_blurb:
The French Revolution began in 1789 with promises of liberty and reason, and within four years it was killing its own people by the thousands. In the Terror of 1793 and 1794, Maximilien Robespierre and the Committee of Public Safety made the guillotine an instrument of government, and the war on the old order became a war on the Church itself.

In 1793 revolutionaries, emptying Notre-Dame for their new Cult of Reason, pulled down the 28 stone kings across its front and knocked off their heads, believing they were kings of France. In fact the carvers had made them Old Testament kings of Judah and Israel from the Bible. On 10 November 1793 they turned the cathedral into a Temple of Reason. They ripped out the altar, raised an artificial mountain crowned by a small Greek temple, and at the centre enthroned a living woman, an actress dressed as the Goddess of Reason, to be worshipped in place of God.

Madame Roland, a leader of the moderate Girondins, went to the guillotine on 8 November 1793. As her cart went by the figure of Liberty beside the scaffold, tradition says she called out to Liberty, lamenting the crimes committed in its name, the most famous verdict on the whole Revolution. The Terror devoured its makers. Maximilien Robespierre, who had sent thousands to their deaths, was overthrown on 28 July 1794: the night before, a pistol shot shattered his jaw, and he was beheaded without trial on the guillotine, the machine of his own Terror, with about 21 of his allies, among them Saint-Just.

Robespierre had defended the killing in February 1794, in his speech On Political Morality: terror, he said, was nothing but justice, prompt, severe and inflexible, an emanation of virtue, and virtue without terror was powerless. In his own words, the Terror grew out of the Revolution's ideals. Its victims were mostly not the rich. Donald Greer, a historian, went through the official death sentences, some 17,000 of them, and found that about 85 percent fell on peasants, servants and day-labourers, ordinary commoners, with only about 8.5 percent nobles and 6.5 percent clergy. Edmund Burke, an Irish-born British statesman, had seen where it would lead. In his Reflections on the Revolution in France of 1790, before the king was killed or the Terror began, he predicted that contempt for tradition would end in bloodshed and in a popular army general seizing power as a dictator, as Napoleon later did. The prophecy made Burke's name as the founder of modern conservatism.

the-gettysburg-address.context_blurb:
In November 1863, months after the great battle fought there, President Abraham Lincoln came to Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, to help dedicate a cemetery for the Union dead. His speech lasted about two minutes and ran to only 272 words, and it became the most famous speech in American history.

The main speaker that day was Edward Everett, the most celebrated orator in America, who spoke for two hours. Then Lincoln rose and spoke for two minutes. The next morning Everett wrote to Lincoln that he would be glad if he had come as near the central idea of the occasion in two hours as Lincoln had in two minutes, and Lincoln replied that he was pleased his few words were not entirely a failure.

In his closing sentence Lincoln named the cause the fallen had given their lives for: a government of the people, run by the people and for the people, which must not perish from the earth. No definition of democracy in English is quoted more often, and the words are carved on the wall of the Lincoln Memorial.

the-gilded-age-industrialists.context_blurb:
After the Civil War, American industry boomed, and a handful of men built fortunes larger than any the world had seen: Cornelius Vanderbilt in steamboats and railroads, Rockefeller in oil, Andrew Carnegie in steel. They rose from nothing, drove their workers hard and gave away fortunes.

Cornelius Vanderbilt, a Staten Island boy born in 1794, earned his nickname on the water long before he built a railroad. As a teenager of sixteen he got a hundred-dollar loan from his mother, bought a little sailing boat and ferried passengers to New York, and from that he built the biggest steamboat business on the Hudson. Commodore is a naval rank, and he became the Commodore. Andrew Carnegie came from Scotland as a poor immigrant boy and at 13 worked as a bobbin boy in a Pittsburgh cotton mill, earning $1.20 a week. A kind man, Colonel James Anderson, lent his books to working boys on Saturdays, and Carnegie vowed that if he ever grew rich he would give boys like him the same chance to read. He kept the vow, paying for about 2,509 free public libraries across the English-speaking world.

Rockefeller, the devout founder of Standard Oil, carried pockets of coins on his walks and pressed shiny dimes on the children he met, urging them to work hard and save. Their wealth had a harsh side. In the Homestead Strike of 1892 at Carnegie's steelworks, his manager, Henry Clay Frick, walled the works in with a fence three miles long and twelve feet high, crowned with barbed wire and pierced with peepholes for rifles, and the workers nicknamed it Fort Frick. On 6 July hundreds of Pinkerton guards floated up the Monongahela on barges to seize the mill, and a gun battle of thirteen hours left about seven workers and three Pinkertons dead.

In his 1889 essay The Gospel of Wealth, Carnegie argued that great wealth beyond a man's needs is held in trust for the public good, to be given away while he lives, and that the man who dies rich dies disgraced. He lived by it, selling his steel empire and giving away most of his fortune.

the-gordian-knot.context_blurb:
Gordium was the old royal city of Phrygia, a kingdom in the hills of central Anatolia, in today's Turkey. There, dedicated to Zeus, stood the ancient wagon of a legendary king named Gordius, lashed fast with a rope tangled so cunningly that no loose end showed anywhere. In 333 BC a young Macedonian king, Alexander the Great, reached the city on his march east against the Persian Empire.

The tangle carried a prophecy. An oracle had foretold that the man who loosened it would become lord of all Asia, so the knot was really a riddle about who would win an empire. For years challenger after challenger had picked at it and gone away beaten.

Alexander came to try his luck. He turned the knot this way and that, hunting for an end to pull, and found none. Then his patience ran out: he drew his sword and cut the knot through with one stroke. He had solved the puzzle not by untangling it but by refusing to play by its rules.

Alexander went on to conquer the whole Persian Empire, and his admirers said the oracle had come true. Ever since, a person who settles a stubborn, complicated problem with one bold, simple act is said to have cut the Gordian knot, a phrase that has lasted more than two thousand years.

the-gracchi-brothers-and-the-republic-s-.context_blurb:
Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus were brothers from a noble Roman family who served as tribunes of the people in the late second century BC. A tribune could summon the people's assembly, propose laws and block almost any act of government with his veto. The brothers used the office to give land to Rome's poor, and the fight over it broke the Republic's oldest rules.

In 133 BC Tiberius proposed a law handing out small plots of public land to landless families, reviving an old limit on how much public land one man could hold. His colleague Marcus Octavius vetoed it. A tribune's person was sacred and his veto final, yet Tiberius had the people's assembly vote Octavius out of office in the middle of his term, then had him dragged bodily off the tribunes' bench. Many senators now saw a tyrant in the making, and later that year a mob led by senators clubbed Tiberius to death with sticks and broken benches.

Ten years later his younger brother Gaius took up the same cause. By 121 BC Gaius and his followers had gathered under arms on the Aventine Hill, and the Senate answered with a new weapon, a decree later known as the ultimate decree, the senatus consultum ultimum. It let the consul Lucius Opimius use deadly force against Roman citizens, as much as he needed, without any trial at all. Opimius attacked, and he had the bodies of Gaius, his ally Fulvius Flaccus and about 3,000 followers thrown into the Tiber. The decree became a standing emergency tool, later turned on Catiline, and Romans came to see the brothers' deaths as the moment their politics turned from the vote to the sword.

the-great-depression.context_blurb:
The Great Depression was the deepest economic collapse in American history, and it dragged much of the world down too. It started with the Wall Street crash: on Black Tuesday, 29 October 1929, panicked investors dumped some sixteen million shares in a single day. For the next decade Americans argued over who was to blame, and economists still do.

The misery reached into ordinary homes. At the bottom, close to thirteen million Americans, a quarter of all workers, had no job, and roughly one household in four had no income whatsoever. Families who lost their homes knocked together shacks from packing crates and tar paper on vacant lots and in Central Park itself. People called these shanty towns Hoovervilles, a jab at President Herbert Hoover, whom they blamed for the misery.

Over nine thousand banks failed in the slump's first years, and a rumour of trouble could send a bank's customers stampeding in to empty their accounts in a day. Such a run ruined families completely, because no government agency yet guaranteed deposits: once the vault was empty, the savings left inside were lost for good. Congress created the FDIC in 1933 to end that danger. Stocks slid for almost three years. From its peak of 381 in early September 1929, the Dow Jones average sank until, in July 1932, it closed at about 41, a loss of nearly nine-tenths and its lowest close of the whole century.

In June 1930 Congress sent Hoover the Smoot-Hawley Tariff, raising duties on over twenty thousand imports. More than a thousand economists urged a veto, and the banker Thomas Lamont later said he had nearly gone down on his knees to plead with Hoover against what he called an asinine tariff. Hoover signed it, other countries retaliated with tariffs of their own, and world trade fell by about two-thirds in five years.

In the summer of 1932 thousands of jobless World War I veterans camped in Washington, asking to be paid early a bonus promised for their war service. Hoover sent in the army, and General Douglas MacArthur drove them out with bayonets, cavalry and tanks and set their shacks on fire. Seeing newspaper photographs of the blaze, Franklin Roosevelt, Hoover's opponent, reportedly told an aide that this scene would win him the election. He beat Hoover that November by seven million votes. In Germany, where American lenders had demanded their money back, over six million people were jobless by 1932. Adolf Hitler's Nazi Party, which had won 2.6 percent of the vote in 1928, took 37.4 percent in July 1932 and became the largest party in the Reichstag.

Roosevelt took office on 4 March 1933 and told a frightened nation that its one real enemy was fear itself. He shut every bank for a bank holiday, and on 12 March, in his first radio fireside chat, he assured listeners that their savings would be safer in a reopened bank than hidden under the mattress. When the banks reopened, the Dow leapt about fifteen percent in a day. Then nature struck. On 14 April 1935, after years of drought on over-ploughed land, a black wall of dust hundreds of feet high rolled across the Great Plains and turned noon into night. Survivors named that storm Black Sunday, the worst of the whole Dust Bowl.

What caused the Depression is still argued, and each school has serious defenders. In his 1936 General Theory, John Maynard Keynes described the paradox of thrift: when frightened people all save at once, shops lose customers and the slump deepens. His cure was for government to spend on public works and jobs, so that money reached people's hands and got spent again. Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz blamed the Federal Reserve: in their 1963 account, the Fed stood by while the nation's money supply fell by roughly a third in four years, a collapse they called the Great Contraction. Murray Rothbard, in the Austrian tradition of Mises and Hayek, blamed the boom built on the Fed's cheap credit in the 1920s and saw the bust as the cure. What dragged the slump out, he argued, was Hoover holding wages and prices up when they needed to fall. Barry Eichengreen blamed the gold standard, the golden fetters that stopped central banks from printing money to save their banks and so spread the collapse worldwide. Britain and Scandinavia, which broke with gold early, in 1931, recovered sooner than most, while France held on and stayed mired.

the-great-mosque-of-cordoba-and-the-alha.context_blurb:
The Great Mosque of Córdoba, the Mezquita, was begun in 785 by the Umayyad emir Abd al-Rahman I, and later rulers kept enlarging it until it was one of the largest mosques in the world. Far to the east, on a hill above Granada, the Nasrid dynasty, the last Muslim rulers of Spain, built the Alhambra palace in the 1300s.

Córdoba's builders reused old Roman and Visigothic columns, which were too short for a lofty roof. Rather than discard them, the masons set a horseshoe arch low to brace each column and stacked a second, rounder arch above it, so two tiers of arches did the work of one tall pillar and lifted the ceiling high. The famous red-and-white stripes on those arches are not paint but alternating bands of red brick and pale stone, repeated across roughly 856 columns. When Córdoba fell to the Christians in 1236, King Ferdinand III reconsecrated the Mezquita as a cathedral.

In the Alhambra's Court of the Lions, built between 1362 and 1391, twelve stone lions hold up a marble fountain and spout water from their mouths. Scholars believe the builders gave the spouts slightly different heights, so that each lion began to flow at its own hour until all twelve ran together at midday. If they are right, the fountain doubled as a water clock marking the twelve hours, though that reading is a reconstruction, not a certainty.

the-great-pyramids-of-giza.context_blurb:
On the desert edge outside Cairo stand the pyramids of Giza, raised around 2600 to 2500 BC as tombs for three pharaohs of Egypt's Old Kingdom. The biggest, the Great Pyramid, may be the most famous building on Earth, and archaeologists keep finding new clues about who built it, how, and why.

The Great Pyramid was the tomb of Khufu, the second king of the Fourth Dynasty, whom the Greeks later called Cheops; it was completed for him around 2560 BC. Ancient writers listed Seven Wonders of the World, and earthquakes, fire and stone robbers destroyed six of them; only the Great Pyramid of Giza, the oldest of them all, still stands.

When it was finished it rose about 481 feet, and nothing built by human hands topped it until the spire of Lincoln Cathedral in England around 1311, so it held the record as the tallest structure on Earth for roughly 3,800 years. The Egyptians never called it the Great Pyramid. They named it Akhet-Khufu, the Horizon of Khufu, and that name appears in the oldest papyrus in the world. It once gleamed. About 144,000 polished blocks of white Tura limestone covered it until an earthquake in 1303 loosened them, and around 1356 Sultan an-Nasir's men stripped the casing and carted it off to build Cairo, which is why its faces now look rough and stepped. Who built it? Not aliens. When the billionaire Elon Musk tweeted in 2020 that aliens had built the pyramids, Egypt's tourism minister, Rania al-Mashat, invited him to come to Giza and see the graves of the workmen who really built them.

Those graves belong to a whole town of builders that the archaeologists Mark Lehner and Zahi Hawass uncovered at Giza. The workers were organised crews, not whipped slaves, and they scrawled their gang names on the stones: one called itself the Friends of Khufu, another the Drunkards of Menkaure. The sides face the four cardinal points almost perfectly, off by only about three and a half minutes of arc, and a leading theory says the builders found true north using the autumn equinox.

Deep inside, in the King's Chamber, stands Khufu's granite coffer, and it is broader than the chamber's only entrance. Since nobody could have squeezed it through that door, the builders must have set it in place first and raised the chamber around it. When explorers looked inside, it was empty. In 2013, digging at Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea, Pierre Tallet found the world's oldest papyrus, the diary of Merer, an inspector, written in Khufu's 27th year. It records Merer leading a crew of about two hundred men who shipped white limestone by boat to Akhet-Khufu, a trip of roughly three days. In 2017 physicists scanned the pyramid without drilling a single hole, using muons, particles born when cosmic rays strike the air, which shower down and pass through rock. They found an empty space at least thirty metres, about 100 feet, long above the Grand Gallery, nicknamed the Big Void, the first major hidden space found inside since the 1800s.

The hardest puzzle is how workers hauled two-tonne blocks up the rising pyramid without machines. At Hatnub, an ancient quarry, archaeologists uncovered a ramp built in Khufu's time, some forty-five centuries ago, flanked by stairs lined with post-holes. Workers tied ropes to wooden posts set in those holes and used them to help drag stone-laden sledges up slopes as steep as 20 percent.

the-great-schism-of-1054.context_blurb:
For a thousand years Christians in Rome and Constantinople belonged to one church, but by the eleventh century the Latin-speaking West and the Greek-speaking East had drifted apart over language, ritual and, above all, whether the pope ruled the whole church. In 1054 the quarrel exploded inside Hagia Sophia, the great domed cathedral of Constantinople, and Christianity split into Catholic and Orthodox halves.

On 16 July 1054 three envoys of Pope Leo IX, led by the hard-edged Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida, walked into Hagia Sophia in the middle of the Divine Liturgy. Humbert laid a bull on the high altar, a written decree excommunicating the patriarch, Michael Cerularius, and cutting him off from the church.

The fight had been simmering over bread. Latin priests baked their Communion bread flat, without yeast, while the Greeks used leavened loaves and refused to accept the flat kind as true Communion. In 1053 Cerularius closed the Latin churches of the city, and his aide Nicephorus burst open their tabernacles and trampled the consecrated bread underfoot.

Their decree delivered, the legates walked out. At the door they turned, shook the cathedral's dust from their sandals, the old gesture of final rejection, and cried out in Latin, Videat Deus et judicet, meaning may God see and judge.

Cerularius struck back with care. On 24 July he gathered twenty-one bishops in Hagia Sophia and pronounced an anathema of his own, but it named only the three legates, one by one, not the pope or the Latin church as a whole. That restraint is one reason historians say the break of 1054 was less total than legend claims. He also had the legates' bull burned in public. The two curses then stayed in force for 911 years, until 7 December 1965, when Patriarch Athenagoras I and Pope Paul VI lifted them in simultaneous ceremonies in Istanbul and Rome, agreeing to consign the old excommunications to oblivion.

The legates' bull had flaws of its own. Pope Leo IX, who had sent them, had died on 19 April 1054, three months before they acted, so strictly speaking they had no authority left to excommunicate anyone. Its list of eleven charges even accused the Greeks of cutting the filioque, Latin for "and the Son", out of the Creed. That was backwards: the West itself had added those words to the Nicene Creed, and the East had never accepted them, holding that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone. Tellingly, the filioque came only seventh on the list, well behind the quarrel over bread.

the-great-sphinx.context_blurb:
The Great Sphinx crouches on the Giza plateau outside Cairo: a colossal lion with a man's head, about 73 metres long and 20 metres high, keeping watch before the pyramid of the pharaoh Khafre. Most Egyptologists think Khafre's workmen made it in the twenty-sixth century BC and gave it his face, though both points are debated.

Unlike the pyramids behind it, the Sphinx was never assembled from blocks. Its sculptors cut the whole creature where it lies, out of a single ridge of the plateau's own limestone bedrock, which makes it the oldest known monumental sculpture in Egypt. For much of its history drifting sand buried it up to the neck, and several pharaohs had it dug out again.

Its nose is gone, and chisel marks show that someone pried it off on purpose. A favourite tale blames Napoleon's soldiers, said to have shot it away with a cannon after France invaded Egypt in 1798. The tale cannot be true: the traveller Frederic Louis Norden sketched the Sphinx in 1737, more than sixty years earlier, and his drawing already shows the face without its nose. The likeliest culprit was a Sufi named Muhammad Sa'im al-Dahr, who defaced the statue in the fourteenth century as an idol.

the-great-wall-of-china.context_blurb:
Across the hills and deserts of northern China runs the Great Wall, guarding the farmland of the old empire against horsemen from the northern steppe. It is the most famous defensive work on Earth, and also one of the most misunderstood: it is neither one wall nor the work of one ruler.

At its eastern end the wall marches down to the shore near Shanhai Pass and runs straight out into the Bohai Gulf. Its builders called that spot Laolongtou, the Old Dragon's Head, since the wall seems to lower its head into the waves to drink like a great dragon.

What historians and archaeologists find on the ground is no single structure. It is many separate walls of rammed earth, stone and brick, raised, abandoned and rebuilt by one dynasty after another for nearly two thousand years, from the Qin in the 200s BC to the Ming. A famous myth says the wall is the one human work you can see from the Moon. It is wrong, because the wall is long but narrow: Yang Liwei, the first Chinese astronaut, looked down from orbit in 2003 and said he could not make it out with the naked eye.

The cost in lives was terrible. Emperors drove peasants, soldiers and convicts to build in bitter cold on steep ridges with too little food, and one common estimate puts the dead at around 400,000, many buried in pits beside the wall itself. That is why the wall earned the grim nickname of the longest cemetery in the world.

In the Ming centuries, engineers rebuilt long stretches in brick and stone and stirred sticky rice into their lime mortar. A starch in the rice bound with the lime into an early composite glue, and it has helped those walls ride out earthquakes and weather for centuries.

In the end the wall fell to treason, not to siege. In 1644 the Ming general Wu Sangui, posted to guard Shanhai Pass, threw its gates open to the Manchu army, and the Ming dynasty was finished.

the-gulag-solzhenitsyn-s-witness.context_blurb:
From the 1920s to the 1980s the Soviet Union ran a vast network of forced-labour camps where millions of prisoners, many of them guilty of nothing, worked, froze and died. Its most famous witness was Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, a former prisoner whose books tore the secrecy off the system and shamed the Soviet regime before the world.

The word GULAG names no place on a map. It is a Russian abbreviation for the Main Directorate of Camps, the government office that ran the whole system. In the far east of Siberia, Kolyma's prisoners hacked a road some two thousand kilometres long from the port of Magadan through frozen ground, and so many died that the guards packed their bodies into the roadbed. It is still called the Road of Bones. The prototype camp opened about 1923 on the White Sea's Solovetsky Islands, inside the walls of an ancient Orthodox monastery, a place of prayer turned into a place of death. Solzhenitsyn said every later camp copied it.

Solzhenitsyn himself was an artillery officer, decorated for bravery, at the East Prussian front in February 1945 when his own side arrested him. His crime was a set of private letters to a school friend, Nikolai Vitkevich, in which he mocked Stalin, and it earned him eight years in the camps. Prisoners were forbidden paper, so he composed poems in his head. To keep count of thousands of memorised lines, he broke matchsticks into small pieces, laid them in rows of tens and units, and ran them through his fingers like the beads of a rosary as he recited. He carried about 12,000 lines out of the camps that way.

His sentence ended in 1953, and his first day out, 5 March, was the very day Stalin died. Even then the state sent him into exile for life in Kazakhstan, where he nearly died of cancer. In 1962 the journal Novy Mir printed his short novel about the prisoner Ivan Denisovich Shukhov, after Nikita Khrushchev approved it himself over the protests of other Party bosses. As its title says, the book covers just one single, ordinary day of Shukhov's life in camp, and it was the first honest account of the camps published openly in the USSR. He won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1970 but dared not travel to collect it, fearing he would be barred from coming home. He ended his Nobel lecture with a Russian proverb that summed up his whole struggle against official lies: a single word of truth will outweigh the entire world.

His great work, The Gulag Archipelago, compared the scattered camps to a hidden chain of islands. He wrote it in secret through the 1960s while the KGB hunted for it, and he never let the whole manuscript sit in one place: he worked on fragments and hid the pieces with trusted friends around Moscow and at a secret retreat in Estonia, so that no raid could seize it all. In 1973 KGB officers broke his typist, Elizaveta Voronyanskaya, after days of questioning, and she gave up the hiding place of one copy; soon afterwards she was found hanged. Solzhenitsyn's answer was to order the book published in the West at once, and it appeared in Paris on 28 December 1973. Early in 1974 the state arrested him for treason, stripped his citizenship and expelled him to West Germany.

Even the book's dates were an accusation. By beginning in 1918, in Lenin's first years, Solzhenitsyn charged that the camps were built into the Soviet state from the start and were no mere aberration of Stalin's. He refused, too, the comfortable idea that evil lives only in other people. The line dividing good and evil, he wrote, runs not between states, classes or parties, but through the heart of every human being, and even the worst heart keeps one small bridgehead of good.

the-hellenistic-age-spread-of-greek-cult.context_blurb:
When Alexander the Great died in 323 BC, his generals carved his empire into kingdoms that stretched from Greece and Egypt to the edge of India. For three centuries, until Rome swallowed the last of them with Egypt in 30 BC, Greek language, cities, art and science spread across that whole belt of the world. Historians call it the Hellenistic Age.

Alexander stamped his name on city after city, some twenty to thirty Alexandrias across three continents. One city in India broke the pattern. When his beloved warhorse Bucephalus died there, Alexander founded a city in the horse's honour and called it Bucephala. His armies also carried a simplified Greek, Koine, the common tongue, which merchants and scholars used from Egypt to India. It long outlived his empire, and centuries later it became the language in which the New Testament was first written, along with the Greek Old Testament.

Alexandria in Egypt became the age's capital of learning. Around 240 BC its librarian Eratosthenes knew that on midsummer's day the noon Sun lit the bottom of a well at Syene, in the south, while upright objects in Alexandria still threw a shadow of some seven degrees. From that small gap between two shadows he calculated how far it is around the entire Earth, its circumference, and landed astonishingly close to the true figure. Rival kings even fought with libraries. Ptolemy of Egypt, hoping to starve the great library at Pergamon, banned the export of papyrus, so the people of Pergamon perfected writing on treated animal skins, and the new material took the city's name: parchment, from the Latin pergamenum.

Greek art travelled east as well. For centuries Buddhist artists would not portray the Buddha's body, showing only an empty seat or a pair of footprints where he should be, but in Gandhara, in today's Pakistan and Afghanistan, sculptors trained in the Greek style were the first to carve him in human form. They draped him like a Greek, in a himation, a toga-like robe falling in deep folds. For his bodyguard, Vajrapani, they borrowed a hero from Greek myth: Herakles, the muscular strongman with his club, became the Buddha's protector. Even the Buddha's serene face came from a Greek model, the Belvedere Apollo of about 330 BC, and from it he inherited his wavy, curling hair drawn up into a topknot, a look that spread across all of Asia.

Far out in Afghanistan stood Ai-Khanoum, a thoroughly Greek city with a theatre for five thousand and a gymnasium. There Klearchos raised a stele carved with the Delphic Maxims, the wise sayings of Apollo's temple at Delphi, and it is the oldest copy to survive, for none remain at Delphi itself. In the 100s BC the Indo-Greek king Menander I ruled what is now Pakistan and north-western India, and his Indian subjects called him Milinda. The geographer Strabo wrote a century later that Menander had subdued more tribes than even Alexander the Great. When Menander died, around 130 BC, Plutarch says his cities quarrelled over his ashes, as cities had once fought over the Buddha's relics. By legend they settled it the same way, dividing the ashes and raising a stupa, a domed shrine, over each share. Heliodorus, a Greek envoy, reached an Indian court around 113 BC and took up the local faith. He set up a pillar at Besnagar, crowned with Garuda, proclaiming himself a devotee of Vishnu, worshipped as Krishna, which makes him one of Krishna's earliest recorded worshippers.

Greek engineers built marvels too. From a sunken ship, divers brought up a crusted lump of bronze gearwheels made around 150 to 100 BC: the Antikythera mechanism, a hand-turned device that tracked the Sun and Moon and forecast eclipses years ahead. No one built anything as intricate for more than a millennium. The Letter of Aristeas tells how Ptolemy II brought seventy-two Jewish scholars to Alexandria to put the Hebrew Bible into Greek, producing the Septuagint. Philo added a bolder legend: each scholar worked alone in his own cell, yet all of them produced translations identical word for word. The architect Sostratus raised the Pharos, the lighthouse of Alexandria, more than a hundred metres tall and one of the Seven Wonders. Legend says the king expected only his own name on it, so Sostratus carved his own name into the stone and covered it with plaster bearing the king's, so that when the plaster wore away, the builder's name would be left.

the-hittites-and-ironworking.context_blurb:
The Hittites ruled a great empire from Hattusa in central Anatolia, today's Turkey, between about 1600 and 1200 BC. They were one of the great powers of the Late Bronze Age, trading letters with Egypt and Assyria, and around 1274 BC they fought the Egyptian pharaoh Ramesses II in the huge chariot battle of Kadesh.

Years after that bloody draw, Hattusili III of the Hittites and Ramesses II made peace, and around 1258 BC they had the terms engraved on tablets of silver. It is the oldest surviving peace treaty in the world, which is why Turkey gave the United Nations a copper copy, and it now hangs at the UN's headquarters in New York near the Security Council chamber.

Iron was still precious in their day. The Hittites are often credited as early ironworkers, and Anatolia has the oldest written evidence of iron smelting, but modern scholars reject the old idea that a Hittite monopoly on iron won their wars. When another king asked Hattusili for good iron, Hattusili admitted in his reply that his storehouse in Kizzuwatna held none ready to give at the moment, and he could send only a single iron dagger-blade. Even a great king could not yet supply the metal that would one day replace bronze.

the-holodomor-stalin-s-terror-famine-in-.context_blurb:
In 1932 and 1933 Joseph Stalin's government starved millions of Ukrainian peasants to death. Stalin had forced Ukraine's farms into state collectives and then demanded grain quotas no village could meet, and when the villages fell short, his officials took everything. Ukrainians call the catastrophe the Holodomor. Its first great witness was a young Welsh reporter, Gareth Jones; its most famous denier was the New York Times man in Moscow, Walter Duranty.

Foreigners were barred from the famine zone, so in March 1933 Jones simply left his train some forty miles short of its destination and walked into Ukraine. He had filled his knapsack with bread and chocolate, and he handed them out to the hungry villagers he met as he tramped from village to village. Everywhere the peasants told him the same thing, and he noted it in the little diary he carried: they had no bread, and they were dying. That line became the heart of the press release he issued in Berlin on 29 March, which the Manchester Guardian printed the next day.

Jones already had a knack for scoops. Only weeks earlier, in late February, he had flown to Frankfurt on the same plane as Adolf Hitler, with the propagandist Joseph Goebbels aboard too, and he wrote that if it had crashed, the history of Europe would have changed. Two days after Jones's famine report, Duranty replied in the Times under the headline "Russians Hungry, But Not Starving". Brushing aside the dead, he wrote that, to put it brutally, an omelette could not be made without breaking eggs.

The famine's machinery was written into law. Under a decree signed on 7 August 1932, gathering a handful of stray ears of wheat from a collective farm's stubble could cost a peasant his life or a decade in the camps. Villagers called it the Law of Spikelets, after the tiny ears of grain it punished, and over 200,000 people were sentenced under it. A village that missed its quota went onto the black board, the chorni doshky: the state shut its shops, cut off all its trade and sealed it, children and teachers included, to starve. Duranty, meanwhile, was rewarded. His admiring series of articles on Stalin's Soviet Union had won him the Pulitzer Prize in 1932, and the Pulitzer Board has never taken it back. Jones was banned from the Soviet Union for life. On 12 August 1935, the day before his thirtieth birthday, bandits in Japanese-occupied Inner Mongolia shot him dead, and suspicion of revenge deepened when his travelling companion, Herbert Müller, turned out to be an agent of the NKVD, the Soviet secret police.

Historians have since shown how deliberate it was. On 22 January 1933 Molotov and Stalin put their names to a directive that sealed the borders of the famine zone so that starving peasants could not flee to look for food, and internal passports kept them trapped where they were. All the while the state sold almost two million tonnes of grain abroad for hard currency. By Michael Ellman's calculation, that exported grain could have kept roughly five million people alive for a year. Duranty knew the truth. In public he told readers there was no famine, but in the autumn of 1933, talking privately with British diplomats, he put the possible dead at up to ten million. His colleagues knew Jones had told the truth, too. Guarding their visas, the Moscow correspondents agreed at a meeting with the Soviet censor Constantine Umansky to brand Jones a liar, then drank vodka with Umansky into the early hours. In Assignment in Utopia, his later memoir, Eugene Lyons confessed it: denouncing Jones was an unpleasant chore, he wrote, but they threw him down, all of them, unanimously.

the-holodomor-walter-duranty-s-cover-up.context_blurb:
In 1932 and 1933 Joseph Stalin's regime turned a grain crisis in Soviet Ukraine into a deliberate famine that killed millions of peasants. Ukrainians gave it a name that refuses the neutral word famine: Holodomor, from holod, hunger, and mor, death, so that it means death by hunger, killing by starvation. The world was slow to learn of it, partly because one of its most trusted reporters chose to hide it.

Stalin had forced Ukraine's farms into collectives and set quotas the villages could not meet. A decree of August 1932, which peasants nicknamed the Law of the Five Spikelets, let officials execute a peasant for gleaning a few leftover stalks from a collective field, or jail him for ten years or more and seize everything he owned. Armed brigades then searched house after house and took everything edible: the potatoes, the animals, even the pets, and cruellest of all the seed grain saved for planting, which was next year's whole crop, so the hunger could only go on. By June 1933 Ukraine, the breadbasket of the whole Soviet Union, was losing about 28,000 people every day, some seventeen every minute.

Most foreign correspondents never left Moscow, passing on whatever the officials said. In March 1933 the young Welsh journalist Gareth Jones did the opposite: he stepped off his train near Kharkiv and walked through some twenty villages and a dozen collective farms, sleeping in peasants' huts so he could see the famine for himself. In his notebook he set down what the villagers kept telling him: there was no bread; they were dying; they were waiting for death. He saw children with swollen bellies. Back in Berlin on 29 March, Jones told the press what he had seen, and his story ran under the headline Famine Grips Russia, Millions Dying. By then starving peasants were boarding trains or walking toward Russia in search of food. In January, Molotov and Stalin had signed an order titled "On preventing the mass flight of starving peasants", and army and NKVD units sealed the borders, trapping the hungry where they stood.

The New York Times bureau chief in Moscow, Walter Duranty, struck back two days after Jones spoke. His reply, headlined "Russians Hungry, But Not Starving", waved Jones's report away as a scare story and told readers flatly that there was no famine or starvation. He also gave the world the excuse it remembers him for. Recasting the dead as the price of building socialism, Duranty wrote that, to put it brutally, an omelet could not be made without breaking eggs. Jones paid for his honesty. Banned from the Soviet Union, he went travelling in Japanese-occupied Inner Mongolia, and there in August 1935 bandits kidnapped him and shot him dead, a day before his thirtieth birthday. Some historians suspect that the NKVD, the Soviet secret police, arranged the killing as revenge for his famine reporting, though that has never been proved.

Duranty knew better than he wrote. Around September 1933 he told the British diplomat William Strang that perhaps as many as ten million people may have died from lack of food in the past year, a figure he never printed. A 1931 embassy memo had already recorded his admission that his dispatches always reflected the Soviet government's official opinion. His prize survived anyway. His flattering Soviet reporting of 1931 had won him the 1932 Pulitzer Prize. Asked to review that work in 2003, the historian Mark von Hagen called it unbalanced and uncritical and urged that the prize be revoked, but the Pulitzer Board declined, saying it saw no clear proof that Duranty had meant to deceive. The cover-up shaped the numbers too. For decades the accepted toll was played down to about half a million, a figure that measured the cover-up; serious historians now put the Ukrainian dead at roughly 3.5 to 7 million. Ukraine's parliament declared the Holodomor a genocide in 2006.

the-horse-returns-to-the-americas.context_blurb:
Horses seem as American as the open plains, yet for some ten thousand years before Columbus there were none in the Americas at all. Their return with the Spanish in the 1490s, and their spread onto the Great Plains, is one of the strangest homecomings of the Columbian Exchange.

The horse family actually evolved in North America over millions of years, then died out there at the end of the last Ice Age, along with the mammoths and the giant ground sloths. When Columbus brought some two dozen horses over in 1493, on his second crossing, the animal was not arriving in a strange land but coming home to the continent where it began.

The Spanish herds multiplied, and in the 1600s escaped and traded horses spread north out of Mexico to the peoples of the Great Plains, who had always hunted bison on foot. Until then their only beast of burden had been the dog, which hauled their tents and gear on poles. So when the Lakota met the new animal, they named it sunka wakan, the sacred or mystery dog: a dog, but a wondrous one. Within a generation the Plains peoples had rebuilt their whole way of life around the horse.

the-house-of-wisdom.context_blurb:
In the 800s Baghdad, capital of the Abbasid caliphs, was the richest city of the Islamic world, and at its heart stood the House of Wisdom, the Bayt al-Hikma. There scholars turned the science and philosophy of Greece, Persia and India into Arabic and then built on them, keeping alive learning that Europe had largely lost.

The city itself was a marvel. In 762 the caliph al-Mansur founded his new capital on the Tigris, calling it Madinat al-Salam, which means City of Peace, and laid it out as a perfect circle, with his palace and its library at the centre. That palace library grew into the House of Wisdom. Its greatest translator was a Christian scholar, Hunayn ibn Ishaq, who ran the translation office, and a later biographer says the caliph paid him the weight of every finished book in gold. Around 830 al-Khwarizmi, a Persian mathematician, wrote a book on solving equations. The title of his book began with al-jabr, meaning restoration, the word for setting a broken bone, and a whole branch of mathematics took its name, algebra, from it. His own name travelled further still: when Europeans translated his books into Latin, the Latin form of al-Khwarizmi became algorithm, the word for every step-by-step procedure a computer follows.

The great patron was the caliph al-Ma'mun. By tradition, his love of Greek learning started with a dream in which Aristotle, seated on a throne, urged him to collect the wisdom of the ancients. After defeating the Byzantines, al-Ma'mun is said to have demanded Greek books from Emperor Theophilus instead of gold or land, and the manuscripts he prized most were works of astronomy and mathematics, among them Ptolemy's Almagest. Hunayn served later caliphs too. When the caliph al-Mutawakkil promised him a fortune to mix a poison for one of the court's enemies, Hunayn refused, saying his oath as a physician bound him to heal and never to do harm, and he spent a year in prison for it. The library lasted four centuries. In 1258 Hulagu Khan's Mongol army sacked Baghdad, and chroniclers claimed the soldiers hurled so many books into the Tigris that the river ran black with ink, a famous image that historians think is likely exaggerated. The astronomer Nasir al-Din al-Tusi is said to have rescued a great hoard of manuscripts.

The scholars did not only copy. On the flat plain of Sinjar, al-Ma'mun had two teams of astronomers set out, one marching due north and one due south, counting their paces and planting arrows, to measure one degree of latitude and so work out how big the Earth is; they came within a few hundred miles of the true circumference. Around 850 al-Kindi, a philosopher, produced the earliest known guide to breaking codes. His trick, now called frequency analysis, was to find the sign that turns up most often in a secret message and match it to the letter used most often in the everyday language, then work outward from there. His manuscript was lost for centuries until a researcher found it in an Istanbul archive in 1987. Of the Greek doctor Galen's writings, Hunayn put 129 into Arabic. For many of them every Greek copy has since vanished, so today those works of Galen can be read only through Hunayn's Arabic.

Some ideas reached astonishingly far ahead. The writer al-Jahiz, an Iraqi, described more than 350 creatures in his Book of Animals and argued that every animal must fight to survive, while its surroundings determine which creatures live on. That idea foreshadows natural selection, which Charles Darwin named a thousand years later, in 1859.

the-human-cost-and-shell-shock.context_blurb:
World War I killed nearly ten million soldiers and wounded more than twenty million, and many more came home with wounds no surgeon could see. Men who had been near exploding shells arrived at field hospitals trembling, mute, blind, deaf or paralysed, with no physical injury to explain it. Doctors at first blamed concussion from the blast; slowly they understood that the damage was to the mind.

In February 1915 the Cambridge psychologist Charles Myers described three British soldiers caught by bursting shells, one of whom lost his taste and smell, and in The Lancet he gave their condition the name that stuck: shell shock. Doctors noted ringing ears, dizziness, nightmares and, above all, a trembling of the whole body that one of them likened to a jelly shaking.

Treatment varied wildly. In 1917, at a hospital for officers outside Edinburgh called Craiglockhart, Dr William Rivers used a gentle talking cure, and two of his patients, the poets Wilfred Owen and Siegfried Sassoon, met there. While he recovered at Craiglockhart, Owen wrote Anthem for Doomed Youth, his lament for the young men dying at the front.

Other doctors were brutal. Dr Lewis Yealland treated soldiers struck dumb by trauma by forcing their mouths open and applying a strong electric current to the back of the throat until they spoke, and he claimed a perfect success rate. The army could be harsher still. One soldier, Private Harry Farr, shook so badly from shell shock that he could not hold a pen, yet in 1916 a court martial condemned him as a coward. When he was marched out to be shot on 18 October, he turned down the blindfold and faced the rifles with his eyes open. In 2006, after a campaign by his granddaughter, the British government pardoned him along with 305 other executed men.

the-hundred-years-war.context_blurb:
From 1337 to 1453 the kings of England and France fought a long, interrupted series of wars over who should wear the French crown. English kings claimed it through a French princess; French kings fought to keep it. The war really lasted 116 years, outliving five kings on each side, so its famous name falls short by sixteen years.

Its first great English victory came at Crécy in 1346, where English longbowmen cut down the charging French. Among the French rode the old King John of Bohemia, who was completely blind but meant to land at least one blow, so he had his knights tie their horses' reins to his and rode into the battle bound to them; next morning they were all found dead together. Tradition says the sixteen-year-old English prince Edward, known as the Black Prince, crossed the field afterwards and took the blind king's crest of three ostrich feathers and his motto, Ich dien, meaning I serve, and it has been the badge of every Prince of Wales since.

Ten years later, at Poitiers in 1356, the Black Prince's army won an even rarer prize: it took the French king, John II, prisoner on the field. That evening the prince honoured his royal captive by standing at the banquet and serving the king his food with his own hands, a gesture of chivalric respect for a brave enemy.

But the French recovered, and the end came at Castillon in 1453. There Jean Bureau's massed French cannon, perhaps more than two hundred guns, shattered the English attack, and John Talbot, the great English commander, died pinned under his horse after a cannon shot struck it. Bows had won Crécy and Poitiers; guns won the war. Of all its old lands in France, England kept only a single port, Calais.

the-iconoclasm-controversy.context_blurb:
For more than a century, from 726 to 843, the Byzantine Empire tore itself apart over holy pictures. The iconoclasts, or image-breakers, said that painting Christ, Mary and the saints and honouring those icons broke the commandment against idols, and emperors smashed icons and punished their defenders. Others answered that God had made himself visible in Christ, so he could be shown.

The sharpest defence came from John of Damascus, a Syrian monk writing under Muslim rule, out of the emperor's reach. He argued that whoever honours an icon is not worshipping wood and paint: the honour passes through the picture to the real person it shows, just as a kiss pressed on a portrait of a loved one is meant for the loved one.

The image-breakers had a clever argument of their own. The emperor Constantine V, who wrote thirteen treatises against icons, argued before a church council at Hieria in 754 that any painter of Christ falls into a trap: picturing his humanity alone would tear it away from his godhead, while picturing the godhead would muddle the two natures together. Christ's only faithful image, he concluded, was the Eucharist itself, its consecrated bread and wine. The Second Council of Nicaea overturned Hieria in 787 and made John's teaching official, and in 843 the empress Theodora restored the icons for good, which is why Orthodox churches are full of them today.

the-ides-of-march-caesar-s-assassination.context_blurb:
In 44 BC Julius Caesar was the master of Rome. He had made himself dictator for life, put his own face on coins and treated the Senate as a rubber stamp, and a band of senators, some of them his friends, resolved to kill him. They struck on the Ides of March, and the date has meant doom ever since.

The Ides was simply the middle of a Roman month: the 15th in March, May, July and October, and the 13th in the rest. A seer, Spurinna, a priest who read omens, had warned Caesar that danger would come no later than that day. As Caesar walked to the Senate that morning, he joked to Spurinna that the Ides had come, and Spurinna answered that they had indeed come, but they had not yet gone. Nobody in ancient Rome said the famous words "beware the Ides of March": William Shakespeare invented that line for his play Julius Caesar in 1599, while the ancient writers Suetonius and Plutarch record only Spurinna's warning.

Omens crowded the night before. By legend, Caesar's wife Calpurnia dreamed that he lay stabbed to death in her arms, and she begged him not to leave the house; he nearly gave in, until the conspirator Decimus Brutus came and coaxed him out. At the door Artemidorus, a Greek teacher, thrust a scroll at him that named every plotter. Caesar tucked it among the papers in his left hand to look at later, and he died with it still unread.

Inside the hall, the senator Tillius Cimber came up as if to plead for his exiled brother, then seized Caesar's toga and dragged it from his neck, the agreed signal. As the cloth tore away, Caesar cried out that this was violence. Servilius Casca struck first, a shallow blow at the neck from behind, and Caesar fought back with what he was holding, driving his iron writing-stylus through Casca's arm. Then about twenty of them closed in and dealt him twenty-three wounds, crowding so tightly that, as Plutarch tells it, several of the conspirators wounded one another. The plotters, at least sixty in all, did not think of themselves as murderers. They called themselves the Liberators, and in their own minds they were rescuing the Republic from a man who had made himself dictator for life. Brutus was so proud of the deed that he minted a silver coin about it: his own face on one side, and on the other two daggers flanking the cap of a freed slave above the words EID MAR, the Ides of March. It was a politician boasting of a killing on his own money, and only about a hundred of these coins survive.

The setting held a bitter irony. The Senate met that day in a hall Pompey the Great had built, and Caesar, who had beaten Pompey in the civil war, died at the foot of Pompey's own statue, its base drenched with his blood. Antistius, a Greek physician, examined the body, in what is often called the first recorded autopsy in history. He announced in the Forum that of all twenty-three wounds only one, the second, in the chest, had actually killed Caesar. And the Liberators had miscalculated. Within a few years Cassius and Brutus had both died, and Octavian, Caesar's adopted son, became sole master of Rome as Augustus, the first emperor. The killing meant to save the Republic ended it for good.

the-inca-empire-and-cusco.context_blurb:
In the 1400s the Inca built the largest empire the Americas had ever seen, running down the spine of the Andes from Ecuador into Chile and Argentina. They spoke Quechua, worshipped the Sun, and ruled without money, writing, iron or the wheel. Everything began at their capital, Cusco, high in the mountains of Peru.

The Inca thought of Cusco as the centre of everything. Its Quechua name, Qosqo, means the navel, and they saw it as the world's navel, the place where the four quarters of their realm joined. They never called their state the Inca Empire; they called it Tawantinsuyu, the Realm of the Four Parts, because four great regions fanned out from Cusco, so the name was itself a map. By legend, Manco Cápac and Mama Ocllo, a brother and sister who were children of the sun god Inti, walked out of Lake Titicaca with a golden staff. Inti had told them to settle wherever it sank into the earth, and at Cusco the staff slid into the ground. Later, legend says, the great ruler Pachacuti laid Cusco out as a crouching puma, the symbol of Inca might, with the fortress of Sacsayhuamán as its head and the main plaza as its belly. Inca masons shaped huge stones and fitted them with no mortar so precisely that you cannot push a sheet of paper or the point of a knife into the joints, which is why their walls still stand where later buildings have fallen in earthquakes.

The empire ran on clever systems instead of writing. To count people, tribute, llamas and stores, record-keepers tied knots in bundles of dyed cords, the height of each knot marking ones, tens or hundreds; the device was the quipu, and specialists called quipucamayocs read it. Chasquis, relay runners stationed a few kilometres apart, carried messages up to about 150 miles a day, fast enough to bring fish caught in the ocean up to the emperor in the mountains still fresh enough to eat. High in the freezing Andes, families preserved potatoes as chuño: they left them out to freeze at night, let them thaw by day and stamped out the water barefoot until the potatoes turned rock-hard. That was freeze-drying, and chuño kept for up to ten years in stone storehouses against famine. Where roads crossed deep canyons, the Inca wove suspension bridges from grass rope. One, the Q'eswachaka over the Apurímac River, still hangs today because every June the local communities take it down and weave it anew from fresh grass, as their ancestors have done for five centuries.

The man who turned Cusco into an empire was a prince who saved the city from an invading Chanca army, smashing it at Yahuar Pampa. He then took the throne name Pachacuti, meaning Earth-Shaker, the one who turns the world over, and set out to conquer the Andes. Cusco's holiest temple, the Qorikancha, the Golden Enclosure, had walls lined with some 700 sheets of gold and a garden of golden and silver maize plants and llamas at full size. The Spanish melted the gold into bars and built the church of Santo Domingo on the temple's foundations, but when earthquakes in 1650 and 1950 wrecked the church, the mortarless Inca walls beneath it stood firm.

The empire fell fast, weakened by a civil war between rival royal brothers. In 1532 the Spanish under Francisco Pizarro captured the emperor Atahualpa, who promised a room full of gold and twice that much silver, piled as high as his raised hand, for his freedom. His subjects brought the treasure in; Pizarro's men melted it into bars and then strangled Atahualpa anyway in 1533. Cusco survived as a Spanish colonial city built on Inca foundations, which is why its old stone walls still line its streets.

the-inca-empire-machu-picchu.context_blurb:
In the 1400s the Inca of Peru ruled the greatest empire of the early Americas, stretching down the Andes for thousands of miles from their capital, Cusco. They had no writing, no money, no iron and no wheel, yet they ruled perhaps ten million people. Their most famous creation is Machu Picchu, a stone city on a ridge high above the Urubamba River.

The Inca had none of the Old World's big work animals. Their one beast of burden was the llama, which could carry only about forty kilograms, so most loads moved on human backs. Their stonework still astonishes. Above Cusco they built the fortress of Sacsayhuamán from many-sided blocks, some over a hundred tons, shaped to interlock without mortar so tightly that not even a sheet of paper can be pushed into a joint.

The empire was laced together by the Qhapaq Ñan, the Road of the Lord: a coastal highway and a mountain highway running side by side down the continent, with some 40,000 kilometres of road in all, built without the wheel. Officials kept the accounts of people, harvests and taxes not in books but on the quipu, cords of coloured string tied with knots, in which the colour, the fibre and the kind of knot all carried meaning. Machu Picchu itself, raised around 1450 some eighty kilometres from Cusco, was neither a fortress nor a temple-city: it was a royal estate built for the emperor Pachacuti, his private retreat in the mountains.

On its highest point stands the Intihuatana, the Hitching Post of the Sun, a carved rock lined up with the winter solstice that worked as a calendar in stone, telling priests when each festival should begin. News moved by chasqui runners. Each man raced his own short leg of road and passed the message to a fresh runner, so news could travel up to 240 kilometres in a day, and the runners could even bring the emperor in Cusco fish from the Pacific while it was still fresh. For years of failed harvests the Inca stored chuño, potatoes frozen under the bitter night sky and trampled by day until all the water was gone; it was the earliest freeze-dried food anywhere, and it kept for years. Grass suspension bridges carried the roads over gorges, and one, the Q'eswachaka over the Apurímac, survives because every June local Quechua communities tear it down and rebuild it from scratch with fresh grass: women twist ichu grass into thin rope, and the whole bridge is rewoven in three days of work, prayer and festival.

The quipu was a true place-value system. Knots sat in base-ten rows for units, tens, hundreds and thousands, and where a number had a zero, the knot-maker simply left an empty space on the cord. The end came in 1532, when Francisco Pizarro reached Cajamarca with fewer than 170 Spaniards and met the emperor Atahualpa amid thousands of his warriors. Pizarro's hidden horsemen charged the crowd in an ambush and seized Atahualpa in the middle of his own army.

To buy his freedom, Atahualpa promised a room full of gold and twice that much silver, piled as high as his raised hand, and for four months llama trains brought in the treasure. When the ransom was paid, the Spanish strangled him anyway. The empire had no coins, so families paid the emperor in work. Each community owed the mit'a, a turn of labour on roads, terraces, bridges or state fields, and the yearly rebuilding of the Q'eswachaka began as just such a duty. It was Pachacuti who began it all. Taking the throne in 1438, he launched conquests that spread across the length of the Andes within three generations, and his chosen name fitted: Pachacuti means the Overturner of the World, a cataclysm in human form.

the-inca-road-system-and-rope-bridges.context_blurb:
The Inca held their mountain empire together with one of the great road networks of the ancient world: tens of thousands of miles of paved, drained roads along the Andes and the Pacific coast, linking Cusco to the farthest provinces. Spanish chroniclers used to Roman roads were astonished by them. Where the roads met deep gorges, Inca engineers slung suspension bridges of twisted grass.

One bridge survives. Every June more than a thousand people from four Quechua communities, Huinchiri among them, rebuild the Q'eswachaka over a gorge of the Apurímac River by hand in about three days. Twisting the grass into six great cables as thick as a person's thigh, they weave the whole bridge from braided grass, then drop the old one into the river. UNESCO named the yearly renewal an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2013.

Along the roads ran the chasquis, relay runners posted in pairs. A fresh runner sprinted beside each arriving one to take the message without stopping, so news moved up to about 150 miles a day, and fish caught in the Pacific reached the emperor's table in Cusco in roughly two days, still fresh. The chronicler Pedro de Cieza de León judged that even the swiftest horses could not have carried news faster, and the Inca had no horses at all.

the-industrial-revolution-as-the-great-e.context_blurb:
For almost all of history nearly everyone lived close to the same bare standard: a modest ration of grain, a few homemade garments, a smoky hut and a short life menaced by famine and disease. Then, beginning in Britain in the late 1700s, output per person began to climb and never stopped. The economic historian Deirdre McCloskey calls it the Great Enrichment.

Before that, the line on the graph was nearly flat. At the birth of Christ the average person lived on roughly two dollars a day in today's money, and when William the Conqueror invaded England in 1066, income had not budged from that two dollars; by 1800 it had crept only to $2.80. That long flat stretch is the handle of a hockey stick, and around 1800 the blade turned sharply upward.

The early factory age, the time of William Blake's dark satanic mills, is remembered for child labour and choking smoke. Yet in that same grim era the death of young children began its long fall for the first time in history. Around 1800 more than a third of all children died before turning five, and a mother of five to seven expected to bury two or three of them. Today the world's rate is around four percent, and that escape from early death, more than the misery of the mills, is the real headline of the age.

the-internal-african-slave-trade-and-the.context_blurb:
Britain outlawed its own slave trade in 1807, but the trade did not stop. African kings and Arab and Swahili merchants kept raiding the interior for captives, and Portuguese, Brazilian and Spanish ships kept carrying them away. Ending it took decades of Royal Navy patrols off both coasts of Africa, and the stubborn witness of men like David Livingstone.

The Navy's most famous hunter, HMS Black Joke, had once been a slave ship herself: the Royal Navy seized the Brazilian slaver Henriquetta in 1827, renamed her and turned her on her old trade, and in one year she caught eleven slavers. On the East African side the greatest slave and ivory trader was Hamad bin Muhammad of Zanzibar, who led armed caravans of thousands deep into the Congo. Everyone knew him as Tippu Tip, a nickname said to echo the tip-tip sound of his men's guns. In 1887 the Belgian-run Congo Free State even made him a district governor.

In West Africa, the Kingdom of Dahomey marched its captives to the port of Ouidah. Tradition says that before the sale, captives were made to walk around a Tree of Forgetfulness, a ritual meant to wipe away their memories of home and family before the ocean crossing. The story is legend rather than documented fact, but it shows what the trade tried to do to a person. Livingstone, the Scottish missionary and explorer, crossed and recrossed central Africa on foot for years, exposing the East African trade. When he died in 1873 in what is now Zambia, his African companions buried his heart there, dried his body in the sun and carried it some 930 miles on foot to the coast, so that it could be shipped home to Westminster Abbey.

On 1 February 1829 the little Black Joke chased the Spanish slaver El Almirante for thirty-one hours, rowing when the wind died, then beat her bigger guns in eighty minutes and freed the 466 people in her hold. In the words of a naval surgeon, this one small ship had done more against the slave trade than all the other ships on the station combined. In 1873 the British made Zanzibar's sultan close East Africa's largest slave market. Anglican missionaries raised a cathedral on the site and set its altar deliberately over the spot where the market's whipping post had stood, turning the cruellest place in the market into the holiest.

The trade also had powerful African defenders. In the 1840s British envoys urged Ghezo, the king of Dahomey, to give up selling captives, and he refused: the trade, he said, ruled his people's whole way of life and was the source of their glory and wealth. It took a Royal Navy blockade in 1851 to force Dahomey into a treaty the following year.

the-internal-african-slave-trade-its-wes.context_blurb:
Slavery in Africa is far older than the Atlantic trade. African kingdoms enslaved war captives and sold people north across the Sahara and east over the Red Sea for a thousand years before European ships arrived, and many of them supplied the Atlantic trade too. What finally broke the trade was a campaign born in Christian Britain, led by William Wilberforce and Thomas Clarkson, and enforced at sea by the Royal Navy.

Once Parliament outlawed the British slave trade in 1807, the Navy's West Africa Squadron patrolled the coast. Its fastest hunter, HMS Black Joke, was no Navy-built warship but the Henriquetta, a swift slave ship from Baltimore that the Navy had captured and then turned against the trade. In East Africa the trade's great lord was Hamad bin Muhammad al-Murjabi of Zanzibar, who started with fewer than a hundred armed men and became one of history's wealthiest dealers in slaves and ivory. He said his nickname, Tippu Tip, came from the tip-tip sound of his guns firing, and by 1895 he held seven plantations and some 10,000 slaves. Dahomey, a West African kingdom, enriched itself by raiding its neighbours, and its most feared raiders were women: the Agojie, an all-female regiment some 6,000 strong at its peak in the 1840s, whom Europeans called the Dahomey Amazons. They seized captives to sell or to be sacrificed at the kingdom's Annual Customs.

On the Gold Coast, the Asante Empire rose to dominance by the mid-1700s through a vicious cycle with British and Dutch traders: it sold them war captives in exchange for firearms, used the guns to conquer more peoples, and sold the new captives for more guns. The Royal Navy's answer took half a century. From about 1808 to 1860 the West Africa Squadron patrolled thousands of kilometres of coast, seizing some sixteen hundred slave ships and setting about 150,000 Africans free. In 1871 David Livingstone, the Scottish missionary and explorer, was deep in the Congo recording what the slavers did. With his paper and ink used up, he made ink from clothing dye and filled the margins of an old copy of The Standard newspaper with his field diary.

Among the Asante, slavery was old, but it differed from the slavery Europeans built in the Americas. In Akan society an enslaved person could rise to real standing and influence in the community, while chattel slavery across the Atlantic fixed a person's status for life. Livingstone's diary recorded the worst day he ever saw. On 15 July 1871 at Nyangwe, a busy market town on the Lualaba, gunmen working for the slaver Dugumbe fired into the crowd of shoppers and killed some 400 to 500 people. That massacre became the emotional heart of Livingstone's campaign against the East African slave trade. Exactly a year before his death, in May 1872, he wrote a prayer asking heaven to bless anyone, American, English or Turk, who would help heal the open sore of the world, as he called the slave trade, and those words are carved on his tomb in Westminster Abbey. The patrol had its own cost. Some sixteen hundred of the squadron's sailors died in the thirty-five years after 1830, almost all of them from tropical disease rather than in battle, and the coast earned the nickname the white man's grave.

The political scientists Robert Pape and Chaim Kaufmann later added up the bill. Britain's sixty-year campaign against the Atlantic trade cost about 1.8 percent of national income, and they called it the costliest example of international moral action on record in modern history. Under the Frere Treaty of 1873, Sultan Barghash of Zanzibar closed East Africa's biggest slave market, which had handled up to 50,000 captives a year. Anglican missionaries raised Christ Church Cathedral on the site, and its altar stands where the whipping post once stood.

the-internal-african-slave-trade-that-fe.context_blurb:
The Atlantic slave trade did not begin from nothing. It plugged into slave systems that had run inside Africa, and across the Sahara and the Indian Ocean, for centuries before any European ship arrived. On much of the West African coast Europeans never went inland at all; they anchored offshore and bought captives that African kingdoms and merchants delivered to them in chains.

The older system shows in the records. In the 1300s, long before the first European slave ship, the Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta crossed the rich Mali Empire and noted that its people showed their rank by competing over how many slaves and servants they owned. European demand later expanded that old internal system enormously.

It became a machine. King Agaja of Dahomey, who reigned from 1718 to 1740, re-armed his soldiers from bows to muskets, and the historian Robert Harms explains why the kingdom then could not stop: the only way to get more firearms and gunpowder was to sell more captives, so Dahomey's wars and its slave sales fed each other in an endless loop. None of this lessens what European buyers did; it means the trade grew to its terrible size because partners at both ends profited from it.
