the-internet-and-the-world-wide-web.context_blurb:
The Internet began as ARPANET, a network the Pentagon paid for in the 1960s so that research computers at American universities could share data over telephone lines. Over two decades engineers stretched it into a worldwide web of networks. Then, at the end of the 1980s, an English physicist built the World Wide Web, the system of linked pages that runs on top of it.

ARPANET's first message went out on 29 October 1969. At UCLA the programmer Charley Kline began typing LOGIN to a computer at Stanford, but the computer at the far end froze after two letters, so the first word ever carried across the network was LO. Leonard Kleinrock, whose lab sent it, loved that the accident spelled lo, as in lo and behold; about an hour later the full LOGIN went through.

The physicist was Tim Berners-Lee, working at CERN, the European particle-physics laboratory near Geneva, and he wrote the first browser and web server himself. He could have patented the Web and charged for every use. Instead, on 30 April 1993, CERN released the Web's source code into the public domain, free for anyone to use forever, because, as Berners-Lee put it, nobody can offer a universal space and keep control of it at the same time. That gift is why the Web belongs to everyone.

the-iron-curtain-descends-origins-of-the.context_blurb:
When the Second World War ended in 1945, the wartime alliance between the Western democracies and Stalin's Soviet Union fell apart within months. Behind the Red Army's lines in Eastern Europe, local communists backed by Moscow seized power country by country through rigged elections, intimidation and show trials, and the continent split into two camps for more than forty years.

In March 1946 Winston Churchill, recently voted out as Britain's prime minister, spoke at a small college in Fulton, Missouri. From Stettin on the Baltic to Trieste on the Adriatic, he warned, an iron curtain had descended across the Continent. He had not coined the phrase, but his speech made the iron curtain the name of the Cold War's dividing line.

Hungary's communist leader, Mátyás Rákosi, bragged that he had wiped out the other parties not with a single ban but piece by piece, demanding a little more every day, the way you cut a costly sausage into slivers. He called it salami tactics, and the name became the textbook term for how Moscow's parties took their opponents apart. Czechoslovakia held out longest as Eastern Europe's last democracy, until the Communist Party grabbed absolute control in February 1948. On 10 March Jan Masaryk, the foreign minister and son of Czechoslovakia's first president, was found dead on the pavement below his bathroom window. The government called it suicide, many suspected murder, and a Czech investigation in 2021 could not rule murder out.

the-iroquois-confederacy-haudenosaunee.context_blurb:
The Haudenosaunee, whom the French and English called the Iroquois, were a league of five nations, the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca, in what is now upstate New York; the Tuscarora joined as a sixth in the 1700s. Their tradition says the league was founded long before Europeans came, by the Peacemaker and his companion Hiawatha.

The five nations had been locked in endless war. To seal the peace, the Peacemaker, Deganawida, pulled up a great white pine, and the nations buried their weapons of war in the hole beneath its roots; then he replanted the pine over them as the Tree of Peace. Haudenosaunee tradition holds that this is where the English phrase about burying the hatchet comes from.

The league's Grand Council seats fifty sachems, with a set number of chiefs from every nation. The men did not choose themselves: the clan mothers, the leading women of every clan, selected the sachems and could strip a chief of his title if he failed his people. Some writers claim the league's Great Law shaped the United States Constitution, but historians such as Jack Rakove and Elisabeth Tooker doubt it, pointing out that the Constitution gave women no such power.

the-italian-renaissance-florence.context_blurb:
In the 1400s Florence, a small city on the Arno River in central Italy, became the heart of an astonishing flowering of art and learning. Its bankers had grown rich enough to pay for genius, and its scholars and artists looked back to ancient Greece and Rome as a living inheritance being handed back to them.

The era took its name from a French word, Renaissance, which means rebirth: the rebirth of ancient art and learning after long neglect. The painter and historian Giorgio Vasari had used the Italian word for it, rinascita, in 1550. Florence's cathedral, Santa Maria del Fiore, is Saint Mary of the Flower. Begun in 1296, it spent more than a hundred years with a gaping hole where its dome should be, because no one knew how to roof so wide a space.

The money behind it all was Florentine. In 1252 the city began minting the florin, a small coin of pure gold so reliable in weight that merchants and kings from London to Constantinople treated it as the yardstick currency of their day. Donatello cast his bronze David around 1440 for the Medici, the banking family that ran the city, and they set it on a column in their palace courtyard. It was the first free-standing nude statue made since the fall of Rome, more than a thousand years before. Around 1485 Sandro Botticelli painted The Birth of Venus, in which the Roman goddess of love, newly born and fully grown, rides to shore standing on a giant scallop shell, blown in by the wind god Zephyr.

Then came the dome. Between 1420 and 1436 Filippo Brunelleschi set more than four million bricks in a herringbone pattern, spinapesce or fish-spine, in which the bricks lock into one another so that each new ring of the dome held itself up while it was built, with no wooden frame beneath. Legend, told by Vasari, says that while competing for the job Brunelleschi challenged his rivals to stand an egg upright on smooth marble. All of them failed; he cracked the bottom of the egg flat against the marble so that it stood, and told them they could have built the dome too, if only they had known how. In 1501 a 26-year-old named Michelangelo took on a scarred marble block the Florentines called the Giant, which two earlier sculptors had hacked at and abandoned, and from it he carved his 17-foot David, set up outside the town hall in 1504. The movement's first great scholar came earlier still. In 1336 Petrarch, later called the Father of Humanism, climbed Mont Ventoux just to stand on top and enjoy the view, a strange thing to do in his day, and that climb has earned him the playful nickname of the first tourist.

For three decades Cosimo de' Medici governed Florence without crown or title, a banker pulling the strings, and Pope Pius II called him king in all but name. When he died in 1464, the city carved Pater Patriae, Father of the Fatherland, on his tomb. His grandsons nearly died for that power. During Mass in the cathedral on 26 April 1478, Pazzi conspirators attacked Lorenzo and Giuliano de' Medici, and the killers struck at the holiest moment, the instant the priest lifted the Host. Giuliano was stabbed nineteen times and killed; Lorenzo escaped with a wound to the neck, and furious Florentines hunted down the plotters and executed about eighty people. Scholars hunted lost books like treasure. In 1417 Poggio Bracciolini, searching in a remote monastery in Germany, found the last surviving copy of Lucretius's great Roman poem On the Nature of Things and put it back into circulation.

the-july-crisis-and-alliance-system.context_blurb:
On 28 June 1914 a young Bosnian Serb, Gavrilo Princip, shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, in Sarajevo. In the six weeks that followed, the July Crisis, a web of alliances and railway timetables dragged every great power of Europe into war, though almost no historian now believes the war could not have been avoided.

The killing was a fluke. Earlier that day a bomb thrown at the archduke's car bounced off and the motorcade sped away; later his chauffeur turned into the wrong street, stopped to back up, and stalled, and the car sat dead in front of Moritz Schiller's delicatessen, exactly where Princip was standing. Austria-Hungary wanted to crush Serbia but feared Russia would defend the Serbs, so in early July Kaiser Wilhelm II promised that Germany would back whatever Austria chose to do. Historians call that open-ended promise Germany's blank cheque, like a signed cheque with the amount left empty.

As war loomed, Wilhelm and Russia's Tsar Nicholas II, who were first cousins, sent each other telegrams as Willy and Nicky, and they wrote them in English, their family's common language. Nicholas even begged Wilhelm to send the dispute to the peace court at The Hague. But the generals' machinery was already turning. Nicholas wanted to mobilise against Austria alone, so as not to frighten Germany, but his generals said Russia's plans allowed only full mobilization, and any half-measure would snarl the train schedules and leave the country defenceless. So the Tsar wired Wilhelm that it was technically impossible to stop Russia's military preparations.

On 4 August German troops invaded neutral Belgium, tearing up an 1839 treaty that guaranteed Belgian neutrality. Britain went to war to uphold that treaty, and the German chancellor, Theobald von Bethmann-Hollweg, sneered that Britain was going to war over a scrap of paper. The jab backfired: British propaganda used it to show that Germany held its sworn word worthless. The evening before, as Britain prepared to declare war, the foreign secretary Sir Edward Grey watched the lamplighters at work from his office window. The lamps were going out all over Europe, he remarked, and his generation would not see them lit again.

the-kamikaze-failed-mongol-invasions-of-.context_blurb:
In the 1270s and 1280s Kublai Khan, the Mongol emperor who had conquered China, twice sent fleets to conquer Japan. Both times Japanese samurai fought the invaders to a standstill on the beaches of Kyushu, and both times a storm finished the job.

The Japanese were sure their gods had sent those storms in 1274 and 1281 in answer to their prayers, and they named them kamikaze, the divine wind. The second invasion, in 1281, was enormous: some 4,400 ships carrying perhaps 100,000 men. Afraid of samurai raiders rowing out at night, the Mongols lashed the fleet into great rafts of ships, hull against hull. When the typhoon struck, the bound ships could not ride the waves separately, and the storm smashed them against one another and against the rocks. Between half and two-thirds of the army died, and the survivors stranded ashore were executed.

For centuries the divine winds were a legend no one could prove. In 2014 Jon Woodruff, a geologist, sampled the mud at the bottom of lakes beside Hakata Bay, the invaders' landing place, and found distinct storm layers dated to the late 1200s, matching the years 1274 and 1281. Japan later revived the name for its suicide pilots in the Second World War.

the-katyn-forest-massacre.context_blurb:
In September 1939 Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union carved up Poland between them under a secret pact. In the spring of 1940 Stalin's secret police, the NKVD, shot some 22,000 captured Polish officers, policemen, priests and civic leaders and buried them in mass graves, the best known in the Katyn Forest near Smolensk.

The NKVD's chief executioner, Vasily Blokhin, killed thousands of prisoners himself over 28 nights, using a briefcase of German Walther pistols rather than Soviet revolvers. He chose them partly because Soviet revolvers kicked too hard for hours of shooting, and partly so that if the graves were ever found, the bullets would point to Germany rather than the Soviet Union. The cover-up was built into the murder weapon itself.

When German troops found the graves in April 1943, the Germans accused the Soviets. Britain's diplomats were privately all but certain the Soviets were guilty, yet Winston Churchill secretly promised Stalin that Britain would vigorously oppose any Red Cross investigation, choosing silence to keep the wartime alliance whole. Moscow kept blaming the Nazis for nearly fifty years, until in 1990 Mikhail Gorbachev's government admitted that the NKVD had done it.

the-khmer-rouge-the-killing-fields.context_blurb:
In April 1975 the Khmer Rouge, the communist guerrilla army of Pol Pot, captured Cambodia's capital, Phnom Penh, and set out to turn the whole country into a classless peasant commune. In less than four years the regime killed some 1.5 to 2 million Cambodians, roughly one person in four, through execution, starvation and forced labour. Its mass graves became known as the Killing Fields.

The regime declared that history was starting over: it abolished money, markets, schools and religion and named 1975 Year Zero. On 17 April its soldiers emptied Phnom Penh, a city of some two million, with a lie blared from loudspeakers, warning that American planes were about to bomb it. Within three days they had marched the whole population out at gunpoint, and almost no one was allowed back. The soldiers emptied the hospitals too, driving some 20,000 sick and wounded into the streets and wheeling out patients too weak to walk still lying in their beds, drip bottles swaying.

The regime's most infamous prison, code-named S-21, stood in Phnom Penh in a former high school, Tuol Svay Prey, whose classrooms became torture and interrogation cells. Some 16,000 people passed through it and barely a dozen survived; today it is the Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum.

Under the Khmer Rouge, education itself was a death sentence. Guards hunted the city-bred "new people" by crude clues such as soft hands, a foreign language and a pair of eyeglasses, all read as marks of the educated class the regime meant to destroy. Real power was faceless. People were ordered to obey Angkar, the Organization, behind which stood Brother Number One, Pol Pot, whose real name was Saloth Sar, and many Cambodians never learned who he was. At S-21 guards photographed new prisoners, made them write out their life stories and tortured them until they confessed to serving foreign masters: the CIA, the KGB or Vietnam. The painter Vann Nath survived because the prison's chief, Duch, wanted his skill: he was kept alive to paint admiring portraits of Pol Pot. After the regime fell he painted the tortures he had seen, and his pictures became evidence. Prisoners were trucked to Choeung Ek, outside the city, and killed beside pits the victims themselves had often been made to dig. To save bullets, the executioners beat most of them to death with hoes, hammers, axes and bamboo. There, guards killed babies and small children against the trunk of a tree, reasoning coldly that a child left alive might one day grow up to avenge its parents. When Vietnam invaded and captured Phnom Penh on 7 January 1979, ending the regime, its soldiers found a ghost city with barely seventy people left in it.

The regime's own words show its logic. Survivors such as Teeda Butt Mam remembered the slogan cadres used on the educated: keeping you brings no benefit, and destroying you brings no loss. Its paranoia turned inward until just six of its original twenty-two top leaders survived. Pol Pot had his former defence chief Son Sen killed in 1997, and with him fourteen of Son Sen's relatives, grandchildren included, a massacre that finally turned his own men against him. That year the journalist Nate Thayer reached the sick old man in his jungle hideout for his first interview in eighteen years. Asked whether he felt remorse, Pol Pot said he had come to carry out the struggle, not to kill people, and that his conscience was clear; asked if he wished to apologise, he said no. Historians still argue over the causes of his rise. From 1969 to 1973 the United States secretly bombed Cambodia, unloading over 500,000 tons of bombs in raids code-named Breakfast, Lunch and Dinner, and many historians argue that the devastation helped the Khmer Rouge recruit and seize power.

the-league-of-nations.context_blurb:
After the First World War the victors created the League of Nations, the first world body meant to stop wars through collective security: its members would stand together against any aggressor. It did useful work on refugees and public health, but its central promise collapsed at its first serious tests.

Its loudest champion was the American president Woodrow Wilson, who received the Nobel Peace Prize for 1919 for promoting it, yet the United States never joined, because the Senate refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles. In 1936 the League moved into the Palace of Nations, a headquarters raised for it on the shore of Lake Geneva.

The first great test came in Manchuria. In September 1931 Lieutenant Kawamoto Suemori of the Japanese army exploded a little dynamite next to a Japanese-owned railway line near Mukden; the blast was so feeble that trains still passed over it. Japan blamed China and used the staged blast as a pretext to seize all of Manchuria, where it set up the puppet state of Manchukuo.

The League's Lytton Commission rejected Japan's claim that Manchukuo was independent, and the Assembly voted 42 to 1 in February 1933 to accept the report. Japan's delegation, led by Yosuke Matsuoka, walked out of the Assembly, and in March Japan quit the League altogether. Italy's invasion of Abyssinia, today's Ethiopia, in 1935 finished the League's authority. Publicly, Samuel Hoare of Britain and Pierre Laval of France supported the League; privately they agreed in the Hoare-Laval Pact to give Mussolini two-thirds of Abyssinia. A French paper leaked the deal in December 1935, and both men had to resign.

The League was built to fail: any single Council member could block action, and it owned no soldiers. On 30 June 1936 the exiled emperor of Abyssinia, Haile Selassie, stood before the Assembly as Italian reporters jeered him, and he warned the great powers that what had happened to his country today would happen to them tomorrow. The Second World War began just over three years later.

the-library-and-lighthouse-of-alexandria.context_blurb:
Founded by Alexander the Great in 331 BC and ruled afterwards by the Greek-speaking Ptolemies, Alexandria in Egypt became the brightest city of the ancient Mediterranean. Its kings poured money into a great library and research institute where Euclid wrote, Eratosthenes measured the Earth, and Jewish scholars put the Hebrew Bible into Greek.

The Ptolemies wanted every book in the world. Harbour officials searched each ship that docked, and when they found a scroll, the scribes copied it, kept the original for the Library and handed the owner the fresh copy. Those confiscated books were catalogued as books from the ships.

In the harbour stood another wonder, the Pharos, a lighthouse more than a hundred metres high, taller than any building of its time except the Great Pyramid. At its top a polished bronze mirror flashed the sun by day and reflected a great fire by night, throwing its warning far out to sea. The lighthouse stood for some 1,600 years before earthquakes toppled it, while the Library declined slowly through neglect and fire.

the-maya-and-their-stepped-pyramids.context_blurb:
Between about AD 250 and 900 the Maya of southern Mexico and Central America built great cities of carved limestone across the rainforest, each ruled by its own divine king. At their hearts rose stepped pyramid-temples, palaces and ball courts. The Maya were never one empire, but they shared a writing system, a calendar and a mathematics as advanced as any of their age.

The jungle city of Tikal, in Guatemala, is so dramatic that the first Star Wars film used it for the rebel hideout on a forest moon: the shot of temples poking through the trees was filmed from the top of Tikal's Temple IV. At Chichén Itzá in Mexico's Yucatán, the great pyramid called El Castillo, raised around a millennium ago to honour Kukulkan, the feathered serpent, has four stairways of 91 steps each. Add the single step of the platform on top and the total is 365, one step for every day of the solar year, a calendar built in stone.

Twice a year, at the spring and autumn equinoxes, the late-afternoon sun throws a zigzag of light and shadow triangles down the edge of El Castillo's north stairway. It meets the carved stone serpent head at the bottom, so that for a few minutes a giant serpent seems to slither down the pyramid: Kukulkan himself descending. Maya scribes wrote numbers with a dot for one and a bar for five, and for zero they drew a shell, making them among the first people anywhere to write zero as a placeholder. Pakal took the throne of Palenque in 615, when he was only twelve, and ruled until about 683, roughly 68 years, one of the longest verified reigns in world history.

Chichén Itzá's Great Ball Court, the largest in the ancient Americas, is longer than a football field, and its builders gave it an uncanny voice: a whisper at the temple at one end carries clearly to the temple at the other, about 140 metres away, and a single clap echoes back again and again. Its wall panels show what the game could cost. One carving shows a ballplayer on his knees, his head struck off, and from his neck, in place of blood, sprouts a tangle of serpents along with a plant, evidence that the game could end in human sacrifice. Beside the city lies the Sacred Cenote, a great natural sinkhole, where the Maya threw offerings of gold, jade, copper and incense to Chaac, god of rain. When divers dredged it, they brought up the bones of roughly two hundred people as well, many of them children: the Maya had offered human lives there too. In a royal tomb sealed deep inside Temple I at Tikal, King Jasaw Chan K'awiil I was laid out on jaguar pelts amid pearls and stingray spines, and around his neck hung a jade necklace of 114 enormous beads, nearly four kilograms of stone.

For centuries no one could read the Maya's more than 800 picture-signs, the only fully developed writing system of the ancient Americas. When scholars finally cracked it, experts ranked the feat beside the reading of Egyptian hieroglyphs as one of history's great decipherments. In 1952 Alberto Ruz Lhuillier raised a stone in the floor of the Temple of the Inscriptions at Palenque and uncovered a secret staircase filled with rubble. After years of digging he reached a sealed crypt about 25 metres down, untouched for some 1,300 years, and so proved for the first time that a Maya pyramid could hold a king's tomb deep inside it, not just a temple on top.

It was Pakal's tomb. His stone coffin was sealed by a carved limestone lid of about seven tons, among the best-known carvings the Maya ever made: it shows the king at the moment of death, falling backward into the open jaws of Xibalba, the underworld, while the great World Tree rises out of his body with the Celestial Bird perched on top.

the-maya-civilization.context_blurb:
The Maya of southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and Honduras built one of the great original civilizations of the world. Their classic cities flourished from about AD 250 to 900 under rival divine kings, and their scholars developed a calendar, a mathematics with zero, a full writing system and an astronomy of startling precision. Millions of Maya people still live in the old homeland today.

Some 1,500 years ago, centuries before Europe had a zero, Maya scribes drew a little shell to mean nothing, and few other peoples on Earth ever devised a zero independently. With a dot for one, a bar for five and the shell for zero, a scribe could write any number: three dots over two bars made thirteen.

The Maya counted in twenties rather than tens, because they counted on their toes as well as their fingers, and each level of a stacked number was worth twenty times the one below. Their nobles prized a drink so highly that owning it marked rank. Scholars deciphered the word kakaw painted on pots from noble tombs, and a Hershey chemist found theobromine, chocolate's chemical fingerprint, in the dried residue inside: the drink was chocolate.

Their solar calendar had eighteen months of twenty days, leaving five days over when the year closed, the nameless Wayeb'. People feared them, stayed home and avoided strangers, because they believed the doors between the living world and the Underworld swung open during those days. No single empire ever united the Maya. The two greatest cities, Tikal and Calakmul, fought a feud so long and bitter that scholars nickname it the Star Wars. In 562 Calakmul's king, Sky Witness, crushed Tikal and began some 130 years of Tikal's decline. In 695 Jasaw Chan K'awiil I of Tikal finally turned the tables, defeating Calakmul and carrying off its patron god, a capture that broke Calakmul's power and made Tikal supreme again. When Alberto Ruz Lhuillier finally broke into Pakal's crypt at Palenque in 1952, he found the king's face covered by a mask made of jade mosaic. Fringe theorists later nicknamed Pakal's strange carved coffin lid the Palenque Astronaut.

Many people feared the world would end on 21 December 2012, when the Maya Long Count reached 13.0.0.0.0. Scholars say the Maya expected no doomsday: the great cycles would simply roll over and keep counting, and one inscription even projects a date into the year 4772. Most Maya books are gone. Diego de Landa, a Spanish friar, condemned the painted books as the devil's lies and had dozens of them burned in one bonfire at Maní in 1562. Only three Maya books from before the conquest survive, plus a scrap of a fourth.

Reading the script took a bold idea. In 1952 the young Soviet linguist Yuri Knorozov showed that the glyphs did not spell words letter by letter, as the so-called de Landa alphabet seemed to suggest, but stood for syllables of speech; that insight unlocked the script, and about 80 percent of Maya writing can now be read. One of the three surviving books, the Dresden Codex, is a manual of astronomy with a table for tracking Venus. The Maya put Venus's cycle at 584 days against a true 583.92, and over five hundred years their table drifts by less than two hours.

the-medici-of-florence.context_blurb:
The Medici were a Florentine banking family who turned money into power. From the early 1400s they ran Florence from behind the scenes, paid for the greatest artists of the age, and went on to produce popes, queens of France and, later, the grand dukes of Tuscany. Their story mixes genius with blood.

Cosimo de' Medici bankrolled the brilliant, debt-ridden builder Filippo Brunelleschi, the one man who knew how to finish a job everyone else had given up on, and by 1436 Brunelleschi had raised the great dome of Florence's cathedral, still the biggest masonry dome in the world.

At Easter in 1478, during High Mass in that same cathedral, the rival Pazzi family struck at Cosimo's grandsons, Lorenzo and Giuliano. The plotters chose as their signal the holiest instant of the Mass, when the priest raised the consecrated Host at the altar and every eye turned forward. The professional soldier hired to kill Lorenzo refused at the last moment to shed blood in a church, so two priests, Stefano da Bagnone and Antonio Maffei, took his place, and both failed to kill him. Giuliano was stabbed nineteen times and died on the cathedral floor. Lorenzo, bleeding from a neck wound, ran into the sacristy, where his friends slammed its heavy bronze doors shut against the attackers and saved his life.

Florence took savage revenge. One conspirator, Bernardo Bandini dei Baroncelli, fled as far as Constantinople before he was caught, dragged home and left hanging from the town hall's window, and in 1479 the young Leonardo da Vinci sketched the dangling body in careful detail, even noting the colours of his clothes.

Two Medici sons became popes. One of them, Clement VII, faced King Henry VIII of England in the 1530s, when Henry, eager to marry Anne Boleyn, demanded that his marriage to Catherine of Aragon be annulled. Clement refused, and his refusal helped push England to break with Rome. The other Medici pope was Leo X, the son of Lorenzo the Magnificent.

the-medieval-catholic-church-the-pope.context_blurb:
In medieval Europe the Catholic Church touched almost every life. It baptised, married and buried, ran schools and charities, and at its head the pope crowned emperors, excommunicated kings and claimed that his spiritual authority outranked any ruler's. It also bred corruption, and reformers spent centuries fighting it.

Every farming family owed the Church a tithe, a tenth of all it produced each year, from the Old English word for a tenth. Since peasants had few coins, most paid in kind, handing over sheaves of wheat and barley, livestock and fish. Parishes stored the grain in great tithe barns, and builders made many of them of solid stone because the danger they feared most for a stored harvest was fire. The Church effectively invented the hospital as an institution, too. In 651 it founded the Hôtel-Dieu, the hostel of God, beside Notre-Dame in Paris to shelter the poor, the sick and pilgrims, and thirteen centuries later it is still a working hospital, one of the oldest on Earth.

Popes and kings fought over who ruled whom. Pope Gregory VII excommunicated the German ruler Henry IV, freeing his subjects from obeying him, and in the bitter winter of 1077 Henry crossed the frozen Alps to the castle of Canossa, where the pope was staying. To prove his penitence he stood barefoot outside the gate, in a rough wool garment, for three days, until Gregory forgave him. To go to Canossa still means to eat humble pie. After the death of Clement IV in 1268, the cardinals quarrelled for nearly three years and could not agree on a new pope. Viterbo's exasperated citizens shut them inside the palace on bread and water, and when that failed, they tore the roof off over the cardinals' heads. The election lasted 1,006 days, and the new pope, Gregory X, ruled that cardinals must be locked in until they chose, which is why a papal election is called a conclave, from the Latin for with a key.

The Church's gravest punishment was the curse of bell, book and candle. A bishop with twelve priests rang a bell, closed the holy book with a bang and threw down a burning candle, stamping it out: as the flame died, so the sinner's soul was cast out from God's light. A pope could punish a whole kingdom. King John of England refused to accept Innocent III's archbishop of Canterbury, so in 1208 the pope struck the entire kingdom with an interdict lasting six years: churches held no services, couples could not marry in church, and the bells that rang the hours and gave the alarm went silent everywhere. Reformers fought the sale of holy things. The sin of buying church office is called simony after Simon, a sorcerer in the Book of Acts who offered the apostles money for the power to give the Holy Spirit; Peter told him that his silver could perish with him, since the gift of God could not be bought. In the early sixteenth century churchmen sold indulgences, pardons said to shorten a soul's stay in purgatory, to pay for rebuilding St Peter's in Rome, and the friar Johann Tetzel became infamous for a sales jingle: the moment a coin clinked in the money chest, a soul leapt up out of purgatory. His selling provoked Martin Luther's 95 Theses in 1517. Through it all the Church guided each life through seven holy rites, the seven sacraments: baptism, confirmation, the Eucharist, confession, marriage, holy orders and the last rites. The theologian Peter Lombard first fixed the list at seven around 1150.

Indulgences did not begin as a money racket. At the Council of Clermont in 1095, Urban II declared that anyone who marched on crusade to free Jerusalem out of pure devotion, not for honour or wealth, would have that journey count in place of all penance: the first indulgence. The friar Thomas Aquinas joined Aristotle's philosophy to Christian faith in his Summa Theologiae, and he taught that a ruler's command counts as real law only when it fits the moral law that human reason can discover. A rule that breaks that higher law, he held, is no law at all but a perversion of law. Innocent III, pope from 1198 to 1216 and perhaps the most powerful man in Europe, drove home the Church's claim with an image from the sky: the pope was like the sun, and kings were like the moon, which shines only with light borrowed from the sun.

the-meiji-restoration-and-japan-s-modern.context_blurb:
For 250 years real power in Japan lay with the Tokugawa shoguns rather than the emperor, hereditary military dictators. In 1868 reform-minded samurai overthrew the last shogun and restored the teenage emperor Mutsuhito to power, and in his name they launched one of the fastest modernizations in history: railways, factories, a conscript army and a constitution within a single generation.

The young emperor, only about fifteen, named his reign Meiji, meaning Enlightened Rule, and the name came to stand for the whole age of change. In 1873 a new law made every fit man liable to serve in the army, ending the samurai's ancient monopoly on bearing arms. The government called military service a blood tax, and frightened peasants took the phrase literally: believing the state would draw the blood out of their veins, they rose in the blood tax riots.

Japan's leaders went to learn from the West in person on the Iwakura Mission of 1871, with five girls who were to study in American schools. The youngest, Tsuda Umeko, was just six years old when she sailed; she stayed about a decade and later founded the school that became Tsuda University.

Not every samurai accepted the new order. In 1877 Saigo Takamori, a great hero of the Restoration, led the Satsuma Rebellion against the government he had helped create. At the last battle, at Shiroyama, his few hundred survivors faced some 30,000 imperial conscripts under General Yamagata Aritomo, and when their ammunition ran out, they melted down metal Buddhist statues smuggled in by civilians and cast them into bullets.

Wounded in the leg on the final morning, Saigo could no longer walk. Beppu Shinsuke, his faithful follower, took him to a quiet spot, cut off his head to give him an honourable death and hid it, so that the enemy could not parade it as a prize. Then the last samurai drew their swords and charged the guns. Saigo died a branded traitor, yet in 1889, on the very day the government proclaimed Japan's first modern constitution, it granted him a posthumous pardon and restored his court rank. The rebel became a national hero, and a famous statue in Tokyo's Ueno Park shows him in a plain kimono walking his hunting dog.

the-mesoamerican-ballgame.context_blurb:
For thousands of years peoples across Mesoamerica, from the Olmecs to the Maya and the Aztecs, played a sacred ballgame on long stone-walled courts. The Aztecs called the game ollamaliztli and the court tlachtli. It was sport and ritual at once, a re-enactment of the struggle between the powers of day and night, and some games ended in human sacrifice.

Players had to keep a heavy ball of solid rubber in play without touching it with their hands or feet. Instead they struck it with their hips and upper thighs, protected by padded gear, until one team failed to return it.

The game is astonishingly old. The oldest rubber balls ever found, recovered from a Mexican bog called El Manatí where people sank offerings, date to about 1700 BC, more than a thousand years before the first Greek Olympic Games, which makes it perhaps the oldest known team sport on Earth.

The balls bounced because Mesoamerican craftsmen blended the milky latex of the rubber tree with sap squeezed from morning-glory vines, turning soft, sticky rubber into a tough, springy material. That trick is vulcanization, the process credited to the American Charles Goodyear, which means the Aztecs and their neighbours were vulcanizing rubber centuries before Goodyear. The Spanish conquerors had never seen anything like those bouncing balls.

the-microscope-and-microorganisms.context_blurb:
In the 1600s the microscope opened a hidden world. Lens-makers in the Netherlands built the first compound microscopes around 1600, and within a century two very different men, an English scientist and a Dutch shopkeeper, used lenses to see things no human eye had ever seen.

Robert Hooke's Micrographia of 1665 showed a sliver of cork seen through his lens, riddled with little hollow compartments like a honeycomb. To him they looked like the plain little rooms where monks slept, so he called them cells, and biology still uses the word.

The Delft draper Antonie van Leeuwenhoek had no scientific schooling; he ground tiny, powerful lenses for his own amusement, some magnifying about 270 times. When he scraped the white matter from between his teeth and put it under a lens, he became the first person to see living bacteria: tiny moving creatures he called animalcules.

In 1676 he reported to the Royal Society that pond water teemed with tiny animals. The scholars would not take an amateur's word for it, so the Society sent its own observers to check, and in 1677 they confirmed what he had seen. His discoveries founded microbiology, and he is remembered as its father.

the-middle-passage.context_blurb:
The Middle Passage was the sea crossing at the heart of the Atlantic slave trade: the middle leg of a triangle in which ships sailed from Europe to Africa, carried chained Africans to the Americas, and brought plantation goods home. For six to twelve weeks captives lay packed below deck in heat and filth, and many died on the way.

From start to finish, slave ships carried roughly 12.5 million Africans across the ocean. Despair drove many to leap overboard, and crews hung netting around the decks to stop them. Many jumped anyway, believing that death would carry them back across the water, home to their families and villages.

Olaudah Equiano, carried across as a child, eventually purchased his own freedom and in 1789 told his story in The Interesting Narrative. When the crew first hauled him on deck, the sailors' pale, red faces and loose hair terrified him so much that he asked the other captives whether these men were going to eat him. Below deck, he wrote, the screams of the women and the moans of the dying made it a horror almost impossible to conceive. Captains needed captives who looked fit enough to fetch a good price, so sailors drove the shackled captives onto the deck and made them leap about, whipping any who would not, and called it dancing the slaves. Crews force-fed captives who tried to starve themselves, using the speculum oris, a screw-driven mouth-opener first made for doctors treating lockjaw, cranked between the teeth to pry the jaws apart.

Abolitionists made the horror visible. In 1788 campaigners in Plymouth printed a diagram of the slave ship Brookes, its decks lined with human figures fitted side by side, each man given a space of six feet by sixteen inches, and a slave trader later admitted the ship had once sailed with 609 people aboard. In November 1781 the crew of the British slave ship Zong, bound for Jamaica, claimed the water was running out, and over several days they threw some 130 living Africans overboard; about ten more leapt to their deaths in defiance. The owners, the Gregson syndicate of Liverpool slave traders, had insured the captives at about £30 a head, and instead of facing a murder trial they filed an insurance claim for their lost cargo.

Their excuse did not hold water. Rain had refilled the casks on 1 December, in the middle of the killings, and the Zong reached port with about 420 gallons still aboard, which leads historians to suspect the drownings were planned insurance fraud. When the case reached court in 1783, the jury, Lord Mansfield explained, treated the drowned people as lost property, just as if horses had been thrown into the sea. Equiano told Granville Sharp, a leading abolitionist, about the massacre, and Sharp fought to have the crew charged with murder, but not one of them ever stood trial. The outrage instead fed the growing movement to end the trade.

the-moche-civilization.context_blurb:
The Moche flourished on the dry northern coast of Peru from about AD 100 to 800, long before the Inca. They raised huge mud-brick temple platforms, dug irrigation canals across the desert, and made some of the most lifelike portrait pottery of the ancient world. Their art also shows human sacrifice, which archaeologists have confirmed in the bones of their victims.

In February 1987 looters led by Ernil Bernal dug their way into an adobe pyramid at Sipán and made off with heaps of gold. Everything else in the burial escaped them only because the looters quarrelled over the spoils and one of them tipped off the police, who alerted the archaeologist Walter Alva. Alva then excavated the first unlooted Moche royal tomb ever found, packed with 451 objects of gold, silver, copper, turquoise and shell around a warrior-priest now called the Lord of Sipán.

The lord was not buried alone. Companions shared his grave, young women, warriors, a child, a dog and llamas, and one of the warrior guardians had had his feet cut off, as if to make sure he could never walk away from his watch over the dead lord. The lord himself stood about 1.63 metres tall and died at around 35 to 45.

the-mound-builders-adena-and-hopewell.context_blurb:
Long before Europeans arrived, the peoples of the eastern woodlands of North America built great earthen mounds and geometric earthworks. The Adena culture of the Ohio Valley, from about 1000 BC, raised burial mounds, and the Hopewell after them built vast linked circles, squares and octagons and traded for copper, mica, obsidian and seashells across the continent.

In Adams County, Ohio, an earthen serpent winds for a quarter of a mile along a wooded ridge: the Great Serpent Mound, built more than 900 years ago, the biggest effigy mound left anywhere in the world. It is shaped like a snake with a triple-coiled tail and open jaws wrapped around a great oval, often read as the serpent swallowing an egg.

In the 1800s many white settlers pushing west refused to believe that the ancestors of living Native Americans could have built such works. Instead they invented a vanished lost race that had supposedly built the mounds and died out long before. In 1894 the Smithsonian archaeologist Cyrus Thomas demolished the myth, proving that the ancestors of living Native Americans built the mounds themselves.

the-mughal-empire-the-taj-mahal.context_blurb:
For three centuries, from 1526, the Mughal emperors ruled most of India from Delhi and Agra. They were Muslims of Central Asian descent who built a rich, cultured empire, and one of them raised the most famous monument of love on Earth, the Taj Mahal.

The dynasty's founder, Babur, descended from the conqueror Timur on his father's side and from Genghis Khan on his mother's, and the very name Mughal is simply the Persian form of Mongol, the name of his mother's people. His memoir, the Baburnama, is often called the first true autobiography in Islamic literature. In 1526, on the field of Panipat, Babur's army of about 12,000 faced the Delhi sultan Ibrahim Lodi and an army four times larger, with a thousand war elephants. Babur won because he had cannons and matchlock guns, which shattered the elephants and infantry of a foe with no firearms at all.

Babur's grandson Akbar, who ruled from 1556 to 1605, refused to force one faith on everyone. Scholars of every faith, Hindu, Jain, Christian and Zoroastrian as well as Muslim, argued openly at his court, and he appointed Hindus to the highest posts, a policy of religious tolerance he called sulh-i-kul, peace with all. He backed that ideal with action by abolishing the jizya, the tax that earlier Muslim rulers had laid on non-Muslims simply for following another religion.

Akbar's grandson was born Prince Khurram in 1592. His father, the emperor Jahangir, rewarded his victories in the Deccan in 1617 with the title Shah Jahan, King of the World. In 1612 he had married Arjumand Banu Begum, and at their wedding he gave her the Persian title Mumtaz Mahal, the Exalted One of the Palace. She bore him fourteen children in nineteen years and died giving birth to the last in 1631. Heartbroken, Shah Jahan spent some twenty years and the labour of 20,000 workers raising a white-marble mausoleum for her on the Yamuna at Agra: at its heart the Taj Mahal is a tomb, built to hold his wife.

Its Makrana marble is slightly translucent, so the Taj seems to change colour through the day: pinkish at dawn, dazzling white at noon and golden under the moon. Its builders planned for disaster, tilting each of the four minarets slightly outward so that in an earthquake the towers would fall away from the tomb instead of crashing onto it. Above the great gateway they carved each line of Quranic calligraphy a little larger than the one below, so that to someone looking up from the ground every line appears the same size. The whole building is a mirror of perfect symmetry, with one exception. Mumtaz Mahal's tomb sits dead centre under the dome, while Shah Jahan's was added later beside hers, off to one side, the only break in the balance. The real graves lie sealed in a chamber below.

Shah Jahan's court in Delhi had a throne of solid gold as well. Seven years in the making, it blazed with 26,733 gems, the Koh-i-Noor diamond among them, and two peacocks fanned their tails behind the seat: it was the Peacock Throne. In 1739 the Persian invader Nadir Shah carried it off to Iran. Shah Jahan's own end was bitter. In 1658 his son Aurangzeb took the throne from him and kept him captive in Agra Fort until his death eight years later. Tradition says that when his eyesight failed, his daughter set a mirror in the wall of his room so that he could still gaze at the reflection of his wife's tomb. When he died in 1666, he was buried beside Mumtaz in the tomb he had built for her. A grisly tale says Shah Jahan cut off the builders' hands to stop them ever making anything so beautiful again. Historians find no evidence for it; the story was passed around as hearsay no earlier than the 1960s, and the records show the same craftsmen went on to build other Mughal palaces.

the-nazca-lines.context_blurb:
Between about 500 BC and AD 500 the Nazca people of southern Peru drew giant pictures on their desert floor: a monkey, a hummingbird, a spider, a condor and many more, along with straight lines running for miles. They made them by scraping away the dark, reddish-brown surface pebbles to expose the pale ground beneath.

The figures are so huge, some hundreds of feet across, that a person standing inside one sees only shallow paths in the dirt; you can see one as a picture only by flying overhead and looking straight down, which is why the lines went unrecognised until pilots flew over the desert in the 20th century. The furrows are only about ten centimetres deep, yet they have lasted some two thousand years, because the Nazca plain is one of the driest and least windy places on Earth, so almost nothing wears them away.

Because the shapes make sense only from the air, some writers claimed aliens must have made them. But wooden stakes turn up where many lines end, and they reveal the real method: the Nazca stretched cords taut between stakes and scaled up a small design on a grid, like enlarging a blueprint. In the 1980s the investigator Joe Nickell and a few helpers reproduced a Nazca figure using only string and stakes. Most scholars think the lines were sacred walkways for processions, perhaps prayers for water in that parched land.

the-nile-river-and-egyptian-geography.context_blurb:
Egypt is almost all desert. Its civilization grew up along the narrow green ribbon of farmland that the Nile, flowing north from the heart of Africa to the Mediterranean, kept alive. Every summer, before modern dams, the river overflowed and laid new, rich black silt over its valley, and that predictable flood fed three thousand years of pharaohs.

The Egyptians named their country after that silt. They called it Kemet, the Black Land, while the dead desert beyond the farmland was the Red Land. Around 450 BC the Greek historian Herodotus visited and saw the thin green strip slicing across endless desert. Without the yearly flood, he wrote, the country would be a wasteland, and he called Egypt the gift of the Nile.

The river also set the Egyptians' sense of direction. Because the Nile flows north, the delta in the north, downstream, was Lower Egypt and the upstream south was Upper Egypt, since they measured up and down by the river's current rather than by the compass. Nature announced the flood. Each summer the bright star Sirius, which the Egyptians called Sopdet, reappeared in the dawn sky just as the river began to rise, and its return anchored their calendar of 365 days. To measure each flood they built nilometers, marked stairways or posts running down into the river, like the one on Elephantine Island at Aswan with its 52 steps. A high flood meant a big harvest, so officials fixed each year's taxes by how high the water rose.

Pliny the Elder, a Roman writer, listed what each height meant: 12 cubits brought famine, 14 joy, and 16 the perfect flood of abundance. A flood higher than 16 cubits was a catastrophe, because it drowned the crops, the houses and the stored grain.

the-northern-renaissance.context_blurb:
In the 1400s and 1500s a second Renaissance flowered north of the Alps, in the Low Countries, the German lands, France and England. Its painters worked in oil with patient, glowing detail, its printmakers spread images across Europe, and its scholars wrote in Latin for the whole continent. It borrowed from Italy but spoke in its own voice.

In Bruges, Jan van Eyck perfected oil painting. His Arnolfini Portrait of 1434 pictures a wealthy pair standing in a bedroom; on the far wall a little convex mirror reflects the scene from behind, showing two more people in the doorway, roughly where the viewer stands, one of whom is thought to be the painter himself. Above the mirror he wrote in curling Latin that Johannes de Eyck fuit hic, signing like a witness on a legal document. The words mean that Jan van Eyck was here, followed by the year, 1434.

In 1515 a live rhinoceros reached Lisbon, sent by an Indian sultan to Portugal's king, Manuel I, the first rhino seen in Europe for more than a thousand years. Pliny had written that rhinos and elephants were natural enemies, and Manuel wanted to test it, so he set the rhino against a young elephant; the elephant took fright and bolted before the fight even began. Word of the beast spread by letter, and the German artist Albrecht Dürer, who never saw it, made a woodcut from a sketch and a written description. He imagined its skin as riveted plates of armour and added a small, twisted extra horn between its shoulders, which no real rhino has. No animal picture in Europe became better known, and German schoolbooks still printed it as a faithful likeness until the late 1930s, more than four hundred years after he carved it.

In his Self-Portrait of 1500 Dürer dared something new. He painted himself facing straight out, his hand lifted near his heart like a blessing, a solemn pose that artists of his day reserved for images of Christ.

Van Eyck's greatest work, the Ghent Altarpiece of 1432, painted with his brother Hubert, has been stolen six times, entire or in pieces, more than any other artwork. Its Just Judges panel vanished in 1934 and has never come back, and a replica made by a forger now hangs in its place in St Bavo's Cathedral. The scholar Erasmus of Rotterdam, the Prince of the Humanists, wrote a witty satire on the follies of his age in 1511 and dedicated it to his friend Sir Thomas More. Its Greek title, Moriae Encomium, In Praise of Folly, hides a joke: moriae is Greek for folly, and it echoes More's own name.

the-northwest-ordinance-1787-bans-slaver.context_blurb:
In the summer of 1787, while the Constitutional Convention met in Philadelphia, the old Congress of the Articles of Confederation passed the Northwest Ordinance. It set up government for the vast territory north of the Ohio River that would become Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan and Wisconsin, promised settlers religious freedom and trial by jury, and let new states join the Union as equals.

It had a bolder forerunner. In 1784 Thomas Jefferson proposed banning slavery from all the western territories after 1800, and his plan fell one vote short in Congress, because a delegate lay ill in bed and missed the vote. Jefferson later wrote that the voice of a single individual would have prevented this abominable crime, and that heaven would not always be silent.

The 1787 ordinance was milder, barring slavery only north of the Ohio, but its Article 6 declared that there would be neither slavery nor involuntary servitude in the territory, except as punishment for crime. Seventy-eight years later the Thirteenth Amendment to the Constitution, which abolished slavery throughout the United States in 1865, copied that wording almost word for word. The 1787 ban became the template for ending slavery across the whole nation.

the-olmec-mother-culture-of-mesoamerica.context_blurb:
Between about 1500 and 400 BC the Olmecs lived along the humid Gulf Coast of Mexico, in today's Veracruz. Later peoples, the Maya and the Aztecs among them, inherited so much from them, the ballgame, jade, the feathered serpent and monumental stone carving, that archaeologists call the Olmecs the mother culture of Mesoamerica.

Their most famous works are colossal stone heads, each carved from a single basalt boulder of more than twenty tons, probably portraits of their rulers. The Olmecs hauled those boulders over 100 kilometres from the mountains without the wheel and without any draft animals, floating them on rafts down the rivers and dragging them on log rollers.

The name Olmec is not their own. It comes from the Aztecs' Nahuatl word Olmecatl, made of olli, rubber, and mecatl, people: the rubber people, because their swampy homeland produced natural rubber from the latex of its trees. At El Manatí archaeologists have found rubber balls from about 1700 BC, the oldest rubber objects in the world.

the-opium-wars-and-china-s-century-of-hu.context_blurb:
In the early 1800s British merchants bought tea, silk and porcelain from China but had little that China wanted in return, so silver drained east. Their answer was to grow opium in British India and smuggle it into China, and by the 1830s millions of Chinese were addicted. The wars that followed began what China still remembers as a century of national disgrace.

In 1839 the emperor ordered Lin Zexu, an incorruptible official, to end the trade at Canton. Lin confiscated some 20,000 chests of the drug and refused simply to burn it: over twenty-three days at Humen, his men dissolved it in trenches with lime, salt and seawater, and the tide flushed the scalding sludge out to sea. China honours him as a hero of the fight against drugs, and one statue of Lin stands far from home, in Chatham Square in New York City's Chinatown, inscribed as a pioneer of the war on drugs.

Britain answered with war. Its steamer Nemesis, built of iron, shattered fleets of wooden junks while barely taking a scratch, and the terrified Chinese called her the devil ship.

Peace came in 1842 at Nanking: China ceded Hong Kong, opened Canton, Shanghai and three other ports to British trade and paid an indemnity of 21 million dollars. Strangely, the treaty's text never names opium anywhere, though opium was the cause of the whole war. The Chinese call the whole stretch from the first war to 1949, with its defeats, one-sided treaties and lost lands, the Century of Humiliation, a memory that still shapes how China sees the West.

Twenty years after the first war, in the Second Opium War, British and French troops reached Beijing. In 1860 Lord Elgin's soldiers took three days to burn the Old Summer Palace, a vast park of halls, libraries and fountains. The French writer Victor Hugo said the two great nations had behaved like a pair of robbers plundering a museum, one filling its pockets and the other its safes.

the-ottoman-empire-fall-of-constantinopl.context_blurb:
The Ottoman Turks began around 1300 as a small frontier dynasty in Anatolia and spent a century and a half swallowing the dying Byzantine Empire, until only its walled capital, Constantinople, was left. In 1453 the young sultan Mehmed II, barely twenty-one, came to take it.

He prepared carefully. In 1452 he threw up a fortress in only four months where the Bosphorus runs narrowest, so that his guns could strangle shipping to the city, and its cannon sank a Venetian vessel that tried to run past. He called it Boğazkesen, the Throat-Cutter. The city's land walls, three thick lines of stone, had turned back every attacker for a thousand years. Mehmed's answer was gunpowder on a scale no army had fielded: above all a single monster cannon, a bombard about 27 feet long cast by the Hungarian gun-founder Orban, which hurled stone balls of some 600 pounds more than a mile.

Orban had tried to sell his gun to Constantine XI first, but the cash-starved Byzantines could not pay his fee, so he took it to Mehmed, boasting that it could blast down the walls of Babylon itself. The monster had a crippling weakness: it took about three hours to reload, so it could fire only some seven times a day, and dragging it into place took sixty oxen and hundreds of men.

The city's defences facing the Golden Horn, its harbour, were weaker, so Constantine XI closed the harbour mouth with a huge iron chain floated on logs, some 1,600 feet of two-foot links fixed to towers on each shore. Mehmed's galleys could not break it, so on 22 April he went around it: his men dragged about seventy ships overland on greased wooden rollers, over the hill behind Galata and down into the Golden Horn, where they appeared overnight behind the chain.

On 29 May 1453 the city fell. Tradition says Constantine XI Palaiologos, the last emperor, refused the chance to escape, tore off his imperial purple so that no one could carry off his body as a trophy, and died fighting on foot, sword in hand, in the breach near the Gate of St Romanos; his body was never identified. Hagia Sophia, the greatest church in Christendom, became a mosque. By right of conquest Mehmed now claimed to be heir to the Roman emperors, taking the title Kayser-i Rum, Caesar of Rome. The city's Greek scholars escaped to Italy with their precious manuscripts, the complete works of Plato among them, and with Gutenberg's new printing press ready to copy them, that rescued learning helped spark the Renaissance.

Under Mehmed's great-grandson Suleiman, who reigned for 46 years from 1520 to 1566, longer than any other sultan, the Ottomans reached their golden age. Europeans called him the Magnificent, but his own people called him Kanuni, the Lawgiver, for reforming the empire's laws. In 1526, at Mohács, Suleiman's army crushed the Hungarians in less than two hours, and the young Hungarian king, Louis II, died fleeing the field, drowned in a river when his horse threw him.

the-pantheon-and-roman-concrete.context_blurb:
The Pantheon in Rome is a huge round temple that the emperor Hadrian built around AD 125, on the site of an earlier temple by Agrippa. Because the Church turned it into a place of worship in the 600s, it has been in use ever since and is one of the best-preserved buildings of antiquity. Its great dome, open to the sky at the top, was the largest in the world for well over a thousand years.

Its builders faced a deadly problem: a dome 142 feet across could crush itself under its own weight. So they graded the dome by weight, with heavy travertine at the thick base, then lighter tile and tufa, and at the very top pumice, a volcanic rock so full of holes that it floats on water. That lightening cut the stresses in the dome by about 80 percent.

The concrete is the other secret. Modern concrete often crumbles within decades, yet the Pantheon's unreinforced dome has lasted almost nineteen centuries. Admir Masic and his MIT team found out why in 2023: small white lumps of lime, once dismissed as sloppy mixing, let Roman concrete heal its own cracks, because rainwater seeping into a crack dissolves the lime, which then crystallises again and fills the gap. The team cracked blocks of Roman-recipe and modern concrete and ran water through them; within two weeks the Roman block had sealed itself, while the modern one kept leaking.

the-parthenon-and-phidias-the-classical-.context_blurb:
In the 440s BC, at the height of Athens' golden age, Pericles had a great marble temple built on the Acropolis for the city's patron goddess, Athena. The architects Iktinos and Kallikrates designed it, and the sculptor Phidias directed its carvings and its giant statue. Its proportions and calm balance became the model for what later ages called the classical ideal.

The temple took its name from one of Athena's titles, Parthenos, the maiden, so Parthenon means the maiden's chamber. Inside stood Phidias's Athena Parthenos, nearly 40 feet tall over a hidden core of cypress wood, made in the chryselephantine style: her skin was carved from ivory and her robes were plated in gold. In her open right hand she held a figure of Nike, the winged goddess of victory, itself as tall as a person.

At Olympia, home of the Games, Phidias outdid himself with a seated Zeus about 41 feet high, also of gold and ivory, on a throne of cedar inlaid with ebony and gems, and it was later counted among the Seven Wonders. He also made a third Athena, the Athena Promachos, a 30-foot bronze under the open sky of the Acropolis. Pausanias wrote that sailors rounding Cape Sounion could see the tip of her spear gleaming in the sun from far out at sea.

The temple's straight lines are an illusion. A truly straight column looks pinched to the eye, so the architects gave every column a gentle outward swell at the middle, called entasis, which makes it look perfectly straight. A long, dead-flat floor would seem to sag in the middle, so they curved the platform up gently, and its middle stands some four inches above its corners. On the shield of the Athena, Plutarch says, Phidias carved a fight between Greeks and Amazons and slipped in two real men: his friend Pericles, and Phidias's own face, as a bald old man lifting a stone over his head. Centuries later the Roman emperor Caligula wanted the Olympian Zeus brought to Rome and given his own head instead, and Suetonius tells the legend that the statue burst out laughing so loudly that the workmen's scaffolding collapsed and they fled for their lives.

Phidias was put on trial, accused of pocketing gold meant for Athena's robe, but he had made the robe's gold panels removable, so the Athenians took them off and weighed them, and the gold matched its recorded amount exactly. He was convicted anyway on a separate charge over the hidden portrait. One last trick is invisible. Every outer column leans inward by a hair, and so precisely that if the columns were extended upward, their lines would cross about 2.4 kilometres overhead, roughly a mile and a half above the temple. The temple stood almost whole for over two thousand years. In 1687 a Venetian mortar bomb, fired on the orders of the general Morosini, struck the gunpowder the Ottomans had stored inside, gutting the building and killing some 300 people. Morosini described the hit as fortunate.

the-pax-romana.context_blurb:
The Pax Romana, the Roman peace, was the long stretch of internal calm that began when Augustus became the first emperor in 27 BC and lasted about two centuries. Legions still fought on the frontiers, but inside the empire the roads were safe, Roman law ruled the courts, trade ran from Britain to India, and cities grew.

Rome's roads were its arteries. In 312 BC the official Appius Claudius Caecus began the first great paved road, the Via Appia, running south from Rome and eventually stretching to Brindisi in Italy's far south-east. Romans called it the Queen of Roads, regina viarum, and long stretches of its tightly packed basalt paving survive today. Augustus raised the Golden Milestone, a gilded bronze column in the Forum, and every distance in the empire was counted from it; hence the saying that all roads lead to Rome. During the peace the Romans built over 50,000 miles of paved road, carrying legions, mail riders and traders from northern Britain to Syria.

Once Rome had swept the pirates from the sea and taken Egypt, its traders reached India with glassware, wine and silver, and a merchant's guidebook, the Periplus, records what they bought there: ivory, pepper and silk yarn. Archaeologists have dug up Roman wine jars and coins at the Indian port of Arikamedu.

Augustus boasted of the peace in his own funeral inscription, the Res Gestae. Janus's temple doors stood open whenever Rome was at war, and Romans remembered them closing only twice in all their history before Augustus, once under King Numa and once after the Second Punic War. Augustus recorded that he shut them three times.

The peace had a dark side, and a Roman recorded it. The historian Tacitus put a bitter verdict in the mouth of the British chieftain Calgacus: the Romans, he said, make a wasteland and call it peace.

the-peloponnesian-war-athens-vs-sparta-4.context_blurb:
From 431 to 404 BC Athens and Sparta, the two great powers of classical Greece, fought the Peloponnesian War with their alliances behind them. It ended in Sparta's victory and the fall of Athens' empire, and an Athenian general, Thucydides, wrote its history as it happened.

Pericles, Athens' leader, refused to meet the Spartan army in open battle. He brought the farmers inside the Long Walls, left the countryside for the Spartans to ravage and fed the city by sea, but in 430 BC a plague tore through the packed city, killing perhaps a quarter to a third of the people inside, and Pericles himself died of it in 429. Thucydides caught the plague himself and lived. The sick, he wrote, burned inside so badly that they tore off their clothes and leapt into cold water, and scavenging birds and animals either stayed away from the unburied bodies or died if they ate them.

Athens then staked everything on invading Sicily in 415 BC. By 413 its fleet was destroyed, the generals Nicias and Demosthenes were executed, and the Syracusans herded thousands of Athenian prisoners into deep stone quarries, giving them a little barley and water each day, until most died of disease and starvation. Plutarch tells a legend from those quarries: the Sicilians loved the tragedies of the Athenian Euripides so much that a prisoner who could recite his verses might win food or even freedom.

The war also showed raw power. In 416 BC Athens demanded the surrender of the small island of Melos. The Melians pleaded that justice was on their side, and the Athenian envoys answered, in Thucydides' telling, that between unequal powers the strong do whatever they can, and the weak suffer whatever they must. Melos refused anyway, and Athens killed its men and sold its women and children as slaves. Thucydides was a general too. When the Spartan Brasidas took Amphipolis in 424 BC, Thucydides arrived too late to save it, and the Athenians banished him for twenty years. He used the exile to travel among both sides and wrote a true history that recorded his own failure at Amphipolis, honesty at his own cost that makes his work the founding book of analytical history.

the-persian-royal-road-and-administratio.context_blurb:
From the 500s BC until Alexander the Great conquered it in the 330s, the Persian Empire was the largest the world had yet seen, stretching from the Aegean coast to the Indus. King Darius I held it together with roads, standard coinage and a tight system of provinces, and his model shaped empires from Rome to the Islamic caliphates.

Darius built the Royal Road, more than 1,500 miles from Susa in Iran to Sardis in western Anatolia, with relay stations along the way. A fresh horse and a fresh rider waited at every station, so each courier galloped one day's stretch and handed the dispatch on, like runners passing a torch, and a royal message crossed in about a week a road that took a walker some three months. The Greek writer Herodotus marvelled at those couriers, saying that no snow, rain, heat or darkness could stop them. The famous inscription over the New York City General Post Office is adapted from his praise of the relay riders of King Darius's Persian Royal Road, and it was never an official postal motto.

Darius split the realm into some twenty satrapies, provinces governed by satraps, a title meaning protector of the realm. To keep these powerful governors honest, he sent out inspectors called the Eye of the King, his roving eyes and ears, who rode the Royal Road, dropped in unannounced and answered only to the king.

the-pharaohs-and-egyptian-god-kings.context_blurb:
For some three thousand years, from about 3100 BC until Rome took Egypt in 30 BC, the pharaoh was more than a king to the Egyptians: he was a god on earth. His crowns, his tools and his tomb all proclaimed it, and even foreign conquerors who seized Egypt had themselves carved on temple walls in pharaoh's dress.

Egypt had once been two kingdoms, Upper and Lower Egypt, and the pharaoh showed that he ruled both by wearing the pschent, a double crown that set the tall White Crown of the south inside the Red Crown of the north. In art he crosses his arms over his chest and grips a crook and a flail: the shepherd's hooked staff, marking him as the guide of his people, and the grain-threshing whip, standing for the land's fertility and his power to punish.

Over his forehead rose the uraeus, a rearing golden cobra, the emblem of Wadjet, guardian goddess of the north, which Egyptians believed could spit fire at his foes. The word pharaoh itself comes from the Egyptian per-aa, Great House: at first it meant the palace and the court around the king, much as the White House can mean an American president, and only in the New Kingdom, after about 1550 BC, did it become the king's own title.

On becoming king, Egyptians believed, the pharaoh turned into Horus, the falcon-headed sky god, walking the earth as the bridge between gods and people. A pharaoh expecting to become a god needed a tomb to match. Khufu's Great Pyramid, raised around 2560 BC from about 2.3 million blocks, was the tomb of that single god-king. Peering into Tutankhamun's tomb by candlelight in 1922, Howard Carter was asked by Lord Carnarvon, who paid for the dig, whether he saw anything. Carter's famous answer was "Yes, wonderful things." Inside lay thousands of treasures, among them a death mask of solid gold. Women could rule too. Hatshepsut held the throne for some two decades in the 1400s BC, and to present herself as king she had her statues carved with a male body and the false beard of a pharaoh, a ceremonial chin-piece. The last pharaoh, Cleopatra VII, was not Egyptian by blood at all but Greek, from the Ptolemies, a dynasty founded by one of Alexander the Great's generals; her death in 30 BC ended three thousand years of pharaohs and made Egypt a Roman province.

Above all the pharaoh had to keep ma'at, the right order of the universe, safe from isfet, chaos. If the god-king failed, Egyptians feared, nature itself would break down: the sun might fail to rise and the river's yearly flood might never come, and a failed flood meant famine. When he died, the king became Osiris, lord of the underworld, and his heir became the new Horus, so kingship passed unbroken from dead father to living son. Akhenaten, king from about 1353 to 1336 BC, attempted to abolish Egypt's crowd of gods. He exalted the Aten, the sun-disk, proclaimed it the one true god, made himself the only go-between for his people, and built it a new capital at Amarna; later Egyptians hated the upheaval so much that they tore his city down.

When Hatshepsut died in 1458 BC, Thutmose III eventually had her statues smashed and her name chiselled from temple walls. Since he did it only near the end of his long rule, historians think he acted not from spite but to make sure his own son, not some rival line, would inherit the crown.

the-phoenician-alphabet.context_blurb:
The Phoenicians were seafaring traders from cities such as Tyre and Byblos on the eastern Mediterranean coast, in today's Lebanon. Around 3,000 years ago they used a simple set of letters, one sign for each consonant sound, that almost anyone could learn. Carried across the sea and reshaped by the Greeks, it became the ancestor of the letters you are reading now.

Scribes in Egypt and Mesopotamia had to master hundreds of signs. The Phoenicians needed just 22 letters, all consonants and no vowels, a system small enough for an ordinary merchant to learn quickly. The people who spread these letters around the Mediterranean were not priests or poets but seafaring traders, the greatest merchant sailors of their age, who needed quick, accurate records of their deals. Even the word alphabet records the borrowing: it is built from the names of the first two letters, aleph and bet, which the Greeks took over as alpha and beta.

Each letter was named after an everyday object and drawn like it. Aleph meant ox and was drawn as a horned ox-head; the Greeks later flipped it upright, so a capital A turned upside down still shows the head and horns. Bet, which became our B, meant house. Even their name was a nickname. Phoenician comes from the Greek phoinikes, the purple people, after the royal purple dye they squeezed from murex sea-snails and sold across the sea, worth more than silver, weight for weight. That Tyrian purple, made by crushing thousands of snails, was a dye fit only for royalty, and unlike every other ancient dye it did not fade: Pliny the Elder reported that sun and weather made it grow richer and brighter the longer the cloth was worn. The letters travelled on: the Greeks reshaped them and passed them to the Etruscans, who handed them to the Romans, and the Romans' Latin alphabet spread across the West to become the letters on this page.

The alphabet's first spark came much earlier. Nearly four thousand years ago, in the mines of Sinai, Canaanite labourers who dug copper and turquoise for the pharaohs borrowed a handful of hieroglyphs to stand for sounds, creating the Proto-Sinaitic script, which Flinders Petrie found at Serabit el-Khadim in 1905. Byblos's King Ahiram, buried around 1000 BC, left the longest early text in these letters on his sarcophagus, and it is a threat: any king who uncovers the coffin will have the sceptre of his rule torn away and the throne of his kingdom overturned. The Phoenician script had one big flaw: with no vowels, the letters bt could stand for bat, but, bit or bet. The Greeks solved it around 800 BC by reusing spare Phoenician consonant letters they did not need as vowels, so aleph became the vowel A, and the world had its first full alphabet. Greek legend gave the credit to Cadmus, a Phoenician prince who killed a dragon and planted its teeth, which grew into armed men; Herodotus said Cadmus brought the letters to Greece, and the Greeks went on calling them Phoenician letters.

the-printing-press-and-spread-of-ideas.context_blurb:
Around 1440 to 1450 Johannes Gutenberg, a goldsmith working in Mainz, combined movable metal type, oil-based ink and a press adapted from the wine press into a machine that printed identical pages far faster than any scribe. Within fifty years presses were running from Venice to London, and ideas could spread faster than any authority could stop them.

Before printing, a monk copying by hand produced only a few pages daily and needed about half a year for one book. In that same half year the press could turn out several hundred identical copies, roughly a thousand times the monk's output.

Gutenberg's masterpiece was a Bible printed in Mainz around 1454. Partway through, he squeezed two extra lines onto each page, going from 40 to 42, to stretch his paper further, and so scholars call it the 42-line Bible; a full copy runs to about 1,282 pages in two volumes.

In 1517 the monk Martin Luther posted his Ninety-Five Theses, complaints against the Church meant for fellow scholars. Printers copied them without his permission, and in a fortnight they were all over Germany, in a month all over Europe. Luther wrote to Pope Leo X that it was a mystery to him how his theses had spread to so many places. Between 1517 and 1520 some 400,000 copies of his pamphlets poured off the presses.
