the-punic-wars-and-hannibal-at-cannae.context_blurb:
Carthage, a rich trading city on the coast of North Africa founded by Phoenician settlers, was the greatest rival Rome ever faced. Rome fought it in three Punic Wars, named from the Latin word for Phoenician, and in the second, from 218 to 201 BC, the Carthaginian general Hannibal came close to breaking Rome.

Legend says Carthage itself began with a trick. Offered no more ground than a single ox-hide would cover, Queen Dido sliced the hide into thin strips and laid them end to end in a ring around a whole hilltop, the Byrsa. Hannibal's hatred of Rome began in childhood. When he was nine, his father Hamilcar agreed to take him to war on one condition: the boy placed a hand on the altar and swore that he would never be Rome's friend, an oath he kept for some 36 years.

Marching from Spain in 218 BC with an army of more than 100,000 men and 37 elephants, Hannibal crossed the Pyrenees, the Rhône and finally the Alps in late autumn. When he came down into Italy he had only about 26,000 men left, having lost most of his army to mountains, rivers and cold before fighting a single Roman battle. Next spring his men slogged for days through the swamps of the flooded Arno valley, and Hannibal rode across on the only elephant left alive after the winter. There he caught a severe eye infection, ophthalmia, and since the army could not halt, he lost the sight of one eye for good and fought the rest of the war half-blind. At Lake Trasimene he tucked his forces into the slopes over a cramped shoreline track, and when the consul Gaius Flaminius marched along it one morning, a thick early-morning fog hid the Carthaginians until they swept down and killed him and some 15,000 Romans.

In 216 BC came Cannae, his masterpiece. He deliberately put his least reliable soldiers, Spaniards and Gauls, at the centre; as the Romans pushed in, the centre bent back, the African veterans on either flank swung in, and his horsemen sealed the back. Surrounded on all sides, the Roman army was slaughtered where it stood, trapped by a double envelopment, a manoeuvre West Point still teaches. Polybius counts about 70,000 Romans dead in a single day. Hannibal's men stripped gold rings, worn only by senators and knights, from the Roman dead, and his brother Mago carried them home and poured them out in a heap on the floor of Carthage's Senate to show how many Roman nobles had fallen.

Maharbal, who led his horsemen, urged an immediate march on Rome, promising dinner on the Capitol within five days. When Hannibal hesitated, Maharbal told him that he knew how to win a victory but not how to use one, and historians still argue over that choice. Rome refused to break. It turned to Quintus Fabius Maximus, who would not give Hannibal the pitched battle he wanted but shadowed him through the hills, where Carthaginian cavalry was useless, and wore him down. Romans nicknamed him Cunctator, the Delayer, and patient avoidance is still called Fabian strategy. At last Rome carried the war to Africa. On the field of Zama, in 202 BC, Hannibal led off with a charge of war elephants, but the young Roman general Scipio had trumpets and horns blare to frighten the beasts and had left open lanes in his lines, so many elephants ran harmlessly straight through and others stampeded back into Hannibal's own ranks.

Carthage lost the war, yet in Rome the old senator Cato the Elder still feared it, and he closed each of his Senate speeches, whatever the topic, with the same words: Carthage must be destroyed, Carthago delenda est. He once let fresh figs tumble from his toga, saying they had been picked in Carthage, just three days' sail away.

the-quran-and-the-five-pillars.context_blurb:
The Quran is the sacred scripture of Islam, which Muslims believe God revealed to the Prophet Muhammad through the angel Gabriel over some twenty-three years in the 600s. Its teaching shapes a Muslim's life through five basic practices, the Five Pillars: the testimony of faith, prayer, giving to the poor, the Ramadan fast and the pilgrimage to Mecca.

Muslims believe the revelation began around 610, when Muhammad was praying in solitude in a cave on a mountain near Mecca and the angel Gabriel seized him and commanded him with one word, iqra, recite. Unable to read, Muhammad replied that he was not a reader, but Gabriel repeated the command three times before the first verses came. Saying the Shahada sincerely is all it takes to become a Muslim: it declares that there is no god except God, and that Muhammad is God's messenger.

Prayer, salah, is the second pillar. Five times a day Muslims stand, bow, kneel and press their foreheads to the ground, and wherever they are, they face the qibla, the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca. The fourth pillar, sawm, is the fast of Ramadan: nothing passes their lips, not even water, between dawn and sunset, and at sunset they break the fast, following the Prophet's example, with dates and water.

The fifth pillar, the hajj, is the pilgrimage to Mecca. At its heart the pilgrims circle the Kaaba, the black cube-shaped shrine, seven times, moving counter-clockwise, in the tawaf, and each tries to touch or kiss the Black Stone fixed in its corner, or at least points toward it through the crowd. The Quran has 114 chapters, called surahs, and all but one open with the Bismillah, a blessing invoking God as most gracious and most merciful; the lone exception is the ninth chapter, At-Tawbah.

the-railway-revolution-and-stephenson-s-.context_blurb:
George Stephenson, the son of a poor colliery worker in northern England, built the steam locomotives and iron railways that launched the railway age. Within a single lifetime his engines changed how far people could travel, how fast goods could move, and how whole countries were mapped.

He started work at eight, keeping cows off the colliery wagon tracks, and was still illiterate at eighteen; then he paid for night school out of his own wages to learn reading, writing and arithmetic. His first locomotive, built at a colliery in 1814, hauled 30 tons of coal uphill and held to plain iron rails by friction alone; he named it Blucher, after the Prussian general who had helped defeat Napoleon. In 1825 he was at the controls of Locomotion No.1 when it opened the Stockton and Darlington line, pulling some 600 passengers and 80 tons of cargo.

In 1829 the company building the line from Liverpool to Manchester staged the Rainhill Trials to choose its locomotive, offering a £500 prize. To win, an engine had to pull a load of triple its own weight and keep up an average of ten miles an hour across seventy miles of shuttling up and down. Five machines entered. One, the Cycloped, had no boiler at all, because a horse on a treadmill belt powered it, until the horse crashed through the belt. The crowd's favourite, John Ericsson and John Braithwaite's Novelty, outpaced Rocket at first at over 24 mph, but a joint in its boiler gave way under the pressure and it never finished. Only one engine finished: Stephenson's Rocket, built with his son Robert, pulling a 13-ton load at up to 30 mph, faster than a horse at full gallop. A Liverpool newspaper said it darted past the spectators as swiftly as a swallow darts through the air.

Rocket owed its speed to two tricks. Its boiler piped the fire's hot gases through 25 slim copper tubes surrounded by water instead of one big flue, so it raised steam far faster than any rival. And a blast pipe blew the spent steam up the chimney, dragging a draught through the firebox, so that the quicker Rocket went, the fiercer its fire became. Its glory was short: so many engineers improved on it that within roughly a year and a half newer engines had left it behind.

The line opened on 15 September 1830 with tragedy. At Parkside the MP William Huskisson stepped down to greet the Duke of Wellington, panicked as Rocket approached, and was caught by an open carriage door that swung into the engine's path; Rocket crushed his leg. Stephenson uncoupled the locomotive Northumbrian and raced the dying man to Eccles at about 36 mph, setting a world speed record by accident, but Huskisson died that evening. Stephenson had faced mockery before. In 1825 a member of a parliamentary committee asked what would happen if a cow wandered onto the track, and by tradition Stephenson answered in his Northumbrian accent that it would be very awkward, for the coo.

His choices outlived him. For the gap between his rails he copied the width of the colliery's horse-drawn wagons, 4 feet 8.5 inches, and that standard gauge is still used by most of the world's railways. Railway mania followed. Britain had 98 miles of railway in 1830 and about 6,000 miles by 1849, as Parliament approved one new line after another. George Hudson, nicknamed the Railway King, ran more than a third of the nation's lines by 1844 and paid old investors their dividends out of new investors' money; when the fraud came out, Madame Tussaud's melted down his wax figure.

the-rape-of-nanking.context_blurb:
In December 1937 the Japanese army captured Nanjing, then called Nanking in English and the capital of Nationalist China. Over the next six weeks Japanese troops murdered an estimated 200,000 to 300,000 civilians and disarmed soldiers and raped tens of thousands of women, one of the worst atrocities of the twentieth century.

A few foreigners stayed to help. John Rabe, a German businessman who ran the Siemens office and was a member of the Nazi Party, led the committee that turned a neutral zone into a refuge for some 250,000 Chinese, and he took more than 600 refugees into his own home and garden. Betting that Japanese pilots would never bomb the emblem of their German ally, he spread a giant swastika flag over his air-raid shelter, and it worked.

After the war the Tokyo tribunal tried General Iwane Matsui, who had commanded the army that took the city, and hanged him in 1948, not for ordering the massacre but for failing to prevent his troops' atrocities. Under the principle of command responsibility, a commander can hang for crimes he did not order if he failed to stop them. The imperial prince who was actually in the city, Prince Yasuhiko Asaka, was never prosecuted.

the-reconquista-fall-of-granada-1492.context_blurb:
For nearly eight centuries the Christian kingdoms of northern Spain fought to push Muslim rulers south, a long struggle later called the Reconquista. Its heroes became legends, and it ended in 1492, when Ferdinand and Isabella took Granada, the last Muslim kingdom in Spain.

Its greatest hero was Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar. Legend says that when young Rodrigo picked a colt from the herd, his godfather thought it weak and blurted out Babieca, roughly stupid or dummy, and the name stuck to what became the most famous warhorse in Spain. Rodrigo fought for Christian and Muslim kings alike, and after King Alfonso VI exiled him he served the Muslim ruler of Zaragoza. His famous title, El Cid, comes from his Muslim soldiers' Arabic al-sidi, meaning the lord or master. He then took Valencia as his own. When he died defending it in 1099, an Almoravid army still surrounded the city, and legend says his wife Jimena strapped his armoured body upright on Babieca and sent him out at the head of one last charge. The terrified besiegers fled to their ships, and so, the saying goes, El Cid won a battle after his death.

By the late 1400s only the emirate of Granada was left. Year by year Ferdinand and Isabella took its towns, and the Spaniards mocked its last sultan, Boabdil, as el rey chico, the little king, not for his height but because his realm grew smaller every year. In January 1492 Boabdil surrendered and rode into exile. At a mountain pass he turned for a last look at the Alhambra and wept, and by legend his mother Aixa told him that he wept like a woman for what he had failed to defend like a man. Historians think a bishop, Antonio de Guevara, invented the taunt around 1526, but the pass is still called the Moor's Sigh. Among those who watched Granada surrender was a foreign sailor, Christopher Columbus, and that same year the monarchs backed his voyage west, which reached the Americas.

Granada's surrender terms of 1491 guaranteed its Muslims their faith, mosques, property and language. Cardinal Cisneros soon tore them up: he forced mass baptisms and boasted to the Pope of 3,000 Muslims converted in a single December day in 1499. The betrayal sparked the Alpujarras revolt and, in 1501, a decree ordering Granada's Muslims to convert or leave.

the-red-baron-and-aerial-dogfights.context_blurb:
Manfred von Richthofen, a young German cavalry officer who became a pilot in 1915, was the deadliest fighter ace of World War I, credited with 80 victories before he was shot down over the Somme in April 1918 at the age of 25. His squadron's brightly painted planes earned it the nickname the Flying Circus.

Around January 1917 Richthofen had his fighter painted blood-red, beginning with his Albatros D.III, and that one vivid colour earned him the most famous nickname of the war: the Red Baron. The plane history remembers best is his Fokker Dr.I triplane: where most fighters had two wings, it stacked three, which let it turn and climb tightly in a dogfight, and he flew it painted all red.

Modern studies suggest the bullet that killed him came from an Australian machine gunner on the ground, not from the Canadian pilot credited at the time. Pilots of his war flew in open cockpits without parachutes, and a new pilot's life expectancy at the front was often counted in weeks.

the-renaissance-rebirth-of-art-learning.context_blurb:
The Renaissance, the rebirth of art and learning, began in the Italian city-states in the 1300s and spread across Europe over the next three centuries. Its scholars hunted down ancient Greek and Latin texts and read the classical authors for themselves, its artists studied ancient statues, and together they set human dignity, curiosity and reason at the centre of the picture.

Its first great humanist was the poet Petrarch. In 1336 he and his brother climbed Mont Ventoux, a peak of nearly 2,000 metres, for no practical reason at all: he wrote that he went up simply for the delight of the view from the summit, which makes him one of the first people known to scale a peak just to look. Looking back in scorn at the centuries before his own, Petrarch called them dark, and the idea of the Dark Ages comes from him. In Florence, Lorenzo Ghiberti spent from 1425 to 1452 on a pair of gilded bronze doors for the Baptistery, and the young Michelangelo said they were beautiful enough to be the Gates of Paradise, the name they still bear.

In 1418 Filippo Brunelleschi was competing to build Florence's great dome. As Vasari tells the legend, he dared the competing masters to balance an egg on end on a slab of marble; when they all failed, he cracked one end flat on the marble and stood it up, and when they protested that anyone could do that, he said they would say the same of his dome once they had seen his design. He won, and his secret was a herringbone spiral, spina di pesce: he laid more than four million bricks at angles so that every ring locked onto the one beneath and the dome held itself up, with no wooden scaffold inside, since all Tuscany did not hold enough timber for one. The money behind such works came from the Medici. On Easter Sunday 1478, assassins sent by the rival Pazzi family attacked the Medici brothers at High Mass in the cathedral, choosing the holiest moment, the elevation of the Host, as a deliberate insult to God. Giuliano de' Medici was stabbed nineteen times and died; Lorenzo escaped with a neck wound.

Lorenzo took revenge in paint. For forty gold florins Botticelli painted life-size figures of the hanged plotters dangling on the wall of the city jail, pictures of infamy that stayed there until the Medici were driven out in 1494. Book-hunters were the movement's explorers. In 1417 Poggio Bracciolini found, in a German monastery far from any city, the last copy of Lucretius's On the Nature of Things, a 7,400-line poem picturing a cosmos built from tiny atoms; he knew it mattered because Cicero had quoted it. Leonardo da Vinci's Vitruvian Man of around 1490 solved an old puzzle: earlier artists could not fit a man's outstretched limbs into both a circle and a square that shared one centre, so Leonardo gave each shape its own, centring the circle on the navel and the square on the groin. When Constantinople fell to Mehmed II in 1453, Greek scholars fled to Italy carrying the treasure they prized most, old Greek manuscripts rescued from Constantinople's libraries, among them the complete works of Plato, and they poured Greek learning into Florence and Venice.

Cosimo de' Medici gave the scholar Marsilio Ficino a villa and the task of producing the first complete Latin Plato. On his deathbed in 1464, though, Cosimo told Ficino to set Plato aside and translate first the Hermetic writings, magical texts said to come from ancient Egypt and believed to hold the wisdom of an Egyptian sage older than Plato. Ficino later finished that Plato and coined the phrase Platonic love. By 1492 he was sure he lived in an extraordinary time, writing that his century, like a golden age, had brought back to light the liberal arts that were almost extinct. In 1486 the 23-year-old Giovanni Pico della Mirandola challenged all comers in Rome to debate his 900 propositions on all knowledge, opening with the Oration on the Dignity of Man, later called the manifesto of the Renaissance. Its claim that a man is free to make himself into whatever he chooses so alarmed churchmen that the Church forbade the debate and accused Pico of heresy.

the-revolutions-of-1848.context_blurb:
In the first months of 1848 revolutions swept across Europe faster than anyone thought possible: Paris, Vienna, Berlin, Budapest, Milan, Prague. Liberals, workers, students and nationalists took to the barricades demanding constitutions, parliaments, a free press and nations of their own, and the order of kings built in 1815 cracked in city after city. Within a year most of the uprisings had been crushed.

In February the Parisians toppled King Louis Philippe. Afraid of sharing the fate of Louis XVI, the king escaped the capital in disguise and fled to England, travelling as plain Mr Smith. In Budapest on 15 March, Sándor Petőfi, a young poet, recited his National Song on the steps of the National Museum, with its cry of Rise up, Hungarian, the homeland calls, and the crowd took over the print shops to run off copies.

Two days earlier the revolution had reached Vienna and forced out the chancellor Klemens von Metternich, the very symbol of the old order since 1815. On hearing the news he reportedly sighed, in French, that it was all over. In the Five Days of Milan, from 18 to 22 March, Milan's citizens built barricades and shot down from roofs and windows at Field Marshal Radetzky's 13,000 Austrian soldiers, and by the fifth day they had driven the whole garrison out of Milan, though Radetzky returned the next year.

The Frankfurt Parliament, elected to unite Germany, offered Prussia's King Frederick William IV the crown of a German empire in 1849. He refused it, scorning a crown handed up from the gutter by a people's assembly instead of granted by his fellow princes, and with that the liberal hope of uniting Germany by consent collapsed. The revolutions also split their own makers. In June 1848 tens of thousands of Paris workers manned barricades against the republicans who had toppled the king, until the army crushed them, and that same spring Marx and Engels published The Communist Manifesto. In 1848 the road of liberal constitutions and the road of socialism visibly parted.

the-rise-of-the-ottoman-empire.context_blurb:
Around 1300 a Turkish warrior chief named Osman ruled a small frontier land around the town of Söğüt in north-western Anatolia, on the edge of the crumbling Byzantine Empire. From that tiny start grew an empire that would stretch from Vienna to Baghdad and last until 1923, and the whole dynasty, the Ottomans or Osmanlis, took his name.

Mehmed II was only twenty-one when he besieged Constantinople, a capital that had sheltered behind its walls for more than a millennium. His gun-founder Urban made him a giant bombard, the Basilica, about 27 feet long; moving it some 120 miles took sixty oxen, a thousand men and forty-two days, and it hurled stone balls of about 600 pounds almost a mile. The Byzantines had sealed the Golden Horn harbour with a massive iron chain, so on the night of 22 April Mehmed went around it: his men built a road of greased logs over the hills of Pera and dragged about seventy warships overland, dropping them into the harbour behind the chain by morning. Constantinople fell on 29 May 1453, and Mehmed rode straight to Hagia Sophia, the great domed church built in 537, and turned it into a mosque. For that conquest at twenty-one, the Turks named him Fatih, the Conqueror, a title he kept until he died.

The empire's elite infantry, the Janissaries, came from the devshirme, the child levy: every few years officers took Christian boys aged 8 to 20 from Balkan villages, raised them as Muslims and trained them as soldiers. Cut off from their families, these soldiers served the Sultan alone, the man who paid their salaries. The levy could lift a boy to the very top. A Christian boy named Joseph, taken from near Kayseri around 1512 and trained as a Janissary, became Mimar Sinan, the empire's greatest architect, who designed some 374 buildings and finished his masterpiece, the Selimiye Mosque at Edirne, when he was over eighty. In the West, Suleiman, who reigned for 46 years from 1520 to 1566, longer than any other sultan, was called the Magnificent, while his subjects knew him as Kanuni, the Lawgiver, for codifying Ottoman law into kanuns; he was also a poet and a goldsmith.

Later Ottoman storytellers gave the dynasty a founding legend. Asleep in the house of the holy man Edebali, Osman dreamed that a tree sprouted from his navel and spread its shade over all the earth, a sign that his family would rule a great empire. The tale was written down in the 1400s, long after his death.

the-roaring-twenties.context_blurb:
After the First World War and the influenza pandemic, Americans plunged into the Roaring Twenties: a booming, carefree decade of cars, radio, jazz and new freedoms, with Prohibition driving drinking into back-room clubs. It ended with Americans far more confident of their prosperity than they had any reason to be in October 1929.

Its signature dance came from a 1923 all-Black Broadway show, Runnin' Wild, whose number with flapping arms and kicking legs spread across the country: the Charleston. Its icon was the flapper, the young woman who bobbed her hair, wore her skirt at the knee, smoked and danced in jazz clubs till dawn, defying all the rules her mother had been raised by.

Cars reached ordinary families because Ford's moving assembly line could build a Model T chassis in 93 minutes instead of more than twelve hours, and so the line never had to pause for paint, every car came out in one colour, black. Charles Lindbergh crossed the Atlantic alone in May 1927, flying the Spirit of Saint Louis from New York to Paris in about thirty-three and a half hours, and when he touched down at Le Bourget more than 100,000 people swarmed the field.

Radio tied the country together. KDKA in Pittsburgh went on air with the election returns on 2 November 1920, the first commercial broadcast, so listeners at home learned of Warren Harding's victory in the presidential race before the morning papers could print it. The Yankees slugger Babe Ruth hit his record 60th home run of the season on 30 September 1927, more home runs than any other American League team managed that whole year.

Duke Ellington's band took up residence at the Cotton Club in Harlem in 1927; the club admitted only white customers and had a plantation theme, and its owners demanded crude jungle music. Ellington turned the order into a proud signature sound of his own, a cornerstone of the Harlem Renaissance.

the-roman-legion-and-the-army-machine.context_blurb:
The Roman legion was one of the most effective fighting machines in history and a main reason a small Italian city came to rule the Mediterranean. A legion of about five thousand heavy infantry was split into cohorts and centuries, each led by a tough professional centurion, and its men trained constantly, carried their own tools and obeyed a discipline that enemies found terrifying.

The legionary's main weapon, the gladius, was unusual among ancient swords: it was short, only about two feet long, and made for stabbing, so that men packed shoulder to shoulder could thrust it past their shields without room to swing. After every day's march into enemy country the soldiers built a complete fortified camp from scratch, digging a ditch, raising an earth rampart and planting a wall of sharpened stakes, in four or five hours, and the next morning they tore it down.

Reforms tied to the general Marius, late in the Republic, required every soldier to carry his own gear on a T-shaped pole: saw, basket, pick, axe, stakes and three days' food, so the men were mocked as Marius's mules. In a siege the front rank locked shields into a wall while the men behind raised theirs overhead as a roof, making the whole unit an armoured box that arrows and rocks bounced off: the testudo, or tortoise. It was only a shelter, and the moment hand-to-hand fighting began it broke apart.

The pilum, a heavy javelin, had a long thin iron shank, and its tip was broader than the rod behind it. When it buried itself in an enemy's shield, the shank stuck fast and could hardly be pulled out, so the enemy usually had to throw away his shield and fight unprotected.

Discipline came from the centurion's vine-wood staff, the vitis, the one instrument the law let him use to beat a citizen soldier. Tacitus tells of a centurion whom the troops nicknamed Cedo Alteram, Bring me another, because he broke staff after staff on soldiers' backs and kept shouting for a fresh one; in the mutiny of AD 14 his men killed him first.

the-roman-republic-as-the-american-found.context_blurb:
The men who founded the United States had read the Roman historians in school, and they saw in the Roman Republic a free society of citizen-farmers that lost its liberty to military strongmen. That lesson shaped how they designed their own republic, from the Senate to the limits on a president's power.

Their favourite Roman was Cincinnatus. In 458 BC messengers found him ploughing his small farm and named him dictator to rescue a trapped army; he beat the enemy within roughly a fortnight, and then, holding full power, he resigned and went straight back to his plough.

George Washington followed his example. In 1783, having won the war, he resigned as commander-in-chief before Congress at Annapolis, returned all command of the army to it and went home to farm at Mount Vernon. On learning that Washington would surrender his power, George III reportedly said this would make him the greatest man on earth.

The 85 essays that Hamilton, Madison and Jay wrote for the Constitution were all signed Publius, after Publius Valerius Publicola, who in Plutarch's Lives saved the young Roman Republic from would-be tyrants, and their opponents wrote back as Brutus and Cato. Every pen name in the fight came from ancient Rome's republic, so the whole debate was argued in Roman costume. Rome is built into the Capitol itself. Flanking the Speaker's chair in the House of Representatives stands a bronze fasces, a bundle of rods strapped around an axe, copied from the emblem carried by the guards of Roman magistrates; its 13 rods stand for the original states, and it teaches that one rod breaks easily, but tied together they hold.

the-roman-republic-s-mixed-government.context_blurb:
The Roman Republic lasted from about 509 BC to the first century BC, and its government fascinated later thinkers. The Greek historian Polybius, who lived in Rome, argued that it worked because it mixed three kinds of rule, kingly consuls, an aristocratic Senate and democratic assemblies of citizens, each checking the others. The American founders borrowed the idea.

When the Romans expelled Tarquin the Proud, their last king, in 509 BC, they put two consuls in his place, chosen side by side for one year only, so that each could block the other; Romans even named each year after its pair. With both in Rome, the lead passed from one consul to the other each month, so neither could build up the power to seize the state, and after their year each had to step down and account for what he had done. The Republic's name for itself, carved on coins and monuments and carried on the army's standards, was SPQR, Senatus Populusque Romanus: the Senate and the People of Rome, the few and the many sharing one name. Legend says Romulus chose a hundred chief men for Rome's first Senate and named them patres, meaning fathers, and their descendants, the patricians, took their name from that word.

Twelve attendants went before each consul, bearing the fasces, rods bound around an axe. Inside the city walls the axe was taken out, because no citizen could be put to death without a trial: the rods were for beating, the axe for beheading, and only outside the walls did the consul hold power of life and death over his soldiers. The commoners, the plebeians, at first could hold no high office, so they invented a weapon. In a series of walkouts, the Secessions of the Plebs, which began in 494 BC, they marched out of the city and camped on a hill nearby, the Sacred Mount and later the Aventine, leaving Rome with no one to fight or farm, history's first general strike. In 494 BC the patrician envoy Menenius Agrippa coaxed them back with a fable: the limbs rebelled and refused to feed the belly, which looked lazy, until the entire body withered, so nobles and commoners, like belly and limbs, needed each other. The plebs won the office of tribune, their protector, whose veto, intercessio or I forbid, could halt even a consul. To shield him, the law made the tribune sacrosanct: whoever harmed him could be put to death at once, with no trial. Until 451 BC no written code existed; only patrician priests knew the law, so a plebeian might be condemned under rules he had never been shown. The plebs forced ten commissioners to write the law on bronze tablets set up in the Forum, the Twelve Tables, and centuries later Roman schoolboys still memorised them. In 458 BC, with a Roman army hemmed in by the Aequi on Mount Algidus, senators hurried across the Tiber to the small farm of Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus and made him dictator. A dictator could hold total power for up to six months; Cincinnatus rescued the army, laid down his power after just 15 days and went back to farming.

In Polybius's view, the Senate's most fearsome power was money. It controlled the treasury, and no coin could be spent without its decree, so even a victorious general in the field could be ruined if the Senate withheld the grain, clothing and pay his army needed. In 449 BC, legend says, Appius Claudius, one of the ten men then ruling Rome, used a crooked trial to have a free plebeian girl, Verginia, declared his slave. Unable to save her by law, her father, a soldier, stabbed his own daughter dead in the Forum rather than let her be taken, and the outrage brought down Appius and the ten and restored the tribunes. Rome's design crossed the ocean. In the sixty-third Federalist essay, in 1788, James Madison defended the new United States Senate by citing the republics of antiquity: history, he wrote, knew of no long-lived republic that lacked a senate, and he named Sparta, Rome and Carthage.

the-rosetta-stone.context_blurb:
In July 1799 French soldiers digging foundations for a fort near Rosetta, on the western mouth of the Nile, turned up a slab of dark granodiorite a little over a metre tall. Carved on it in 196 BC was a decree from the priests of Ptolemy V. That slab would let the world read ancient Egypt again.

The priests had the same decree cut three times, one version above another: sacred hieroglyphs at the top, Demotic, the everyday Egyptian handwriting, in the middle, and Greek, the language of Egypt's rulers, along the base. Nineteenth-century scholars could make nothing of either Egyptian script, but they read the Ancient Greek at the bottom with ease, so the Greek told them what the two texts above it must say.

Even so, hieroglyphs had been a dead script for some fourteen centuries. The Frenchman Jean-François Champollion broke through in September 1822. As the legend tells it, he burst in on his brother shouting that he had it, and then fainted dead away, so overcome by the shock that he lay in bed for days.

His proof that the signs could spell out sounds came from cartouches, the ovals drawn around royal names. Champollion set the oval for Ptolemy beside the oval for Cleopatra. Both names contain the sounds p, t, o and l, and the very same signs sat in the matching places in each, so those signs had to be letters standing for sounds, much like an alphabet. His knowledge of Coptic, the late descendant of Egyptian, then let him guess what the words meant, beating his English rival Thomas Young.

the-salamanca-school-the-birth-of-natura.context_blurb:
In the 1500s, while Spanish conquistadors were seizing whole empires in the Americas, a circle of Catholic theologians at the University of Salamanca, most of them Dominican friars, asked an uncomfortable question: what right did Spain really have to those lands and peoples? Working from natural law, Thomas Aquinas and Aristotle, they built much of what later thinkers called natural rights, a century before John Locke.

Their founder, Francisco de Vitoria, told a crowded lecture hall in 1539 that the peoples of the New World were already the true owners of their lands, veri domini in his Latin, so stumbling upon those lands handed Spain no title at all. To show how hollow the discovery excuse was, he turned it around: if finding a country made it yours, then the Indians might just as well have "discovered" Spain and France and owned them by that identical right.

Francisco Suárez, a Jesuit who carried the Salamanca tradition into the next century, pushed further in his 1613 book Defensio Fidei. He rejected the divine right of kings and argued that power passes from God to the whole people, who consent to be governed and who may, in extreme cases, throw down a tyrant. Crowned heads took fright: England's King James I had the book publicly burned, and the French capital followed suit the next year. Lord Acton later named the Salamanca scholars among the roots of Locke, Rousseau and Adam Smith, an early link in a chain that reached the American Founding.

the-salon-and-the-republic-of-letters.context_blurb:
Long before the telephone, the scholars and writers of eighteenth-century Europe kept up their arguments by post, sending hand-written pages across borders, faiths and languages. They called this scattered network the Republic of Letters. In Paris its meeting rooms were the salons, evening gatherings hosted by clever, well-connected women, where philosophers and scientists tried out new books and ideas in conversation.

Voltaire was the network's most tireless writer: nearly 19,000 of his letters still survive. A Stanford project that mapped where they travelled found that the web ran heavily through Paris and Geneva, a slow paper internet linking thinkers who mostly never met face to face.

The hostesses held real power, as one famous quarrel shows. Madame du Deffand, a blind hostess, took on a sharp young assistant, Julie de Lespinasse, in 1754. Ten years on she learned that Lespinasse had been receiving her finest guests, among them the mathematician d'Alembert, for an hour ahead of the hostess's own entrance, and she dismissed her. Lespinasse simply left, taking d'Alembert, Turgot and the rest of the literary circle along, and opened a rival salon that soon matched her old employer's.

the-scientific-method-bacon-and-descarte.context_blurb:
In the first half of the 1600s two men set out to explain how the new science should work, and how anyone could tell a true claim about nature from a false one. Francis Bacon was an English lawyer and statesman; René Descartes was a French soldier turned mathematician and philosopher. They pointed in opposite directions, and modern science grew from both of them.

Bacon put his idea in a picture of three creatures. A pure experimenter, he wrote in 1620, is like an ant, which only piles up what it collects, and a pure reasoner is like a spider, spinning webs out of its own body. The true scientist is the bee, which collects from the flowers and then, by a power of its own, digests what it collects into honey: real evidence, worked over by careful thought.

Descartes took the other road. In the 1640s he resolved to doubt everything he could: his senses, whether he might be dreaming, even whether some wicked demon was conjuring a false world around him. Doubting is itself thinking, and thinking needs a thinker, so no demon could trick him out of existing: because he was thinking, he had to exist, or as he put it, "I think, therefore I am."

A favourite story, which historians count as legend, has Descartes watching a fly crawl over his bedroom ceiling one morning and seeing that two numbers, its distance from each of two walls, could pin its position exactly. From that one idea, the story says, grew the graph, with its x and y axes. Whatever the truth about the fly, Descartes really did join algebra to geometry in his 1637 book La Géométrie, and the system still bears his name: Cartesian coordinates, from Cartesius, the Latin form of Descartes.

Bacon aimed his great 1620 book squarely at Aristotle, whose logic books were known as the Organon, the instrument. He titled his own Novum Organum, the New Instrument, announcing that the old way of reasoning was broken and here was a tool to replace it. He believed you learn most by prodding nature in a controlled test, and his last experiment killed him. Travelling through freezing weather in the spring of 1626 and wondering whether cold could keep meat fresh, he stuffed a chicken full of snow to find out. The chill he took turned to pneumonia, and he died on 9 April.

Descartes dated his own calling to a November night in 1619, when the young soldier sat alone in a stove-heated room and had three vivid dreams that he took as a summons to rebuild all human knowledge.

Bacon also warned of four Idols, traps that fool the mind before it starts to think. Worst of all, he said, were the Idols of the Marketplace: the muddle that comes from loose, empty words passed around in everyday talk. His most famous slogan is not quite his own. He wrote in 1597 that knowledge itself is power, but the crisp Latin form, scientia potentia est, was printed later by Thomas Hobbes, who had worked for Bacon as a secretary in his youth, so the apprentice polished the master's line.

Bacon rose to be Lord Chancellor, England's top law officer, and then fell hard. In 1621 Parliament accused him of taking bribes on twenty-three counts; he confessed, and begged the lords to show mercy to a broken reed, meaning himself. They fined him 40,000 pounds and held him briefly in the Tower of London. Descartes had his own brush with danger. In 1633, just as he finished a book called The World arguing that the Earth moves, the Inquisition found Galileo guilty of teaching the same idea. Descartes, a sincere believer, judged silence wiser: he shelved the finished book and would not let it be printed.

Side by side, the two men mark the great split at the root of modern science. Bacon began with evidence, gathering many observations and working up to general laws, which is called induction. Descartes began by doubting everything and then rebuilt knowledge, by pure reason alone, from a few certainties such as his own thinking existence, which is called deduction. The Scientific Revolution needed both.

the-scramble-for-africa-and-the-berlin-c.context_blurb:
Between about 1880 and 1914 the powers of Europe conquered nearly the whole of Africa, a land grab so fast that it is remembered as the Scramble for Africa. In 1870 Africans still governed most of their continent, from desert sultans in the north to Congo kingdoms at its heart. The rules for the carve-up were written at a conference table in Berlin.

In November 1884 the German chancellor Otto von Bismarck gathered fourteen nations in his capital to agree how to divide the continent without fighting one another, and over three months they drew their claims across a great map. Not a single African sat among them: the delegates did not treat African states as lawful parties at all, so men who governed none of the continent shared it out. By 1914 Europe held about nine-tenths of Africa, and only two African states, Ethiopia and Liberia, had kept their freedom through the whole Scramble.

The biggest single prize went to one man. On 1 August 1885 the vast Congo basin became the Congo Free State, the personal property not of Belgium but of King Leopold II of Belgium, who ruled some twenty million people as his private estate and never once travelled there.

Leopold's fortune came from wild rubber, which his private army, the Force Publique, forced Congolese villagers to gather. Bullets were counted: for every cartridge he fired, a soldier had to bring back a severed right hand to prove he had shot a person rather than wasted the round, and baskets of smoked hands became a grim kind of bookkeeping.

The truth leaked out through paperwork. In Belgium a young shipping clerk, E.D. Morel, studied the cargo lists. Ships sailed for the Congo with chains, guns and ammunition and almost no trade goods, yet came home heavy with rubber and ivory. If nothing was being sold to the Congolese, nothing was being paid for either, so Morel saw that the rubber was simply being taken at gunpoint. He quit his job and founded the Congo Reform Association to expose it.

Photographs did even more. In 1904 Alice Seeley Harris, a missionary, photographed a father, Nsala of Wala, sitting on her mission's porch and gazing at all the Force Publique had left of his five-year-old daughter after his village fell short of its rubber quota: her severed hand and foot. A picture could not be denied the way words could. In Mark Twain's furious 1905 satire, King Leopold's Soliloquy, the king grumbles that the Kodak camera, which he can neither bribe nor silence, has become his most powerful enemy. Twain gave every penny of the proceeds to Congo relief, and Arthur Conan Doyle also lent his fame to the cause.

Behind the race lay one Berlin rule. A power could claim African land only by effective occupation, by really holding it: it had to raise its flag, sign treaties with the local chiefs and post troops or police to control the ground. So every power rushed to get there first.

Historians still argue over the death toll of Leopold's rule, which lasted until 1908. Roger Casement, the British investigator, reckoned three million and warned that the true number was higher. Adam Hochschild and Jan Vansina, two later historians, estimate about ten million deaths, roughly half the population, from murder, starvation, exhaustion and disease.

the-seven-kings-and-the-birth-of-the-rep.context_blurb:
The Romans believed that before their Republic their city had been ruled by seven kings, from its legendary founder down to a tyrant named Tarquin. Much of it is legend, written down centuries later by the historian Livy, but Romans told it as the story of how they became a free people.

The last king, Lucius Tarquinius, ruled by fear and expelled from the Senate anyone who crossed him. Romans tagged him Superbus, the Proud, an insult he earned by his arrogance rather than by birth, and it has clung to him for 2,500 years. In about 509 BC Rome threw him out, and its people swore that no king would ever rule them again; that hatred of one-man rule became the bedrock of the Republic. So that no one man could hold power for life, the Republic handed its highest authority to two consuls, equal in power and serving one year each, so either could block the other.

Tarquin had won his throne by crime. He killed his own father-in-law, King Servius Tullius, and as the body lay in the road the dead man's daughter, Tullia, drove her chariot right over it. Horrified Romans named that road the Vicus Sceleratus, the Street of Crime, and still pointed it out as a real place. Legend tells, too, how an old prophetess, the Cumaean Sibyl, asked Tarquin a high price for nine prophetic books. Each time he refused, she burned three, yet asked the same sum for the rest, until Tarquin paid the full nine-book price for only the last three, now too precious to lose. Rome kept those Sibylline Books for emergencies.

Tarquin had murdered leading Romans, and one man stayed alive only by acting the harmless fool. Lucius Junius Brutus, whose own brother was among the dead, played the part so well that his nickname, Brutus, means dullard, or idiot. The fool was the cleverest man in Rome. When the king's sons asked the Oracle of Delphi who would rule next, they were told that supreme power would go to the first of them to kiss his mother. While the princes planned a dash home, Brutus, who had come with them, read the mother as the Earth, mother of all, and pretended to stumble so that he could kiss the ground.

The end began during the siege of Ardea. Over wine the young noblemen argued about whose wife was the most virtuous, then galloped back to Rome after dark to catch the women off guard. The princes' wives were found at a rich banquet, but Lucretia, wife of Collatinus, was spinning wool by lamplight among her maids, the very picture of a good Roman wife, and she won the wager. Soon afterwards the king's son Sextus wronged her. In Livy's telling she summoned her husband and father, bound them by oath to avenge her and declared that her shame must never excuse a faithless wife; then, too quickly for anyone to stop her, she pulled out a knife she had hidden and stabbed herself.

As she lay dying, Brutus the supposed half-wit astonished them all. He drew the bloody blade from her wound and vowed on her blood that Tarquin and all his house would be driven out by sword and fire. Then he handed the knife from man to man so that each swore the same oath on it, turning a private grief into a shared vow against the monarchy.

The new Republic soon tested its founder. As consul, Brutus learned that two of his own sons were conspiring to restore the king, and the law's penalty was death. Livy says Brutus sat and watched them die, a father's anguish plain on his face, and never once halted it: the law had to bind even the men who made it. He persuaded Lars Porsena, an Etruscan king, to march on Rome, and only a wooden bridge over the Tiber stood between his army and the city. Horatius Cocles held its far end alone while his comrades hacked it down behind him, and when it fell he swam back across the river in his armour, saving Rome.

the-silk-road.context_blurb:
For some fifteen hundred years, caravans carried silk west out of China and brought horses, glass and new beliefs east, along a web of overland routes linking China, Central Asia, Persia, India and the Mediterranean. There was never just one road, and goods changed hands many times on the way. A nineteenth-century German geographer gave the network its modern name, the Silk Road.

The deadliest stretch lay just west of China: the Taklamakan Desert, a vast, waterless sea of sand whose heart no caravan dared to cross. At Dunhuang, the last place to stock up going west and the first safe haven coming home, the route forked in two, one branch curving around the northern edge of the sands and one around the southern edge. Each branch survived by hugging a chain of oasis towns along the desert's rim, kept alive by meltwater running down from the surrounding mountains.

Silk-making was China's jealously kept secret, and sending silkworms, their eggs or even mulberry seeds out of the country was a crime punished by death. Around 552 two monks broke the monopoly for good, bringing the Byzantine emperor Justinian I a cargo of living eggs tucked inside canes of hollow bamboo. Dunhuang shows that the road carried ideas as well. From the 4th century to the 14th, monks there cut more than 700 caves into a cliff, the Mogao Caves, and covered their walls with Buddhist paintings, proof that Buddhism travelled into China along the trade routes.

The desert kept other treasures. In 1907 the archaeologist Aurel Stein found near Dunhuang a lost mailbag of letters in Sogdian, written around 313 and never delivered. One came from a woman named Miwnay, whose husband had left her stuck there for three years and would not come for her, and she signed off by telling him she would sooner be the wife of a dog or a pig than his. Another cave, a library walled up for some nine centuries, held the Diamond Sutra, printed in 868 and the oldest dated printed book anywhere. A note at its end says that one Wang Jie paid for it to be printed and given away on behalf of his two parents, a book offered as a gift of love for his mother and father.

The merchants who did most of the carrying were seldom Chinese or Roman. They were Sogdians from Samarkand and Bukhara, the great middlemen of the route, and sheer business need made their language the common trading tongue all along it. Educated Sogdians often spoke four or five languages.

the-sistine-chapel-ceiling.context_blurb:
Between 1508 and 1512 Michelangelo, who thought of himself as a sculptor rather than a painter, covered the vaulted ceiling of the Sistine Chapel, the pope's private chapel in the Vatican, with scenes from the opening chapters of Genesis. Pope Julius II had hired him, and the finished ceiling astonished Rome.

The most famous panel, the Creation of Adam, shows God surging forward among his angels as the first man lifts his arm toward him. Michelangelo left their outstretched fingers just short of touching, a thin gap of empty air between them, so the scene freezes at the instant before life passes across, and that gap is the most copied detail on the whole ceiling.

Popular pictures show him painting flat on his back, but that is a myth. In truth he stood on a scaffold for four years with his head cranked backwards, reaching up above him to paint, and Vasari, who knew him, wrote that the work cost him the greatest discomfort.

the-socratic-method-as-a-way-of-thinking.context_blurb:
Socrates, a stonemason's son, spent his days in the streets of Athens in the 400s BC, stopping generals, priests and politicians to ask what courage, justice or piety really were. He accepted each answer politely, then tested it against one case after another until it fell apart. That stubborn habit of questioning became one of the great ways of thinking in the Western world.

Strangely, the man remembered as the West's great teacher of thinking never wrote a single page. Everything we know of his method comes from two pupils who set it down after his death, the philosopher Plato and the soldier-historian Xenophon. His mission began with a god's reply. His friend Chaerephon made the journey to Delphi to put a question to the priestess: was anyone wiser than Socrates? She replied that there was no one wiser. Socrates, sure that he knew nothing, set out to prove the oracle wrong by hunting for a wiser man among the poets, craftsmen and politicians, and his method grew out of that search. He was no beauty. In Plato's Symposium the drunken Alcibiades describes him as snub-nosed, goggle-eyed and ugly as a satyr, and likens him to one of those cheap Silenus figurines that open up: crack it apart, he says, and it is packed with little golden gods, a treasure hidden inside a plain outside.

The Greeks called his technique elenchos, which means a cross-examination: not teaching but testing, a string of questions under which a confident man's answers give way. He had his own picture for it. His mother, Phaenarete, was a midwife, and in the Theaetetus Socrates says he delivers ideas the way she delivered babies: barren of wisdom himself, he helps others give birth to their thoughts and then tests whether each is healthy or a mere phantom. His victims did not always enjoy it. In the dialogue Plato named after him, Meno, a wealthy youth questioned into helplessness, complains that his mind and tongue have gone numb and compares Socrates to the torpedo fish, the electric ray that numbs whatever touches it. Socrates turns the insult around: he leaves others confused, he says, only because he is more confused than anyone.

Outside the court one day he met Euthyphro, a self-styled expert on religion, who had come to prosecute his own father after a hired labourer died bound hand and foot in a ditch. In 399 BC Athens put Socrates himself on trial for corrupting its young men. He compared the city to a fine, well-bred horse made sluggish by its own size, and said the god had set him on it as a gadfly, a stinging fly that rouses, persuades and scolds it all day long.

Five definitions of piety later, Euthyphro remembered an appointment and fled, never seeing the puzzle buried in his own certainty, which philosophers still call the Euthyphro dilemma: do the gods love what is pious because it is pious, or is a thing pious simply because the gods love it? Socrates left it open; his work was to bring it into the light. People often quote him as saying he knows that he knows nothing, but Plato never puts those words in his mouth. The real line is sharper: after testing a politician famed for his wisdom, Socrates decided he was slightly better off, because the politician knew nothing yet believed he knew, while Socrates knew nothing and did not believe he knew.

In the Meno, Socrates also set out to show that learning is really remembering. He questioned a slave boy who had never been taught geometry about how to draw a square twice as big in area as one already drawn. The boy first doubled each side, which only made the area four times bigger; then, led by nothing but questions, he found that the new square has to be built on the diagonal of the old one. Socrates told him nothing, and argued that the boy had recollected it, an idea called anamnesis. In the Republic, Thrasymachus, a sophist, bursts into the talk like a wild animal, shouting that justice is only the advantage of the stronger. Socrates questions him until he must concede that injustice belongs to the ignorant and the bad, and Plato records the sign of his defeat: sweating in the summer heat, the loud sophist did what no one had seen him do before and blushed.

the-space-race-sputnik.context_blurb:
On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union put the first artificial satellite into orbit, and the Space Race between the Soviets and the United States began. For twelve years the two superpowers chased one first after another, from the first dog in orbit to the first man in space, until Americans walked on the Moon in 1969.

The satellite, Sputnik 1, was a polished sphere no bigger than a beach ball. Its chief designer, Sergei Korolev, gave it a simple one-watt radio on easy frequencies on purpose, so that radio amateurs and ordinary people everywhere could tune in to its steady beep, beep, beep as it crossed the sky overhead. The batteries lasted 22 days. A month later, on 3 November, Sputnik 2 carried the first living creature into orbit: Laika, a stray dog picked up off the streets of Moscow. Her flight was one-way from the start, since there was no way to bring her home, and she died of overheating within hours.

On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin, a 27-year-old Soviet air-force pilot, became the first human in space. As his rocket lifted off from Baikonur, he shouted Poyekhali, Russian for "Let's go!", and the word went round the world. He circled the Earth once in 108 minutes, and he had been chosen partly because, at 5 feet 2 inches, he fit the cramped capsule. Gagarin did not ride Vostok 1 all the way down. High above the farmland near Saratov he ejected and came down under his own parachute, apart from the capsule. A startled farmer and his family backed away as he landed, and he assured them he was a Soviet citizen like them, just back from space. The Soviets hid the ejection until 1971, because record rules required a pilot to land inside his craft.

Sputnik's beep frightened Americans, since a rocket able to put a satellite overhead every hour and a half could also deliver a nuclear bomb to American cities. Within months the United States founded NASA and the research agency ARPA, later renamed DARPA, to carry its science into space. Congress also passed the National Defense Education Act, and America's own first satellite, Explorer 1, reached orbit on 31 January 1958, where its detector let James Van Allen discover the radiation belts that bear his name.

the-spanish-armada.context_blurb:
In 1588 Spain's Catholic king, Philip II, sent about 130 ships and some 30,000 men north to invade Protestant England, overthrow Queen Elizabeth I and end years of raids by English sea captains on Spanish treasure fleets. Spain was so sure of winning that its fleet has gone down in history as the Invincible Armada, a boast that became a bitter joke when about half the ships never came home.

Lord Howard of Effingham commanded the English fleet. His vice-admiral, aboard the Revenge, was Francis Drake, who had plundered Spanish treasure for years, and the Spanish called him El Draque, the Dragon, a name that was half curse and half dread.

The Armada sailed up the Channel in a tight crescent that English guns could not break. As it lay at anchor off Calais late on 28 July, the English sent old ships loaded with gunpowder, tar, pitch and brimstone drifting into it, ablaze. The fireships did not burn a single Spanish vessel, but terrified crews hacked through their anchor cables and fled in all directions into the night, losing some 120 anchors, so the fleet could never again hold position or form up.

On land, Elizabeth came to Tilbury wearing a silver breastplate to stir her troops. Granting that she had the body of a weak and feeble woman, she declared that she had a king's heart and stomach, and an English king's at that. The words survive in a 1654 account by Leonel Sharp, and most historians accept them as genuine.

Beaten again at Gravelines, the Armada could not fight its way back down the Channel, so it fled the long way round, north of Scotland and down the west coast of Ireland. Gales the English called the Protestant wind wrecked ship after ship, about 24 off Ireland alone. England struck a medal for the victory, and its Latin, Afflavit Deus et dissipati sunt, gave the glory not to the sailors but to God, whose breath had scattered the enemy.

the-spanish-armada-1588.context_blurb:
In the summer of 1588 King Philip II of Spain sent about 130 ships north to invade Protestant England, overthrow its queen and bring the kingdom back to the Catholic faith. The plan was to collect a Spanish army waiting in the Netherlands and ferry it across the Channel. For a week the faster English ships harried the great fleet without breaking it.

Then, on the night of 7 to 8 August, while the Armada lay in a close half-moon off Calais, the English sent eight blazing hulks drifting into it. The Spanish dreaded hellburners, ships packed as floating bombs, so captains cut their anchor cables and scattered in the darkness, breaking their formation for good. Not one Spanish ship actually caught fire: terror alone did the damage.

With the wind against it, the beaten fleet could not return the way it came. It fled north, round the top of Scotland and down past Ireland, storms wrecked as many as 24 ships on those coasts, and around half the fleet never reached Spain. Elizabeth's victory medal gave the credit to God, who had blown with his winds and scattered them, and that storm has been called the Protestant Wind ever since.

the-spanish-flu-pandemic-of-1918.context_blurb:
In 1918, as the First World War drew to its end, a new strain of influenza swept the planet in waves. It infected about 500 million people, roughly a third of everyone alive, and killed somewhere between 50 and 100 million of them.

The flu took far more lives than the whole war, whose four years of fighting killed some 17 to 20 million. It almost certainly did not start in Spain. Britain, France, Germany and the United States censored news of the sickness to protect wartime morale, but neutral Spain did not, so Spanish newspapers alone told the world about the outbreak, and the world wrongly pinned it on Spain. The Spanish themselves blamed France.

On 28 September 1918, though the flu had already reached it, Philadelphia went ahead with a Liberty Loan parade to sell war bonds, and more than 200,000 people crowded the streets. Within three days all 31 of its hospitals were full; about 2,600 people were dead by the week's end and some 12,000 in the weeks after, which made it the deadliest parade America has ever held. St. Louis, which cancelled its parade and closed public gatherings, fared far better.

Most flu seasons kill babies and the elderly, but a chart of 1918's deaths makes a W, with a third great spike among strong, healthy people between 25 and 35. Their strong immune systems overreacted in a cytokine storm that flooded their lungs with fluid and suffocated them, so the disease struck hardest at the people expected to survive it.

The key to the killer lay in Alaska. At Brevig Mission, a tiny Alaskan village, 72 of the 80 people died of the flu within five days, and they were buried in ground that never thaws. In 1997 Johan Hultin recovered lung tissue, still carrying the virus, from a woman's frozen grave, and by 2005 Jeffery Taubenberger's team had used it to rebuild the whole 1918 virus and show that it began in birds.

the-steam-locomotive-and-railroads.context_blurb:
Steam engines running on iron rails were the first great leap in mechanised transport, and they began in Britain. The Cornishman Richard Trevithick built the earliest working locomotives in the first years of the 1800s, and in the 1820s George Stephenson put them to work on public lines. Within decades railways ran across Britain, Europe and America.

The turning point came at the Rainhill Trials in October 1829, a public contest of locomotives. In an age when a galloping horse set the speed limit, Stephenson's Rocket raced past at roughly 30 miles an hour, faster than any machine most people had ever seen. Rocket was the only engine to finish: Sans Pareil broke down, and so did Novelty, the crowd's favourite. Its secret lay inside. Instead of one flue, its boiler was pierced by 25 copper fire-tubes, and a blastpipe shot used steam up the chimney so that it sucked air hard through the fire, giving far more heat and power than older designs. Robert Stephenson built it with his father George and Henry Booth in Newcastle, and it survives today in the National Railway Museum.

Forty years later America finished something grander. On 10 May 1869, at Utah's Promontory Summit, the Central Pacific's engine Jupiter and the Union Pacific's engine Number 119 stood face to face with a single tie between them, after six years of laying track toward each other from opposite coasts, completing the first railroad to cross the continent. Leland Stanford, the Central Pacific's boss, raised a silver hammer before a great crowd to drive in the last spike, made of gold, and missed it entirely. It did not matter: the spike was wired to the telegraph, and the operator flashed the single word DONE across the nation.

That line was built at a cost. The Central Pacific could find few white workers for the mountains, so by 1867 more than nine-tenths of its crews were immigrants from China, between ten and fifteen thousand men, earning less than white men and buying their own food. They did the deadliest work on the line, blasting tunnels through the Sierra Nevada's granite, and more than a thousand are thought to have died in avalanches, rockslides, explosions and cold. The Union Pacific's crews, building west, were mostly Irish immigrants and Civil War veterans.

the-suez-canal.context_blurb:
The Suez Canal is a channel dug across the Isthmus of Suez, the narrow neck of Egyptian land between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea. The French diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps drove the project, and after about ten years of digging, much of it by forced Egyptian labour, the canal opened with great ceremony in November 1869.

Before it, ships sailing between Europe and Asia had to go the long way, all around Africa and its southern tip, the Cape of Good Hope; now they could pass straight from one sea into the other. The saving was enormous. A voyage from London to Bombay became about 4,500 miles shorter, and ships could skip the long, dangerous passage round the Cape.

The opening day brought a famous trick. Seventy-seven ships were to file in behind L'Aigle, the French imperial yacht carrying Empress Eugénie, wife of Napoleon III. But under cover of night the British warship HMS Newport slipped ahead of the whole line, so a ship of Britain, not France, was the first ever through the canal.

Britain soon owned a large share of the canal itself. In 1875 Egypt's bankrupt ruler, Khedive Ismail, offered his big block of canal shares for sale, and Britain's prime minister, Benjamin Disraeli, meant to buy nearly half the company, though Parliament was not sitting to vote the money. As the story is told, Disraeli borrowed the 4 million pounds from the banker Lionel de Rothschild on nothing more than a gentleman's word, without any contract signed. The canal became Britain's imperial lifeline to India.

the-sumerian-base-60-number-system.context_blurb:
In southern Mesopotamia, more than four thousand years ago, the Sumerians built some of the world's first cities and one of its first systems of mathematics. Instead of counting in tens, as we do, they counted in sixties, a method called sexagesimal, and the Babylonians who came after them used it to build up advanced astronomy and algebra.

That habit has outlived them by thousands of years. Every time you read a clock you are counting like the Sumerians of Mesopotamia, because our 60-minute hour and 60-second minute come straight from their sixties, the oldest counting system still in daily use. So does the 360-degree circle.

Sixty was a clever choice. It splits evenly into 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 or 30 parts with nothing left over, and it is the smallest number that every whole number from 1 to 6 divides without a remainder. That is why an hour can be cut neatly in two, three, four, five or six. Ten cannot even be split into thirds.

the-swahili-coast-city-states.context_blurb:
From southern Somalia down to northern Mozambique, a chain of Muslim trading cities grew up along the East African coast between about the 700s and the arrival of the Portuguese around 1500. There African coastal peoples met Arab, Persian and later Indian and Chinese merchants who sailed the Indian Ocean, and from that meeting grew a new people, culture and language.

Arab sailors gave them their name. Swahili comes from the Arabic sawahil, meaning the coasts, a plain description of where the towns stood. The language itself is Bantu at its core, rich in Arabic and Persian borrowings.

Their seamen rode the open ocean in boats called mtepe, built without a single piece of iron. The coconut-wood planks were sewn together edge to edge with coir, rope twisted from coconut-husk fibre, and pegged with wood, so a hull that scraped the razor-edged coral reefs flexed instead of shattering. A Greek trading guide of the first century AD, the Periplus, already describes such sewn boats.

The richest city was Kilwa. Its merchants rode the monsoon winds across the Indian Ocean to India and Arabia, and their trade paid for the sultan's coral-stone palace, Husuni Kubwa, with more than a hundred rooms, an octagonal pool and running water indoors. Kilwa's own chronicle tells, as legend, how a prince from Persia, Ali ibn al-Hasan, purchased the island from the Bantu king who ruled it, paying in coloured cloth, enough to go right round the island's edge. When the king regretted the bargain and tried to take Kilwa back, he found that the Persians had dug away the narrow land bridge, turning it into a true island, cut off and no longer his.

Kilwa struck its own copper coins from about 1150 to 1330, and some of them travelled astonishingly far. During the Second World War a soldier named Morry Isenberg found a few strange coins on the sand of the Wessel Islands, off Australia's northern tip, and kept them in an old tin for 35 years. When experts identified them in 1979, they turned out to be medieval Kilwa coins, the oldest foreign objects ever found in Australia, and no one knows how they crossed the whole Indian Ocean. The coast's reach ran even to China. In 1414 the Swahili city of Malindi sent envoys with a giraffe for the Ming court, handing it to the fleet of Admiral Zheng He. At court, nobody had ever beheld such a creature, and the Chinese took it for the qilin, a unicorn-like beast of legend that appeared only when a wise and virtuous ruler sat on the throne.

The Portuguese brought the golden age to an end. In 1502 Vasco da Gama forced Kilwa's ruler to pay yearly tribute in gold and pearls, and Francisco de Almeida came in 1505 with some 500 soldiers, battled street by street and left the town looted and burning. To hold its harbour for Portuguese ships on the way to India, Almeida built a stone fort there, the Gereza, then sailed north to sack and burn Mombasa as well.

Underneath it all lay the monsoon. For a season of three or four months the winds pushed ships toward Africa; then they swung round toward Arabia and India, so a trader who came in on one wind often had to wait months to sail home. Stranded ashore through the season, many merchants married into local Bantu families, and over generations the African and Arab worlds fused into the Swahili people.

the-telegraph-and-morse-code.context_blurb:
In the 1830s and 1840s the American painter and inventor Samuel Morse, with his partner Alfred Vail, built a simple electric telegraph that sent letters down a single wire in a code of dots and dashes, long and short pulses, now called Morse code. In 1844 Congress paid for a test line about 40 miles long, from Washington to Baltimore. It was the first technology to send a message faster than a rider on horseback.

The half-built line proved itself before it was finished. On 1 May 1844 news that the Whig party had chosen Henry Clay for president came down the wire from Baltimore, and it reached Washington roughly an hour, some 64 minutes, ahead of the train carrying the same report. For the first time, news had travelled faster than the person bringing it.

Three weeks later, on 24 May, Morse sat in the old Supreme Court chamber of the Capitol and tapped out the first official message to Vail in Baltimore: What hath God wrought, a verse from the Book of Numbers. Seventeen-year-old Annie Ellsworth chose the words; Morse had promised her the first message because she had rushed to tell him that Congress had passed his funding bill.

the-ten-commandments-and-the-decalogue-a.context_blurb:
The Ten Commandments are the short list of laws that the Hebrew scriptures say God gave to Moses on Mount Sinai after the Israelites escaped from Egypt. They command worship of one God and a weekly day of rest, and they forbid murder, theft, adultery and false witness. Through Judaism and Christianity they became the most influential ancient law in Western civilization.

Exodus tells the giving of the law as a terrifying scene. The mountain smoked like a furnace and shook, thunder rolled, lightning flashed, and through it all came the blast of a ram's-horn trumpet, the shofar, sounding long and growing ever louder until the whole camp shook with fear. Moses climbed into the cloud and came back with two stone tablets inscribed by the finger of God, the only thing in the whole Bible described as written by God himself.

Meanwhile, below, the people were dancing around a golden calf they had made. Moses' anger burned, and he hurled the tablets from his hands and broke them to pieces there on the ground at the mountain's foot. He burned the calf, ground its gold to fine powder, scattered it on water and made the Israelites drink it, forcing them to swallow their own false god. Aaron had cast the calf from the people's gold, but when Moses demanded an answer he gave a famously feeble excuse: he had only thrown the gold into the fire, he said, and out came this calf, as if the fire had done it rather than his own hands.

For the second set of tablets, the work was split. God told Moses to cut two new blank stones himself, and God then wrote the words on them again, so the renewed covenant was cut by human hands but inscribed by God. The people had already learned to fear that voice. Terrified by the fire, the smoke and the sound, they stood far back and begged Moses to talk to them himself and not let God speak to them, for fear that they would die. One of the laws commands a weekly day of rest, the Sabbath, and it protected people whom no other ancient law shielded: besides the family's own children, Exodus gives the same day off to its male and female slaves, its ox and donkey, and the foreigner living within its gates.

Set beside the older law of Babylon, the difference is plain. On the black stone that carries Hammurabi's laws, more than seven feet tall, the king stands before the seated Shamash, the sun god and patron of justice, who presents him with a rod and a ring, the signs of power to make law: a god's mandate given to one ruler. Exodus says the Ten Words came another way, spoken by God aloud to the whole assembled nation at once, not handed privately to priests or a king, so the entire people became party to the covenant.

The grammar differs too. The Ten Words are flat commands with no penalty attached, such as "You shall not steal," while Hammurabi's code, like every other law code of the ancient Near East, is case law, set out as "if a man does this, then that shall follow." Scholars call the first kind apodictic and the second casuistic. Hammurabi's justice was also graded by rank. A noble who put out another noble's eye lost his own, but a slave's eye was settled in silver, valued at half of what the slave had cost, while the Decalogue bound everyone alike.

Even the name in English is a translation. The Hebrew Bible never calls them commandments; three times it names them Aseret ha-Devarim, the Ten Words, or Ten Utterances. The Greek translation called the Septuagint rendered that as deka logoi, which gave us the word Decalogue.

the-toltecs-and-tula.context_blurb:
The Toltecs were a people of central Mexico whose capital, Tula, flourished north of today's Mexico City from about AD 900 to 1150, in the centuries between the fall of Teotihuacan and the rise of the Aztecs. Their state collapsed in the 1100s for reasons no one fully understands, but its ruins and its legend lived on.

Four stone giants, each some 15 feet high and assembled from four drum-shaped blocks, still stand atop Tula's Pyramid B. Each one shows a Toltec warrior in full battle dress, with a tall feathered headdress, a butterfly-shaped breastplate, a round sun-disk on his back and an atlatl, a spear-thrower, in his hand. Nicknamed the Atlanteans, they probably once held up a temple roof as columns, and they are so alike that Toltec workshops must have turned out huge sculptures to a standard pattern.

To the Aztecs, who rose long after Tula fell, the Toltecs were a vanished people of a golden age, masters of every art. They even turned the name into an everyday Nahuatl word: a toltecatl was an artist, a master craftsman or a wise man. Toltecayotl, Toltec-ness, meant art and civilization itself, the opposite of the wild nomad's life, and to say a person had a Toltec heart meant that he or she excelled at a craft.

the-transcontinental-railroad-and-the-go.context_blurb:
On 10 May 1869 America's first transcontinental railroad was finished at Promontory Summit in Utah Territory, where the Central Pacific, building eastward out of California, met the Union Pacific, building westward out of Nebraska. Once the rails joined, a coast-to-coast journey shrank from more than four months to about a week.

To mark the joining, the bosses tapped in a ceremonial last spike of gold, 17.6-carat and engraved for the occasion, set into a polished laurelwood tie. It never stayed in the track: it was pulled out after the ceremony and now sits at Stanford University. The two locomotives, the Central Pacific's Jupiter and the Union Pacific's Number 119, stood nose to nose, and a camera caught men from the two companies reaching across the gap to shake hands. The meeting was hailed as the Wedding of the Rails, and that photograph of it became an instant American icon.

Leland Stanford, the Central Pacific's president, raised a heavy silver maul and swung at the spike, which was linked by telegraph wire so that every blow would sound across the country, and he missed it completely. The Union Pacific's Thomas Durant missed too, so the telegraph operator simply tapped out one word, DONE, and the nation celebrated anyway.

Days earlier, on 28 April, Central Pacific crews had laid ten miles and fifty-six feet of track in a single day, a record for work by hand that still stands. Eight Irishmen handled the rails, each lifting an estimated 125 tons of iron, and when fresh men were offered to take over at lunch, the eight refused and kept hauling rails until the day was done.

The hardest work had come two winters before, high in the Sierra Nevada. Through the winter of 1866 to 1867 the Central Pacific's Chinese crews, the great majority of its workers, kept blasting rock tunnels near Donner Pass while storm after storm, 44 in all, buried the summit in snow deeper than forty feet. They dug tunnels through the snow itself, 50 to 500 feet long with air shafts bored through the walls, and lived and worked down there by lantern light for months, hardly ever seeing the sky. Leland Stanford himself testified that without them the western part of the line could never have been finished.
