the-transistor-and-the-digital-revolutio.context_blurb:
Just before Christmas 1947, at Bell Telephone Laboratories in New Jersey, John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley built the first transistor, a tiny solid switch made from a semiconductor crystal. It could do the work of the hot, fragile vacuum tubes that filled the first room-sized computers, and every chip of the digital age grew from it.

In the 1950s engineers ran into a problem they named the tyranny of numbers: a single machine needed thousands of separate parts, far too many for anyone to wire together by hand. The cure was the integrated circuit, which put the transistors, resistors and capacitors of a whole circuit together on one small chip.

Jack Kilby built the first one at Texas Instruments in the summer of 1958. He was so new that he had no holiday time, so he worked by himself in the deserted lab while everyone else was away. On 12 September he showed his bosses a rough patch of germanium holding a transistor, a capacitor and resistors joined by fine gold wires, and when he flipped the switch, a green wavy line rolled across the oscilloscope screen: the chip worked. Robert Noyce at Fairchild made a version in 1959 that printed the wires onto the chip, which made mass production practical, and Kilby later won the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physics.

In 1971 the Intel 4004 went further, cramming a computer's entire central processor, 2,300 transistors, onto one chip about 12 square millimetres in size: the first microprocessor. Federico Faggin, who designed it, signed his work: he etched his own initials, F.F., right into the silicon.

the-trojan-horse-and-the-fall-of-troy.context_blurb:
In Greek legend, told by Homer and later by the Roman poet Virgil, the Greeks besieged the city of Troy, on the coast of Asia Minor, for ten years without breaking its walls. In the end they won not by force but by a trick, and its name is still a byword for a gift with a trap inside.

The Greeks built a huge horse of wood, hollow inside, hid a band of their best warriors in its belly, left it by the city and sailed off as if beaten. The Trojans dragged it into the city themselves, and that night the hidden men climbed out and opened the gates to the returning army. Today a Trojan is also a computer program that hides an attack inside something harmless.

One man saw the danger. The priest Laocoön hurled his spear into the horse's flank and warned the Trojans that he feared the Greeks even when they came bearing gifts, a line Virgil wrote as Timeo Danaos et dona ferentes. Then two huge sea serpents came up out of the waves and crushed him to death along with his two sons. The Trojans took it as a sign that the gods wanted the horse brought in, so the warning that should have saved Troy doomed it. A marble statue of Laocoön and his sons in the serpents' coils, dug up in Rome in 1506, stands in the Vatican Museums.

the-twelve-tables-rome-s-first-written-l.context_blurb:
Around 450 BC, a couple of generations into the Roman Republic, Rome's ordinary citizens, the plebeians, demanded that the law be written down. Until then it lived only in the memories of a few patrician priests, the pontifices, who alone interpreted the old customs and so held the law in their hands. A commission set the rules down on twelve bronze tablets, the Twelve Tables.

Some of those rules were harsh. Table III dealt with debtors: a man who could not pay was loaded with chains of at least fifteen pounds; if nobody had bought his freedom by the third market day, his creditors were allowed to cut his body into pieces and share them out. The Latin says partis secanto, let them cut the parts, and the clause even adds that taking more or less than one's share is no crime.

The decisive step was where the Romans put the tablets: they fixed them up in the Forum, the open square every Roman crossed, so a plebeian and a patrician could read exactly the same law with their own eyes. No one could claim any longer that the law said something secret, and historians see in it a distant ancestor of the Western ideal that law is written, public and the same for everyone.

the-umayyad-caliphate-and-damascus.context_blurb:
The Umayyads were the first great dynasty of Islam. In 661 Muawiya, the governor of Syria, took power after the murder of the fourth caliph, Ali, and moved the capital to Damascus. From there the Umayyad caliphs led the fastest Muslim expansion in history, reaching the Pyrenees in the west and the Indus River in the east within a single lifetime.

Tariq ibn Ziyad, a Berber general, led the Umayyad invasion of Spain in 711, crossing the strait from Africa and landing beside a great rock. The rock took his name, Jabal Tariq, the Mountain of Tariq, which English speakers later wore down to Gibraltar.

The dynasty fell in 750, when a revolt led by the rival Abbasid family destroyed Umayyad power at the river Zab and tracked down the princes one by one. Only Abd al-Rahman I, a young prince, got away: he fled across the whole of North Africa and founded a new Umayyad state at Cordoba, in Spain, which became a famous centre of learning.

the-valladolid-debate-las-casas-vs-sep-l.context_blurb:
In 1550 the emperor Charles V, ruler of Spain and its new American empire, took a step that hardly any empire in history has taken. He halted every new conquest in the Americas and summoned a panel of judges to the Spanish city of Valladolid, where two learned men argued out, in public and under his own crown, what Spain was doing in the New World.

The judges had to settle whether it was just for Spain to make war on the native peoples of the Americas at all: an empire had paused its own expansion to ask, openly, whether what it was doing was right.

The scholar who spoke for the war was Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda. He leaned on the natural slave, a notion he took from Aristotle: some people, he claimed, are born to be ruled. He ranked the natives below the Spaniards as children rank below adults and women below men, and even placed them somewhere between apes and men, so Spanish rule was, in his view, natural and right. It was a serious, learned argument for its day, made in the open. Bartolomé de las Casas answered that the native peoples had real laws, farming and religion and were fully capable of reason.

the-wars-of-religion.context_blurb:
After Martin Luther's Reformation split Western Christendom, Catholics and Protestants fought a long series of wars over faith in the 1500s and 1600s, first in Germany, then in France, and finally across much of Europe in the Thirty Years' War. Kings, dukes and popes made the decisions, and ordinary worshippers paid for them.

In Germany the Peace of Augsburg of 1555 allowed every German prince to decide whether his lands would be Lutheran or Catholic, a rule summed up as cuius regio, eius religio: whose realm, his religion. But it made room for no third faith and shut out the fast-growing Calvinists, an omission that helped pave the way to the much deadlier Thirty Years' War.

In France the killing started in the spring of 1562: on the first of March Duke François de Guise led his men against Huguenots, French Protestants, as they worshipped in a barn in the town of Wassy, and killed about a hundred of them. It lit the fuse for thirty-six years of civil war. The worst horror came ten years later. In the dark hours of 24 August 1572, St Bartholomew's Day, church bells near the Louvre gave the signal, and Catholic mobs began hunting Huguenots door to door across Paris; so as not to kill one another in the confusion, the attackers tied white scarves or bands on their sleeves.

Among the first victims was Admiral Gaspard de Coligny, who led the Huguenots. The Duke of Guise's men pulled him out of bed, murdered him and then threw his body from the window into the street below. One of the killers reportedly said he had never seen a man meet death more steadfastly. In Rome, Pope Gregory XIII greeted the news with celebration. He had a Te Deum sung in thanks and a medal struck whose blunt Latin, Ugonottorum strages, means the Slaughter of the Huguenots, with an angel bearing a cross and a sword striking down the fallen Protestants.

King Henry IV finally ended the French wars in 1598 with the Edict of Nantes. Catholicism stayed the state religion, but Huguenots could worship in much of the kingdom, though not in Paris, hold office and enter the universities. As a guarantee stronger than any promise, they also kept more than a hundred fortified towns, places of safety such as La Rochelle and Montauban, held by their own garrisons.

Germany's turn came in 1618. On 23 May Bohemian Protestants in Prague hurled two Catholic imperial regents and their secretary from a window of Prague Castle, some 70 feet up, and all three survived because they landed on a heap of dung. Catholics hailed a miracle; Protestants gave the credit to the manure. The Thirty Years' War that followed lasted until 1648.

the-wright-brothers-and-powered-flight.context_blurb:
Wilbur and Orville Wright were brothers from Dayton, Ohio, sons of a church bishop, who taught themselves the science of flight in the 1890s. On a cold December morning in 1903, among the sand dunes at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, they flew the first powered, controlled airplane, and within one lifetime flight had carried men to the Moon.

It started with a toy. In 1878 their father, Milton Wright, brought home a little helicopter made of paper, bamboo and cork and threw it into the air, and the boys watched it whirr across the room to the ceiling, flutter there awhile and drop. Neither brother finished high school, and neither was a trained engineer. They taught themselves from books while earning a living at the Wright Cycle Company, where they built and sold their own bicycles, and the skill they learned there let them build a flying machine.

Other inventors had wings and engines, but their machines kept crashing because no one could keep them level. The Wrights' answer was wing-warping: twisting the two wingtips in contrary directions let the pilot bank the plane and steer it. Wilbur reportedly got the idea while idly twisting an empty cardboard inner-tube box in the shop.

Their success rested on measurement. In 1901 they knocked together a wind tunnel of wood and tried out between 100 and 200 miniature wings, and they found that the published tables of the famous German glider pioneer Otto Lilienthal were badly wrong: their wing gave only about a third of the lift his figures promised. So they built their own tables. They even caught an error in the Smeaton coefficient, a figure engineers had relied on for over a hundred years in working out air pressure and lift: the accepted value, about 0.0054, was nearly twice the true figure, which was closer to 0.0033.

No company could supply a gasoline engine light enough, so their shop mechanic, Charlie Taylor, made one himself in roughly six weeks from rough sketches. It had four cylinders and about 12 horsepower, and to save weight he cast the block from aluminium, the first aluminium engine ever used in an aircraft. Propellers needed a science no one had written. The brothers realised that a propeller is no screw boring into the air but a wing turned on its side and spun in a vertical circle, so they shaped theirs from their own wing data and predicted the thrust to within about one per cent.

A coin toss settled which brother would fly first. Wilbur won, but on 14 December he climbed too steeply, stalled and nosed into the soft sand after about three seconds, so three days later it was Orville's turn at the controls, and he made the famous first flight. On 17 December 1903, at 10:35 in the morning, into a wind of 27 miles an hour, Orville took off lying on his stomach across the lower wing, with Wilbur running beside him. The Flyer stayed up for about 12 seconds and covered 120 feet: a tiny hop, but the first time a powered machine heavier than air had carried a person under control.

They flew four times that day, each flight longer than the last, and Wilbur's fourth covered 852 feet and stayed up for 59 seconds, ending the age of hops. Orville's telegram home, garbled by the operator, gave the longest as 57 seconds. Soon after, a gust of wind caught the resting Flyer and sent it cartwheeling over the sand, rolling a helper, the lifesaver John Daniels, along inside it. He was shaken but unhurt, but the plane was wrecked beyond easy repair and never flew again. Sixty-six years later Neil Armstrong took wood cut from the 1903 Flyer's propeller, and a scrap of the unbleached muslin that covered its wings, all the way to the surface of the Moon.

thermopylae-480-bc-leonidas-and-the-300-.context_blurb:
In the summer of 480 BC Xerxes, king of Persia, led a vast army into Greece to take revenge on the Greek cities that had defied him. To slow him, the Spartan king Leonidas led about 7,000 Greeks, among them 300 Spartans, to a narrow pass north of Athens. For three days they held it, and their last stand became the most famous in history.

The mountains there came down almost to the sea, leaving a road barely wide enough for a few men abreast, so a small force could hold off a huge one. Steaming sulphur springs gave the place its name, Thermopylae, the Hot Gates. When Xerxes demanded that the Greeks hand over their weapons, Leonidas, as later tradition tells it, answered in two words, molon labe: come and take them. The line comes from Plutarch, writing centuries afterwards, not from the earlier historian Herodotus, so it is a celebrated tradition rather than a proven quotation.

The Spartans met fear with jokes. When a Greek warned the Spartan Dieneces that the Persians had so many archers that their arrows would hide the sun, Dieneces replied that they would then fight in the shade, and Herodotus named him the bravest man there. A Persian scout sent ahead came back puzzled, because the Spartans were calmly combing out and grooming their long hair. Demaratus, an exiled Spartan king riding with Xerxes, explained that this was how Spartans prepared to die well, and the sight unnerved the Persians.

Xerxes asked Demaratus why so few men would stand instead of running. Herodotus says Demaratus warned him that the Spartans served a master stronger than any commander: the Law, which forbade them to flee and ordered them to conquer or die, and which they feared far more than Xerxes's own men feared their king.

For two days the Greeks threw back every assault. Then Ephialtes, a Greek from the district, hoping for a reward, led the Persians to a secret path over the mountain, the Anopaea, that came out behind the pass. The Greeks never forgave him: in Greek his name is the very word for a nightmare, and it came to mean traitor too. Xerxes sent his elite guard up the path by night under the commander Hydarnes. They were ten thousand picked men known to the Greeks as the Immortals, because whenever one was killed, wounded or fell sick, a waiting replacement stepped into his place at once, so the corps never dropped below ten thousand and seemed never to die. A thousand Phocian Greeks guarded the mountain path, but in the still night their first warning was the crackle of fallen oak leaves under thousands of feet, and they realized too late that the enemy was upon them.

On the third day, surrounded, Leonidas and his remaining men fought with spears until the shafts broke and then with swords until those broke too. Herodotus says that even then they fought on with their hands and teeth, until Persian arrows overwhelmed them. Greeks held it sacred to give an enemy's body back for honourable burial, but Xerxes, enraged that so few had cost him so dearly, had Leonidas's head struck off and fixed on a stake.

Two of the 300 had been sent away before the end with a disease of the eyes. One, Eurytus, had himself led blind into the fight by a slave and was killed; the other, Aristodemus, went home alive, and Sparta branded him the Trembler: no one would speak to him or even give him fire to light his hearth. A year later he wiped out the disgrace by fighting with reckless courage at Plataea. Long afterwards the Greeks raised a memorial stone where the Spartans fell, and the poet Simonides of Ceos gave it the best-known soldiers' epitaph in history, spoken in the voice of the fallen: it asks any passing stranger to go and tell the Spartans that here they lie, obedient to their laws.

thomas-aquinas-the-summa-theologica.context_blurb:
Thomas Aquinas was an Italian friar of the 1200s who argued that what the mind can reason out and what the Church believes must in the end agree. His giant Summa Theologica, a summary of all Christian teaching, made him the most influential thinker of the medieval Church.

He was born into the powerful Aquino family, and as its youngest son he was given to the Church: at about five years old he was sent to the great Benedictine abbey of Monte Cassino, where his family hoped he would one day rule as its wealthy abbot. At nineteen, in 1244, he wrecked the plan by joining the Dominicans, wandering friars sworn to poverty who begged for their bread. His own brothers ambushed him on the road and shut him up for almost a year in the family stronghold of Roccasecca to break his will. They even pushed a woman into his room to seduce him into breaking his vow. According to the records later gathered for his sainthood, he grabbed a blazing log out of the fireplace and chased her from the room. In the end his mother, Theodora, gave up the fight and had him let down through a window after dark, and he went off to study in Paris.

There he sat at the feet of Albert the Great, the famous Dominican master. Huge, heavy and silent in class, Thomas struck his fellow students as slow, and they mocked him as the Dumb Ox; Albert silenced them, saying that one day the ox's bellowing would be heard throughout the world.

His grand project was to marry the logic of Aristotle, a pagan Greek dead for some sixteen centuries, to Christian faith. He admired Aristotle so much that he seldom bothered with the name and simply called him the Philosopher. In his last years he wrote the Summa, about 3,000 pages divided into 512 Questions and thousands of short Articles, working through every great debate of the Church in his day. Yet its opening lines say he wrote it as a textbook for beginners in Christian doctrine.

Every Article follows the same fighting pattern. He poses a question beginning "Whether", sets down first the best case against himself, the Objections, stated fairly, and only then argues his own side: a line from authority beginning "On the contrary", his answer, "I answer that", and a reply to each objection in turn. Near the start he gives five brief arguments, any one of which, he held, was enough to show that God exists, drawn from motion, first causes, things that must exist, grades of perfection and the order of nature. They are called the Five Ways, and each one ends by naming God. Above every human law, he argued, stands a natural law that anyone can grasp by reason, beginning with the command to do good and avoid evil. Through John Locke that idea grew, centuries later, into the self-evident natural rights written into the American Declaration of Independence.

A legend tells that when he finished writing about the Eucharist, the bread and wine of the Mass, the carved figure of Christ on a crucifix spoke to him as he prayed, praising his work and asking what reward he wanted. He answered, in Latin, Non nisi te, Domine: nothing but you, Lord. On 6 December 1273, while saying Mass, he had a vision that shattered him, and he never wrote another word, so the Summa stayed unfinished. When Reginald, his secretary, pleaded with him to continue, he said he could not, because everything he had written now seemed to him like straw.

Travelling to a Church council in 1274, he fell ill and died at Fossanova, a Cistercian abbey. Whispers already called him a saint, and holy bones would draw pilgrims and gifts, so the monks, afraid his own Dominicans would carry him off, beheaded the corpse and stewed the flesh off the bones to keep the relics. Two rival skulls are still each claimed as his. Pope John XXII made him a saint in 1323, and in 1880 the Church named him patron of every Catholic school and university, honoured as the Angelic Doctor: the mocked ox of the classroom had become its teacher of teachers.

thomas-becket-s-murder-1170.context_blurb:
Thomas Becket was King Henry II's close friend and chancellor until Henry made him Archbishop of Canterbury, expecting a loyal servant at the head of the English Church. Instead Becket defended the Church's rights against the king, and for years the two men feuded bitterly over who held power over the Church in England.

Tradition says that Henry, in a fury at court, asked whether no one would rid him of this turbulent priest. The famous line appears in no account from the time and is almost certainly invented; chroniclers report him cursing the low-born clerks he had raised who let one man shame him. Four of his knights, Reginald FitzUrse, Hugh de Morville, William de Tracy and Richard le Breton, took his anger as an order and murdered Becket inside Canterbury Cathedral on 29 December 1170.

When the monks undressed the body for burial, they found a secret under his fine robes: a rough shirt of goat hair, crawling with lice, that he had worn next to his skin, day after day, as a hidden penance. It convinced people of his holiness even more than his murder did. Miracle cures were soon reported at his tomb, and Pope Alexander III made him a saint in 1173, barely three years after his death.

thomas-edison-and-the-light-bulb.context_blurb:
Thomas Edison, born in Ohio in 1847, began as a telegraph operator and became the most famous inventor of his age. In the 1870s he set up a laboratory in the little village of Menlo Park, New Jersey, and from it came the phonograph, a better telephone microphone and, most famously, a practical electric light.

Menlo Park was the world's first industrial research laboratory, a workshop where a whole staff of skilled hands, with all their tools in one building, produced invention after invention on purpose. Edison called it his Invention Factory, and while there he applied for about 400 patents. By 1878 newspapers around the world were calling him the Wizard of Menlo Park. The year before, he had built the phonograph, a hand-cranked cylinder wrapped in tinfoil, with one needle to cut grooves and another to play them back. He recited the nursery rhyme about Mary and her little lamb into it, and even Edison was startled when the machine said it back to him on the first try. He himself was deaf in his left ear and mostly deaf in the right. A famous story, told as legend, says he would bite into the wooden case of a piano so the music travelled through his jaw, explaining that he could hear through his teeth. A surviving Steinway grand bears bite marks believed to be his.

The light took longer. In 1879 at Menlo Park his first practical lamp glowed for about thirteen and a half hours, and its filament, the fine thread that glows inside the glass, was nothing rare: a loop of ordinary cotton sewing thread, baked to carbon and sealed in a vacuum. On New Year's Eve that year Edison lit rows of lamps around the Menlo Park grounds, special trains brought the crowds, and eight of the bulbs disappeared into visitors' pockets as souvenirs. He went on testing thousands of materials. Legend says he told a reporter he had not failed but had found 10,000 ways that would not work; the earliest written version, from 1910, is gentler, with Edison saying he knew several thousand things that would not work. His agents combed the globe for plant fibres to carbonize and test. The winner, sent home in 1880 by his scout William Moore from a bamboo grove beside the Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine near Kyoto, was Japanese bamboo, which lasted some 1,200 hours alight and remained his standard filament for close to a decade.

On 4 September 1882 at three o'clock Edison threw the switch at Pearl Street Station in Manhattan, America's first central power plant, driven by 27-ton dynamos he nicknamed Jumbo after Barnum's famous circus elephant. His real breakthrough was the system, not the bulb alone. Rival lamps used fat filaments that swallowed big currents, but Edison chose a filament as fine as a hair that resisted the current strongly and needed only a little of it, so thin, cheap copper wires could carry power to many bulbs at once, and lighting a whole city became affordable. Around the bulb he built everything else, from the central plant and the cables running into houses to the sockets and switches, plus an electric meter that measured how much power each customer used, so the company could bill each home fairly.

Edison did not invent the light bulb; he made it practical. In Britain Joseph Swan had already demonstrated a carbon-filament lamp and patented it in 1878, and when the two men clashed in the British courts, Edison lost and had to take Swan in as a partner, forming the Edison and Swan United Electric Light Company in 1883.

thomas-hobbes-and-the-leviathan.context_blurb:
Thomas Hobbes was an English philosopher who saw his country torn apart by civil war in the 1640s and came to hate the chaos it brought. In 1651, in exile in Paris, he published Leviathan, a book arguing that only a strong, undivided government can save people from their own fear and violence.

Fear was there from the start. On 5 April 1588 his mother heard that the Spanish Armada was sailing against England and went into early labour, and Hobbes later joked that fear and he had been born twins together. Fear of violent death drives his whole philosophy. Without government, he argued, there would be a war of each against all, and life in that state of nature would be solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short, his single most famous sentence.

He wrote Leviathan just after King Charles I had been beheaded. The way out of that disorder, he argued, was a social contract: every man surrenders his right of governing himself, on condition that everyone else does the same, and they all transfer it to a single ruler, receiving in return protection. Hobbes began from the same kind of state of nature as John Locke but reached absolute rule rather than limited government. He named the book after the Leviathan, the monstrous sea serpent of the Book of Job, because his ruler must overawe everyone the way that beast did in order to keep the peace.

Abraham Bosse's engraving for the title page shows a giant in a crown rising above the countryside, a sword in one hand for worldly power and a churchman's crosier in the other for the power of the Church. Peer at it and you see that the giant is made of over 300 little human figures: the people themselves make up the sovereign.

Hobbes lived to 91 and died at Chatsworth House, home of the Cavendish family, on 4 December 1679. The man who built his philosophy on the fear of death reportedly met it calmly, calling it a great leap into the dark, though those last words are tradition rather than proven fact.

thomas-jefferson-author-and-third-presid.context_blurb:
Thomas Jefferson was a Virginia planter, lawyer, architect and tinkerer who wrote the Declaration of Independence and later served as America's third president. He gave the new nation its creed of equal rights and doubled its size, and he lived a life full of contradictions, above all the people he held in slavery.

In June 1776 the Continental Congress named a Committee of Five to draft a declaration, among them John Adams of Massachusetts and its youngest member, the 33-year-old Jefferson. Adams insisted that Jefferson do the writing, telling him that he wrote far better than Adams did himself. Jefferson wrote that all men are created equal and are born with rights no one can rightly take from them. Yet over his lifetime the same man enslaved more than 600 people at Monticello and his other estates, about 130 of them at his death: the sharpest contradiction of the founding.

Congress argued over his draft for two days and cut about a quarter of it, while Jefferson sat by in pained silence. The deepest cut was a fierce passage of 168 words that accused the king of waging the slave trade as a war on human nature. The South Carolina and Georgia delegations, deeply tied to that trade, demanded it go, and so the Declaration as adopted is silent on slavery.

As president, in 1803, Jefferson seized Napoleon's offer to sell the whole Louisiana Territory, from the Mississippi to the Rocky Mountains, for about 15 million dollars, roughly three cents an acre, and the purchase doubled the size of the United States at a stroke. Privately he doubted whether the Constitution gave him any power at all to buy foreign land; he admitted he was acting beyond it and trusted the nation to forgive an act done for its good. To learn what he had bought, he sent out the Corps of Discovery under Meriwether Lewis, once his own secretary, and William Clark, who set out up the Missouri in May 1804, crossed the Rockies, reached the Pacific and came back. In 1802 he also wrote to a group of anxious Danbury Baptists in Connecticut that the First Amendment had built a wall of separation dividing Church from State, words the Supreme Court later adopted as its reading of the religion clauses. His own 1786 Virginia statute on religious freedom, which barred forcing anyone to support or attend a church, had been their model.

At home on his Virginia mountaintop, Monticello, he tinkered for decades, calling all his building up and pulling down a favourite amusement. In the front hall stands his Great Clock, kept going by weights that sink slowly on ropes, and those weights are cannonballs. Buffon, a French naturalist, had sneered that America's animals were smaller and weaker than Europe's, and Jefferson took the claim personally. He collected huge mastodon bones to prove Buffon wrong and argued that the giant beasts might yet be living somewhere in the uncharted West. He loved books too, telling John Adams he could not live without them. When British troops burned the Capitol in August 1814 and wiped out the young Library of Congress, the 71-year-old Jefferson sold the government his own library, nearly 6,500 volumes, for $23,950, and it became the new heart of the Library of Congress.

He died on 4 July 1826, exactly half a century after the Declaration was adopted. He had written out his own tombstone, ordering only three things carved on it, the Declaration, his Virginia statute on religious freedom and the University of Virginia, and he deliberately left out his two terms as President. John Adams, his friend, then bitter rival, then friend again by letter, died the same day a few hours later. His reported last words were that Thomas Jefferson survives, but Jefferson was already dead.

three-fifths-compromise-slavery-in-frami.context_blurb:
At the Constitutional Convention of 1787 the delegates had to decide how to share out seats in the House of Representatives, which went to each state by population. Slavery was legal across the South, and the question was whether enslaved people would be counted. The answer, counting three of every five, became one of the Constitution's most misunderstood clauses.

Many people believe the clause called a slave three-fifths of a person. The real fight ran the other way: the slave states pushed hardest to count enslaved people, the very people they held as property, because more heads meant more seats in the House and more votes for president, while antislavery delegates resisted. Three-fifths was a grim bargain to hold the union together, not a measure of anyone's humanity.

Frederick Douglass, who had fled slavery as a young man, read the clause as a weapon against it. Because a freed person counted as a whole person rather than three-fifths, every slave a state set free would win it more seats, so the clause handed the South a standing reward for every slave it freed. Against William Lloyd Garrison, who burned the Constitution as a pact with slavery, Douglass insisted it was an antislavery document.

three-sisters-agriculture-and-the-domest.context_blurb:
Corn, one of the world's great food crops, did not exist in the wild. Over thousands of years Native farmers in Mexico bred it from a scrawny, branching wild grass called teosinte. Later, farmers across the Americas grew it beside climbing beans and sprawling squash, the Three Sisters: the stalks held up the beans, the beans fed the soil, and the squash leaves shaded out weeds.

Teosinte looks nothing like an ear of corn. Its tiny ear held just two rows of five to twelve kernels, and every kernel was locked inside a shell as hard as stone, like a tiny acorn, nothing like the naked kernels of a modern cob.

Geneticists found that a change in one single gene, teosinte glume architecture 1, or tga1, did the crucial work: it freed the kernels from those armoured cases, turning teosinte's locked seeds into corn's naked, ready-to-eat kernels. A second gene, tb1, collapsed the bushy grass into one upright stalk.

tiananmen-square-1989.context_blurb:
In the spring of 1989 hundreds of thousands of students, workers and ordinary citizens filled Tiananmen Square in Beijing, calling for political reform and an end to official corruption. China's Communist leaders declared martial law, and on the night of 3 to 4 June they sent army units with tanks and automatic weapons to clear the square, killing many hundreds and possibly thousands of unarmed civilians.

On 5 June, the day after the massacre, a single man, dressed in a white shirt, stepped out into Chang'an Avenue and stood in front of a column of tanks, carrying nothing but two shopping bags. When the lead tank tried to steer around him, he stepped sideways to block it again, and he even climbed onto it to speak to the crew. To this day no one knows his name or what became of him.

The picture almost never got out. The Associated Press photographer Jeff Widener shot it from a sixth-floor hotel balcony half a mile away, sick with flu and concussed by a rock that had hit him the day before. With police confiscating film across the city, an American student, Kirk Martsen, smuggled the roll to the AP office hidden inside his underwear.

timbuktu-and-trans-saharan-trade.context_blurb:
Timbuktu stood where the Niger River bends north toward the Sahara, which made it the southern end of the great camel caravans that crossed the desert in the Middle Ages. Gold, ivory and captives went north; salt, cloth and horses came south. Salt was so scarce in West Africa that miners cut it straight from the earth at desert mines and camels carried it for months.

In 1352 Ibn Battuta, the Moroccan traveller, reached one of those mines, Taghaza, deep in the Sahara. The ground there was solid salt, and the people built homes, and a mosque too, from slabs of it, and since there was no timber anywhere in that bleak place, they roofed them with camel skins.

Timbuktu itself grew rich on that trade, yet when Leo Africanus visited around 1510 he wrote that selling books brought more profit than any other business. Handwritten manuscripts out-earned even gold and salt there. The city's libraries came to hold hundreds of thousands of volumes on astronomy, medicine, law and poetry.

timbuktu-city-of-books-and-scholars.context_blurb:
Timbuktu, where the Sahara meets the Niger in what is now Mali, grew from a trading camp into one of the great centres of Islamic learning between the 1200s and the 1500s. Under the empires of Mali and then Songhai its scholars filled family libraries with tens of thousands of handwritten books, and many of those books survive today.

The city grew rich at the meeting of sand and river. Salt came down by camel from mines far out in the desert and gold came up by boat from the southern forests, and because the body cannot live without salt in that heat, a pound of gold could fetch roughly its own weight in salt. The salt came from places like Taghaza, a lonely mining town deep in the Sahara. When the Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta arrived there in 1352, he found that the people had cut the very ground into thick slabs of salt to build their homes and a small mosque, because nothing grew there but sand and salt. The great Djinguereber Mosque, nearly seven hundred years old, is made of sun-dried earth, straw and timber from palm trees, without a single stone. So every year, when the brief rains are over, the whole town turns out to replaster it by hand, sealing the cracks so that the next rains cannot wash it away.

Mali's emperor Mansa Musa made the region famous. On his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324, the legends say, 500 servants walked ahead of him, each one carrying a solid-gold staff weighing about six pounds. In Cairo he handed out gold to officials, shopkeepers and beggars alike, and so much of it flooded the city that the price of gold crashed by about a fifth and took some twelve years to recover. The Catalan Atlas, drawn by a European mapmaker around 1375, shows him enthroned as the wealthiest king in the south, a sceptre in one hand and, held up in the other, a huge lump of raw gold, a nugget.

The traveller Leo Africanus, who visited in the early 1500s, found salt, gold, cloth and piles of manuscripts for sale in the markets, and he wrote that selling handwritten books brought more profit than all other goods together. Those books were never only about religion. Timbuktu's manuscripts cover astronomy, mathematics, medicine, plants, law, poetry and history, and a diagram in one astronomy text shows the rotating sky, drawn to teach students the motions of the planets and how to find the direction of Mecca by the stars.

In 1591 a Moroccan army conquered the city. Its most famous scholar, Ahmad Baba, was carried off in chains to Morocco, and he told the sultan that his soldiers had stolen more than 1,600 of his books, adding that his was the smallest library in his family. Learned Timbuktu families owned books by the thousand.

Our best record of the Mali and Songhai empires comes from two Timbuktu chronicles, known as the Tarikh al-Fattash and the Tarikh al-Sudan. Historians treasure them because they are among the oldest histories of West Africa written by West Africans themselves, telling their own story. The scribes made their own inks from plants, green from boiled mango leaves and a deep red from the ground and boiled stalks of the sorghum plant, and they kept their lines straight with a little frame of stretched threads.

When armed fighters took the city in 2012 and vowed to burn its libraries, the librarian Abdel Kader Haidara organised a rescue. He bought every metal trunk in the city's markets, and when those ran out he had old oil drums hammered into more trunks. Volunteers carried some 350,000 manuscripts out by donkey, road and river, past armed checkpoints, working by flashlight after the power was cut. When the city was retaken in 2013, only about 4,000 of nearly 400,000 books had been destroyed.

timur-tamerlane-samarkand.context_blurb:
Timur, called Tamerlane in the West from the Persian for Timur the Lame, was a Turko-Mongol conqueror of the 1300s from Central Asia. From his capital, Samarkand, in today's Uzbekistan, he carved out an empire from Turkey to India, razing city after city while filling Samarkand with turquoise-domed buildings raised by craftsmen he had deported from the places he destroyed.

When Isfahan rose against him in 1387, Timur crushed it and had his soldiers build towering pyramids of human heads to terrify every other city into obedience. Eyewitnesses counted more than 28 towers, each piled from some 1,500 heads, and he did the same at Delhi in 1398. The same man raised the Registan and the Bibi-Khanym Mosque in Samarkand.

He died in 1405, marching to invade China, and was buried in Samarkand, in the Gur-e-Amir, beneath its ribbed turquoise dome. Ulugh Beg, Timur's grandson and an astronomer-king, later had a single enormous slab brought from distant Mongolia to cover the tomb: the largest block of dark-green jade in the world. The Persian conqueror Nadir Shah tried to carry it off, and it cracked in two when it was dropped crossing a river.

trajan-and-the-empire-at-its-greatest-ex.context_blurb:
Trajan ruled Rome from AD 98 to 117. Born in Spain, he was the first emperor from outside Italy, and under him the Roman Empire reached the greatest size it would ever have. He conquered Dacia, north of the Danube in today's Romania, and then drove deep into the east against the Parthians.

By 117, after Trajan had taken Dacia, Armenia, Mesopotamia and even the Parthian capital, Ctesiphon, the empire ran from Hadrian's Wall in northern Britain to the shore of the Persian Gulf, the only time Roman soldiers ever stood there. At its peak Rome ruled some five million square kilometres and sixty million people, but Trajan's successor, Hadrian, gave up much of the eastern conquest within months.

In Rome, Trajan's Column, a marble shaft about a hundred feet tall dedicated in 113, celebrates the conquest of Dacia. A single carved band winds 23 times around it from bottom to top, telling the Dacian Wars from start to finish, one scene after another, with thousands of figures; unwound, it would stretch about 190 metres.

One scene shows the end of the Dacian king Decebalus in 106. With Roman cavalry closing in on his mountain hiding place, meaning to take him alive and parade him through Rome, he knelt beneath a tree and turned his curved Dacian sword, a falx, on his own throat. The first rider to reach him, Tiberius Claudius Maximus, cut off the dying king's head and carried it to Trajan. He was so proud of it that he had the feat carved on his own tombstone, which turned up centuries later at Philippi in Greece, boasting that he had captured Decebalus and brought the emperor his head.

A bronze statue of Trajan once crowned the column, but it vanished in the Middle Ages. Pope Sixtus V replaced it in 1587 with a bronze of the apostle Saint Peter, so a Christian saint now stands on top of a monument to a Roman conqueror. A hidden spiral staircase of 185 steps climbs the hollow shaft inside.

The Senate named Trajan Optimus, the best, and for centuries Romans held him up as the model ruler. Whenever a new emperor took power, senators wished that he might be luckier than Augustus and better than Trajan, in Latin felicior Augusto, melior Traiano.

trans-saharan-trade-the-salt-gold-carava.context_blurb:
For some eight hundred years, from the 700s to the 1500s, camel caravans crossed the Sahara in both directions, linking the Mediterranean coast of North Africa with the lands south of the desert. Salt went south and gold went north, and the trade built the wealth of great West African empires such as Mali.

None of it was possible without the camel, the ship of the desert. Broad padded feet held it up on loose sand, it could march for days with no water, and it could carry about 240 kilograms some 48 kilometres a day, four times what a pack horse could manage.

Salt came from desert mines like Taghaza, where the earth was so salty that miners sawed it into slabs. Visiting in 1352, the Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta found the houses and even the mosque built of blocks of salt and roofed with camel skins, since the place had no wood, stone or clay at all. The forest country of the south had gold but no salt of its own and no sea nearby, yet in that climate people sweat salt away and need it, and food spoiled without it. So the slabs hauled south became among the costliest goods on earth: at Timbuktu a block of salt was said to trade almost pound for pound with gold.

Near the goldfields, an Arab traveller of the 900s recorded a strange silent trade between peoples who never met or shared a language. Traders from the north would lay out their wares, sound a drum and pull back out of sight, and the Wangarans, who held the gold, would then come forward and place gold next to the wares. The northerners returned and, if they thought the gold a fair price, took it and left; if not, they withdrew again and waited until more gold was added. The Wangarans guarded the secret of where their gold came from, the upper Niger and Senegal country, so fiercely that for centuries no Arab or Berber merchant learned it.

For everyday buying and selling, West Africans used no coins at all but the cowrie shell, a small, glossy seashell from the Maldives in the Indian Ocean, hard to forge and quick to count. Caravans carried cowries across the desert from at least the 600s, and billions eventually circulated.

In 1324 Mansa Musa of Mali crossed the desert to Mecca with some 60,000 people and a hundred camels laden with gold. In Cairo he gave away and spent so much that the price of gold crashed and stayed low for about twelve years.

treaty-of-paris-1783.context_blurb:
The Treaty of Paris, signed in 1783, ended the American Revolutionary War and forced Britain to recognize the United States as an independent nation. Its American negotiators, among them Benjamin Franklin, John Adams and John Jay, won remarkably generous terms for the new country.

The treaty roughly doubled the young nation's size. Its borders ran from the Atlantic in the east to the Mississippi River in the west, with British Canada to the north and Spanish Florida to the south: a continent's worth of future land.

One negotiator, Henry Laurens, had been captured at sea and held for fifteen months in the Tower of London, the only American ever imprisoned there. On 31 December 1781 Britain exchanged him for Lord Cornwallis, the general who had surrendered his whole army at Yorktown that October.

The painter Benjamin West set out to record the signing, but the British negotiator Richard Oswald and his secretary, Caleb Whitefoord, refused to pose, since Britain had no wish to celebrate its defeat. So West painted only the five Americans on the left, and the right side of his unfinished canvas is still bare, an empty patch where the British should be.

treaty-of-tordesillas.context_blurb:
Within two years of Columbus's first voyage, Spain and Portugal were close to war over who owned the lands being found across the Atlantic. In 1494, in the Treaty of Tordesillas, they agreed to split the world with a single line drawn from pole to pole, about 370 leagues beyond the Cape Verde Islands: the lands to the west went to Spain, and those to the east to Portugal.

No one in 1494 could measure longitude at sea, so for a while the line was one nobody could find on the ocean. The Portuguese captain Pedro Álvares Cabral gave it meaning. On 22 April 1500 his thirteen ships came upon a coast no European had charted, near Porto Seguro, where his men held Mass, planted a wooden cross and claimed the land for Portugal, because it fell east of the Tordesillas line, in Portugal's half.

When mapmakers charted South America, its great eastern bulge turned out to poke across the line, which fell at about 46 degrees west, onto Portugal's side. That is how Brazil became Portuguese, and why it speaks Portuguese while the rest of the continent speaks Spanish.

treaty-of-versailles.context_blurb:
The Treaty of Versailles, signed in June 1919, was the peace the victorious Allies imposed on Germany after the First World War. Written at the Paris Peace Conference by the leaders of Britain, France and the United States, among them France's Georges Clemenceau and America's Woodrow Wilson, it stripped Germany of land, arms and money, and its bitter legacy helped bring on the next war.

The Allies made the Germans sign in the Hall of Mirrors, in the palace the old French kings had built at Versailles, a room the French chose as payback. There, in 1871, after beating France in war, the Germans had declared the birth of their German Empire and hailed Wilhelm I as its emperor. Even the date was chosen: 28 June 1919 marked exactly five years since the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo, the shot that had set off the war. When the ink was dry, the great fountains of Versailles were switched on for the first time since 1914, and guns boomed out a salute to tell Paris that the treaty had been signed. Wilson's dearest dream came first among the 440 articles: Part I created the League of Nations, and he had fought to put it first.

Clemenceau wanted every delegate to feel the cost of the war. At the entrance, where each of them had to pass, he placed five French soldiers whose faces had been torn apart by shrapnel, the gueules cassées, or broken faces, and the sight reportedly moved even Clemenceau to tears. Marshal Ferdinand Foch, the French commander of all the Allied armies, thought the treaty far too soft on Germany rather than too harsh. He refused to celebrate and reportedly warned that this was no peace, only an armistice for twenty years; the Second World War began in September 1939, twenty years and two months later.

The treaty took about 13 per cent of Germany's land and some six to seven million of its people. The loss that hurt most was the Polish Corridor, a band of territory taken from Germany so that the reborn Poland could reach the Baltic, which sliced East Prussia away from the main body of Germany and left it stranded. Article 231 became infamous as the war-guilt clause. It said Germany must accept responsibility for causing all the loss and damage of the war, as a legal hook for reparations, yet the word guilt never appears in it. Germans took it as a verdict that they alone were to blame, and that resentment helped feed the rise of the Nazi Party.

The British economist John Maynard Keynes walked out of the conference, appalled. He attacked the settlement as a Carthaginian peace, so crushing it would ruin the loser and all of Europe, in a book called The Economic Consequences of the Peace, which appeared in December 1919 and soon spread through Germany in translation. Not everyone was heard. A young kitchen helper from a Paris hotel, Nguyen Tat Thanh, brought the conference a petition demanding rights and self-government for the Vietnamese, and the Great Powers ignored him; he later took the name Ho Chi Minh and led the fight for Vietnam's independence.

The reparations bill, set in 1921, sounded staggering, 132 billion gold marks, but the fine print split it into A, B and C bonds. The 82 billion marks of C bonds were a paper figure for angry Allied voters, and Germany was privately told it would never truly have to pay them, so the real bill was about 50 billion. The American historian Sally Marks, after decades in the payment records, argues that Germany could easily have paid that real bill through taxes but defaulted again and again on purpose, as a political strategy to break the treaty. Other historians still contest her case. The debt outlived everyone who signed: Germany had borrowed through bonds during the 1920s to make its payments, and it paid the last installment, 94 million dollars, on 3 October 2010, more than ninety years after the war and twenty years to the day after German reunification.

Germany never forgave Versailles. In June 1940, after defeating France, Hitler had the railway carriage in which Germany had signed the 1918 armistice dragged out of its museum to the same spot near Compiègne, and he made the French sign their surrender inside it.

trench-warfare-and-the-western-front.context_blurb:
After the German advance stalled at the Marne in 1914, the Western Front settled into two lines of trenches running some 475 miles from the English Channel to the Swiss border. For nearly four years millions of men lived, fought and died in them, and the line in the west barely moved.

The ordinary British soldier was called Tommy. An army record book of 1815 used the sample name Thomas Atkins to show a soldier how to fill it in, so the whole British infantry ended up named after the example on a blank form. Between the enemy lines lay No Man's Land, a strip of ground choked with wire, craters and the dead, in places barely 50 yards across. When an officer's whistle shrieked, the men climbed ladders out of the trench and ran across that ground toward the enemy's machine guns. They called it going over the top, and the phrase came to mean any all-out attack.

A trench was a home as well as a fort. Its floor was often knee-deep in icy mud, so the men laid slatted wooden walkways called duckboards along it, a word born in those trenches and still in use. To shoot, a soldier stepped up onto the firestep, a ledge two or three feet high against the front wall, so he could see and aim over the sandbagged parapet.

Days of standing in freezing water brought trench foot: the feet went numb, turned red or blue and puffed up to double or triple their normal size, and gangrenous cases meant amputation. In the first winter of the war alone, upwards of 20,000 British soldiers had to be treated for it. To fight it, men changed their socks several times a day and rubbed whale oil into their feet, and one battalion at the front could use ten gallons daily. Rats swarmed everywhere, fattened on the unburied dead; some, according to Major Walter Vignoles, grew almost the size of cats, and veterans such as Harry Patch never forgot them. Body lice were everywhere too. In idle hours men ran a lit candle, or a thumbnail, along their shirt seams to pop the lice, which they called chats, and that grumbling pastime is the likely origin of chatting, meaning idle talk.

Heavy German shells, which exploded in clouds of black smoke, were nicknamed Jack Johnsons, after the first African-American heavyweight boxing champion, Jack Johnson, known as the Big Smoke. A head raised above the sandbags drew a sniper's bullet. Men watched No Man's Land through trench periscopes, and in May 1915 Lance Corporal William Beech fitted mirrors to a rifle, creating the periscope rifle, so that a man could shoot over the sandbags with his head safely a foot beneath the parapet.

Trenches were never dug straight. They zigzagged in short sections called fire-bays, each walled off from the next by a bank of earth called a traverse, because, as the soldier John Raws explained, that kept a shell burst inside one bay and meant an enemy who captured part of the line could not pour fire straight along its whole length.

At Christmas 1914 an unofficial truce spread along parts of the line, and soldiers met between the lines to trade food and bury the fallen. By legend the two sides even played football on the frozen ground, and both The Times, in a soldier's letter, and the German officer Johannes Niemann gave the same score: the Germans won 3-2.

truman-doctrine-containment.context_blurb:
In the spring of 1947 Harry Truman asked Congress to help two countries resist communism, and in doing so he set the course of American foreign policy for the next forty years. The idea behind it, containing Soviet expansion wherever it pushed, came from a diplomat named George Kennan.

The crisis began when Great Britain, exhausted and nearly bankrupt after the Second World War, told Washington on 21 February 1947 that it could no longer prop up the Greek government against a communist rebellion and would end its aid by 31 March. Truman requested emergency aid of 400 million dollars for Greece, then fighting communist rebels, and for Turkey, which the Soviets were pressing to give up control of its straits. Congress was reluctant. The Republican senator Arthur Vandenberg reportedly told Truman that he would have to go before the nation and scare the hell out of it. Behind closed doors Undersecretary of State Dean Acheson warned doubtful senators that one communist state could spoil its neighbours the way one rotten apple spoils a whole barrel, with Greece infecting Turkey, then the Middle East, then Western Europe: the idea later called the domino theory.

In the speech itself Truman painted Greece's misery, with more than a thousand villages burned and eighty-five per cent of the children tubercular. Then came the sentence that defined the Truman Doctrine: it must be American policy, he said, to support free peoples resisting attempts to subjugate them by armed minorities or by pressure from outside. That open-ended promise bound America to oppose communist expansion nearly everywhere in the world. Truman also offered a theory of why tyranny spreads. The seeds of totalitarian rule, he said, are fed by misery and want and take root in poverty and strife, which he called evil soil, so giving desperate people hope was the real cure. The bill passed by huge margins in May 1947, though critics later said the scare had oversold a smaller threat.

Kennan had laid the groundwork a year earlier. In February 1946, serving at the embassy in Moscow, he was asked a narrow question about Soviet hostility to the new World Bank and answered with a cable of some 5,000 words diagnosing the whole Soviet outlook, known ever since as the Long Telegram. The historian John Lewis Gaddis called it the basis of American strategy toward the Soviet Union for the rest of the Cold War. In July 1947 Kennan set out containment for the public in an essay in Foreign Affairs, calling for patient but firm and vigilant containment of Russian expansion; because he was still a government official, he signed it with the single letter X. A columnist unmasked him within about a week.

Kennan predicted that patient pressure would one day force Soviet power to break up or gradually mellow, and when the Soviet Union broke apart in 1991, forty-four years had passed since his essay. Yet for decades afterwards he insisted people had got him wrong. He meant political and economic pressure, not a global arms race or a war like Vietnam, which he testified against in 1966, and in 1996 he complained that the very people who championed his idea had distorted it into a mainly military concept.

Containment's fiercest critic, the columnist Walter Lippmann, attacked the open-ended promise in fourteen columns as a strategic monstrosity that handed the initiative to Moscow and chained America to weak client states, and the book he wrote against it that year gave the whole era its name: The Cold War. The deepest irony lay in a deal made earlier. At a meeting in Moscow in 1944, Winston Churchill had jotted on a scrap of paper a plan to share out Eastern Europe, giving Britain 90 per cent of the say in Greece, and pushed it over to Stalin, calling it his naughty document. Stalin kept that bargain and had already written off the Greek rebels, who collapsed when Tito closed the Yugoslav border in July 1949.

tuskegee-airmen.context_blurb:
During the Second World War a segregated airfield at Tuskegee, Alabama, trained the first Black pilots ever to fly for the American military. The Tuskegee Airmen flew combat missions over North Africa and Europe while the army that sent them still kept them apart from white units.

Their 332nd Fighter Group painted the tails of its P-51 Mustangs bright red, and by 1944 the Red Tails guarded bombers so well that white bomber crews, many of whom scorned Black airmen, asked for them by name as their escorts.

On 24 March 1945 their commander, Benjamin Davis Jr., led them 1,600 miles to Berlin and back, and no escort mission of the war went farther. Over the target they met something new in the sky, the German Me-262 jet fighter, the first jet in combat service and far faster than any propeller plane, and they shot down three of them.

Davis had been tested long before. At West Point, where he was the lone Black cadet, he was shunned by his classmates, who refused to speak to him for four years in the hope he would quit; he roomed alone and ate alone. Davis answered by graduating near the top of his class in 1936, 35th of 276, and he later became the first Black general in the Air Force, as his father had been the Army's first Black general.

tutankhamun-and-his-tomb.context_blurb:
Tutankhamun became pharaoh of Egypt around 1330 BC as a boy of nine and died before he was twenty. Later kings almost erased his name, and the world all but forgot him until 1922, when Howard Carter, a British archaeologist paid by Lord Carnarvon, found his tomb in the valley where Egypt buried its kings.

What made him famous was the tomb itself. Almost alone among royal burials it had escaped serious looting, and Carter found it with its seals largely intact and packed with untouched treasure after more than 3,000 years. The first sign came on 4 November 1922. As the popular story tells it, a boy who carried water for the diggers found a single stone step, the top of a staircase leading down to a sealed door. On 26 November Carter chiselled a hole in the door and held up a candle, and when Carnarvon asked whether he could see anything, Carter replied that he could see wonderful things: gold glinting everywhere, statues, dismantled chariots, shrines and furniture. His own diary records the plainer "Yes, it is wonderful"; the famous line is the polished version.

The body lay inside three coffins fitted one within another, the outer two of gilded wood and the innermost of solid gold, weighing about 110 kilograms. Over the mummy's face lay the famous death mask, more than ten kilograms of gold hammered from two sheets, with eyes of quartz and eyebrows of blue lapis lazuli. On the back of his golden throne, Queen Ankhesenamun rubs scented oil on her husband, and in one homely touch he wears one sandal of a pair and she wears the other.

Most of the other royal tombs there had been stripped long ago. Tutankhamun's survived because of an accident: when workers later cut the tomb of Ramesses VI nearby, their rubble and a cluster of workmen's stone huts ended up over his hidden entrance, hiding it so well that later diggers camped right over it unawares. Among the treasures was a dagger whose iron blade holds about 11 per cent nickel, forged six centuries before Egyptian smiths learned to smelt iron. That nickel, with a trace of cobalt, is the fingerprint of a meteorite: the blade was made from sky-metal that had fallen to Earth, more precious than gold. He was born Tutankhaten, living image of the Aten, the son of Akhenaten, a king who had swept away Egypt's old gods in favour of one, the sun-disc Aten. As king he changed his name to Tutankhamun, living image of Amun, to proclaim that he had brought back the old gods.

Carter's boast of a tomb untouched for 3,000 years was not quite true. Twice, not long after the funeral, robbers broke in, but both times necropolis officials caught the thieves, hastily repacked the treasures and sealed the tomb again. One fleeing gang dropped a linen scarf knotted around eight gold rings, which the guards stuffed back into a box, and Carter found it still tied.

A 2010 study of his DNA and CT scans, published in a leading American medical journal, showed a harder life than the golden image suggests. He had a club foot and walked with a cane, his parents were brother and sister, and he probably died when a broken leg turned deadly as malaria struck. When Lord Carnarvon died on 5 April 1923 of an infected mosquito bite he had cut open while shaving, the papers blamed a pharaoh's curse, and even Arthur Conan Doyle believed it. Yet Howard Carter, the man who broke into the burial and unwrapped the king, lived on for about seventeen more years and died of natural causes in 1939.

tycho-brahe-and-the-war-on-the-data.context_blurb:
Tycho Brahe was a wealthy Danish nobleman of the later 1500s who became the greatest astronomer of the age before the telescope. A towering, hard-drinking figure, he spent decades measuring the sky, and his records transformed astronomy after his death.

In December 1566 he and his third cousin, Manderup Parsberg, fell out at a party over who was the finer mathematician, and in the sword fight that followed a blade sliced away the bridge of Tycho's nose. Ever after he wore an artificial nose, said to be made of silver and gold, but when scientists examined his exhumed remains, the traces showed that his everyday nose was brass.

For two decades Tycho measured the planets with giant instruments and no telescope, to within one or two arcminutes, the sharpest readings ever made by the naked eye. After he died, his assistant Johannes Kepler found that no circle fitted Tycho's figures for Mars: a stubborn gap of eight arcminutes remained. Because he trusted Tycho's accuracy, Kepler chased that gap until he proved that the planets move not in circles but in ellipses, overturning two thousand years of astronomy.

tycho-brahe-s-observations.context_blurb:
Tycho Brahe was a Danish nobleman of the 1500s who measured the night sky more accurately than anyone before the telescope. The Danish king gave him an entire island in the Baltic for his observatory, and his careful records later let Johannes Kepler work out how the planets move.

As a student of twenty, in 1566, Tycho lost part of his nose in a duel with a fellow student, Manderup Parsberg, over which of them was the better mathematician, and ever after he wore a metal replacement. Legend made it gold and silver to suit his rank, but when his body was exhumed in 2010, the stains on his nasal bones held equal parts copper and zinc, the recipe for brass: his everyday nose was cheap brass, and he perhaps kept a finer one for special occasions.

On 11 November 1572 Tycho saw a dazzling new star flare up among the stars of Cassiopeia, outshining Venus and visible even by day. Ancient astronomy taught that nothing ever changed in the heavens, so by that teaching a new light had to sit nearby, under the Moon. But a nearby object shifts against the background stars when seen from different angles, and night after night Tycho's star never moved at all, so it had to sit far past the Moon, among the distant fixed stars. The supposedly perfect heavens had changed, and his book De nova stella of 1573 helped give us the word nova.

urbanization-and-the-growth-of-industria.context_blurb:
In the 1800s the industrial cities of Europe and America grew faster than any cities ever had. London doubled and doubled again, but its water supplies and drains could not keep up, and diseases spread by filth killed thousands. The fight to clean up London's water became the birth of modern public health.

In 1854 cholera tore through London's Soho district, killing about 500 people in ten days. Dr John Snow plotted every death on a map, saw that they clustered around one street pump on Broad Street, and persuaded the parish to remove its handle, leaving the pump useless. On 7 September the handle came off and the outbreak died away, and Snow's map is remembered as the founding moment of epidemiology. One clue had stood out. Men at the Lion Brewery, right on Broad Street, almost all escaped, because they drank their free daily ration of beer and never touched the pump.

The Reverend Henry Whitehead, a local clergyman, hoped to disprove Snow and to show that the outbreak was God's doing, but his interviews with survivors ended up confirming the water theory and tracing the source to a leaking cesspool. A sick baby's nappies, rinsed by its mother at 40 Broad Street, had seeped into the pump's well.

During the scorching summer of 1858 the sewage dumped into the Thames baked in the sun, and the Great Stink drove the lawmakers out of the Houses of Parliament, which stand right on the river. Disgust finally pushed Parliament to pay for a proper sewer system. In the 1860s Joseph Bazalgette laid out a vast new web of sewers for London. As the celebrated story goes, he worked out the pipe sizes the city needed and then doubled every diameter, reasoning that London would get just one chance to tear up its streets for sewers, and that spare room is why his sewers still cope with a far bigger London.

v-e-day-and-v-j-day.context_blurb:
The Second World War ended in two stages in 1945. On 8 May, Victory in Europe Day, the Allies celebrated Germany's surrender, and on 2 September Japan formally surrendered aboard the American battleship USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay, closing the war in the Pacific.

In London on V-E Day the 19-year-old Princess Elizabeth, the future Queen Elizabeth II, slipped out of Buckingham Palace with her 14-year-old sister, Princess Margaret, hiding in the crowd with her uniform cap pulled low. The two princesses danced the hokey-cokey and the Lambeth Walk and joined a conga line right through the Ritz hotel, and she remembered it all her life as one of her most unforgettable nights.

At the surrender in Tokyo Bay, General Douglas MacArthur signed with six pens and handed two to the generals standing beside him, Jonathan Wainwright and Arthur Percival. Wainwright had been forced to give up the Philippines and Percival Singapore in the dark early days of the war, and both had lived through years as Japanese prisoners, so MacArthur gave them the pens that ended the war they had once lost.

valley-forge-winter-1777-78.context_blurb:
In the winter of 1777 to 1778, after the British had taken Philadelphia, George Washington camped his Continental Army at Valley Forge, about twenty miles to the north-west. Some 12,000 soldiers crowded into 1,500 to 2,000 log huts, briefly making the camp one of the largest towns in America.

About 2,000 of them died there in six months, roughly one man in six. The popular image is of men frozen in the snow, but the real killer was disease: influenza, typhus, typhoid and dysentery swept through the packed huts and killed far more men than the cold.

That spring a Prussian officer, Baron von Steuben, turned the hungry, half-trained army into a disciplined force. Late each night, by candlelight, he drafted the coming day's lesson in French, which his aides then put into English, and those pages became the first drill book of the American army, the Blue Book. It stayed the army's official guide until 1812, and its diagrams were drawn by Pierre L'Enfant, who later designed the city of Washington.

van-gogh-starry-night-and-the-ear.context_blurb:
Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch painter who worked for only about ten years, lived in poverty on money from his brother Theo, and battled a mental illness that was never properly diagnosed. Almost unknown in his own lifetime, he is now among the most famous painters who ever lived, and his works sell for more than 100 million dollars.

In those ten years he painted roughly 900 pictures, about one every four days, yet only one is known to have found a buyer while he lived, The Red Vineyard, which the Belgian painter Anna Boch bought for 400 francs at an exhibition in Brussels in 1890. In December 1888, in Arles in southern France, he quarrelled bitterly with his housemate, the painter Paul Gauguin. That night he cut off part of his left ear with a razor, parcelled it up and took it to a young woman, asking her to guard it with care; she fainted. Newspapers called her Rachel, but researchers later identified her as Gabrielle Berlatier, a teenage farm girl working as a maid.

In 1889 he checked himself into the asylum of Saint-Paul-de-Mausole at Saint-Rémy, and there, in June, he painted The Starry Night from his room in the asylum, looking out through a barred window. The year he spent there was the most productive of his life, with more than 150 works. Cypresses, tall and dark, became one of his favourite subjects, and he told Theo that the tree had lines and proportions as beautiful as an Egyptian obelisk.

He did not paint The Starry Night out under the night sky but by day, from memory. The scene behind it was a dawn: he wrote to Theo that long before sunrise he had looked out over the countryside with nothing in the sky but the morning star, which looked very big, and that morning star was the planet Venus. The church steeple in the painting could not even be seen from his window.

In July 1890, in the fields near Auvers-sur-Oise, he shot himself, and he died at his inn some thirty-six hours later, Theo at his side. Theo reported that among his last words was the line that his sadness would never end: la tristesse durera toujours.

vasco-da-gama-and-the-sea-route-to-india.context_blurb:
In 1497 King Manuel I of Portugal sent Vasco da Gama with four ships to finish a quest Portugal had pursued for most of a century: a sea route around Africa to the spices of India. Da Gama rounded the southern tip of Africa and worked his way up the east African coast.

At Malindi, on the East African coast, he faced the open Indian Ocean with no coast to follow. A skilled local pilot, said in legend to be the famous navigator Ahmad ibn Majid, showed him the summer monsoon, which for part of each year blows steadily out of the south-west, and riding it the fleet crossed the ocean and anchored off the spice port of Calicut on 20 May 1498. No ship had ever before sailed all the way from Europe to India.

Spices had always passed overland or up the Red Sea through the hands of Arab and then Venetian merchants, each adding to the price. When da Gama's ships sailed straight home to Lisbon in 1499, the new sea route broke the old monopoly of those Venetian and Arab middlemen, and a single cargo of pepper could sell for many times its cost. The first ship home, the Berrio, reached Lisbon on 10 July 1499, almost two years after the fleet set out.

vasco-da-gama-reaches-india.context_blurb:
Vasco da Gama was the Portuguese captain who finally completed the plan Prince Henry the Navigator had set in motion decades earlier: to reach India by sailing around Africa. His voyage of 1497 to 1499 opened a sea road between Europe and Asia, and his second voyage was marked by a terrible crime.

He left Lisbon on 8 July 1497 with four ships built for the voyage, and on 20 May 1498, ten months later, he reached Calicut, the spice port on India's south-west coast, the first European to sail from Europe to India. To claim the coasts for Portugal, he set up tall carved stone pillars topped with a cross along the shores of Africa and India; each of these markers was called a padrão.

The open Indian Ocean was unknown water to the Portuguese. At Malindi, in modern Kenya, da Gama took aboard a local pilot who already knew the way, and the fleet ran straight across and sighted the mountains of India in about 23 days. The old tale that the pilot was the famous Arab navigator Ahmad ibn Majid has been disproved. When the first of his men went ashore near Calicut, two Moors from Tunis who spoke Spanish cursed him and asked what had brought him there, and he answered that they came in search of Christians and spices, the twin goals of the voyage.

For the Zamorin, who ruled Calicut, da Gama laid out cheap goods: some striped cloth, hats, hoods, coral beads, and honey, oil and sugar in casks. The king's officials laughed that this was no gift for a king, since even the humblest trader from Mecca brought more, and that a real present should be gold.

His second voyage, in 1502, came for vengeance. Off the Indian coast he intercepted the Miri, full of Muslim pilgrims returning from Mecca, took everything of value and then burned the ship with several hundred pilgrims still on board, women and children among them. Then he bombarded the unfortified port of Calicut for two days, nearly destroying it.

vasco-n-ez-de-balboa-sights-the-pacific.context_blurb:
Vasco Núñez de Balboa was a Spanish adventurer who had escaped his debts on Hispaniola by stowing away in a barrel and ended up leading a small settlement in what is now Panama. In September 1513, chasing native tales of a great sea to the south, he led his men across the jungle-covered isthmus.

On 25 September, just short of the summit, Balboa halted his party and climbed the final slope alone, so that no other European would see the new ocean before him. Only then did he call his men up to look.

Days later he came down to the water on the Gulf of San Miguel. Armoured, with drawn sword and a banner bearing the Virgin Mary, he waded into the surf and claimed the ocean and every shore it touched for the Spanish crown. Because his march had crossed Panama heading south, he named it the South Sea, Mar del Sur, and it kept that name until Ferdinand Magellan renamed it the Pacific in 1520.

velazquez-las-meninas.context_blurb:
Diego Velázquez was court painter to King Philip IV of Spain and spent most of his life at the royal court in Madrid. In 1656 he painted Las Meninas, a huge canvas showing the king's small daughter and the maids of honour who wait on her in a room of the palace, with Velázquez himself standing at his easel.

The king and queen, who ought to be the subject, are not among the figures. They appear only in a little mirror hanging on the far wall, as a faint reflection, which means they must be standing exactly where we stand, looking into the room. That puzzle of who is looking at whom is what makes the painting famous.

The painter wears the red cross of the Order of Santiago, a badge of knighthood, yet he finished the picture in 1656 and only became a knight in 1659. By tradition, King Philip IV himself, the painter's royal master, painted the cross on after Velázquez died, honouring a painter the snobbish Order had refused to treat as a true nobleman. This is tradition rather than documented fact.

vermeer-girl-with-a-pearl-earring.context_blurb:
Johannes Vermeer was a Dutch painter of the mid-1600s who spent his whole short career in the small city of Delft, sold most of his work to a few local collectors and died in debt. Today he counts among the greatest of the Dutch masters, and his Girl with a Pearl Earring, a girl in a blue turban, her eyes shining, is one of the best-loved faces in art.

His fame rests on very few pictures: only about 34 of his paintings survive, with a 35th disputed, so each one is precious. Girl with a Pearl Earring is small too, about 44 by 39 centimetres, signed in the top-left corner but never dated; scholars place it around 1665.

Look closely at the famous pearl and there is nothing to hold it on, and hardly any detail. Vermeer made it with two strokes of white: a bright highlight at the top catching the window light, and a soft reflection below catching light bounced up from her white collar. Experts are not even sure it is a pearl; some think it was glass, or simply invented, and the astrophysicist Vincent Icke argued that it looks more like polished tin.
