vesalius-and-human-anatomy.context_blurb:
Andreas Vesalius was a Flemish doctor of the 1500s whose great book on the human body, De Humani Corporis Fabrica, published in 1543, overturned more than a thousand years of medical teaching. Before him, European doctors learned anatomy almost entirely from the books of Galen, a Greek physician of the Roman Empire in the second century AD.

As a medical student at Louvain in the 1530s, Vesalius wanted a real human skeleton, but the law forbade cutting up bodies. So he climbed a gibbet outside the city walls, cut down the body of a hanged criminal and carried the bones home in pieces to put back together, risking prison to do it.

When he dissected human bodies himself in the 1540s, he found that Galen had gone wrong more than two hundred times. Galen's knowledge came from cutting up apes, dogs and pigs; he had never opened a human body, and he had simply assumed that people were built the same way. Galen claimed that blood soaked through the dividing wall of the heart, from one chamber to the other, by way of pores too small to see. Vesalius searched real human hearts for those pores and found no holes at all, only a thick, solid wall, a crack in Galen's theory that helped open the way to the later discovery that blood circulates.

vietnam-war.context_blurb:
The Vietnam War pitted communist North Vietnam, backed by the Soviet Union and China, against South Vietnam, backed by the United States, which sent its own soldiers to fight. In April 1975 the North's tanks rolled into Saigon. The war tore America apart at home and left terrible crimes on every side.

In June 1963, at a busy Saigon crossroads, Thich Quang Duc, a Buddhist monk of 73, set himself alight in protest at cruel treatment of his fellow Buddhists, and what stunned the world was his stillness: he sat perfectly calm and never moved or made a sound as the flames killed him. In August 1964 Congress let President Lyndon Johnson wage war in Vietnam through the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, which leaned on reports that North Vietnamese boats had struck the USS Maddox a second time on 4 August. Investigators later found that no enemy boats were there that night: the second attack never happened, and the National Security Agency had skewed the intelligence.

The turning point came at Tet, the Vietnamese New Year, when the communists launched a huge offensive at the end of January 1968. Militarily it was a communist defeat, but General Westmoreland had just promised light at the end of the tunnel, and now the evening news showed Viet Cong commandos fighting inside the walls of the American embassy compound in Saigon. During Tet, North Vietnamese troops also held Hue, Vietnam's old royal capital, for weeks. Afterwards mass graves held an estimated 2,800 to 6,000 civilians and prisoners, and the killings were plainly planned, because the soldiers had brought ready-made blacklists of the people they meant to execute as enemies of the revolution. In February Walter Cronkite, the most trusted anchor on CBS, set aside his rule against giving opinions and declared on air that the war was unwinnable, concluding that America was mired in stalemate.

Americans committed atrocities too. On 16 March 1968 soldiers of Charlie Company massacred between 347 and 504 unarmed villagers at My Lai. The helicopter pilot Hugh Thompson set his little helicopter down in the line of fire, between the soldiers and villagers running for their lives, and ordered his two crewmen to open fire on the Americans if they kept on shooting. Lieutenant William Calley was the only man ever convicted. The navy pilot John McCain, shot down and locked in the prison the captives called the Hanoi Hilton, was offered an early release because his father was a powerful admiral. McCain refused and insisted that prisoners go home in the order they had been captured, and he stayed more than five years.

In May 1969 soldiers of the 101st Airborne spent ten days clawing up Hill 937, a slaughter they nicknamed Hamburger Hill, and the Army abandoned it two weeks after taking it. A soldier pinned up a cardboard sign naming the hill, and under it someone wrote: Was it worth it? That June, Dan Bullock, who had faked his birth certificate to join the Marines at fourteen, was killed by an enemy bomb in his bunker at An Hoa, less than a month after arriving. No American who died in the war was younger: he was 15.

In June 1972 South Vietnamese planes mistakenly napalmed a village near Trang Bang, and Nick Ut photographed nine-year-old Kim Phuc fleeing along the road, naked and burning. Then he set the camera down, gave her water and raced her to the closest hospital, saving her life. By 29 April 1975 communist tanks were closing on Saigon. Americans had been told to make for the pickup points when they heard a fake weather report, 105 degrees and rising, followed on Armed Forces Radio by Bing Crosby singing White Christmas.

Over the next twenty years more than a million Vietnamese fled their new communist rulers in tiny, crowded boats, and between 200,000 and 250,000 died at sea. Storms and hunger killed many, and Thai pirates preyed on the refugee boats, robbing, killing and kidnapping. Next door, the communist Khmer Rouge seized Cambodia and killed roughly a fifth of its people. At S-21, a Phnom Penh high school they had made into a secret jail, over 18,000 people were tortured until they confessed to spying for the CIA or the KGB, and then executed.

viking-raids-lindisfarne-793.context_blurb:
In 793 longships out of Scandinavia struck the monastery of Lindisfarne, on a tidal island off the coast of Northumbria in England, and Christian Europe had never seen anything like it. For the next two and a half centuries Norse raiders, traders and settlers sailed to Britain, Ireland and France and, across the Atlantic, as far as North America.

Their name is usually traced to vik, Norse for a bay or inlet, the sheltered water a crew launched from. Going a-viking meant going raiding, and the English word Viking was revived only in the 1800s. On 8 June 793 the raiders beached at Lindisfarne. Old monks too slow to escape were cut down, the young ones were carried off as slaves, and the church was stripped of its treasure, a raid that traditionally marks the start of the Viking Age.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says terrible omens came first: huge flashes of light in the sky, violent whirlwinds, and fiery dragons seen flying through the air, followed by famine and then the heathen raiders. Alcuin of York, a Northumbrian scholar then serving at Charlemagne's court, told Bishop Higbald that the raiders had trodden the holy dead underfoot in God's own house as if they were animal dung in the street. He asked what church in Britain could be safe if St Cuthbert would not defend his own.

Raids like that were possible because of the longship. It drew so little water that it needed no harbour and could row far up rivers, and it could drive its bow right up onto the sand of an open beach, which is exactly why an island monastery was so exposed. Its hull was clinker-built from overlapping oak planks riveted with iron, light enough to flex with the waves. The most feared Norse fighters were the berserkers, who hurled themselves at the enemy in a howling frenzy, sometimes biting their own shields. Their Old Norse name, berserkr, is thought to mean bear-shirt, for the animal pelts they were said to wear.

Later the Norse came not just to plunder but to settle. The Great Heathen Army that came ashore in 865 was commanded by sons of Ragnar Lothbrok, a hero of legend, among them Ivar the Boneless and Halfdan, and it overran Northumbria, East Anglia and Mercia. At Edington in 878 the West Saxon king Alfred defeated the Danish leader Guthrum, and rather than kill him, Alfred made him accept Christian baptism as a term of the peace. A border was drawn across England, and the north and east, left under Norse law, became the Danelaw, where town names ending in -by and -thorpe still survive. Lindisfarne's monks clung on for more than eighty years. When Danish armies drew near in 875, they left the island for good, taking the glittering Lindisfarne Gospels and, just as precious, the coffin holding St Cuthbert's body, the holy bishop whose shrine had made the island sacred. They wandered for seven years, and Cuthbert came at last to rest at Durham.

The Norse sailed west as well. Around the year 1000 Leif Erikson sailed out of Greenland and came to the coast of Newfoundland, about 500 years before Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492. One of the lands he named there was Vinland, Wine Land, because his crewman Tyrker rushed back, the Saga of the Greenlanders says, to report that it was full of vines and grapes. The Norse camp at L'Anse aux Meadows, on Newfoundland's northern tip, was cut from wood felled in 1021, a date fixed by a spike of carbon-14 left by a cosmic-ray burst in 993. In its rubbish lay butternuts and a butternut burl cut with metal tools, from a tree that grows only far to the south, proof that the Norse ranged toward the Gulf of Saint Lawrence.

No magnetic compass guided them; Europe would not have one for centuries. On grey, foggy days, tradition says, the navigator found the hidden sun with a sunstone, a crystal of Iceland spar. They also steered by latitude with a wooden sun-compass, a fragment of which was dug up at Uunartoq in Greenland.

virgil-s-aeneid-and-roman-literature.context_blurb:
The Roman poet Virgil composed the Aeneid, Rome's national epic, in the decade after 30 BC, under the patronage of the emperor Augustus, and it is counted the greatest work of Roman literature. Its hero is Aeneas, a prince who flees the flames of Troy and, after years of wandering, becomes the ancestor of the Romans.

The epic opens with three Latin words, Arma virumque cano: of arms and the man I sing. Arms stands for war, echoing Homer's Iliad, and the man is the wandering hero, echoing the Odyssey.

When Virgil died in 19 BC, after some eleven years' labour, the poem still lacked its last revision, and he asked that it be burned. Augustus overruled that dying wish and ordered the executors, Varius and Tucca, to publish the Aeneid with as few changes as possible. More than 1,300 years later Dante chose Virgil himself as his guide through Hell and Purgatory.

voltaire-and-freedom-of-speech.context_blurb:
Voltaire was the most famous writer in Europe in the 1700s: a French playwright, poet, historian and troublemaker who spent his life mocking the powerful and fighting for tolerance. His campaigns against injustice made him a hero of free thought.

His real name was François-Marie Arouet, but in 1718 he took the pen name Voltaire, most likely an anagram of the Latin form of Arouet le jeune, and over his life he used more than a hundred other false names to slip past the king's censors. In 1726 he mocked a nobleman, the Chevalier de Rohan-Chabot, who had his servants beat Voltaire with clubs. When Voltaire demanded a duel, the powerful Rohan family had him locked in the Bastille prison instead, freeing him only on condition that he leave France, and he spent nearly three years in exile in England.

In Toulouse in 1762 a Protestant merchant of 64, Jean Calas, was accused without real proof of killing his own son. The court condemned him to be broken on the wheel: on 10 March his limbs were smashed with an iron bar before he was strangled, and he proclaimed his innocence to the end. Voltaire spent almost three years clearing Calas's name, writing letters across Europe and publishing his Treatise on Tolerance in 1763. Louis XV annulled the verdict, judges cleared the dead man in 1765, and the king paid the ruined family 36,000 livres, and historians have called Voltaire's fight the first modern human-rights campaign.

His most famous saying is not his. The words everyone quotes, about disapproving of what someone says yet defending to the death that person's right to say it, were coined in 1906 by his English biographer Evelyn Beatrice Hall to sum up his attitude, so they are her paraphrase, not his words.

wall-street-crash-of-1929.context_blurb:
Through 1928 and 1929 share prices in New York climbed to dizzying heights, driven partly by ordinary Americans buying with borrowed money. In the last week of October 1929 the boom came apart in a crash that opened the way to the Great Depression, and historians still argue about why it happened.

Many people bought on margin, paying perhaps a tenth of the price themselves and borrowing the other nine-tenths. By that August such loans topped 8.5 billion dollars, more than all the paper money then circulating in the United States. When prices fell, lenders called in their loans, and the borrowers had to sell in a panic. On 15 October, nine days before the crash, Irving Fisher, the celebrated economist of Yale, assured a business dinner that stock prices had reached what looked like a permanently high plateau. It became the most mocked forecast in financial history, and the crash wiped out Fisher's own fortune.

Panic broke out on Black Thursday, 24 October. At noon the bankers sent Richard Whitney, vice-president of the Exchange, striding across the floor, where in a loud voice he bid 205 dollars a share for 25,000 shares of United States Steel, above the going price, and the bluff briefly steadied the market. It did not last, and the worst day of all was Black Tuesday, 29 October, when a record 16.4 million shares changed hands. So much was sold that the ticker tape machine, which printed prices on a ribbon of paper, fell hours behind and did not finish the day's prices until about a quarter to eight that evening, so for hours nobody on the floor knew what anything was worth.

Some stocks collapsed almost completely. Shares of White Sewing Machine, worth about 48 dollars that summer, had sunk to 11 by the eve of Black Tuesday, and in the next day's chaos one buyer reportedly picked up a share for a single dollar. The next morning Variety, the entertainment paper, summed it up with stage slang for a flop: Wall Street, it said, had laid an egg. The Dow Jones average had peaked at 381 on 3 September 1929, and anyone who bought at the top and held on waited twenty-five years, until November 1954, just to break even.

Everyone pictures ruined brokers leaping from windows, but Charles Norris, the city's chief medical examiner, checked the records. Manhattan had 44 suicides in the four weeks after the crash, fewer than the 53 in the same weeks a year earlier. Winston Churchill, who was visiting New York and had lost money himself, still wrote in London's Daily Telegraph that right under his window a man had flung himself down fifteen storeys, a dramatic personal account rather than a verified event.

Historians still argue about the cause. Two economists of the Austrian school, Friedrich Hayek and Ludwig von Mises, blamed the cheap credit the Federal Reserve had poured out in the 1920s, which in their view inflated an artificial boom: the boom itself was the sickness, and the crash was the cure, the painful correction. Hayek had warned early in 1929 that the American boom would collapse, while others, such as John Kenneth Galbraith, blamed runaway speculation instead. The Austrians pointed to a secret gathering of the world's central bankers on Long Island in 1927, where the New York Fed's Benjamin Strong backed a cut in interest rates and reportedly called it a little shot of whisky to perk up the stock market, un petit coup de whisky. Other historians dispute how much it mattered.

war-of-1812-burning-of-washington.context_blurb:
The War of 1812 set the young United States against Britain from 1812 to 1815, while Britain was also at war with Napoleon in Europe. Americans had real grievances against British interference with their ships and sailors, but the war went badly for them, and in August 1814 a British army marched on their capital.

On 24 August 1814 a British force entered Washington and burned the Capitol and the President's house, the only time a foreign enemy has ever captured and burned the American capital. As the British closed in, Dolley Madison, the president's wife, would not go until the full-length portrait of George Washington by Gilbert Stuart was saved; it was screwed to the wall, so the frame was broken and the canvas carried away. That is the famous version. Paul Jennings, enslaved in the White House at fifteen, wrote in his memoir of 1865 that Dolley Madison did not take the painting down herself: the doorkeeper, John Susé, and the gardener, Magraw, did.

Before she fled, a fine dinner had been laid on her orders, and the British officers who entered the deserted house found the meal still warm. They sat down, ate it and drank a mocking toast to Jemmy's health, sneering at President James Madison, and then set the house on fire. Admiral George Cockburn had a personal grudge. The National Intelligencer, a Washington newspaper, had branded him a ruffian, so at its office he had his men destroy every piece of type for the letter C, so that the rascals could no longer print his name.

The British held the city for only about 26 hours. The next day, 25 August, a violent storm and tornado ripped roofs off houses, tossed cannons about, killed some thirty British soldiers and put out the fires, and the British withdrew. Three weeks later they bombarded Fort McHenry at Baltimore through the night of 13 to 14 September. When morning came, Francis Scott Key, who had watched all night, saw the great flag still waving over the fort and wrote a poem that, set to music, became The Star-Spangled Banner. That flag, 30 by 42 feet, with fifteen stars and fifteen stripes, was sewn by Mary Pickersgill and hangs in the Smithsonian.

The war's most famous American victory came after it was over. On 8 January 1815 General Andrew Jackson, leading a mixed force that included pirates and free Black volunteers, crushed a British army at New Orleans and became a national hero overnight. But the Treaty of Ghent had already been signed on 24 December 1814; word of the peace simply had not yet crossed the Atlantic, and the treaty left things as they had been before the war.

washington-crossing-the-delaware-trenton.context_blurb:
By December 1776 George Washington's Continental Army had been chased out of New York, across New Jersey and over the Delaware River into Pennsylvania. Most of his men's enlistments ran out at the New Year, and one more defeat might finish the Revolution, so Washington gambled on a surprise attack on the Hessian garrison at Trenton.

For the night attack he chose a grim password. A sentry would challenge with the word Victory, and the man who answered had to say Death: Victory or Death, the motto of a gamble in which failure could end everything.

On the freezing night of 25 to 26 December some 2,400 soldiers, with their horses and big guns, had to get over the ice-choked river in flat wooden boats while, as one soldier said, it blew a hurricane. The men who rowed and poled the army through the ice were Colonel John Glover's Marblehead mariners, seamen and fishermen from Marblehead, Massachusetts.

washington-resigns-his-commission-the-am.context_blurb:
At the end of the Revolutionary War George Washington took the most important political step of his career. Instead of using his victorious army to seize power, as so many generals in history had done, he handed his command back to Congress in December 1783 and went home to his farm at Mount Vernon.

Eight years earlier he had spent Christmas very differently. On the night of 25 December 1776 he took his soldiers over the ice-choked Delaware and fell on the Hessian garrison at Trenton by surprise, a stunning win that revived a collapsing cause. He would not spend another Christmas at home until 1783, days after giving up his command.

In March 1783 at Newburgh his own officers, furious over unpaid wages, were close to mutiny and talking of a march on Congress. Washington came to face them, and as he fumbled on a pair of spectacles, which few of them had ever seen him wear, he begged their pardon, saying he had grown grey in their service and was now going blind. Officers who had been ready to revolt wept, and the plot collapsed. Across the ocean, the painter Benjamin West told King George III that the victorious general intended to surrender his power and return to farming, and the king is said to have replied that if he did, he would be the greatest man on earth. The story was written down years later, in the diary of the artist Joseph Farington, so it is beloved testimony rather than a proven quote.

At the Maryland State House that December every detail of the ceremony made one point: the army answered to Congress. The printed rules told the members of Congress to keep their seats and their hats on and, when Washington bowed, simply to raise their hats without bowing in return: the soldier bowed to the people's government, and the government did not bow to him.

washington-s-farewell-address-precedents.context_blurb:
In 1796, after eight years as president, George Washington chose not to seek a third term and stepped down of his own free will. Before he left office he gave the nation his Farewell Address, full of advice and warnings about the dangers ahead for the young republic, and his choice to go home after two terms became a model for the presidents who followed.

Despite its name, the Farewell Address was never spoken aloud. Washington wanted it to reach plain citizens all over the country, not only a crowd in the capital, so he gave it to a Philadelphia newspaper, Claypoole's American Daily Advertiser, which printed it on 19 September 1796 for anyone to read.

Its gravest warning, made in the most solemn manner, was against the spirit of party, the rivalry of political factions. Washington feared that party feeling, sharpened by revenge, might turn into a frightful despotism, the worst enemy a free people could have.

watson-crick-franklin-and-the-dna-double.context_blurb:
By the late 1940s most biologists accepted that DNA, the long thin molecule inside our chromosomes, carried the instructions for life, but nobody knew its shape. In 1953 two scientists at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, the American biologist James Watson and the English physicist Francis Crick, solved it, with crucial evidence gathered by Rosalind Franklin, an X-ray expert in London.

DNA turned out to be a double helix: two long strands wound around each other like the two railings of a spiral staircase, joined in the middle by rungs, a shape that now turns up on logos and stamps. The rungs are made of paired chemicals called bases, and the four bases, A, T, G and C, are fussy about partners. A links only with T, and G only with C, fitting together like puzzle pieces, so the two strands always match exactly.

The key clue was a blurry X-ray picture known today as Photo 51, taken on 2 May 1952 by Franklin's PhD student Raymond Gosling, who blasted a single fibre of DNA with X-rays for about 62 hours to get it. For an expert, the smudged X in the middle was the fingerprint of a helix, proof that DNA twists like a spiral. Franklin had not finished her own analysis or published it, but her colleague Maurice Wilkins showed the photograph to James Watson without her knowledge or permission. Watson later wrote that the instant he saw it his mouth fell open and his pulse began racing.

The race was close. Linus Pauling, the world's best-known chemist, put out a DNA model of his own early in 1953 with three strands, built inside out so it could never have held together. His son Peter Pauling, a student at Cambridge, passed a copy of the paper to Watson, who saw that the race was still open. Watson and Crick did not rely on equations alone. They built a tall tabletop model of the molecule out of metal plates and rods and adjusted it until every piece fitted, and the picture of Watson and Crick posing proudly beside their metal model of DNA is one of the best-known images in science.

On 28 February 1953, as Watson told it, Crick burst into the Eagle, the pub where the Cavendish scientists lunched, and announced to everyone that they had found the secret of life. Crick himself had no memory of saying it. Their paper ended with one modest sentence noting that the specific pairing they proposed immediately suggested a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material: because each base has only one partner, each strand is a mould for the other, so DNA can unzip and copy itself. It is often called the greatest understatement in science.

In 1962 Watson, Crick and Wilkins shared the Nobel Prize in Medicine. Franklin was left out, though her photograph had been the vital proof: she had died in 1958, and the prize is never given after death. She had moved on to new work. At Birkbeck College she used X-ray methods to map the tobacco mosaic virus, turned out seventeen papers before her death and helped found structural virology, the mapping of the shapes of viruses. She died of ovarian cancer at only 37, and Crick later said her part in the DNA discovery had been critical.

weimar-republic-and-hyperinflation.context_blurb:
After defeat in 1918 Germany became a republic, called the Weimar Republic after the small town where its constitution was written. Born in defeat, debt and street violence, its governments printed money to pay their bills, and in 1923 the currency collapsed in one of the worst hyperinflations in history.

By late 1923 prices rose by the hour: bread priced at 250 marks in January sold for billions by November. A bundle of banknotes was worth less than the firewood it could buy, so families burned the money in their stoves for heat. Some pasted notes on their walls because they were cheaper than wallpaper. Children played with stacks of banknotes like toy blocks, and in one well-known Berlin picture two youngsters stand by a tower of bundled notes worth about one American dollar in all.

Prices could jump within hours. A student who ordered a coffee at a café for 5,000 marks found that by the time his second cup arrived, it cost 7,000. In 1914 a dollar had bought about four marks; at the peak, in November 1923, it bought about 4.2 trillion. As faith in the mark collapsed, people turned to something divisible, portable and steady in value, and cigarettes became everyday money, traded for goods when shopkeepers refused the worthless notes.

The cure came in November 1923 with a new currency, the Rentenmark, swapped at one for a trillion old marks and capped at 3.2 billion units. Hjalmar Schacht, who became president of the Reichsbank that December, turned down every request for more notes, and because the supply could not grow, people trusted the new money and prices settled within days.

westward-expansion-and-the-plains-indian.context_blurb:
In the decades after the Civil War the United States completed its conquest of the Great Plains. Railroads crossed the buffalo country, hunters shot the great herds nearly to extinction, and the army fought the Plains nations who resisted the loss of their land.

In 1868, in the Treaty of Fort Laramie, the United States pledged the Black Hills to the Lakota for all time. In 1874 George Custer led soldiers into those hills and found gold there, more than 15,000 miners poured in, and when the Lakota would not sell the land they had been promised, the United States broke the treaty and the Great Sioux War began in 1876.

In June 1876, at a Sun Dance by Rosebud Creek, Sitting Bull, the Lakota holy man, gave a hundred small pieces of his own flesh and danced till he collapsed. In his vision he saw soldiers tumbling head-first into the Lakota camp, as thick as grasshoppers, and heard a voice say they had no ears, meaning they would not listen; his people took it as a promise of victory. Weeks later, on 25 June, Lakota and Cheyenne warriors wiped out Lieutenant Colonel George Custer and his whole column at the Little Bighorn. When searchers came two days later, the only living thing left of Custer's force was a cavalry horse, Comanche, ridden by Captain Myles Keogh, with seven bullet wounds. The regiment ordered that no one should ever ride him again.

Crazy Horse, the most feared Lakota war leader, had in 1866 drawn a whole army detachment under Captain Fetterman into a deadly trap, and he struck Custer's flank at the Little Bighorn. Famous for his humility, he refused all his life to sign any document or to let anyone photograph him, and no verified photograph of him is known.

By 1890 a new faith, the Ghost Dance, had spread among the Lakota. It began with a vision of the Paiute prophet Wovoka during a solar eclipse on 1 January 1889, promising that if the people danced, the dead would rise and the settlers would vanish. Believers wore painted muslin Ghost Shirts, trusting that the shirts themselves would turn aside bullets. Fear of the dance brought soldiers to Wounded Knee Creek. On 29 December 1890 soldiers of the 7th Cavalry ringed a camp of some 350 Lakota led by the ailing Spotted Elk, with rapid-fire cannon on the rise above. A rifle went off in a scuffle over one man's gun, the troopers began shooting, and 250 to 300 Lakota were killed, most of them unarmed women and children. The holy man Black Elk said that a people's dream died there.

whiskey-rebellion-1794.context_blurb:
In 1791 Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton pushed a federal tax on distilled spirits through Congress as part of his financial program. Farmers in western Pennsylvania, who turned much of their grain into whiskey, hated the tax, and in 1794 thousands of them chose rebellion over paying.

President George Washington raised about 13,000 militiamen to crush the revolt and rode west at their head himself, reviewing the troops at Bedford, Pennsylvania: the only time a sitting president has led an army in the field. He then handed command to Henry Lee, governor of Virginia, and went back to Philadelphia, while Hamilton stayed with the army.

Short of supplies on the march, the soldiers raided farms along the way for food, and the mocking locals nicknamed them the Watermelon Army. By the time they reached western Pennsylvania the rebels had melted away, and the show of force ended the rebellion without a battle.

why-roman-concrete-still-stands-the-self.context_blurb:
Many great Roman concrete structures, from the dome of the Pantheon in Rome to harbour walls that have stood in salt water for two thousand years, still stand, while much modern concrete crumbles within decades. Scientists have only recently worked out why.

For years experts dismissed the little white specks in Roman concrete, lumps of lime called lime clasts, as a sign of sloppy mixing. In 2023 a team at MIT showed that they heal the concrete: when a crack reaches one and rainwater seeps in, the lime dissolves and grows back as crystals of calcium carbonate that seal the crack. In their test, a cracked sample made to the Roman recipe had sealed itself within two weeks, while a modern-style sample never healed; the secret was hot mixing with quicklime.

Today's builders take care to use stone that stays inert in cement, because a chemical reaction could swell and crack the concrete. The geologist Marie Jackson discovered that Roman harbour builders chose volcanic ash precisely because it reacts: seawater seeping through dissolves the ash and grows rare interlocking crystals, so over two thousand years the walls have grown stronger as the new crystals bind the rock together. Pliny the Elder had already described sea piers that became a single mass of stone, every day stronger.

william-harvey-and-blood-circulation.context_blurb:
William Harvey was an English physician of the 1600s, doctor to two kings, who overturned the teaching of Galen, the ancient Greek physician whose word had ruled medicine for some fourteen centuries. Galen's followers held that the liver made blood fresh from food and that the organs used it up; Harvey proved them wrong.

His proof was arithmetic. The heart pushes out about two ounces with each beat, and at some 72 beats a minute that comes to more than 500 pounds of blood an hour, far more than a body contains or a liver could ever produce, so the same blood must go round in a circle and come back to the heart. He published the discovery in 1628 in De Motu Cordis.

Harvey was famously calm. When King Charles I fought at Edgehill in 1642, he left his two young sons in Harvey's care, and the story goes that as the cannon boomed he settled the boys under a hedge, took a book out of his pocket and read to them, until a cannonball landed close enough to make him move.

He died in 1657, aged 79, after a brain haemorrhage left him unable to speak. The man who had proved that blood circulates rather than being consumed made signs asking to be bled, the standard cure of the age, and he died before the night was out.

winston-churchill-s-wartime-leadership.context_blurb:
Winston Churchill spent most of the 1930s out of office, warning in lonely speeches that Nazi Germany was rearming and that appeasement would end in disaster. When war proved him right, he became Britain's prime minister in its darkest hour, and his words held the country together.

In those years he recited the swelling numbers of German planes and tanks to an almost empty chamber, and the first book of his war memoirs takes its title from that looming danger: The Gathering Storm. Only after the Munich deal of 1938 and Hitler's seizure of Czechoslovakia did opinion turn his way. On 10 May 1940, the morning German armies smashed into Western Europe, the King asked Churchill, then 65, to form a government. That night, he later wrote, he felt as if he were walking with destiny, as though all his past life had been a preparation for that hour and that trial.

Three days later he told the House of Commons he had nothing to offer but blood and toil, tears and sweat, and that his aim was victory at all costs, because without victory there could be no survival. When small boats plucked over 338,000 men from the sands of Dunkirk, far more than the 45,000 first hoped for, he reminded the Commons that a rescue is not a victory. Then he vowed that Britain would fight on the beaches, in the fields and in the streets, and ended: we shall never surrender. On 18 June, with France fallen and Britain alone, he warned that defeat would sink the world into a new Dark Age, but said that if the British Empire lasted a thousand years, men would still call that moment their finest hour.

In August 1940, during the Battle of Britain, he watched from an underground operations room as RAF squadrons rose to meet the German attack, and afterwards he told General Hastings Ismay that he had never been so moved. On 20 August he told the Commons that never in the field of human conflict had so many owed so much to so few. He liked to salute crowds with a V for Victory, made with two fingers, an idea first broadcast on the BBC in January 1941 by the exiled Belgian politician Victor de Laveleye. At first, though, he made it the rude way, with his palm facing inward, the British working-class version of a very insulting gesture, until his staff begged him to turn it palm-out.

He often worked from his bed or even his bath, and for air raids he had his tailor create a siren suit: a one-piece jumpsuit that zipped up the front, quick to pull on when the sirens sounded. His staff called it his rompers. Addressing the Canadian Parliament at the end of 1941, he recalled the French generals' forecast that Britain's neck would be wrung like a chicken's within three weeks, paused, and answered: Some chicken! Some neck! The chamber roared.

The real turning point came in private. On 28 May 1940 the Foreign Secretary, Lord Halifax, urged his colleagues to seek Mussolini's help in arranging a peace with Hitler. Churchill replied that a nation which falls fighting can rise again, but one that gives in meekly is finished, and he told his ministers that if Britain's long island story must end, it should end only when each of them lay choking in his own blood upon the ground. The minister Hugh Dalton recorded not a flicker of dissent, and the peace idea died.

Few people actually heard the beaches speech in wartime: he delivered it in the Commons, and the Commons was not broadcast. The famous recording everyone knows was made by Churchill himself for a gramophone record in 1949, and the story that an actor impersonated him on the radio is a debunked myth. In 1953 Churchill, who privately hoped for the Nobel Peace Prize, was given the literature prize instead, partly for those speeches. The American broadcaster Edward Murrow summed up what they had done: Churchill, he said, had mobilised the English language and sent it to war.

woodrow-wilson-s-fourteen-points.context_blurb:
In January 1918, with American troops pouring into the war in Europe, President Woodrow Wilson set out his plan for the peace to come: a new world of open diplomacy, free seas and nations governing themselves. His proposals inspired millions, were largely shelved by the victors at Paris, and ended in personal tragedy for Wilson.

On 8 January 1918 he presented it to a joint session of Congress as a numbered list of fourteen points, his blueprint for peace. Point one attacked secret diplomacy, the hidden treaties he blamed for the war: from now on, he said, peace treaties should be open covenants, openly arrived at. Point two called for freedom of the seas. The points were not his work alone. His close friend Colonel Edward House had secretly gathered about 150 scholars, mostly historians, geographers and political scientists, into a team called The Inquiry, which produced some 2,000 reports and more than 1,200 maps.

The idea that ran through the whole plan was self-determination, the right of each people to govern itself. Robert Lansing, Wilson's Secretary of State, dreaded it, warning privately that the phrase was simply loaded with dynamite and would stir up hopes that could never be satisfied. He was grimly proved right in the 1930s, when Adolf Hitler made self-determination a central plank of Nazi policy to justify grabbing German-speaking lands. His last point proposed a lasting association of nations, in which great and small countries alike could settle quarrels without war, and from it grew the League of Nations.

At the peace conference in Paris, Georges Clemenceau, the tough old French premier they called the Tiger, resented Wilson's academic idealism and mocked his list, remarking that God himself had been content with ten commandments while Wilson gave them fourteen. The Allied leaders cared more about punishing Germany than about Wilson's ideals, so they diluted or discarded most of his points, and the League of Nations was the one major piece that made it into the Treaty of Versailles.

To win Americans over to the League, the 62-year-old Wilson set out by train in September 1919, travelling 8,000 miles in three weeks of speeches while headaches pounded. He spoke for the last time at Pueblo, Colorado, on 25 September, and on 2 October a massive stroke paralysed his left side. For months he could not govern, and his wife, First Lady Edith Bolling Galt Wilson, together with his doctor, controlled all access to him, turning away even the Vice President and the Secretary of State: historians call it the shadow presidency. Meanwhile Henry Cabot Lodge led the Senate's opposition, fearing that Article X of the League could drag America into war without the consent of Congress. In March 1920 the Senate rejected the treaty 49 to 35, so the country that dreamed up the League never became a member.

wwi-poetry-and-remembrance.context_blurb:
The First World War produced English poetry still read in schools a century later, much of it written by men who served in the trenches. Their poems swing from grief to fury at the old ideas of glorious war.

In May 1915, during the Second Battle of Ypres, the Canadian army doctor John McCrae looked out from his dressing station at Essex Farm over fresh graves among wild red poppies, and the day after his friend Alexis Helmer was killed by a shell he wrote In Flanders Fields. Poppy seeds sprout in churned-up earth, so the flowers bloomed blood-red over the shell-torn battlefields, and the poppy became the flower people wear every year in memory of those killed in war.

Wilfred Owen's poem Dulce et Decorum Est shows a man dying in a gas attack, drowning as the gas fills his lungs, then turns on the Latin boast of the Roman poet Horace, some two thousand years old, that dying for your country is sweet and fitting, and calls it the old Lie. Owen fell to gunfire at a canal crossing near Ors, in France, on 4 November 1918, just seven days before the guns fell silent. The telegram with the news reached his parents in Shrewsbury on Armistice Day, 11 November, as the church bells rang out to celebrate the peace.

xerxes-invasion-and-the-greco-persian-wa.context_blurb:
Between about 500 and 449 BC the Greek city-states fought the Persian Empire, the greatest power the Mediterranean world had yet seen. Twice the Persians invaded Greece, first under King Darius in 490 BC and then under his son Xerxes in 480 BC, and twice the outnumbered Greeks drove them back.

In 490 BC ten thousand Athenian citizens in arms met Darius's far bigger army on the coastal plain of Marathon. Their general Miltiades ordered something no Greek army had dared: they charged the whole way across the open ground at a run, getting through the deadly zone of Persian arrows fast and hitting hard. Herodotus counts 192 Athenians dead against 6,400 Persians. Before the battle Athens had sent the runner Pheidippides across the mountains, about 140 miles, to plead for Spartan help, and he reached Sparta on the second day. Herodotus reports that on the lonely mountain road the god Pan appeared to him and demanded to know why the Athenians paid him no honour. The famous tale of a runner who raced from Marathon to Athens and dropped dead, giving us the word marathon, is a later invention.

Ten years later Xerxes came with an even greater army. To get it from Asia into Europe across the Hellespont, the narrow strait between the continents, his engineers lashed some 674 boats side by side with huge cables of flax and papyrus and laid planks, brushwood and earth over them, making a floating road across the sea. When a storm smashed the first bridge, Xerxes took the storm as the sea's own defiance and had the water punished: it was given three hundred lashes and a pair of iron fetters, and he had the bridge builders beheaded. At Abydos, gazing down at his vast army and fleet at the height of his power, Xerxes suddenly wept. Artabanus, his uncle, asked the reason, and the king said he had been seized by pity, because not one of all those men would be alive in a hundred years. His elite guard was the Immortals, a corps kept at exactly ten thousand men: the moment one was killed or wounded, another took his place.

At the pass of Thermopylae, King Leonidas of Sparta and a small Greek force barred the way. According to Plutarch, writing some 500 years later, Xerxes offered peace if the Spartans would hand over their weapons, and Leonidas answered in two words, molon labe: come and take them. The line is not in Herodotus, so it is best treated as tradition. Told that the Persian bowmen would darken the sky with arrows, the Spartan Dienekes said that was good news, since they would fight in the shade, a retort Herodotus called the finest of the day. Then Ephialtes, a Greek of the district, sold Xerxes the secret of a hidden mountain trail, the Anopaia path, that led around behind the defenders, and his name became the Greek word for traitor.

Xerxes also fought at sea. Before the sea battle, the oracle at Delphi had told Athens that only a wooden wall would save the city. Some Athenians wanted to fence the Acropolis with timber, but their leader Themistocles argued that the wooden wall was Athens's navy, its warships, and he staked the city on its ships. He wanted the battle in the narrow waters of Salamis, where Persian numbers would be a burden, so he sent his trusted servant Sicinnus over to the Persians with a false message: the Greeks were about to flee, and the king should block the exits. Xerxes sealed the exits and trapped his own oversized fleet, and Herodotus says some 300 Persian ships were lost to about 40 Greek. Among his commanders at sea was Artemisia, queen of Caria. Chased by a Greek ship, she drove her ram into a ship from her own fleet and sank it, so that she looked Greek and slipped away, and Xerxes, believing she had sunk an enemy, exclaimed that his men had become women and his women men.

A year later came the last great land battle, at Plataea, where the Spartan regent Pausanias led the largest army of armoured hoplites Greece ever gathered. The battle swayed back and forth until the Persian general Mardonius fell fighting the Spartans, and his leaderless army broke and ran, ending the invasion.

yorktown-1781-cornwallis-surrenders.context_blurb:
In October 1781 the last major battle of the American Revolutionary War ended at Yorktown, on the Virginia coast. The British commander in the South, General Charles Cornwallis, had fortified himself at Yorktown, counting on the Royal Navy to come down from New York and take his army off by sea.

Instead, on 5 September 1781, Admiral de Grasse's French fleet defeated the British navy at the Battle of the Chesapeake and then blockaded the bay, so Cornwallis had no escape by water and no rescue by sea. The fleet he hoped for, under Admiral Thomas Graves, never came, and with Washington's army and the French closing in by land, he was trapped.

On 19 October Cornwallis's defeated regiments filed out to surrender their arms to the colonists they had long called rebels. According to legend, the British musicians struck up The World Turned Upside Down, a fitting tune for an army giving up to its own rebellious subjects, though the evidence for it is thin.

yuri-gagarin-first-human-in-space.context_blurb:
Yuri Gagarin was a Soviet air force pilot, the son of a carpenter and a dairymaid from a village west of Moscow, who had grown up under Nazi occupation. Chosen in 1960 from among thousands of pilots, he became on 12 April 1961 the first human being to travel into space.

As his Vostok 1 rocket lifted off, the 27-year-old called out over the radio Poyekhali, Russian for "Let's go!", a word that rang round the world. He circled the whole Earth once in about 108 minutes, the first person to see the planet turn beneath him.

He survived the fiery plunge back through the atmosphere, but he did not stay in the capsule all the way down. About seven kilometres up he ejected and came down under his own parachute, apart from the capsule, landing near Engels in the Saratov region. Because record rules said a pilot had to land inside his craft, Soviet officials at first hid the ejection; when it came out, the rules were changed and his records stood.

zheng-he-s-treasure-fleet-voyages.context_blurb:
In the early 1400s the Ming emperor Yongle sent seven great voyages across the Indian Ocean under the Muslim court eunuch Zheng He. His fleet was the most powerful on Earth, and over the years it sailed as far as the shores of Africa.

Columbus would need just three little ships and some ninety sailors in 1492. Almost ninety years earlier, in 1405, Zheng He sailed on his first voyage with about 62 giant treasure ships leading hundreds of other vessels, carrying about 28,000 men.

In 1414 his fleet brought home a live giraffe from Africa, an animal no one in China had ever seen. Courtiers declared it a qilin, the legendary beast that showed itself only in the reign of a wise and good emperor, a sign of heaven's blessing on Yongle, who had seized the throne by force. The court painter Shen Du painted it with a poem, and the scroll survives in the Philadelphia Museum of Art.

After Zheng He died around 1433, the Ming court turned inward, stopped the voyages and left the shipyards idle. So that no later emperor could ever revive the fleets, court officials, linked by tradition to the minister Liu Daxia, destroyed the voyage records, by the usual account burning the logs and sea charts. That helped hand the oceans, and the coming age of exploration, to Europe.

ziggurats.context_blurb:
A ziggurat was a huge stepped temple-platform of mud brick, faced with fired brick, the signature building of ancient Mesopotamia, the land of the Sumerians and Babylonians, from the late third millennium BC onward. Each rose in tiers toward a shrine at the top, where the city's god was believed to dwell among his people.

The Great Ziggurat of Ur, built by King Ur-Nammu around 2100 BCE, still stands in southern Iraq, better preserved than any other. Its summit shrine, now lost, was the house on earth of Ur's protector, Nanna, also called Sin, the god of the moon.

Around 600 BCE King Nebuchadnezzar II rebuilt the great ziggurat of Babylon, Etemenanki, whose name links heaven and earth, and dedicated it to Marduk, king of the Babylonian gods. It rose in seven tiers above the city, and most scholars think this real tower lies behind the Bible's story of the Tower of Babel.

august-coup-and-the-end-of-the-ussr-1991.context_blurb:
By the summer of 1991 the Soviet Union, the communist state Lenin's Bolsheviks founded in 1917, was coming apart. For seven decades the Communist Party had ruled through censorship, the secret police and the Gulag camps, and its command economy could no longer feed its people. Mikhail Gorbachev had loosened the Party's grip, and the fifteen republics were pulling away. That August, hardliners tried to stop it.

When the plotters sent tanks into Moscow on 19 August, Boris Yeltsin, the newly elected president of Russia, walked out of the Russian parliament building, climbed on top of a tank and spoke to the crowd, and that photograph came to stand for the coup's collapse. Four months later the country itself was gone. On the evening of 25 December 1991 the Soviet red flag with its hammer and sickle was lowered from the Kremlin, and in its place rose the white, blue and red tricolour of Russia from before the 1917 revolution.

The coup's eight leaders, among them the KGB chief Vladimir Kryuchkov and Defence Minister Dmitry Yazov, struck while Gorbachev was vacationing by the sea at Foros in Crimea, holding him prisoner in his own villa and cutting every phone line. State television dropped its normal programmes and played Tchaikovsky's ballet Swan Lake over and over, a signal older viewers recognised: something was being concealed at the very top. At a press conference the plotters' stand-in president, Gennady Yanayev, was asked whether this was a coup, and viewers saw at once that the plotters had lost their grip, because his hands trembled visibly and his voice wavered.

Tens of thousands of unarmed Muscovites ringed the parliament, and for all its tanks the coup killed only three people, young defenders crushed in a tunnel under Moscow's ring road while trying to stop armoured vehicles. Dmitry Komar, Vladimir Usov and Ilya Krichevsky were honoured as heroes, and the plot fell apart within days.

On 8 December Yeltsin and the presidents of Ukraine and Belarus slipped away to a hunting lodge deep in the Belovezha Forest of Belarus, one of Europe's last primeval woods, and signed an accord pronouncing the Soviet Union finished. On 25 December, before his farewell speech even aired, Gorbachev quietly handed Yeltsin the briefcase that controlled the Soviet nuclear missiles. When Gorbachev sat down on live television to sign his resignation, his Soviet pen would not write, so the CNN president, Tom Johnson, handed him his own Montblanc pen, and the USSR ended with a borrowed Western pen.

On 8 December, right after signing the accord, Yeltsin telephoned not Gorbachev, still the Soviet president, but the American president, George H. W. Bush, telling him he could not wait even ten minutes to call. Behind it all lay money: the Soviet arms race ran on oil sales, and when Saudi Arabia dropped its production limits in 1985 and pumped far more, world oil prices crashed and Moscow lost the hard currency it needed. A superpower that had survived Hitler's invasion ended without a war, brought down by its own failures and by citizens who stopped obeying.

fall-of-the-berlin-wall-1989.context_blurb:
After World War Two, Berlin lay deep inside communist East Germany, split between a free West and a Soviet-run East. In August 1961 the East German regime built a wall through the city to stop its people from fleeing, and it ordered its guards to shoot anyone who tried. On 9 November 1989, after weeks of protest, the wall suddenly opened.

That night crowds of East Berliners packed the checkpoints, chanting Tor auf!, which means open the gate. In the days that followed, people attacked the concrete with hammers and chisels, knocking loose painted chunks to keep, and the endless tapping earned them the nickname Mauerspechte, wall woodpeckers.

The opening began with a blunder. That evening the government spokesman Günter Schabowski read out new travel rules at a live televised press conference, though he had barely looked at the note himself, and when a journalist asked when they would begin, he fiddled with his glasses, leafed through his papers and made a guess. The rules were supposed to begin on the following day, but Schabowski said they applied immediately, sofort in German, and that single word sent thousands hurrying to the border crossings. At the Bornholmer Strasse checkpoint the officer Harald Jäger was eating in the guards' break room when the radio carried the news, and he nearly choked on his sandwich. Over the weekend upward of two million people crossed from East Berlin, greeted by strangers with champagne and flowers, and one writer called it the greatest street party the world had ever seen.

The wall had never been just a wall. Behind the concrete lay the death strip, a patrolled no-man's-land of watchtowers, guard dogs and buried mines, and at least 140 people were killed at the wall between 1961 and 1989. Two days after it opened, the cellist Mstislav Rostropovich flew in from Paris, borrowed a chair and sat before a graffiti-covered slab to play Bach's cello suites, in honour of those who had died trying to cross. On the first New Year's Eve after the wall opened, the American star David Hasselhoff, lifted high in a crane's cage at the Brandenburg Gate and wearing a jacket of flashing lights, sang his hit Looking for Freedom to about a million people.

The hidden story turned on a few people. That first night Jäger, a guard who had obeyed orders for decades, kept calling his commanders for orders and received none, until one sneered that perhaps Jäger was simply a coward, and that insult made him open his gate, the first breach in the wall. He told his commander he was ending all controls and letting the people out. Earlier the guards had tried the valve solution, letting the loudest protesters out one at a time while secretly stamping their passports to strip their citizenship, but it collapsed when young parents pushed through realised they could never go back to their children. Two years before, on 12 June 1987, President Ronald Reagan had stood at the Brandenburg Gate and challenged Mikhail Gorbachev by name to tear down this wall! The Soviet news agency called the speech war-mongering. Germany reunited less than a year after the wall opened.

gorbachev-glasnost-and-perestroika.context_blurb:
Mikhail Gorbachev was the eighth and final leader of the USSR. Born in 1931 to a peasant family in southern Russia, he rose through the Communist Party to become its General Secretary in March 1985, at fifty-four. He inherited a superpower in deep trouble, with empty shops, a war in Afghanistan and an arms race it could not afford, and he set out to save communism by reforming it.

He grew up in the village of Privolnoye, and as a teenager on a state farm he drove a combine harvester, a skill his father Sergei taught him. His first famous policy was glasnost, openness: after decades of silence the press, writers and ordinary citizens could talk freely about shortages, corruption and the crimes of Stalin. The second was perestroika, restructuring, a plan to loosen the grip of the central planners in Moscow, allow more local decisions and permit some private ownership for the first time since the 1920s. In May 1985 he launched a campaign against drinking, raising prices, cutting production and tearing out vineyards, and people mocked him as the mineral-water secretary instead of the general secretary.

On 26 April 1986 a reactor exploded at Chernobyl in Soviet Ukraine, and officials at first tried to cover it up, but Gorbachev later called the disaster a turning point, after which the old secretive system could no longer go on. In October 1989, visiting East Berlin, he warned the hardline East German boss Erich Honecker not to fight reform, telling him that life punishes anyone who comes too late, and within weeks Honecker had fallen and the Berlin Wall had opened. On 19 August 1991 Communist hardliners seized Gorbachev at his holiday home and sent tanks into Moscow, but the Russian president Boris Yeltsin clambered onto a tank outside the parliament building and read out a defiant appeal, and within days the coup collapsed.

At the Reykjavik summit in October 1986 he and President Ronald Reagan nearly agreed to scrap all their nuclear weapons, but the deal collapsed because Reagan would not limit testing of SDI, his Star Wars missile defence, to the laboratory. Gorbachev allowed Moscow's satellite states in Eastern Europe to choose their own paths instead of crushing them with tanks, and his spokesman Gennadi Gerasimov quipped that the old Brezhnev Doctrine had given way to the Sinatra Doctrine, because, as in the song My Way, each country would choose its own road. He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1990. On 25 December 1991, signing the papers that dissolved the Soviet Union, he found his Soviet felt-tip pen had run dry, and when CNN's president Tom Johnson offered a Mont Blanc, Gorbachev first asked whether it was an American pen.

The reforms carried hidden traps. Taxes on vodka had paid for a big slice of the state budget, so the anti-drinking drive tore a hole in it, and the government covered the gap by printing more money, feeding the inflation that helped wreck the economy. The deepest irony was that perestroika tore down central planning without building a working market to replace it, so prices rose, shelves emptied and shortages grew, and a system that could not survive even partial honesty about itself dissolved in 1991.
